11575-notes-and-queries-number-12-januar:
Notes and Queries number 12, dated Saturday, 19 January 1850 and priced at threepence, keeps its motto from Captain Cuttle: when found, make a note of it. Notes cover a passage in Hudibras, the field of the brothers' footsteps, notes on books and authors, and receipts of The Beggar's Opera.

Queries follow on St. Thomas of Lancaster, the shield of the Black Prince, the fraternity of vagabonds, and the name of Shylock, with minor queries on snob, cannibal, and Queen's messengers. A query on flaying in punishment of sacrilege, with a piece of human skin from Hadstock church door, shows the journal's antiquarian range.
11653-notes-and-queries-number-11-januar:
Notes and Queries number 11, dated Saturday, 12 January 1850 and priced at threepence, opens with Sir E. Dering's household book and Bayswater and its origin. Eva, daughter of D. MacMurrough, plagiarisms, Billingsgate, and notes from fly leaves follow.

Queries ask about catacombs and bone-houses, contradictions in Don Quixote, and ancient alms-basins. Minor queries cover Cupid crying, Sir G. Jackson as Junius, and the ballad of Dick and the Devil. One note quotes O'Flaherty on the bernacle goose, engendered by the sea out of timber long lying in water. The number is antiquarian talk at its liveliest.
11707-notes-and-queries-number-13-januar:
Notes and Queries number 13, dated Saturday, 26 January 1850 and priced at threepence, opens with Domingo Lomelyn, jester to Henry VIII, by Edward F. Rimbault. Marlowe and the old Taming of a Shrew, beetle mythology, and churchwardens' accounts of St. Margaret's, Westminster, follow.

Queries ask about Catherine Pegge, William Basse and his poems, and minor matters from Christmas hymns to Oliver Cromwell and Luther and Erasmus. One note quotes Basse's elegy, where a young muse runs forth in ceaseless currents of complaining verse. The number is a January antiquarian exchange, brisk and crowded.
11929-notes-and-queries-number-15-februa:
Number 15 of Notes and Queries, dated Saturday, February 9, 1850, offered literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists a medium for exchanging questions and answers. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, urged readers: when found, make a note of it. The issue cost threepence, fourpence for the stamped edition.

Notes include wages in the seventeenth and nineteenth centuries, Marlowe and the old Taming of a Shrew, and the vanished streets of St. Giles's, Dyot Street and Denmark Street, with their owners and clubs. Replies to minor queries close the number, on topics from a French maxim to the fall of rain in England, in the journal's characteristic miscellany of small, exact knowledge.
11958-notes-and-queries-number-21-march-:
Number 21 of Notes and Queries, dated Saturday, March 23, 1850, continues the journal's exchange for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, at threepence, fourpence stamped. Its motto, when found, make a note of it, from Captain Cuttle, still heads the number.

Notes include early statistics from Chart in Kent, the Latin tag bis dat qui cito dat, parallel passages, errors corrected, direct and indirect etymology, and an error in Pope's Homer. The issue's value lies in its small corrections and comparisons, the kind of scholarly housekeeping that larger histories depend on and that only a correspondence journal could supply week by week.
12018-notes-and-queries-number-17-februa:
Number 17 of Notes and Queries, dated Saturday, February 23, 1850, continues the journal's work as a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto from Captain Cuttle, when found, make a note of it, heads a threepenny number, fourpence stamped.

Notes in this issue include Alfred's Orosius by R. T. Hampson, folk lore on omens from cattle, a horse's head, and rush-bearings, and a piece on authors and books. Short queries and replies follow the same pattern as earlier numbers: small points of history, language. Custom, answered by readers who knew something exact and were glad to share it.
12198-notes-and-queries-number-22-march-:
Notes and Queries, number twenty-two, dated March 30, 1850, shows a Victorian weekly built entirely from reader letters. Priced at threepence, it called itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists.

Notes in this number debate the authorship of The Taming of the Shrew, trace proverb origins, and collect folk lore on salting, weather sayings, and death-bed superstitions. Queries ask about bishops papers, Bristol riots, and the etymology of Dalston, while replies settle points on the dodo, Robert Crowley, and old poems. The issue captures scholarly conversation before journals and search engines: curious readers pooling small facts in public.
12505-notes-and-queries-number-23-april-:
Notes and Queries number 23, dated 6 April 1850 and priced threepence, calls itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries and genealogists. Captain Cuttle's motto fronts it: when found, make a note of it. Contents list notes on Hanno's Periplus, Pope vindicated and the Supper of the Lord, with folk lore on Palm Sunday wind and the Wild Huntsman.

Queries follow on Breton, the sword Curtana, the Domesday of Alfred, Wycliffite scriptures, gloves and law courts. Readers wrote in, answered and argued, building a shared notebook in print. The number shows Victorian scholarship as conversation, small questions answered by many hands.
12589-notes-and-queries-number-31-june-1:
Notes and Queries number 31, Saturday 1 June 1850, priced threepence, continues its medium for literary men, artists, antiquaries and genealogists. Captain Cuttle's motto returns: when found, make a note of it. Notes cover parish registers and statistics, Hudibrastic verse by Singer, gloves presented by custom, and folk lore on exhumation, Suffolk lore, cures for fits, and Bible and key.

Notes on Jeremy Taylor, unpublished epigrams in the British Museum, and authors and books by Corney follow. Queries ask about death by burning, Cornelis Drebbel, verses attributed to Charles Yorke, geometry in Lancashire, and ransom of an English nobleman. The number shows Victorian scholarship as a shared, weekly conversation.
13350-the-vanity-of-human-wishes-1749-an:
Samuel Johnson's Vanity of Human Wishes, 1749, with two Rambler papers of 1750, appears here in the Augustan Reprint Society edition, number twenty-two, with an introduction by Bertrand H. Bronson, published in Los Angeles in 1950. The poem, Johnson's great satire on human hopes, follows Charles XII of Sweden to Moscow's walls, where famine guards the solitary coast. The Rambler papers add Johnson's prose on habit and observation.

One paper praises a mind disengaged from fixed thoughts, able to turn every new object to entertainment, finding in nature an inexhaustible stock of materials without envy or malice. The volume is a compact, scholarly reprint, useful for students of Johnson and Augustan satire. Its notes and introduction frame the poems for modern readers.
13361-notes-and-queries-number-36-july-6:
Notes and Queries for July 6, 1850, opens with Samuel Hickson on the derivation of the word news and S. W. Singer on borrowed thoughts. C. Ross writes on strangers in the House of Commons, while folk lore notes treat high spirits as a presage of calamity and explain the hydro-incubator.

Queries and notes chase the etymology of Parliament, the line about falling into Scylla while shunning Charybdis, and the Earl of Norwich and his son Lord Goring. A learned note traces a Latin line to Galeottus Martius in 1476 and to Philippe Gualtier's Alexandreis. The number is typical of the journal: short, sharp, and keen to set a small fact right.
13362-notes-and-queries-number-38-july-2:
Notes and Queries number thirty-eight, Saturday, July 20, 1850, price threepence, is a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Contents list notes on the meaning of delighted as used by Shakespeare, authors of the Rolliad, notes on Milton, derivation of Easter, and folk lore on passages of death. Queries ask about Nicholas Ferrar, Stukeley's Stonehenge, and smoke money.

One footnote quotes a prophecy that death draws nigh and a violent fate awaits, slain in fight by Achilles, son of Peleus. Another piece argues that Caxton printed at Cologne, citing a life of Caxton and noting a Norfolk parochial library said to hold books by Caxton and other early printers. The number is a dense, learned weekly for antiquaries.
13389-notes-and-queries-number-40-august:
Notes and Queries for August 3, 1850, gathers translations of Juvenal, a dedication to Milton by Antonio Malatesti, Pulteney's ballad of The Honest Jury, and notes on Milton. Folk lore treats high spirits as a sign of coming calamity, Norfolk rhymes, salt thrown over the shoulder, and charms for warts.

A Shakespeare note contrasts dreams that promise joy with the messenger who brings Juliet's death, showing how high spirits precede bad news on stage as in life. Another note traces Celtic pipes found at Brannocktown and in the Bog of Cullen, with a skeleton found holding a pipe between its teeth. Small facts, well sourced, make the number.
13393-notes-and-queries-number-41-august:
Notes and Queries for August 10, 1850, notes Sir William Gascoigne, an old Guy, and folk lore of south Northamptonshire, from mice and snakes to poultry, crows, owls, and cuckoos. Minor notes cover gloves, death by burning, and India rubber, then new in common use.

Queries ask about the Bar of Michael Angelo, annotated copies of Bishop Andrewes, a Grub Street poet named Robert Innes, the Sicilian Vespers, and treasure trove. A note on India rubber as an eraser, sold by Mr. Nairne opposite the Royal Exchange for three shillings a cube, shows how everyday inventions entered scholarship. The number is lively, learned, and full of small discoveries.
13406-notes-and-queries-number-43-august:
Notes and Queries for August 24, 1850, is a weekly exchange for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Short notes cover the Collar of SS, Tennyson and Coleridge, and folk lore such as prophecy, bay leaves at funerals, old shoes thrown for luck, and mice roasted for hooping cough.

Queries ask who wrote Shakespeare's Henry VIII, with Samuel Hickson setting out a discovery he had held back for years. Readers chase the authorship of old tracts and the errors of learned writers. The number shows Victorian scholarship at work in public: small facts offered, challenged, and corrected, one letter at a time.
13411-notes-and-queries-number-42-august:
Notes and Queries for August 17, 1850, offers the same weekly trade in small scholarship as its sister numbers. Notes take up Alfred's Orosius, a remarkable proposition about Ireland, old materials for the history of the word news, and folk cures such as charming for warts.

Minor notes record the capture of Henry VI, betrayed by a Talbot and carried bound to the Tower, and the new Temple. Queries chase paradox poems, church rates, and the accomplices of Thomas of Lancaster. One long note weighs the Countess of Desmond, said to have lived to great age and bred teeth three times. It is antiquarian talk, precise, gossipy, and eager to correct the record.
13426-notes-and-queries-number-44-august:
Notes and Queries for August 31, 1850, keeps up its weekly exchange of antiquarian notes. Readers write on Gravesend boats, Cunningham's Handbook of London, devotional tracts once owned by Queen Katherine Parr, and cheap books of reference. Minor notes touch Cinderella's glass slipper, mistletoe on oaks, omnibuses, and church property.

Queries ask for the life of Sejanus by P. Mathieu, the antiquity of smoking, and Sir Gregory Norton. A quaint essay asks why Eve was formed from a rib, and what that choice says about husband and wife. Other notes date when gentlemen stopped wearing swords in daily life, near 1770 to 1780. Small questions, answered in public, build the number.
13427-notes-and-queries-number-45-septem:
Notes and Queries for September 7, 1850, notes folk lore from Cornwall and beyond: the first mole in Cornwall, a whistling wife, a charm for warts, and hanging out the broom. Lord Plunket and St. Agobard, Cunningham's Handbook of London, and Coleridge's Aids to Reflection get longer notes, with minor notes on Henry VI and the Mentmore register.

Queries ask for Joachim the French ambassador, Roman Catholic translations of Scripture, and the lost tribes, with lists of theories and publications. A correspondent asks whether Luther left any account of early familiarity with Scripture to test a story about him, and another weighs wizards that peep and mutter in Isaiah. The number keeps antiquarian talk moving briskly.
13462-notes-and-queries-number-46-septem:
Notes and Queries for September 14, 1850, offers Shakespeare notes, antiquarian gossip, and folk lore in its usual compact form. S. W. Singer writes on the meaning of risell in Hamlet, Pitman Jones on the body of James II. Readers note the authors of the Rolliad and a prophetic spring at Langley in Kent.

Queries ask for quotations in Bishop Andrewes, a lexicon of types for emblems on monuments, coins, and title pages, and the custom of wearing the breast uncovered. A note on delighted argues that the word means refined, dainty, and delicate in Measure for Measure and Othello. The number is a busy workshop of small literary questions.
13463-notes-and-queries-number-48-septem:
Notes and Queries for September 28, 1850, notes riots in London, satirical poems on William III, Shakespeare's grief and frenzy, etymological notes, and mistakes in Gibbon by J. E. B. Mayor. Minor notes cover the history of Saracens, the hippopotamus, America, Pascal's letters, and a parson's epigram.

Queries ask for the Orkneyinga Saga and for incumbents of church livings, the York Buildings Company, a saying ascribed to Montaigne, and the wife of Edward the Outlaw. A note corrects a writer who called Rachelius a translator of Pascal, when Placcius shows him merely a German editor. The number keeps the journal's habit of catching small errors in big books.
13480-notes-and-queries-number-49-octobe:
Notes and Queries for October 5, 1850, notes stray points on Cunningham's London, a satirical song on Villiers, Duke of Buckingham, by Dr. Rimbault, and Baker's notes on the author of The Whole Duty of Man. A mistake about George Wither and the uses of useful against useless learning fill the notes.

Queries ask for Bishop Cosin's conference and Engelman's Bibliotheca Scriptorum Classicorum, while a writer proposes a classified catalogue for a great library, hampered only by finding a room to hold it. Another note weighs whether Bishop Berkeley wrote a disputed book, citing booksellers' catalogues and internal evidence. The number is full of London history, authorship puzzles, and library dreams.
13540-notes-and-queries-number-53-novemb:
Notes and Queries for November 2, 1850, opens with Samuel Hickson on Shakespeare and Marlowe. A plan for a church-history society, Burnet as historian, epigrams from Buchanan, and mistakes about George Chapman the poet. Minor notes cover Shakespeare and George Herbert, Old Dan Tucker, Lord John Townsend, and Croker's Boswell.

Queries seek early poetry in five bibliographical questions, while a note lists works by Lord John Townsend and Tickle, from ballads to odes to Sir Elijah Impey. Another correspondent, holding music to nearly twenty jigs, defends a project on the subject against a rival who spent many years on it. The number shows literary scholarship as friendly rivalry in print.
13544-notes-and-queries-number-18-march-:
Notes and Queries for March 2, 1850, prints an unpublished letter of Horace Walpole, a note on Lady Arabella Stuart, and the name Martel by W. Robson. Queries ask about Junius and a new edition of Dr. Owen's works, with minor queries on a book of hours, Bess of Hardwick, Caesar's wife, and Cromwell's estates.

Replies trace the origin of the Jew's harp and the fate of Astle's manuscripts. Astle's manuscripts were bought for five hundred pounds after his death in 1803, kept at Stowe, and sold to the Earl of Ashburnham for eight thousand pounds. A witchcraft note tells of Agnes Sampson and two hundred witches sailing to sea in riddles and sieves with flagons of wine. The number blends letters, manuscripts, and folk belief.
13551-notes-and-queries-number-50-octobe:
Notes and Queries for October 12, 1850, its fiftieth number, notes small words, Gray's Elegy. Gray's Elegy in Portuguese, further notes on the authorship of Henry VIII, and Queen Elizabeth with Sir Henry Nevill. Minor notes touch whales, bookbinding, Scott's Waverley, and Satyavrata.

Queries ask for the Black Rood of Scotland and for Trogus Pompeius, mortuary stanzas, the Laird of Grant, Bastille records, Orkney under Norwegians, and Swift's works. A correspondent seeks original sources for Bishop Durdent, who held the privilege of coining money, beyond Godwin and Shaw. Eisell and wormwood wine, drunk by Pepys's friends, prompts a note on Shakespearean propoma. The journal reaches fifty with its curiosity intact.
13558-notes-and-queries-number-14-februa:
Notes and Queries for February 2, 1850, notes reprints of old books by J. P. Collier, catacombs and bone-houses, lines attributed to Hudibras, notes from fly-leaves, and The Pursuits of Literature. Queries ask for Barryana and nine queries by the Rev. J. Jebb on a confraternity's Sunday schools.

Minor queries cover Mowbray coheirs, Drayton and Yong, the fraternity of Christian doctrine, Engelbert's treatise, New Year's customs, under the rose, Norman pedigrees, and Dr. Johnson's library. A note on Armagh traces its name to Macha, wife of Nemedius, buried there, with other derivations from Gomer and Bullet. The number is antiquarian work at full stretch.
13638-notes-and-queries-number-19-march-:
Notes and Queries for March 9, 1850, opens with progress and notes on the captivity of the Queen of Bruce, Robert Herrick, and the meaning of Laerig. Folk lore covers St. Valentine in Norwich, cook-eels, old charms, superstitions in the north of England, decking churches with yew, and strewing chaff before houses.

Welsh folk lore adds Cron Annwn and Gwrach-y-rhybin, while William Basse and his poems, John Stowe, transposition of letters, and pet names fill later notes. A letter attributed to Sir Robert Walpole to George II, printed in Banks's Dormant Peerage to expose Pulteney's vanity, is examined with care. The number keeps its antiquarian range wide.
13684-notes-and-queries-number-28-may-11:
This May 11, 1850 issue of Notes and Queries keeps the journal's brisk weekly mix. Notes report findings on London streets, old letters, and folk custom. Queries ask for help with obscure books, names, and phrases. Replies settle earlier puzzles with fresh evidence and polite correction.

Contents include notes on Cunningham's London and a letter of Peter Le Neve. Folk lore covers superstitions of the middle counties and rainbows in the morning. Queries chase the Purvey of the Apocalypse and Bonner on the Seven Sacraments. Replies range from Luther's translation to the Worm of Lambton. The issue shows a community of readers building knowledge together, one small fact at a time.
13712-notes-and-queries-number-27-may-4-:
Number 27 of Notes and Queries, dated May 4, 1850, is a weekly medium of exchange for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, sold for threepence. Short notes and questions fill its pages, from the Mosquito Country and the Duke of Monmouth's correspondence to folk charms for toothache and the evil eye.

Contributors debate Bacon and Jeremy Taylor, early English and German literature, Arabic and Roman numerals, and errors in Hallam's history, while Latin notes weigh the merits of Shakespeare, Jonson, and Fletcher. The charm of the paper lies in its miscellany: small facts, corrections, and queries passed among readers. It is a window into mid-Victorian antiquarian life.
13713-notes-and-queries-number-30-may-25:
Notes and Queries for May 25, 1850, continues its weekly trade in small facts. Notes treat Dr. Johnson and Dr. Warton, Spenser's monument, and borrowed thoughts. Folk lore items list Easter eggs, cures for warts, charms for wounds, and the fifth son. Queries ask about Dr. Richard Holsworth and other obscure names.

A longer note follows Bartholomew Legate, burned as a martyr under James I. Other items note Bohn's Milton, Jeremy Taylor's works, and a legal history of Britain. Replies correct and extend earlier answers. The issue feels like a crowded commonplace book. It shows how much Victorian scholarship grew from reader cooperation.
13729-notes-and-queries-number-37-july-1:
Notes and Queries began in 1849 as a weekly exchange for readers who studied books, history, and old customs. This issue, dated July 13, 1850, follows the same small format. Short notes answer earlier questions, and new queries ask for help with names, texts, and local lore. Contributors write from libraries, parishes, and private collections across Britain.

Here, notes touch Caxton's printing office, old sanitary laws, and midsummer fires. Queries chase letters of Queen Elizabeth and Philip II of Spain and the author of the Characteristics. Replies correct small facts and add fresh sources. The whole issue reads like a public notebook. It shows how Victorian readers pooled knowledge before modern reference works existed.
13736-notes-and-queries-number-39-july-2:
Notes and Queries for July 27, 1850, offers its usual weekly bundle of notes, queries, and replies. Notes explain the words Whitsuntide and Mass and report folk cures, including sympathetic cures and a charm for growing young. Long Meg of Westminster gets a careful note, as does spelling of words like sanatory.

Queries ask about the story of the Three Kings and other lore. Replies correct earlier items and add new sources. Minor notes touch Shakespeare as a brass-rubber, California news, and the Mayor of Misrule. The issue reads as a lively exchange among antiquaries. It shows Victorian readers building a shared reference work week by week.
13747-notes-and-queries-number-25-april-:
This April 20, 1850 issue of Notes and Queries follows the journal's usual weekly pattern. Short notes report new findings on books, people, and places. Queries ask readers for help with puzzles of wording, authorship, and local history. Replies correct earlier answers and add evidence from manuscripts and parish records.

Topics here include Roger Bacon, Craik's Romance of the Peerage, and notes on Cunningham's London. Folk lore items cover toothache charms, Easter eggs, and cures for whooping cough. The Duke of Monmouth's pocket-book gets a careful note. The issue shows Victorian antiquaries at work, trading small facts that later grew into larger histories.
13822-notes-and-queries-number-26-april-:
Notes and Queries for April 27, 1850, mixes literary notes with folk lore and bibliography. Notes cover Nicholas Breton, Cunningham's London, the dodo, and the words sterling and penny. Hanno's Periplus and Pope's translators get scholarly attention. Folk lore items include cook-eels, divination by Bible and key, and weather proverbs.

Queries and replies continue the journal's cooperative method. Readers correct a supposed Portuguese discovery of Bourbon in 1545, tracing a copied stone pillar through several hands. Other items chase books, names, and local customs. The issue shows antiquaries checking each other with care. It remains a snapshot of Victorian learning in progress.
13925-notes-and-queries-number-24-april-:
Dated April 13, 1850, this Notes and Queries number keeps the journal's compact weekly form. Notes treat Skinner's Life of Monk, Cunningham's lives of Whitgift and Cartwright, and an inedited letter of the Duke of Monmouth. Lydgate and Coverdale get a note from E. F. Rimbault. Queries ask about Speculum Exemplorum and the second Duke of Ormonde.

Minor queries cover mayors' correct prefix, Quevedo and Spanish bull-fights, and Gilbert Browne. A note on Monk quotes his profession of content with the condition God set him in. Replies and corrections follow the usual pattern. The issue shows antiquaries trading evidence in small doses. It is a useful sample of early Victorian scholarship.
13936-notes-and-queries-number-47-septem:
September 21, 1850 brings another weekly Notes and Queries, priced threepence. Notes treat old songs, Junius Identified by J. Taylor, and a passage in The Tempest by S. W. Singer. Folk lore covers spiders as a cure for ague, funeral superstition, and folk lore rhymes. Punishment by burning and morganatic marriages get notes.

Minor notes touch Alderman Beckford, a frozen horn, and George Herbert's poems. A correspondent corrects an attribution error, asking a lord to stop crediting his work to Mr. Dubois. Replies and queries follow the journal's cooperative pattern. The issue shows Victorian antiquaries at their busiest. It offers a dense sample of mid-century learning.
15197-notes-and-queries-number-29-may-18:
Number 29 of Notes and Queries, dated May 18, 1850, serves as a medium of exchange for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Notes cover Cromwell as a feoffee of a charity at Ely, Dr. Parr, provincial words, and folk lore on deathbed superstition, May marriages, and throwing old shoes. Queries seek numismatic facts and more.

Replies answer points on Surrey's poems, evangelist symbols, complexion, and a ballad of Dick and the Devil. Minor queries chase painters, autographs, and old diaries. The issue shows Victorian scholarship as a conversation, with readers helping readers across the country, one small fact at a time.
15199-the-reformed-librarie-keeper-1650:
John Dury's 1650 tract on the reformed librarie-keeper was reprinted by the Augustan Reprint Society in 1983. Richard Popkin and Thomas Wright wrote its introduction. Dury sets out how a library keeper should serve learning. He argues that the keeper is no mere guard of books, but a worker who gathers, orders, and shares knowledge for scholars.

His plan covers buying, cataloguing, and helping readers, with an eye to public benefit rather than private hoarding. The tract is short, practical, and ahead of its time. Students of library history will find it a founding text for the modern idea of the librarian as a guide to knowledge.
15216-notes-and-queries-number-55-novemb:
Number 55 of Notes and Queries, dated November 16, 1850, continues the weekly exchange for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Notes debate the authorship of Henry VIII, review a handbook of London, and record folk lore on laying a ghost and testing witchcraft. Minor notes touch cards, Herodotus, and America.

Queries ask about Dryden's Absalom and Achitophel, a widow of the wood, and hoods worn by Aberdeen doctors of divinity. Replies and short notes fill the rest. The issue shows Victorian readers pooling small facts, a habit that built modern antiquarian study one letter at a time.
15232-notes-and-queries-number-51-octobe:
Number 51 of Notes and Queries, dated October 19, 1850, offers notes on Roberd the Robber, a passage in Merry Wives of Windsor, and Chaucer's Damascene. Minor notes chase Long Friday, hip hip hurrah, and Albanian literature. Queries seek Fairfax's Tasso, Jeremy Taylor, St. Cuthbert, and bells in churches.

Replies take up Gaudentio di Lucca and a bibliography of classic writers, with minor queries on coins, egg cups, and Luther's hymns. The mix is typical of the journal: small, exact, and collaborative. Antiquaries will enjoy the issue as a snapshot of Victorian learning in conversation.
15354-notes-and-queries-number-56-novemb:
Number 56 of Notes and Queries, dated November 23, 1850, notes the Oldenburg Horn, Greek particles in Eastern languages, and Samuel Rowlands's claim to a work on change. Etymology of apricot, peach, and nectarine follows, with minor notes on Chaucer's monument, Herrick, and camels in Gaul.

Queries seek bibliographical facts, Dryden on satire, and meanings of phrases like please the pigs and save one's bacon. Replies and short notes round out the issue. The journal's collaborative spirit shines through, as readers pool learning across Britain, one small query at a time. The issue rewards slow browsing through its many small discoveries.
15405-notes-and-queries-number-57-novemb:
Number 57 of Notes and Queries, dated November 30, 1850, notes a portrait of Cardinal Beaton and the pointing of a passage in All's Well That Ends Well. Folk lore follows: the bigger the ring, the nearer the wet, prophesying before death, strange remedies, mice as medicine, and omens from birds. Interest computation and Lancashire geometry add variety.

Minor notes chase sermon's pills, an infant prodigy, and a hint for publishers, while queries seek Timothy Thruscross, echo songs, and the meaning of Thwaites. The issue closes the year's run in the journal's collaborative style. Antiquaries will enjoy its curious, exact, and very Victorian mix.
15427-notes-and-queries-number-59-decemb:
This number of Notes and Queries, dated December 14, 1850, is a weekly paper where literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists traded notes and questions. It cost threepence and ran to short, dense items rather than long essays. The motto on its head, from Captain Cuttle, urges readers to make a note when they find a fact.

Notes in this issue cover England's first paper mill, folk lore on May dew, pixies, the Dun Cow, and Lady Godiva, and small points on words, blood circulation, and portraits. Queries ask about the Wise Men of Gotham, Herstmonceux Castle, Yorkshire ballads, and church customs. Together they show Victorian antiquarian life in action: many minds pooling scraps toward answers no single scholar held.
15996-notes-and-queries-number-32-june-8:
Notes and Queries, number thirty-two, dated Saturday, June 8, 1850, at threepence, fourpence stamped. The paper calls itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, bids readers, when found, make a note of it. Notes and queries share the pages in equal part.

Notes treat strangers in the House of Commons, the Agapemone, and London Irish registers. Folk lore follows, with divination by Bible and key and a charm for warts. Queries ask about poet laureates, wood paper, a Latin line, a new Milton, and Barum and Sarum. The number shows Victorian scholarship at work: curious, exact, and eager to share.
16031-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Dated October 21, 1897, number fifty of The Great Round World leads with a change of government in Spain. After days of doubt, the Queen named Sagasta prime minister, and rumor at once said General Weyler had resigned and would be removed from Cuba. Weyler, the paper reports, meant to stay if he could, and had just sent Madrid a long report claiming western Cuba was pacified and much improved since his arrival.

For young readers, the number turns a distant colonial war into names, offices, and short, clear facts. Spain, Cuba, and the fate of a hard-handed general become a story a child could follow from week to week. The issue is a crisp snapshot of empire and politics on the eve of the Spanish-American War.
16193-notes-and-queries-number-16-februa:
Number sixteen of Notes and Queries, dated Saturday, February 16, 1850, served as a medium of exchange for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Priced at threepence, it prints notes on Daniel Defoe and his ghost stories, pet names, Spartan black broth, hints to editors, and folklore on Easter eggs, buns, and Gloucestershire customs. Queries ask about the White Hart Inn at Scole, passages in Pope, and Belvoir Castle.

Replies cover Aelfric's Colloquy and a long list of minor queries, from French leave to Cromwell relics and a Kentish ballad. The paper's motto, from Captain Cuttle, urges readers to make a note when found. Scholars still value it as a lively record of Victorian antiquarian curiosity.
16404-notes-and-queries-number-61-decemb:
This December 28, 1850 number of Notes and Queries leans into the season, with folk lore notes on St. Thomas's Day, pixies, straw necklaces, and breaking Judas' bones. Scottish ballads, the Holt and Vincent families, Vondel's Lucifer, and a myth of Midridge fill the notes pages, while Devonshire rhymes and a Christmas carol add local color.

Minor notes chase odd words like Passilodion and Berafrynde, and an alms-dish inscription gets its turn. The issue feels like a winter evening among antiquaries, swapping scraps of lore. It is a charming sample of the journal at its most miscellaneous and most English.
16409-notes-and-queries-number-20-march-:
This March 16, 1850 number of Notes and Queries shows the journal doing exactly what its title promises. Short notes cover Alfred's geography of Europe, the first coffee houses in England, folk lore, old records, and lines from Milton. Readers then send in queries of their own, from old songs at Christ's Hospital to the sense of odd words.

No single topic rules the issue. Instead, scholars, clergy, and keen amateurs swap facts, correct each other, and chase small points of history and language. The mix feels like a club journal: brief, learned, and full of odd corners. It is a fine snapshot of mid-Victorian antiquarian life in print.
21528-the-international-monthly-magazine:
The International Monthly Magazine began at New York in August 1850, priced at twenty-five cents a number. Stringer and Townsend issued it from Broadway, with a year's run costing three dollars. Its first volume runs from August to November of that year.

An opening essay treats the great change in how letters reach readers through periodicals. Since the Edinburgh Review, it argues, the finest minds have written for magazines. Contents range over art, portraits, tales borrowed from Household Words, and notes on statues and painters. Sir David Brewster's portrait and an essay on learning show the mix of science and letters inside.
24303-the-philadelphia-magazines-and-the:
Albert H. Smyth, of Johns Hopkins University and professor of English literature in the Philadelphia High School, wrote this history of Philadelphia magazines from 1741 to 1850, published by Robert M. Lindsay in Philadelphia in 1892. The study began at the request of Professor H. B. Adams, and its results were first read before the Historical and English Seminaries of Johns Hopkins, then before the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.

Smyth warns that a complete list is impossible, since many magazines vanished and left not a rack behind. He worked at first hand, refusing to see an inaccessible magazine through another investigator's eyes. Friends learned in local lore, including George W. Childs and George R. Graham, aided him. Readers get a fond, scholarly history of a city's lost periodicals.
26121-notes-and-queries-number-33-june-1:
Number 33 of Notes and Queries, dated Saturday, June 15, 1850, shows a Victorian weekly built as a shared notice board for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its contents list notes on Dr. Whichcote and Lord Shaftesbury, a piece on the rebel, notes on the hippopotamus, and Northamptonshire folk charms for wens, cramp, and toothache.

Queries from readers ask about Sir George Buc, Spanish phrases, and York Cathedral drawings, while replies settle small points on numismatics, Pope Felix, and old sayings. The issue is a good sample of how scholars and keen amateurs pooled facts in print long before reference works went online.
29655-harper-s-new-monthly-magazine-volu:
Number three of Harper's New Monthly Magazine, volume one, dated August 1850, opens with a pilgrimage to the home of Sir Thomas More, by Mrs. S. C. Hall. Living near Chelsea, Hall and her party sought the few broken walls that once enclosed More's residence, reading Erasmus, Hoddesdon, Roper, and Aubrey first. More, she writes, died upon a point of religion, respected as a martyr by the side for which he suffered.

The issue mixes travel, biography, and letters in Harper's early manner, with a portrait of More from the Art-Journal. It is pleasant, Hall says, to muse over the past and to know that much malice and bigotry has departed. Readers of Victorian magazines will find a rich, early number of a great American monthly.
31187-harper-s-new-monthly-magazine-volu:
Number two of Harper's New Monthly Magazine, dated July 1850 and opening the magazine's first volume, shows the new American monthly finding its voice. Its leading piece, reprinted from the London Eclectic Review, profiles Thomas De Quincey, son of a Liverpool merchant, as the last great argosy among a gallery of literary shipwrecks. It promises his history, faults, genius, and works.

The issue's miscellany of essays, tales, and sketches, drawn from British and American sources, set the pattern Harper's would follow for decades. For modern readers, this early number is a time capsule of mid-century magazine culture, when a New York monthly introduced British writers to American parlors.
31358-harper-s-new-monthly-magazine-volu:
Number four of Harper's New Monthly Magazine, for September 1850, opens with memories of Miss Jane Porter by Mrs. S. C. Hall, illustrated with a portrait from the London Art Journal. Hall reflects on the place of celebrated women in England, arguing that celebrity rarely adds to a woman's happiness or usefulness. Her essay sets a thoughtful, domestic tone for the number.

The rest of the issue follows the magazine's early pattern: varied articles, stories, and sketches for a general American readership. Harper's, still in its first volume, was building the mix that would make it a fixture of American periodical life. This number shows the young magazine finding its voice, with biography and moral reflection beside lighter fare.
a-suggestive-inquiry-into-the-hermetic-m:
A Suggestive Inquiry into the Hermetic Mystery, published anonymously in 1850, is Mary Anne Atwood's attempt toward the recovery of the ancient experiment of nature. Atwood argued that the alchemists guarded a real spiritual science behind their symbols. With the inquiry stands a dissertation on the more celebrated of the alchemical philosophers, surveying the famous adepts and their teachings.

The book appeared without her name, which was attached only to later editions. It became one of the most influential occult books of the nineteenth century, read as a key to the hermetic tradition. Readers meet Atwood's central claim throughout: that alchemy's furnaces and metals record an inward, experimental knowledge of nature and the soul.
alchemy-and-the-alchemists-1850: Alchemy and the Alchemists, dated 1850, is a survey of the old art and its practitioners. Its author is not named. The copy here is held by the University of Glasgow Library, in its Ferguson collection of alchemy books. The work belongs to the Victorian writing that retold the history of alchemy for general readers. It appeared between the rise of the new chemistry and the start of the occult revival.
anima-magica-abscondita-or-a-discourse-o:
Anima Magica Abscondita, printed in 1650, is Thomas Vaughan's discourse of the universal spirit of nature. Vaughan, the Welsh philosopher and alchemist, published it under his pen name Eugenius Philalethes. The full title promises an account of that hidden spirit, with its strange, abstruse, and miraculous ascent and descent through the world.

Vaughan's subject is the living soul he believed moves inside nature, the agent behind growth, decay, and magic. The discourse argues for that universal spirit in the language of hermetic philosophy, against a merely mechanical account of things. It is one of the works that made Vaughan the most distinctive English hermetic writer of the Commonwealth years.
ars-et-theoria-transmvtationis-metallica:
Ars et Theoria Transmutationis Metallicae, printed in 1550, is the Venetian author Giovanni Agostino Pantheo's art and theory of metallic transmutation. With it stands his Voarchadumia, and the whole is illustrated with proportions, numbers, and figures fitted to the subject, as the title promises. The volume runs to two sequences of leaves with woodcut illustrations and a map.

Pantheo, who flourished in the early sixteenth century, wrote as a priestly adept who separated true transmutation from fraud. His diagrams and number schemes try to give the art a visible order. This mid-century edition preserves that system in print, a Venetian theory of how metals might be perfected and changed.
arxiv-2412-03050:
Shivanagouda Biradar and Deepak Patil wrote this engineering paper, published in 2024. It tackles a detective problem: from a few electrical measurements at a network's edge, work out the network's wiring and each link's conductance. Or at least list every network that fits.

The networks in scope are circular, flat, and passive, built from resistors and simple reactive parts with matched values. The authors find a clean link between the edge measurements, called Thevenin impedances, and the network's Laplacian matrix. That link turns the puzzle into polynomial equations whose solutions are all matching networks. Two inequality families, triangle and Kalmanson, prune impossible shapes. Gröbner basis methods then do the algebra. The paper shows the inequalities hold broadly under stated boundary conditions, making the reconstruction trustworthy.
arxiv-2412-04750:
Wenyong Huang and Xiang Zhang reduce elementary integrability of polynomial vector fields in two thousand twenty-four. Prelle and Singer showed a key trait of elementary first integrals in the eighties. Such integrals must build from algebraic parts, powers, and logarithms. Their planar result gave an integrating factor of a set form.

The pair extend that result to any dimension here. An elementary integrable field has many independent first integrals of that build. Galois theory then yields a rational Jacobian multiplier for the field. The proof tightens the classic theory in a broad way.
arxiv-2412-05450:
Arend Hintze and Christoph Adami ask whether artificial intelligence agents can rescue cooperation in public goods games, in a two thousand twenty-four paper. The tragedy of the commons shows how individually rational choices wreck shared resources.

Using an evolutionary computational model, the authors test three designs. In one, AI agents are forced always to cooperate. In another, players evolve control over their agents' cooperation. In the third, agents simply mimic player behavior. Only mimicry lowered the critical synergy threshold for cooperation, effectively resolving the dilemma. The suggestion is practical: build AI agents that imitate people if the goal is collective well-being.
arxiv-2412-09250:
Abdessalam Ed-dib, Zhanibek Datbayev, and Amine Mohamed Aboussalah make a popular fine-tuning shortcut choose its own size, layer by layer. The shortcut, LoRA, trains small low-rank patches instead of the whole model. Rank is the dial: low saves compute but dulls the patch, high costs more. Prior adaptive schemes set the dial without theory.

Their method, GeLoRA, reads the geometry of each layer's hidden states. A layer's intrinsic dimension, how many directions its signals truly use, bounds the rank it needs. The framework sets each layer's rank from that measure. Layers that carry simple signals get lean patches, rich layers get wider ones. Across several tasks, GeLoRA beat recent rivals under the same parameter budget. The work gives rank choice a principled base instead of a guess.
arxiv-2412-11850:
Zhenyu Wang, Yifan Hu, Peter Bühlmann, and Zijian Guo learn causal outcome models by hunting for what stays fixed across settings. Their paper from twenty twenty-four uses data from many environments. The direct causes of an outcome should act the same way in each one. That invariance is the lever for telling cause from mere correlation.

Their NegDRO frame scores a model by its worst weighted mix of risks across settings. Negative weights are allowed, which forces true invariance rather than a safe average. Three results follow. Set terms say when the invariant model is the causal one. The loss landscape is benign: all flat points sit near the truth. A gradient method provably homes in, with rates in both sample size and steps. The method skips the vast subset searches of older work.
arxiv-2412-13950:
Jan Stock, Till Schmidt, André Xhonneux, and Dirk Müller lay out a recipe for building computer models of whole district heating networks from open data and free tools. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. District heating is central to cleaning up building heat. Yet each real network needs a model before upgrades can be tested.

Their workflow merges public structural data with computed estimates to fill the gaps. The result is a digital twin ready for simulation and optimization studies. Planners can test renewable and waste-heat feeds, lower supply temperatures, or new controls. Two example networks built this way are presented. The authors discuss where the method applies and where it strains. Open ingredients mean any city can replicate the work. That lowers the cost of planning the heat transition.
arxiv-2412-16450:
Chang and Lai design in twenty twenty-four a family of quantum error-correcting codes that fix energy-loss errors while shrugging off shared phase errors. Real quantum hardware suffers both: qubits leak energy, and whole registers can drift in phase together. Their codes, built in the spirit of Shor's classic scheme, pack many logical qubits per block and can correct a set number of loss events.

They prove the family meets the conditions for near-perfect correction. Checking for errors needs only local operations plus a few helper qubits, thanks to a structured measurement layout. Layering the codes with a dual-rail scheme yields a combined family immune to both error kinds. The authors pitch high-rate storage for noisy quantum machines.
arxiv-2412-18150:
Shuhao Han and ten co-authors present EvalMuse-40K in two thousand twenty-four. The benchmark grades text to image models with human annotations. Auto metrics for image text alignment lacked large test sets. Fine grained checks were missing from the small sets that existed.

Their set holds forty thousand image text pairs with rich labels. Balanced prompt sampling and re-annotation keep the data sound. Two new scorers come with the benchmark itself. FGA-BLIP2 fine tunes a vision language model end to end. PN-VQA uses a positive negative question style for zero shot checks. Both score well, and model rankings follow.
arxiv-2501-03750:
Guandi Zhao, Jiajun Zhang, Peng Wang, and Ji Yao use simulations to see how an interacting dark sector would twist the spin and shape of dark matter halos. Models where dark matter and dark energy exchange energy substantially affect how large-scale structure forms. Halos growing inside that structure carry the imprint in their shapes and orientations.

Using a modified N-body simulation pipeline, the team compares interacting models with the standard cosmological model. When dark matter converts into dark energy, halo shapes align more strongly with the surrounding tidal field while halo spins align less. When the energy flows the other way, both effects reverse. The authors provide fitted functions describing these alignment signals. The study lays groundwork for modeling future observations, such as those from the China Space Station Telescope. There, halo orientation statistics could betray whether the dark sector's two halves talk to each other.
arxiv-2501-04350:
Zhuo-Yang Song, Feng Ding, and Wanying Kang wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It asks how a lava planet's own spin bends the supersonic winds of its rock-vapor sky.

Lava planets hug their stars, so rock melts and boils off near the point that faces the star. Past models let the flow run in rings around that point and skipped spin. But close-in planets can spin fast, which breaks the ring shape. The team builds a two-dimensional model that starts from the ring solution and adds the lopsided part as a small term tied to the Rossby number. The bent flow matters for how such skies will look to telescopes, and for the magma currents below.
arxiv-2501-09450:
Domenico Dona' and four co-authors teach a network to plan robot arm paths that use near-minimal energy, fast enough for live use. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Factories burn much power moving arms. The best paths come from hard math problems that solve too slowly for real-time work.

Their method learns from precomputed best paths. It starts from a standard path and learns only the fix needed to reach the best one. Start and end conditions are baked into the design. Near its training cases, the planner kept most of the energy gains of the slow solver. Far from them it kept about half. It ran hundreds of times faster either way. The work could cut power bills on busy factory floors.
arxiv-2501-10250:
Kamila Moriová, Petr Koutenský, Marius-Constantin Chirita-Mihaila, and Martin Kozák clock electron pulses inside an ultrafast electron microscope using only light. Knowing a pulse's duration at the exact spot where it meets the sample is essential and hard. Their all-optical method lets electrons interact with the ponderomotive push of an optical standing wave. The measurement happens in situ, across electron energies from one to thirty kiloelectron volts.

Single-photon photoemission from a Schottky tip, driven by ultraviolet femtosecond pulses, launches the electrons. Durations ran from half a picosecond at the top energy to under three picoseconds at lower energy, once Coulomb effects were negligible. Halving the photon energy halved the emitted electrons' energy spread and shortened pulses further. The technique gives ultrafast microscopy a stopwatch at the interaction point.
arxiv-2501-11450:
Chen, Liu, Sun, and Wang settle an extremal tiling problem for a letter-shaped tree in this 2025 mathematics paper. Tiling asks how a dense graph can be covered by copies of a fixed small graph. The target here is the H-shaped tree, a specific branching pattern.

The authors determine the two extremal constructions asymptotically, meaning the densest graphs that just avoid perfect tilings. The first construction sits near the complement of two cliques. That shape contrasts with earlier bipartite cases, where one clique's complement ruled. The result disproves a conjecture of Lang that tried to generalize the classic Erdős matching conjecture. The paper redraws the map for this tiling problem.
arxiv-2501-14550:
Ariel E Kellison, Laura Zielinski, David Bindel, and Justin Hsu present a programming language for backward error analysis. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Backward error gauges how well a numeric program copes with the small rounding errors of machine maths. Past ways to bound it take much human work, with no tools to do it by machine.

Their language, Bean, has a type system that tracks error flow through a program in a sound way. Each program stands for a triple of linked maps that meet an error pledge. They code classic matrix methods in Bean and get fine bounds by typing. A test tool infers bounds that match known worst-case results.
arxiv-2501-15550:
David Fisac wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author. It restates Markov's uniqueness conjecture, a classic open claim about whole-number necklaces, in combinatorial terms.

The geometric form of the guess speaks of the simple length spectrum on the modular torus. Fisac uses that form to write the set of lengths in plain combinatorial terms. The rewrite turns a guess from geometry into one that counting can attack directly. The note is short and pure, in the line of work on Markov numbers and their kin across number theory.
arxiv-2501-15950:
Florian Neukart and Valerii Vinokur propose a bold link between heat physics and computing cost. Their paper from twenty twenty-five argues that how hard a task is to compute should count as a state trait, like heat or size. They add a cost term to the first law of thermodynamics. The new law charges energy for hard tasks, not just for erasing bits.

The authors draw on Landauer's rule, which ties erasing data to heat. They extend it to hard tasks such as NP-complete problems. They suggest hard tasks may leave marks like the sharp shifts seen at phase changes. Spin glasses and random logic tasks serve as test beds. They also sketch lab tests with reversible computing rigs. The frame aims to fold computing limits into physical models.
arxiv-2501-16950:
Dyatlov, Nozdrin, Sergeev, and three colleagues build optical elements that twist deep ultraviolet light into vortex beams, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. A vortex beam carries orbital angular momentum, its wavefront spiraling like a corkscrew, and making such beams gets harder at short wavelengths.

The team fabricated spiral zone plates, in both amplitude and phase versions, using advanced lithography and etching. The plates reshape an ordinary Gaussian beam into a twisted mode. Tests ran on the laser driver of a radio-frequency photoinjector at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research. The elements produced deep ultraviolet vortices, at wavelengths near two hundred sixty nanometers, with a topological charge of one. Twisted ultraviolet light could help steer and diagnose relativistic electron beams. The work shows structured light techniques can be pushed into a spectral range where tools are scarce.
arxiv-2501-17650:
Manuel Colaço, Orlando Oliveira, and Paulo J. Silva reported a lattice QCD calculation in twenty twenty-five of the four-gluon vertex. Gluons are the particles that carry the strong force between quarks. The four-gluon vertex describes how four gluons meet at one point, and it feeds into many other quantities in particle physics.

This quantity is still poorly known, and its deep structure is only now coming into view. The authors computed it with large computer simulations of QCD on a space-time grid, working in the Landau gauge. They explain the hard parts of the task and report several measured values that pin down the vertex's shape. The results help efforts to pin down the gluon propagator, a basic part of QCD.
arxiv-2501-18250:
Mehdi Sattari, Deniz Gündüz, and Tommy Svensson cut the cost of updating channel models for huge antenna systems. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with feedback of channel state in split band systems. Deep learning squeezes that feedback well, but its edge fades when radio settings shift. Tuning the full model on fresh samples from the new setting can fix it. Yet the tuned decoder must be sent to the receiver, which adds fresh cost.

The team built a tuning scheme that keeps that send cost in check. Both ends are tuned on a small set of recent samples. Readers who build wireless systems get a way to adapt smart squeezers to new settings. The aim is top scores at a low update price.
arxiv-2502-01750:
Mattia Cesàro and David Osten wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It builds two families of deformations of gravity cut down to two dimensions, in ways that keep the cut-down theory integrable.

When gravity is shrunk along set symmetry directions, the result is a sigma model with a dilaton and a scale factor, and the system can be solved by Lax means. One family grows from a fresh auxiliary field trick. The other plants the Yang-Baxter sigma model inside the shrunk gravity. Both keep flat Lax forms. The first keeps the old algebra so well that its integrability can be proved in the Hamiltonian sense too.
arxiv-2502-02050:
Lahari Anne and co-authors brought in RECCS in 2025, a maker of true-to-life fake networks for testing group finding methods. Judging such methods needs networks whose true groups are known, which real data rarely provides, so research staff plant groups in synthetic networks. A leading maker group, stochastic block models seeded from real networks, turns out to have a flaw: it can produce ground-truth groups that fall apart into disconnected pieces. Even when the real groups they copy are connected.

RECCS starts from that same block model output, then modifies the network to restore a true-to-life fit to group connectivity while roughly keeping the other network and group traits. The authors checked it on settings drawn from real clustered networks reaching nearly fourteen million nodes, a scale at which trustworthy test data are otherwise scarce.
arxiv-2502-03650:
Eduardo Santos de Oliveira Marques and co-authors propose, in twenty twenty-five, an upgraded evolving fuzzy system for forecasting chaotic time series. Real data carry uncertainty from external factors and from chaos itself. Evolving fuzzy systems handle such data well, since they adapt on their own. Type-2 fuzzy sets, which add a band of uncertainty to each fuzzy value, can beat type-1 sets when uncertainty is high. Their model merges participatory learning, a kernel least squares method, type-2 logic, and data transforms into fuzzy sets.

They call the model ePL-KRLS-FSM+. It creates and measures type-2 fuzzy sets to handle data uncertainty better. Tests use the chaotic Mackey-Glass equation at varied chaos levels, and Taiwan's main stock index. The aim is more accurate forecasts of chaotic series.
arxiv-2502-04350:
Yongchao Chen, Yilun Hao, Yueying Liu, Yang Zhang, and Chuchu Fan teach language models, in a 2025 preprint, when to reason in words and when to write code. Symbolic tasks often need exact computation, which plain text does badly. Yet models rarely switch to code at the right moments. The authors build a guide model that steers a bigger model between the two modes. They first create a benchmark of thirty-seven symbolic tasks with adjustable difficulty. Then they make training data of guidance exchanges.

The guide, CodeSteerLLM, is a tuned mid-size model with checkers that verify symbols and answers. Paired with a leading commercial model, it lifted the average task score sharply. The pair beat the strongest known reasoning models on the same set. The guide also transferred to other big models, boosting each by a wide margin. The authors argue that steering, not scale alone, unlocks symbolic skill.
arxiv-2502-06550:
Xie took a first step in twenty twenty-five to fold fast wave kinds into a lean fluid model of hot charged gas. Full wave models are true but cost much to solve. His plan swaps two hard sum forms for neat fits that stay sound.

One fit tracks the wave spread sum, the other the ring sum across all sizes. With both fits the whole model stays in clean frac-tion form. That lets Bernstein waves, a known kind, sit in a fluid frame. A grid solve then reads when such waves can pass in hot gas.
arxiv-2502-08150:
Yang Cao, Bo Chen, Xiaoyu Li, Yingyu Liang, Zhizhou Sha, Zhenmei Shi, Zhao Song, and Mingda Wan wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It builds a generative model on a physics trick from special relativity: a hard cap on speed.

Their frame, Force Matching, adds the Lorentz factor so sample speeds stay below a fixed limit as a sample forms. That cap steadies the whole sampling path. The authors prove the cap holds through the run. On a twin-moons test set the method beats plain flow matching by a wide gap in distance loss. Knock-out tests pin the gain on the speed cap. The work seeds a physics-led path for stable generation.
arxiv-2502-09050:
Kim, Choi, Park, and Shin introduced a fast method in twenty twenty-five for recommending items to groups rather than single users. Group picks, like a film for friends, must blend tastes at member and group level. Neural methods do this well but train slowly and at high cost.

Their method, Group-GF, skips training entirely. It builds three item similarity graphs, each capturing a different view of member-group ties. A tailored polynomial filter is run on each graph, and the three results are combined. Tests showed runtimes far below neural rivals while matching or beating their accuracy. The approach suits platforms that must refresh group picks often and cheaply, from streaming services to team travel planning. The work reframes group recommendation as a filtering problem on graphs.
arxiv-2502-09150:
Suhail, Goel, and Sethi tested in twenty twenty-five how prone three kinds of pic sort tools are to learn-ing short cuts in place of true traits. Short cuts are false cues in data that cut train loss but fail on new pics. They plant cues tied to class by spot and by bright-ness in a test set.

Tools are then read on sets with and without the planted cues to gauge their lean. At low learn rates one tool kind, the swirl net, held back from the cues most. Glass-like tools with no spot code took the cues in near full and lost the true traits. Learn rate shifts the lean in all kinds.
arxiv-2502-09250:
Jacopo Moi, Davide Spallarossa, Stefano Bonetti, Raffaella Burioni, and Guido Caldarelli reviewed in twenty twenty-five how network theory and machine learning can speed the hunt for new materials. Sets of data on materials now grow fast. They grow faster than researchers can search them. The hard part is no longer to gather data. The hard part is to search a vast space of compounds in a wise way.

The review calls for descriptors at many scales. They range from the layout of atoms to bulk traits. Each material then sits in a space with many dimensions. Network theory sets out the links between materials. It brings hidden patterns into view. Machine learning adds forecasts. It shrinks the space and ranks strong candidates. Used as one, the two give a clear route through material space. The authors survey wins and open problems for this joint approach.
arxiv-2502-10950:
Xiangyu Zhang, Hexin Liu, Qiquan Zhang, Beena Ahmed, and Julien Epps detect depression, in a 2025 preprint, from the timing of speech rather than its words alone. Language models asked to judge depression from text do only fairly. Adding a standard retrieval step barely helps. The missing signal, the authors argue, sits in how speech unfolds in time: pauses, pace, and rhythm. They first compare those timing patterns between healthy speakers and speakers with depression. Clear differences show up.

Their system, SpeechT-RAG, retrieves reference cases by timing traits instead of text. The same traits drive a confidence score, so the system knows when to trust itself. It matched fine-tuned models on accuracy with no extra training. Unlike them, it also reports how sure it is. The authors frame that pairing, accuracy plus honesty about doubt, as what mental health tools require before real use.
arxiv-2502-12050:
Yasmin Moslem and five co-authors report on the first mentorship program devoted to speech translation, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The program ran across two months and paired learners with guidance on a fast-growing field. Speech translation turns spoken words in one language into text or speech in another.

Participants worked through data preparation, model building, and advanced research tasks. They tried ways to stretch limited training data and compared direct systems with chained ones that first transcribe and then translate. Projects covered Arabic, Bengali, Galician, Indonesian, Japanese, and Spanish. The paper shares what the teams built and what they learned, as a record for future rounds of the program.
arxiv-2502-13050: Kool, Oh, Rennemo, and Thomas define a Hopf index for isotropic sections of orthogonal bundles in twenty twenty-five. The classic Hopf index equates how often a section of a vector bundle vanishes with a winding number. Their version adapts that match to sections that stay isotropic, meaning null for a quadratic form carried by the bundle. Eight analogues of the index are given. The tools feed into cosection localized virtual cycles and DT4 virtual cycles, two counting schemes in modern geometry.
arxiv-2502-13250:
Ricardo Ferreira da Silva and five co-authors automate the tuning of atomic structure calculations for heavy elements, where errors feed directly into models of neutron star mergers. The Flexible Atomic Code needs a fictitious mean configuration chosen well, or its energy levels drift far from experiment. Lanthanides and actinides are the hardest and most important cases.

Their sequential model-based optimization iteratively adjusts that configuration to minimize disagreement with measured levels. Case studies covered gold, platinum, praseodymium, and erbium ions in two charge states each. Average level errors fell from twenty to sixty percent down to ten percent or less. Transition wavelengths matched experiment within ten percent for about ninety percent of lines in the best-tested ions.
arxiv-2502-15350: Rowena Ball opened a series on Indigenous math in 2025 for the Gazette of the Australian Mathematical Society, starting with smoke telegraphy. Ball frames Indigenous math knowledge as a key but neglected part of humankind's shared math heritage. She writes with respect for the Mithaka peoples of south-western Queensland. She also states that the content includes no culturally restricted knowledge or images. The series aims to widen the horizons of research staff, students, and teachers.
arxiv-2502-15950:
Lior Belenki, Alekh Agarwal, Tianze Shi, and Kristina Toutanova tune the recipe of data used to pretrain language models. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The mix of sources shapes what a model learns. Trying every mix by full training is far too costly. A regression model can predict loss for untried mixes. Older regressions used only the mix rates as inputs.

Their Mixture of Data Experts approximates each mix's loss more richly. Expert models trained per source supply extra features. The regression then forecasts candidate mixes far better. Experiments span models from small to a billion parameters on SlimPajama. Adding end-task loss to the goal lifts few-shot scores further. Pretraining budgets stretch further with smarter mixes.
arxiv-2502-17150:
Andrea Bertazzi, Tim Johnston, Gareth Roberts, and Alain Durmus established privacy guarantees in twenty twenty-five for Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms. These samplers underpin Bayesian statistics, but releasing their output can leak information about the data behind them. The question is when the samples themselves count as differentially private.

The first part ties privacy to how fast the underlying chain converges, with a sharp warning: the target distribution must itself be differentially private. The second part specializes to two workhorse algorithms, the unadjusted Langevin algorithm and its stochastic gradient cousin. A new proof method, built on Girsanov's theorem plus a perturbation trick, handles unbounded domains and non-convex targets. Guarantees cover both a single released state and the whole trajectory, giving concrete guidance for private sampling.
arxiv-2502-17650:
Sameer Neupane, Poorvesh Dongre, Denis Gracanin, and Santosh Kumar study their own use of a stress aid that joins a wrist-worn sensor with a smart chatbot. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

For twenty-two days, the two lead authors used chatbots they built for the study. When the worn tool sensed strain in the body, it sent a prompt. Each man logged the cause of stress in a short phrase, then sought a tailored step from his chatbot. They kept diaries and met each week to weigh the tips for fit, clarity, and effect. Most prompts flagged real stress, but just one in five called for a step to be taken.
arxiv-2502-18850:
Jongbae Hong investigates a long-debated feature of tiny electrical constrictions in a 2025 physics study. In a quantum point contact, conductance climbs in steps as a gate voltage opens channels, but a shoulder appears near a fraction of the expected step, the famous anomaly in this field. The author reads the gate-dependent conductance as entangled-state tunneling and extracts the energy of quasiparticles near the Fermi level.

At zero temperature that energy signals a quantum phase transition between two coupling states of a localized spin, split by the conductance threshold. Gate-driven migration of the localized state drives the switch, tying the anomaly to Kondo physics.
arxiv-2502-19150:
Lopez-Miguel and three co-authors offered controller verification as a service in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Programmable logic controllers run safety-critical gear in factories and labs. Safety standards recommend proving their code correct with formal methods. Few organizations keep that expertise in-house, though.

The proposed service supplies the experts from outside, sparing costly internal training. It also models time-dependent parts whose internals stay trade secrets. A case study applied the service at a particle accelerator in Germany. CERN provided the verification for a safety installation at GSI. The authors present the model as a cost-effective route to compliance.
arxiv-2502-20350:
Kai Zhang and co-authors taught a language model to recommend drugs and explain itself in 2025. Drug find is a core language task in biomedicine, yet systems that must justify a recommendation, the trait that makes a suggestion usable in research or care, remain underexplored. The authors first built the teaching substance: a clear drug recommendation data set built from open drug knowledge graphs, medical trial records. And the PubMed literature, tying likely drugs to the evidence for them.

On that base they trained KEDRec-LM, an instruction-tuned large language model that distills knowledge from the built medical corpus. The model does two things at once: it recommends drugs for a stated need and generates the rationale behind each recommendation. So a human can audit the thinking rather than merely the answer. The data set and model are offered as infrastructure for further work on clear biomedical recommendation.
arxiv-2503-02650:
William Brach, Kristian Kostal, and Michal Ries test how well large language models convert free text into strict formats in a 2025 paper. Huge amounts of useful data sit in unstructured text, and turning them into standard forms by hand is slow. The team used recipe text and a structured cooking format as their test case.

Four models were tested, from two major model families and at two sizes. The largest model, given a few examples, scored near perfect on their measures, a first proof that such conversion can be reliable without heavy training. Smaller models lagged but showed promise for targeted fine tuning. The authors suggest the approach could extend to medical records and technical documents.
arxiv-2503-02850:
Ekkehard Glimm and Lillian Yau proposed exact matching in twenty twenty-five as an alternative to propensity score matching in medical comparisons. Comparing treatments across studies is confounded by differences in patients and trial entry rules. Propensity matching reweights patients to roughly balance those differences, but 'roughly' has no accepted standard.

The authors recast matching as a constrained optimization problem: choose weights so the average confounder values are exactly identical across groups after matching. Unlike a known related method, they impose no fixed formula on the weights. The approach handles individual patient data from several groups and mixtures of individual and summary data. The paper investigates when exact matching is feasible, offering a principled standard where the field has relied on judgment calls.
arxiv-2503-03950:
Pedro Marquez-Zacarias, Andres Ortiz-Munoz, and Emma Bingham ask what stays fixed in a live thing while its stuff is swapped out. The work came out in 2025. Live things trade stuff with the world round them all the time. Yet one trait lasts through that swap. The team calls that trait the form of the whole.

They set out a math frame and a set of core terms for that form. In their view, the form does not hinge on which bits of stuff are there at one time. The form also comes from inside the thing itself. So the frame must show how self-made form starts and holds. They build up from small base steps to the whole forms that life science studies. They also link their terms to past work in the field and in thought about life.
arxiv-2503-04850:
Minh Trung Tran, Nasrin Sohrabi, and colleagues dissect a slow-bleeding scam in decentralized finance in a 2025 security study. Unlike rug pulls that empty a pool at once, a slow liquidity drain siphons funds gradually over long periods, staying under alarms tuned for sudden theft. The authors name the scheme and call it a large, growing risk to the ecosystem.

Their empirical analysis covers hundreds of thousands of liquidity pools across six major decentralized platforms. Mapping the drain's fingerprints is the first step toward detectors that watch rates, not just events. Slow theft punishes exactly the patience that investors are told to practice.
arxiv-2503-06150:
Huan Tian and colleagues ask if making a classifier fairer makes it leak more private data. In-processing fairness methods curb biased forecasts. But their effect on privacy was little studied. The team tests fair binary classifiers against two standard attacks. One is membership inference, which tests if a person's data was in training. One is attribute inference, which guesses traits that are sensitive.

Fairness steps did not, as a surprise, hurt privacy as a rule. Fair models often fought off both attacks better. The steps seem to strip sensitive facts from traits that are pulled out. They also lower confidence on most training cases. But the study also found a threat path. To use gaps between fair and biased models powers stronger attacks of both kinds. Broad tests confirm the results.
arxiv-2503-08050:
Yi Shuen Lee, Siddhant Doshi, Margaret Millhouse, and Andrew Melatos test how well an unmodeled gravitational wave pipeline can certify that a burst carries only the polarizations Einstein allows. General relativity predicts two tensor modes. The BayesWave algorithm offers two signal models: one insisting on elliptical polarization, one relaxed enough to describe generic content through Stokes parameters. Synthetic black hole mergers, plain and precessing, serve as truth.

Both models reconstruct nonprecessing signals accurately; the stricter model wins on evidence because it has fewer parameters. Heavy precession with three or more detectors flips the verdict for some events, the relaxed model reconstructing better and evidencing stronger. On real events from the third observing run, the strict model is preferred throughout. More detectors, the study shows, will sharpen polarization forensics considerably.
arxiv-2503-08650:
Zhenchen Wan and co-authors wrote this computer vision paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on virtual try-on that needs no masks. Shoppers want to see a garment on a photo of themselves, but older systems demand a hand-drawn mask of the body area to replace, and sloppy masks ruin the result.

Their framework, MF-VITON, takes just two inputs: a person photo and the target garment. In a first stage, a mask-based model builds a rich training set of person and garment pairs with varied backgrounds. In the second stage, that model is fine-tuned on the set until it can swap garments with no mask at all. Tests show the mask-free system beating the mask-based ones it learned from, on both accuracy and looks. The authors present it as a simpler path to try-on tools people will actually use.
arxiv-2503-08750:
Yuhan Zhi, Xiaoyu Zhang, Longtian Wang, and four colleagues expose a bias in language model investment advice in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Language models increasingly act as recommendation engines, including for investing. The authors show the models systematically prefer specific products when recommending investments. Such preferences could quietly steer users, inflate valuations, and feed financial bubbles, risking harm to investors and market stability.

To study the bias they built an automated pipeline producing over half a million samples across stocks, mutual funds, cryptocurrencies, savings products, and portfolios. Clear preferences emerged, including for well-known technology stocks from Apple and Microsoft. Notably, the bias persisted even after standard debiasing techniques were applied. The authors urge researchers to treat product bias as a fairness and security concern for AI-driven financial advice.
arxiv-2503-09050:
Alvin Kimbowa and five co-authors introduced Mono2D in twenty twenty-five, a layer that helps ultrasound AI read knee cartilage on unfamiliar machines. Point-of-care ultrasound could widen care for knee osteoarthritis, but segmentation models falter when a new device or setting changes the image style. Their fix extracts features that ignore contrast and brightness shifts.

Mono2D computes local phase features at several scales with trainable filters, and sits before a standard segmentation network, learning alongside it. On multi-domain knee ultrasound data it beat rival domain-generalization methods on overlap score and surface distance. It also won on a multi-site prostate MRI data set, suggesting the trick travels across imaging types. The authors note more clinical testing is still needed.
arxiv-2503-09350:
Alex Kehagias, Davide Perrone, and Antonio Riotto wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It works out the non-linear part of the ringing tones of a Schwarzschild black hole, the simplest kind with no charge or spin.

When struck, a black hole rings at set tones called quasi-normal modes, and those tones mix at second order. The authors use the Penrose limit, a trick that links a plane wave shape to the ring of light paths around the hole. With it they pull out the second-order tones for one mixing channel by hand. The result does not hinge on the tone index, and a symmetry check backs it up. The work gives a clean test case for studies of black hole rings.
arxiv-2503-10650:
Tabia Tanzin Prama and co-authors wrote this paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on rating how severe online bullying is for each victim. The same cruel comment can wound one person far more than another, so a flat label misses the real harm.

Their model reads the comment plus facts about the user: self-esteem, anxiety, depression, time online, past discipline, and background traits. A relabeling step sorts comments into not bullying, mild, and severe with those personal factors in mind. A sequence model trained on one hundred forty-six features beat prior systems, reaching about ninety-eight percent accuracy. Explanation tools then showed which inputs drove each call. Victims from some racial and gender groups, and those bullied before, drew harsher treatment and deeper harm. The authors argue severity tools should weigh the person, not just the words.
arxiv-2503-12650:
Denis Sedov and Mathias Scheurer work out how a scanning tunneling probe can reveal the pairing state of a graphene superconductor. Stacked graphene sheets with a rhombohedral twist have shown hints of superconductivity. The normal state there favors one valley, breaking time-reversal symmetry. Which pairing pattern wins is unknown.

The authors build a microscopic tunneling theory that treats any pairing pattern on equal footing, even ones with moving pairs. In weak tunneling, the single-valley asymmetry stamps distinct marks on commensurate versus incommensurate pair momenta.
