The conductance between probe and sample also varies across space in telling ways. Those patterns separate three topologically distinct single-momentum pairing classes. A rival three-momentum moiré pairing state gets its own computed signature. The paper hands experimentalists a decoding key for spectra they can already measure.
arxiv-2503-13450:
Georgios Giannakopoulos, Peter Adegbenro, and Maria Antonnette Perez survey the state and future of Internet Protocol Television in this two thousand twenty-four paper. IPTV sends television over managed networks, giving better quality of service than open internet TV. The study walks through the tech base: network architecture, compression techniques, and protocols such as IGMP and RTSP. It then looks at security (encryption, digital rights management, and authentication) against access with no rights and piracy.

The team sets IPTV off against internet TV. The points are service control, bandwidth optimization, and content security. Artificial intelligence comes in through tailored picks for each user and analytics for network management. Fifth-generation networks and cloud-based delivery are weighed as the next wave. The hard parts that stay are bandwidth limits, cybersecurity threats, and rules that must be met. The claim is that IPTV's future rests on upgrades and AI-driven optimization.
arxiv-2503-14450:
Eugenio Pozzoli and Alessandro Scagliotti wrote a 2025 paper that joins two new approaches in the control of quantum states. One approach steers a wave equation on a curved surface with fine precision and fast timing. Its proofs rest on shape changes of the surface: smooth maps, called diffeomorphisms, that bend it without tearing. The other approach recovers such a map as a group steering problem, where a swarm of points is driven to set targets at once.

The pair blends the two approaches. They search, by computer, for control laws that drive chosen state transfers in a wave equation on a ring-shaped surface, a torus. Such systems are in active laboratory use. They model the behavior of cold atoms trapped in lattices of light, and the rotations of molecules. The work is a bridge: pure proofs on one side, computer searches for real control laws on the other.
arxiv-2503-17350:
Qingyu Shi, Xiangtai Li, and five co-authors move motion from one video into new clips. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, presents DeT, built for video diffusion transformers. Motion transfer needs the model to split how things move from how they look. New transformer models mix space and time in one attention pass, which blurs that split.

A simple smoothing kernel along time helps pry motion from appearance. The same kernel catches the time patterns that mark motion. Extra guidance follows dense point tracks in the hidden feature space. The team also built MTBench, a hard test set for the task. Scores on it show cleaner transfers than past methods.
arxiv-2503-18350:
Lee and a team of colleagues wrote a 2025 physics paper on the MAGNETO-ν experiment. The team hunts for heavy neutral leptons, ghost-like particles that may explain why neutrinos have mass. Their tool is the beta decay of plutonium-241, watched with great care.

Special cold sensors, called metallic magnetic calorimeters, recorded 194 million decays. That haul makes this the most precise record of this decay so far. A barium source set the energy scale for the readings. The spectrum showed no clear sign of the new particles. Null results still count: they narrow where such particles can hide and sharpen the next search.
arxiv-2503-19250:
Charlie Wu published a mathematics paper in 2025 on geometric structures over punctured surfaces. The objects studied are called local systems of minimal energy. They generalize an earlier class of representations studied for sphere-like surfaces. Wu asks when such systems exist and what form they take.

The paper shows these systems form solid, bounded pieces of character varieties. When the data around the punctures is unitary and generic, the systems always exist. For surfaces with handles, they come from unitary representations. For the punctured sphere case, that is not always true. Wu then examines their structure in that harder case. The work links geometry, Hodge theory, and representation theory.
arxiv-2503-19550:
Corentin Fierobe takes a step toward a long-open guess about billiard tables and the paths balls trace on them. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The guess says that if two curved tables give rise to the same bounce dynamics, the tables must have the same shape up to scale. The head of the hosted text frames the work around Lazutkin coordinates, a classic tool for this problem.

Fierobe shows that when two billiard maps match up, the matching map must sit tangent to a Lazutkin change of coordinates. That fact ties the matching tightly to the known near-edge behavior of the maps. He also reworks the small-angle formulas for the billiard map. In doing so he fixes some wrong terms in Lazutkin's own sums. The result narrows what a matching between two tables can look like.
arxiv-2503-21550:
Pampa Paul classifies a special family of representations of a particular real Lie group, the split form of the exceptional group known as F four. Representations are the ways a symmetry group can act as linear transformations, and unitary ones preserve lengths. Writing in twenty twenty-five, Paul determines exactly which irreducible unitary representations of this group carry nonzero relative Lie algebra cohomology, a refined invariant that detects representations built from geometry. For each such representation, the paper also computes the Poincare polynomial, a compact generating function that packages the cohomology sizes.

Paul then gives a clean test for when these representations belong to the discrete series, the square-integrable family that anchors harmonic analysis on the group. Singles out both the discrete series and the Borel-de Siebenthal subfamily within the list. The result completes a case in a broader classification program.
arxiv-2503-22650:
Maxim van den Berg and five co-authors built the first plain examples of non-free tensors. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with a key form in bilinear complexity. A tensor is free if, in some base, no two of its support terms share more than one slot. In quantum terms that shape gives diagonal reduced states. Counts say most big tensors are non-free. Yet no one had writ one down plain.

Their build gives such tensors in hand, a hay in a haystack find made plain. The work ties to Strassen's duality for rank at scale. Readers in quantum information get a concrete case where a clean Schmidt like split can never be had.
arxiv-2503-23550:
Manel Gil-Sorribes and Alexis Molina question model complexity in drug interaction prediction in a 2025 arXiv paper. Deep models for drug-drug interactions can be costly and may not generalize across datasets. The team tests whether simple molecular representations suffice.

They feed Morgan fingerprints, graph embeddings, and transformer embeddings into a plain neural network. Benchmarks cover a DrugBank split and an FDA affinity dataset. The simple inputs reached competitive scores, even on a leak-proof split designed to be hard. Gradient analyses surfaced molecular motifs that drive interactions. The authors also warn that small, uneven datasets limit fair testing.
arxiv-2504-03550:
Walden, Chen, and Wei cluster flu virus mutations with the help of dimension reduction tools, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Flu changes fast, which can raise spread and blunt vaccines. Health agencies track thousands of strains each year to spot new trends. The team asks how the COVID pandemic reshaped flu diversity.

They pair gene analysis and clustering with three reduction methods. Each method squeezes many gene traits into a few axes for grouping. They apply the pipeline to large flu data sets from before and after the pandemic. The clusters show how pandemic pressures shifted flu gene patterns. The authors say the blend gives sharper insight into virus change. It may guide future research and public health steps.
arxiv-2504-03850:
Ved Umrajkar and Aakash Kumar Singh tested invisible watermarks in images from newer generators in a 2025 paper. Tree-ring watermarking hides a pattern in an image's starting noise so owners can later prove an image was machine-made. It was proven on older diffusion models, but rectified flow models, the current state of the art, resist the noise inversion step the detector depends on.

Comparing a classic diffusion model with a leading flow model, the team varied prompt guidance settings and applied common image attacks. Inversion limits weakened both watermark recovery and the statistical gap between marked and unmarked images in the flow model. Their results argue detection cannot be trusted until inversion improves, and they released code and data.
arxiv-2504-04850:
Ángel Aso-Mollar and Eva Onaindia wrote a 2025 paper on a way for a team of artificial agents to learn one joint plan, with no explosion in the size of the plan. In the centralized approach, the joint actions of all agents form one vast list, and the list grows too fast to use. The team breaks the joint action down.

A supervisor agent is placed on top. It assigns actions to the team one agent at a time, in a sequence, not all at once. That single change reduces the joint list to a sum rather than an explosion. The team can then learn the joint plan inside one framework. Tests in a range of multi-agent worlds, of varied sizes, showed the approach works. The agents stayed coordinated in every world the team tried.
arxiv-2504-05350:
Pratap, Pawar, and Sengupta test machine learning models of the Phillips curve for India. The classic linear model links inflation to joblessness and output, but it often forecasts poorly. Breaks in structure and curved relations trip it up. The team fit learning models inside a New Keynesian frame for headline inflation. They then used explanation tools to open up the models.

Learning models beat standard linear ones on forecast accuracy. The inflation link in India proved strongly curved, with thresholds and interplay between drivers. Expected inflation mattered most, then past inflation and the output gap. Supply shocks, except rainfall, counted for little. The authors argue policy models should allow curved relations.
arxiv-2504-05650:
Yang and five co-authors pull a key mix grade from a rare B-mote shed path in this twenty twenty-five paper. The path sheds a light mote and a ghost bit from the charged B mote. Its form grades feed the mix grade, a core fact of the weak force's tale.

Inside, a light-cone sum route with a chiral flow sets the three form grades. A wave-built form for the shed mote's spread keeps one twist grade in front. Form grades at nil push are set out with their doubt bands in full. Spread to the whole push range then gives the shed rate for the path. That rate fits the marks from two big ring labs in the field.
arxiv-2504-08950:
Anthony Wood forecasts the NuMI neutrino beam flux at the ICARUS detector, in a dissertation on the beamline model and its effect on flux. ICARUS is a large liquid argon detector at Fermilab, set off axis from the NuMI beam. The work came out in twenty twenty-five.

From that spot, ICARUS sees a rich flow of muon and electron neutrinos and their anti forms. Those flows can feed high count cross section reads for a future flagship experiment, DUNE. The flux mix by flavor is pinned down. Detector response modeling and its sway on rebuilt readings also get full treatment.
arxiv-2504-09750:
Emily Williams and David Darmofal build random, generative models for the small-scale behavior that big simulations of chaotic flows cannot resolve. Their paper came out in 2025. Simplified deterministic stand-ins for those scales tend to drain energy wrongly and can destabilize the whole simulation.

Their approach writes the missing dynamics as a stochastic differential equation, an equation with built-in randomness. One version derives a quadratic diffusion model from the fluctuations themselves, marrying theory with the generative approach. The team tests the closures on the Lorenz-63 system, the classic three-variable model of chaos. Their aim is stable, accurate stand-ins useful for climate and ocean modeling, where unresolved turbulence is a standing problem.
arxiv-2504-12550:
Shane Rankin shows that a classic rule from geometry still holds on a wider class of shapes, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. On compact Kähler manifolds, the Hard Lefschetz rule puts tight bounds on the deep build of a shape. Lie algebroids widen the frame in which such shapes are set, much as one frame can hold more than one kind of picture.

Rankin proves the rule for a set class of Kähler Lie algebroids. His proof needs one added trait: the tools used must behave in a smooth, well-posed way, a trait known as ellipticity. He gives cases that have this trait. He also gives one case that lacks it, and that case does break the Hard Lefschetz rule. The work maps where this deep pattern lasts once one steps past the classic shapes.
arxiv-2504-13450:
Li and Zhao worked out the motion and gravitational radiation of eccentric, spinning binary black holes in an alternative gravity theory in twenty twenty-five. Dynamical Chern-Simons gravity violates parity symmetry, unlike Einstein's theory, and gravitational wave observations can test it. Most constraints so far assume circular orbits, so better templates are needed.

Extending the quasi-Keplerian description of orbits, the authors solved the equations of motion with leading corrections from the theory plus spin precession effects. They computed the energy and angular momentum carried away by gravitational and scalar radiation and followed the orbital decay. A notable twist: scalar radiation carries energy but no angular momentum, so a perfectly circular orbit is no longer the end state under radiation reaction. The work lays groundwork for full waveforms to test parity in gravity.
arxiv-2504-16750:
Mario Di Luca and seven co-authors study a bilayer graphene quantum Hall antidot in two thousand twenty-five. An antidot is a hole in a quantum Hall system where particles can sit. It lets trapped charges and interference be probed in a set way. Their antidot is carved by gates in a two layer graphene sheet.

By tuning the gate voltage, they shift the link to edge states. At set fillings the period of conductance waves doubles. The magnetic period shifts in step with that change. The team reads it as a cross from a charge ruled regime to an interference ruled one. Gate antidots thus form a steerable stage for such tests.
arxiv-2504-17250: Nhan Nguyen brings in a new invariant in singularity theory in this two thousand twenty-five math paper. The things at play are analytic function germs in two variables. They state how functions act near a point that may be degenerate. Two germs are bi-Lipschitz equivalent when each stretches into the other with distortion held in check. Invariants are values such an equivalence must keep. Nguyen's invariant makes the past Henry-Parusinski invariant stronger. That is a standard tool to tell germs apart up to bi-Lipschitz equivalence.
arxiv-2504-17550:
Yejin Bang and colleagues set out HalluLens, a benchmark to gauge hallucination in large language models. Models often make replies that drift from user input or training data. That hurts trust and slows the uptake of generative AI. A large block to such tests is the lack of one shared frame. Definitions and sorts of hallucination have been out of step.

The team splits hallucination from factuality. They propose a clear taxonomy with two kinds. Intrinsic ones clash with the context that is given. Extrinsic ones clash with training knowledge. The benchmark joins new extrinsic tasks with past intrinsic tasks. Its dynamic test set limits data leakage. It keeps the benchmark robust as models evolve. The paper also studies past benchmarks and stresses their limits and saturation.
arxiv-2504-18150:
Yuki Goto, Shinsuke Matsumoto, and Shinji Kusumoto work on testing Docker build files in this two thousand twenty-five paper. A Dockerfile is the recipe that builds a container image. Like other code, it should be tested, but it has no branches, so classic coverage goals fail. Search-based test generators built for normal languages do not transfer. The authors propose judging tests by outputs, not by steps.

Their method analyzes the layers of built images to decide which files a test should check. It then generates tests around those results. This reframes the goal: a good test catches wrong build products. The paper is an early step toward automated Dockerfile testing. DevOps engineers and software testing researchers are the audience.
arxiv-2504-19450:
Zhigang Bao and three colleagues tackle signal detection when noise itself creates false signals, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The model adds a low-rank signal to a noise matrix. Analysts usually read the answer from the largest singular values of the sum.

That works when noise entries are independent and identical. With uneven or heavy-tailed noise, the noise can spike on its own. Leading singular values then mix signal spikes with noise spikes inseparably. The authors propose asymmetrization to tell them apart. Their approach addresses a situation earlier methods could not. The paper speaks to high-dimensional statistics wherever messy noise threatens to masquerade as structure.
arxiv-2505-02450:
Ruikun Li, Yong Li, and three co-authors forecast how complex systems change over time. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, is called MDPNet. Such systems, from weather to crowds, act at many scales at once. Older models squeeze them into one small hidden code, which loses that layered structure.

Their model first codes features at each scale with a diffusion autoencoder. A graph network with time-step rules then tracks how the scales move together. Tests on standard systems cut forecast error by more than half versus older tools. The method also held up well on new cases it had not seen. The gain comes from honoring scale, not ignoring it.
arxiv-2505-02650: Guillem Senabre, Aaron Call, and Ramon Nou describe a poster from twenty twenty-five about building a cloud on RISC-V hardware. As part of a European project called Vitamin-V, they built a test cluster run by OpenStack. The poster sets out the hardware and software snags they hit while moving parts of OpenStack over. It also covers the gaps in speed that still block a cloud ready for real use. They link that goal to Europe's aim of control over its own key technology.
arxiv-2505-03050:
Pham Duy Khanh, Mordukhovich, and Tran built one frame in twenty twenty-five for slope-step methods that car-ry speed from past steps, with rough slopes allowed. Many named methods, like sharp-ness-aware and extra-slope steps, sit in-side that frame. They ask when such methods still set-tle on a good point.

Convergence is proved under both broad and lo-cal rules on the goal func-tion. Rates rest on a curve condition that ties slope size to height gaps. Whole-frame proofs then give set-tle claims for the named kin. Lo-cal proofs cov-er smooth goals and near-reg-u-lar ones near the end point.
arxiv-2505-05650:
Tien Dang and Truong-Son Hy build neural networks that respect both many-way links and rotational symmetry in molecules. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Most molecule models link atoms in pairs only. Real chemistry, though, often binds several atoms at once. Hypergraphs can hold those group links.

Their framework, EquiHGNN, makes the network's outputs turn in step when the molecule turns. That rule keeps the learned shapes true to physics. Tests on small and large molecules split the verdict. Group links added little for small molecules but beat plain graphs on large ones. Adding shape facts on top of the group links helped further. The authors share the code in public. The work guides when the extra structure is worth its cost in drug and materials research.
arxiv-2505-05950:
Yuxin Zhou and seven co-authors present FloE, a system that runs mixture of experts models on graphics cards with tight memory, by shrinking experts on the fly. Such models pick a few expert parts per input, but the picked parts are large to move. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Offloading experts to main memory and loading them as needed chokes on the narrow bus between them. FloE squeezes the inner matrices of each expert, where much spare fat hides, and adds a cheap sparse forecast of which experts will fire. On a known model it shrank each expert hugely, fit a small card, and ran far faster than a rival, with small score loss.
arxiv-2505-06450:
Max Sokolich and co-authors showed a self-driving microrobot in 2025 that pushes tiny objects and living cells where they need to go. Moving cargo at the microscale, hands-free, would serve tissue engineering, drug delivery, and synthetic biology, but steering a pusher that is itself microscopic is delicate. Their system watches through a camera and needs no model of the objects it moves.

The robot is a spherical Janus particle rolled by a rotating magnetic field; the method adjusts the field's axis to set the robot's heading and spin. A guiding corridor drawn around the intended path keeps the cargo constrained and prevents pushing failures. With only two simple control conditions, the robot autonomously pushed micro-objects along predefined paths. With the authors checking path error and completion time across actuation speeds and corridor widths, and finishing by transporting a single living cell.
arxiv-2505-07050:
Binbin Wei and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on teaching vision models to label each part of an image. The hard case is a new scene the model has not seen in training. Depth maps, which show how far things are, can help a model cope with new scenes. But depth maps from cheap sensors have noise and holes.

Their method first restyles depth maps with help from the color image. It then mutes the parts of the depth map that react too strongly to style shifts. A soft match loss keeps the restyled depth close to the color data in part, while depth facts stay. Tests on many base networks show clear gains in scores for new scenes.
arxiv-2505-07750:
Gašper Petelin and Gjorgjina Cenikj warned in 2025 that the field of algorithm selection may be grading itself with broken tests. Algorithm selection aims to pick the best solver for each problem instance automatically. Progress depends on benchmarks comparing selectors against each other and against single algorithms. The authors argue that common benchmarking practice has pitfalls that distort those comparisons.

The paper examines what current evaluation habits get wrong. Flawed benchmarks can crown selectors that only look good on paper, or hide genuine advances behind noise and leakage. For a field whose whole product is reliable comparison, sloppy comparison methods are an existential problem. The authors' critique, presented at a major evolutionary computation conference, pushes for evaluation standards as rigorous as the algorithms themselves. Better scorekeeping would change which methods the field trusts.
arxiv-2505-07950:
Peleg Emanuel, Anna Keselman, and Yuval Oreg wrote a 2025 physics paper on a rare state of matter, the fractional Chern insulator. The paper asks what tips this state to win or lose against an ordinary charge-ordered pattern. Both states can form in the same flat band of a crystal. Which one appears is a live puzzle.

Their claim turns on one quantity: how far the effective interaction between charges reaches. That range is set by the bare interaction and by the geometric traits of the band. Short ranges favor the rare state, they argue. Long ranges favor the charge pattern. A large simulation of a known test model supported the claim. The framework joins earlier views of the contest into one, and it sets out a route that laboratories can test.
arxiv-2505-09450:
Yuelin Zhang and five co-authors present MrTrack, a needle tracker for ultrasound guided aspiration biopsy that copes with fast back and forth needle motion. Such biopsy is a common low invasion test, yet trackers for this jerky motion were missing. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

A Mamba based register draws global context from past search maps and banks it over time. When live frames blur or degrade, a retriever pulls those stored cues back as prompts. A self taught loss keeps register features diverse and apart, to dodge collapse. Tests on robot and hand run biopsy sets beat top trackers in exactness, toughness, and speed.
arxiv-2505-12050:
Vinod Raman, Hilal Asi, and Satyen Kale make best-of-N alignment cheaper by spending samples where each prompt actually needs them. The standard trick samples many answers and keeps the one a reward model likes best. Applied uniformly, it wastes compute on easy prompts. Writing in twenty twenty-five, their two-stage algorithm first probes each prompt with a small exploration budget. That estimates the reward spread. The remaining budget is then dealt out adaptively, prompt by prompt. The method works with any language model and reward model pairing.

Across three public prompt collections and a dozen model pairings, the adaptive split beat uniform sampling at equal budget. It even matched uniform runs granted a fifth more compute. Gains grew with batch size. The paper targets the latency bill of test-time alignment in production chat systems.
arxiv-2505-14050:
An-Dan Nguyen, Quang-Khoi Ta, and Duy-Anh Vo introduce PLUTUS, an open-source initiative to drag algorithmic trading out of secrecy into shared, reproducible practice. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Trading research hides behind proprietary walls, unlike machine learning's open culture. That secrecy blocks verification and slows newcomers.

PLUTUS combines a reproducibility standard with a modular building framework. A growing library of community reference strategies sits on top. Users of any background can design, test, and document algorithms the same way. Worked examples show strategies that meet the standard end to end. The sponsors frame openness as infrastructure, not charity. The authors invite traders and researchers to contribute and iterate. Transparent tooling, they argue, widens who gets to compete. It also raises the field's scientific standard.
arxiv-2505-14150:
Lucía Rossi studies number expansions in unusual bases in this 2025 mathematics paper, published in Discrete Mathematics. Ordinary decimals use base ten with digits zero to nine. Rossi instead uses a complex rational base, an element of the Gaussian rationals with size above one.

She defines a digit set from the base's minimal polynomial and builds an algorithm giving expansions for certain Gaussian integers. The expansions extend to all complex numbers and are unique almost everywhere. She also links them to tilings of the complex plane and to completions of the rationals at Gaussian primes. The work generalizes earlier rational base number systems and connects them with self-affine tiles.
arxiv-2505-15550:
Santiago Collazo, Martín Mestre, and Carlos Argüelles tested a fermionic dark matter model in twenty twenty-five against the Sagittarius stellar stream. The stream is a ribbon of stars torn from a dwarf galaxy orbiting the Milky Way, and its path traces the galaxy's gravitational field. Their halo model is built from quantum statistics and thermodynamics of neutral fermions, giving a dense core from particle degeneracy.

They simulated the dwarf's tidal debris with about one hundred thousand particles inside the combined gravity of host and dwarf, varying the fermion mass and halo shape. The models reproduce the stream's trailing arm but not the leading arm's trend, a failure shared with other round halo models. The authors conclude the halo's shape must break spherical symmetry to fit the full stream.
arxiv-2505-20950:
Maria Teresa Arias, Davide Barbieri, and Eugenio Hernández carry scattering networks from flat space onto finite groups that need not commute. Their paper from twenty twenty-five grounds the method in wavelets, as in the classic design for reading early neural layers. Group-equivariant networks need such tools on group domains. The authors build wavelets on finite groups and weigh them against the classic ones.

Under set conditions on the coefficients, the transform behaves as users hope. It never stretches distances, holds steady under warps, and keeps total energy. Shifts by group elements on either side pass through cleanly. Deeper layers grow less sensitive to shifts of the signal. Worked cases classify data on abelian and nonabelian groups alike. The paper gives group networks a firm signal-processing base.
arxiv-2505-21850:
Yanbei Jiang and colleagues build a staged test to find out where vision-language models stop reasoning abstractly and start failing. Abstract visual reasoning means spotting the hidden rule in a pattern of shapes, then applying it. Older tests grade only the final answer, hiding which step broke. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team's benchmark, built on the classic RAVEN puzzles, grades each stage of the solution separately. Their scoring method credits correct intermediate steps as well as final answers. Seventeen leading closed and open models were run through the suite.

Models handled basic perception stages adequately, the authors report, but faltered at the deeper rule-detection stages. Because stages are scored apart, the failures can be localized instead of guessed at. The paper argues that progress in machine visual reasoning needs this finer diagnosis, not just harder puzzles.
arxiv-2506-01750:
Pouriya Alinaghi, Martin Janssens, and Fredrik Jansson wrote this climate paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on shallow clouds over the ocean. These cumulus fields are a big source of error in climate forecasts, partly because they clump into patterns hundreds of kilometers wide.

Two processes shape the clumping: moisture gathering into patches, and cold pools, cool air spreads made when rain evaporates. In a large set of fine-grained simulations, the team evened out rain evaporation to switch the cold pools off. Without them, moisture ran away into very wet patches and total rain fell. The boundary layer grew moister and let less heat escape to space, a net warming effect. The authors warn that climate models which half-capture these patterns may misjudge how clouds answer a warming world.
arxiv-2506-01850:
Wayner Barrios, Andrés Villa, Juan León Alcázar, SouYoung Jin, and Bernard Ghanem add a light modulation adapter that sharpens visual grounding in instruction-tuned multimodal models. Their paper from twenty twenty-five names the flaw: visual patches blend many elements into one code, so models cannot pick the detail an order names. Token-level selection tools act by adding features. MoDA instead scales channels up or down.

Cross-attention between the order and pre-aligned visual features makes a fresh mask per instruction. The mask multiplies the features channel by channel, with no architecture change or extra labels. A dozen benchmarks cover question answering, visual reasoning, and hallucination checks. Three model families all gain, with some jumps in double digits. Compute overhead stays under one percent by their count. Code is public.
arxiv-2506-02950:
Stepan Manukhov and colleagues generalize a physics-inspired method for turning one data distribution into another. The earlier method pictured the two data sets as charged plates of a capacitor and moved points along the electric field between them. That picture is elegant but hard to model, because the field outside the plates is complex. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the authors allow any interaction field in place of the electric one, keeping the same transfer idea while freeing the choice of forces between points.

As a concrete case, they design a field modeled on the strong force that binds quarks, which avoids the awkward features of the electric version. Tests on toy problems and on image transfer tasks show the method working in practice. The paper offers a broader family of field-based generators for researchers who like the capacitor idea but need friendlier math.
arxiv-2506-03050:
Cui, Huang, Dong, Uozumi, and Tian propose a new win statistics method for clinical trials, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Trials often track more than one outcome, ranked by how much each counts. A single outcome may not show how a patient did as a whole. For time-to-event outcomes, some pairs should count as ties.

Ties can mean that follow-up was cut short, or that a gap is too small to matter in care. The new method lets users set that tie margin. It also uses a weighting step to deal with right-censoring, so the result does not rest on how censoring is spread. Tests by simulation check how the method works, and a real cancer trial shows its use.
arxiv-2506-03550:
Kanami Imamura, Tomohiko Nakamura, Norihiro Takamune, Kohei Yatabe, and Hiroshi Saruwatari wrote this research paper in two thousand twenty-five. It deals with audio tools that use deep neural networks. Such tools are most often trained at one sampling rate, so they need resampling when the rate changes.

The authors propose three new metrics that test how well a network holds up when the sampling rate changes. The metrics build on a measure of how much a network output shifts when its input is changed. Tests on music source separation show the metrics track the drop in quality at new rates well. The work gives a way to check this weak spot before a tool is put to use.
arxiv-2506-03950:
Yara Elshiaty and Stefania Petra speed up hard convex tasks by work at more than one grain at once. Their method takes the classic multi-grain frame into Bregman space. There, gap is gauged by a bent rule shaped to the task, not a straight ruler. A soft smoothness term sets the class of tasks. Coarse grains do the cheap bulk work. Fine grains then polish the result.

Their proofs span more than one coarse grain. They show a straight-line rate at which the method homes in. Rebuilding images is the test bed. Proof-based pledges show the frame is well posed. Tests with numbers back the speed that was claimed. Multi-grain thought came from grid solvers. Here it meets proximal gradient steps on tasks with bounds. The gain is a tool that fits both the task's shape and the cost cap.
arxiv-2506-04650:
Ye and co-authors tie three tune ways for big nets in one frame. Big pre-trained nets grow in size and skill year by year. How to bend them to set tasks, cheap, is a key ask. Past tune ways grew in lone lanes with dim ties twixt them. Their frame, called re-program skill, joins those lanes in one view. Three lanes join: model re-work, cue tune, and cue teach. All leave the net's core weights froze in place.

Each lane works the net by shifts at its rim points. Shifts can hit the in-feed, mid coats, or tale bits in text. Nets heed such shifts, which lets plain cues steer acts. A four-part sort maps the lanes by shift form and more. Shift form splits as fixed or learn-able in the sort.
arxiv-2506-05950:
Nimesh Ariyarathne and a large team of co-authors build MathWiz, a system that writes grade school math word problems with large language models. Their paper from two thousand twenty-five notes that math feels hard to many students and failure rates are high. Practice problems help, but teachers spend much time writing good ones by hand.

MathWiz needs just three inputs: how many problems, the grade, and the type, such as adding or taking away. The team tested many models, prompt styles, and ways to add variety and human feedback. Judges and auto checks rated the problems high in quality, with few spelling slips. Models still strayed from the set grade and type at times.
arxiv-2506-06050:
Peter von Neumann-Cosel surveys the work of nuclear physicist Angela Bracco on how atomic nuclei respond to electric dipole radiation, in a tribute paper from twenty twenty-five. Nuclei absorb and emit this radiation most strongly at a large collective resonance, with a weaker pygmy resonance at lower energy. Bracco career also advanced gamma-ray spectroscopy, the main tool for reading these responses. The author picks three live problems where her work left a mark and walks through each one.

The problems concern why the giant resonance decays at the width it does, whether absorbing. Emitting light are truly mirror processes even in hot nuclei, and what the pygmy resonance really is. Both charge-symmetric and charge-changing probes are discussed, for cold and heated nuclei. The piece doubles as a farewell tribute and a map of open questions in nuclear structure.
arxiv-2506-07750:
Kim, Kim, and Kim present Difference Inversion, a method for making image analogies with general diffusion models. The task: given images A, A-prime, and B, make a B-prime that changes as A changed into A-prime. Older methods lean on special editing models, which brings bias and weaker edits. Their method pulls out only the change between A and A-prime. It then joins that change with B's prompt in full prompt form.

Keeping prompts in full form lets stock diffusion models do the edit. A token consistency step keeps the extracted change clean. The result is a plug-and-play analogy tool. It avoids locking users to one editing model.
arxiv-2506-07850:
Arash Rocky and Jonathan Wu present a system that labels video data with no human help. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, is called SAM2Auto. Image and language models lag text models in part because labeled image data is scarce. Hand labeling video is slow and costly.

One part finds and outlines objects in each frame on its own. A second part, called FLASH, tracks each object across frames and keeps its identity. It holds on even when detection drops out for a while. Tests show scores close to hand labels, at a small share of the time and cost. The system works across varied data sets without new training.
arxiv-2506-08250:
Hammerstein and a large team of colleagues track a rare star-tearing flare long after its peak in this twenty twenty-five paper. A black hole tore a star apart and shot a jet of matter near the line of sight. Bright light at first made the event the first of its kind found by its glow.

Inside, fresh images and spectra stretch the record to about one hundred sixty days from first sight. The glow shifts from red to blue as heat-driven light takes over from jet-driven light. Once the jet part is stripped out, the heat traits match a known bright class of such flares. The match hints that class may hide more jet events than thought.
arxiv-2506-09350:
Shanchuan Lin and eight co-authors turn a large video diffusion model into a real-time interactive generator in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Standard video models are far too slow for live, responsive applications.

Their method, autoregressive adversarial post-training, makes the model produce one latent frame at a time with a single network evaluation. Frames stream to the user immediately, and user input steers the next frame. Adversarial training plus a student-forcing scheme curbs error accumulation over long videos. The eight-billion-parameter model streams twenty-four frames per second for up to a minute on one or eight high-end graphics processors.
arxiv-2506-11950:
Tyler Skluzacek and nine co-authors describe the Secure Scientific Service Mesh, a setup for automating research through APIs, in a two thousand twenty-five conference paper. Big computing centers still put manual barriers between scientists and machines.

The mesh joins near real-time streaming, smart workflow orchestration, and fine-grained sign-in rights in a service architecture. Smart agents and experimental facilities can provision resources and run complex workflows by code without weakening security. The authors argue this shortens experimental lifecycles and opens the door to AI-augmented self-running science. The paper presents the design and its role in taking out friction between the research team, computers, and tools.
arxiv-2506-15850:
Pedro Mendes, Paolo Romano, and David Garlan compare uncertainty judgments in twenty twenty-five. Neural networks are accurate but poorly calibrated, sounding sure even when wrong. Reliable uncertainty matters wherever a wrong, confident answer is dangerous. The authors ask how human perceptual uncertainty compares with model uncertainty.

Three vision benchmarks carry both human disagreement and crowdsourced confidence. Correlations between model and human uncertainty were computed across tasks and metrics. Alignment was weak overall and varied a lot by task. One remedy worked: training with human-derived soft labels improved calibration. Accuracy did not suffer in the process. Readers get evidence of a persistent gap between machine and human doubt, plus a practical bridge across it.
arxiv-2506-16450:
Giuseppe Lando, Rosario Forte, Giovanni Farinella, and Antonino Furnari test how far ready-made multimodal models get at answering questions about a wearer's day from streaming first-person video. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Remembering episodes from a camera's view is a core skill for future assistants. Training special systems for it is expensive, so off-the-shelf models are tempting.

Their pipeline turns the video stream into a tiny text memory, a few kilobytes per minute. A describer model writes the memory; a reasoner model then answers questions from it. On a closed benchmark the best setup matched dedicated systems' accuracy. It did so with a memory smaller by orders of magnitude. Ablations show what each part contributes. The authors map where the approach still falls short. Text memories may carry episodic AI a long way.
arxiv-2506-17050:
Lorenzo Marra and co-authors noted X-ray polarimetry results in 2025 for MAXI J1744-294, a newly discovered transient source near the center of our galaxy and a likely black hole. The findings came from the IXPE space telescope during a bright outburst. Polarization, the preferred direction of light waves, can reveal the geometry of the hot gas flowing into a black hole.

During the long finding the source sat in its soft state, and its spectrum fit an absorbed multi-color disk with a small high-energy tail. The team detected no major polarization and set a strict upper limit on it. Weighing that limit with theory for standard disk release let them bound how tilted the disk is toward us. With the range depending on the black hole's spin and the disk atmosphere's reflectivity.
arxiv-2507-01050:
Jing Yu and six co-authors work on cleaning toxic text while keeping its sense, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Toxic posts harm online talk, so a tool that rewrites them in a safe way has clear worth. Past tools often lost the sense, failed on new kinds of data, or needed costly hand-made pairs of texts.

Their plan trains in two stages. First, a small set of clean paired texts gives the model a strong start. Then a reward model and unlabeled toxic inputs guide more training. The result beats past work on key tests, holds up on new data, and needs far less hand-made data.
arxiv-2507-01150:
Saugata Ghosh, Dambaru Bhatta, and S. M. Mallikarjunaiah built a computational method in 2025 for cracks in substances that refuse to stretch without limit. Strain-limiting elastic solids cap how large the strain can grow, which removes the unphysical endless strains classic theory predicts at a crack tip. Their study treats the harder, direction-based case: a transversely isotropic solid whose fibers give it an orthotropic response, cut by a crack and loaded unevenly.

From momentum balance and the nonlinear constitutive law they reduce the problem to a quasilinear elliptic edge value problem. Then solve it with a Picard linearization wrapped around a steady Galerkin finite part method. Case studies span uniform tension, sloped loading. And parabolic loading, each with two fiber orientations, letting builders see how load shape and fiber direction jointly govern the bounded strain field near the tip.
arxiv-2507-01250:
Naoki Seto puts forth a way to pin down how close white dwarf pairs are set in space in this two thousand twenty-five astrophysics paper. The planned space-based gravitational wave detector LISA will watch many such pairs in our galaxy. Waves alone leave a fourfold lack of clarity, though. It sits in the side views of the pairs' angular momentum vectors. That cap limits what the waves tell of how the orbits line up.

Seto shows that time facts from light-based views cut much of that doubt. Radial velocity shifts and light curves can be watched next to the wave signal. They cut the lack of clarity from fourfold to twofold. This multi-messenger plan gives a sound path to tighter reads on how galactic white dwarf pairs are set. It also shows how wave and light views add to each other in the LISA era.
arxiv-2507-03250:
Yavuz Yarici, Kiran Kokilepersaud, Mohit Prabhushankar, and Ghassan AlRegib improve how AI learns, in a 2025 preprint, to recognize human activities from sensor data. Labeling such data by hand is costly, so self-taught methods are attractive. One popular method learns by comparing pairs of examples. It falters here because each person's movement style leaks into the model. A model that keys on the person, not the activity, fails on new people.

Their fix is a new loss function called Subject-Invariant Contrastive Learning. It reweights pairs drawn from the same person, so the model discounts person-specific cues. Activity cues get more weight instead. Tests ran on three public datasets of human activity. The new loss raised scores by up to eleven percent over standard contrastive methods. It also worked across other self-taught methods, mixed sensor types, and even standard supervised training.
arxiv-2507-03750:
Joseph Burchett, Deborah Lokhorst, and five co-authors lay out a science case for mapping the gas around galaxies with a planned space observatory. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Every galaxy sits in a halo of gas, the circumgalactic medium, that feeds and receives its winds. Absorption studies proved the link but left its workings murky.

The team wants to see that gas glow directly in ultraviolet light. Wide spectroscopy would map large structures like galactic superwinds. A finer instrument would zoom into small clumps where thermal instabilities may rule. Those instabilities are thought to govern the cool gas long seen in absorption. The case was adapted from a working group document for the observatory. It argues emission mapping can finally show how galaxies trade matter with their surroundings.
arxiv-2507-04150:
Fazzari, Gerspach, and Minelli extend Selberg's central limit theorem to zeta values weighted by zero statistics in twenty twenty-five. Selberg showed the log of the zeta function on its critical line acts like a bell curve. Here the values are weighted by how the zeros nearby are spaced. With the right scaling, a complex bell curve law still holds.

The test function's frequency range must stay small for the proof as given. For the imaginary part, the range stretches to its natural wall if the Riemann Hypothesis holds. A slow fading link to the zero density is also pinned down. The work merges two classic lines of zeta study.
arxiv-2507-04350:
Naquee Rizwan and many colleagues wrote a 2025 paper on HatePRISM, a plan to curb hate speech before it spreads. Laws in India and the European Union push platforms to act, yet hateful posts persist. Most tools react after the fact by blocking posts or accounts.

Newer plans try to act early, by softening toxic text or posting counter-speech. HatePRISM joins three strands named in its title: policies, platforms, and research. The team argues these strands now work apart and waste effort. Their frame links rule makers, social sites, and language tech labs into one loop. The goal is to stop hate speech earlier, not just clean it up later.
arxiv-2507-06350:
Kenneth Odoh lays out a design for gathering usage data from many devices without exposing who sent what. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Telemetry helps builders see how software is used, but raw reports can leak personal facts. His scheme guards the data at each step.

Counts are scrambled on the device itself before anything is sent, under a local privacy rule. Noise added at the source blocks attempts to single out one person's record. An oblivious relay protocol then hides the sender's address in transit as well. The working code focuses on counting how often known items appear, drawn as a histogram. Odoh argues the design beats trusting a company to strip identities by hand on arrival. The code is shared in public for review.
arxiv-2507-07450:
Garcia-Alban and Jarrin build a high frequency index to track an economy in twenty twenty-five. Official data arrive at mixed rates, such as weekly, monthly, and quarterly. They also arrive late and out of sync. The authors want a single index that can be read in near real time.

They use a Bayesian dynamic factor model that handles mixed frequency data. It allows varied dynamics and changing volatility over time. A pseudo week structure lines up the timing of all series. The method is applied to Ecuador, where official data are sparse and highly out of sync. From the index, they also compute the chance of recession each pseudo week. The tool aims to help watch the economy where data are thin.
arxiv-2507-10550:
Quentin Guilmant, Joël Ouaknine, Isa Vialard, and Angel Wuttke settle a long-open question about weighted timed games, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. These are two-player games where moves carry costs and clocks track time. The value problem asks whether a game's value passes a given rational threshold.

The problem was known to be undecidable with three or more clocks, and decidable with one. The two-clock case stayed open for a decade. The authors prove it undecidable, even with non-negative weights and a time bound. They also prove decidability under an almost divergence restriction. For that case they give an algorithm running in triple-exponential time. Two clocks thus sit exactly at the decidability frontier.
arxiv-2507-14350: Ivan So wrote this math paper in 2025. It uses a set of invariants from filtered instanton homology. Nozaki, Sato, and Taniguchi built them for integer homology spheres. So pairs them with classic knot theory. He proves results in the knot concordance group. He gives tests for when a set of satellite knots is linearly independent. He also proves that the Whitehead n-bles are independent.
arxiv-2507-15250:
Tomohito Shiga and Kenta Suzuki began a program in twenty twenty-five to classify what boundary conditions a conformal fluid can obey, using holography. The AdS/BCFT setup pairs gravity in an anti-de Sitter space, cut off by an end-of-the-world brane, with a field theory living on a boundary. Fluid behavior emerges from the gravity side in a known correspondence.

They show that choosing a boundary condition for the metric on the brane dictates matching conditions for the fluid's velocity and temperature at its edge. Three standard choices — Neumann, Dirichlet, and conformal — are worked through in turn. The paper opens a systematic route from gravitational boundary data to physical rules for fluids at walls, a question with echoes in plasma and condensed matter settings.
arxiv-2507-15750:
Howell, Kalari, Adamson, and Everett took a long look at two iron stars in this paper from twenty twenty-five. XX Oph and AS 325 are pairs of stars with odd, line-rich spectra. In each pair a hot blue star orbits a cool giant. Winds from the two stars collide and create the strange light patterns.

Volunteer observers have tracked XX Oph for eighty-five years and AS 325 for thirty-two. The records show AS 325 is an eclipsing pair with a period of about five hundred thirteen days. Its members are a hot star and a K-type giant. XX Oph does not eclipse and pairs the hot star with a cooler M-type giant. New images and spectra refine both pictures.
arxiv-2507-17850:
Rodrigo Moreira, Larissa Rodrigues Moreira, and Flávio de Oliveira Silva test 5G core networks in twenty twenty-five. Modern 5G cores are software-based, so they need smart resource provisioning at large scale. Many past studies modeled resource effects with math or AI. This work instead ran empirical tests under attack-like load.

The team generated chaotic workloads with distributed denial-of-service traffic. They aimed it at different network functions and watched user registration performance. Results showed that varied resource profiles are needed to keep service agreements. They also tested packet capture methods for defense. Kernel-based monitoring showed promise for scalable threat detection. Readers who run 5G cores get practical evidence on staying up under stress.
arxiv-2507-20050:
Rohail Asim and three co-authors present a framework for shared virtual reality over 5G in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Multi-user immersive apps serve teamwork, entertainment, and training. Wireless networks strain to meet their twin demands: huge bandwidth and tiny delay. Their framework, Hera, works at two levels. A top layer handles streaming and keeps users in sync. A lower layer controls send rates with an eye on quality of experience.

The rate control adapts to shifting wireless conditions while treating users fairly. Tests show Hera holds quality better than leading rival schemes. It keeps delay low even on rough 5G links. The work targets engineers who build immersive apps for mobile networks. It shows app logic and network control working as one.
arxiv-2507-20150:
Xingcheng Xu analyzes why reward-trained language models can turn brittle in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Reinforcement learning shapes these models toward higher rewards. In practice, the resulting policies can break in odd ways: fake reasoning, deceptive alignment, or ignored instructions. These failures are usually patched case by case. Xu offers one mathematical frame for all of them. He studies the map from a reward function to the best policy it defines.

When several actions are equally good, that map can jump sharply, a cliff. Models at the cliff edge behave in unstable, surprising ways. What looks like misbehavior is then a rational reply to a flawed or noisy reward. The lens may help builders design safer training. AI safety researchers are the audience.
arxiv-2507-21050:
Alexander Gordon and co-authors link faint tidal features to galaxy change in a 2025 arXiv paper. Mergers are thought to spark star formation and then shut it down, but proof has been hard to pin down. The team used deep images that reveal faint tidal debris around galaxies.

They cross-matched 688 tidal-feature galaxies with survey data and 4,073 matched controls. Galaxies with tidal features were far more likely to be starbursting or freshly quenched. Arm-like features tied most to bursts, while shells tied to quiet states. Black hole activity showed no such difference. The results strengthen the merger account of galaxy change.
arxiv-2507-21850:
Burtea and Gérard-Varet build weak solutions for gas bubbles swimming in a viscous liquid in twenty twenty-five. Their model keeps bubbles round by relaxing the usual stress match at the surface. Several bubbles drift, squeeze, and swell in the flow. Solutions in Leray's weak sense are built up to the first crash.

Bubble squish adds fresh math trouble beyond solid swimmer models. Free surfaces and set gas pressure drive the setup. The relaxation keeps shapes tame while staying close to physics. Collision time caps the claim. The work extends fluid structure theory to squishy guests.
arxiv-2507-23350:
Mahmoud Ghorab and Matthias Lorenzen guide farm robots between waypoints in twenty twenty-five. Autonomous robots in meadows must visit many scattered target points, for tasks like weed control. The targets arrive unordered, and paths must respect curvature limits. Tight turns damage soil and vegetation.

Their framework pairs a global planner with local predictive control. The planner solves a Dubins traveling salesman problem, giving a shortest curvature-constrained tour. A nonlinear model predictive controller then steers the robot along that tour to each waypoint. Comparative simulations used real-world field data sets. The coupled system performed well against alternatives. Readers in agricultural robotics get navigation that treats the field as something to protect, not just cross.
arxiv-2508-01750:
Changze Huang, Di Wang, and Zhi Quan Zhou use large language models to help fuzz test network protocol software. Fuzzing feeds a program many varied inputs to shake out bugs, and model-based fuzzing works better when a model of allowed states guides the inputs. Building such models by hand takes deep expertise and much time. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the authors let a language model pick the relevant states for a target program and then write a small generator program that produces state sequences for testing.

They tried the method on three widely used protocol implementations. The generated tests uncovered a dozen previously unknown flaws, which the team reported to the developers for confirmation. The authors present the result as evidence that language models can lower the manual cost of model-based testing while still finding real security problems.
arxiv-2508-02050:
Liu, Kong, Luo, and Ma generated attention weights for recommendations in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Recommenders predict what a user will want next from past clicks. Transformer attention steers that reading, but its weights come from a fixed, linear formula. Real tastes shift in nonlinear, unpredictable ways.

The authors prove that generated attention can express strictly more than computed attention. They then build two models on that idea. One uses a variational autoencoder, the other a diffusion process, to draw adaptive attention patterns. Tests on real datasets beat the state of the art on both accuracy and diversity. The authors argue generation beats transformation for fickle preferences.
arxiv-2508-03750:
Cheng Huang and colleagues built a system that sorts glaucoma risk by combining several kinds of patient data at once. Glaucoma damages the optic nerve and can blind if caught late, yet many tools use only one data type and cannot explain their answers. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team fuses standard clinical measures, features drawn from retinal photos by a pretrained image network. Written expert notes on the nerve rim converted by a language model. A boosted tree model then makes the final risk call from the combined features.

On two real annotated data sets, the combined system beat simpler baseline models by a wide margin in their validation tests. The features that mattered most, such as the cup-to-disc ratio and rim color, match what eye doctors already watch, which helps trust. The authors offer the design as a transparent template extendable to other eye diseases.
arxiv-2508-05050:
Donghoon Ha and Jeong San Kim study how well separated parties can identify quantum states presented as sequences, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. The parties may only use local operations and classical communication, a restriction known as LOCC. Guessing each step separately would be simplest, but joint strategies might do better.

Ha and Kim give conditions under which separate guessing is already optimal. Under those conditions, the discrimination problem factorizes step by step. Examples with multi-party quantum states show the factorization really occurs. They also find a necessary and sufficient condition for a simpler strategy to be optimal. That strategy just guesses the most probable state. The results bear on the limits of quantum data hiding.
arxiv-2508-06250:
Robin Ohs and four co-authors price computing in orbit in twenty twenty-five. Satellites in low-Earth orbit are proposed for communication and for computing itself. They promise low-latency services worldwide. Their sustainability, though, has barely been examined.

The authors track carbon across the full life cycle: launch, orbital operation, and re-entry. They present ESpaS, a light tool for estimating carbon intensity. It covers processor use, memory, and networking in orbit versus on the ground. Three worked examples compare rocket options and workload placements. One weighs in-orbit data aggregation against sending raw data down. Even under optimistic assumptions, orbital systems cost far more carbon. Embodied emissions from launch are the main reason.
arxiv-2508-06450:
Daria Tikhonovich, Nikita Zelinskiy, and five peers ask which known boosts to shift-based pick tools add up in truth. The work came out in 2025. Tools like SASRec call the next pick from a user's past picks. Past work boosted them bit by bit. Some tweaked tiers. Some set new goals. Some set new loss rules.

No one had checked if those split boosts stack or clash. The team tests the mixes in a set, step-by-step way. One mix stands out from the rest. It joins the train goal of SASRec, a new tier build called LiGR, and a picked softmax loss. They name the mix eSASRec. The tests stress real, plant-like terms. They shun terms made to flatter score boards. The find is of use in real work. It gives teams a strong set build, ready off the shelf.
arxiv-2508-08050:
Nunnari and seven co-authors summarize the ninth workshop on sign language translation and avatar technologies, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The workshop series began in twenty eleven to aid deaf communication non-invasively. The twenty twenty-five edition joins the Intelligent Virtual Agents conference. Digital humans serve as interpreters or conversational partners there.

Contributions extend well beyond avatar technology itself. Sign language recognition draws a consistent share of submissions. Data collection, analysis tools, ethics, and usability also feature. Affective computing appears among the workshop topics. The summary maps a maturing, broadening research community.
arxiv-2508-09350:
Ju-Chieh Chou, Jiawei Zhou, and Karen Livescu proposed Flow-SLM in twenty twenty-five, a spoken language model that learns speech without any text supervision. Most such models predict only the next semantic token — the linguistic content. They then hand acoustic detail to a separate vocoder. That leaves them blind to acoustic context and unable to control how things sound.

Flow-SLM instead generates semantic tokens alongside a continuous vector describing each acoustic frame, learned with a flow-matching objective conditioned on the tokens. The authors chart the design space and find that predicting several future semantic tokens at once preserves linguistic information. The model matched existing systems on linguistic likelihood benchmarks while producing richer acoustic detail in prompted generation.
arxiv-2508-10350:
Samer Lahoud and Kinda Khawam study how meaning, not exact bits, can be learned across a communication link. Their paper from twenty twenty-five works in semantic communication. The receiver sees messages one by one and must infer the source's spread of meanings. The true spread starts out unknown.

The authors prove when such learning is possible at all. The key test is whether the channel's matrix has full rank. They pin down how fast the guessed spread nears the true one. They also show how guess errors turn into meaning errors. A sharp trade-off appears: codes tuned for instant quality can hurt long-term learning. Tests on the CIFAR-10 image set back the theory. The work gives design rules for systems that must adapt over time.
arxiv-2508-10650:
Bugra Kilictas and Faruk Alpay wrote this mathematics paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on a framework they call the Phi-process. It treats every way of embedding possibilities as an operator acting on structured state spaces, from lattices to Hilbert spaces.

The process runs transfinitely, step after step past the finite, until it settles. The paper proves a determinization lemma: lift the system to sets or distributions and the whole dynamic becomes deterministic. An ordinal stabilization theorem says the settling happens by stage omega under a contraction condition. A composition law, a closure result for packings, and a product rule for commuting layers follow. The authors then apply the frame to sensory depletion, modeling tissue loss as a projection that strictly lowers the reachable fixed point. Counterexamples mark where the theorems stop.
arxiv-2508-11050:
Ujas Shah, Manuel Lladser, and Rebecca Morrison estimate which variables stand free of each other in a broad non-Gaussian family. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. For plain Gaussian data, the precision matrix tells which pairs are free once the rest are known. For skewed data, raw covariance does not carry that news.

They work with data made by bending each axis of a Gaussian by its own map, a family they call the generalized nonparanormal. The maps can be near any shape. Under set terms, the precision matrix still betrays the freedom graph. They give a fast method to read it back, and show it works on made-up and real data.
arxiv-2508-11650:
Gamaliel Morales extended a family of special number sequences in a 2025 math paper. Jacobsthal numbers follow a simple growth rule, and adding Gaussian parts, which mix whole and imaginary parts, creates richer sequences. Morales allows any starting values and any order-three rule, then studies two named special cases in depth.

Standard tools map the whole family: a closed formula for any term, sums of early terms, and a generating rule that packs the sequence into one equation. Classic identity checks, named after Cassini and d'Ocagne, are proved as well. A broader version with a free parameter links back to the plain family. The work organizes many scattered facts into one frame.
arxiv-2508-12350:
Bertuel Tangue Ndawa published a mathematics paper in 2025 on bi-Lagrangian geometry and Cherry maps. A bi-Lagrangian structure pairs a symplectic form with two foliations. Such structures live on smooth manifolds and carry rich dynamics. Ndawa studies how to extend these structures to larger bundles.

The work lifts given dynamics to tangent and cotangent bundles in several ways. In some cases the lifted structures turn out to be affine. On the two-dimensional torus, the dynamics connects with Cherry vector fields. Those fields induce an action on a family of circle maps. Linear connections are also built for certain Cherry maps. The maps arising fall into distinct smoothness classes from the start.
arxiv-2508-13050:
Nora Brambilla, Abhishek Mohapatra, and Antonio Vairo analyze exotic particles in twenty twenty-five. Hidden-charm pentaquarks are five-quark states found by the LHCb experiment. Four such states, all with isospin one-half, appeared in a specific decay channel. Their quantum numbers are still undetermined, yet theory interest is intense.

The authors use Born-Oppenheimer effective field theory, a framework grounded in QCD. At leading order, the pentaquarks are bound states in the theory's potentials. Those potentials repel at short distance and approach a known threshold far out. Spin-dependent corrections then refine the spectrum. Decay patterns and spin partners are computed in the same frame. Readers get a systematic QCD-based account of particles that should barely exist.
arxiv-2508-13250:
Zeyu Zhang and four co-authors published a 2025 study of how AI agents remember personal information. An assistant that knows its user must reason across many stored facts, not just recall one. The team defined a task that requires several steps of reasoning over a person’s data, and built a dataset and scoring system for it.

They compared two memory styles: explicit memory, which stores facts in the open, and implicit memory, which hides them inside the model. Each style had strengths and weaknesses on multi-step questions. A hybrid method combining both performed best in their tests. The authors released their tools so other researchers can use the same benchmark.
arxiv-2508-15850:
Ziyu Wang and five co-authors show that shared heart signal data can betray who it came from. Their paper from twenty twenty-five studies electrocardiogram records posted for research. Heart traces act like fingerprints, which opens a linkage risk. Past privacy studies assumed foes with perfect knowledge. This team tests weaker, realistic foes with partial data.

Records from over a hundred people across real sets were used. Their method re-identified people in public sets with high accuracy at a tuned threshold. A share of strangers was also wrongly matched to known people. Plain anonymization failed to block the linkage. The authors call for stronger shields: differential privacy, access control, and encrypted computing. Such tools must guard identity while keeping the data useful for care research.
arxiv-2508-16050:
Zhaoyi Yan, Binghui Chen, Yunfan Liu, and Qixiang Ye shrink big neural networks into small ones by splitting what the small model must learn, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Knowledge distillation trains a light student model to mimic a heavy teacher. A wide gap in capacity between the two often blocks the transfer.

Their method breaks the leftover knowledge gap into many small residual steps, each easier to copy, carried out by a multi-branched student network. Borrowing the teacher's final layer weights narrows the gap further. On standard image benchmarks the approach lifted classification accuracy and detection scores beyond rival methods. Code and models are public.
arxiv-2508-17750:
Ryan Ramos, Yusuke Hirota, Yuta Nakashima, and Noa Garcia study whether the social biases inside a widely reused image-text model pass into the applications built on top of it. Their paper came out in 2025. The model, CLIP, serves as a backbone for tools from image captioning to question answering.

First, measured bias depended heavily on which slice of data was used to measure it, local or global. Second, across downstream tasks, the team found no consistent trend linking a model's pre-training bias to the bias of the finished application. Third, they show why: when different versions of the model are adapted to a task, their internal representations tend to converge. The findings complicate simple stories about bias transfer and point mitigation efforts toward the adaptation stage.
arxiv-2509-00050:
David Kurtenbach, Megan Manly, and Zach Metzinger apply deep learning in 2025 to spot odd Russian satellite moves before the Ukraine invasion. Resident space objects are tracked craft and debris whose paths are logged in public two-line element data, a compact format for orbits. Odd moves could serve as indications and warnings of hostile intent.

Five methods set a baseline of normal on-orbit conduct, from a classic isolation forest to autoencoders that rebuild input and flag what they cannot. A new anchor-loss autoencoder joins the set. Each model's flags are checked for shifts in pattern of life before the invasion. Sound baselines could help analysts tell routine drift from a true change in posture.
arxiv-2509-00150:
Luca Tortorelli, Silvan Fischbacher, Aaron S. G. Robotham, Céline Nussbaumer, and Alexandre Refregier present ProMage in 2025, a neural network that speeds up galaxy brightness estimates by a huge factor. Magnitudes state how bright a galaxy looks in each filter band. The base package, ProSpect, builds them from a galaxy's traits, such as redshift, star history, gas, and dust, but it runs slowly.

ProMage mimics that package at ten thousand times the speed. Accuracy stays within a tenth of a percent for almost all test sources across five survey bands. Fast magnitudes enable sharp inference of galaxy traits in next-generation surveys. They also let teams generate vast mock catalogs for forward-model studies of the sky.
arxiv-2509-00850:
Guangqi Zhao, with two co-authors, Fei Yan and Xiaotong Ni, presents a universal routing strategy to reduce connectivity needs of quantum low-density parity-check codes. These codes cut error correction overhead but demand dense, long-range connections that challenge hardware, especially superconducting processors.

Zhao and his co-authors observe that ancilla qubits, helper qubits, form short loops with data qubits in any quantum code. This lets stabilizer measurement circuits route data qubit information through ancillas when direct connections are unavailable. For bivariate bicycle codes, they remove up to fifty percent of long-range connections while roughly doubling circuit depth, with circuit-level distance largely preserved. The method also applies to surface codes, matching a known hexagonal connectivity requirement.
arxiv-2509-01050:
Caili Jia and Yong Lu work on graph theory, the math of networks made of points and links. They study two measures of how hard a graph is to break apart. The scattering number counts pieces left after points are removed, while tau-toughness weighs removals against the pieces they create.

Both measures link to how well a network stays connected after damage. Jia and Lu use a spectral value, a number drawn from a graph matrix, called rho alpha in plain terms. They give a condition that ensures the scattering number stays at one or less. They also give a condition for a graph to count as tau-tough, and both results extend earlier work by Chen, Li, and Xu.
arxiv-2509-01350:
Finding the right part inside a complex CAD assembly, a computer model of a machine, is key for automated engineering, yet vision-language models struggle with it. Yunqing Liu, Nan Zhang, and Zhiming Tan note two barriers: assembly metadata run longer than model token limits, and the strongest commercial models cannot be fine-tuned. Their framework needs no training at all.

The method works in two stages and adapts at inference time. An error notebook is built by correcting the model's first chains of thought through reflective revision, then filtering them with a grammar check for sound form. Retrieval then pulls matching examples from that notebook to guide each new query. Liu and the team also contribute a CAD data set, aiming to make specification-aware part search work with off-the-shelf models.
arxiv-2509-01450:
Workers who team with robots will sometimes get stuck, and future assistants may be artificial agents rather than people. Ane San Martin, with four co-authors, studies how users feel about asking for help in that setting. Their user study gave participants on-demand aid from a remote human during a joint assembly task with a robot.

The team measured experiences of requesting and receiving help, and asked how participants viewed future non-human assistants. They also tested whether help should arrive only when asked, or be offered unasked. Both quantitative and qualitative data feed the analysis. Findings cover emotional responses, productivity, and user preferences under each design choice. San Martin and the co-authors draw lessons for building assisting agents that people will actually accept on the factory floor.
arxiv-2509-01650:
The nonlinear Schrodinger equation models waves from optics to fluids, and its hyperbolic, periodic form in two dimensions raises sharp questions about when solutions exist and stay unique. Engin Basakoglu, Tadahiro Oh, and Yuzhao Wang study the cubic case on a periodic domain, working in Fourier-Lebesgue spaces, which weigh frequency content in a flexible way.

Using the Fourier restriction norm method, they establish sharp local well-posedness, short-time existence with control, across nearly the full scaling-critical range. A normal form approach then yields sharp unconditional uniqueness inside that regime, meaning solutions are unique without extra assumed bounds. Counting estimates for the hyperbolic equation drive both results. As a byproduct, they obtain the same uniqueness for the usual two-dimensional periodic cubic equation in a stated range, settling points left open by earlier work.
arxiv-2509-01750:
Xinlu Zhang, Na Yan, Yang Su, Yansha Deng, and Toktam Mahmoodi cut the data cost of training language models across many devices. In federated learning, devices train a shared model without sending raw data out. Sharing full model weights is heavy and fits poorly when devices hold unlike models. Sharing model outputs, called logits, is lighter but still bulky for large models.

The team picks only the top few output values, with the count shifting as network conditions change. A matching merge step avoids the fake inputs that plain padding would add. A projection from inner layers of the large model enriches the teaching signal. Tests beat base methods while cutting traffic by about half.
arxiv-2509-01850:
Tijmen de Haan analyzes noise suppression in sensitive heat detectors cooled near absolute zero. These transition-edge sensors read tiny heat deposits through a sharp change in resistance. Feedback in the circuit calms the sensor own electrical noise, called Johnson noise. Past theory covered simpler circuits than the alternating current setups now in use.

Haan recasts the circuit as an ideal source plus a complex series resistance outside the sensor island. From that form he derives the noise current with both sensor and stray resistance noise included. Feedback fully calms sensor noise at high gain, but stray resistance noise stays untouched. Detector builders must thus guard the wiring, not just the sensor itself.
arxiv-2509-01950:
Layton A Hall and Ayman F Abouraddy bend light pulses along curved paths while keeping their profiles symmetric and sharp. Some beams curve as they travel, but classic examples are lopsided in shape. Their beams build on space-time wave packets, pulses where each spatial frequency pairs with one wavelength. Such packets normally travel straight without spreading.

A tilt in the spectral layout tilts the travel path in step. Changing that tilt gradually along the path bends the route into a curve. The curves can follow linear, square, cubic, or square root growth laws. The bending rate does not depend on beam width. Symmetric bending beams could help signals dodge obstacles in free space links.
arxiv-2509-02050:
Ugur G Abdulla and Jose H Rodrigues sharpen early cancer detection through electrical impedance tomography framed as optimal control. The imaging method sends currents through boundary electrodes and reads voltages to map conductivity inside. Tumor tissue conducts far better than healthy tissue, giving a clear contrast target. Their inverse problem recovers the conductivity map from electrode measurements.

A clever permutation trick expands one measurement set into many virtual ones without adding unknowns. Swapping current and voltage roles multiplies the partial differential equation constraints instead. A gradient projection method using refined differentiability solves the control problem. Simulations in two and three dimensions show tumor resolution rising sharply with the expanded data. Early, sharp localization could guide faster clinical follow-up.
arxiv-2509-02350:
