Jindong Li and eight co-authors wrote a 2025 survey of implicit reasoning in large language models, where thinking happens silently inside the network rather than as written step-by-step text. Silent reasoning can cut cost, speed replies, and match how models compute internally.

Earlier surveys covered hidden representations, but none mapped the mechanisms in depth. The authors sort methods into three styles based on where internal work happens: latent optimisation, signal-guided control, and layer-recurrent execution, where layers get reused. They review evidence from structure, behaviour, and representations that silent reasoning really occurs. Benchmarks and scoring methods for checking such reasoning are also catalogued, giving researchers a shared map of a fast-moving area.
arxiv-2509-02450:
Lingzhi Shen and five co-authors wrote a 2025 natural language processing paper on detecting personality traits from a person's social media writing. Labelled personality data is scarce, and most methods treat emotion and personality as separate signals.

Their EmoPerso framework learns without heavy labelling. Generative steps create extra training text and richer representations. The model then extracts pseudo-labelled emotion features, guesses made without human labels, and trains them jointly with personality prediction. A cross-attention module links traits with the inferred emotions in fine detail. A self-taught loop refines the model's reasoning over rounds. On two benchmark datasets, the framework beat leading rivals, and the authors release the code openly.
arxiv-2509-02650:
Henrique Correia da Fonseca and seventeen co-authors wrote a 2025 game theory paper asking whether media coverage can push AI developers toward safer products without formal regulation. Developers chasing profit may skimp on safety unless misconduct carries a visible cost.

The authors model reputation loss through media as that cost, using evolutionary game theory on artificial populations of creators and users. Media coverage did foster cooperation in many runs. It failed when reporting quality was unreliable, or when reading media or building safely cost too much. Under the right conditions, media acts as a soft regulator, holding developers to account through public perception. The study maps where that informal pressure works and where it breaks down.
arxiv-2509-02750:
Albert Nazeeri and four co-authors present a 2025 experimental physics paper coupling a nuclear transition to a surface acoustic wave, a ripple travelling along a solid's surface. Wiggling a nucleus mechanically lets researchers steer its gamma-ray emission and absorption.

A film enriched in iron-57 sits on the acoustic device, driven near ninety-eight megahertz, almost a hundred times the nuclear linewidth. The drive prints a comb of sidebands onto the Mössbauer absorption spectrum, the fingerprint of periodic modulation. The authors describe the result as the highest frequency yet for a mechanically driven Mössbauer resonance. The solid, single-piece platform opens an interface linking nuclear transitions with high-frequency acoustics, with uses in gamma-ray quantum optics and precision nuclear spectroscopy.
arxiv-2509-02850:
Michael Aizenman wrote a 2025 mathematical physics paper, the third in a series, on the Ising model. That model places tiny magnets on a grid and studies how order spreads or breaks down as conditions change. It is a basic test case for understanding phase transitions, where matter shifts from one state to another.

Aizenman works with a picture that turns the model into random paths and currents on the grid. He stretches that picture to cover mildly frustrated systems, where some influences pull in opposing directions. He then applies the same ideas to a related lattice gauge model and its shift toward deconfinement. The paper also gives shorter proofs of useful inequalities about how distant points in such systems relate.
arxiv-2509-03050:
Xinyi Wang and Shuangning Li proved a 2025 statistics result about adjusting for covariates when experimental units interfere with each other. In a drug trial or classroom study, covariates are background traits used to sharpen effect estimates. Interference means one person's treatment can change another person's outcome, which breaks standard assumptions.

The authors work with neighborhood interference, where effects spread only through nearby contacts, and allow low-order interactions among them. Building on an existing estimator for the total effect, they define a family of adjusted versions. Under sparsity conditions on the contact network, these versions stay unbiased in the long run. Better, they carry a no-harm guarantee: their variance never exceeds the unadjusted estimator's. They also give a variance estimator that is safe yet tighter than earlier ones.
arxiv-2509-03150:
Dániel Garamvölgyi, Bill Jackson, and Tibor Jordán proved 2025 results in graph rigidity theory, the study of when a framework of bars and joints can flex. A graph is rigid or flexible depending on how its edges constrain its vertices in space. Counting edges against vertices, a sparsity condition from Maxwell in 1867, gives a basic test.

The authors study stress-independent graphs, a broad family that covers many natural cases, including minimally globally rigid ones. They show every such graph stays independent one dimension higher, a stepping-up property. A key device is the stress-linked pair, two vertices tied through internal forces. From it they derive conditions for pairs to be globally linked, strengthening earlier work. Their results settle two open conjectures in the field.
arxiv-2509-03250:
A. Warmuth and 41 co-authors presented a 2025 list of solar energetic electron events recorded by the Solar Orbiter spacecraft. Such electrons blast from the Sun and can be tied to flares and to coronal mass ejections, eruptions that remote telescopes watch in many wavelengths. Linking the two views shows how particles speed up and travel through space between planets.

The list covers every electron event the probe measured in place. It adds the linked flares, eruptions, and radio bursts seen from afar. Entries draw on instruments for particles, X-rays, imaging, radio waves, plasma, and magnetic fields. A modeling tool gives its own estimate of where on the Sun each event began. The first release holds several hundred events, from late 2020 through 2022. Early stats link impulsive events to flares and gradual ones to wide eruption-driven shocks.
arxiv-2509-03350:
Somiya Chhillar and 3 co-authors exposed a privacy attack on anonymized clinical data in 2025 that needs no outside information. The k-anonymity standard hides each person among at least k similar records, and it remains popular for its simplicity and regulatory fit. Defenders often claim that, without auxiliary data, its protections hold.

The new combinatorial refinement attacks refute that claim for datasets anonymized by local recoding, a common utility-preserving variant. The attacks exploit how a widely used open-source anonymizer optimizes usefulness, turning that behavior into a linear program that shrinks the plausible values of sensitive fields. Tests used real microdata from a network of free community clinics, a setting where outside information is genuinely scarce. Even there, promised privacy levels failed.
arxiv-2509-03450:
Vladimir Hinich and Ieke Moerdijk explained in a 2025 category theory note how to localize lax symmetric monoidal categories fiber by fiber. Localization formally adds inverses to chosen arrows in a category. A monoidal structure lets objects combine, much like tensors. The lax version lets that combining hold maps in one direction only. It is a setting used in modern homotopy theory.

A stronger result is proved in this version of the note. Start with a locally cocartesian fibration, a family of categories varying over a base. Mark arrows in the fibers that respect the fibration structure. The localization then remains a fibration of the same kind. Each fiber of the result is the localization of the matching original fiber. The construction describes localizations used in the authors' work comparing two models of infinity-operads.
arxiv-2509-03750:
In a 2025 research paper, Shohei Hayashida and ten co-authors examine the lattice dynamics of lanthanum nickel oxide, a member of the infinite-layer nickelates. Those materials form a young class of superconductors, but making them is technically hard, so they exist mainly as thin films or powders. Bulk lattice vibrations, called phonons, had therefore stayed poorly measured.

The team grew many bulk crystals, aligned them together, and probed them with time-of-flight inelastic neutron scattering, which reads phonon energies from scattered neutrons. Several dispersive phonon branches appear, spreading across the crystal as expected. They agree well with calculations based on density-functional perturbation theory. Selected modes are compared with those of cuprate superconductors, the older copper-based family the nickelates resemble. The findings give future studies a reference point for how lattice motion and electronic behaviour interact in these materials.
arxiv-2509-04050:
Huy Che and four co-authors present a 2025 computer science paper on finding the same person again across camera images. Systems first rank likely matches, then a re-ranking step cleans up that list. Older methods leaned on features from one view only, so pose changes, blocked views, and new angles caused errors. The team's fix builds richer features by blending each image with its nearest look-alikes.

Their method, called K-nearest weighted fusion, needs no extra training or hand labels. Tested on three public data sets, it lifted top-match accuracy sharply on the two hardest ones. It also ran faster than rival re-ranking methods, which suits large camera networks.
arxiv-2509-04250:
Shota Arai and three co-authors ask how many trial patients could be spared by borrowing knowledge from large language models in a 2025 research paper. Safety trials track harmful side effects across many hospitals, and strong background knowledge can shrink the needed sample. Their framework asks a pre-trained language model for prior distributions, the starting beliefs inside a Bayesian statistical model, rather than inventing fake patient data. Hyperparameters, the settings governing those beliefs, come straight from the model's answers.

Tests on real trial data included checks for sensitivity to sampling randomness and careful cross-validation. Language-model priors predicted better than classic methods that pool earlier studies. Safer, smaller trials could follow if regulators accept the approach, the authors argue.
arxiv-2509-04350:
Maria Sabitova, writing alone, asks whether a computer can decide when two dimension groups are the same in a 2025 mathematics paper. Dimension groups are ordered algebraic objects built here from columns made by repeated powers of a fixed integer matrix. The isomorphism set collects all structure-preserving matches between two such groups. Sabitova assumes the matrix's characteristic polynomial, a key defining equation, cannot be split into factors, with an added condition when the size is not prime.

Under those assumptions, that matching set is computable, meaning a step-by-step method finishes the job in finitely many steps. Worked examples show the process at work. Questions of this kind sit where algebra meets the theory of computation, and explicit methods matter for both sides.
arxiv-2509-05050:
Spin waves could carry information in devices far smaller than today's chips, if they travel far enough. Andrey A. Voronov, lead author with nine co-authors, study spin-wave propagation in gallium-substituted yttrium iron garnet nanowaveguides in a 2025 paper. The material's lower magnetisation favours exchange-dominated spin waves with better transport.

Combining light scattering spectroscopy, simulations, and analytical calculations, they examine waveguides down to very small widths and thicknesses. The waves reach high group velocities that stay constant across widths, giving longer propagation lengths than unsubstituted material. The authors present gallium substitution as a route to nanoscale spin-wave devices.
arxiv-2509-05250:
A magnet model that is hard to solve in one form becomes easier in a mirror form, in a 2025 physics paper by Dario Benedetti and three co-authors. They study the one-dimensional Ising model, a line of spins with long-range links that fade with distance at a rate set by one parameter.

In the middle range of that parameter the model forms a family of conformal field theories, models with scale symmetry. The usual description is weak at one end of the range and strong at the other. Their dual description flips that pattern and becomes exactly solvable at the crossover point. Two separate methods then compute the theory's data near that point and agree fully.
arxiv-2509-05350:
Testing whether synthetic data leak who was in the original records is done better by teams of attacks than by any single one. Joshua Ward and three co-authors show this in a 2025 privacy paper. Membership inference attacks try to guess whether a person's record trained a data generator.

In practice an attacker must pick one attack with no promise it will work best. The authors run what they call the largest benchmark of its kind and find no single attack wins across model types and data domains. They then build unsupervised ensembles, combinations that need no labelled answers to tune them. These ensembles proved more robust and lost less, on average, than any lone attack.
arxiv-2509-05650: A moving surface that drifts at constant speed, called a translator, cannot end like an upright wall unless it is one, Yunfan Zhao proves in a solo 2025 geometry paper. Zhao studies complete translators set in Euclidean space of dimension at least four, with finite topology. Their ends are assumed to approach upright hyperplanes in a smooth-once way. The only such translator, the theorem states, is the vertical hyperplane itself.
arxiv-2509-05750:
Design choices inside graph-based vector search are compared at billion scale by Ilias Azizi and three co-authors in a 2025 database paper. Vector search over learned embeddings now underpins many business and scientific tools, and graph methods lead where exact answers are not required.

Five design paradigms, from seed selection to divide-and-conquer, have produced many competing algorithms with no systematic comparison. The authors evaluate twelve leading methods on seven real collections, up to a billion vectors. Incremental insertion plus neighbourhood diversification usually won, while the choice of base graph could hurt scaling. Open directions include smarter data-adaptive seed choice and diversification. The study is a map for builders of in-memory search.
arxiv-2509-06250:
Proving a big system safe piece by piece is the method Ian Dardik and Eunsuk Kang develop in a 2025 paper. Inductive invariants, formulas that overapproximate reachable states and imply safety, are notoriously hard to infer for whole systems because they must close over every transition. The authors instead decompose the system and give each component an assume-guarantee contract.

Each component is verified by a local invariant that only needs to close over that component's transitions, a simpler job. The conjunction of local invariants is then an invariant for the whole system by construction. Two case studies show faster inference than the global technique, plus modular insight into the specification that global invariants hide.
arxiv-2509-06650:
Search inside specialized collections gets a domain-aware upgrade from Hao Lin and five co-authors in a 2025 information retrieval paper. Retrieval-augmented generation depends on a coarse ranking stage that picks candidate documents. Methods for improving that stage often fail to balance subject knowledge against better queries.

Their system, MoLER, trains in two stages. Continual pretraining uses a mixture of losses to add domain knowledge without erasing general language skill. Reinforcement learning then tunes how queries and passages are generated, aiming to recall the right documents. A late-fusion trick runs many queries against one passage during training to cut cost, while inference fuses across many passages for scale. Experiments on benchmark sets show top results, well ahead of baselines, which the authors offer as a way to close the knowledge gap in specialized search.
arxiv-2509-06850:
Counting two-colored planar maps with control over both colors' face sizes is achieved by Marie Albenque and one co-author in a 2025 combinatorics paper. Hypermaps generalize planar maps and can be read as maps whose faces are colored in two colors properly. Physics models, including the two-matrix model and the Ising model on random maps, had produced counting formulas still lacking direct bijective proofs.

The slice decomposition cuts maps along shortest paths. For hypermaps those paths are directed, following the orientation the coloring imposes, so a new kind of slice is defined with its own recursive decomposition. Built from slices, the authors decompose disks, cylinders, and disks with a mixed boundary condition, each expressed through constrained walks. The result supplies bijective proofs of known generating function formulas and explains their algebraic character.
arxiv-2509-06950:
Imagining a scene from new viewpoints, with help from synthetic training data, is scaled up by Nithin Gopalakrishnan Nair and five co-authors in a 2025 computer vision paper. Transformer models can synthesize novel views from a few input images without per-scene tuning. Public scene datasets lack diversity, though, so real-world scenes often fall outside what the models know.

Training data generated by diffusion models adds variety and scale, but its artifacts become the new bottleneck for reconstruction quality. The authors add a token disentanglement process inside the transformer, separating features more cleanly so learning uses the synthetic data better. The refined model beat existing systems on both in-dataset and cross-dataset tests, reaching state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks while cutting computing costs significantly. Synthetic data plus cleaner internal features is the recipe offered.
arxiv-2509-07050:
Juan Manuel Contreras, writing alone in a 2025 paper, automatically tests gender bias across thirteen large multimodal models. They can also carry forward the unfair social patterns hidden in the data they learned from. Earlier studies did find gender bias in such models.

Contreras answers with a benchmark that scores fairness in images made by AI. He tested thirteen models that anyone can buy access to. The prompts named no gender, and they asked for people in three kinds of jobs: ones stereotyped as male, ones stereotyped as female, and ones with no strong stereotype. A judge system, checked for validity, then scored each picture for how gender was represented. The results were stark. The models did more than copy the gender patterns of real working life. They made those patterns stronger, putting men in the large majority of pictures for the male-stereotyped jobs.
arxiv-2509-07150:
Andy Xu and 4 co-authors present PLaID++ in 2025, a language model tuned to design new inorganic materials. Inorganic materials include metals, salts, and crystals that lack carbon-based chemistry. The goal is not one right answer but many fresh crystal structures that meet set limits and stay stable. The work borrows training methods first built for text models.

A compact text form based on Wyckoff positions, which describe where atoms sit in a crystal pattern, helps the model learn faster and generalize better. A temperature setting during training keeps outputs varied instead of collapsing to a few repeats. The model makes stable, unique, and new structures at a rate about half again higher than earlier methods. It can also aim at chosen symmetry traits, which speeds the hunt for useful new materials.
arxiv-2509-07250:
Lucas G. Câmara and 2 co-authors propose a fix in 2025 for a nagging flaw in thermal field theory calculations. Perturbation theory, which builds answers as a series of small corrections, often depends too much on an arbitrary renormalization scale. That dependence clouds studies of phase transitions, the sharp changes matter undergoes when heated, in the early universe and in materials.

Their method, called variational renormalization group, joins a scale-improvement recipe with an optimized resummation technique. They test it on the quartic scalar field theory, a standard benchmark model with a four-way self-interaction. Key outputs such as the effective potential, the critical temperature, and the pressure become much more stable when the scale changes. The authors present the method as a sturdier tool for precision studies of hot phase transitions.
arxiv-2509-07650:
Judging whether someone acted selfishly or kindly requires knowing what they value, which observers rarely see. Victor Villin and Christos Dimitrakakis tackle that inference problem in a 2025 research paper. They use multi-agent inverse reinforcement learning, which works backward from behavior to the rewards behind it. Their simple model lets each agent weigh its own welfare against the welfare of others.

With new Bayesian techniques, the authors show intrinsic rewards and altruistic tendencies can be told apart. The trick is watching agents placed in different groups. Once separated, the two ingredients can be recombined to synthesize behavior at any desired level of altruism. That ability matters for autonomous agents that must cooperate with people. It could help designers build assistants whose social behavior is understood, not just imitated.
arxiv-2509-07750:
John Byrne and 1 co-author construct large nonabelian Sidon sets and link them to extremal graph problems in a 2025 paper. A Sidon set in a group has a near-uniqueness property. If two products of its elements agree, the factors must match. The nonabelian setting means the group operation need not commute. Permutation groups are the setting used here.

Explicit constructions give large sets of the two defined types in symmetric groups and their products. Probabilistic constructions handle other nice groups. Upper bounds improve the trivial bound by a constant factor for certain groups. The authors then draw links to Turán-type problems in graph theory. They pin down, up to constants, the minimum outdegree that forces certain even cycles in digraphs. They improve a bound on Hamilton paths. They also show that a directed form of the Erdős-Simonovits compactness conjecture is false.
arxiv-2509-08050:
Lucia Angel and 4 co-authors forecast how sharply a future gamma-ray observatory can hunt dark matter in a 2025 astroparticle physics paper. If dark matter particles annihilate, they could produce gamma rays at one exact energy, a line that astrophysics rarely mimics. Searches so far have found none, but the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory promises better sensitivity and energy resolution.

The team models expectations toward the Galactic Centre and toward dwarf galaxies, using effective field theory operators for scalar and fermion dark matter. Upper limits on annihilation into gamma-ray lines are derived for the lowest-order operators. Even a continued non-detection would squeeze the allowed properties of dark matter candidates, guiding both theory and future telescope time.
arxiv-2509-08350:
How many dimensions does a network secretly live in? Aina Ferrà Marcús and 4 co-authors estimate that hidden dimensionality with topological tools in a 2025 network science paper. Many social and biological networks show patterns matching an underlying hyperbolic geometry, and the latent space's dimension shapes navigation, community structure, and behaviour.

Their weighting scheme for graphs builds on chordless cycles, loops with no shortcuts across them, inside a topological data analysis filtration. The resulting descriptors feed a neural network trained on synthetic examples to estimate dimensionality in a data-driven way. A reliable dimension estimate would tell modellers which geometric machinery fits a given network before they commit to an embedding.
arxiv-2509-09250:
Yuzhou Tian and 1 co-author prove that key systems for eigenvalue sum bounds are not integrable in a 2025 paper. Sturm-Liouville operators are a classic class of differential operators. Best bounds on sums of their first eigenvalues come from solving linked critical systems.

Those systems are Hamiltonian, with one parameter per degree of freedom. Differential Galois theory, which reads the symmetry of differential equations, is the tool. All but two known cases are shown not to be meromorphically integrable, meaning no full set of conserved laws in that form exists. The negative result shows deep complexity hides in the eigenvalue task.
arxiv-2509-09350:
Topological data analysis turns shapes into algebra, and its most useful outputs are the generators that locate the holes. Yann-Situ Gazull, Aldo Gonzalez-Lorenzo, and Alexandra Bac characterize which homology bases standard algorithms actually produce, in a 2025 technical report. Many methods compute homology, but which representatives they return has been loosely understood.

The proof runs through a combinatorial structure called the homological discrete vector field. That structure underlies several standard methods, from persistent homology to discrete Morse theory. By characterizing the computed class of bases, the authors refine combinatorial homology theory. Their results promise more control over generator computation. Control matters when the generator is the deliverable. A scientist locating a tunnel in a protein needs the specific cycle, not just a count of holes.
arxiv-2509-09450:
Magnetic fields thread the disks where planets form, steering how gas flows onto the young star, but measuring them has been nearly impossible. Richard Teague and 7 co-authors present a new detection approach in a 2025 research paper. They use the differential broadening of unpolarized molecular emission from cyanide radicals. The well-studied disk of TW Hydrae is their demonstration case, observed with the ALMA array.

Their model folds in the disk's velocity structure, the molecule's excitation, and the Zeeman effect, magnetism's fingerprint on spectral lines. The recovered field varies with radius and reaches a modest strength across the planet-forming zone. Its shape changes character with distance, lying mostly vertical inside and flattening beyond a known gap. Gas density limits from the same data constrain how strongly the field can push on the gas. A practical field meter for planet-forming disks opens a missing chapter of disk physics.
arxiv-2509-09550:
Compressing audio into tokens a language model can speak requires a codec that survives bad connections, not just clean benchmarks. Harry Julian and 4 co-authors introduce NeuCodec in a 2025 research paper. Most neural audio codecs quantize with a residual method that stacks codebooks. NeuCodec uses finite scalar quantization, which trains more simply and needs one codebook.

Two experiments reveal a hidden virtue. Different encoders can write the same audio into wildly different token sequences of equal quality, showing the code carries redundancy. When noise corrupts the transmitted tokens, the scalar method degrades far more gracefully than the residual rival. That baked-in redundancy is exactly what streaming through noisy channels demands. As language models take over audio generation, codecs that forgive transmission errors become infrastructure, not a nicety.
arxiv-2509-09650:
Siddarth Mamidanna and 3 co-authors look inside language models doing mental arithmetic in a 2025 interpretability paper. The models answer direct calculations as next-token guesses, with no written working. Theory says attention could let every position compute from all earlier ones, but the authors test how much of that power is actually used by blocking computations and rerouting information flow.

Two new probing tools locate a small working subgraph they name All-for-One. Real computation happens late and only at the final token, which collects what it needs from other positions in a few middle layers. Across many models and expression types that subgraph proves both enough for the answers and necessary for them.
arxiv-2509-09850:
František Bartoš and Eric-Jan Wagenmakers wrote this 2025 paper, the second part of a series on meta-analysis with the free JASP software. Meta-analysis pools results across studies, and the Bayesian version offers extras: it measures uncertainty, weighs rival claims, and updates cleanly as new studies arrive. Until now, many of those methods called for programming skill.

The authors describe Bayesian tools they built into JASP's Meta-Analysis module, including meta-regression, multilevel models, and models that adjust for publication bias. Results can be read through forest plots, bubble plots, and estimated group means. Their aim is practical: researchers with no coding background should still be able to run advanced Bayesian meta-analysis and read the output with confidence.
arxiv-2509-09950:
Pouneh Nikkhah Bahrami and 2 co-authors catch browser fingerprinting at the level of single functions in a 2025 privacy paper. Fingerprinting scripts quietly identify a visitor across sites, and blocking whole scripts either misses disguised code or breaks pages people need. Their system, ByteDefender, reads the V8 engine's bytecode instead of surface code, so renaming tricks and address games cannot hide what a function truly does.

A transformer classifier trained offline on bytecode sequences spots fingerprinting behaviour function by function. Lightweight signatures drawn from that model let a browser match suspicious functions during compilation, before they run, adding only a few percent to page load time. Tested across the hundred thousand most visited sites, the design promises surgical blocking that leaves honest scripts alone.
arxiv-2509-10050:
Aryan Esmailpour and 2 co-authors map the unavoidable trade between memory and speed for spatial questions over joined data in a 2025 database theory paper. A conjunctive query first combines tables, and users then ask spatial things about the outcome: is anything in this box, how many points fall there, what sits nearest. Such questions power analytics from attribute filtering to counting shapes inside temporal graphs.

Known indexes either answer slowly or balloon to the size of the full result list, neither acceptable at scale. The authors prove lower bounds that fence the whole trade-off for star-shaped and path-shaped queries, showing exactly how answer time and storage must relate. Any future index for spatial conjunctive search now has a proven frontier it cannot cross, and a target to aim at.
arxiv-2509-10450:
Alexander Taveira Blomenhofer and Benjamin Lovitz give a fast algorithm for Chow decompositions in this 2025 algebraic geometry paper. A Chow decomposition writes a symmetric tensor, a multiway array of numbers, as a combination of simplest-possible pieces. Their algorithm runs in linear time for the cases they target, handling concise symmetric three-variable-style tensors whose Chow rank is a third of the number of variables.

The method is pencil-based, leaning on generalized eigenvalue computations rather than slow searches. The authors also push further: sub-quadratic algorithms for higher-order Chow decompositions, and for decompositions of three-tensors into products of linear forms that avoid the generic orbit. One concrete gain is a sub-quadratic way to split a symmetric three-tensor into a combination of W-tensors, a benchmark case in tensor theory.
arxiv-2509-11150:
Yuriy A. Drozd is the sole author of this 2025 algebra paper. He introduces a new class of rings. They are called pseudo-krullian orders. He studies the module categories built over them. The aim is to extend older results by I. Beck. Those results covered Krull rings.

Drozd forms quotient categories from these modules. Modules that differ only by a pseudo-isomorphism are identified. He describes the injective objects inside those quotients. He also works out their global homological dimension. That number measures how complex their resolutions can get. One outcome concerns maximal Cohen-Macaulay modules. Drozd pins down the dimension for their category over certain orders. The base ring there is noetherian and two-dimensional.
arxiv-2509-11450:
Chinonso Onah and Kristel Michielsen propose a standard health check for quantum processors. This 2025 quantum computing paper looks ahead to quantum chips inside big computing centers. Users there need a steady, repeatable way to judge a device. Run-to-run sameness is the gate for real work.

Their probe asks the device to repeat known best answers. The tasks are single-layer QAOA circuits, a known optimization routine. Harmonic analysis supplies the yardstick. The team derives exact upper bounds for the count of stationary points in that landscape. A cheap grid test can then check a device in full. Run-to-failure statistics and confidence ranges fold into one score. The score grades hardware maturity for hybrid workflows.
arxiv-2509-11550:
Shane Stevenson and Maryam Sabagh survey compressed sensing in a 2025 paper covering its mathematical foundations, implementation, and advanced optimization techniques. Compressed sensing reconstructs a signal from far fewer measurements than traditional methods require.

The key idea is sparsity: many real-world signals can be represented with only a few nonzero components in a suitable basis. The paper works through the mathematical formulation behind that idea, explaining its logic and its pathologies, meaning the cases where reconstruction can fail. It then applies compressed sensing to real-world signals. As an expository treatment, the paper serves readers who want the full path from theory to practice in one place, rather than a single new algorithm.
arxiv-2509-12050:
Twenty years of X-ray observations of an ultraluminous source in galaxy M74 anchor a 2025 study by Aman Upadhyay and two co-authors. Chandra and XMM-Newton data from 2001 to 2021 let the team compare the source's flaring and quiet states in detail.

Flaring visits show two-component spectra at lower average brightness, while quiet visits show a single component at higher flux, a counterintuitive split. Several models fit, and a two-temperature disk picture gives a cool and a hot emitting region, hinting at an outflowing wind beside the disk. A spectral line near one kiloelectronvolt in the flaring state matches wind features seen in similar systems. Brightness grows harder as it rises, suggesting beaming, and the hot component points to a stellar-mass black hole feeding above the Eddington limit.
arxiv-2509-12350:
Recommending the next place a person will visit is a natural job for a large language model, once places are turned into tokens the model can read. Ke Sun and one co-author argue in 2025 that the usual tokenizers throw away the mixed signals in mobility data, and that training ignores behavior beyond place visits.

Their system, KGTB, first arranges the data as a knowledge graph so the varied signals survive. A graph-guided tokenizer then assigns each node a structural code. Training adds tasks for category and region visits alongside place visits. Tests on four city datasets beat prior generative recommenders.
arxiv-2509-12750:
Rishab Parthasarathy, Jasmine Collins and Cory Stephenson ask in this 2025 study what makes people judge one computer-made image as better than another. They compare human choices with the choices made by large vision and language models that are now used to grade images on their own.

The team built pairs of made-up images and tracked six traits, from looks and clean detail to correct body shapes and match with the prompt. People linked those traits in clear patterns, while the models linked them far less. Controlled tests also showed that body shape was hard for the models to judge. The work helps explain where model grades still miss human taste.
arxiv-2509-12850:
Laxmi Iyer and Ali Minai model in 2025 how the brain might learn word chains that mean something faster than random word chains. People grasp a new sentence in a known scene with ease, and the team asks what stored links make that ease possible.

They load a large word-link data set into a spiking network built on a known memory model. With those links in place, short poems are learned much faster than random word strings. The loaded network also stands up better to noise. The result backs the idea that prior word sense, not just repeat practice, speeds new learning.
arxiv-2509-12950:
Pietro Armenante, Kai Huang and two co-authors ask in 2025 whether trip tables should hide persons or whole groups. Trip tables count moves between zones. Small zones show travel well but risk privacy.

Rich survey data lets the team split tables by age, work, and more. Each person stands for a weighted slice of the true crowd. That fact shifts the goal: guard the crowd, not just those asked. They test zone-merging ways and add a fast greedy method. The goal is tables that stay useful yet meet the guard rule for the full crowd.
arxiv-2509-13150:
Shima Mohammadi, Mohsen Jenadeleh and three co-authors grade in 2025 how well quality scores track near-perfect image compression. Pro uses need even faint artifacts caught, from archives to web delivery. Scores tuned for coarse damage may miss faint harm near the just-notice line.

New grade methods use the JPEG AIC-3 set built for high fidelity. A new score folds in human score doubt. Fresh stats tests split metrics with care. Full, high, and mid ranges are all checked, plus crop effects in human tests. Data, ranks, and tools are shared openly for later work.
arxiv-2509-13250:
Andi Kuswoyo, Christos Margadji, and Sebastian W. Pattinson present an intelligent vacuum thermoforming process in a 2025 paper. In thermoforming, a heated plastic sheet is shaped over a mould with the help of a vacuum. Keeping every part up to standard is hard. The material changes from batch to batch, and so do the tooling setups.

First they built a full data set of formed samples, made under many different settings, and recorded each sample visually. A k-nearest neighbour method then took over the tuning. For a part that came out poorly, it looked for similar parts that came out well, and read off the settings those good parts had used. The model did well at adjusting the heating power, the heating time, and the vacuum time. The goal throughout was fewer defects and smoother production, without needing much data to get there.
arxiv-2509-13350:
Es-said En-naoui extends in 2025 Mittag-Leffler stability for fuzzy fractional systems in the Caputo sense. Lyapunov-type analysis for fuzzy nonlinear fractional equations gains stronger, broader results. Variable order and delay cases are both in scope.

Five strands anchor the work: uniform stability, input-to-state stability with bounds, a converse Lyapunov theorem, a LaSalle invariance rule, and practical tests. Delay tools use Krasovskii functionals. Linear tests use matrix inequalities level by level. Assumptions and lemmas are stated with proof sketches, with full proofs and cases following in later sections.
arxiv-2509-13450:
Vincent Siu, Nicholas Crispino and six co-authors benchmark representation steering in 2025 across nine safety views with SteeringSafety. Steering edits internal directions to shift conduct. Prior work stressed general skill; safety trade-offs were under-mapped.

Eighteen datasets and five top methods share modular blocks, with conditional steering included. Three models are tested. Strong results hinge on method, model, and view pairing. Entanglement is rife: gains on one view shift others. Social conduct degrades most. Refusal steering harms moral judgment. Hallucination steering swings political views by model. Single-target grades mislead.
arxiv-2509-13650:
Amena Amro and Manar H. Alalfi test GitHub Copilot's code review feature in a 2025 software security study. The tool promises to comment on code before it is committed, and the authors ask whether it can actually spot security flaws, a skill developers increasingly assume such assistants have.

They ran the reviewer over a curated set of labeled vulnerable code samples drawn from open-source projects across languages and domains. The reviewer often missed critical flaws such as SQL injection, cross-site scripting, and insecure deserialization. Its comments mostly flagged low-severity matters like style and typos instead. The authors conclude that dedicated security tools and manual audits remain necessary, whatever the marketing suggests.
arxiv-2509-13750:
H. M. Maridi, writing alone in a 2025 paper, presents a proof-of-concept study of nuclear radii and binding energies within a framework called NUCLEI-PACK. Treat each proton and neutron as a sphere. Pack the spheres inside the nucleus as well as they can be packed, clusters included.

A packing algorithm places the protons and neutrons under set constraints, giving every nucleon the same radius. A global search then improves the arrangement, and the search is run across the whole nuclear chart, from the lightest nuclei to heavy ones. With the geometry fixed, the charge radius, the matter radius, and the binding energy all follow by calculation. The model gets the broad patterns right: how big nuclei are, and how stable they tend to be, across the chart. Fitting terms of the semi-empirical mass formula to the model's output gave values in remarkable agreement with what theory expects.
arxiv-2509-13850:
Joseph J. Webber and Thomas D. Montenegro-Johnson show that two linked gel spheres can swim in a 2025 soft matter paper. The spheres are self-oscillating gels that swell and shrink as an oscillating chemical reaction washes over them, expelling and drawing in water. Joined by a rigid rod, with no hinges or moving parts, the pair forms a minimal swimmer.

Working in the inertialess Stokes regime, the authors build a continuum model where a Brusselator reaction generates the oscillating solute field, then derive the swimming speed analytically. Placed in a bath with traveling reaction-diffusion waves, the swimmer shows two behaviors: bobbing in place and surfing along with the wave. It moves slowly, but its simplicity suits mass production.
arxiv-2509-14050:
Wael Albayaydh and three co-authors study AI as a privacy protector in smart homes in a 2025 paper. Owners worry about unauthorized access and opaque data collection, fears the authors trace partly to misunderstanding how devices gather and guard information. The question is whether AI-powered tools can protect privacy in ways users actually understand and control.

Through twenty-three in-depth interviews with users, developers, designers, and regulators, analyzed with grounded theory, two themes emerged. People aspire to AI that empowers them, rebalances power, and stays easy to use. At the same time, security, compliance, and ethical challenges loom over any such tool. The authors turn both themes into concrete recommendations for designers and developers building privacy-conscious smart home AI.
arxiv-2509-14450:
Davide Gabrielli and Giovanni Jona-Lasinio introduce a notion of equivalent transformations for diffusive systems in 2025, systems where particles spread by random motion. The work sits inside macroscopic fluctuation theory and takes inspiration from Clausius in thermodynamics.

Beyond a new proof of a known formula that grounds equivalence, the authors show equivalent slow transformations can still be told apart. A renormalised work quantity captures the finite difference between them. That distinction lets them ask which slow transformation in an equivalence class is optimal. Nonequilibrium theory needs such comparisons: many driving paths reach the same endpoint, but they do not cost the same. A principled optimal choice sharpens both theory and protocol design.
arxiv-2509-14650:
Jun-Wei Yeow and four co-authors build a lightweight system in 2025 to restore situational awareness for wearers of noise cancelling headphones. Active noise control improves comfort but masks alarms, traffic and voices. Isolation can become a safety risk outdoors.

Their framework first classifies the acoustic scene with a small model. The scene prediction then retunes a sound event localisation and detection network toward sounds that matter in that context. A siren matters on a street, less in an office. Tests on simulated headphone data assess the coupled design. Context aware tuning aims to surface the right warnings without flooding the listener with every faint sound the microphones capture.
arxiv-2509-14950:
Sergei Bogdanov leads a team of fourteen authors demonstrating ghost imaging with electron-photon pairs in a 2025 physics paper. Ghost imaging forms a picture from correlations between two particles: one interacts with the object but is not spatially resolved, while the other carries the spatial information without ever touching the object. Most demonstrations so far used only photons.

Here the pairs mix a massive, charged electron with a massless, neutral photon, produced through cathodoluminescence inside a transmission electron microscope. A custom free-space setup collects the photons outside the microscope. The team reconstructed images of complex patterns with resolution down to a few micrometers. Pairing the two flagship microscopy particles opens a path toward quantum-enhanced electron imaging methods.
arxiv-2509-15050:
Peng Chen and six co-authors dig into why aluminium scandium nitride films are ferroelectric in a 2025 materials physics paper. These nitrides can hold a switchable electric polarization, which makes them attractive for memory devices. The team combines first-principles calculations with a Landau-type model whose energy expression respects the crystal symmetry and whose parameters come from the calculations.

Two energy minima appear for scandium fractions up to forty percent: the familiar four-fold coordinated wurtzite polar structure, and a five-fold coordinated hexagonal phase with no polarization. The nonpolar phase sinks lower in energy as scandium content rises. The model pinpoints the coupling between polarization and strain as the ingredient that creates the wurtzite minimum, beyond the separate polar and elastic energies. Such insight guides growers tuning the alloy for devices.
arxiv-2509-15350:
Yitong Wang and co-authors ask a sharper question about machine text. A language model may write a whole page, fix grammar, or translate a draft. Each use carries a different risk, yet most detectors only sort text into human or machine. The team builds a detector that can tell these uses apart.

Their system, called HERO, sorts text into four groups: human written, machine made, machine polished, and machine translated. It joins models trained for different text lengths, with extra guidance for groups that are easy to mix up. Tests across five language models and six fields show it beats older methods. The work helps readers judge not just whether a machine helped, but how.
arxiv-2509-15850:
J. Matthew Douglass, Götz Pfeiffer, and Gerhard Roehrle revisit the structure of normalizers in finite Coxeter groups. A Coxeter group is built from reflections, like the symmetry group of a regular solid. A parabolic subgroup is generated by a subset of those reflections. Its normalizer holds all elements that map the subgroup to itself.

Howlett described that normalizer long ago. Building on his lemma and a recent trick of Serre, the trio recast it as a subdirect product, using a classic lemma of Goursat. A Galois link on the lattice of parabolic subgroups drives a new split into named parts. Each part mirrors a feature of the whole reflection setup. They classify the outcome case by case for all irreducible groups.
arxiv-2509-16150: Jeffrey Shallit and Ingrid Vukusic prove new facts about a way of writing whole numbers based on the golden ratio. Among their results is a proof of a guess made by Kimberling in 2012 about this number system. They used a theorem-proving program called Walnut as a software helper for parts of the work. One proof also drew on help from an AI chat tool, which the authors note in the text.
arxiv-2509-16350:
Layered materials that lack a center of symmetry can turn spin flow into charge flow, a trick behind tiny light emitters that pulse at terahertz rates. Armando Pezo and eight co-authors simulate one such stack, where a ferroelectric layer's polarity can be flipped. They count both spin and orbital contributions to the response, going beyond the usual spin-only view.

Spin and orbital parts behave in distinct ways as the polarity flips, which gives a handle on the emitted signal. The findings clarify how angular momentum turns into charge in these stacks. They may also explain varied lab results and guide spin-based torque devices.
arxiv-2509-16450:
Data markets ask each holder to weigh the value of data gained against the cost of data given up. A deal lasts only if no group can do better by breaking away. Jiaxin Song and three co-authors import the core idea from cooperative game theory to judge such deals. A core-stable exchange is one no subset of agents wants to leave.

Such a deal is sure to exist when gains bend one way and costs the other. Dropping either shape can kill it. Finding one is provably hard in a strong sense, a first for core-like results in data economics. A classic pivoting method still works well in practice.
arxiv-2509-16950:
Xuan Chen and co-authors craft stealthy backdoor attacks on self-driving learners in a 2025 paper. A backdoor makes a model act wrongly only when a trigger appears. Past triggers were pixel patterns, which are hard to plant on real roads. Their attacks use temporal logic patterns across several vehicles instead, tied to driving trajectories.

Tests cover five offline learning driving agents and six trigger patterns. Varied target actions show the attack bends flexibly. Stealth rises because the trigger looks like normal traffic flow. The work exposes gaps in end-to-end driving systems. Builders need defenses against multi-vehicle triggers before such learners reach public roads.
arxiv-2509-17250:
Yigit Berkay Uslu, Samar Hadou, Sergio Rozada, Shirin Saeedi Bidokhti, and Alejandro Ribeiro present a 2025 arXiv paper on making up graph signals with diffusion models. A graph signal assigns values to the nodes of a network, and stock prices on linked assets form one such signal. Fixed forecasts miss the spread and the rare swings that matter most in finance.

The team's network copies the U shape of a well-known image model, with an encoder, a decoder, and skip links between them. A pooling step pads with zeros rather than merging nodes in an ad hoc way, so deep layers still respect the source graph. Graph convolutions on top capture local links. Trained as a denoising diffusion model, the system learned to sample fresh signals. On stock price forecasting, it gave full probability forecasts rather than single guesses.
arxiv-2509-17350:
Haoran Zhou, Yangwei You, and Shuaijun Wang teach two robot arms to toss and catch objects in mid-air. Their 2025 arXiv paper takes on dynamic handover, a task that needs sharp perception, tight coordination, and natural motion. Older methods lean on dynamics models, strong priors, or depth sensors, which limits how well they generalize.

Their framework, DyDexHandover, trains the arms with multi-agent reinforcement learning and a policy that sees only normal color images. A human-policy regularizer guides the throwing arm toward fluid, lifelike motion. Training ran in a dual-arm simulator built in Isaac Sim. The system hit near-perfect success on training objects and strong success on unseen ones, while moving in a human-like way. The authors say it is the first dual-arm in-air handover driven by raw color images alone.
arxiv-2509-17650:
Soroush Mahdi, Fardin Ayar, Ehsan Javanmardi, Manabu Tsukada, and Mahdi Javanmardi bound the memory of streaming 3D vision models. Their 2025 arXiv paper starts from StreamVGGT, a transformer that reads video and builds three-dimensional understanding as frames arrive. Its key-value memory grows without limit, which caps how long a stream it can handle.

Their policy, Evict3R, discards redundant tokens at inference time and keeps the most informative ones, with no retraining. On long sequences in the 7-Scenes data set, peak memory fell by about half while accuracy barely moved. Under tight budgets, eviction frees room to sample frames more densely, which can even raise reconstruction quality. Tests span video depth, 3D reconstruction, and camera pose tasks. The authors offer the policy as a practical route to long-horizon streaming perception.
arxiv-2509-17750:
Inkyu Jang and five co-authors grade the safety of learning-based robots with spectral tools. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that robot dynamics are stochastic, from sensor noise and a messy world. Classic reachability and barrier methods struggle to give a safety critic that matches the true probability of staying safe.

Their framework, EigenSafe, derives a linear operator that governs how safety probability evolves under a policy. Its dominant eigenpair turns out to carry the key safety facts, for single state-action pairs and for the closed-loop system as a whole. The framework learns that eigenpair and uses it to inform or constrain policy updates. It supports safe reinforcement learning directly. It also audited policies learned by imitation, in robot manipulation trials with a UR3 arm on a food preparation task. The spectral view gives safety work a single number with a clear meaning.
arxiv-2509-17950:
Bradley Hauer and 4 co-authors test if a famed coded note by composer Edward Elgar hides music, not words. The Dorabella cipher has resisted all reading tries for more than a hundred years. Most past guesses read it as an English text.

The team weighs proof for and against the music view, then builds a simple music script. Models of music style, checked on known coded scores, guide a rebuild of a tune from the cipher. The tune is then shaped by hand into a piece folk can hear. The authors stress their tune is one take, not a sole true answer.
arxiv-2509-18150:
Kean Shi and 3 co-authors make multimodal model training cheaper by cutting waste where it sits. Their 2025 frame deals with models that read text, image, and more at once. Long mixed inputs and under-used layers waste compute, and that waste shifts as training goes on.

Their Sparse Training Scheme adapts its cuts by stage. A visual token press shrinks image load while modes are aligned. A layer skipper drops unneeded layers while the model learns to follow prompts. The frame fits many model shapes. Bench tests show gains in both score and training speed.
arxiv-2509-18450:
Sharp spectra of starlight let astronomers measure star motions and chemistry. Devika K Divakar, Phillip MacQueen, and Joseph Strubhar present a redesign of the fiber feed for a major spectrograph in this 2025 paper. The instrument is the High Resolution Spectrograph on the Hobby-Eberly Telescope. The upgrade targets better light flow and image quality from near-ultraviolet to near-infrared.

A fixed corrector made of two matched prisms undoes the air's spreading of colors at the telescope's set tilt. The glass types were picked for very high clarity. New relay optics boost sensitivity at the blue end while keeping spots well under the fiber core size. Simulations show leftover color spread stays tiny across the band and tilt range. Light efficiency lands between 91 and 94 percent. All parts sit in one rigid head unit for stable alignment.
arxiv-2509-18550:
A real smile and a posed smile differ in subtle muscle cues that machines can learn to spot. Mohammad Junayed Hasan, Nabeel Mohammed, Shafin Rahman, and Philipp Koehn present HadaSmileNet for that task in this 2025 paper. Older systems mixed deep features with hand-crafted smile markers through multi-task training. That route was heavy and needed careful loss balancing.

The new framework fuses transformer features with the hand-crafted markers by direct multiplication, a Hadamard product with no added parameters. The team compared fifteen fusion styles in a systematic sweep. Direct multiplication won, giving top deep-learning scores on four benchmark sets. Scores reached near-perfect levels on two of them. The design cut parameter count by about a quarter versus multi-task rivals. Feature plots showed cleaner separation of real and posed smiles. The authors aim it at real-time emotion tools.
arxiv-2509-18750:
Multilingual models chop words into shared pieces, and the same piece can appear in many languages. Julie Kallini, Dan Jurafsky, Christopher Potts, and Martijn Bartelds ask whether that overlap helps or hurts in this 2025 paper. Such shared pieces are called false friends when their meanings differ. Prior evidence was mixed, tangled with frequency and segmentation effects.

The team trained bilingual models under controlled overlap levels, holding other factors steady. They added a new lens: how similar the shared pieces' meanings are across the pair. Inside the models, any overlap built embedding spaces that captured cross-language meaning links. Disjoint vocabularies showed that effect only weakly. On two standard cross-lingual tests, overlap models beat disjoint ones, and more overlap generally helped more. The authors conclude shared vocabularies remain a sound design choice. False friends, on balance, are not foes.
arxiv-2509-18850:
Powerful galaxies fire jets that accelerate cosmic rays to extreme energies. Dimitrios Kantzas, Francesca Calore, and Marco Chianese ask whether dark matter could be cooling those rays in this 2025 paper. If light dark matter particles scatter off jet electrons, the jets should glow a touch less across the spectrum. The test case is Markarian 421, a well-studied active galaxy.

The team fit a multizone jet model to the galaxy's full light spectrum, radio to gamma rays. Jet traits and the dark matter interaction were fit together, with jet uncertainty fully counted for the first time. No cooling signal was required by the data. They set an upper limit on the scattering strength for a light dark matter mass. The limit beats older approaches by a factor of two to ten. Careful handling of jet unknowns, they show, is what makes the bound trustworthy.
arxiv-2509-19050:
Ryo Nikkuni, writing alone, adds a new example to a strange family of shapes in topology. A simplicial complex is a shape built by gluing triangles and their higher-dimensional cousins along shared faces. Some complexes are intrinsically linked. However they are placed in space one dimension higher than twice their own, they must contain two sphere-like parts. Those parts are linked in a way that cannot be split apart. Several earlier authors gave examples of such complexes for every dimension.

Nikkuni's example comes by a short argument from piecewise-linear topology. The proof leans on the van Kampen-Flores theorem, a classic result about how such shapes must intersect themselves. He also shows that more examples arise from a higher-dimensional version of a graph move called the triangle-Y exchange. The work widens the known stock of shapes that force linking no matter how they are embedded.
arxiv-2509-19150:
Supercomputers increasingly run simulations and AI training as one coupled job, and moving data between the parts can dominate the cost. Harikrishna Tummalapalli and seven co-authors present SimAI-Bench, a tool to prototype and measure such workflows. They use it on the Aurora supercomputer for two common patterns. In one, each simulation feeds its own AI instance side by side. In the other, many simulations feed a single shared model.

For the paired pattern, node-local staging and a system called DragonHPC beat a Redis store and the shared file system clearly. For the many-to-one pattern, data transport grew into the main bottleneck as the ensemble grew. There, the plain file system turned out best among the options tested. The study gives workflow designers measured guidance on where data should sit while coupled jobs run.
arxiv-2509-19350:
Tiny internet-of-things devices at the network edge cannot call the cloud for every decision, so Wojciech Kalka and six co-authors ask how such devices can manage themselves. Their proposal, TinyAC, carries autonomic computing principles, self-configuration, self-healing, and kin, down to resource-starved hardware. The design is hybrid: small on-device learning supplies bottom-up intelligence, while large language models supply top-down guidance. Together they aim for adaptation that is both scalable and explainable.

The authors argue that self-management itself must be self-adaptive, able to handle faults that appear during operation. Much of the paper maps the problems and challenges of autonomic methods on constrained devices. It closes by naming research gaps and future directions. As a position-style contribution, it offers a framework and an agenda rather than a finished deployed system.
arxiv-2509-19550:
Translation surfaces are flat shapes glued from polygons, and they split into families called strata. Sam Freedman and Bradley Zykoski study regions where the best triangle mesh on a surface keeps the same pattern. These regions, named for Delaunay, cover each family with finitely many pieces. The question is whether those pieces are convex, meaning free of dents, when viewed in angle coordinates.

For meshes with a pairing symmetry, the authors prove the regions are convex. As a payoff, all such regions in the hyperelliptic families are convex too. Convex pieces are easier to count, sample, and reason about. The result ties together two lines of flat-surface theory. It may help later work that classifies surfaces by their geometry.
arxiv-2509-19650:
Malware written for quantum computers is still rare, but the systems it could strike guard defense, energy, and space assets. Dehinde Molade and four co-authors review how researchers classify malware and ask what those schemes miss for the quantum era. Their systematic review sorts past work with knowledge frameworks such as ontologies and taxonomies. A European framework for quantum skills helps frame the needed expertise.

Sorted knowledge lets the team map how known malicious behaviors could translate into attacks on quantum hardware and software. That map exposes gaps where defenses and vocabulary do not yet exist. Early classification work is cheap insurance against later chaos. The authors urge the field to prepare mitigations before quantum malware matures. Their review gives security teams a shared language for that preparation.
arxiv-2509-19850:
Jets of energetic particles plowing through dense quark matter lose energy in a branching cascade. Yacine Mehtar-Tani presents an analytic framework that treats that cascade as one nonlinear story. Medium-driven splitting joins the vacuum's own collinear splitting instead of replacing it. Energy carried outside the jet obeys a rate equation that sums splittings at any angle.

At very high energies, the loss pattern for a single hard particle takes an exponential, Poisson-like form. That pattern seeds a further evolution that handles early fragmentation and the medium's angular resolution. Jet quenching is a key probe of the matter made in heavy-ion collisions. A unified resummation sharpens what jet shapes can reveal about that matter.
arxiv-2509-19950:
Solvable systems are the rare motions that math can finish in full, and geometers lift plain ones into rich ones. Ondřej Kubů and Piergiulio Tempesta bring two classic lifts under one roof, Stäckel geometry. Their lift covers both the space-like and time-like forms of the older Eisenhart lift. Systems built with a Stäckel matrix that depends on momentum gain a rich geometric frame for free, they prove.

Magnet systems that split in round coordinates show the method at work. Lift matrices that depend on momentum also give rise to Platonic-wave shapes. Those shapes may serve new theories of gravity and bent-path metrics. A lift helps when a hard low-space problem turns solvable once raised. One frame now shows the old tricks as a single idea.
arxiv-2509-20150:
Alberto Bonollo and seven co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on high-energy astrophysics. Some objects, nicknamed PeVatrons, accelerate particles to extreme energies. Young massive star clusters are leading candidates for that role. A photon of record energy was seen coming from the direction of the cluster Cygnus OB2.

The team modeled gamma-ray emission from five young massive clusters and their surroundings. They asked what the next generation of Cherenkov telescopes will be able to resolve. Simulated observations used the response of the CTAO and ASTRI Mini-Array instruments. The authors built ways to classify clusters seen as unidentified extended sources. They also estimated how long telescopes must observe to tell cluster shapes from the halos around pulsars. Features like the emission peak look key to that task.
arxiv-2509-20250:
Quantum contextuality limits how far classical hidden-variable stories can explain quantum outcomes. Colm Kelleher and Frederic Holweck present a quantum algorithm for measuring that limit in a 2025 arXiv paper. The relevant quantity, the degree of contextuality, is NP-hard to compute in general. It connects to a broader family of hard optimization problems.

Their algorithm builds on Grover's search method and computes the degree far faster than classical brute force. Variants encode the needed information in phases of the quantum states. Those variants shrink the circuit width and depth a machine must support. The team also ran the method on current IBM quantum hardware. Noise in today's machines made those outputs inconclusive. The authors expect better hardware to settle what the theory promises.
arxiv-2509-20350:
Nonlocal games test whether separated players share genuine quantum entanglement. Honghao Fu and three co-authors study those games under heavy noise in a 2025 arXiv paper. Players may share many copies of a noisy entangled state. In that regime, older rigidity theorems could certify nothing nontrivial, leaving device-independent protocols without support.

The authors compute the best possible quantum winning chances for the CHSH game, the Magic Square game, and a family of variants, each as an explicit function of the noise rate. Those formulas also let users estimate the noise level itself from game outcomes. Building on them, they prove the first rigidity results that survive high noise. The games certify one, two, or many pairs of anticommuting Pauli measurements, matching the variant played. The work draws on sum-of-squares and Pauli analysis methods.
arxiv-2509-20550:
A warehouse robot meets objects it has never seen, and grasping them reliably takes data at scale. Srinidhi Kalgundi Srinivas and three co-authors release GraspFactory, a grasping dataset, in a 2025 arXiv paper. The dataset holds more than one hundred nine million six-degree-of-freedom grasps. They cover tens of thousands of objects for two common grippers, the Franka Panda hand and the Robotiq two-finger gripper.

Object-centered geometry is the design principle: grasps are computed per object in rich variety, which suits training data-hungry models. The authors trained one such model on a subset of the data. It generalized to new objects in both simulation and the real world. The dataset and its tools are free to download. The release aims to give grasping research the same data scale that transformed other robot skills.
arxiv-2509-20850:
Genes can affect not only a trait's average level but also how much it varies between people. Qiong Wu and five co-authors build a tool for that second effect in a 2025 paper on polygenic scores. Variance effects can reveal where genes interact with the environment.

Their algorithm, snpboostlss, uses cyclical gradient boosting on a Gaussian location-scale model. It builds sparse polygenic models for the mean and the variance of a trait at the same time. To handle huge genotype datasets, each boosting step considers only a batch of the most relevant variants. Finding variance-linked variants can guide personalized interventions, the authors argue, because it flags people whose outcomes depend more strongly on their surroundings.
arxiv-2509-20950:
Gaussian processes give principled forecasts for physical systems but scale badly, so learned stand-ins have stepped in. Kaustubh Sharma, Simardeep Singh, and Parikshit Pareek improve one such stand-in in a 2025 paper. The stand-ins are prior-data fitted networks, which mimic Bayesian inference in a single forward pass of a learned model.

Standard transformer attention limits these networks on high-dimensional regression tasks. Their fix, decoupled-value attention, copies how a Gaussian process truly predicts. Inputs alone set the similarity scores, while labels flow only through the values. The forecast mean then forms as a weighted sum of past targets, as in the classic method. The authors argue this match in structure restores lost accuracy, which matters for fast physics surrogates.
arxiv-2509-21450:
Diabetes affects more than half a billion adults, yet early diagnosis stays hard. Vague symptoms, borderline lab values, and pregnancy related complexity all cause delays. Gaurav Kumar Gupta and 2 co-authors evaluate a large language model as diagnostic support in a 2025 study. Their test bed uses man made cases only. Cases align with the American Diabetes Association standards of care for 2025.

Five scenarios were tested with the GPT-5 model. They cover symptom recognition, laboratory interpretation, and gestational diabetes screening. Remote monitoring and multimodal cases complete the set. Public data sources inspired the man made cases. The study maps opportunities and challenges for model based support. Structured, interpretable, patient friendly outputs are the promise under scoring.
arxiv-2509-21650:
Mask based pre training underlies modern models in language, vision, and now biology, but its theory lagged its success. Mingze Dong and 2 co-authors describe that behaviour in a 2025 paper. Test risk in high dimensional minimum norm linear regression describes mask based pre training directly, they show. No further model specification is needed for that link. Linear analysis then uncovers several new aspects of the method.

Checking spans multilayer perceptrons, convolutional networks, and transformers on vision and language tasks. Guided by the theory, a simple pre training scheme is proposed. Randomly Random Mask AutoEncoding enforces capturing multi scale traits from data. The scheme was overlooked despite its simplicity, the authors argue. Performance gains over standard masking are reported for the new method.
arxiv-2509-21750:
Segment Anything Models segment medical images poorly where limits are ambiguous and anatomy matters. Yu Li and 2 co-authors add form constraints to the model in a 2025 paper. Their system, KG-SAM, integrates anatomical priors with limit refinement and uncertainty estimation. A medical knowledge graph encodes fine grained anatomical relationships. Probabilistic graphical models carry those constraints into outputs.

An energy based conditional random field enforces anatomically steady outputs. An uncertainty aware fusion module enhances reliability for high stakes clinical use. Multi centre medical data sets supplied the tests. Segmentation scores improved over the base model, the authors report. Anatomical knowledge, rather than more pixels, is the lever used to fix medical segmentation failures.
arxiv-2509-21950:
Judging how well a multimodal model reads emotion in images has given mixed answers, and Daiqing Wu and four co-authors blame the tests themselves. Existing evaluations overlook plausible answers, use narrow emotion lists, ignore context, and cost heavy human labeling. Their 2025 paper, accepted at ICLR 2026, proposes a custom-built way to evaluate visual emotion understanding.

The core is a new task: the model judges emotion statements about an image, rather than picking one label. An automated pipeline builds such statements with little human effort, so the tests scale. Running leading models through the frame, the authors find them strong at interpreting emotion and judging it in context. The models are weaker at grasping that different viewers may feel differently about the same image. Even the best model trailed humans by a wide margin, which marks where work is needed.
arxiv-2509-22650:
Anna Kukleva and 6 co-authors find that filler words in a prompt act like magnets for attention. Referring segmentation asks a model to outline the object a text phrase points to. Most methods fine-tune or chain several models. The team instead reuses attention scores inside diffusion transformers, with no training and no architecture change. Stop words soak up surplus attention, and filtering them cuts noise.

Deeper layers grow global attention sinks that blur the maps. Suppressing or redirecting those sinks sharpens the grounding. Appending stop words splits background activity into small clusters, which sharpens maps further. Their framework, RefAM, led training-free methods on image and video benchmarks.
arxiv-2509-22750:
Jeonghyun Park and 7 co-authors built a benchmark where multi-hop questions are also ambiguous. A real user query can branch into several reasoning paths, each needing its own resolution. Ambiguity can strike at any step, so a model must manage layered uncertainty through the whole chain. Prior benchmarks studied single-hop ambiguity only. Their set, MARCH, holds over two thousand curated questions, verified by multiple models and human annotators.

Even top models struggled on the set. The team also proposes CLARION, a two-stage agent that separates ambiguity planning from evidence-driven reasoning. That split beat existing approaches by a clear margin. The work maps a harder, more realistic corner of question answering.
arxiv-2509-22850:
Roie Kazoom and 3 co-authors attack tabular data models with only yes-or-no access to their outputs. Adversarial work has focused on images and text, leaving structured data underexplored. Their black-box, decision-based attack estimates descent directions without gradients. An iterative boundary search then walks each record across the decision edge with few queries. The method handles both discrete and continuous features.

Across models from classic classifiers to language-model pipelines, the attack compromised nearly the entire test set. Success rates stayed above ninety percent while using only a small number of queries per record. The authors present the results as a warning: real-world decision systems built on tabular models need stronger defenses.
arxiv-2509-22950:
Supantha Dey and Ratul Chowdhury predict how strongly two proteins bind, using sequence text alone. Their network, Twin Peaks, has two heads on one shared body. One head predicts binding strength, and the other predicts how a mutation shifts that strength. Most rivals need 3D structure data, which many proteins lack.

The shared body uses transformer encoders and a cross-attention step for protein pairs. Training mixed the SKEMPI v2 and PDBbind data sets, split by protein domain to stop leakage. Scores for mutation shifts and raw strength both held up on held-out data. The pair stress gains for viral and disordered proteins that resist structure work.
arxiv-2509-23050:
Vision-language models often answer from memorized text habits and slight the image in front of them. Lin Long and 3 co-authors trace that language prior inside the network layers. Their lens is the chain of embeddings, layer by layer. Every model they tested shows a visual integration point. At that layer, visual data starts to reshape the hidden code in earnest.

Past that point, a new estimator sums how much the image shifts the code. That total predicts how strong the language prior will be. The pattern held across sixty model and data combinations. The toolkit offers a principled way to diagnose text bias in multimodal models.
arxiv-2509-23250:
Step-level reward models for vision-language reasoning are held back by noisy training labels. Brandon Ong and 4 co-authors map the design space of such models. Tree search builds most current labels, which injects noise. Their hybrid synthesis mixes tree search with judgments from a strong vision model. A second idea adds perception-focused supervision.

That supervision teaches the reward model to catch visual grounding errors early. Five multimodal benchmarks frame the tests. As outcome judges, the models beat step-selection use in scaling tests. Small reward models matched or beat larger ones at error spotting. Perception supervision gave significant scaling gains.
arxiv-2509-23550:
Doctors dictating notes in Greek need speech software that knows medical terms, not just everyday speech. Vardis Georgilas and Themos Stafylakis built a domain-specific transcription system for Greek medical dictation. Their goal is to cut the load of manual paperwork and speed clinical workflow. The system pairs automatic speech recognition with a text correction model that fixes domain terms and language quirks.

Both sound modeling and text modeling were adapted to the Greek medical setting. Fine-tuning on domain data handled complex terminology and inconsistent phrasing. The result was more accurate and coherent transcripts, offered as practical language technology for Greek healthcare.
arxiv-2509-23850:
The hottest known exoplanet bakes its dayside until molecules split apart, which makes finding any molecule there a prize. Yuanheng Yang and 3 co-authors report the first detection of OH in the dayside atmosphere of KELT-9b, using two thermal emission observations with the SPIRou spectrograph. They also confirm iron. A self-consistent retrieval under chemical equilibrium pins down abundances and metallicity, and confirms a strong thermal inversion layer.

The planet's spin matches its tidally locked value, with no clear Doppler shifts. Oxygen looks solar to supersolar, while the carbon-to-oxygen ratio and metallicity run subsolar to solar, with wide error bars. The authors read the pattern as tentative evidence of volatile enrichment and formation beyond the water snowline.
arxiv-2509-24250:
Teaching a system a team sport is harder than teaching a solo one, since teammates must guess each other's intent. Edward Kim and 9 co-authors frame that learning task as program synthesis. Their system stores behavior as editable programs, so users can inspect and fix what it learned. Teaching happens through narrated demonstrations, pairing physical actions with speech.

Users never need to see or write code, yet they can correct the logic directly. In a study, twenty users taught multiplayer soccer tactics to the system. Most users refined the learned programs to match their intent, and most found correction easy. The study also surfaced hard spots in showing learning as programs.
arxiv-2509-24550:
