Numbers alone miss context that images and text can supply, but blending them well is hard. Fine time patterns get lost, fusion turns clumsy, and features at mixed speeds resist one fixed recipe.

MGTS-Net answers with three layers. The first tunes a reader for each data type, pulling out fine-grained time patterns. The second builds a graph linking the streams, so each can borrow strength from the others as it learns. The third runs short-, mid-, and long-range forecasters and weighs their mix on the fly. Across experiments it beats top rival models while staying light and efficient. That is a practical step for forecasting where data comes in many forms.
arxiv-2510-16850:
Uday Gopan and six co-authors present DiRAC, a framework for assigning tasks and planning paths in very large robot swarms. Warehouse fleets can grow past what one central planner handles well. DiRAC splits the space into zones, elects a leader in each zone, and runs a tick-synchronized consensus protocol, so decisions stay consistent and repeatable.

Path planning uses a force-based method spread across the robots, which resolves collisions in real time as they arise. The team built the system on ROS 2 middleware and tested it in simulated warehouse settings. Early results point to a modular design that scales, laying groundwork for real fleets in industry and logistics.
arxiv-2510-17050:
Hibiki Kunisawa and four co-authors probe a magnetic mineral under extreme fields in a 2025 paper. The mineral is karpenkoite, a candidate kagome antiferromagnet. Kagome means its magnetic atoms sit on a woven triangular lattice. Antiferromagnet means neighboring spins point in opposing directions.

The team measured torque on single crystals in strong magnetic fields. Fields reached forty-five tesla along two crystal directions. No sudden phase transition appeared at any field strength. Instead, the spins rotated smoothly toward alignment with the field. The authors say one interaction likely governs that smooth turning. It is the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, which twists neighboring spins. The result narrows theories for this candidate material.
arxiv-2510-17150:
Heng Zhang and three co-authors build a robot controller that adjusts its stiffness in this 2025 paper. A variable impedance controller, which sets how stiff or soft a robot arm feels, aids safe touch tasks. Fixed settings fail when tasks and places change. The team adds vision and language sense to tune stiffness on the fly.

Their system recalls past tasks from a memory bank to guide new ones. Live force feedback keeps push forces inside safe bounds. Tests in sim and on real robots beat set baselines. Success rose from about one quarter to over three fifths on hard tasks. Fewer force breaches also made contact work safer overall.
arxiv-2510-17350:
Transport equations describe how a quantity is carried along by a flow, and small changes to the flow can have outsized effects over time. Gabriel Rivière and Maria Teresa Rotolo study wobbling, time dependent changes to such equations on a two dimensional torus, a surface shaped like a ring doughnut. They ask whether smooth starting data can grow wildly under these steady perturbations.

Rivière and Rotolo prove that, for typical perturbations, a large class of starting data sees its Sobolev norms, a measure of roughness, grow exponentially fast. The same holds in higher dimensions when the repeating part of the change meets a stated condition. Their proof reshapes the equation into a simpler normal form and then draws on tools from the study of chaotic motion.
arxiv-2510-18250:
Xiaohan Qin, with Xiaoxing Wang and six co-authors, proposes ssToken in a 2025 paper on training language models. Fine-tuning means extra training that adapts a general model to a task. Picking the best tokens, meaning small text pieces, to train on can beat using all data.

Older token pickers need a separate reference model or trust loss scores alone. Loss here means a score for how wrong the model is on each token. ssToken instead compares past and current model versions, and adds an attention-based check on meaning. Each part alone beat full-data training in tests, and together they did better still.
arxiv-2510-18450:
Sombuddha Bhattacharyya works with Tuhin Mondal and Suman Kumar Sahoo. They study a transform built on light rays. The transform adds up values along each ray. Powers that track momentum weight the sum. It acts on plain functions. It also acts on tensor fields. Such fields assign data with direction at each point of space-time.

The key question is uniqueness. Could two distinct fields give the same readings? If so, no rebuild from data could work. The authors find terms that rule this out. The proof covers tensors of any order. It needs two or more space dimensions. It works for full and for partial data. For partial data, they give a rebuild method. The method draws on tensor tomography, geometry, and analysis.
arxiv-2510-18550:
Enhan Li and Hongyang Du look at how language models choose which external tool to call for a user's request. Matching the words of a request to a tool's function is not enough, they argue. Requests are often vague, and the user's real experience also depends on network delay and whether servers are actually available, facts that pure meaning matching cannot see.

Their framework, JAUNT, aligns two views at once. It interprets what the user intends, and it uses model agents to turn raw network numbers into profiles written in the same semantic space, so routing can weigh both together. The authors also built a benchmark that pairs varied request styles with mixed network conditions. In tests, JAUNT improved quality of experience over several baselines, supporting their claim that scalable tool services must route by intent and network state together.
arxiv-2510-18750:
Reinosuke Kusano works with Keith Horne, Friedrich Koenig, and Miguel Yulo Asuncion. They pile light onto a special orbit near a black hole. The setting is an alternative theory of gravity. It is called Weyl conformal gravity. Its Mannheim-Kazanas solution plays the Schwarzschild role. The orbit is the stable photon sphere. Light can circle there in a stable way.

The light matter is modeled as an infinitely thin shell. Its arrival creates a jump in radial pressure. That jump vanishes only at a photon sphere radius. Loading the stable sphere leaves its area unchanged. That invariance is striking. At a critical load, a surprise appears. The metric gains an extremal horizon. Its geometry ignores the universe's background curvature. The authors note this is unseen in standard theories.
arxiv-2510-18850: M. Koshelev, writing alone, completes a stability theorem in graph theory. It concerns the independence number of graphs denoted G(n, r, 1). That number is the size of the largest set of vertices with no edges among them. The theorem was stated earlier by M. Pyaderkin. The proof offered there was incorrect. Koshelev supplies a correct proof of the key lemma. With that repair, the full proof of the theorem is finally complete.
arxiv-2510-18950:
Subham Dutta Chowdhury, Sean A Hartnoll, and Aditya Hebbar connect Lieb-Robinson causality with the physics of non-Fermi liquids. Lattice models with local, bounded interactions cannot spread influence faster than a set limit, and the authors show this limit forces a region where a key response function stays analytic.

Low-energy theories of strange metals must respect that microscopic limit. Checking two standard forms, the marginal Fermi liquid and the Hertz liquid, they find the constraint caps the strength of the non-Fermi liquid coupling in some cases. The result ties everyday causality limits to exotic metal behavior.
arxiv-2510-19050:
Wenqian Ye and two co-authors tackle shortcut behavior in reward models trained from human preferences, the models that steer large language models toward helpful answers. Such models often chase high scores by copying shallow cues, like long answers, agreeable tone, or flattery, instead of the qualities people actually wanted.

Rather than fixing one shortcut at a time, the authors treat reward hacking as a general shortcut problem and propose a principled, flexible remedy. Cleaning up reward learning matters because a fooled reward model quietly trains the final system to please raters rather than serve users well.
arxiv-2510-19150:
Yunzhe Wang, Soham Hans, and Volkan Ustun build tools for team-level tactical awareness from first-person game video. Good team play grows from each player's own view plus the ability to guess what teammates intend, yet most video research uses third-person broadcast views and misses that shared first-person structure.

Their benchmark holds many hours of Counter-Strike 2 footage from professional-level matches, with synchronized first-person streams for every player plus records of states and actions. A cross-egocentric learning method then builds representations across those views. The dataset gives multi-agent research a realistic test bed in a complex three-dimensional setting.
arxiv-2510-19250:
Yuheng Wu and four co-authors present FadeLead, a method that lets self-driving cars share perception efficiently by sending foreground features while quietly packing background context into them. Cars that pool sensor views handle rare road situations better, but vehicle networks cannot carry full feature maps for every car.

Earlier foreground-only schemes threw the background away, losing context that matters. FadeLead instead teaches the model during training to fold background information into compact foreground features, guided by a curriculum that uses background cues progressively. At sending time, little is transmitted, yet receivers keep much of the scene's meaning.
arxiv-2510-19350:
Varsha Suresh and three co-authors model turn-taking in conversation using gestures that carry meaning, not just movement. People manage who speaks next through words, voice, gaze, and gesture together, and gesture cues have often been left out of computational models of these transitions.

The team extends a multi-party gesture corpus with thousands of semantic annotations, covering gestures that picture ideas, point, or organize discourse. A mixture-of-experts model combining text, audio, and gestures predicts turn changes better with the semantic gestures than without. The gains show gesture meaning, not motion alone, carries real conversational signal.
arxiv-2510-19850:
Mostapha Kalami Heris presents Prompt Decorators, a compact syntax for steering how a large language model reasons and writes. Normal prompt craft buries behavior rules in long plain-language text. That hurts reuse and makes results hard to repeat. Decorators are short tokens, for tone, reasoning style, or calling in a topic. Each one shifts a single facet of how the model acts, without touching the task itself.

The scheme fixes twenty core decorators in two families. They span reasoning, interaction, expression, and session control, under one syntax and one fixed processing pipeline. By splitting what the user wants done from how the model should act, decorators promise prompt design that can be audited and mixed freely. Worked cases show clearer reasoning and shorter prompts.
arxiv-2510-19950:
Shaocong Ma and Heng Huang make reinforcement learning for trading robust to the market impact the learner itself causes. Agents trained on historical data assume their trades move nothing, but live trading shifts prices, and that mismatch can wreck performance. Standard robust methods guard against worst cases inside symmetric uncertainty sets, which miss impact's directional character.

The authors introduce elliptic uncertainty sets shaped to reflect directional price pressure, and they derive closed-form worst-case solutions that keep robust policy evaluation efficient. On single-asset and multi-asset trading tasks the method earned superior Sharpe ratios and stayed robust as trade volumes grew. The approach aims to give financial reinforcement learning a more faithful model of the markets it will actually face.
arxiv-2510-20250:
Zhiqin Yang and five co-authors build FedGPS, a federated learning frame built to stand up when client data sets clash. Data clash is a core block in such learning, since it hurts scores and slows the fit. Their broad tests show most past ways are weak when the form of clash shifts. Shared stats, by contrast, help each client learn with a full view in mind.

FedGPS first reshapes each client aim with proxy stats, so it tracks the full data spread in a quiet way. It then steers each local step with slope facts from peer clients at each round. Broad tests in mixed clash states show FedGPS ahead of top rivals on scores and on strength.
arxiv-2510-20650:
Santanu S Dey, Dahye Han, and Yang Wang extend a strong branching method from whole number problems to problems with squared terms and squared limits. Branching means testing a choice, solving relaxed versions of the task, and keeping the split that improves the goal value most.

For a binary choice the split point is fixed, but for a smooth value someone must also pick where to split, and past methods fixed that point in advance. The new rule tests several split points per value and picks the value and point together, gaining tighter bounds as a side benefit. On some squared problems, tests show the rule beats leading paid solvers, a notable result for hard design and planning tasks.
arxiv-2510-20950:
Federico Zahariev leads two co-authors on cutting qubit needs for quantum chemistry by fragmenting the virtual orbital space. Correlated calculations demand large active spaces, and qubits are the scarcest resource on current quantum hardware.

Their Q-FVO method keeps the full occupied space, splits the localized virtual space into chemical fragments, and recovers correlation energy through a many body expansion with inclusion exclusion counting. Across six molecular benchmarks, one body calculations cut qubit needs by roughly half, while two body versions cut less but recover most correlation energy with small errors. The trade offers a practical dial between hardware cost and accuracy.
arxiv-2510-21250:
Anh Nguyen and six co-authors work on shortcut models, a kind of generative model that can create samples in one step, a few steps, or many steps using a single trained network. Despite that promise, five flaws have held the models back from wider use in image generation.

The flaws include guidance that quietly compounds and ruins images, fixed guidance that users cannot adjust, a bias toward coarse detail over fine detail, and training conflicts that bend the generation paths. Their framework, iSM, adds adjustable guidance built into the model, a wavelet-based loss that restores fine detail, a transport method that straightens paths, and a doubled averaging scheme for stability. On ImageNet images, quality scores improve clearly at every step count.
arxiv-2510-21450:
Federico Danieli and four co-authors remove the speed limit that kept recurrent neural networks, the original sequence models, small. Recurrent designs read inputs step by step, which blocks parallel computing, so giant models moved to Transformers and state space models, whose linear structure trains fast but cannot express some nonlinear patterns.

Their framework, ParaRNN, rewrites a whole sequence of nonlinear recurrence steps as one system of equations and solves it in parallel with Newton iterations plus custom parallel reductions. Speedups reach several hundredfold over naive step-by-step runs. Retooled long short-term memory and gated recurrent designs train at seven billion parameters, matching the perplexity of similar-sized Transformers and Mamba2 models. The code is released openly so others can train new nonlinear recurrent designs at scale.
arxiv-2510-21550:
Christian Kremer records a proof about group actions on curved spaces that bend nowhere positively. Geometry strongly restricts symmetry in that setting. For isometric actions on complete spaces of that kind, genuine fixed points and homotopy fixed points coincide. The two notions capture stability under a group in different ways, so their agreement is not obvious.

The result speaks to the Nielsen realisation problem for aspherical manifolds. That problem asks whether a finite group of outer symmetries can be realized by actual symmetries of the manifold itself. Kremer gives a unifying account of the problem's different formulations. The same methods make that account possible. He also extends the fixed-point statement to certain quotients of universal spaces. Those spaces are built for families of subgroups.
arxiv-2510-21650:
Erhan Bayraktar, Bingyan Han, and Jingjie Zhang help an investor fund several life goals at once when every trade costs money. Each goal carries its own deadline and target sum. A strictly positive transaction fee on stock trades breaks the clean strategies known from frictionless models. In those models, the best plan traces a simple V shape.

Using a stochastic version of Perron's method, they show the problem's value function is the unique well-behaved solution of a system of quasi-variational inequalities. Those equations mix optimization with free switching. They also prove an optimal trading strategy and goal funding scheme actually exist. Numerical experiments map out surprisingly intricate regions where the investor should buy, sell, or wait. The optimal policy departs substantially from the frictionless V-shaped rule.
arxiv-2510-21950:
Nnamdi Daniel Aghanya and Romain Leemans study Heaven-Hell dynamics, a stylized model of how a network of agents reaches agreement when a central hub pulls on everyone. An earlier result fixed an exact threshold for one-step agreement with a single uniform hub, stated in terms of the strongest pull arriving from outside the hub.

The pair makes that threshold practical. They show it survives different tie-breaking rules, per-node tolerance levels, deliberate seeding of key nodes, several hubs at once, and updates that arrive out of order. New viewpoints include a conservation-law reading, sharper per-node bounds, and a fairness guarantee for one-pass asynchronous updates. Every proof is mechanized in the Coq proof assistant, and experiments on rings, grids, and uneven weighted networks check that the bounds are tight.
arxiv-2510-22050:
Marcus Thomas argues that machine learning aims at the wrong target. Today's best systems chase predictive accuracy, yet their inner workings stay causally opaque: nothing inside them says what would change if you intervened. The only fix for a bad mechanism is retraining the whole thing and hoping.

Thomas proposes treating intelligence as the craft of building and refining explanations, claims about manipulable structure that state plainly what changes and what stays fixed when you act. That can be tested and repaired piece by piece. His concrete vehicle is the Energy-Structured Causal Model, where mechanisms are written as constraints in the form of energy functions. The paper is a conceptual reorientation, offering a framework in which learned knowledge carries causal commitments instead of mere correlations.
arxiv-2510-22250:
Jongwan Ko, Woowon Byun, and Kwang-Il Seon lead a thirty-four-author team building telescopes to photograph the faintest structures in the sky. Low-surface-brightness features, tidal streams, and diffuse halos record how galaxies collided and assembled and where dark matter sits. They drown in stray light and shifting sky glow, which is why they remain underexplored.

The K-DRIFT project answers with off-axis, freeform three-mirror telescopes designed from the start for faint imaging, paired with observing strategies that protect the dim signal. The first-generation instrument is complete and its survey is about to begin. The paper lays out the science case, the technical fights along the way, and the design choices meant to open the low-surface-brightness universe to systematic study for the first time.
arxiv-2510-22450:
Amin Omidvar introduces SmartMixed, a training plan that lets each neuron in a network pick its own activation function instead of sharing one fixed choice. Activation choice shapes how a network learns, yet most designs force one function on every neuron. SmartMixed learns the choice in a first phase and then locks it in for cheaper further training.

During the first phase, neurons choose among six common functions through a smooth mixing method. Tests on a handwritten digit data set with several network shapes show different layers prefer different functions. The learned mix competes with strong single function models while keeping running costs low.
arxiv-2510-22650:
To edit a made image in just one way is still hard. Tharun Anand wrote a 2025 paper on that task. His co-authors are Mohammad Hassan Vali and Arno Solin. Green Rosh and B H Pawan Prasad are co-authors too. Their method needs no new training of the model.

The key is found in the model's own weights. Some weight sets hold rich facts about what the model learned. The team takes special directions from those sets. Those directions turn out to be clear edit paths. No extra data is used at all. Tests on many data sets show good edits. Edit time fell by about sixty percent from the best prior marks.
arxiv-2510-22750:
Matching markets can stall when people fear a bad match. Kaibalyapati Mishra, writing alone in 2025, refines the idea of stability for such markets. Information is incomplete in his setting. Pairs can pay for tests before they decide to leave. Tests can reveal facts about match quality.

His concept is called Information-Credible Pairwise Stability. It rules out matches held together only by fear. When tests teach nothing, it matches Bayesian stability. When tests are perfect and free, it matches full information stability. He proves stable outcomes always exist. Blocking moves raise total expected surplus. Strong tests can make the outcome unique.
arxiv-2510-22850:
Finding a community in a network means balancing two goals. Members should connect well to each other. They should also share similar attributes. Nikolaos Georgiadis, Eleftherios Tiakas, and Apostolos N Papadopoulos tackle that balance in 2025. Their method mixes hop based and random walk tools.

A domination score rates node influence from attributes. A k-core step then enforces strong cohesion. K-core keeps nodes with many internal links. Tests used large real world datasets. The method found cohesive, similar communities fast. Uses include social network analysis. Recommendation systems are another target use. The work joins structure and attribute views in one search.
arxiv-2510-22950:
Yuepeng Jiang and nine co-authors introduce DiffRhythm 2, a system that creates full songs with vocals matched to lyrics. Long songs are hard because words and music must stay in step over minutes, not seconds. Older fast methods often let vocals drift from the written lyrics.

The new design works block by block with flow matching, which keeps lyric alignment tighter across a song. It also learns from human feedback to suit varied tastes without merging many models, a step that hurt quality before. The authors present it as an end-to-end route to high-quality, controllable song creation.
arxiv-2510-23150:
Alban Etienne and five co-authors revisit how trend-following returns are built across time horizons. Traders often blend trend signals from several lookback windows, with six months to one year seen as the sweet spot. Equal weighting assumes every asset gains equally from every horizon, an assumption the authors challenge.

Using Bayesian optimization, they reallocate exposure across horizons separately for each asset, learning weights from data. The results suggest diversification across horizons can hide redundant signals. Allocations tuned per asset may earn the trend premium more cleanly, a practical lesson for systematic funds that blend many lookback periods.
arxiv-2510-23350:
Alcino Cunha and Nuno Macedo test whether large language models can write test cases that validate formal specifications. Validation is central when building a formal spec, and one sound technique is to define scenarios in advance that the spec must pass or fail. Writing those cases by hand is burdensome and error prone, so users often skip it.

Their empirical study uses pretrained models to generate test cases from natural language requirements, focusing on structural requirements. Automated generation could make validation routine rather than rare. The results help spec authors judge when model-written tests are trustworthy.
arxiv-2510-23850:
Enrico Lampetti constructs good moduli spaces for two classes of objects in algebraic geometry: constructible sheaves and Stokes functors. A moduli space is a single geometric home whose points stand for a whole family of objects, letting geometers study the family as one space. Constructible sheaves are sheaf-like data that stay constant on the pieces of a layered split of a space.

Stokes functors encode a related kind of layered data, tied to how solutions of certain equations behave near singular points. Lampetti's constructions give both settings the good moduli spaces they lacked. He also treats derived enhancements of the same moduli problems, the richer versions of these constructions used in derived algebraic geometry.
arxiv-2510-24050:
Connor van Rossum and two co-authors study how noise affects quantum models that are tuned by a classical computer. These models are a hope for useful work on today's noisy quantum hardware, in tasks like planning, simulation, and learning. Most work asks how easy the models are to train, not how noise shapes that training.

The team finds a surprise. A common step that makes noise more even can hurt results, while keeping uneven noise can help the search find better answers. They prove this in a simple model and test it more broadly. The work suggests noise should not always be cleaned up in the same way.
arxiv-2510-24450:
Špela Vintar leads a team of four authors on testing AI language models. Benchmarks are test sets that score what a model can do. New benchmarks appear fast, but most still favor English. For other languages of Europe, the test landscape is thin and messy. The team survey recent work and sort it into a new scheme.

Their taxonomy, a sorting scheme, fits tests for many languages well. It weighs language and culture, not just raw task scores. They also set out best practices for building such tests. Shared quality standards could help teams across Europe work in step. Care with local culture is a core point of their advice. The paper gives test builders a map and a rule book.
arxiv-2510-24550:
Anna Deza and Georgina Hall, two authors, link two fields of optimization. Submodular functions show diminishing returns: later additions help less. Testing if a set function is submodular is known to be hard. Sum of squares methods certify that polynomials are never negative. The pair blend the two into a new ladder of tests.

Each rung of the ladder is a stronger algebraic test. For a fixed rung, a semidefinite program checks the test fast. That check runs in time polynomial in the ground set size. They give equal forms of the test and operations that keep it. They also sort when the test matches submodularity exactly. Three uses follow: regression, ratio bounds, and splitting hard functions. The work bridges discrete optimization and real algebraic geometry.
arxiv-2510-24650:
Nitin Rai, Daeun Choi, Nathan S Boyd, and Arnold W Schumann review how new base models could change crop pest and plant ill control. Old tools used hand made traits, then deep nets learned traits on their own. Base models add text and image sense, plus plain talk with growers.

The team screened about forty works on these models for site based care. They found use rose fast in the past two years, and image text models led text only ones. Smart spray with learn by trial is still new. Twin models in code may let farms test spray plans in a safe fake field first.
arxiv-2510-25350:
Yvann Gaudillot-Estrada studies a q-deformation of a Lie group. His 2025 math paper works in feature theory. The group is SL(2,R), a classic real group. A q-deformation alters its algebra with a setting q. He studies convolution algebras attached to that deformation. His method is algebraic and goes beyond unitary cases.

Many classic results transpose to this deformed context. Real semisimple groups supply the classic comparison theory. He proves an analogue of the Harish-Chandra isomorphism. That isomorphism is a central tool in feature theory. He also presents an analogue of parabolic induction. Induction builds new features from smaller subgroup data. These tools classify non-unitary irreducible features there. He shows how they converge to classic ones. At q equals one, the theory recovers classic results. A quantized enveloping algebra version supports the construction.
arxiv-2510-25550:
Dominik Sturm and Ivo F Sbalzarini select variables for spatial point processes. Their 2025 paper handles readings corrupted by noise. Spatial data increasingly come from remote sensing and imaging. Automated acquisition often produces noisy event records. Reading errors cause displacements. Events can be missed too.

They study noise impact on sparse point-process estimation. Poisson and Thomas processes are among models considered. Their method mixes sparsity-promoting estimation with robust choice. Stability choice uses point-process subsampling for robustness. A non-convex best-subset penalty enhances choice results. Extensive runs show reliable recovery of true covariates. Diverse noise scenarios were tested in those runs. Choice quality and stability both better largely. They apply the method to forestry data afterward. Tree distribution relates to elevation and soil nutrients. A tropical rain forest supplied that dataset. Useful utility is shown without extra process knowledge.
arxiv-2510-25850:
Kevin Qiu and Marek Cygan present a system where language model agents debate their way to a better robot design. Robot co-design means shaping the body and the control rules together, since each affects the other. Their system, Debate2Create, splits the work between a design agent and a control agent that argue in a thesis, counter point, and synthesis loop.

Special judge models score each proposal on several goals, and a physics simulator grounds the debate in real performance. Across five MuJoCo locomotion tasks, a standard robot simulation suite, the method earned the highest normalized scores among the methods tested. Debate added clear gains over one shot generation with the same computing budget.
arxiv-2510-25950:
D. Manzoni and A. Ferrara argue that light from young stars can limit how efficiently gas clouds turn into stars. The light is Lyman alpha radiation, a strong ultraviolet line from hydrogen, whose pressure can push on gas. High efficiency has been suggested to explain the many bright galaxies the Webb telescope sees in the early universe.

Manzoni and Ferrara build a shell model with this feedback and check it with one dimensional fluid simulations. They find clouds are disrupted in less than a free fall time, before supernovae, for dense clouds. At low metal content typical of early galaxies, efficiency stays well below unity except at extreme density and near solar metal content.
arxiv-2510-26050:
S. Abubakar and M. Acsencio-Sosa lead sixty six co-authors in a report on reconstructing neutrino events in the ANNIE experiment at Fermilab. ANNIE uses a twenty six ton water Cherenkov tank, which detects faint light rings from charged particles in water, fed by the Booster Neutrino Beam. Its goals are to measure neutron production when neutrinos hit oxygen and to test new detector technology.

The paper describes reconstruction performance using only the conventional light sensors and a downstream muon spectrometer, before newer picosecond detectors and a water based scintillator vessel are added. That baseline matters because later gains can be measured against it. Even the baseline methods differ from larger water detectors, due to the small size of ANNIE.
arxiv-2510-26650:
Feranmi V Olowookere, with four co-authors, cleans up the training data for coarse-grained molecular models. Molecular dynamics simulations track atoms in materials, but they are slow for large systems. Coarse-grained models group atoms into beads to save time, at the cost of detail and of mapping noise in the forces used for training machine-learned versions.

Olowookere and the team apply knowledge distillation: a first, teacher network learns from the noisy mapped forces and smooths them, then a student network trains on the teacher's force and energy predictions. They test the frame on a deep eutectic solvent, a complex molecular fluid, checking two-, three-, and many-body traits against all-atom results. Students trained on ensemble teacher forces and per-bead energies gave better, more stable force fields.
arxiv-2510-27050:
Isaac Malsky, Tiffany Kataria, Natasha Batalha, and Matthew Graham speed up a costly step in modeling planetary atmospheres. Radiative transfer tracks how light and heat move through an atmosphere, but standard calculations are slow. Climate-scale models therefore cut corners, losing accuracy in the process.

The team trains a transformer neural network, a model that weighs context across an input, to mimic the exact calculation for hot Jupiter atmospheres. On test cases it reproduces layer energy fluxes with errors near one percent while running about a hundred times faster. Faster, faithful transfer could let large circulation models keep more physical detail. The work frames the task as a clean mapping well suited to machine learning emulation.
arxiv-2510-27250:
Xin Jiang and Haitang Yang show how the Einstein equation of gravity can be derived from entanglement entropy in a conformal field theory. Conformal field theories are quantum theories with scale symmetry that anchor modern ideas linking gravity to quantum information. Entanglement entropy measures how strongly two parts of a quantum system are linked.

The derivation works between codimension-one disjoint regions, meaning separate regions one dimension below the full theory space, inside a conformal theory in one fewer dimension. From that entropy structure the authors explicitly obtain the Einstein equation in the higher dimension. Results of this kind support the holographic view that spacetime dynamics can emerge from quantum entanglement patterns, a guiding idea in current gravity research.
arxiv-2511-00050:
Dhananjaya Gowda, Seoha Song, and Junhyun Lee propose FLoRA, a family of fused forward-backward adapters for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large language models. Low-rank adapters already cut training cost, but much of the design space remains unexplored. Their adapters fuse operations in the forward and backward passes, aiming also to reduce inference-time latency, not just training parameters.

Language model practitioners get a new adapter family positioned against established low-rank methods. Efficiency at both training and deployment matters because fine-tuned models are served many times. Fusing passes attacks overhead that parameter counts alone do not capture, widening the practical gains of adapter tuning.
arxiv-2511-00150:
Christopher Baldwin asks whether a quantum method for hard search problems really beats a well-matched classical rival. The quantum method, adiabatic reverse annealing, starts from a good first guess to dodge harmful phase changes. Baldwin reads its gains through the shape of the free energy landscape, the map that guides the search.

From that view he builds a classical twin, simulated reverse annealing, that copies the same trick without quantum hardware. In a solvable mean-field model, the classical method wins wherever the quantum one does. It even succeeds in a narrow range where the quantum method fails, which weakens claims of a quantum edge here.
arxiv-2511-00250:
Courtney Watson, Elizabeth Blanton, Scott Randall, Tracy Clarke, and John ZuHone report very deep X-ray observations of Abell 2029, a galaxy cluster with a cool, dense core. Data from the Chandra telescope, gathered over a long exposure, reveal one of the longest sloshing spirals ever seen, reaching far from the cluster core. Sloshing is gas swaying after a past disturbance.

Fainter features tell the merger story: a broad splash of cooler gas and a possible merger shock. Radio lobes at the center bend along the sloshing flow, not the host galaxy's motion. Comparison with simulations points to a smaller cluster that passed through long ago. Even calm-looking clusters, the team shows, hide busy pasts.
arxiv-2511-00350:
Yu-Peng Wang, Chuo-Kai Chang, Ryo Okugawa, and Chen-Hsuan Hsu study localization in a non-Hermitian system, a quantum setup where energy can leak, patterned by a quasiperiodic potential. They track when states stay extended and when they collapse into small regions, using several measures at once: participation ratios, fractal dimensions, and spectral statistics.

Even without the usual self-dual symmetry, a critical potential strength exists, and it grows in a straight line with the antisymmetric hopping strength. Adding longer-range hopping enriches the picture: mobility edges appear, separating localized from extended states by energy, and fractal patterns show in the complex energy spectrum. Self-similar structures recur as the potential varies, linking localization physics with fractal geometry in a leaky system.
arxiv-2511-01150:
D. Schuricht and J. Sirker study paraparticles, hypothetical particle types with statistics beyond the usual boson and fermion kinds, arranged in interacting chains. Their Hamiltonians sum over the particles' internal flavors and use a constant interaction matrix, making the Hamiltonians blind to flavor.

For such flavor blind chains they prove the Hilbert space factors into occupation and flavor parts, with the energy acting only on occupation. With open ends, the spectrum matches the occupation Hamiltonian, flavors merely adding degeneracy. With periodic boundaries, flavor reordering splits the problem into flux sectors, making the parastatistics directly visible in the spectrum. In key cases the occupation part reduces to the solvable XXZ chain, whose gapless regime shows shifted conformal towers and a temperature dependent chemical potential.
arxiv-2511-01650:
Ayesha Gull and six colleagues argue that grading a final answer alone misjudges the work. The answer may belong to an engineering student or to a language model. Right answers can hide flawed steps. Wrong ones can rest on mostly sound derivations. Their benchmark, EngTrace, grades the derivation itself.

EngTrace holds 150 expert-certified problem templates. They span five branches, 15 domains, and 42 areas of engineering. Each template generates problems with a gold reasoning trace. In that trace, every intermediate quantity is exact. An automated evaluator checks final answers, coverage of the trace's milestone quantities, and the displayed arithmetic, mostly without a language-model judge. Testing 11 models, final answers barely separated the leaders. Their derivations differed clearly. Wrong answers still stated about half the gold milestones. Experts traced most errors to calculation slips.
arxiv-2511-01750:
Matus Rybak and nine colleagues survey the dense gas in galaxies that formed stars furiously in the early universe. Dense gas is where stars are born, but its standard tracer lines, from HCN, HCO+, and HNC molecules, are faint, so high-redshift dense gas stayed mostly unexplored.

With the ALMA and NOEMA telescopes, the team targeted those lines in eleven mostly gravitationally lensed dusty star-forming galaxies at redshifts 1.6 to 3.2. They detected at least one line in ten galaxies. There were 34 dense-gas transitions in all. That more than quadruples the known high-redshift detections. Two targets also yielded rarer carbon monoxide isotopologues and CN. The excitation of these molecules runs systematically higher than in nearby infrared-luminous galaxies. Dense gas depletes faster: in a median of about 23 million years, versus about 60 million locally. Star formation efficiency per free-fall time runs a few times higher.
arxiv-2511-01950:
Prasanth K K and Shubham Sharma rebuild the memory of a recurrent network around self-reflection. Long short-term memory networks still lose long-range dependencies, especially when sequences contain distracting or misleading material. The authors' principle, output-conditioned gating, lets the model modulate its own memory gates using its past inferences, a feedback loop meant to stabilize what it retains.

Their EchoLSTM adds an attention mechanism on top of that principle. On a custom distractor signal task it reached about 69 percent accuracy, beating a standard LSTM baseline by 33 percentage points. On the ListOps benchmark it scored about 70 percent, close to a modern Transformer's roughly 72 percent, while using over five times fewer parameters. A trigger sensitivity test adds qualitative evidence that the self-reflective loop makes the memory fundamentally more robust.
arxiv-2511-02050:
Faouzi Thabet, Gliia Braek, Marwa Mansouri, and Mondher Chouikhi study the cubic oscillator, a quantum system whose potential energy curve has three turning points, using geometry rather than direct analysis. Their approach rests on a correspondence that links the oscillator to critical graphs of a quadratic differential, a geometric object whose shape encodes the spectral data. Extra data attached to the potential determine when quantisation conditions hold.

The work proceeds on two levels. First comes an inverse spectral problem: recovering information about the oscillator from its spectrum through the graph picture. Second, the authors describe where the zeros of the eigenfunctions lie. They suggest the geometric route may yield proofs of open questions about cubic potentials that analytic methods have not settled.
arxiv-2511-02350:
Ya. S. Greenberg, A. A. Shtygashev, and O. V. Kibis analyse how a superconducting qubit loses its excitation when it sits in a wide-band cavity. The qubit is a transmon, an artificial atom with three relevant levels, coupled to a continuum of electromagnetic modes in a one-dimensional, broadband resonator. Using resolvent methods, the authors derive formulas for how the resonance frequencies shift and broaden, then evaluate them numerically for a Gaussian distribution of modes.

Two regimes emerge, separated by the ratio of coupling strength to the continuum's bandwidth. Weakly coupled, the decay is Markovian, with a width nearly constant across the band. Stronger coupling turns the decay non-Markovian, the width varying sharply with energy because the continuum remembers the qubit's past. Coupling between the transmon's levels also opens a fast two-photon decay channel that broadens the second level.
arxiv-2511-02550:
Iqra Liaqat and Faisal Akram compute the masses of the lightest mesons, the particles built from up, down, and strange quarks, from the equations of quantum chromodynamics itself. Their tools are the Dyson-Schwinger equation for the quark propagator and the Bethe-Salpeter equation for bound states, a coupled framework that keeps the theory's chiral symmetry intact when truncated consistently. The gluon propagator is modelled with the Maris-Tandy form, realistic both at low and high momenta.

Two models for the quark-gluon vertex, the bare vertex and the Ball-Chiu construction that respects gauge symmetry, are compared under the same truncation, policed by the axial-vector Ward-Takahashi identity. Meson masses come from locating poles of the Bethe-Salpeter amplitude through a Padé approximation, avoiding calculations in the awkward timelike region. Both vertex choices, paired with the Maris-Tandy gluon, gave consistent spectra for flavoured and unflavoured light mesons.
arxiv-2511-02750:
Priyanka Majethiya and Shivam Bajpeyi build new tools for approximating complex-valued functions, which carry both size and phase. Their 2025 paper extends work by Paul Nevai, a noted mathematician in approximation theory. They define a family of complex Nevai operators meant to fit smooth functions, rough ones, and functions where higher derivatives matter too.

One operator uses Chebyshev polynomials for continuous functions, with accuracy tied to a modulus of continuity. A Kantorovich type handles functions that are merely integrable, and a Hermite type preserves higher derivatives. The authors prove boundedness and convergence for each kind. Worked examples, including an image processing case, test the theory against real approximation tasks.
arxiv-2511-02850:
Youssif Abuzied, Hassan AbdEltawab, Abdelrhman Gaber, and Tamer ElBatt built ECGXtract, a deep learning tool that pulls clear features from heart tracings. Doctors read such tracings for signs of cardiovascular disease, but older extraction methods are brittle, and black-box models hide their reasoning. Their 2025 paper trains convolutional networks to output features that match a clinically checked ground truth.

At first each model extracts one feature, keeping outputs precise and readable. Across setups, global features matched the truth with a mean correlation score of 0.80, and lead II worked best. Lead-specific features scored 0.822 on average. The tool beat the open-source ECGdeli on ninety percent of features. Grouping related features into one model worked for global features, though wide grouping hurt accuracy.
arxiv-2511-02950:
Rohith Vaidyanathan, Srinath Srinivasa, Praseeda, and Dev Shinde tackle consent in digital public infrastructure, the shared digital rails countries build for public good. Consent at population scale is tricky because ownership of a digital asset can take many forms, each with different rights. Their 2025 paper proposes basic building blocks, called ownership and flow primitives, to represent those forms.

The proposed design aims for traceability of consent from end to end, fine-grained control over sharing, and fit with changing laws. It also weighs personal autonomy against public well-being and national sovereignty, tensions the authors treat as design inputs rather than afterthoughts. The work is architectural: it sets out the abstractions a consent system needs before any code is written.
arxiv-2511-03050:
Katharine E Fisher, Matthew Li, Youssef Marzouk, and Timo Schorlepp ask what changes when a neural model learns from both values and slopes. That style of training, called Sobolev training, is common in practice yet poorly understood for very large models. The team studies random feature models as data, width, and input size all grow together in fixed ratios.

With tools borrowed from physics and advanced probability, they derive exact formulas for test error in that large limit. Their setup mirrors real practice by compressing slope data into smaller spaces before use. The closed forms show how slope data helps or hurts in each regime. Such sharp predictions can guide how much gradient data to collect before training begins.
arxiv-2511-03250:
Ryuta Miyata and colleagues built a small sealed detector to keep radon gas out of dark matter searches. Radon and its decay products create stray signals that can hide the faint hits such searches chase. Their device uses a plastic vessel pressed between quartz flanges with soft gaskets, sealing the active gas inside away from outside air.

Over a run lasting hundreds of hours, the team pumped radon around the device and watched for leaks with two separate tools. Both tools agreed that only about one part in a hundred of the outside radon level built up inside. Scaled to a huge future detector, that leak would add a tiny amount next to natural sources. Flange sealing therefore looks like a practical way to shield the inner volume.
arxiv-2511-03350:
Silvia Manconi, Christopher Eckner, Francesca Calore, and Fiorenza Donato revisit a gamma-ray glow at the center of our galaxy. That excess glow was once read as a possible sign of dark matter particles destroying each other. Newer work favors a crowd of fast-spinning dead stars in the galactic bulge as its source instead.

Taking the stellar reading as the base, the team asks how well dark matter could still be hunted there. Adaptive fitting plus photon counting lets them separate a faint dark signal from the stellar crowd more cleanly. The center then becomes a strong target again rather than a lost cause. Their results set sharper limits and show where future telescopes should look hardest.
arxiv-2511-03650:
Debarshi Chanda improves how few questions an algorithm needs to estimate a graph's average degree. Sublinear methods peek at tiny parts of a huge graph through degree checks and random edge picks, never reading the whole thing. Chanda's randomized method needs no advance knowledge of the graph's traits.

Query counts drop below the best earlier method, which also had access to neighbor queries this one forgoes. A matching lower bound shows no method with those query types can do better in the worst case, up to small factors. Arboricity, a sparseness measure, governs where the savings land. Fast degree estimates help audit giant social and web graphs where full scans are impossible.
arxiv-2511-03850:
Shakil Ahmed, Amika Tabassum, Ibrahim Almazyad, and Ashfaq Khokhar propose QSAFE-V, a lightweight login protocol for vehicles in tactile wireless networks tied to 6G and smart transport. Control commands and swarm behaviour must stay trusted, since attacks could threaten road safety directly.

Many current schemes resist classical attacks but weaken under quantum-enabled adversaries. QSAFE-V builds security on quantum key sharing and quantum adversary models, with formal proofs and behaviour-based fresh login checks as vehicles move. Tests described in the abstract show strong protection against quantum and context-driven attacks, with strong performance. The design targets fast, frequent checks without heavy cost for edge-enabled vehicles.
arxiv-2511-03950:
Zhejia Cai, Puhua Jiang, Shiwei Mao, Hongkun Cao, and Ruqi Huang present a joint method for rebuilding real objects from multi-view images. That step is needed for 3D editing, augmented reality, and content creation. Older methods favour either shape accuracy or photo-like rendering and fit shape and appearance apart, which hurts later editing.

Their framework fits mesh vertices and faces together with vertex colours, guided by Gaussians that render the mesh. Photometric consistency from the input images and shape regularisation from normal and depth maps steer the fit. The resulting rebuilds support downstream tasks such as relighting and shape change, and code was promised for public release.
arxiv-2511-04050:
Zenan Chen, Ruijiang Gao, and Yingzhi Liang test whether showing AI reasoning helps people judge when to trust it. People often hold unique private context that should decide whether to accept or override a suggestion, and openness is widely assumed to improve that balance.

In a pre-registered, paid experiment with seven hundred fifty-two participants, revealing reasoning, brief or long, acted as a strong cue. Trust and agreement with the system rose sharply. Rather than balancing trust, openness produced over-trust and crowded out use of participants' own unique knowledge. Careful information design, not automatic openness, is the lesson for joint systems that display model reasoning.
arxiv-2511-04450:
Yaniv Ohayon and two colleagues teach a computer to solve convex partition jigsaw puzzles. Most earlier solvers handled only square pieces, which limits real use. Convex partition puzzles use convex polygon pieces that must return to their exact poses.

Their solver scores piece pairs by both shape fit and picture fit along shared edges. A greedy strategy then assembles the full image step by step. The team also releases the first benchmark dataset for this puzzle type and reports several quality measures. Automatic solving of richer puzzle forms could aid fields from archaeology to document repair.
arxiv-2511-04650:
Dražen Glavan and two colleagues study how a complex scalar field falls onto a black hole. Such fields, carrying a global U(1) symmetry, appear often in cosmology and astrophysics. The setup is steady, spherically symmetric Bondi accretion onto a Schwarzschild black hole.

At lowest order, the field behaves like a perfect superfluid, a known result. Going beyond that approximation cuts the accretion rate below the fluid value, they show. A generic quartic potential is used, with cases that keep or break the symmetry. The correction matters for models that treat scalar clouds around black holes as simple fluids.
arxiv-2511-04850:
Olena Podladchikova, writing alone, asks whether MHD oscillations set the rhythm of plasma release from coronal streamers. The slow solar wind carries periodic density structures of uncertain origin. She separates two jobs: what releases the plasma, and what sets its cadence.

Reconnection at web, cusp, or current-sheet sites likely does the releasing. Structured wave responses may then modulate the density or the release rate. Her informed parameter scan finds slow-mode periods spanning roughly twenty to two hundred thirty minutes. Matching the observed range needs effective path lengths under about one solar radius, a concrete test for streamer models.
arxiv-2511-05050:
Masahiro Tanaka builds a scalable online kernel method to estimate causal effects that run in both directions at once. Many real systems have mutual links, where each side shapes the other, yet classic causal work often treats effects as one-way only.

His method joins a likelihood estimator for joint equations with large-scale online kernel learning. Random Fourier features let it fit curved means and spreads, while a step-by-step gradient rule keeps it fast on streaming, high-dimension data. In wide simulations, the method beat rivals on both accuracy and speed for such two-way systems.
arxiv-2511-05250:
Mohamed Sanim Akremi and co-authors build an online system that spots actions and gestures as a skeleton stream arrives, not after a clip ends. Online spotting fits real use, but most past work judges whole segments at once.

Their system pairs a detector with a classifier. Both use a matrix form for the joint data, and the classifier is a Siamese network built on those matrices. The detector marks when an act starts, then the classifier names it. Tests check how well the pair keeps up with live motion data.
arxiv-2511-05550:
Daniel Chenyu Lin, Michael Freeman, and John Thickstun ask whether large audio language models truly know facts about music. These models answer open questions about songs and recordings. The team shows that a popular test set, MusicQA, fails to check whether those answers are factually right.

They propose a stricter protocol instead. The model must give facts that can be checked, and its prose answer is parsed into a fixed form scored for precision and recall. Their benchmark covers six fact-finding tasks across three music data sets. They ran nine recent models through it, from frontier systems to open ones, and released the scoring code for future use.
arxiv-2511-05650:
Yichen Wang and co-authors address a trade-off in aligned language models: their answers are better, but also more alike. Fine-tuning for quality tends to flatten variety, above all in open-ended tasks like story writing. Their framework, BACo, mixes a base model with its aligned twin while generating, token by token.

Routing rules use uncertainty and content signals to pick which model supplies each token. The mix runs in a single pass, with no extra training or costly decoding. Across three open-ended tasks and many quality and diversity metrics, BACo beat prior inference-time methods. The best router lifted diversity and quality together by about a fifth, and human raters agreed.
arxiv-2511-05850:
Max McKinnon rechecks a famous weakness of large language models: forgetting facts buried in the middle of long inputs. Prior work named the effect Lost in the Middle, after accuracy fell for facts placed centrally. McKinnon tests whether a current model, Gemini 2.5 Flash, still shows it.

He poses needle-in-a-haystack questions, where one fact hides in a long document. The model answered with high accuracy no matter where the fact sat. That held even when the document nearly filled the model's whole input limit. McKinnon concludes the effect is absent for simple fact questions in this model. The result suggests long-context retrieval has improved a great deal since the effect was first reported.
arxiv-2511-06050:
V Roatti, G Picogna, and F Marzari simulate how several small planets together carve gaps in the dust of a young star's disk. Single-planet studies cannot capture the interplay. The team ran two-dimensional fluid simulations with dust as particles of many sizes, sweeping a large grid of disk and planet properties.

Planets just above Earth's mass can open dust gaps without much disturbing the gas. Which grains gap depends on coupling: small grains in dense warm disks, large grains in thin cold ones. Fast inward or outward migration can drag the gap off the planet's orbit, and gaps can sit on resonance locations. In weakly coupled disks the planets can clear a central cavity, stack rings, or hide inside one shared gap.
arxiv-2511-06150:
Haoran Wang and co-authors build a neural audio codec that treats speech, music, and sound with one system without slighting any of them. Codecs compress audio into compact codes. Speech energy hugs narrow bands near pitch harmonics, while music and sound need the full spectrum, above all the high frequencies that carry timbre.

Speech-tuned codecs degrade on other audio, and full-band designs spread capacity evenly despite uneven needs. Their BSCodec splits the spectrum into bands and compresses each on its own. Trained on a combined set of speech, music, and sound, it beat baselines on sound and music reconstruction while staying competitive on speech. Downstream task tests backed its promise as a general audio tokenizer.
arxiv-2511-06450:
Seulgi Kim and co-authors stop sensor fusion from collapsing into a single dull signal. When data streams merge, feature collapse drains the variety from individual dimensions, and modality collapse lets one loud sensor drown the rest. Human action anticipation, which must fuse many sensors, suffers from both failures at once.

Effective rank, a measure of how richly a representation spreads across dimensions, becomes the shared yardstick for both problems. Their Rank-enhancing Token Fuser blends weak features from one modality with complementary features from another, provably raising the fused rank. Depth paired with ordinary video kept balance instead of collapsing, and tests on three action datasets beat prior methods.
arxiv-2511-06650:
Norbert Hegyvari, Janos Pach, and Thang Pham extend Raimi's theorem, a classic result saying the natural numbers can be split so that some color class, after a shift, meets both parts endlessly. Their version allows polynomial shifts instead of plain translations, and works in any dimension with any fixed number of pieces.

Given non-constant integer polynomials that vanish at zero, the authors partition the integer lattice points accordingly. For any finite coloring, one single color class meets every piece after shifts built from one base point plus polynomial values along each axis, for infinitely many shift sizes. Weyl equidistribution, Pontryagin duality, and polynomial relation lattices drive the proof, with finite analogues for abelian groups also included.
arxiv-2511-06850:
Lu Zhou and five co-authors search for pulsars living in open star clusters, something never yet confirmed. Globular clusters host about a tenth of the roughly four thousand known pulsars, yet open clusters are twenty times more numerous and have none confirmed. Using the Gaia DR3 catalog, the team cross-matched pulsars with measured distances against thousands of open clusters.

Four pulsars look like current cluster members. The standout is the binary pulsar J1302-6350, which the evidence places in the open cluster UBC 525, with an updated distance and a companion star of about seventeen solar masses. Tracing past motions through the Galaxy adds nineteen pulsars that were probably born in open clusters and later escaped, opening a new window on pulsar origins.
arxiv-2511-06950:
M Doostmohammadian, U A Khan, and N Meskin study how connected self-driving vehicles can estimate the states of nearby human-driven vehicles in mixed traffic. They derive a distributed state-space model that supports both estimation and observability analysis. Each self-driving vehicle runs a local observer and shares estimates and observations with its network neighbors, so no central processor is needed.

The authors prove that strong connectivity of the communication network, along with a properly built observer gain, guarantees every human-driven vehicle's state is observable to every autonomous one. They then design for redundancy: with a suitably node- and link-connected network, a certain number of faulty sensors and unreliable links can be isolated or removed without losing observability. Simulations illustrate the approach, which matters for safe cooperation between automated and human traffic.
arxiv-2511-07050:
Marco Grzegorczyk studies mixtures of Gaussian Bayesian networks, probabilistic models that blend several network structures to capture heterogeneous data. Earlier work let every mixture part carry its own covariance matrix. Grzegorczyk instead proposes tied covariance, where all parts share one common covariance matrix, a simpler and more constrained model that can resist overfitting.

His main contribution derives the model's marginal likelihood, the BGe score used to compare structures, and shows it remains available in closed analytic form. Unlike the full-covariance case, however, the tied score no longer splits into separate part-certain factors. For inference he implements Markov Chain Monte Carlo schemes that combine structure search with a fast Gibbs sampler for the mixture assignments. Compares tied against full covariance on simulated and benchmark data.
arxiv-2511-07450:
Florian Neukart asks what pushed the interstellar comet 3I ATLAS off a purely gravitational path. The comet showed a small extra acceleration as it crossed the inner solar system. One possible cause is uneven outgassing, where jets of vapor act like tiny thrusters.

Thermophysical modeling with random sampling of jet layouts tests that idea. Carbon monoxide activity can match the observed push for nuclei between half a kilometer and three kilometers across, with active areas that remain physically plausible. Less volatile gases alone fall short. The findings favor ordinary volatile outgassing over exotic explanations for the comet motion.
arxiv-2511-07650:
Mingrui Wang and Prakash Chakraborty derive fluid limits for call-center style systems whose demand changes through the day. Many servers face arriving jobs with general service times, and zero waiting room means late arrivals are lost. Blocking happens instantly, making the limiting equations discontinuous.

A functional strong law shows the busy-server fraction follows a nonlinear Volterra integral equation. A careful solution concept makes that equation well-posed and yields time-varying acceptance odds without hand-waving. Finite waiting room versions get parallel treatment for busy, waiting, and lost fractions. Service operators gain exact large-scale laws for staffing systems that never sit still.
arxiv-2511-08050:
Olaf Beyersdorff, Ilario Bonacina, Kaspar Kasche, and Meena Mahajan introduce semi algebraic proof systems for QBF Boolean rules. Such rules add for all and there exists choices to usual logic, making proof analysis harder. The new systems mirror plain Nullstellensatz, Sherali Adams, and Sum of Squares methods in the QBF setting.

Techniques come from both QBF formula research, through strategy extraction, and plain proof complexity, through size degree relations and pseudo expectations. With them, the authors prove strong lower bounds and separations between these systems. The separations hold even when plain hardness is set aside, showing genuinely QBF difficulty.
arxiv-2511-08450:
Luis Yague Bosch and Sandro Wimberger compare two ways to design a high fidelity quantum gate on Rydberg atoms: an analytic shortcut to adiabaticity and brute force numeric tuning. The counterdiabatic approach mimics a helpful extra Hamiltonian with fast oscillating fields, giving an understandable recipe for fast, exact gates. The rival protocol was optimized numerically on the Boulder Opal platform under realistic pulse limits.

The numerically optimized gate reaches higher fidelities while matching the counterdiabatic gate robustness against errors. Pulse constraints in time and amplitude prove decisive for judging either method fairly. The study serves as a concrete benchmark of analytic shortcut inspired design against numeric search on a leading quantum computing platform.
arxiv-2511-08550:
Rachael Boyd and three co-authors study the homology of Temperley-Lieb algebras, algebraic objects that arise from diagrams of strands and loops. They restrict attention to algebras built on an even number of strands, where the homology turns out to be rich and often far from trivial.

The key claim is that one smaller structure controls all of this homology: a differential graded algebra built from planar loops. The authors construct a small model for that algebra, small enough to compute with directly. Feeding the model back into the problem yields concrete consequences for the homology of the original algebras. The work ties a diagram-based algebra to loop geometry in a precise, usable way.
arxiv-2511-08850:
Yuzhe Song and five co-authors simulate the millisecond pulsars that crowd globular clusters, the dense star cities where over three hundred such pulsars are already known, more than half the galactic total. These neutron stars spin hundreds of times per second after stealing mass from companions, and cluster dynamics assemble many of their binaries.

The simulations run on NBODY6++GPU, a direct N-body code the team extended with pulsar physics: spin-down from magnetic braking and spin-up from accretion. Intermediate-mass clusters are the laboratory, and the cluster M71 is modeled in detail as a test case. Beyond counting and characterizing the pulsar population, the study watches for gravitational wave transients the systems might produce. The framework aims to explain why clusters manufacture millisecond pulsars so efficiently.
arxiv-2511-10150:
Feng Ding, Wenhui Yi, Yunpeng Zhou, Xinan He, Hong Rao, and Shu Hu make deepfake detectors fairer without giving up accuracy. Detectors can misjudge demographic groups such as gender and race at different rates, which in identity security settings compounds social inequity. Earlier fairness fixes usually traded detection accuracy away, limiting their appeal. The aim is fair treatment for every group without giving up accuracy.

Their framework combines two mechanisms: it decouples channels sensitive to demographic attributes inside the architecture, and it aligns the overall feature distribution with each group's distribution. Experiments showed gains in both between-group and within-group fairness while overall detection accuracy held across domains. The authors release their code publicly.
arxiv-2511-10250:
Yongji Zhang, Siqi Li, Yue Gao, and Yu Jiang build FineSkiing, the first benchmark for scoring aerial skiing with fine-grained annotations. Existing action quality datasets grade whole performances but lack the sub-scores and deduction items that explain a judge's number. FineSkiing adds those annotations for aerial skiing, and the authors release it as a public benchmark for the field.

Their scoring method, JudgeMind, imitates professional referees: it splits a performance video into stages and scores each stage separately. A stage-aware module enhances the key regions of each stage and stays robust when camera viewpoints switch, while a grade-aware decoder uses known deduction items as prior knowledge. The system reached state-of-the-art scoring performance with better interpretability than whole-video baselines.
arxiv-2511-10350:
J. J. Chebly, C. K. Louis, A. Strugarek, J. D. Alvarado-Gómez, and P. Zarka predict which exoplanet systems are worth pointing radio telescopes at. Radio emission from a planet interacting magnetically with its star has never been firmly detected: signals are weak, beamed, and often blocked by Earth's ionosphere. Their framework simulates the interaction to estimate emission frequencies and power before telescope time is spent.

Magnetic maps of the star feed three-dimensional stellar wind simulations, and a dedicated code models the resulting radio emission, with intensity from a radio-magnetic scaling law. Applied to Tau Boötis, HD 179949, and HD 189733, the method rates detectability with current and future instruments. The authors offer it as a data-driven way to prioritize targets and schedule observations.
arxiv-2511-10450:
T. Devolder and eleven co-authors watch, in real time, how a driven magnetic vortex splits its energy into two kinds of waves. The system is a magnetic disk in the vortex state, excited near its first azimuthal spin wave frequencies. Earlier work showed such driving feeds the vortex's gyration motion and grows Floquet spin waves that form a frequency comb.

Using time-resolved microwave measurements, the team timed the process. The strongest Floquet mode appears at the same moment as the gyration mode, after a shared incubation delay. That delay grows without bound near the scattering threshold. It shrinks to about three nanoseconds at the highest power tried, when the drive is resonant. This timing identifies three-wave splitting of a regular spin wave into a gyration magnon and a Floquet wave as the first mechanism at work.
arxiv-2511-10650:
Felix George and five co-authors go hunting for a hidden failure mode of AI agents: execution cycles that loop quietly, burning compute without ever raising an error. Standard observability tools miss these loops because nothing technically crashes.

Their unsupervised framework works in two passes. A fast temporal call stack analysis catches explicit loops first, then semantic similarity analysis uncovers subtler cycles where the agent keeps generating redundant content. Evaluated on 1,575 trajectories from a LangGraph-based stock market application, the hybrid method reached an F1 score of 0.72, far above either the structural method alone at 0.08 or the semantic method alone at 0.28. The authors note substantial room remains to refine the approach.
arxiv-2511-10850:
Stefan Horoi and six co-authors improve task arithmetic, the trick of moving a skill between language models by adding the difference of their weights. The catch is interference: once two models have diverged in training, their parameter spaces no longer line up, and naive arithmetic can damage both.

The authors align the parameter spaces first, exploiting the permutation, rotation, and scaling symmetries built into transformer architectures. They adapt the alignment to modern grouped-query attention and SwiGLU layers using both weight-based and activation-based methods. With spaces aligned, they moved advanced reasoning skills into a model that had none. On challenging reasoning benchmarks, the alignment-first approach consistently beat standard task arithmetic, offering a way to reuse specialized skills as model families evolve.
arxiv-2511-11150:
Miguel Aguilera, Daniele De Martino, and their colleagues build a new class of continuous-time recurrent networks whose inner workings can be read through physics. Such networks model complex time patterns, but their internal motion is often opaque. Their design rests on Hopfield-like associative memory, which stores patterns as stable states, with uneven links between units.

The math lets them track the stored features directly as they evolve, plus the system's entropy and its loss rate at each instant. That gives a bridge between low-level motion rules and the statistical physics of large out-of-balance networks. The authors suggest the models can serve as clearer tools for sequence tasks.
arxiv-2511-11250:
Biagio Boi and Christian Esposito compare prompt engineering against fine-tuning for using large language models to find flaws in smart contracts on Solana and Algorand. Smart contracts automate deals on blockchains, but sloppy code can lock in serious vulnerabilities. Most detection research targets Ethereum-style contracts, leaving these two platforms understudied and short of labeled data.

The authors built a synthetic data set of annotated code snippets in Rust and PyTeal, sorted by a flaw taxonomy drawn from OWASP guidance. Prompting alone proved broadly robust, while fine-tuning sharpened precision and recall on the leaner TEAL language. Platform design shaped how flaws appear and how well each method detects them.
arxiv-2511-11350:
Karl Kunisch and Jesper Schröder extend the Kalman-Bucy filter, the classic tool for reconstructing a system's hidden state from noisy data, to systems whose state operator carries parametric uncertainty. Standard filters assume the model is exact, so uncertain parameters can cause large reconstruction errors. The authors take a deterministic viewpoint and favor risk-averse designs that cut the chance of such large errors.

Their theory derives error bounds stated through the variance of the uncertainties, which tells designers how risk shrinks as uncertainty is pinned down. A numerical section implements two examples, letting readers compare risk-neutral and risk-averse estimators side by side on the same tasks.
arxiv-2511-11450:
Maximilian Rokuss and ten co-authors present VoxTell, a vision-language model that cuts three-dimensional medical scans into labeled regions from plain text prompts. A user can type anything from a single word to a full clinical sentence, and the system returns a matching 3D mask.

Training covered more than sixty-two thousand CT, MRI, and PET volumes across over one thousand body structures and disease classes. Layered fusion ties words to image features at several scales, giving strong zero-shot results on scans the model never saw. It also handles varied wording and moves well between scan types, pointing toward faster, more flexible medical image analysis.
arxiv-2511-11550:
J. Antonio Dantas Macedo, Hugo Fernandes, and J. Eduardo Ferreira Ribeiro address a tension in aerospace software: agile teams thrive on change, while safety certification under rules such as DO-178C demands strict documents, traceability, and testing. Their proposal, CertiA360, tries to keep both sides workable.

Rather than treating certification as a final hurdle, the approach uses agile flexibility to automate and manage change requests across the whole development cycle. Requirements stay linked across levels, and verification evidence is maintained as the software evolves. For builders of safety-critical systems, the goal is compliance that keeps pace with iteration instead of forcing teams to choose between speed and approval.
arxiv-2511-11850:
Ali Mashhadireza and Ali Sadighi pair iterative learning control with a small neural network to keep a linear Lorentz force actuator on trajectory despite friction. Iterative learning improves with each repeated pass, but changing commands and time-varying friction leave residual errors that fixed learning cannot fully cancel.

The network estimates the needed learning effort for new reference commands, so the controller adapts at reference changes and converges faster. Deliberately simple network design keeps online training and implementation practical for real-time use, unlike heavier predecessors. Experiments confirm precise tracking across varied conditions. Precision motion systems, from stages to scanners, are the natural beneficiaries of cheap, adaptive friction compensation.
arxiv-2511-12050:
Jing-Hui Huang and Xiang-Yun Hu tackle timing jitter, a stubborn source of error in pump-probe tests that measure tiny time delays. Their simulations work at a scale of a few attoseconds, which is far below what direct timing can hold steady. They combine weak value amplification with deep learning to recover the delay.

Weak values make the small delay shift the interference pattern more, but they also distort that pattern. Two neural networks then read the pattern: one estimates the delay directly, and one sorts it into set classes. Both beat the older Fourier method, and the classifier still works in a hard phase case where the older method fails.
arxiv-2511-12350: Armand Kanga and Etienne Pardoux extend an earlier result on a spatial epidemic model of SIR type, where people are susceptible, infected or recovered and do not move. Infectivity depends on how long each person has been infected, and infections can act at a distance. The domain is now an unbounded region. As the population size grows without limit, they prove a law of large numbers for the model.
arxiv-2511-12550:
Edward Elliott, C. M. Baugh and Cedric Lacey revisit a controversy about distant sub-millimetre galaxies, bright dusty systems seen at high redshift. Models that build galaxies hierarchically have struggled to match these objects, and some argued a top-heavy distribution of stellar masses in starbursts is required. The authors test that claim with a semi-analytical galaxy model.

Using Bayesian optimisation, they search the model's fifteen-dimensional parameter space in under two hundred evaluations, far fewer than older searches. They demand a match to local galaxy brightness, sub-millimetre counts and redshift spread at once. With a universal mass distribution no parameter choice fits all three, which sets up the comparison with a version where the starburst slope can vary.
arxiv-2511-12750:
Ahmed Hussain, Asmaa Abdallah, Abdulkadir Celik, and Ahmed M. Eltawil compare two antenna layouts for near-field communication, circular arrays and linear arrays. Circular arrays are known to widen the angular region where near-field focusing works. The question is whether wider coverage improves spatial multiplexing, serving separate streams at once. To compare fairly, the authors define a new boundary for the effective near-field region, tied to where beam focusing stays effective at each angle.

They derive closed-form formulas for beam depth and for that boundary in circular arrays. With the same number of antenna elements, linear arrays focus more tightly and reach farther. With the same total aperture length, circular arrays edge ahead slightly. Simulations match the theory: linear arrays give higher total data rate under the element limit, circular ones a small gain under the aperture limit. The right choice depends on which constraint binds.
arxiv-2511-12850:
Saranzaya Magsarjav, Jonathan Tuke, Lewis Mitchell, and Melissa Humphries warn against a tempting shortcut in topic modeling: trusting a model because it gives the same answer twice. Analysts often judge topic models by consistency across runs, quietly assuming repeatable topics are the true ones.
