To test that, the authors generate synthetic text corpora from a known Latent Dirichlet Allocation process. The true topics are known, then run the model fifty times on each corpus and score both consistency and recovery of the truth.

The model reliably found the right number of topics and often settled into highly consistent solutions. Those stable solutions often missed the true topics. Repeatability and recovery are different properties, and internal stability is not evidence of correctness. The authors advise validating topic models with several complementary criteria before drawing conclusions, especially in high-stakes work. The title states the moral plainly: repeatability is not recovery.
arxiv-2511-13450:
Álvaro Corrochano López and Carlos García Sánchez test whether Apple's Neural Engine, built for machine learning, can run classic high-performance computing tasks well. Specialized chips now sit in most systems, and graphics processors already crossed over to general use. The question is whether a neural engine can do the same for science codes.

They ran matrix multiplication, Jacobi, and multigrid methods on the engine across M1 and M4 chips and compared speed and power with the graphics unit. With careful adaptation, the engine reached competitive speed on matrix work in their tests. Its power draw was far lower than the graphics unit's, a strong point for energy-aware computing.
arxiv-2511-13550:
Irene Cazzaniga and Toni Giorgino release MDIntrinsicDimension, a Python package that measures the intrinsic dimension of molecular motion paths. Such runs record high-dimensional motion over time, but the true motion often lives on a far smaller set of variables. That minimal count reveals how complex a molecule's collective motion really is.

The package uses rotation- and translation-invariant features such as backbone angles and residue distances with modern tools. Users can measure the whole molecule, slide a window along the sequence, or focus on single structural elements, in total or over time. Tests on fast folding data showed local flexibility that standard measures miss.
arxiv-2511-13650:
Aayush Saxena and 20 co-authors present Webb observations of a massive galaxy taking shape at redshift four. Imaging and integral-field spectroscopy show the radio galaxy TGSSJ1530+1049 sits inside one of the densest known gatherings of objects at that era. Distinct continuum sources, diffuse interaction traces, and strong line-emitting regions fill the small field.

Bright hydrogen emission runs linearly along the radio axis, hinting at twin illumination cones from a hidden active nucleus, while gas motions show jet impacts over kiloparsec scales. At least four nearby objects already hold high stellar mass and brisk star formation. The group should merge into one massive galaxy within a few billion years, much like simulated cluster giants.
arxiv-2511-13750:
E. Zhixuan Zeng, Yuhao Chen, and Alexander Wong introduce SCALEX, a framework that maps the hidden concept space of image diffusion models at scale. Generators absorb social stereotypes about gender, race, and profession, but older audits either check a short fixed list or need hand reading of latent directions. Subtle associations can hide from both styles of audit.

SCALEX pulls meaningful directions out of the model's hidden space using only natural language prompts, with no retraining or labeling. Auditors can then compare any concepts systematically across the whole space. Tests detected gender bias in profession prompts, ranked how identity words align, and exposed clustered concept structure without supervision, making bias hunting broader and more repeatable.
arxiv-2511-13850:
István Juhász, Jan van Mill, and Lajos Soukup answer open questions in topology about shrinking spaces without changing their basic form. A condensation is a continuous one-to-one map onto another space, and the authors ask when extra demands can be met at the same time. Their note gives cases where the target must give up compactness, group structure, or both.

They show some locally compact spaces can be condensed onto separable spaces but never onto compact separable ones. They also build, for every cardinal size, a locally compact group of that doubled size that condenses onto a compact space but not onto a compact group. The results settle questions raised by Arhangel'skii and Buzyakova.
arxiv-2511-14050:
Liqian Qin, Aviv Gibali, Cuijie Zhang, and one co-author design faster algorithms for monotone inclusion problems, a general form behind many optimization and equilibrium tasks. Their setting mixes three operators: one maximally monotone, one monotone and Lipschitz, and one cocoercive. They extend three classical splitting schemes by adding a nonlinear momentum term to each.

Under suitable step-size conditions all three methods converge weakly, and under strong monotonicity they converge at a linear rate. Early numerical tests on synthetic data and on real portfolio optimization problems, cast as quadratic programs, show the new algorithms beating their classical counterparts. The work targets structured problems where splitting is the natural attack.
arxiv-2511-14150:
Luyang Li, Min Zhou, Zhiyang Liu, and three co-authors compute how neutral meson masses shift in hot, magnetized matter. Their tool is a three-flavor Polyakov-extended Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model, which adds a gluon background through the Polyakov loop and mimics inverse magnetic catalysis with a field-dependent parameter. They track the kaon pair, the pion, and the eta mesons through rising temperature.

Kaon mass is governed by chiral symmetry breaking and jumps at the Mott transition, where the meson falls apart into quarks. The pion behaves differently at high temperature because of flavor mixing with the eta family. The eta mesons also feel the axial anomaly, and their masses fall, jump, then recover as temperature climbs.
arxiv-2511-14250:
Jonathan Yaffe, Ben Maman, and Meinard Müller train music transcription systems with note counts instead of precise timing. Turning audio into symbolic scores normally needs frame-perfect annotations, which are costly and often impossible. Weakly supervised rivals still lean on alignment tools that are error-prone and heavy. CountEM supervises with histograms: how many times each note occurs in a segment.

An expectation-maximization loop refines the network's predictions using only those counts, never an explicit local alignment. Annotation effort drops sharply while accuracy holds up. On piano, guitar, and multi-instrument data sets, CountEM matched or beat existing weakly supervised methods, improving the robustness and reach of automatic transcription.
arxiv-2511-14350:
Sourav Ballav, Wen-Yu Wen, and Chi-Hsien Tai model black hole evaporation as a small quantum circuit with a dial for forbidden leakage. Semi-causality says information may fall in but never propagate back out across the horizon. Building on an earlier evaporation circuit, the authors add a controlled gate that leaks a tunable amount of information outward while keeping the whole evolution unitary.

With the dial at zero the circuit reproduces the classic Page-like entropy curve with full late-time purification. Any positive setting leaves residual entropy and lingering entanglement at late times, meaning the radiation never fully purifies. The small-leak regime shows a distinctive scaling that resembles logarithmic corrections from generalized uncertainty scenarios.
arxiv-2511-14550:
Dimitrios Dimopoulos and four co-authors evaluate how scheduling and congestion control affect multipath TCP performance. Multipath TCP lets one connection use several network paths at once. Gains shrink when paths differ greatly in speed or delay. The study reviews how the protocol works and surveys known scheduling and congestion algorithms.

The team then run broad experiments that pair other schedulers with other congestion controls. Conditions vary widely in path heterogeneity. Results show which combinations hold up and which degrade when paths mismatch. The work gives practical guidance for deploying multipath transport on mixed networks. It also maps where new algorithm design is most needed.
arxiv-2511-14650:
Jingyi Jia and Qinbin Li present AutoTool, a method that cuts the cost of letting language model agents pick their own tools. Popular agent designs ask the model at every step which tool to use next, and those repeated calls are slow and costly. The authors notice that tool use follows habits: one tool tends to follow another in predictable chains.

AutoTool builds a directed graph from past agent runs, where nodes are tools and edges carry the odds of each switch. New tasks then follow the graph instead of asking the model each time. Parameter filling is folded into the same scheme. The result aims at agents that act faster and cheaper on routine work.
arxiv-2511-14850:
Sebastiano D. von Fellenberg, Joseph M. Michail, and eleven co-authors measure how much dust dims mid-infrared light on the way from the center of our galaxy. The galactic center is the best laboratory for studying a supermassive black hole up close, but dust along the line of sight distorts every observation. The team uses Webb telescope data over a small patch around the center.

Two independent methods, one modeling the glow of hot dust and one comparing hydrogen lines, give the dimming across wavelengths. The dimming varies across the field, with dustier spots showing more, and the team releases a public code for the modeling. Every study of the center's black hole flares depends on corrections like these.
arxiv-2511-15150:
Bhargabi Saha and Malay K. Nandy follow warm inflation through its full nonlinear life, with no simplifying shortcuts. In warm inflation, the inflaton field that drives the early expansion leaks energy into radiation as it rolls, so the universe stays warm instead of supercooling. Their model uses the classic quartic potential and a friction that grows with temperature, with settings matched to Planck satellite limits.

Solving the three coupled equations for the field, the radiation, and the expansion exactly, they find two regimes. Weak friction stalls the handover to radiation, while strong friction exits inflation smoothly into a hot, radiation-filled universe. That graceful exit is exactly what a warm model must deliver to connect with the later cosmos.
arxiv-2511-15350:
Nathanael Bosch, Oleksandr Shchur, and three co-authors show that stacking, the workhorse ensemble trick for tables, finally pays off for forecasting time series. Forecasters still mostly blend models with simple averages, even though learned stacking wins in other areas of machine learning. The authors test dozens of ensemble recipes, old and new, across fifty real-world data sets.

Stacking improves accuracy consistently, but no single stacking model wins everywhere. Their answer is a multi-layer stacking framework that layers several stackers so their strengths combine. Across the diverse test suite it delivers superior accuracy more reliably than any one recipe. The result gives forecasting teams a principled upgrade path from plain averaging.
arxiv-2511-15450:
Rémy Mosseri and Jean-François Sadoc explore several attempts to generalize phyllotaxy patterns to three dimensions. Phyllotaxy describes the spiral patterns seen in plants, defined as point sets on surfaces. Known constructions cover flat, spherical, and hyperbolic 2D surfaces. Extending that orderly structure to volumes has no single standard solution.

The authors try stacking shifted planar sets, then a radially triggered building. A promising set on the three sphere follows from the Hopf fibration. A four dimensional product example and a cut and project candidate are also presented. Comparing distinct routes clarifies what 3D phyllotaxy could mean. The paper is exploratory, mapping options rather than crowning one building.
arxiv-2511-15850:
David G. Radcliffe proves elementary lower bounds for the digital sums of several fast-growing number sequences. The digital sum of a number adds its decimal digits, a simple quantity that becomes surprisingly hard to control for powers, factorials, and least common multiples. Radcliffe goal is to show these sums must grow at least logarithmically, using only elementary number theory.

Separate arguments cover powers, multiples of powers, factorials, and the least common multiple of the first several integers. The paper closes with an expository proof of Stewart theorem on digital sums of powers. That closing proof uses Baker theorem on linear forms in logarithms, a deep result, and is presented for exposition rather than as part of the elementary bounds.
arxiv-2511-16450:
Ziyue Xu and five co-authors optimize federated learning for large language models through message quantization and streaming. Federated training keeps data local, but billion parameter models overwhelm memory and communication links. An open federated learning toolkit is enhanced for this regime. Quantization shrinks messages between clients and server, while streaming manages large objects efficiently in memory.

Together the techniques improve scalability and integration with existing systems. Local resource constraints ease because full models need not sit in memory at once. Privacy preserving training of very large models becomes more practical. The engineering advances target hospitals, banks, and other settings where data cannot move. Communication efficiency is the binding constraint the work directly attacks.
arxiv-2511-16850:
Kritti Sharma and five co-authors ask whether the messy selection effects behind fast radio burst surveys corrupt the cosmology drawn from them. Bursts probe the universe's baryons through the dispersion measure-redshift relation, but instrument sensitivity, search efficiency, and source evolution all filter which bursts get seen.

Forward-modeled population simulations explore more realistic survey scenarios. A neural network emulator, trained on fifty thousand halo-model simulations, supplies the cosmic dispersion variance to within a few percent out to high redshift, and enables fast likelihoods. The headline is reassuring for today: selection effects reshape the joint distribution strongly yet barely move the conditional distribution used for inference. Biases stay under one standard deviation for hundred-burst samples. For ten-thousand-burst surveys the biases can exceed three standard deviations, so future analyses must model selection explicitly.
arxiv-2511-17350:
The LUX-ZEPLIN collaboration, listing more than two hundred authors, reports a search for new physics in low-energy electron recoils. The LZ detector, a large tank watched for tiny flashes, gathered data over its first two science runs amounting to a four point two tonne-year exposure. The team looks for signs that go beyond known physics, such as particles of dark matter being absorbed or extra interactions of solar neutrinos.

The data match a background-only account, so no new signal is claimed. Instead the team sets fresh limits on several ideas, covering solar axion-like particles, mirror dark matter, and bosonic dark matter. Some of these limits are the tightest yet for their class, which narrows where such particles could still be hiding.
arxiv-2511-17750:
Zhimin Shao, Abhay Yadav, Rama Chellappa, and Cheng Peng present SPIDER, a system for finding matching points between images so that three-dimensional structure and camera poses can be recovered. Matching across aerial, indoor, and outdoor views is hard because look, scale, and angle shift so much. Recent three-dimensional foundation models give spatially aware matches, but those matches tend to pile onto flat areas like walls and floors and miss fine detail.

The team first probes several vision foundation models with simple tests to see which carry the best matching signals. Building on those findings, they design their estimator to spread reliable matches more evenly and hold up under large viewpoint changes. The goal is sturdier spatial perception for mapping and navigation systems.
arxiv-2511-18550:
Oguzhan Akgun and Ryo Okui build tests for panel data where units fall into hidden groups with distinct slopes. If groups are split from the data, standard tests treat that split as known truth and can mislead. Worse, the groups may not truly split at all, a case where many past methods lose their base.

Their fix conditions on the found group form: tests use the distribution of slope estimates given that form. The tests stay valid even when no true split exists, and they beat standard limits in small samples when a split does hold. Exact validity holds for Gaussian noise with known spread, with a broad form for other noise. The work targets general linear claims, not just group sameness.
arxiv-2511-18650:
K. Aivazelis and 96 co-authors report the performance of new time projection chambers in the upgraded T2K near detector. T2K is a neutrino beam experiment; its off axis near detector checks the beam close to its source. The upgrade adds two chambers with resistive Micromegas readouts and thin composite field cage walls.

The report details the new parts: gas system, gas watch chambers, and data capture. Tests with neutrino beams and cosmic rays are matched against simulations. The chambers give sharper position reads and better particle identification than the old set. Both gains serve the precision goals of the experiment. The work is a builder's record of a detector that must run for years.
arxiv-2511-18750:
Samya Praharaj and Koulik Khamaru show that chasing the best worst case loss can break sound inference in bandit problems. A bandit algorithm learns which arm pays best by trial, and its data are adaptive, not independent. Sample means under such sampling can fail the central limit theorem, which voids standard confidence claims.

A stability test by Lai and Wei marks when normal limits hold. The famed UCB method passes it, yet UCB is not minimax optimal. The pair give broad structural terms under which optimism based methods, the family UCB heads, break the stability test. As a result, minimax optimal optimism methods fall in that trap. Best loss and sound inference may not coexist in this family.
arxiv-2511-18950:
Juntao Gao, Feiyang Ye, Jing Zhang, and Wenjing Qian present Compressor-VLA, a method for slimming the visual input to robot control models. Vision-language-action models are powerful but slow, because they process many redundant visual tokens, which blocks real-time use on robots. Plain pruning cuts tokens without regard to the task and can discard details the action depends on. Their framework instead compresses under the guidance of the instruction itself.

Two modules divide the work: one distils the holistic, task-relevant context, and one preserves fine spatial detail. Together they aim to keep both the scene's gist and the precise features a gripper needs. The authors present the hybrid design as a route to robot models that run fast enough for live deployment without going blind to what matters.
arxiv-2511-19050:
Wei Wei and twelve co-authors chart the critical current density across a family of iron selenide superconductors that shows two separate superconducting domes as its composition changes. Each dome sits beside a distinct quantum critical point tied to nematic order, the tendency of electrons to pick a direction, with the second point also entangled with magnetism. The team tracks how the current capacity evolves with doping through both domes in single crystals.

Surprisingly, they find three peaks. Two sharp maxima sit exactly at the endpoints of the nematic phases, one in the tellurium-doped series and one in the sulfur-doped series. The authors explore vortex pinning and argue that fluctuations near the quantum critical points contribute to the boost. The link between critical fluctuations and practical current capacity is the paper's central thread.
arxiv-2511-19150:
Georgios Maragkopoulos, Lazaros Chavatzoglou, Aikaterini Mandilara, and Dimitris Syvridis build a quantum neural network for credit risk that keeps its reasoning visible. Finance models must balance accuracy with interpretability, since a loan decision carries real consequences. Their network runs on a single qudit, a quantum unit with more than two levels. Encoding both the data features and the trainable parameters inside one unitary evolution that explores the full space of states.

Because feature importance shows up in the size of the learned coefficients, the model's ranking of risk factors stays transparent. On a real, imbalanced credit data set from Taiwan, it beats logistic regression and matches random forests on a balanced accuracy score. Two new metrics quantify how faithful its feature ranking is, addressing the audit needs of lenders.
arxiv-2511-19350:
Nikita Neveditsin, Pawan Lingras, and Vijay Mago cluster short texts without being told how many groups to find. Guessing that number in advance is a standing weakness of short-text clustering. Their spectral method reads the count off the structure of the graph Laplacian's spectrum, built from cosine similarities between text embeddings.

An adaptive sampling step keeps the method fast on large data. To grade clusters without true labels, they propose the Cohesion Ratio, which compares likeness inside clusters against the global background. On six data sets and four embedding models, the ratio tracks standard external scores well, and guided versions of K-Means and hierarchical clustering perform strongly.
arxiv-2511-19450:
M. Zeeshan Haider, Tayyaba Noreen, M. D. Assuncao, and Kaiwen Zhang design a smarter way to split blockchain work across shards. Sharding lets parts of a ledger process transactions in parallel, but fixed assignments create hot shards, congestion, and heavy cross-shard traffic. Their protocol forecasts workloads and assigns accounts ahead of time.

A temporal forecasting model predicts load several blocks ahead, while a safety-limited reinforcement learning controller reconfigures shards within strict bounds. A safety gate caps stake concentration, migration cost, and usage levels, and migrations happen atomically in bounded steps. The goal is steady load balance without weakening the rules validators rely on.
arxiv-2511-20050:
Yan Li, Yingzhao Li, and Gim Hee Lee present Active3D, a framework that explores a scene in order to rebuild it in fine detail. Instead of scanning blindly, the system keeps a multi-level map of its own uncertainty and plans where to look next. A hybrid representation fuses neural fields with Gaussian primitives, joining global structure with local surface detail.

From that state, the authors derive a layered uncertainty volume covering both global structure quality and local surface confidence. High-uncertainty viewpoints become sparse attention anchors for keyframe choice, and a sliding window refines local areas. Next views are picked by expected information gain, with a risk-sensitive path planner for safe motion. Benchmarks show top accuracy, completeness, and rendering quality.
arxiv-2511-20150:
Ehrhardt, Günther, and Ševčovič show how to merge and split energy-based system models safely. Their 2025 paper works with port-Hamiltonian systems. Such models track energy storage, loss, and exchange. Ports connect the parts to each other and the world. Coupling port-Hamiltonian parts normally preserves the structure.

The team gives a systematic two-way transformation method. Coupled parts become one single joint system. In reverse, a single system splits into weakly coupled parts. The single-system form favors stability and soundness. The split form favors distributed, parallel simulation. Operator splitting or dynamic iteration can then run it. Linear input-output relations underpin the constructions here. Energy conservation and dissipation survive both directions. Nonlinear ordinary equation systems are covered too. Future work targets adaptive coupling strategies. Structure-preserving time stepping is another open direction. Algebraic and stochastic extensions are planned as well.
arxiv-2511-20350:
McGrath measures the size of symmetry groups defined by shift rules. His 2025 paper builds size formulas for difference algebraic groups. Ordinary algebraic groups are cut out by polynomial equations. Difference versions use equations involving shift maps too. With several shifts that commute, the theory is called partial. Two main results anchor the paper.

First, the defining ideal of such a group is finitely generated. Only finitely many difference equations are ever needed. That finite generation unlocks the second result. A dimension polynomial exists for every such group in this setting. The polynomial counts the sizes of finite approximations as they grow. A special case is restated in symbolic dynamics language. There, the group is fixed by one finite window plus shift invariance. The work was supported by an EPSRC doctoral studentship. It puts this branch of algebra on the same footing as the classical theory.
arxiv-2511-20450:
Wirth settles a conjecture about distances between quantum states. His 2025 mathematics paper proves the triangle inequality for a quantum Wasserstein divergence. Wasserstein distances measure optimal transport cost classically. Quantum versions try to do the same for quantum states. De Palma and Trevisan defined one such modified distance. Whether it obeyed the triangle inequality stayed open.

A distance needs that inequality to behave like a true metric. Wirth's proof resolves their conjecture affirmatively. Complex analysis methods power the argument. The key step is a new integral representation of transport cost. Static definitions like this one generalize the Monge-Kantorovich formula. Dynamical rivals instead follow the Benamou-Brenier viewpoint. The distance has zero self-distance and symmetry by construction. Non-degeneracy depends on the chosen cost operators. Quantum optimal transport has grown rapidly in recent decades. This result firms up one of its central definitions.
arxiv-2511-20550:
Bryant, Huerta y Munive, and Foster machine-check the numeric recipes machine learning stands on. Their 2025 paper builds a checking framework inside Isabelle/HOL. Numeric methods approach solutions step by step, from root-finding to gradient descent. Bugs or shaky proofs in them undermine trust in systems built on top. Formal checking of such methods is still young.

Their language lets users state numeric programs directly. Programs carry loop invariants for correctness reasoning. A generator produces proof goals that automated methods discharge. Lemmas from the HOL-Analysis library close those goals. The bisection method shows the workflow end to end. Fixed-point iteration serves as the second worked example. Checked code exports to runnable source through Isabelle's generator. The library gained higher-order derivatives as a by-product. Taylor's theorem in Peano form was formalized too. Users need not grasp the generator's internals to use it.
arxiv-2511-20650:
Tooba Tehreem Sheikh and co-authors at MBZUAI present in 2025 MedROV, a detector that finds objects in medical scans even when it was never trained on their names. Ordinary detectors only recognise a fixed list of categories. A scan showing pneumonia is missed if pneumonia was never on that list. MedROV instead takes a text description at run time and searches the image for whatever the words describe, across scan types from X-rays to microscope slides.

To teach it, the team built Omnis, a training set of 600,000 labelled examples drawn from 35 datasets covering nine kinds of medical imaging, with machine-generated labels filling gaps. MedROV beat the previous best medical foundation model by an average of 40 points on the mAP50 accuracy score. It also topped closed-set detectors by more than 3 points on the same measure, and runs at 70 frames per second, fast enough for live clinical use.
arxiv-2511-21050:
Dongkyu Derek Cho and colleagues challenge in 2025 the belief that making a language model more capable must make it less safe. Fine-tuning normally erodes safety alignment even on benign data, across supervised tuning and human-feedback reinforcement learning alike. The team studies reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where the reward is an objective check, such as whether an answer is exactly right. Its safety behaviour had never been analysed.

Theory comes first: under KL-constrained optimisation they bound how far safety can drift, and prove conditions under which degradation vanishes entirely. Experiments across five adversarial safety benchmarks then show the method improving reasoning while holding, or even strengthening, safety guardrails. Ablations vary the optimisation algorithm, comparing GRPO with REINFORCE++, plus model scale and task domain. The authors argue the safety-capability trade-off is an artefact of training method, not a law, with direct lessons for deploying reasoning models.
arxiv-2511-21150:
Multimodal language models read images through a vision encoder, then compress the flood of visual tokens before the language model sees them. Encoding whole images at native resolution works better than slicing, but the cost balloons with resolution. Shichu Sun and colleagues present LLaVA-UHD v3 in 2025, built on progressive visual compression, a method that plugs into a Vision Transformer. Refined patch embedding allows finer patch sizes, while windowed compression inside the transformer layers merges local tokens step by step.

The rebuilt encoder, ViT-UHD, matched the strong MoonViT encoder's benchmark scores while cutting time-to-first-token by a factor of 2.4 in identical model setups. The full LLaVA-UHD v3 system matched Qwen2-VL's performance with a 1.9-fold cut in that latency. Tests span 15 benchmarks for the model and six for the encoder alone. Code and checkpoints are promised for release, aimed at cheaper high-resolution multimodal models.
arxiv-2511-21450:
Per Austrin, Johan Håstad, and Björn Martinsson ask when a promise makes a hard problem easy, in a 2025 theoretical computer science paper. Promise constraint problems hand the solver a guarantee, like a graph being 3-colorable, and ask only for a weaker prize, like a 5-coloring. A predicate is called promise-useful if some nontrivial promise version built on it is efficiently solvable, and promise-useless otherwise.

Austrin and his coauthors derive conditions settling both sides, assuming P differs from NP. Their criteria classify every Boolean predicate of arity at most four, and almost all of arity five. For large arities, they prove the vast majority of predicates are promise-useless, so helpful promises are rare gems. The engine of the work is a close study of Promise-SAT, combining the LP plus affine integer programming algorithm of Brakensiek and coauthors with new NP-hardness tests.
arxiv-2511-21550:
Thai-Khanh Nguyen and five coauthors give a sequence model a sense of momentum for recognizing human activity, in 2025. Watches and phones identify walking, sitting, or falling from inertial sensors, but the signals are noisy and activities unfold over long spans. Mamba, a state-space sequence model, handles long sequences cheaply, yet its first-order memory fades. The team borrowed momentum, the physics trick of carrying velocity, to enrich its memory.

Their Momentum Mamba adds a second-order dynamics pathway to the hidden state, damping vanishing gradients and improving robustness and long-range modeling. Two extensions push further: Complex Momentum Mamba scales memory by frequency, and Adam Momentum Mamba adapts by variance. Across multiple benchmarks, the models consistently beat both plain Mamba and transformer baselines in accuracy, noise robustness, and convergence speed. The gains cost only moderate extra training, making momentum-augmented models a scalable default for sensor data.
arxiv-2511-21650:
Francesco Capozzi, Eligio Lisi, Francesco Marcone, Antonio Marrone, and Antonio Palazzo sharpen two fundamental neutrino numbers with brand-new data, in 2025. The parameters govern how the two lightest neutrino states mix and split in mass, and they are probed by solar and reactor neutrino oscillations. A 2024 global analysis knew them only to within a few percent.

Adding the latest SNO+ constraints shifted the best fits slightly. Then the first results from China's JUNO reactor experiment cut the uncertainties dramatically. The updated global bounds put the squared mass difference at 7.48 units of a hundred-thousandth of an electronvolt squared, and the mixing measure at 0.3085, give or take 0.0073 in the same units. Those are errors of just over one percent for the splitting and about two and a half percent for the mixing. The authors also flag subtle effects that may one day break the remaining degeneracy over neutrino mass ordering.
arxiv-2511-21750:
Di Feng and eleven coauthors introduce SO-Bench, the first systematic benchmark of whether multimodal models can emit correctly structured output from images, in 2025. In real deployments, answers feed downstream software, so they must match predefined JSON schemas exactly. Text-only structured generation had been studied; the visual side had not.

SO-Bench spans four visual domains: interface screens, natural images, documents, and charts. It draws on over 6,500 diverse JSON schemas and 1,800 curated image-schema pairs with human-verified quality. Testing exposed persistent gaps. The strongest systems, GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5-Pro, followed schemas with over 95 percent accuracy yet produced fully correct outputs only up to nearly 19 percent of the time on a fuzzy match. Small 3 and 7 billion parameter models lagged far behind. Follow-up training substantially improved structured output, showing the weakness is trainable rather than fixed.
arxiv-2511-21850:
Alpern and Rachev blend environmental, social, and governance scores, known as ESG ratings, into a classic portfolio-building method called Black-Litterman allocation. In their strategy, ESG scores bias the estimated equilibrium returns fed into the allocation, via shrinkage toward a stable centre. Asset returns are modelled with a heavy-tailed normal-inverse Gaussian distribution rather than a normal one, and risk is measured by CVaR, which focuses on the worst tail outcomes instead of average swings.

Portfolios were reallocated daily over a 4.7 year test period, 2017 to 2021, across many risk aversion and ESG weighting combinations. A soft limit on how much the portfolio could change each day proved important. The most successful strategies returned approximately 40 to 45 percent annually over that test period in the authors' backtest, a striking backtest result for a simple, carefully constrained ESG tilt.
arxiv-2511-21950:
Liu and colleagues study a large system of coupled random wave equations, the hyperbolic O(N) linear sigma model, with N interacting fields. Each field obeys a damped, noisy nonlinear wave equation on a two-dimensional torus, the surface of a donut, coupled to all the others through their shared average energy term. The question is what the whole system looks like when N becomes enormous, in physics language, its mean-field limit.

After proving global well-posedness, the authors prove the finite-N dynamics converge to a single mean-field equation. For local time intervals they obtain an explicit convergence rate, of order N to the power of minus one-half plus epsilon for any positive epsilon. They extend the same rate to the invariant Gibbs dynamics on large time intervals.
arxiv-2511-22050:
Bian, Wang, Tang, and Lee, neuroscientists at Carnegie Mellon, map how brain area V4. A mid-level stage of the primate visual system, organizes its coding of shape, texture, color, and three-dimensional form. Classic experiments probed each feature separately, leaving open how one neuron's preferences across features relate and how the preferences tile the cortical surface. The team attacks the question with V4 'digital twins,' neural network models fitted to wide-field calcium imaging from tens of thousands of natural images.

Probing the twins systematically, they find neurons preferring two-dimensional contour shape also prefer 3D solid surfaces and object form, while texture-preferring neurons prefer flat surfaces. The pattern suggests V4 splits its work into a shape module encoding 3D geometry and an appearance module encoding surface properties, arranged as interleaved clusters across the topographic map. A division of labor future physiology experiments can test directly.
arxiv-2511-22150:
Rottach and colleagues study how text embedding models arrange meaning in geometric space. Embeddings turn text into lists of numbers, and models differ in the shapes those numbers form. Researchers use topological and geometric measures to describe those shapes. The team compares many such measures across a wide set of models and datasets. A full view, the authors argue, is essential for understanding these spaces.

They find the measures overlap heavily, so most add little new information. Single measures also fail to tell embedding spaces apart reliably. Their answer is Unified Topological Signatures, a combined profile of a space from many angles. The signatures predict model-specific traits and reveal similarities driven by model architecture. They also link structure to ranking quality and predict how easily documents can be retrieved. That gives practitioners a fuller way to judge and compare embedding models.
arxiv-2511-22250:
Jiang, Wang, Cheng, and Ge, medical imaging researchers, reconstruct the colon's 3D shape from a single camera's video. Colonoscopy images defeat geometry models: surfaces are glossy rather than matte, the light moves with the scope, and long stretches are textureless. Their ColonAdapter fine-tunes a pretrained 3D geometric foundation model for this domain with self-supervision, keeping its priors while adapting them to clinical imagery, crucially without needing the camera's ground-truth internal parameters.

Two additions target the failure modes: a Detail Restoration Module recovers structure in low-texture regions, helped by a geometry consistency loss enforcing scale coherence. A confidence-weighted photometric loss stabilizes training where reflections corrupt the signal. On synthetic and real data it reaches state-of-the-art pose, depth, and point-map results, fixing DUSt3R's textureless-scene errors. The framework needs no ground-truth geometry labels for the colonoscopy data.
arxiv-2511-22550:
Idir and colleagues compare ten statistical models for mapping city air pollution from cheap sensors. Low-cost sensors on vehicles promise far denser coverage than fixed monitoring stations, but their data quality is questionable. Working in Nantes, France, the team fed fixed and mobile low-cost sensor data, plus auxiliary variables, into ten literature models. They validated outputs against reference stations. They tested both gap-filling in time and forecasting ahead.

Two lessons stand out. First, models fed low-cost data showed a pronounced bias against reference station data, in both interpolation and prediction. Second, machine learning models, random forest, XGBoost, and a hybrid, performed best at forecasting, with correlations above 0.4 on every indicator. The authors conclude that data quality matters more than model sophistication: low-cost sensors should never be used alone, but integrated with, and calibrated against, fixed station data.
arxiv-2511-22650:
Budzinskiy, Kazeev, and Olshanskii generalise tensor compression to arrays whose entries are functions. Reduced-order modelling of parametric partial differential equations needs stand-ins for the parameter-to-solution map. Low-rank tensor approximation is a compressor, except that a PDE solution at each parameter value is a whole function, not a number. The authors show Hilbert space inner-product geometry is enough: they define Tucker rank, a higher-order singular value decomposition, and a Tucker-cross decomposition for function-valued tensors, despite the field arithmetic.

On that foundation they build a cross-approximation algorithm sampling only tensor fibres, making the method non-intrusive. The PDE solver is a black box. The reduced model reads as an encoder-decoder pair: nonlinear encoder, multilinear decoder. Numerical experiments on two nonlinear parametric PDE systems demonstrate the approach, positioned for parametric workloads, inverse problems, optimal control, uncertainty quantification, and digital twins.
arxiv-2511-22750:
Mouli settles a classification question linking number fields and group theory. Drungilas and coauthors asked which triples of positive integers can occur as the degrees of two number fields and their compositum. Via the Galois correspondence, degrees become subgroup indices. A triple is index-realizable if some group has finite-index subgroups realising the first two numbers as indices and the third as the index of their intersection.

The main theorem characterises index-realizable triples completely. A triple is realizable if and only if a bipartite graph exists, with no isolated vertices and degree conditions on its parts, encoding the intersection pattern. Non-realizable triples are pinned down just as sharply, by graph-theoretic obstructions. Since every compositum-feasible triple must be index-realizable, the classification gives necessary conditions for the original problem while standing as a clean combinatorial result, proved largely by explicit constructions.
arxiv-2511-23450:
Agarwal and colleagues tackle the annotation bottleneck in object detection. Teaching a model a new object category normally demands large amounts of hand-labeled images that rare, long-tailed classes do not have. They define the object-centric data setting, in which the only material available for a new category is object-centric data such as multi-view images or 3D models. They ask how far synthetic training images can carry a detector.

Four synthesis routes are compared, from cut-and-paste compositing through 3D rendering to image diffusion models, generating cluttered scenes with realism and context for fine-tuning. Enhanced paste methods that add geometric, lighting, and perspective cues plus contextual backgrounds beat the plain cut-paste baseline. A combined 3D copy-paste method does not. The authors warn that realistic constraints like surface placement can shrink viewpoint diversity enough to cancel their own benefit.
arxiv-2512-00250:
Angular applications often suffer subtle bugs in how they handle reactive data streams. Shrinivass Arunachalam Balasubramanian presents ng-reactive-lint in 2025, a smarter linting tool for Angular apps. Misuse of Observables, Signals, and change detection can cause slowdowns that are hard to diagnose.

Later Angular versions introduced a signal-first model, yet many enterprise codebases still rely on older RxJS patterns. Those patterns can create unpredictable update flows, memory leaks, and excessive change cycles. A linter that catches such misuse early helps large teams keep web applications fast and maintainable as they grow. Linting shifts bug catching to the moment code is written, when fixes are cheapest. The tool targets reactive patterns specifically, rather than style rules in general.
arxiv-2512-00450:
Judging personality and interview performance from video and audio could speed up hiring, but datasets are scarce. Amit Kumar Gupta and co-authors at Manipal University Jaipur present RecruitView in 2025, a multimodal dataset for human resources applications. Automated assessment remains challenging because traits have geometric structure that simple methods miss.

The dataset supports predicting personality and interview performance from multimodal behavioral data. Shared data lets researchers compare methods fairly instead of training on private recordings. The work also raises the stakes for care: tools trained on such data influence real people's job prospects. Multimodal data combine face, voice, and movement, each carrying part of the signal. Personality prediction from behavior is contested, which makes shared benchmarks even more important. For firms that hire at scale, the gain is a shared test bed. New tools can be tried on the same clips, and the scores can be checked side by side.
arxiv-2512-00550:
Cells inside tissue live under constant mechanical stress, and measuring that stress explains much of development and disease. Lucas Anger and co-authors present tissue stress measurements with Bayesian Inversion Stress Microscopy in 2025. Mechanical forces shape morphogenesis, collective migration, cell division, and cell death.

Stress inside tissue cannot be probed directly, so it must be inferred from observed deformations. A Bayesian inversion states its uncertainty along with the estimate, which keeps biologists from overreading noisy maps. Better stress maps help researchers understand how tissues grow, heal, and sometimes turn cancerous. Bayesian inversion also regularizes the inference, keeping wild stress maps in check. Stress microscopy serves developmental biology, where forces sculpt growing tissues. For folks who grow tissues in the lab, the gain is a map they can trust. The pull and push in each part, with a fair sense of how sure the map is.
arxiv-2512-00850:
Haishan Wang, Mohammad Hassan Vali, and Arno Solin present Smol-GS in a 2025 computer graphics paper. A popular way to store 3D scenes is Gaussian splatting, which fills space with soft colored blobs called splats. Full scenes can take huge storage, especially when fine detail matters.

Smol-GS learns compact codes for such scenes. Splat positions are stored through a recursive voxel hierarchy, a tree of nested cubes. Features on each splat keep abstract cues like color, opacity, shape change, and material. Spatial and semantic information are packed together. Smaller scene files would help stream detailed 3D content to phones and headsets.
arxiv-2512-00950:
Arnaldo Spalvieri works out a probability law for bosonic systems in a 2025 physics paper. Bosons are particles that can share the same state, so a system is described by occupancy numbers, counts of how many sit in each state. The canonical setting fixes the temperature and lets energy be exchanged with an environment.

Spalvieri derives the canonical distribution of those occupancy numbers. He shows that canonical typicality applies here. Almost any pure state of the whole universe gives the same mixed state for the system, once the environment is traced out. In the limit, the distribution tends toward a multinomial one.
arxiv-2512-01250:
Geng Zhao, Yun Chen, Jiayuan Zhang, Jing Tang, and Yuangang Deng propose a scheme for unusual light in a 2025 physics paper. Nonclassical light, whose photon patterns no classical wave can mimic, is a resource for quantum technology. The authors work with atomic arrays that can be reconfigured, coupled to an optical cavity.

By controlling the collective interference phase of the atoms, the system switches behavior. On one side sits single-photon blockade, where photons enter one at a time. On the other, it emits high-purity bundles of several photons together. The pattern of correlations follows atom-number parity and cavity detuning, giving experimenters clear knobs to turn.
arxiv-2512-01350:
Songting Li and a large team map the halo of stars around our galaxy. The halo is a vast, sparse cloud of old stars. Its shape tells how our galaxy grew by eating smaller ones. The team used giant stars from the DESI survey's second data set.

They track stars from near the core to far out in the halo. They find the halo is both twisted and split in two zones. They also map how star counts thin with range. A twisted, split halo points to a past merger that still marks our galaxy's form today.
arxiv-2512-02050:
Gravity might be carried by a particle with a small mass, a massive graviton, and that idea has a famous catch. Th. A. Rijken and J. W. Wagenaar present in 2025 a quantization of massive and massless spin-2 particles using an auxiliary-field method, and revisit the catch directly.

The catch is the vDVZ discontinuity: a massive graviton's predictions may fail to approach Einstein's as its mass shrinks, spoiling agreement with data such as the precession of Mercury's orbit. The authors study perihelion precession in their spin-2 theory at tree level. The paper continues a long effort to learn whether massive gravity can survive contact with the solar system.
arxiv-2512-02150:
On a triangular lattice, neighboring spins cannot all oppose each other at once, and this frustration breeds exotic magnetic phases. Anna Keselman and four co-authors map in 2025 how one such antiferromagnet behaves when a magnetic field is applied, across all its coupling strengths.

They combine large-scale density matrix renormalization group simulations with self-consistent spin-wave theory, two methods that check each other. The resulting phase diagram shows quantum fluctuations stabilizing coplanar spin order everywhere in the range studied. Triangular magnets are test beds for quantum materials, and a full field-and-coupling map guides experiments hunting new phases.
arxiv-2512-02250:
Random tensors arise when analysts average noisy high-dimensional data, and one key estimate about them was proved in 2022 by Deng, Nahmod, and Yue using the moment method. Claire Kaneshiro gives a new proof of that abstract random tensor estimate in 2025, with a different central tool.

Her proof leans directly on the non-commutative Khintchine inequality, together with a probabilistic decoupling of products of Gaussians. A cleaner proof is not just elegance: it shows which parts of the original argument were essential and may extend to cases the moment method cannot reach. Tensor estimates of this kind underlie work on nonlinear waves and random data problems.
arxiv-2512-02350:
Robots and agents in different places can learn together without sharing data, but offline federated reinforcement learning inherits two problems at once. Nan Qiao and three co-authors show in 2025 that most existing methods collapse when the logged data differ in quality from client to client, and propose FOVA to fix it.

In the offline setting, agents learn from fixed logs of past behavior rather than fresh interaction, and those logs come from policies of varying quality. A method that stays robust under mixed-quality data is essential for real deployments, where no one can re-collect every client's history. The work targets federated learning's promise of collaboration without centralizing sensitive experience.
arxiv-2512-02450:
Estimating a room's 3D layout from one image works in tidy synthetic rooms and fails in real buildings with several floors. Valentin Bieri and four co-authors introduce HouseLayout3D in 2025, a benchmark for layout estimation in the wild, plus a training-free baseline that needs no task-specific learning.

Models trained on simple single-room data cannot natively handle multi-floor buildings, and splitting scenes by floor destroys global context like staircases. A benchmark drawn from real complexity exposes that gap honestly. Progress here serves augmented reality, renovation tools, and robots that must understand whole homes, not single rooms.
arxiv-2512-02750:
Kiev Gama and five co-authors study how beginners engage with vibe coding, building software by prompting AI. Instead of writing code directly, the programmer describes intent in natural language and steers the result. The style promises to open software building to far more people.

Its effects on learning, though, remain largely unexplored. Novices may gain confidence quickly, or may skip the struggle that builds real skill. The team's exploration of engagement offers early evidence for teachers. Schools need such evidence to decide how AI coding should enter the classroom. Prompt craft is a new skill, and how schools teach it will shape who gets to build with code at all.
arxiv-2512-02950:
Sungjun Lee and four co-authors create ultracold molecules from sodium and potassium atoms as a step toward dipolar gases. Feshbach molecules form when atoms bind loosely near a magnetic resonance. Coherent transfer can then move them to the ground state of rotation and vibration.

Those ground state dimers would form stable gases with strong, tunable long range interactions. The team reports creating bosonic sodium potassium Feshbach molecules by radio frequency association. Each step toward controlled dipolar gases opens studies of matter governed by long range forces. Each bound pair is a step on a stair. The stair climbs from loose pairs of atoms to a gas of true dipoles that labs can probe at will.
arxiv-2512-03150:
The Bullet Cluster is a famous crash of galaxy clusters. Boseong Young Cho, M. James Jee, and co-authors weigh its parts in this 2025 work. Past estimates of its mass ratio ranged widely, from about two to one to more than ten to one.

The team joins data from the Webb telescope and DECam in a lensing study. They report the first robust masses for the cluster's three parts from weak and strong lensing. Their title calls the crash a minor merger. Firm masses help test dark matter ideas built on this system. Mass ratios shape how the crash is read as evidence about dark matter behavior.
arxiv-2512-03450:
Finding key points on 3D objects without labels is a core challenge. Rhys Newbury and co-authors present KeyPointDiffuser in this 2025 work. Key points summarize an object's structure for grasping, matching, and generation.

Most unsupervised key point methods are not built for unconditional generation settings. That limits their use in modern 3D generative pipelines. The authors use latent diffusion models to learn key points, bridging that gap. Learned key points could help robots and design tools reason about shapes automatically. Generative key points could seed new shapes, not just describe shapes already given, extending their use in design and animation tools.
arxiv-2512-03950:
Ants leaving scent trails and cells laying chemical tracks share a trick: past paths steer future motion. Paul Pineau, Samuel Bell, Raphaël Voituriez, and Ram M. Adar build a minimal model of many such trail-following particles in a 2025 statistical mechanics preprint. Earlier work treated single particles or averaged theories, leaving collective behaviour largely unexplored.

In their model, particles wander randomly while depositing long-lasting trails that attract or repel those who come later, forming a shared memory field. Using stochastic density functional theory, the authors derive equations for the collective density and study them on paper and in simulation. With repelling trails, densities spread unusually and form temporary clusters. With attracting trails, the system condenses in finite time into frozen, localised clumps. Memory plus noise, they conclude, generates instabilities and self-organisation of its own.
arxiv-2512-04150:
A Fermi surface, the boundary in momentum space between filled and empty electron states, is usually something a material happens to have. Minho Luke Kim, Salvatore D. Pace, and Shu-Heng Shao prove some systems cannot avoid having one, in a 2025 preprint. They construct a symmetry forcing every model that respects it to be gapless in exactly this way.

The symmetry mixes ordinary fermion number conservation with a non-local Majorana translation, generating a noncompact Lie group related to the Onsager algebra. For any Fermi surface this symmetry enforces, the authors show the symmetry group always contains the even part of the ersatz Fermi liquid symmetry that such surfaces carry. They also prove these enforced surfaces generically have at least two noncontractible components, like open orbits wrapping momentum space.
arxiv-2512-04650:
Halina Wiśniewska studies a family of functions named for Weierstrass that stretch a classic inequality between sums and products. The classical rule bounds the product of two numbers by their sum in a tidy double inequality. A Weierstrass function keeps that double rule alive on a chosen interval: the sum minus one sits below the function of the product, which sits below the product of the function values. Her 2025 arXiv paper maps what such functions can do.

With these functions, the old inequality extends to trigonometric functions, the Euler gamma function, and logarithms. One case stands out: the function built from the log of one plus x, scaled to fit. It yields a new multiplicative inequality that in turn generalizes the classical rule. Such extensions give analysts fresh bounds for special functions, useful wherever products must be fenced in by sums.
arxiv-2512-05050:
Natalie Hogg, Daniel Johnson, Anowar Shajib, and Julien Larena measure a subtle distortion in strong gravitational lenses, the systems where a massive galaxy bends a distant source's light into arcs. Matter scattered along the line of sight adds its own stretch, called shear, and if that stretch can be measured reliably it becomes a new way to probe the cosmos. An earlier group study modeled a first batch of lenses from the SLACS survey.

Here the team successfully models most of a second batch, bringing the total sample to forty-five lenses. The average stretch comes out larger than expected, and a good fraction of the lenses show surprisingly strong values even under the most flexible models of the lensing galaxy. Checks against redshift, filters, image quality, and brightness explain none of the big values, leaving the strength of the effect an open puzzle.
arxiv-2512-05150:
Zhenglin Cheng, Peng Sun, Jianguo Li, and Tao Lin present TwinFlow, a training recipe that teaches large generative models to produce images in a single step. Diffusion and flow models need dozens of steps per image, which makes them slow. Existing shortcuts either distill a teacher model through procedures that degrade at very few steps, or add adversarial training with networks, unstable and hungry for memory.

TwinFlow drops both the fixed teacher and the separate adversary, using a self-adversarial flow design instead. On text-to-image tasks it reaches a strong quality score in one evaluation step, beating few-step baselines. The team also retrained a twenty-billion-parameter image model at full scale and turned it into a few-step generator. At a single step it matches the original hundred-step model on two standard benchmarks. That cuts computing cost roughly a hundredfold, with minor quality loss.
arxiv-2512-05450:
Pawel Weichbroth sorts out the messy catalogue of things that go wrong when people use mobile apps. Usability research on apps is plentiful but fragmented: studies vary in method, inputs, and depth, leaving practitioners without a shared map of the problems users actually hit. Weichbroth triangulates — a systematic literature review plus expert interviews, scholarly and practitioner knowledge side by side — to extract the traits that underlie usability issues.

The result is a catalogue of sixteen issue categories with keywords, extended into a taxonomy, plus a three-tier classification linking app, user, and resources. At the app level, issues arise from interface design, efficiency, errors, and operability. At the user level they tax cognition, learning, and memory. At the resource level they stem from network quality and hardware limits. Interface design emerges as the root cause. The paper closes with takeaways for researchers and vendors alike.
arxiv-2512-05550:
Marvin Klinger and six co-authors test rare-earth borates as working materials for magnetic refrigeration below one kelvin. Cooling by adiabatic demagnetization — magnetize a paramagnetic material, let it absorb heat, demagnetize to grow colder — is gaining importance as helium-3 supplies tighten. The classic hydrated salts degrade under heating and vacuum; frustrated rare-earth oxides promise higher entropy density and toughness, and borates are the new candidates under test here.

The team reports the structure, magnetism, and thermodynamics of two barium rare-earth borate families carrying ytterbium or gadolinium. Three of the four materials stay paramagnetic down to the lowest temperatures measured; one gadolinium compound orders just above a tenth of a kelvin. Cooling performance from two kelvin in a strong field is checked against the literature. The results add practical options to a refrigeration technology that low-temperature physics depends on more and more.
arxiv-2512-05650:
Dhorasso Temfack and Jason Wyse work on tracking an epidemic while it unfolds, from noisy and partial case reports. Health officials need estimates of hidden states, like how many people are truly infected, plus the parameters that drive spread. Fully Bayesian methods give both, but the leading algorithm is very slow. It nests one particle filter inside another, which blocks use during a fast moving outbreak.

Their 2025 paper swaps the inner filter for an ensemble Kalman filter, a cheaper approximation. A corrected density estimate keeps the swap from biasing results, and the filter is adapted to the clumpy counts typical of disease reporting. In simulations with known truth, and on United States monkeypox data from 2022, the new method matched the slow one's answers at a fraction of the cost. It rebuilt the epidemic's path and recovered key parameters well. That speed makes careful Bayesian tracking realistic during an actual response.
arxiv-2512-05850:
Haipeng An and five co-authors re-examine a puzzling excess in the world's great dark matter detectors. Three liquid xenon experiments, LZ, PandaX-4T, and XENONnT, have recorded nuclear recoil like events at energies too high for ordinary WIMP scattering to explain. Using a shared framework on public data, the team performs the first combined fit.

Two families of interaction can reproduce the spectrum: speed dependent collisions, and inelastic hits that gain or lose a fixed bite of energy. Local significance reaches about three and a half sigma. A background from double electron capture in xenon has poorly known charge yields. Varying them can move the signal from nothing to the full three and a half sigma. The decisive test will be extending the analysis to still higher recoil energies, where that background should vanish. A discovery claim is only as strong as its murkiest background.
arxiv-2512-05950:
Zalish Mahmud, Anantaa Kotal, and Aritran Piplai fill holes in datasets with a generative adversary that learns what real data looks like. Missing values are everywhere: sensors die and records conflict. Classic fixes assume tidy linear relations and fail on messy reality. Impugan instead trains a conditional generative adversarial network on complete records, learning how missing variables depend on observed ones.

At work, the generator proposes values for the gaps while a discriminator grades them against real data, pushing the fills toward realism. That contest captures bent, multi humped relationships regression cannot express. On benchmarks and on a multi-source integration task, the distance between filled and true data fell by up to about four fifths compared with leading baselines. A second measure of information mismatch fell by about seven tenths. Principled imputation decides whether the final analysis deserves trust.
arxiv-2512-06050:
L. Horoto and F. G. Scholtz propose rebuilding gravity as a genuine force, carried by a physical field, rather than as the geometry of spacetime itself. In Einstein's theory, gravity can be transformed away at a point. Their field strength tensor is the difference between the curved connection and a flat one. That object cannot be removed by any coordinate choice, so in this picture gravity has true physical degrees of freedom. The dynamics follow a Yang-Mills type Lagrangian with an extra scalar tied to the Newtonian potential.

Coupling off, the theory is general relativity; on, it is a gauge theory of gravity. Dark energy and dark matter like effects are also claimed as consequences. Gravity speaking gauge theory could ease the bridge to a quantum description.
arxiv-2512-06250:
Chris Tava asks a plain question about self guided agents: with two ways to move through a maze, when should the agent swap between them? One mode sweeps the maze in a tidy pattern, while the other heads straight for the goal. Fixed swap rules waste time in mazes that do not fit the rule.

Tava lets the agent learn the swap point on its own during each run. It needs only the maze size and the goal spot, not a map of the walls. The agent groups its state by ground covered and distance left, then tests swap points across a mid range of coverage. Across many test mazes, the learned swap beat both single mode agents and a fixed rule, cutting finish times by a clear margin. The work shows that timing a swap can be learned from progress signals alone.
arxiv-2512-06350:
Ozgecan Kocak, Phanish Puranam, and Nghi Truong ask why smart people clash so hard over the risks of artificial intelligence. Rather than count opinions, they pull apart the chains of reasoning behind them: the premises each side leans on, sorted into facts, forecasts, definitions, causal beliefs, and values. Knowing exactly where a chain splits can help policy makers answer the real points of dispute.

They test the method on guest interviews from the Lex Fridman podcast that deal with AI risk. For risks to human survival and to jobs, the guests split mainly over causal beliefs and forecasts of what comes next. For risks to human social bonds, values and definitions carried more weight, such as what counts as a genuine human connection. The team used a panel of language models to parse the talks at scale. The approach can be reused wherever public debates need their bones laid bare.
arxiv-2512-06450:
Mauli Pant, Linda Fernandez, and Indranil Sahoo model where Arctic whales gather, and in what group sizes, from a decade of aerial survey sightings. Their data cover beluga and bowhead whales in United States Arctic waters across ten years of flights. The two species share some waters but answer to different conditions. The authors model them jointly. Each species keeps its own response to the setting, while both share one hidden spatial field for their broad patterns.

Group size enters through a marked point process, so where whales appear and how many gather are read in one frame. The hidden field is built over a mesh that respects the coastline, and a fast approximation method fits the model to the full decade of effort. Results show lasting hotspots shared by both species, alongside clear differences in what draws each.
arxiv-2512-06750:
Weiqi Li and ten co authors unify three jobs that image software usually splits apart: judging an image's quality, restoring it, and enhancing it. The jobs are natural partners. A restorer that knows what damage looks like should repair better, yet most systems treat assessment and repair in isolation. Their model, UARE, is a vision language model that does all three, built to test how far quality judgment can guide repair.

Training comes in two stages. A progressive schedule moves from single distortions to stacked, mixed damage, so the model learns to handle real world mess. Then quality reading and restoration are fine tuned together on interleaved text and image data, tying the judgment signals to the repair goals. Across assessment, restoration, and enhancement tests, the unified model performed strongly, with the quality side measurably lifting the repair side. One model that both critiques and fixes is the authors' point.
arxiv-2512-06950:
Enrico Camporeale tackles a forecasting trap: when rare events matter most, standard training teaches models to please the common cases and neglect the tail. Reweighting losses or inventing extra rare examples can add noise or warp the data. His method, PARIS, instead improves the training set itself by pruning it. A theorem about how models represent data lets him compute, in closed form, exactly how removing one training point would change the validation score.

With a fast updating scheme, PARIS removes unhelpful points one by one without retraining from scratch. The test case comes from space weather, where rare storms carry outsized impact. There, pruning cut the training set by up to three quarters while matching or beating the accuracy of the full set. It also outperformed reweighting, synthetic oversampling, and boosting. Camporeale presents pruning guided by exact deletion math as a clear, cheap route to better rare-event forecasts.
arxiv-2512-07150:
Jonghyun Park and Jong Chul Ye speed up a class of solvers that reconstruct images from partial measurements using generative flow models as priors. Such solvers face a trade-off at practical step counts. Heavy optimization nails the measurements quickly but can slide into unrealistic images, especially in the warped latent spaces of flow models. Pure sampling stays faithful to the prior yet crawls toward measurement agreement.

FlowLPS mixes the two at every step of the reverse process. A few Langevin updates, random kicks guided by the posterior, jitter the current clean estimate toward plausible regions. A local refinement then rapidly enforces the measurements starting from that jittered point. Controlled re-noising steadies the whole path without breaking its coherence. Across five linear imaging problems on two standard photo sets, the balance between fidelity to the measurements and perceptual quality was strong.
arxiv-2512-07450:
Imran Ahsan, Hyunwook Yu, Jinsung Kim, and Mucheol Kim wrote this 2025 paper on privacy in graph neural networks. Such networks learn from linked data, but laws like the GDPR can require them to forget. Proving that data is truly gone is hard, since these models act like black boxes.

The authors propose a checker driven by explanations rather than raw scores. It snapshots the model before and after a deletion request. Shifts in which parts of the graph the model credits then serve as visible evidence. Five measures track those shifts, from leftover attribution to changes in graph structure. The team tests two network types and four forgetting methods on five benchmarks. Full retraining and one deletion method erase nearly all traces. Another method erases only part, and a fourth leaves clear signals behind. The readable evidence, they argue, makes forgetting claims open to audit.
arxiv-2512-07750:
Roozbeh Bostandoost and ten co-authors wrote this 2025 cloud computing paper. Public clouds place virtual machines using pipelines rich in learned models. Separate models predict processor load, memory need, and machine lifetime.

Each prediction can look harmless while quietly shifting the others. Together, those shifts compound and can badly degrade placement quality. No existing tool stress-tests how the models interact as a system. Deterministic attackers cannot capture how the models behave by chance either. The authors build SANJESH, an analyzer built as a two-level search. The outer level hunts for adversarial conditions the models could produce. It searches across what predictions are plausible under distributional uncertainty. The inner level runs the allocator against those predictions. Applied to production traces from the cloud operator, the tool bites. It uncovers scenarios far worse than the operator's own evaluator found. Correlated model drift, the paper shows, is a real risk.
arxiv-2512-08350: Zeev Nutov, a computer scientist who works on network design, posted a short paper on arXiv in December 2025. He studies the Small Cuts Cover problem. The task is to find the cheapest set of edges covering every small cut in a graph. A classic primal dual algorithm was recently shown by Simmons to guarantee an approximation ratio of five. Simmons asked whether that bound is tight. Nutov answers yes. His example makes the ratio between the algorithm solution and the optimum come arbitrarily close to five.
arxiv-2512-08450:
Besm Osman, Ruben Vink, Andrei Jalba, and Maxime Chamberland, researchers in medical computing, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their task is filling the brain cortex volume with a tetrahedral mesh, the grid that biomechanical simulations run on. For cortical simulations, the mesh must preserve exactly how the input surface is connected, or the anatomy is quietly changed.

The trouble is that automatically extracted brain surfaces arrive flawed, full of self intersections, small holes, and broken geometry. Existing meshers, constrained or not, then fail to keep the surface connectivity. The authors develop a new tetrahedralization method that maintains the input connectivity even in the presence of such defects. They also propose a metric that measures how well connectivity is preserved, so methods can be compared honestly. On that metric, their method kept connectivity correctly where existing solutions did not.
arxiv-2512-08750:
A J D Farias Junior and coauthors study vacuum energy in a system where a mass dimension one fermion field, called Elko, interacts with a real scalar field. Both fields are placed between two large parallel plates and must vanish at the plates, a setup used to study the Casimir effect. Distance between the plates sets the scale for the vacuum response.

Using the effective potential method from quantum field theory, the authors compute the vacuum energy density and its first correction from the interaction couplings. They also compute, for each field on its own, the topological mass that arises from the plate conditions and depends on the couplings. The work extends Casimir studies to this less standard fermion type. It shows how boundaries and interactions together reshape vacuum energy and effective mass in a controlled four dimensional setting.
arxiv-2512-08850:
Mohamed Benelmekki and Brahim Boulayat introduce a weaker notion of atomicity for integral domains in factorization theory. A domain is called atomic when every nonzero nonunit element factors into a finite product of irreducible elements. The new notion relaxes that demand in a specific way.

A domain is called sub atomic when every nonunit divisor of an atomic element is itself atomic. The authors study this property and several related factorization properties. They develop the basic theory, give examples, and test how the property behaves under standard constructions. Those constructions include localization, polynomial rings, and a classic composite construction for domains. Results show the sub atomic property is independent of other classical factorization properties. The work identifies a class of domains that sits strictly between atomic and non atomic domains, widening the map of factorization behavior.
arxiv-2512-09250:
Mao Nishino, Martin Bauer, Tom Needham, and Nicolas Charon work on optimal transport, the mathematics of moving mass from one distribution to another at least cost. The dynamic Benamou-Brenier form of the theory follows the moving density over time. An unbalanced version allows mass to be created or destroyed along the way, at a price.

The authors generalize an earlier constrained model. Constraints can now act on the density, the momentum, and the source term together, and they can be equalities or inequalities. Under stated assumptions they prove the resulting problems are well-posed. The paper then builds a numerical pipeline using finite differences and parallel proximal splitting methods that can actually solve them. The framework covers standard balanced and unbalanced transport plus many natural constraints, and the authors show its range on synthetic and real data examples.
arxiv-2512-09750:
Shun Inoue leads a team clarifying where the iron fluorescence line in stellar flares comes from, using a superflare on the RS Canum Venaticorum star UX Arietis. The iron K-alpha line can reveal a flare loop's latitude and size, but only if its origin is known. It could be produced by photoionization from hard X-ray photons, or by collisions from non-thermal electrons. Far-ultraviolet and X-ray observations break the tie.

Japan's Hisaki satellite watched the ultraviolet while NICER on the space station recorded X-rays. The flare released energy in both bands. The ultraviolet emission, a proxy for such activity, peaked an hour and a half before the X-rays. The iron line peaked together with the X-ray maximum instead of the non-thermal peak, supporting the photoionization origin. Calculations using the line's intensity back the conclusion and show the line can recover flare geometry.
arxiv-2512-09850:
Simone Cuonzo and Nina Deliu present Conformal Bandits, a framework that merges conformal prediction with bandit decision making. Bandits are a classic setup for choosing repeatedly among options with unknown rewards. Standard strategies chase low regret but rest on assumptions about distributions or hold only in the long run, and they ignore statistical properties. Conformal prediction instead gives coverage guarantees that hold at finite sample sizes.

The test setting is portfolio allocation, where the rewards of different arms differ by tiny amounts. In that weak separability regime, classic policies are not optimal in finite samples. Tests and the study show the new approach's regret edge, plus coverage at the promised level where a classic method can fail. Adding hidden Markov models to capture regime switching in markets improved the balance between exploring and exploiting, raised risk adjusted returns, and preserved the coverage guarantee.
arxiv-2512-10050:
Christian Millichap and Rolland Trapp classify the symmetries of a family of knots and links built from flat pieces, called flat fully augmented links. The question is which symmetry groups can occur, for the links whose crossing structure is prime in a suitable sense. Their answer is complete: exactly the finite subgroups of the rotation and reflection group of space occur, no more and no fewer. The proof builds a dictionary between symmetries of the link and automorphisms of an associated planar cubic graph.

The same machinery gives a construction kit. For any finite subgroup of that spatial symmetry group, the authors explicitly build infinitely many distinct links in the family whose full symmetry group is exactly the chosen one.
arxiv-2512-10250:
Sicheng Liu, Alexander Fengler, Michael J. Frank, and Matthew T. Harrison prove that a popular shortcut for fitting decision models is unsound in math terms. Drift diffusion models describe choices as evidence accumulating toward a threshold; they anchor computational neuroscience and the math of psychology. When drift varies within and across trials, exact likelihoods are expensive, so teams replace the varying drift with its time average, the time averaged drift approximation. Inference then runs on fast formulas for constant drift models. The authors show this estimator is inconsistent: with infinite data it still does not converge to the true drift.

The proof is by design elementary, set in perhaps the simplest possible case: Brownian motion with piecewise constant drift hitting one boundary. Numerical work shows the approximation misestimates attentional effects and can flip hypothesis test conclusions.
arxiv-2512-10850:
J Socorro and co-authors work out classical solutions for a modified gravity cosmology.
