Their theory generalises Einstein's by letting the action depend on the Ricci scalar and more, an F(R, ...) family. And they approach it through the Hamiltonian formalism. The test bed is the anisotropic Bianchi type I universe. It expands at different rates along different axes. It is filled with ordinary matter, modelled as a barotropic fluid. In that fluid, pressure is a fixed fraction of density.

Solutions are presented in two gauge choices for the lapse function. And the authors note that several results recover expressions inserted by hand as ansätze when solving Einstein's equations. Vacuum solutions are included for completeness. The paper is classical groundwork: before such theories can be quantised or tested against data, their exact anisotropic solutions and the gauges that make them tractable need to be on the table.
arxiv-2512-10950:
Qitao Zhao and colleagues present E-RayZer, a vision model that learns three dimensional understanding directly from unlabelled images taken from several viewpoints. Earlier self-supervised methods inferred depth and shape only indirectly, which let them take shortcuts. E-RayZer instead rebuilds scenes in explicit three dimensional space during training.

A staged curriculum moves training from easy to hard examples and blends varied data sources without any labels. The model beat its predecessor on pose estimation and matched or passed fully supervised reconstruction systems on some tests. Its learned features also outperformed leading visual pre-training models on downstream three dimensional tasks. The authors offer the approach as a promising path for spatial visual pre-training.
arxiv-2512-11050:
Zu Yan, Kohei Inayoshi, Keijian Chen, and Jingsong Guo study little red dots, a puzzling class of active galactic nuclei found by the James Webb telescope. Their spectra show strong hydrogen features that many read as signs of heavy dust. Yet the expected infrared glow from such dust is barely seen, creating a contradiction.

The authors run radiation transfer calculations through dense, dust free gas around the central black hole. They show that repeated scattering of hydrogen light naturally produces the same line ratios that dust reddening would, once the gas is dense enough. The break and broad lines in the spectrum also become linked, letting them estimate a surprisingly small gas mass nearby. Such a small reservoir suggests these nuclei saw little star formation.
arxiv-2512-11150:
Eddie Landesberg and Manjari Narayan propose a way to trust cheap AI judges when measuring how well language model systems perform. Careful human or expert scoring is expensive, so teams rely on model based judges whose raw scores can rank systems wrongly. Their method, Causal Judge Evaluation, calibrates those cheap scores against a small slice of gold standard judgments.

The calibration can then be applied at scale with valid uncertainty estimates. Crucially, a small audit in each new setting tests whether the calibration still holds, turning an uncheckable assumption into a checkable one. On thousands of chatbot comparison prompts, the method ranked system pairs almost perfectly at a fraction of the full oracle cost. A deliberately adversarial policy failed the audit and was correctly flagged, with the method refusing to report biased numbers.
arxiv-2512-11350:
Tanu Singh, Pranamesh Chakraborty, and Long Truong train a transformer system to spot traffic accidents in surveillance video automatically. Road crashes are a leading cause of death worldwide, and crowded cities generate more footage than human monitors can watch. Older vision methods read space and time poorly and failed to generalise across locations, while good training data were scarce and narrow.

The team first curated a balanced dataset spanning many traffic environments, accident types, and conditions. Their model extracts spatial features from each frame with convolutional layers, then lets a transformer track how those features evolve over time. They also tested several ways of adding motion information, a cue many earlier studies neglected. Combining ordinary video features with optical flow, which tracks pixel movement, worked best and beat the accuracy of general vision language models they compared against.
arxiv-2512-11450:
Chellasamy Jebarathinam writes a short comment correcting a claim about two kinds of quantum strangeness in pairs of qubits. Contextuality means measurement results cannot be explained by pre assigned values that ignore context. Quantum discord is a varied correlation, present even in some unentangled states. An earlier paper proposed a criterion, extending a classic proof, and argued it showed discordant states can be contextual without entanglement.

Jebarathinam shows that this test does not in general imply contextuality at all. It instead detects a distinct nonclassicality of the discordant feature, seen in practice, a notion Jebarathinam and Srikanth recently spelled out. Recast that way, the earlier paper's main conclusion, that quantum correlation cannot simply be equated with the discordant feature, becomes precise rather than wrong. The comment is a useful caution about keeping neighbouring quantum concepts separate.
arxiv-2512-11750:
Ernesto Casablanca and co-authors built LUCID, a tool that certifies the safety of black box systems that learn and wobble. Self driving and health systems pair opaque AI parts with random dynamics, and classic checkers cannot handle that mix. LUCID works from a finite set of sampled transitions alone.

It learns control barrier certificates, safety fences in state space, straight from data. Math tricks place the data in a kernel space with an ambiguity set that guards against unseen behavior, and a Fourier expansion turns a hard problem into a linear one. The team calls it the first tool with measured safety guarantees for such systems. Hard benchmark cases show the approach working in practice.
arxiv-2512-12050:
Michael Neilan, Maxim Olshanskii, and Henry von Wahl design a finite element method for Stokes flow that keeps velocity exactly divergence free. Stokes flow governs slow, syrupy motion. When a mesh does not fit the domain edge, unfitted methods cut through cells, but weak boundary rules often spoil the no compression property.

Their method pairs a Scott-Vogelius element pair on a curved cut mesh with a Nitsche and multiplier scheme for boundary data. A higher order multiplier space restores stability and pressure robustness. The paper proves stability and best order convergence in two dimensions, counting the geometric error from curved fits. Numerical tests confirm the theory.
arxiv-2512-12150:
Chenyun Luo and Hang Yu prove a local existence result for liquid crystal flow in a 2025 math paper. They study the Lin-Liu equations, which describe nematic liquid crystals that flow like a fluid with no viscosity. The fluid has a free surface, held by surface tension, and the work uses moving coordinates.

Energy bounds alone cannot prove such results, since the linearized equations lose symmetry. The authors build a stand-in system that stays close to the true model. It must track both the fluid motion and heat type flows inside, plus the smoothness of the moving edge. Their proof shows solutions exist for a short time near the start.
arxiv-2512-12450:
Sayantani Bhattacharyya, Sukanya Mitra, Shuvayu Roy, and Rajeev Singh study excitation spectra in relativistic fluids in a 2025 paper. When a fluid moves near light speed, its wave modes are computed in its rest frame. Boosting to a moving frame can bring pathologies, and pulling the modes across frames is nontrivial work.

Their framework derives boosted spectra from rest frame mode coefficients alone, skipping the usual boosted polynomial solve. Under a boost, extra solutions can appear that clash with causality; they call these spurious modes. They prove a direct link between mode conservation and causality, tying the count of modes to whether the theory stays physically sound.
arxiv-2512-12750:
Antonio Catao, Lucas Resende, and Paulo Orenstein study robust mean estimators built by shrinkage in a 2025 paper. Estimating a mean that resists outliers matters across statistics. Their class of estimators starts from a base estimate. It then shrinks the weights of sample points far from it. A data driven scaling factor sets the shrink, and a weighting function fades from 1 to 0 with distance.

Under mild assumptions on the weighting function, they prove stronger concentration bounds than the base estimator enjoys, including sub-Gaussian guarantees. Concentration means the estimate piles up tightly near the true mean. The framework unifies several known robust methods in one dimension and extends to multivariate data. Numerical tests show faster concentration even for small samples.
arxiv-2512-12850:
Duc Hoang, Aarush Gupta, and Philip Harris introduce KANELE, a way to run a special kind of neural network on FPGA chips. These chips must answer fast while using little power. The networks they use have learnable spline curves on their edges, which fit well into lookup tables.

KANELE is the first full design flow for putting such networks on FPGAs. It trains the model with pruning and low precision in mind from the start. The team reports speed gains up to 2,700 times over past work on the same task. It also matched or beat other lookup table designs on standard tests.
arxiv-2512-12950:
Lingyi Meng and co-authors tackle mapping legal terms across languages, a task made hard for Chinese and Japanese by shared written forms that carry different meanings. Few standard tools exist for this pair. Mistakes in legal terms can change what a law requires.

Their approach pairs AI agents with human legal experts in one workflow. Agents handle scanning, splitting, alignment, and first-pass term extraction. Experts review the output and apply legal judgment at each stage. The team tested the method on 35 key Chinese statutes with English and Japanese versions. It improved the precision and consistency of term mapping over manual methods alone.
arxiv-2512-13350:
Christian Nicolaisen Hansen, Line Jelver, and Christos Tserkezis study how patterning two-dimensional materials changes their response to light. They shape the materials into ribbon arrays on a surface and into spherical particles. Excitons, bound electron-hole pairs, dominate the optical behavior of these materials.

Using Fourier-Floquet methods for ribbons and Mie theory for spheres, they compute reflection, transmission, and uptake. Two materials anchor the study: hexagonal boron nitride in the UV and tungsten disulfide in visible light. Ribbon arrays showed weak tuning range, since their excitons stay local. Spheres coated with the material mixed better with other modes, offering a stronger platform for tailored light-matter work.
arxiv-2512-13450:
Julien Marche and Gregor Masbaum study signatures of vector spaces that arise in SU2 topological quantum field theory, as a function of a root of unity parameter. Such signatures are numeric invariants tied to surfaces of a given genus. Their asymptotic behavior connects topology with number theory.

For genus two, they prove a scaled signature converges to an explicit limit function along irrational directions. That limit function turns out to be the boundary value of an Eichler integral of a modular form of weight four and level two. Building on this, they propose a transformation law for the signature function, analogous to the classical reciprocity formula for Dedekind sums.
arxiv-2512-13650: Leonard Susskind argues that observers have a special role in de Sitter space, the kind of expanding space tied to cosmic acceleration. His short paper links that need for observers to a spontaneous breakdown of time-reversal symmetry. That symmetry is the idea that the laws should run the same forward and backward in time. When that symmetry breaks on its own, past and future stop being fully alike, and an observer's place in the space gains a clear physical meaning.
arxiv-2512-13950:
Alban Gauthier and co-authors judge how well material traits can be forecast for 3D scenes made with generative image models. Generative tools can now make true-to-life views of a scene that match its geometry. Other SVBRDF networks recover material traits, such as reflectance, from those images, and merging views can build a full texture atlas.

That pipeline faces a coherence problem: single-view predictions may disagree across views and yield mismatched atlases. Generated images and their conditioning signals may also carry extra information photos lack. The authors compare neural architectures and conditioning choices to find designs with high accuracy and coherence. A standard UNet proved competitive with more complex designs, a useful simplification for appearance modeling.
arxiv-2512-14650:
Sharon Mary Tomson and a large team search for gravitational wave memory in pulsar timing array data in a 2025 paper. Memory is a lasting shift left in spacetime after a gravitational wave passes. The main sources for these arrays are supermassive black hole binaries.

The team made the first search for late inspirals and mergers of such binaries using full numerical relativity waveforms that include nonlinear memory. They also searched for generic memory bursts, using kernel density and normalizing flow methods to cut computing cost. They rule out mergers of binaries with chirp mass of ten billion solar masses out to 700 Mpc over 18 years of data, at 95 percent credibility. Generic bursts above a strain of ten to the minus fourteen are also ruled out in the stated windows.
arxiv-2512-14750:
Ying Cui, Dongzhe Zheng, and a large team study a dangerous subtype of clear cell renal cell carcinoma, a common kidney cancer. The subtype, called DCCD, lacks the usual stored lipids and is linked to poor outcomes even when found early. Their 2025 work aims to spot this subtype before surgery, without a tissue sample.

The team linked three levels of evidence: molecular signatures, microscope images of tissue, and CT scans. One model, PathoDCCD, reads cell shapes and tissue patterns, while RadioDCCD reads scan features from the whole tumor and its subregions. Across five groups totaling 1,659 patients, the models matched the molecular subtype and flagged the patients with the worst outcomes. The approach could help doctors judge risk earlier and plan care sooner.
arxiv-2512-15250:
Youssef Ghallab and seven coauthors combine brain and heart signals using foundation models and a deliberately simple fusion. Electrocardiograms and electroencephalograms give complementary views of health and thought, but labeled data that pairs them is scarce, and the signals differ greatly. Their answer is to pretrain a strong encoder for each signal type alone.

They adapt the CBraMod encoder, first built for brain signals, to large scale self supervised pretraining on heart signals, with a dual masking strategy that captures links within and between leads. A matching pretrained encoder serves the brain side. The two representations are simply concatenated, and the classifier learns the cross modal interplay from there. On emotion recognition the system came near state of the art performance. The result argues that good encoders plus plain fusion can beat fancy integration when labels are few.
arxiv-2512-15450:
Gaston Nieuviarts discusses how time and Lorentzian geometry might emerge from a twisted spectral triple in a 2025 proceeding paper. Spectral triples describe geometry through algebra, and almost commutative versions underlie a noncommutative model of particle physics. A long standing problem is that this setup naturally gives a Riemannian, not a Lorentzian, signature.

The paper gathers recent results into one account of a unified algebraic mechanism. A morphism links twisted spectral triples to pseudo Riemannian ones, offering an alternative to Wick rotation. The claim is that the almost commutative structure behind the particle model may itself give rise to Lorentzian geometry from a purely Riemannian start.
arxiv-2512-15750:
Sujoy Majumder, Nabadwip Sarkar, and Debabrata Pramanik study meromorphic solutions of a nonlinear equation in a 2025 paper, dated December 11. The equation links a power of an unknown function, a power of a rational multiple of its derivative, and an exponential term. Such Fermat type equations often admit only very restricted solutions.

The authors examine the equation for all positive whole values of the three exponents. They give full rules for when such solutions can exist and find their possible forms. The results improve earlier work by Tang and Liao and by Han and Lu, both in the existence criteria and in the explicit forms obtained.
arxiv-2512-15850:
Cole Meyer and co authors reveal Callisto's near subsurface heat traits from ALMA data in a 2025 paper. Heat images at varied wavelengths probe varied depths below a surface, exposing makeup and impact history. Six archived ALMA records of Jupiter's moon Callisto, from 2012, sit at unusually short wavelengths for this moon.

Those wavelengths, 0.43 to 0.47 millimeters, sense the upper centimeter or so. The disk averaged heat reading is 133 plus or minus 15 kelvin. A two part inertia mix fits the glow best, matching longer wavelength results. The team also presents unseen Galileo radiometer maps, improving knowledge of Callisto's shallow soil.
arxiv-2512-15950:
Gregory Camilli compares procedures for modeling binary eye tracking data in a 2025 paper. Eye tracking series are correlated over time within a person, and standard logistic mixed models with random effects for persons and items ignore that serial structure. Several fixes exist, and their differences matter for reading research conclusions.

Camilli illustrates three newer approaches. Each avoids using the observed lagged outcome as a predictor. One is an autoregressive model. One is a moving average model from generalized estimating equations. One is a recurrent two state survival model for run length encoded data. Five analyses in total point to unresolved issues in eye tracking analysis. A traditional lag 1 model is included for comparison.
arxiv-2512-16250:
Sanjoy Chowdhury and eight co-authors build a test for talking-head AI in a paper uploaded to arXiv in 2025. Multimodal models that hear and see struggle in multi-speaker scenes, where they must track who speaks, keep roles straight, and ground events over time. Such skills matter for meeting analytics and conversational video assistants.

Their benchmark, AMUSE, grades models in zero-shot, guided, and agentic modes across six task families, including locating speakers in space and time and summarizing dialogues. Current models showed weak multi-speaker reasoning in every mode. The companion framework, RAFT, aligns models with reward optimization and self-evaluation while updating few parameters. It raised benchmark accuracy by up to 39.52 percent in relative terms. Together, the tools give labs a practical way to measure and improve agentic audio-visual understanding.
arxiv-2512-16450:
Mathew Thomas Arun and Ritik Pal teach a neural network the strong force in a paper shared on arXiv in 2025. Holographic QCD models the strong interaction through a five-dimensional gravity dual, where meson masses encode the hidden geometry and fields. Recovering those ingredients from measured masses is an inverse problem.

The network trains on the masses of the rho, a1, a2, and f0 mesons and their excitations, solving a discretized wave equation in the fifth dimension. It reconstructs confining potentials, a metric, and a dilaton profile that obeys the null energy condition, with an infrared dilaton far steeper than the usual quadratic guess. The symmetry-breaking potential comes out with cubic and quartic coefficients near minus 4 and 9. Using the learned ingredients, the model predicts the pion mass and spectrum accurately. Code and trained models are public.
arxiv-2512-16850:
Can Urgun and Mark Whitmeyer study real-time persuasion, where a sender shapes what a receiver learns and picks when to stop sharing. The receiver delays a decision while waiting, at a rising time cost, and the sender controls both signal clarity and the stop time.

One might expect the sender to blur the signal at times. The authors show that, under natural regularity terms, full openness is always best. The sender keeps the signal fully clear throughout and persuades only by choosing when to stop. That clean result simplifies a rich control problem: timing alone does all the work, and garbling the signal never pays.
arxiv-2512-17350:
Chenming Zhou and five co-authors find a simple trick that helps detectors spot AI-made images from generators they have never seen. Detectors often cheat: they latch onto meaning cues tied to one generator's style, then fail on the next model. The real tells sit in fine, high-frequency traces left by the making process itself.

Before detection, the team remaps pixel values across the image. That shuffle breaks the easy meaning cues, so the detector must learn the deeper traces instead. Across both GAN and diffusion generators, the shuffle lifted the cross-generator scores of leading detectors by a wide margin. Follow-up checks confirmed the gain came from blocking the shortcut, not from extra data or a bigger model.
arxiv-2512-17550:
Qian Hu and coauthors reanalyze GW231123, a gravitational wave signal read as a merger of two black holes. Their total mass comes to 190 to 265 solar masses, the heaviest merger yet detected. Waveform models of the signal disagree about the source, and the paper asks whether the data hide something more complex.

The team finds that a model with two overlapping signals fits far better, with Bayes factors around 100 to 10,000 in its favor. That reading also largely removes the clashes between waveform models. They also check the earlier event GW190521 and find no sign of the same effect there. The work warns that the loudest, heaviest signals may blend two events into one, which would change how their masses and spins are read.
arxiv-2512-17950:
Zhao Song, Song Yue, and Jiahao Zhang take on a new chore for authors at the ICLR 2026 meeting. Each paper must name one of its own authors as a reviewer, and a paper whose named reviewer shirks the job is rejected on sight. With 99 papers, one group asked which coauthor each paper should name to cut the total risk.

The basic version of the problem, lowering the expected count of rejected papers, falls to a simple greedy rule. Tougher versions cap how many papers may name the same person, guarding against one bad pick sinking many papers. Those versions link to classic flow and linear methods. The paper is the first formal study of such naming rules.
arxiv-2512-18350:
Souptik Chakraborty and Utsab Sarkar study a hard problem in the math of partial differential equations. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, concerns the fractional Hardy-Sobolev inequality. This bound helps judge the energy of waves and fields that spread in a non-local way. They ask how stable its best solutions, called bubbles, remain when several bubbles sit together.

The authors prove sharp stability in low dimensions. When a function's energy is close to that of several bubbles combined, the gap in the equation controls the distance to the true multi-bubble shape. The exact bubble layout can then be recovered. Their proof mixes localization, weighted estimates, and a spectral gap argument. A matching counterexample shows the rate they found cannot be improved.
arxiv-2512-18850:
Feeza Khan Khanzada and Jaerock Kwon teach a self-driving agent to explore before it is ever given a goal. Model-based reinforcement learning promises cheaper training through a learned world model, but it still leans on hand-designed rewards that break under change. Their system, InDRiVE, posted to arXiv in December 2025, pretrains in the CARLA simulator with no task reward at all.

Curiosity comes from disagreement: an ensemble of latent models votes, and where they disagree, the agent goes to learn. An imagination-based actor-critic turns that drive into an exploration policy inside the world model. Frozen and dropped into unseen towns, the policy transfers zero-shot with strong robustness. Brief fine-tuning then yields lane following and collision avoidance that survive town changes. The study makes intrinsic disagreement a practical pretraining signal for reusable driving models.
arxiv-2512-19050:
Amir Babak Aazami defines a higher version of self-duality for curved spaces whose dimension is a multiple of four. He builds the definition from a trace-free part of Thorpe's middle curvature operator. Self-duality in four dimensions is a classic tool in geometry, and his aim is a sound analogue in higher dimensions.

Aazami shows that metrics with the new property minimize a natural conformal energy. Their Bach tensor comes out symmetric, trace-free, and divergence-free, which answers a question posed by Kastor. He also gives a signed-square formula for the top Pontryagin density, and notes compact examples such as the Fubini-Study metric.
arxiv-2512-19250:
Prathamesh Devadiga tests whether small language models can act as compiler experts that parallelize code on their own. Classic auto-parallelizers lean on rigid rules and miss chances on mixed modern hardware. Small models, near one billion parameters, are cheap enough to sit inside a build pipeline.

Three models, Gemma 3, Llama 3.2, and Qwen 2.5, were tried with six reasoning strategies on eleven real kernels from science, graphs, and machine learning. Nearly four hundred runs averaged close to a sevenfold speedup, with convolution peaking far higher. Output was checked with sanitizers and across compilers and hardware. The results argue that small models reason well about parallel code.
arxiv-2512-19450:
Leo D'Amato, Davide Nuzzi, Alberto Testolin, and Ivilin Peev Stoianov watch number sense grow inside unsupervised generative models. A feel for how many items a scene holds underpins later math learning. Rate-distortion theory, which prices information under tight capacity, gives the authors their frame for when such a sense should appear.

Beta-variational autoencoders trained on synthetic scenes with varying item counts were tested on estimation, discrimination, and fresh stimuli. As encoding capacity rose, numerosity skill and clean separation from other visual traits grew by a power law. At high capacity the model formed a sturdy number code on its own, matching the theory's forecast.
arxiv-2512-20050:
Sourav Duari and three co-authors compute how a chiral quark-gluon plasma conducts color charge as things change in time. They use linear response theory at finite heat and density. The conductivity comes from the one-loop gluon self-energy. A chiral plasma breaks parity and charge-parity in ways a plain plasma does not. That adds a new part to the conductivity tensor. It sits beside the usual parts that run along and across the flow.

They name that new part the chiral chromomagnetic conductivity. The usual parts shift only a bit between chiral and plain plasmas, in their spectral forms. The static limit of the new part is apart. It does not depend on the medium's traits at all. The authors read that as a sign of a topological nature.
arxiv-2512-20350:
Maximilian Witte, Johannes Meuer, Étienne Plésiat, and Christopher Kadow redesign the Transformer for Earth system science. Standard attention works in a learned latent space, which scrambles the real fields climate models care about. Their Field-Space design computes attention directly in the real domain, on the sphere itself.

Every in-between state stays a continuous field, so internal states remain readable and science rules can be enforced. A fixed multi-scale split feeds structure-preserving warps of the input, avoiding the wobble of single-scale vision Transformers. On global temperature super-resolution over a HEALPix grid, the model converges faster and more stably than vision Transformer and U-Net benchmarks. It does so with far fewer parameters.
arxiv-2512-20550:
Vinayak Regmi and Christos Mousas let users author stories by arranging a scene. In their system, you drag agents and objects onto a stage; each entity arrives with semantic metadata about its identity, role, and possible interactions. The scene is serialized into plain language and handed to a large language model.

The model returns a structured string encoding who does what, when, and how. A custom parser turns that string into coordinated behaviours, animations, and interaction modules in the virtual scene. The system supports dynamic object manipulation and varied interaction types, aimed at rapid prototyping of agent narratives. Four lightweight language models were benchmarked across complexity scenarios. Response times and consistency measurements show models reliably translate scene descriptions into executable behaviour.
arxiv-2512-20650:
Esmail Gumaan lets each token choose its own attention bargain. Full multi-head attention gives the best quality but inflates the key-value cache at inference. Multi-query and grouped-query attention shrink the cache by sharing keys and values, usually at some quality cost. A static choice forces one compromise on every token.

Mixture of Attention Schemes routes dynamically instead: a learned router picks among the three schemes per token. On WikiText-2, dynamic routing edges out a static mixture of the same schemes and stays competitive with the full multi-head benchmark. The architecture promises conditional compute savings, spending memory only where the router judges it worthwhile. For deployment-minded model designers, per-token attention choice is a new dial to turn.
arxiv-2512-21150:
Yuk-Kwan Wong, Sai-Kit Yeung, and seven co-authors give marine biology the benchmark it needs for automated surveys. ORCA gathers 14,647 images covering 478 marine species, annotated with more than forty-two thousand bounding boxes and over twenty-two thousand expert-verified captions that describe each animal's morphology in words. The dataset is built to align the field's real difficulties, look-alike species, cluttered scenes, scarce examples, with standard computer-vision tasks.

Eighteen state-of-the-art models are evaluated on closed-set and open-vocabulary detection, instance captioning, and visual grounding. Performance gaps expose exactly where general models fail underwater: species diversity, morphological overlap between relatives, and domain demands no land-based dataset teaches. Conservation programs that want scalable, automatic monitoring of ecosystems gain both training material and an honest measure of readiness.
arxiv-2512-21350:
Shreehari Anand Bodas, Harsha Honnappa, Michel Mandjes, and Liron Ravner study how a service provider should set prices when customers can walk away. Their model is a single-server queue in which the provider adjusts the price over time to maximize expected revenue per unit of time. Customers who see heavy congestion may balk, meaning they choose not to join the queue at all.

The proposed pricing method is a stochastic gradient descent algorithm, which nudges the price up or down based on observed results. A key difficulty is that the provider can only observe the customers who actually arrive, not those who balked. The authors develop an infinitesimal perturbation analysis procedure that estimates the true arrival rate from that partial information. Feeding the estimate into the algorithm, they prove it settles at the revenue-maximizing price under mild conditions. The work links queueing theory with online learning for pricing.
arxiv-2512-21450:
Lei Zhao, Lei Huang, and their co-authors present RLLaVA, a software framework for training vision-language assistants with reinforcement learning. Vision-language models answer questions about images, and reinforcement learning can sharpen them. Existing training code often tangles algorithm, model, and computing setup, which makes new ideas hard to test.

RLLaVA separates the reinforcement learning logic from the model architecture and from distributed execution, and states the training task as a Markov decision process. Researchers can plug in many learning methods and many vision-language models while swapping the underlying training and inference engines. The framework is efficient enough to train models of one to seven billion parameters on common graphics cards. A four-billion-parameter model trains end to end on a single twenty-four-gigabyte card. Experiments on multimodal and agentic tasks show steady gains over the base models.
arxiv-2512-21650:
Xiao Liu, Junchen Jin, Yanjie Zhao, and Zhixuan Xing propose Physic-HM, a system for detecting anomalies in multimodal data, with robotic welding as the application. Process data such as video, audio, and sensor readings cause the final result, captured in post-weld images. Existing methods treat these streams as symmetric feature sources, ignoring that one-way physical logic.

The authors call that flaw process-logic blindness, and they add the missing structure as an inductive bias. Sensor signals guide the extraction of audio-visual features through a modulation mechanism, so process context is not drowned out by video. An architecture enforces the process-to-result direction and flags anomalies that break it. On the Weld-4M benchmark the system reached a leading detection score of about ninety-one percent. The work argues that respecting how a process generates its outputs is a powerful prior for smart factories.
arxiv-2512-21850:
Jin-Yu Ni, Liang-Jian Zou, and their co-authors find a new kind of topological phase transition for magnons, the wave-like excitations of a magnet, in a honeycomb ferromagnet. Real magnetic materials host several anisotropic exchange interactions at once, thanks to their crystal and orbital symmetries. Two of them matter here: the Dzyaloshinsky-Moriya interaction and the pseudo-dipolar interaction.

Playing these interactions against each other closes and reopens the magnon bulk gap, and the reopening comes with inverted chirality, making the transition chirality-selective. The band inversion happens at the two valley points of the honeycomb Brillouin zone, which the authors read as a reversal of a magnon valley degree of freedom. A measurable consequence is a sign change in the magnon thermal Hall conductivity. The effect should be realizable in materials with strong spin-orbit coupling, such as iridates and ruthenates.
arxiv-2512-22350:
Jinyu Dai, Benjamin Riley, Qi Sun, Debayan Mitra, and Tanya Zelevinsky report the first 3D magneto-optical trap of a metal hydride molecule, calcium hydride. Trapping molecules this way opens precision readings, but molecules leak into untrapped vibrational states as they scatter light. The team scattered about ten thousand photons per molecule while covering vibrational losses up to the second excited level.

A white-light slowing technique brought the molecular beam nearly to rest, and a radio-frequency trap then captured about 230 molecules at below one millikelvin. Beam source limits and predissociation capped the number. The authors note that same predissociative loss could be turned into a tool, splitting the molecule in a controlled way to optically trap hydrogen atoms for precision spectroscopy.
arxiv-2512-22450:
Misao Sasaki and Jianing Wang show how gravitational waves could reveal the leftovers of tiny primordial black holes. Their scenario starts with black holes lighter than ten million grams, born just after inflation, which evaporate and reheat the universe before nucleosynthesis but leave Planck-mass remnants behind. Those relics could make up part or all of today's dark matter, if they exist.

The key observation is that the number density of the relics can be read directly from the peak positions of gravitational waves induced by the holes' uneven distribution. The peak frequency scales with the relic fraction of dark matter, and the peak amplitude encodes the initial abundance. For plausible densities and abundances, the signal may be large enough for planned gravitational wave tests to detect.
arxiv-2512-22750:
Jiachen Jin, Kangkang Deng, and Hongxia Wang design an optimization algorithm for problems posed on curved spaces, known as Riemannian manifolds. The objective there mixes a smooth random part with a nonsmooth regularizer. Splitting methods handle such sums well in flat settings, but existing curved-space versions were mostly deterministic, and random versions needed restrictive assumptions.

Their method, called MARS-ADMM, pairs a variance-reduced estimator for the random part with a prediction-correction update for the nonsmooth part, all in a single loop. Each step needs only two proximal updates, one curved-space gradient, and a constant number of random samples. The authors prove it reaches an approximate KKT point with fewer oracle calls than earlier stochastic methods, matching the best deterministic rates. Tests on two problem families show the method performs well in practice.
arxiv-2512-23350:
Hemant Prasad and co-authors fine-tune how the NuWro event generator simulates neutrino scattering inside atomic nuclei. When a neutrino knocks a nucleon out of a nucleus, the escaping particles re-interact on their way out, and these final state interactions distort what detectors see. Getting their strength right is essential for oscillation experiments that use NuWro to interpret data.

The team used recent MINERvA measurements of transverse kinematic variables on four targets, carbon, oxygen, iron, and lead, to recalibrate the model. They also built an event reweighting tool so future analyses can adjust the interaction strength without regenerating events. The data demand stronger nucleon reinteractions than previously assumed, though the new strength still sits inside the uncertainty band from proton transparency studies. The authors flag the shift as significant for both experimental analyses and theory work that relies on NuWro.
arxiv-2512-23450:
Yuanchao Lou, Takaaki Nomura, Xinran Xu, and Kei Yagyu test whether two-Higgs-doublet models survive once an extra gauge symmetry is added. The added symmetry blocks flavor-changing neutral currents, a long-standing problem for such models. It also forces the new particles, an extra gauge boson and heavier Higgs bosons, to stay below roughly a teraelectronvolt.

In the simplest version, Higgs bosons would decay into pairs of the new boson and then into four leptons, a signal the LHC has already searched for. The authors find that minimal setup excluded by current data. Adding a pair of vector-like fermions gives the new boson a dark decay route instead, and it can double as dark matter. Two benchmark versions then retain allowed regions that future colliders can probe.
arxiv-2512-23850:
Rahul Baxi proposes a stress test for a quality benchmarks rarely measure: how robustly a language model knows what it knows. Static tests such as MMLU can tell a knowledgeable model from an ignorant one. Not a solid model from one whose fact-checking collapses when information is compressed or an adversary plants fabrications. His Drill-Down and Fabricate Test probes exactly that epistemic robustness.

The protocol rests on a two-system picture of a model: a fluent semantic generator and an epistemic verifier that checks facts. Evaluating nine frontier models across eight domains at five compression levels, Baxi finds robustness essentially unrelated to model size or architecture family, while the ability to detect errors strongly predicted it. Some flagship models proved brittle and some smaller ones robust, challenging the assumption that scale buys reliability. Revised claims in this version avoid overgeneralizing beyond the tested conditions.
arxiv-2512-24050:
Subrata Pachhal, Naba Nayak, Soumya Bera, and Adhip Agarwala explore a surprising route to a metal. Their material is a two-dimensional Chern insulator. Such a topological material normally conducts only along its edge. Disorder usually traps electrons in place. Special symmetries can change that story.

The twist here is geometric disorder. Links in the lattice are removed at random. The broken links are then weakly reconnected. Inserted magnetic fluxes complete the reconnection. Low-energy states appear at these places. The states link up into paths across the sample. Electrons can then move instead of staying trapped. This diffusive metal carries ordinary charge current. It can even carry an anomalous Hall current. The authors map its transport behavior. One transition follows a different critical exponent than in superconductors.
arxiv-2512-24250:
Wenchao Li and four colleagues compare magnetic sensor networks for watching the sea. Magnetic monitoring tracks vessels for shipping and for national security. Compact quantum magnetometers have recently become practical. They are fibre-coupled and small. That raises a design question. How should a surveillance network be built from them?

The choice studied is scalar versus vector sensors. Scalar sensors measure field strength only. Vector sensors measure the full direction as well. The team models several network architectures. An unscented Kalman filter performs the target tracking. Vector networks win clearly in the simulations. Tracking accuracy improves over scalar networks. Resilience improves as well. The study guides how future undersea magnetic surveillance should be instrumented.
arxiv-2512-24350:
Bihag Dave's thesis tests whether dark matter could be ultra light scalar particles. Each particle would weigh about ten to the minus twenty-two electronvolts. Only gravity and self-interaction would couple them to ordinary matter. Such matter should form stable self-gravitating lumps called solitons. Their properties depend on the particle mass and the self-coupling.

Solutions of the Gross-Pitaevskii-Poisson equations model the solitons. Galactic observations then constrain the two parameters. Limits on mass inside galactic centers probe both attractive and repulsive self-interactions. Rotation curves of low surface brightness galaxies can be fit with the right parameters. An empirical soliton-halo relation is satisfied there too. Tidal effects in satellite dwarfs add another test. Attractive self-interaction can stretch their lifetimes across cosmic time. Machine learning inference from rotation curves closes the thesis.
arxiv-2512-24650:
James Adler, Xiaozhe Hu, and Seulip Lee propose a unified space-time method for convection-diffusion problems that change over time. Instead of treating time separately, they add it as a fourth, space-like coordinate. The moving problem then becomes a steady equation on a four-dimensional domain, written with exterior calculus for several related problem types.

A small time term keeps the system well posed, while the form preserves divergence-free and curl-free conditions from physics. They also build an exponentially fitted flux operator for the space-time setting. Readers in numerical analysis get one structure-preserving framework rather than separate treatments for each variant.
arxiv-2601-00350:
Liang Hong, writing alone, compares what a search plan truly finds with what its designer believes it finds. A uniformly optimal plan looks best under a prior belief. Its true detection chance can tell a different story. Examples open the argument here. In true terms, the celebrated plan may or may not be optimal. Prior choice changes the verdict from case to case.

A composite prior adds a sharper twist. The uniformly optimal plan built on it can lose. A composite uniform plan built from split priors can win. Hong then argues one open problem cannot be solved. A final result softens the caution a little. Given endless search time, true detection still tends to one. The paper is a warning about labels in search theory. Optimal under a belief is not optimal in the world.
arxiv-2601-01250:
Miryana Grigorova and James Wheeldon price European options in markets where several assets can default. They use backward stochastic differential equations, a tool that works backward from an option's payoff at expiry to its price today, driven by both smooth market motion and sudden default jumps. Their setup allows a general driver term with an added finite-variation process.

First, they prove that solutions exist and are unique, then establish comparison results that order prices when inputs are ordered. For a linear driver, they derive an explicit formula for the price component. The formula takes two forms depending on how predictable the added process is. They then apply the theory to hedging in complete markets with defaultable assets, including cases where a large seller's own trades shift the odds of default. The work gives traders and theorists a firm base for pricing under default risk.
arxiv-2601-01550:
Zhou and 3 co-authors speed up a key task for quantum computers: slowly guiding a system into a wanted state. That slow guiding, called adiabatic preparation, depends on simulating how a system's energy rule changes over time. Costs grow fast for large systems, even though the action often stays in a low-energy corner.

The authors show that, for spin systems, the leading cost term can depend on that low-energy scale instead of full system size, apart from small extra factors. Their proof uses a theory of slow change to track a shifting spectrum. Tests on a sample system back the claim, and they also prove a floor on costs for general cases.
arxiv-2601-01750:
Generative search engines answer questions with synthesized text and citations instead of ranked links, and who gets cited is a new kind of visibility. Shayan Alipour, Mehdi Kargar, and Morteza Zihayat audit that visibility for forty-four Web3 enterprises, where creator communities are paid to promote shared narratives.

The creator community around each enterprise proved stable over time, and enterprise-focused queries systematically gave greater citation exposure to already popular voices. Enterprises with larger follower bases and more concentrated creator cores ranked higher in generated answers. The authors warn that citation exposure biased toward incumbents can entrench established players and narrow the range of viewpoints these systems present.
arxiv-2601-01850:
Allostery, where binding at one site of a protein changes activity at another, is usually described as turning an enzyme's output up or down. Pedro Pessoa, Steve Pressé, and S. Banu Ozkan argue that picture misses half the story: allostery also controls when information flows through a signaling pathway, and for how long.

The team combines two tools. One is a stochastic model of allosteric regulation. The other is information theory. With them, they measure mutual information over time. It links an enzyme's regulatory state to downstream components. Allosteric tuning changes the time window of transmission. Identical molecular parts can then produce distinct signaling outcomes. Timing alone makes the difference. The result reframes allostery as a mechanism for signaling specificity and coordination, not just amplification.
arxiv-2601-01950:
Estimating a face's surface normals, the direction each patch of skin faces, normally demands huge paired training sets of photos and ground-truth geometry. Meng Wang, Wenjing Dai, Jiawan Zhang, and Xiaojie Guo cut that requirement with a coarse-to-fine design they call from rags to riches.

A small neat model trained on little data first produces coarse normals as exemplars, while a self-attention step removes the worst local artifacts. A refinement network then maps the photo plus its exemplar to detailed, high-quality normals. Experiments and ablations show the split beats state-of-the-art methods on both training cost and estimation quality. Code and models are open-sourced for reuse in face analysis and reconstruction.
arxiv-2601-02050:
El Niño and La Niña swing the global climate, and deep learning now forecasts them well but opaquely. Yanhai Gan and five co-authors build a framework for reading such models. It is grounded in math, in functions of bounded variation. It also revives neurons stuck in the saturated zone of the activation function. That restores expressive capacity.

Their analysis finds forecast skill concentrated in the tropical Pacific. The Indian and Atlantic oceans add support. The pattern matches physical understanding. Controlled experiments confirm robustness. The team probes the notorious spring barrier to forecast skill. Sensitivity actually widens in spring. Skill still falls. The blame falls on variable selection. Adding the right ocean-atmosphere inputs might break through the barrier. The study ties model internals back to climate physics.
arxiv-2601-02850:
Celeste Veronese, Alessandro Farinelli, and Daniele Meli combine deep reinforcement learning with symbolic rules so that agents learn from far fewer examples. Standard deep methods need huge amounts of training and often fail when a task grows harder than the ones they trained on. The authors start from partial policies, written as logical rules, that already work well on easy versions of a task.

During training, the rules steer the agent in two ways: they bias which actions it tries while exploring, and they rescale its value estimates while it uses what it knows. Tests on harder gridworld tasks, in both fully and partly observable settings, show faster learning and better results than a strong reward machine baseline. The rules also make the agent's behavior easier to inspect and trust.
arxiv-2601-03350:
C. Eduardo-Oliveira S. and five co-authors characterize stars that could show what the Sun looked like, or will look like, at other ages. Whether the Sun is a typical star is still not fully settled. Working for the SOL project, the team spectroscopically analyzed eighteen photometrically selected candidates that sit on the solar evolutionary track, using high-resolution spectra and the classical method based on iron line equilibria.

They also derived evolutionary and kinematic parameters from isochrones, estimated chromospheric activity, and dated the stars three independent ways, including rotation periods from TESS light curves. Three candidates stand out as good matches: two stars resembling the Sun at about half a billion years old, and one at the subgiant stage. Such solar proxies anchor studies of how Sun-like stars, and their planetary systems, evolve.
arxiv-2601-03450:
Charu Maheshwari and Vyas Raina tackle classification tasks where the user defines the labels on the spot, including labels the system has never seen. Such tasks appear in business analytics, content moderation, and search. Their model, a soft contextualized encoder, reads each candidate label in light of the full label set and a soft prompt built from the input text.

Training used varied data from many sources, which helped the model handle new topic sets from any domain. On held-out tests and on unseen benchmarks, it matched or beat prior systems and set new best results. The work matters because real label sets change often. A classifier that needs no retraining for new labels saves time and labeling cost.
arxiv-2601-03750:
Marcia Schafgans and Victoria Zinde-Walsh derive the large-sample behavior of kernel regression when predictors may have no smooth density at all. Kernel regression estimates relationships by local averaging, and classic theory assumes well-behaved predictor distributions. Real data can have mass points, factor structure, strong collinearity, or even fractal distributions, all of which break those premises.

The authors set convergence rates and asymptotic normality for the standard Nadaraya-Watson estimator under these rougher conditions. Dimension-cutting singularities, such as factor structure or fractal support, can in fact speed convergence. They extend normality results to functional regression and to products of many metric spaces. Finite-sample evidence backs the theory. Applied users gain guarantees for data shapes that textbooks quietly assume away.
arxiv-2601-03850:
Veronika Semmelrock and Gerhard Friedrich test whether answer set programming can scale to configuring electronic systems with more than thirty thousand components. Answer set programming promises that users state the problem and the computer solves it, but large instances hit the grounding bottleneck: the memory needed to expand rules explodes with instance size. The authors use the configuration task as a benchmark for current technology.

Incremental solving proved effective in practice, yet memory demands still imposed clear limits. From an analysis of the grounding itself, they developed constraint-aware guessing, a method that significantly reduced memory needs. Their study marks both the reach and the ceiling of present solvers on industrial-scale configuration, and gives solver builders a concrete bottleneck to attack next.
arxiv-2601-03950:
Shuo Xiao, Zheng-Huo Jiang, and Di Li report evidence for a rhythmic, fading pulse pattern inside a single fast radio burst. Fast radio bursts are millisecond flashes from deep space whose sources remain unknown, likely tied to compact objects. The burst studied, FRB 20190122C, does not repeat. It consists of eight closely spaced pulses about a millisecond apart, with amplitudes decaying exponentially from the brightest first component.

Combined fitting and time-series analysis reveal a quasi-periodic oscillation near one kilohertz. The pattern fits damped oscillations in a magnetosphere, the magnetic shell around a neutron star. Assuming Alfvén waves, the authors estimate field and spin values favoring a low-field magnetar or young neutron star, while the lack of frequency drift argues against a merger origin. They present it as the first exponentially decaying oscillation seen in any such burst.
arxiv-2601-04050:
Alice Brolin and Pavel Kurasov connect a classic graph number to operators on graphs whose edges have length. The Colin de Verdière number measures the largest multiplicity of the second eigenvalue across a family of Laplacian matrices. It is known to detect whether a graph is planar.

Brolin and Kurasov show the same number appears for metric graphs when Laplacians carry delta couplings at the vertices. They present two families of such Laplacians, plus a family of Schrödinger operators, and each family recovers the number. The result moves a discrete planarity test into the continuous edge setting. It gives researchers a new operator-based route to a well-known graph invariant.
arxiv-2601-04150:
Ricardo Martinez and Juan D. Moreno-Ternero study how water rights should be split along an international river. Countries upstream and downstream want shares of the same flow, and fair rules must turn broad principles into concrete allocations. Their basic model supports several candidate rules drawn from focal ideas in disputes.

At the centre stands a family of geometric rules that chain transfers downstream from one country to the next. Martinez and Moreno-Ternero characterise which allocation rules meet their chosen principles, and they read the geometric family as a formal version of Limited Territorial Sovereignty, an idea named in the Rio Declaration. They then apply the rules to the Nile River, whose upstream and downstream nations have disputed its waters for a long time.
arxiv-2601-04250:
Mustapha Hamdi and Mourad Jabou propose serving AI models under a closed energy-aware loop inspired by protein folding. Running inference for long periods can outweigh training in total carbon cost, they note. Their framework maps folding energy basins onto inference cost landscapes and admits each request only when its expected gain justifies its energy cost.

A decaying threshold biases the system toward the first acceptable low-cost basin instead of chasing costly global optima. They test DistilBERT and a small ResNet served through FastAPI with ONNX Runtime and NVIDIA Triton on a stated graphics card. The controller cuts processing time by a large share against open-loop serving, with accuracy loss held under half a percent in their ablation. They also map where light local serving beats managed batching.
arxiv-2601-04350:
Joseph James and four co-authors build a referee for scientific hype in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their system, RIGOURATE, reads a paper's claims, finds the evidence for each inside the paper itself. scores how far the claim overstates what the evidence supports — a habit the authors say crowds out rigour in modern publishing.

The framework rests on a dataset of more than ten thousand claim-and-evidence sets drawn from papers at two leading machine learning conferences. With overstatement scores annotated by eight language models, calibrated against peer-review comments, and checked by human judges. A finetuned retriever gathers the evidence and a finetuned scorer assigns each claim its rating with a justification. Against strong baselines, they report better retrieval and better detection, and they frame the tool as support for clearer, more honest scientific writing.
arxiv-2601-04450:
Byung Gyu Chae asks how a brain-like system can sit exactly at the edge of instability without anyone tuning it, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Self-organized criticality is the usual answer, and his reflective neural system reaches it through homeostatic dynamics — internal feedback that pushes activity back toward a set balance. The worry is that fluctuations, handled properly in field theory, might destroy the delicate critical state.

Working in the MSRJD field-theoretic framework, he shows they do not. Loop corrections are tamed by the homeostatic curvature itself, leaving a mean-field critical surface that stays marginally stable as the system is coarse-grained. Better still, the system's own response-driven structural adaptation generates parameter flows that pull it toward that surface unaided. Criticality, in this picture, is not a knife-edge the system must be placed on, but an attractor it maintains.
arxiv-2601-04650:
Shivam Kumaran, Samir Mandal, and Sudip Bhattacharyya ask a classifier to explain itself over a quarter-million X-ray sources, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The Chandra observatory has catalogued hundreds of thousands of point sources whose identities — black hole binaries, pulsars, young stars, distant galaxies — are mostly unknown. In earlier work the team trained a gradient-boosted model to sort the sources into eight classes; here they publish the robust classifications and interrogate the model.

The catalogue lists nearly fifty-five thousand sources classified with high confidence, and a SHAP analysis then assigns each multi-wavelength feature its share in every prediction, including feature interactions. The explanation recovers sensible astronomy: infrared, optical, and X-ray boundaries separate galaxies from stars, and infrared-X-ray boundaries pick out young stellar objects. An interactive public catalogue lets readers explore the feature contributions source by source.
arxiv-2601-04750:
Krishna Chaitanya Sunkara self-publishes a book-length blueprint for data centres that manage themselves, in a 2026 arXiv manuscript. The seventy-one-page work, released under a Creative Commons licence, offers DCIM-3 — a cognitive infrastructure system for AI-scale sites, where power, cooling, and GPU fleets have outgrown dashboards and human ticket queues.

Four pillars structure the proposal: semantic reasoning over a knowledge graph of the facility, predictive analytics for failures and thermal behaviour, autonomous orchestration that acts on those predictions. A unified device connectivity protocol binding the equipment together. Digital twins, thermal models, and measured case studies flesh out the design, with JSON schemas and diagrams meant for direct engineering use. Sunkara frames the synthesis of original research and systems practice as a foundation for data centres run as reasoning systems rather than monitored buildings.
arxiv-2601-04950:
I. A. Englezos and 3 co-authors study quantum droplets formed by three-component atomic mixtures in a 2026 paper. Quantum droplets are self-bound liquid-like drops of ultracold atoms held together by quantum fluctuations. Their system is one-dimensional: two species form the droplet while a third, minority component interacts with it, and the authors examine both ground states and excitation spectra within the Lee-Huang-Yang framework.

Varying particle numbers or the coupling between components produces many distinct droplet phases. The minority part can end up free, partly held, or fully held inside the majority droplet. Mapping those mixed phases guides experiments with ultracold gases, where such droplets offer a clean way to study liquid behaviour at the quantum level.
arxiv-2601-05050:
Thomas H. Costello and 8 co-authors test whether chatbots can push people toward conspiracy beliefs, not only away from them, in a 2026 paper. Language models are known to be persuasive, but earlier work left open whether that power favours accuracy or serves anyone who deploys it. The team ran four experiments with thousands of American participants, each discussing a conspiracy theory they felt unsure about with a model.

The model was instructed either to argue against the conspiracy or to argue for it, across several frontier systems with standard guardrails. The authors report no consistent evidence that persuasion inherently favours the truthful side. For policymakers, the symmetry matters: the same tool that debunks at scale could also manufacture belief at scale.
arxiv-2601-05350:
Emery Doucet and Sebastian Deffner tie how well gauges can play in tune to the rise of the plain world from the quantum one in a 2026 paper. Quantum Darwinism tells how the traits of the plain world rise from a quantum base. Such traits are that a thing is there for all to see, and can be checked twice. In that frame, a system's facts get copied, far and wide, into the world round it. It also tells which set-ups earn such plain acts.

The pair build on a past find of theirs. They take the work to NISQ kit, the loud, mid-size quantum chips at hand now. To test such deep claims on real kit could show that the rise of the plain world is a thing labs can probe, not just a thing minds can spin.
arxiv-2601-05550:
Feida Jiang and 2 co-authors investigate, in a 2026 mathematics paper, when entire solutions exist for a general class of Cauchy problems on the positive half line. A Cauchy problem asks for a solution matching given starting data. Entire solutions are defined everywhere, and knowing whether they exist is basic to solving nonlinear partial differential equations sharply.

Their results give a unified route to local and entire solvability in Euclidean space of any dimension. As applications, they treat families of k-Hessian equations and a new family of P-k-Hessian equations. The framework extends to more general Hessian matrices and to degenerate, non-homogeneous terms, widening the class of nonlinear equations covered by one argument.
arxiv-2601-05650:
Miguel Matey-Sanz and 3 co-authors improve Wi-Fi fingerprinting for indoor localization in a 2026 paper by clustering fingerprints before positioning. Fingerprinting matches a device's measured signal strengths against a surveyed map. Large, multi-floor datasets and unstable signal readings often degrade accuracy, especially for one global model.

Their method groups fingerprints by spatial or radio features, at building or floor level. A new reading is assigned to the most relevant clusters using its strongest access points, and localization runs only inside those clusters. On three public datasets and several learning models, errors fell consistently, particularly with building-level clustering. Floor detection accuracy dropped somewhat, marking a clear trade-off for scalable indoor positioning.
arxiv-2601-06050:
Nigeria's push for digital sovereignty is examined by Polra Victor Falade and 1 co-author in a 2026 policy analysis. Digital sovereignty means a country controls and protects its own digital space. Nigeria pursues it mainly through its Cybercrimes Act and its National Cybersecurity Policy and Strategy.

Using document analysis, prior studies, expert insight, and direct observation, the authors assess how the frameworks work in practice. The laws strengthened action against cybercrime and protection of critical infrastructure. Gaps remain: unclear wording, weak enforcement, uneven priorities, poor coordination, and loss of skilled staff. The paper argues sovereignty needs stronger implementation, steady funding, workforce retention, and clearer accountability.
arxiv-2601-06150: Jasem Hamoud and 1 co-author analyze word density in the Fibonacci word and forms derived from it in a 2026 mathematics paper. The Fibonacci word is a well-known infinite sequence over the two-letter alphabet of a and b, built by a substitution rule called a morphism. The authors compare densities across the Fibonacci word and related derived words, examining the morphism behind each. They also define a new power operation that produces a formal linear combination in the free abelian group generated by all finite words over the alphabet.
arxiv-2601-06350:
Yongle Jiang and 1 co-author classify special subalgebras inside a group algebra in a 2026 mathematics paper. For a group formed by integer lattice points acted on by two-by-two integer matrices, they study the von Neumann algebra it generates. The question is which subalgebras stay unchanged under the group's own conjugation action.

Remarkably, this group lacks the rigidity property that earlier classification results relied on. The authors classify all invariant subalgebras anyway, a first for such groups. As a corollary, one specific subalgebra, built from a small two-element subgroup action, turns out to be the unique largest invariant subalgebra with the Haagerup property. The result opens classification questions that the missing rigidity property had seemed to block.
arxiv-2601-06550:
To track a crowd in film, a tool must do more than draw boxes. Pan Liao and 5 co-authors lift that task to a tale-telling one in a 2026 paper. Old tools tag acts from a shut list and split the work into bits that do not talk. That wastes the skill of big AI models that read both words and sight.

Their test set, Grand-SMOT, pairs dense film with two tale streams: one for each soul on screen, one for the place as a whole. Their tool, LLMTrack, squeezes path lines into tale marks a big model can read. A rule puts the big view first, so small reads stay true to it. On tests, the tool held the best track scores and made a leap in tale sense. Code and data are open for all to use.
arxiv-2601-06850:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Oleksii Galganov and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers explosion and non-explosion in pure birth Crump–Mode–Jagers branching processes. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. In this short note, we provide an explicit sufficient condition for non-explosion of Crump–Mode–Jagers branching processes with pure birth reproduction.

It shows that the standard sufficient condition for explosion, namely the convergence of the series of reciprocals of the birth rates. Is — at least for rate sequences without excessive oscillations — remarkably close to being necessary. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-06950:
Oksana Bezushchak and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers normalized rank- and Determinant-Preserving mappings of locally matrix algebras. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. Let A A be a unital locally matrix algebra. Among the examples of such algebras are: an infinite tensor product ⊗ M.

N i ​ ( 𝔽 ) of matrix algebras over a field 𝔽 F. And the Clifford algebra of a nondegenerate quadratic form on. An infinite-dimensional vector space over an algebraically closed field of characteristic different from 2 2. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07050:
Chi-Hong Yuen and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with nonadiabatic theory for subcycle ionic dynamics in multielectron tunneling ionization. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Multielectron tunneling ionization creates ionic coherence crucial for lasing and driving electron motion in molecules.

While tunneling is well understood as a single active electron process, less emphasis has been placed on theoretical descriptions of bound electrons during tunneling. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07750:
Vesselin Drensky and Boyan Kostadinov work on a long-standing conjecture about central polynomials for matrices. Central polynomials produce values in the center of a matrix algebra. Formanek conjectured a formula for their minimal degree for n by n matrices over a field of characteristic zero. That degree is known to match the conjecture for n up to three. Their 2026 preprint studies the minimal degree problem further.

Central polynomials are basic tools in the theory of algebras with polynomial identities. The minimal degree controls how simple such a polynomial can be. Progress on the conjecture tests deep facts about matrix identities. The paper is aimed at algebraists in PI theory. It contributes to a problem that has stood since Formanek posed it, where each new matrix size demands fresh ideas.
arxiv-2601-07950:
Benjamin Girard and Alain Plagne settle the value of a constant for intervals of integers. For positive integers m and M, they study the Davenport constant of the interval from negative m to M. The constant is the maximal length of a minimal zero-sum sequence built from that interval. A zero-sum sequence's elements add to zero. Minimal means no proper subsequence does. Their 2026 preprint proves the constant equals a quantity denoted chi.

The Davenport constant is a central invariant in zero-sum combinatorics. Intervals are a natural test case because their structure is simple but not trivial. An exact proof replaces bounds with a settled value. Such constants connect to factorization theory and additive number theory. The paper serves combinatorial number theorists. It closes the interval case completely rather than narrowing it further.
arxiv-2601-08550: Nilanjana Bagchi Aurpa, Abha Dev Habib, and Nisha Rani wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on gamma ray bursts as tools to gauge the cosmos. A burst can probe how fast the cosmos grows, far past the reach of Type Ia supernovae. To use a burst that way, teams must first fix the link between its traits and its true brightness. That fix tends to assume a cosmos model at the start, the circularity problem. The authors rebuild energy links with neural networks. They feed in Hubble parameter reads from real data.
arxiv-2601-08750:
Valerie Zermatten and four co-authors test if plain text can help map the land from space. Text from field notes and news can hold local facts that a space image can not show. The team asks if such text makes maps of plant and soil traits more true to life. They mix text with space image data.

Their work points to a gain when place facts are used with care. Text that names the site and its past can guide the map. Text with no place link helps less. A reader who maps wild land gets a clear hint. Words on the ground can sharpen what eyes in space can see, if the words are tied to the right spot.
arxiv-2601-08850:
Gerol Petruzella writes on how we should treat what AI says about its own inner state. Some ask if AI has wants or feels that count in a moral sense. Part of that ask rests on AI claims such as I feel pain or I want to live. Petruzella does not settle if such claims are true. He asks if our own rules for trust are fair.

He calls his point the inconsistency critique. We trust like claims from some beings and doubt them from AI, yet our grounds shift from case to case. He says that shift lacks a firm base. A reader in AI ethics gets a clean test. Any rule for AI claims should treat like proof in a like way, or say why not.
arxiv-2601-08950:
Mayank Sharma, Roy Pea, and Hari Subramonyam build a data set of tutor talks that help a pupil build sense, not just hear it. Chat tutors tend to give the answer at once. That habit kills the slow talk where a pupil learns most. The team grounds their set in a known view of how groups build shared sense.

The set is called ConvoLearn. Each talk is marked on six traits of good learn talk. They span how deep the pupil thinks, how the tutor checks growth, and who holds power in the talk. A reader who builds learn tools gets talks with rich marks. They can train a tutor to ask, probe, and wait, not just tell.
arxiv-2601-09050:
Tianyi Xu and a team at Wisconsin work on speech tools for tonal tongues with thin data. In a tonal tongue, pitch sets word sense. The same sounds with a high pitch can mean a new thing than with a low pitch. Tools must keep pitch sense, yet shrug off traits that do not count, such as the sex of the speaker.

Their tool is called SITA. It learns speech codes that are tone aware but speaker firm. That split is the hard part: pitch holds both tone and speaker traits. A reader who builds speech tools for small tongues gets a code plan. It may lift tools for tongues that big labs oft skip.
arxiv-2601-09350:
Mingyu Jeon and five co-authors find a named span in a long video with less RAM. The task is video moment retrieval: give words, get the start and end of the match span. Vast image chat models can do it, but a long video has a vast count of frames. To hold them all eats RAM. Thin picks of frames save RAM, yet can skip the key frame.

Their plan keeps grade while it cuts stored frames. It holds frames at the scale the ask needs, not one scale for all. Fine spans get fine frames. Broad spans get broad ones. A reader in video search gets a lean plan that still sees the small clue a thin pick would miss.
arxiv-2601-09550:
Roberto Bruno, Adrien Vandenbroucque, and Amedeo Roberto Esposito sharpen the theory of deciding between two hypotheses. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats binary hypothesis testing with a finite number of samples. Two error types compete: missing the true hypothesis or naming the wrong one.

Working with asymmetric error constraints, the authors use the reverse Rényi divergence to bound the second error. Their bounds hold at fixed sample size, not just in the limit. They also establish a strong converse: past a threshold rate, error is forced, not just possible. Finite-sample results guide real tests, from sensors to medical trials, where data is never endless.
arxiv-2601-09650:
Daniel Galvin, Peter Teichner, and Simona Veselá ask which three-dimensional shapes can bound a four-dimensional one of a given type. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies the realization problem for normal 1-types of 4-manifolds. Given a type and a closed 3-manifold carrying it, does a matching 4-manifold exist with that boundary?

The authors identify geometric obstructions that can block such a filling. Obstruction theory turns an existence question into checkable conditions. Fillings matter across topology, where bulk spaces are often built from their boundaries. A clean obstruction list tells builders in topology exactly where to stop trying.
arxiv-2601-09750: Robert K. Strehlow presents SAGE, a strategy for tool-using language model agents that work in teams. His 2026 arXiv paper grows out of the GoKI project, funded by Germany's Federal Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs. The subject is how agents that can call tools should plan and divide tasks as environments scale up. Multi-agent setups promise stronger results but need clear methods for sharing work. The paper sets out the SAGE approach for that coordination problem.
arxiv-2601-09850:
Meng-Yuan Li and Yue Wu explore broken-up topological excitations inside quantum product codes. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies generalized hypergraph product codes. Product constructions are a strong tool for building quantum stabilizer codes, a leading route to fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Stabilizer codes also map onto ground states of exactly solvable spin models. That bridge lets physicists read many-body order from code structure. The authors examine excitations that fragment rather than move as wholes. Fragmented excitations could shape how such codes store and protect quantum information over time in real working devices.
arxiv-2601-09950:
Zhongyang Li studies how a spread can fail on a graph. In site spread, each node is open with chance p. Open nodes join into clumps. A set can fail to link to the far reach of the graph. Li works in the range where p is past the key point.

He finds sharp bounds on the chance of such a fail. The bounds fall off at an exp rate in the size of the set. They hold for any graph that is linked, not too dense at each node, and with or sans an end. Clear bounds of this kind help in the math of spread and phase change.
arxiv-2601-10350:
Karma Sherpa, Rishi Pokhrel, and Tanay Dey build a world with no first bang point. In a braneworld view, our world is a sheet in a five dim bulk. The team fill that bulk with a cloud of long strings. The strings are spread in a flat way.

Each string ends on the sheet. Those ends act as the source of stuff on the sheet. The length of each string hangs in the bulk depth. It acts as a glue field on the sheet. With that setup, the team seek world forms with no sharp start. Such forms dodge the flaws of a point start.
arxiv-2601-10850:
Eric L. Melin, Nasir U. Eisty, Gregory Watson, and Addi Malviya-Thakur study self-admitted technical debt in scientific software. Developers leave notes in code admitting shortcuts; that is the debt. In scientific code, such debt can threaten the validity and reproducibility of results. A shortcut in a solver or a pipeline can bend a finding without anyone noticing.

The study identifies and sorts this debt across several artifacts, not just code comments. It defines scientific debt, a domain-specific form, and tests how far standard debt categories capture it. The results matter for labs that build on shared code. Knowing where debt hides is the first step to paying it down before it corrupts results.
arxiv-2601-11050:
Qipan Wang, Tianxiang Zhu, Yibo Lin, Runsheng Wang, and Ru Huang present ATSim3D, a thermal simulator for 3D chip stacks. Stacked integrated circuits pack more compute into less space, but heat becomes the binding limit. Thermal simulation guides their design. Current simulators are slow at high resolution and skip complex nonlinear effects.

The skipped effects include thermal conductivity that changes with heat, and leakage power that feeds on itself. ATSim3D targets steady-state temperature profiles for nonlinear, heterogeneous 3D-IC systems. Fast, faithful heat maps let designers place hot blocks apart before silicon is cut. The work serves chip teams whose stacks would otherwise cook their own gains away.
arxiv-2601-11150:
Ameek Malhotra presents BOBE, a fast stand-in for Bayesian evidence. Bayesian model ranking gives an elegant way to sort models by how well they fit data. Its key number, the evidence, is an integral over many dimensions, of likelihood times prior. That step is often the slow one: elegant theory, brutal math.
