BOBE learns the likelihood's shape so the evidence can be found far faster. It needs only a few true evaluations of the real likelihood. Cosmology teams face this cost on every model check. A fast, faithful stand-in could make strict model ranking routine instead of a luxury.
arxiv-2601-11650:
Jingkang Liang, Niklas Groll, and Gurkan Sin put an LLM agent on process simulators. Their 2026 preprint makes chemical process simulation user-friendly. Modern simulators give detailed design and optimization tools. Building and reading such simulations takes time and expertise.

That barrier limits early exploration by new users. The team integrates an LLM agent with AVEVA Process Simulation. The link runs through the Model Context Protocol, or MCP. Users can then speak to rigorous simulations in plain words. The agent sets up runs and explains results in chat. Early design stages could open to far more engineers. Expert staff would spend less time on routine setups.
arxiv-2601-11750:
Mo Houtti, Moyan Zhou, Daniel Runningen, and their co-authors study AI help for fair, open team meetings. Good meetings need all voices heard, yet social strain makes frank notes hard to give. They test a meeting tool with an AI agent that takes and shares notes.

They propose that an AI go-between feels safer to talk to than a boss or peer. Their tests probe both the gains and the blocks for such AI notes. The work speaks to teams that want more fair talk but fear the social cost of plain speech. It also flags care needed when a tool sits in team talk.
arxiv-2601-12950:
Zining Liang, Runbang Wang, Xuzhou Ye, and Qiuqiang Kong generate spatial audio with flow matching. Immersive spatial audio grows critical for AR and VR, home entertainment, and automotive sound. Existing generative methods stay constrained to low dimensional formats. Binaural audio suits only headphone playback, for example.

First order ambisonics suffers from spatial aliasing and weak resolution at high frequencies. Their system, ImmersiveFlow, converts stereo input into a 7.1.4 spatial format. That format adds height channels for a true three dimensional sound field. Flow matching drives the generation, a modern alternative to diffusion sampling. Rich generated audio could upgrade media made from plain stereo sources.
arxiv-2601-13050:
Lars Kloeser, Mika Elias Beele, and Bodo Kraft look at how well large language models make German text simpler. Simple text helps many readers, yet teams who build such tools lack a good way to check what a model tends to do. Style can shift in ways that plain scores miss.

The team built a tool they call the Simplification Profiler. It turns a batch of plain texts from one model into a rich print of that model. The print joins many traits into one view that people can read. By stacking prints from many texts, teams can spot habits, compare models, and repeat the check later. The aim is a full, fast, and repeatable test of how each model simplifies.
arxiv-2601-13250:
Ante Maric and co-authors use touch sense to guess how an object sits in a hand. Touch can help when sight is blocked or light is poor, as in many grip tasks. Yet one touch read can fit many poses of the same object. That one to many flaw caps old pose tools, most of which were built for sight.

The team built an inverse model based on diffusion. It reads data from a spread out touch sensor skin. From one touch read it can draw the range of poses that fit. That range fits the true flaw of the task, where one read is not one pose. Grip and robot teams gain a pose tool that owns its own doubt.
arxiv-2601-13450:
Cheongho Han and co-authors find four cold super Jupiter worlds from long and complex lens signals. A lens event swells a far star's light as a near star and its worlds pass in front. Most world marks are brief blips. The team re-read KMTNet data for marks that stray from that brief form.

Four events pass their screen. They are named for the years 2020 to 2025. Each shows a long and rich warp in its light curve. Such warps fit cold huge worlds far from their suns. A cold super Jupiter is a hard class to find by other means. The re read shows old data can still yield new worlds.
arxiv-2601-13650:
Ngoctu Bui and Jihoon Lee study how the long-run states of damped wave equations shift in 2026. A global attractor is the set that solutions drift toward over time. If the domain, the region where the wave lives, is slightly perturbed, the attractor may move too. The team asks if that move stays small and controlled.

They use Gromov-Hausdorff distance, a way to measure gaps between whole spaces. With it, they prove continuous dependence of the attractors on the domain. They also prove stability in that same distance. Such results back models where the true domain is known only roughly.
arxiv-2601-14050:
Yuxin Chen and co-authors open up how multilingual mixture-of-experts models route words in 2026. Mixture-of-Experts, or MoE, models use only some sub-networks for each input. MoE designs have shown strong multilingual capabilities. The internal mechanisms behind performance gains and cross-language gaps remain insufficiently understood.

The team conducts a systematic analysis of MoE models. They examine routing behavior and expert specialization across languages and network depth. Layerwise steering tests how to nudge the model per layer. Clear internals could help close the gap between rich and poor languages. The tests span many tongues and depths in the net. That breadth makes the trends they find hard to brush off as quirks of one tongue.
arxiv-2601-14150:
Alejandra Martinez studies how firms adjust when trade ties break for a short time in 2026. International trade relationships often run through relational contracts, built on trust. Martinez exploits an extreme, plausibly exogenous weather shock as a natural test. The shock hit during the 2010-11 La Niña season in Colombia.

Heavy weather restricted Colombian flower exporters' access to cargo terminals. Transaction-level data from Colombian-U.S. trade tracks the response. The study asks how firms adjust during and after such a crisis. Flower exports are time-critical, so the case shows stress in sharp relief.
arxiv-2601-14650:
Hiroma Okubo and nine co-authors present a data analysis framework in this 2026 paper. Their data are ALMA Band 3 observations of the galaxy NGC 1068. Galaxies emit many spectral lines at once, and multi-line analysis tries to read them together. Their framework combines two machine learning tools. Kernel principal component analysis is an unsupervised method that finds patterns. Kernel SHAP is an explainable AI technique that shows which inputs drive a result.

Pairing the two gives patterns plus reasons. The case study is a famous nearby active galaxy. Readers get a worked example of explainable machine learning on real telescope data. Each found pattern can be traced back to the lines that made it.
arxiv-2601-14850:
Fake speech made by computers is hard to spot, and the authors of a 2026 arXiv paper build a tool to catch it. Their system is a transformer, a type of neural network, trained to do more than one task at once. It works from the sound shape of speech itself.

As it listens, the model tracks formants, the resonant tones that shape vowels. It also tracks voicing patterns over time. It then sorts the clip as real or fake. The design also shows if the call leaned more on voiced or unvoiced parts of speech.
arxiv-2601-15150:
A classic model of competing species gets pushed to an endless roster in a 2026 arXiv paper. The Volterra model dates to 1937 and tracks how species grow and compete. Two recent papers showed that an integrable version of the finite-species model is in fact maximally superintegrable.

That is a strong form of order for a dynamical system. The new work extends those results much further. It treats the case of infinitely many species. The count may be countable, like the whole numbers, or uncountable. The integrable structure is shown to survive that leap.
arxiv-2601-15350:
Esmat Sangari and Rajni Kant Bansal study two rival shops that sell goods which go together. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with mixed bundling and price-matching guarantees. Customers differ in what they value, and the two retailers sell complementary products.

One retailer offers mixed bundling, selling items alone or as a bundle. The rival sells only a bundle. The authors characterize the unique pure-strategy equilibria across the subgames. They compare them with a no-bundling benchmark. Their result: mixed bundling strictly dominates its rivals whenever an equilibrium exists at all in the game.
arxiv-2601-15550:
Sangmitra Madhusudan and five co-authors probe regional bias in language models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Cultural commonsense benchmarks often treat a nation as one uniform block. Real practice varies within borders, though. The team asks whether commonsense holds evenly across a country or shifts by region. India is their test case. It has 28 states, 8 union territories, and 22 official languages.

Their benchmark is called Indica. They describe it as the first built to test models on sub-national cultural knowledge. A model can know a national average yet miss local custom. That miss matters when models serve users in specific states. The work pushes evaluation past country-level scores. It asks builders to check whose culture a model actually knows.
arxiv-2601-15750:
Toshiyuki Kobayashi and Michael Pevzner survey Rankin-Cohen brackets in a 2026 arXiv paper. These brackets are basic examples of differential symmetry breaking operators. They can be seen as bi-differential operators, acting on pairs of functions. Their striking trait is how they mirror fusion rules. Those rules govern holomorphic discrete series representations of the Lie group SL(2, R). The brackets are also tied to classical special polynomials.

Representation theory studies how groups act as symmetries of spaces. Symmetry breaking asks what happens when a group shrinks to a subgroup. Operators that respect that breaking are rare and prized. The Rankin-Cohen brackets are the textbook case. A survey from two leading figures maps their role for researchers entering the area.
arxiv-2601-16150:
Maximos Kaliakatsos-Papakostas and coauthors teach a lone coder to add chords to a tune. Their 2026 preprint deals with melodic harm, the task of chords for a set tune. A lone coder frame treats the task as masked chain fill. Past drills for that frame came from spread out fill plans. Those plans can lead to weak or dull chord picks.

The team sets a step drill that masks chords in a set order. The order is named in the title as a staged mask plan. Staged drills aim to teach chord sense step by step. The coder then fills chords with more care for the tune. The work targets music tools that write with users.
arxiv-2601-16350:
Milad Panahi and coauthors learn full sets of growth task answers with physics led solvers. Their 2026 preprint deals with growth tasks that shift with set terms. To learn all answers at once is a core hard task. Mixed ground, as in water flow in rock, makes it more hard. Past nets oft learn one case at a time with no law guide.

Solvers that can be tuned by train steps join laws to learning. The team uses such solvers to learn the full answer set. Full sets let users ask new term cases at low cost. That speed serves water and rock work where terms shift oft. The work joins solver craft to set learning.
arxiv-2601-16450:
Sejun Park, Yeachan Park and Geonho Hwang test what float based coders can state. Their 2026 preprint deals with coder nets, called transformers. Past proofs say coders can match all fair swap fair maps. Those proofs use true real counts and exact steps. Real gear uses float counts with capped fine grain.

Float caps cut what a coder can state in true runs. The team maps which maps stay in reach under float rules. Reach maps warn teams where proofs and gear part ways. They also guide safe depths and widths for real nets. The work joins proof maths to gear facts.
arxiv-2601-16750:
The BESIII team shares new results on charm decays from its vast data sets. No lab holds more threshold data on charm bits than BESIII. The team has now grown those sets by a wide mark. More pairs of D mesons and charm baryons sit in hand. Their 2026 preprint sums the fresh results on weak decays.

Weak decays of charm bits test the base theory's rules. They show how quarks swap types through the weak force. Clean gauges of those swaps bound new physics hunts. The team's larger sets cut the blur on key rates. This sharpens the world pool of charm facts for all labs.
arxiv-2601-16850:
C. L. Sarkis and a large team map spin waves in a famed crystal, RuCl3. The crystal may host a rare spin liquid state. In that state, spins stay fluid down to deep cold. A strong magnet field can push it to a blurred phase. Their 2026 preprint maps that phase with neutron beams.

At and past eight tesla, the spin waves show a clear gap. The team took maps for two field aims in the plane. Those maps show how spins stir in the blurred phase. Such facts test tales of the spin liquid's parts. They guide the long hunt for this odd state.
arxiv-2601-16950:
Ferran Maura, Francesc Wilhelmi, and Boris Bellalta test Wi-Fi for cloud VR streams. Cloud VR sends rich shots to a head set by air. That stream needs high flow and low lag at once. One user can strain a home net. Many users can drown the air band fast. Their 2026 preprint gauges that strain with real film traffic.

The film used a top codec, HEVC, for true load shape. The team counts how many users one net can hold. Those counts guide net design for VR halls and homes. They also warn where 802.11 nets hit their wall. Such facts help plan gear for smooth VR.
arxiv-2601-17450:
Qingchao Shen builds a data-driven way to test AI compilers. Compilers turn AI models into code for many chips. Bugs in them can break models in silent ways. Quality checks are thus key, but hard to write by hand. Shen presents one framework that covers the full test path. It treats stage-specific flaws in a unified way.

The method generates tests from data, not fixed scripts. That lets it probe new models and chips as they come. Compiler teams gain a repeatable hunt for bugs. Early finds protect the apps built on those models. As AI spreads to cars and clinics, such checks matter more. The framework aims at scale and depth at once.
arxiv-2601-17550:
Deepak Singh, Shreyas Khobragade, and Nitin J. Sanket present AsterNav for drone flight in total darkness. Rescue work often runs after power fails. Tiny drones fit tight rescue spaces well. They lack the power for heavy sensors and lights. AsterNav uses passive computation to navigate without light. That keeps the drone light and its power draw low.

Finding survivors fast is the core goal. A drone that works in the dark extends search hours. It also spares human teams the worst risks. Passive methods suit tiny craft that cannot haul lidar. The work joins robotics with disaster response. It aims at rubble, smoke, and blackout zones.
arxiv-2601-17750:
Jan Schröeder, Yair Censor, Philipp Süss, and Karl-Heinz Küfer tackle inverse robustness in radiotherapy planning. Treatment planning is a multi-criteria optimization problem. Planners must balance dose goals against each other. Uncertainty adds a second balance, on robustness itself. Their method handles inverse robustness with semidefinite programming. That class of optimization gives sound, tractable solutions.

A decision maker needs plans that state their trade-offs clearly. Inverse robustness asks what robustness level a chosen plan implies. Making that link explicit aids clinical judgment. Cancer care gains when plans are both strong and honest. Semidefinite tools fit the convex parts of the task. The work joins math programming with bedside needs.
arxiv-2601-17950:
Matthew Walmer, Saksham Suri, Anirud Aggarwal, and Abhinav Shrivastava present UPLiFT, a method for making vision features denser at low cost. Their 2026 preprint sits in a growing area: task-agnostic feature upsampling. Pretrained vision backbones output coarse feature maps. Many tasks, like segmentation, need fine maps instead. Upsampling methods learn to turn the coarse maps into dense ones, giving a shortcut to detail at a fraction of the full cost.

UPLiFT uses local attenders to do that lifting with care. Local focus keeps the cost down while detail goes up. Since the features are task-agnostic, one lifted map can serve many tasks. The work aims at dense vision that stays cheap enough for wide use.
arxiv-2601-18050:
Mickaël Montessinos ties together several hard computing problems about special surfaces. His 2026 preprint deals with superspecial abelian surfaces with a principal polarization. The problems include computing the endomorphism ring of such a surface. They also include computing a certain matrix named for Ibukiyama, Katsura, and Oort, and finding isomorphisms between unpolarised surfaces. The author shows reductions and equivalences between these problems.

Equivalence means a solver for one problem yields solvers for the rest. That web of links lets progress on any one front lift the others. These surfaces matter for cryptography based on isogenies. Clear problem links help judge how hard that cryptography really is.
arxiv-2601-18350:
Junyi Zou studies a clash between two kinds of training in medical language models. His 2026 preprint examines adapter interference. A 14-billion-parameter base model went through a two-stage LoRA pipeline. First came domain-oriented pre-training to inject medical knowledge. Then supervised fine-tuning taught it to follow instructions on medical questions. Zou studies what happens when the two adapters are merged. Domain training and instruction alignment can pull against each other in safety-critical settings.

Interference means the merged model can be worse than either stage alone. In medicine, that loss can touch real advice. Knowing when merging harms helps teams choose safer recipes. The study is a warning and a guide for adapter use.
arxiv-2601-18450:
Jamolidin Abdurakhmanov, of Andijan State University in Uzbekistan, studies when a grid of ones and zeros must hold a heavy column. Each row of the grid is unlike each other row. A column counts as heavy when at least half of its cells hold a one. The ask is plain to state but hard to settle for all grid sizes.

He checks for which widths and heights such a column must show up. Grids like these show up in codes, in tests, and in plans for trials. A heavy column marks a trait that shows in at least half the rows. Proofs about when such a column is forced help teams know what a data set must hold, sight unseen. The work adds one more stone to that base of pure maths.
arxiv-2601-18550:
Bo Gao, Henkjan Gersen, and Simon Hanna study a side push that light can give to tiny forms. When light hits a form that is not the same on both sides, the push can have a side part as well as a front part. Their test form is a small triangle that repeats in a grid. The grid is made of a glass-like stuff that bends light but does not soak it up.

By computer runs, they map how the side push shifts as the form and the light change. In wide zones the push holds firm. In thin bands it flips all at once. The flip bands bear the marks of a known wave clash that boosts some tones and kills the rest. Side pushes could one day move or sort tiny bits with light alone. A firm map is a first step.
arxiv-2601-18650:
Liheng Yu and five colleagues tackle a flaw in tools that make a model forget set facts. To forget is a right in law: a user can ask that their facts be cut from a trained model. Most tests of forget tools use a fair mix of facts to drop. Real asks are not fair: some kinds of fact may fill most of the drop list.

That skew is called long-tailed, since a few kinds hold most of the asks. A forget tool that works on fair tests may fail on skewed ones. The team add a loss tweak that gives more weight to the rare kinds in the drop list. That should help the model drop the rare facts with the same care as the common ones. Fair forget tools count for trust in the firms that hold our facts.
arxiv-2601-18750:
Francesco Chiossi and three colleagues use brain waves to tell a look of choice from a look of mere sight in mixed-world head sets. In such sets, the eyes do much of the work a hand once did. That brings a flaw: a look can mean I pick this, or mere I see this. Kit that can't tell the two will act on mere looks by slip. That flaw has a name, the Midas touch.

The team use a brain wave that comes just ahead of a pick. That wave can serve as a hid yes, with no click or word. They test how the wave shifts when the user means to pick or to just watch, and when the set talks back or stays mute. A sound hid yes could make eye kit fast and safe at once.
arxiv-2601-18850:
Sven Kirchner and three colleagues set out how to fit smart nets into cars in a way that is safe by the book. Nets of the kind in use for sight and text top the charts on many tasks. But a car is a place where a flaw can kill. Safe design there needs proof that a part will act right, or fail in a safe way. A net's acts are hard to prove in that strict way.

Their frame uses the car's many sensors as a check net. If one path fails, the next can catch its work. That spread of paths can lift the whole car's trust grade. The frame is a plan, not a built car. It maps what must be shown for nets to earn a place in cars. Such maps guide firms that must pass strict safe tests.
arxiv-2601-18950:
Harsh Vardhan studies how many computers can agree on an average while sharing very little. In spread out learning, many machines each hold a vector, and the group needs the mean. Bandwidth is tight, so each vector must be squeezed before it is sent.

The twist here is teamwork: the squeezers, called compressors, can work together rather than each acting alone. Shared plans for squeezing can cut the error of the mean for the same small budget of bits. The result speaks to big training jobs where talk between machines, not math, is the main cost.
arxiv-2601-19050:
Everett W. Howe counts a rare family of curves that map onto one fixed curve at every degree. A genus two curve is a smooth shape with two holes, and an elliptic curve has one. Howe asks when maps of every whole number degree exist from the first kind onto one fixed second kind.

He shows that, up to sameness of shape, exactly twenty such pairs exist over the complex numbers. A count that ends in a small, exact list is rare in this area of math. The full list gives number theorists a closed case to test wider ideas about maps between curves against.
arxiv-2601-19350:
Tathagata Raha and three co-authors grade text generation by cross examining the texts themselves. Classic scores like BLEU compare word overlap and miss whether meaning survived. The team adapts a cross examination framework that needs no reference answer.

It treats the source and the new text as two knowledge bases and asks each verifiable questions drawn from the other. Three scores come out: coverage, conformity, and consistency. Interpretable scores that track fidelity would help anyone who uses machine summaries, translations, or reports and needs to know what was lost or bent.
arxiv-2601-19450:
Pravabati Chingangbam reads the shape of the early universe's hydrogen signal to hunt for traces of inflation. The redshifted 21 centimeter signal from the cosmic dawn and the age of reionization encodes both star driven history and primordial physics. Morphological statistics describe the signal's shapes, not just its average strength.

Chingangbam uses Minkowski functionals, a set of shape measures, to test how sensitive the signal is to early features and to reionization at once. Shape based reads could spot the fingerprint of inflation in data that plainer statistics would wash out. The work guides how future radio maps get mined.
arxiv-2601-19650:
Richard M. Milbradt and four colleagues speed up a core routine in quantum simulation. Tensor network methods represent large quantum states as webs of small tensors. A common step applies an operator, itself a tensor network, to a state. That step is a bottleneck in many calculations.

The authors introduce a new algorithm for applying tree-shaped operators to tree-shaped states. It draws on the density matrix method and on the Cholesky decomposition from linear algebra. A faster application step lifts the whole family of methods. Chemists and physicists use tensor networks to study materials that no direct method can handle. Shaving cost from the central subroutine widens what they can simulate.
arxiv-2601-19850:
Binzhu Xie and a large team of colleagues rebuild hands in three dimensions from head-mounted cameras. Egocentric video shows hands from the wearer's own view. Reconstructing their pose is hard: depth is ambiguous, fingers hide each other, and objects get in the way. Earlier systems scaled up training data or added extra cues, yet still struggled with new contexts.

Their method, EgoHandICL, uses in-context learning. The model adapts from examples shown at run time rather than only from fixed training. That flexibility targets unseen situations directly. Reliable hand tracking underpins augmented reality and robot learning from human video. The work aims at hands that stay accurate in the wild.
arxiv-2601-20150:
Laurence G. Yaffe revisits a variational method for studying gauge theories, the theories behind the strong nuclear force. The goal is to compute properties of QCD-like theories in infinite volume when the number of colors, N, is large. Coherent state methods were proposed for this long ago, but their practical use stalled.

Yaffe describes an entirely new implementation of the approach. It applies to lattice gauge theories with or without fermions, on lattices of up to four dimensions. If the method works at scale, it could open a fresh route to questions about confinement that are hard to reach with standard simulation.
arxiv-2601-20550:
Ryotaro Hoshino and Yoshitaka Tanimura build a numerical framework for simulating two-dimensional vibrational spectra of molecular liquids. Their base is the multi-mode anharmonic Brownian motion model, a general frame for molecular vibration in condensed phases. When vibrational energy passes thermal levels, quantum effects grow strong and system-bath entanglement needs rigorous treatment.

Their method, HEOM-2DVS, rests on the hierarchical equations of motion, a powerful tool for open quantum systems. Such spectra are fingerprints that chemists read to learn how molecules move and exchange energy in liquids, so faithful simulation matters. A two-part spectrum shows more than a flat trace can. It shows how the parts of a molecule trade energy as time runs on.
arxiv-2601-20650:
Jing Wu and six colleagues present OS-Marathon, a benchmark for computer-use agents on long, repetitive tasks. Such workflows are common in professional life: processing expense reports from receipts, or entering student grades from exam papers. They are tedious for humans, and their length grows with the size of the data to process.

The benchmark tests agents over these extreme-length chores. Staying accurate across hundreds of near-identical steps is a different challenge from solving one hard problem. OS-Marathon gives agent builders a measure of stamina and consistency, not just cleverness. That is a trait most short tests never touch at all.
arxiv-2601-21050:
Haokun Zhou builds an anomaly detector for streams whose sensors keep changing. The 2026 paper presents SMKC, based on sketch-based kernel correlation images. Conventional detection for multivariate time series assumes a fixed set of variables. Operational systems break that assumption daily. Sensors appear, disappear, or get renamed. Data windows then vary in cardinality. They may include values unseen during training.

A detector that needs a fixed input shape fails in that world. SMKC instead turns each window into a correlation image. Sketches keep the image compact as variables churn. Anomalies then show up as odd patterns in the image. The method targets real monitoring, from factories to data centers. It accepts messy, shifting inputs as the normal case.
arxiv-2601-21350:
Yupei Yang and seven co-authors fix a weakness in the reward models that steer language models toward human tastes. A reward model scores answers so the main model can learn from feedback. Standard reward models can latch onto surface traits that are not truly linked to what people liked.

That flaw invites reward hacking, where high scores stop meaning better behavior. The authors split the model's inner features into causal parts and spurious parts. Training leans on the causal parts, so the score tracks real quality. A steadier reward signal should make feedback training safer and more honest.
arxiv-2601-21450:
Donghuo Zeng, Hao Niu, Zhi Li, and Masato Taya compare the loss functions that teach models to place similar items close together. Metric learning powers search by image and face matching. Yet how each loss shapes the learned space, and how training unfolds, is poorly understood.

The authors build a diagnostic frame with two lenses. One lens tracks the spread of points inside and between classes. The other tracks how greedily each loss uses hard cases, via active ratios and gradient sizes. They compare seven well-known losses across five image search datasets. The frame helps builders pick a loss with open eyes.
arxiv-2601-21650:
Alexander Erlei, Federico Cau, Radoslav Georgiev, Sagar Kumar, Kilian Bizer, and Ujwal Gadiraju study how hidden gaps in knowledge about AI systems warp consumer markets. Buyers cannot easily tell a strong system from a flawed one. A product can look highly accurate while hiding costly errors or defects.

The classic economics of lemons predicts that such gaps drive good products out. Disclosure rules try to close the gap, but large parts remain open. The authors examine how these asymmetries shape adoption and market outcomes. Their analysis helps regulators aim disclosure where it protects buyers without choking useful tools.
arxiv-2601-21850:
Dražen Adamović, Boris Feigin, and Shigenori Nakatsuka prove a structural result in representation theory. Their subject is the center of an affine Lie algebra at the critical level, a special setting where the center becomes large and rich. For the algebra built from the general linear superalgebra with one odd direction, the structure was not fully pinned down.

The authors prove that this center is generated by the coefficients of one pseudo-differential operator, a product of simple factors and one inverse factor. Their 2026 preprint ties the algebra to the theory of opers, geometric objects used in the Langlands program. Identifying a center explicitly is prized in this field, because the center controls how all representations of the algebra behave.
arxiv-2601-22050:
Ghazal Kalhor and Behnam Bahrak test whether language models understand Persian proverbs. Models now sit inside daily life, so they must handle conversational language well, including figurative speech. Most figurative language research covers high-resource languages, leaving low-resource ones unmeasured.

Their 2026 preprint introduces MasalBench, a benchmark for contextual and cross-cultural understanding of Persian proverbs. A proverb's meaning rarely sits in its words alone; it depends on culture and situation. Testing models on such material reveals whether their multilingual skill is deep or only grammatical. Benchmarks like this push developers to serve smaller language communities with the same care given to English.
arxiv-2601-22450:
Jianhao Huang and Baharan Mirzasoleiman tune a hidden brake inside masked diffusion language models. These models build text by filling masked slots, not word by word. Their 2026 preprint notes that their learning traits are little studied next to the standard left-to-right kind. The team study a toy task: the parity, or XOR sum, of a few key bits.

That task is famed for grokking, where a model stalls, then grasps all at once. Tuning the brake aims to make that grasp come sooner and hold. The work guides how this new model class should be trained.
arxiv-2601-22750:
Carlos Marante and a team catch a peak in double-ion yield from ethylene at a fifteen-femtosecond delay. Doubly charged molecules carry marks of electron links and of electron-nucleus ties in the parent. Their 2026 preprint fires an extreme ultraviolet pump pulse, then a near-infrared probe.

The yield peak marks a fleeting window where confinement shapes the outcome. Femtosecond timing — millionths of a billionth of a second — lets them film chemistry as it happens. Such films test how molecules break and bond. The work is precision basic science. It reads a very fast signal.
arxiv-2601-22850:
Glaydston C. Bento and three co-authors sharpen the theory of a classic optimization method. The method, alternating minimization, solves a hard problem by fixing one part and improving the other, back and forth. It was set out for structured, non-smooth problems in a noted 2010 work.

The new results give much faster convergence rates under a key condition named in the abstract. In some cases the method can finish in finite steps, or speed up beyond the linear rate known before. Faster guarantees help users trust the method on real problems.
arxiv-2601-22950:
Petar Veličković and four co-authors question a favorite yardstick for language models: perplexity. Perplexity measures how surprised a model is by a text, and it serves both as a training loss and a quick quality score. Earlier work noted flaws in it, mostly from experiments.

The authors give a sharper account of when perplexity can, and cannot, tell right answers from wrong ones. A metric that looks simple can quietly mislead model choices. Knowing its limits helps teams judge models by measures tied to real correctness. The authors move past scattered empirical complaints, aiming for a principled account of what perplexity can and cannot certify.
arxiv-2601-23150:
J. M. Alcaine-Cuervo and four co-authors design a superconducting circuit that hosts a lattice gauge theory. Gauge theories describe fundamental forces on a grid of sites and links. Their compact U(1) version uses the circuit's own phase and charge variables, which live in infinite-dimensional spaces.

Gauge and matter fields are encoded directly in the circuit nodes' rotor variables. Gauss's law then holds exactly from charge conservation, with no added penalty terms or cutoffs. Clean encodings make quantum simulation of gauge theories more faithful. Exact Gauss law without stabilizers or truncations is the design's prize, keeping the simulated physics faithful by construction.
arxiv-2602-00150: Xinyun Wang and colleagues propose Reversible Diffusion Decoding, a fix for diffusion language models that stall on early bad choices. Such models generate tokens in parallel blocks, but once a block is fixed, a poor context can halt progress. RDD spots stagnation when the reverse process stalls in a state dependent manner, then backtracks to earlier blocks using cached states without recomputation. Confidence guided re masking then restarts uncertain tokens while keeping reliable context intact. Tests show stronger robustness and quality over baselines with only small extra compute.
arxiv-2602-00250: Shreshth Saini and colleagues propose TABES, a steering method for masked diffusion models that looks ahead instead of trusting local confidence. Search methods ease that lock in at prohibitive cost, with many forward passes per step. Backward-on-Entropy steering approximates infinite horizon lookahead with a single backward pass, deriving a Token Influence Score from a first order expansion of trajectory cost. Thus, the gradient of future entropy over input embeddings becomes an optimal control signal for cutting uncertainty.
arxiv-2602-00350: Ignacy Kolton and team introduce ReLAPSe, a reinforcement learning trained adversarial prompt search for erased concepts in unlearned diffusion models. Machine unlearning strips text to image diffusion models of unauthorized concepts, yet latent visual information often survives unlearning. Optimization based attacks cost much through per instance iterative search, while reasoning and heuristic methods lack direct feedback from latent visual representations. That closed loop design directly aligns textual prompts with latent visual targets to recover erased concepts.
arxiv-2602-00650: Mohammadreza Gholipour Shahraki and colleagues adapt the Segment Anything Model to 3D medical segmentation, where domain shift, a 2D design, and costly fine-tuning limit it. Their Mamba-SAM hybrid keeps the SAM encoder frozen and adds Mamba modelling for long-range, linear-time context. Two variants are tested: a dual-branch design fusing frozen SAM features with a trainable VMamba encoder, and an adapter injecting volumetric Tri-Plane Mamba modules.
arxiv-2602-01050: Avinash Ajit Nargund and co-authors test three face-work tip displays in augmented reality: screen-fixed, on a dummy head, or on the user's own face. In tests with 24 folk doing face drills, on-face tips felt lighter on the mind and won more favor, while screen-fixed tips gave sharper fixes and truer moves. Talk after showed a trade: on-face tips felt nicer yet made folk shy and harder to read. The team boils that trade down into design notes for rehab, stage work, and skill drills.
arxiv-2602-01150: Jialong Sun and co-authors build a train-free audit for machine forgetting, since dodging a membership test does not prove true forgetting. Past audits lean on membership attacks, but unlearned cases sit in trait space apart from true non-members, so those audits flatter the model, and shadow-model training costs much. Their SMI plan reframes audit as gauging the non-member share in the unlearned trait mix, with bootstrap bands for audit trust. Tests show it beating all attack-based audits, with no shadow training at all.
arxiv-2602-01350: Arnav Khinvasara and Alexander Pikovski survey ways to count and list set partitions, splits of distinct items into groups. Partition counts, the Bell numbers, climb fast and lack a closed form, so the team tests literature guesses. A Moser-Wyman asymptotic guess proves shockingly true even for small sets, while a plain Berend-Tassa guess serves handily there. For listing, they weigh non-recursive plans with no Gray-code tricks, pitting Hutchinson's classic against three newer ones. All scale exponentially, with Djokic and co-authors' plan fastest in practice.
arxiv-2602-01550: The S1-NexusAgent Team proposes S1-NexusAgent, a self-evolving framework for multidisciplinary research. Current models and tool agents falter at long-horizon planning, goal upkeep, and learning from execution. It splits global planning from subtask tool execution via a hierarchical plan-and-code-act dual-loop design. It supports the model context protocol, orchestrating thousands of tools via intention-aware retrieval and hot-plug links. Object-reference sparse context isolates subtask contexts and compresses results. A critic distills strong trajectories into reusable skills, closing the self-evolution loop.
arxiv-2602-02050: Zeping Li and colleagues rethink entropy's role in optimizing tool use for agents, which trigger excessive calls in long trajectories. Pilot experiments link entropy reduction to quality calls. They propose entropy reduction as a signal with two rewards: sparse rewards for coarse guidance and dense rewards. Experiments show both rewards improve use: the former cuts calls by seventy two point zero seven percent, while the latter improves performance by twenty two point two seven percent. Entropy reduction thus emerges as a key mechanism.
arxiv-2602-02150: Chu Zhao and colleagues propose ECHO for test-time reinforcement learning, steering tree rollouts with local entropy plus group confidence. High-entropy branching can collapse search onto a few paths. Noisy early majority-vote labels can lock the policy into premature overfitting. ECHO therefore prunes persistently low-confidence branches and shapes updates with confidence-aware clipping. Tests on mathematical and visual reasoning show steady gains, clearest when the rollout budget is tight.
arxiv-2602-02250: Viktor Stein and others present transport-based analogues of Kullback-Leibler divergence for regularized control in reinforcement learning. Standard KL regularization blows up under support mismatch and can degenerate when noise is low. Between elliptic spreads, the new divergences stay finite for degenerating equal covariances and give shape meaning to Kalman ensemble regularization heuristics. In linear time-invariant systems with Gaussian noise, standard KL collapses to a singular quadratic penalty as noise vanishes. The variants remove the singularity and preserve nontrivial feedback with better closed-loop results.
arxiv-2602-02550:
Hao Zeng and 5 co-authors route annotation work among language models and human experts while guaranteeing the error rate, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Labeling data can use fast cheap models, slower reasoning models, or expensive humans, each with a different cost-quality balance. The challenge is picking the cheapest adequate source per item without losing control of test errors.

HyPAC calibrates two decision thresholds using importance sampling and upper confidence bounds. Inputs split into three uncertainty regions, each routed to an appropriate source. The authors prove the method achieves minimum expected cost with a probably approximately correct guarantee on annotation error. The guarantee is distribution-free and does not depend on pretrained models. Benchmark experiments cut annotation cost by about seventy-nine percent while holding the error tightly at its target. Hybrid labeling becomes a provable saving, not a gamble.
arxiv-2602-03050:
Milko Estrada's solo 2026 paper offers a gentler interior for a charged black hole. The Reissner-Nordstrom black hole has two known pathologies. Its center holds a destructive singularity, and its inner horizon threatens predictability. Estrada shows the familiar exterior geometry can arise from an interior with an integrable singularity and no inner horizon, where tidal forces stay finite.

Radial infall could then be nondestructive. The pointlike mass is replaced by an extended spread of strings. Two realizations are given, a cloud of strings and a new fluid of strings. The fluid version can carry finite conserved energy. Matching the interior to the exterior requires equal temperatures at the interface. Pressure jumps there can signal gravitational phase shifts.
arxiv-2602-03250:
Collision finding that robots can differentiate through is built by Anup Teejo Mathew, with 4 co-authors. Gradient-based robotics methods need contact distance, location, and normal as smooth functions of robot state. For shapes with zero or undefined curvature, that mapping turns non-smooth in degenerate setups, breaking the gradients planners rely on for tuning through contact-rich motions and interactions with the environment.

Their system, iDCOL, regularizes such geometries into strictly convex implicit representations, restoring uniqueness and smoothness. Colliding bodies become implicit surfaces, and contact quantities come from solving a fixed-size nonlinear system. Analytical derivatives follow from the implicit function theorem. A fast Newton-based solver and an open-source implementation accompany the method. Extensive runs benchmark strength, with demonstrations in path planning and differentiable contact physics.
arxiv-2602-03650:
A massive star with an invisible companion could be hiding a black hole, a key stage on the road to merging black hole pairs. K. Deshmukh and 11 co-authors examine one candidate, VFTS 812 in the Tarantula Nebula, in a 2026 paper. The system is a 17-day spectroscopic binary whose O-type primary shows no light from its partner.

The team analyzes 30 epochs of high-resolution observations plus archival spectra, carefully removing nebular contamination. Spectral disentangling reveals no companion signature at all. Injection tests rule out any main-sequence partner above about six solar masses. Weighing the star's rejuvenated youth, the orbit's eccentricity, and the companion's silence, the authors favor a black hole. Follow-up observations are still needed to confirm it.
arxiv-2602-03950:
Aditya Basarkar and 3 co-authors improve math problem solving in language models by letting code talk back. Their 2026 method, IIPC, builds reasoning as a program, runs it, and uses the execution feedback to revise earlier steps. Ordinary chain-of-thought stays in charge of the high-level plan.

Rigid agent pipelines cannot fix early mistakes, and self-grading is unreliable. Execution gives an objective check instead. Across most reasoning benchmarks and several base models, IIPC beat competing approaches. The authors released all code openly. The design suits education and engineering uses, where a wrong intermediate step should be caught, not rationalized.
arxiv-2602-04550:
Cristina Butucea, Jan Johannes, and Henning Stein ask how gently a quantum state can be checked without destroying it, in a 2026 paper on state certification. Standard measurements collapse the state, using it up to gain information.

Their setting limits each measurement's disturbance to a small amount, so samples can be reused. The task is deciding whether an unknown state equals a reference state or is far from it. The authors derive the smallest possible sample size and build measurements that achieve it. Gentleness carries a clear price in extra samples. That price grows with the state's dimension, but more slowly than in related private estimation problems.
arxiv-2602-05050:
Galaxy cluster MACS J0018.5+1626 shows a radio glow that could be a halo at its center or two relics seen face-on. P Domínguez-Fernández and 11 co-authors modeled the system in this 2026 astrophysics paper, accepted by The Astrophysical Journal. It is the third study in the ICM-SHOX project, which pins down cluster mergers by matching many kinds of observations to simulations.

The combined evidence points to two clusters caught mid-merger, close to their nearest pass, viewed almost along the merger axis. The team ran three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations with tracer particles and a solver for the radio-emitting electrons. Across plausible starting conditions, the merger reliably drives two shocks of moderate strength. Within that picture, ordinary shock acceleration can reproduce the LOFAR radio data if the apparent halo is really two relics overlapping along the line of sight.
arxiv-2602-05150:
Most multilingual benchmarks for Greek are translated from English, which misses how Greek speakers actually write and think. Yang Zhang and 8 co-authors built GreekMMLU to fix that in this 2026 computational linguistics paper. The benchmark is sourced natively, with every question drawn from or written for Greek academic, professional, and government examinations.

The full set holds 21,805 multiple-choice questions across 45 subject areas, grouped under a new taxonomy and labeled by educational level from primary school to professional exams. About 16,900 questions are public; the rest are held back for a private leaderboard to resist contamination. Testing more than 80 open and closed models exposed large gaps: frontier systems led open-weight ones, and models adapted for Greek beat general multilingual models. The authors also analyze how scale, adaptation, and prompting move the scores.
arxiv-2602-05550:
ArkTS is the main language of the OpenHarmony system, yet it has no public data sets for code search research. Yulong He, Artem Ermakov, and 3 co-authors build one from open-source repositories on GitHub and Gitee. Their task is single search: given a natural language comment, retrieve the ArkTS function it describes, a basic test of code understanding tools.

Comment and function pairs were extracted with a tree-sitter parser, cleaned across platforms, and analyzed by function type. The team then benchmarks existing open-source code embedding models on the task. Fine-tuning with both ArkTS and TypeScript data produced a strong model for ArkTS code search. Both the data set and the tuned model are released publicly. The authors present the work as the first systematic benchmark for ArkTS code retrieval, aimed at a young developer ecosystem.
arxiv-2602-05750:
Quantum field theory in anti de Sitter space talks to a conformal field theory on its boundary, and loop corrections are where that dictionary gets tested. Weichen Xiao and Ivo Sachs study a conformally coupled phi to the fourth theory in three dimensional anti de Sitter space and its two dimensional dual. The one loop diagram cannot be written with known transcendental functions, a real obstacle.

The authors show the diagram equals an infinite sum of tree level diagrams that are well understood, and they evaluate that sum using several number theoretic conjectures. From it they extract, recursively, analytic expressions for the anomalous dimensions of all dual double trace operators. Checks in one channel agree with established bootstrap results. Their results in the other two channels are, to their knowledge, new to the literature. It gives bootstrap practitioners fresh data from a direct bulk computation.
arxiv-2602-05850:
Concurrent programs spawn threads dynamically, and giving them a complete set of equations has been a long standing goal in semantics. Ohad Kammar, Jack Liell-Cock, and 3 co-authors use algebraic effects to axiomatize dynamic threads. The theory builds on two primitives: fork, which creates a child thread and hands its name to the parent, and wait, which blocks until children finish.

Their parameterized algebraic theory adds basic atomic actions and laws such as associativity of fork. The axiomatization is complete in two senses. It captures equality of labelled posets, an established model of concurrency. It also proves any two open expressions that agree under all closing substitutions. The team then extends the analysis to a small concurrent language with operational and denotational semantics, shown sound, adequate, and fully abstract at first order. The paper was published at a leading programming languages conference.
arxiv-2602-06050:
Big vision and language models often lack facts about specific people, places, and things. Jongha Kim and 4 co-authors improve how such models use facts fetched from an outside store. Their method is called Relevance-aware Multi-context Contrastive Decoding, or RMCD for short.

Older decoding tricks handle fetched passages one at a time, so weak passages can still mislead the model. RMCD instead runs the model once per passage and mixes the answers, giving more weight to passages that fit the question well. Off-topic passages lose their pull. Across three hard question benchmarks, RMCD beat rival methods for several models, and it needs no extra training.
arxiv-2602-06150:
A new diagnostic for quantum systems, called the Krylov distribution, is introduced by Mohsen Alishahiha and Mohammad Javad Vasli. Krylov space organizes a quantum state by repeatedly applying the energy operator, building a ladder of levels. The distribution shows how a response state spreads across that ladder.

The response state comes from inverting the energy shifted by a chosen value. Unlike standard spectral tools, which only sort response by energy, this one shows which parts of the reachable space get used. The authors find three broad regimes: flat behavior outside the spectrum, steady growth inside it, and slow growth near edges and critical points. Known response measures split neatly in these terms.
arxiv-2602-06250:
Waves passing through a material bump sometimes scatter, and sometimes, at special frequencies, they pass as if nothing were there. Fioralba Cakoni and Michael S Vogelius survey recent results on this non-scattering puzzle for the Helmholtz equation, the basic model of wave motion. They cover both uniform and direction-dependent media.

At most frequencies, any incoming wave must scatter off a real contrast. The special frequencies, called transmission eigenvalues, only open the door to non-scattering. The bump usually must be smooth, and many smooth shapes still scatter natural waves even at those frequencies. The survey gathers these fine-grained results and explains where the field now stands.
arxiv-2602-06450:
Reading text in photos of real scenes, from signs to storefronts, needs training data that hand labeling cannot supply at scale. Xingsong Ye and 5 co-authors ask what is wrong with the synthetic data usually used instead. Auditing mainstream rendering-based sets, they find the same flaws: too little variety in wording, fonts, and layout.

Their answer is UnionST, a synthesis engine built to cover hard cases and complex scenes more faithfully. Its data set, UnionST-S, trained recognizers that beat models raised on older synthetic sets, sometimes beating real-data training. A self-evolution scheme then labels real data so effectively that competitive results came from under a tenth of the usual human labels.
arxiv-2602-06550:
Reinforcement learning agents that must infer hidden context often break when that context flips how actions work. Jan Benad and 5 co-authors present DMA-SH, a framework built for such discontinuous shifts. A single hypernetwork, trained only to predict dynamics, generates a small set of shared adapter weights for the dynamics model, the policy, and the value function.

That shared modulation matches the structure of context-to-dynamics jumps, while input scaling and random masking steady context inference. Theory backs the design with expressivity separation results and variance bounds showing how compression within each mode helps learning. A new benchmark suite isolates the hard cases: actuator inversion, actuator permutation, and weakly overlapping continuous dynamics.
arxiv-2602-06750:
Diego Morales, Pedro Pérez-Aros, and Emilio Vilches establish how fast certain smoothed estimators close in on the objects they approximate. The estimators come from smooth approximations of infimal convolutions, a way of blending two functions. They are used to stand in for proximal mappings and metric projections, two workhorse operations in optimization. The paper's goal is explicit rates with explicit constants.

For weakly convex, possibly nonsmooth problems, the authors prove a square-root rate that spells out the dependence on dimension. Under stronger smoothness assumptions the rate improves to linear, again with constants in plain view, and projection estimates are refined for sets with smooth boundaries. Examples included in the paper show these rates cannot be improved in general.
arxiv-2602-06950:
Sam Spiro turns a bracket pool puzzle into a math question. Suppose friends fill out March Madness brackets and you learn every score. When can you work out exactly how the tournament went? The answer is not plain, because scores hide as much as they reveal, and the scoring rule itself may vary.

Spiro finds the exact smallest number of brackets that always suffices for any March Madness-style tournament, no matter which scoring system is used. He also proves workable bounds for arbitrary single-elimination tournaments, beyond the March Madness format. In metric dimension terms, the brackets act as landmarks, and their scores act as distances that pin down every point in the space.
arxiv-2602-07050:
Sonia Joseph and seven co-authors probe what video world models hold about physics inside. Video models score well on intuitive physics tests, yet it is unclear if they store physical variables in neat, factored form, like a physics engine, or in a distributed, task-tied form. This is the first study to look directly at physical representations inside large-scale video encoders.

Four tools drive the probe. The team probes layer by layer. They map subspace geometry. They decode at patch level. They ablate targeted attention heads. Across designs, a sharp mid-depth transition appears, which the team calls the Physics Emergence Zone. Physical variables become accessible there, peak just after, and fade toward the output layers. Speed and acceleration show up from early layers, but direction shows up only at the transition, coded in a high-dimensional population with circular geometry. The models predict physics without factoring it.
arxiv-2602-07150:
Benchmark scores for AI agents usually come from one run per task, as if that number were stable.  Bjarni Haukur Bjarnason and two co-authors test that assumption with 60,000 agent trajectories on SWE-Bench-Verified, across three models and two scaffolds.

Single-run scores swing by 2. 2 to 6. 0 percentage points depending on which run is picked, even at temperature zero.  That means a reported gain of two or three points may be noise rather than progress.  Tracing tokens shows runs splitting early and cascading into other strategies.  The paper argues for repeated runs and honest error bars in agent testing.
arxiv-2602-07250:
Doubling methods solve important non-linear matrix equations by tracking an eigenspace basis. They depend on that basis taking one of two special forms, which cannot always be guaranteed.  Changli Liu and four co-authors remove that restriction with a new Q-doubling method.

The new method includes the older methods as special cases while dropping the form requirement, and the paper applies it to eigenvalue problems with numerical tests.  Builders and numerical analysts who rely on doubling methods for control and engineering equations get a more general tool that no longer fails when the basis refuses to cooperate.
arxiv-2602-07650:
Glasses under shear are usually simulated at constant volume, but real deformation involves volume changes: shear bands dilate and lose density.  Krishna K Tiwari and one co-author investigate yielding of glasses under shear at constant pressure, where those volumetric effects can speak.

For uniform shear, stress-strain curves at other pressures differ only by stress scale.  Under cyclic shear, stable shear bands widen with external pressure while their density stays below average. Well-annealed glasses yield with a discontinuous dilation while poorly annealed glasses compact first.  Materials experts get a constant-pressure picture of yielding that constant-volume studies suppress.
arxiv-2602-08350:
Learning theory usually hopes that the simplest fit to the data will also predict well, but that hope has limits. Tal Burla and Roi Livni show that even the best-case empirical risk minimizer can fail in stochastic convex optimization. Their arXiv paper builds an example where learning is possible and the sample size grows with the dimension, yet the minimizer is unique and still overfits.

The result settles an open question posed by Feldman, and it extends to near-minimizers as well. The same construction shows that gradient descent can overfit when its horizon and step size grow with the sample size. A new lower bound narrows the gap to the best known upper bound sharply. Readers get a cautionary tale about trusting the most natural fitting rule.
arxiv-2602-08650: Eduardo García-Río, Rosalía Rodríguez-Gigirey and Ramón Vázquez-Lorenzo ask which four-dimensional Lie groups have harmonic curvature, a geometric condition on how curvature spreads across the group. Their 2026 arXiv paper answers by pinning down every such group in four dimensions. That answer then yields a full account of pp-wave Lie groups in four dimensions, a related family singled out by the same result. Readers get a compact, complete classification for a small, sharply defined corner of geometry.
arxiv-2602-08950:
Building spin-based devices from topological insulators and magnetic multilayers demands precise growth control. B. A. Brereton and ten co-authors optimize a stack that pairs a bismuth selenide layer with platinum, cobalt-boron, and ruthenium repeats. The topological layer is grown by molecular beam epitaxy, then moved under ultrahigh vacuum for sputtering of the metal layers.

X-ray and neutron reflectometry plus electron microscopy reveal a key rule: the buffer must pass a threshold thickness for every magnetic layer to gain uniform out-of-plane anisotropy, 1.5 nanometers for tantalum and 0.9 for molybdenum. Buffered samples show clean out-of-plane domains, ready for spin-orbit-torque control.
arxiv-2602-09350:
Xuhua He and Kaitao Xie study the totally nonnegative part of a twisted flag variety, built from a Kac-Moody group and a twisted Borel subgroup. The ordinary flag variety appears as a special case, and earlier work had mapped its nonnegative part in detail. This 2026 paper extends that picture to the twisted setting, where the geometry is richer and less charted.

The main result is a decomposition of the totally nonnegative part into cells, with the closure of each cell forming a regular CW complex. That extends results of Galashin, Karp, and Lam, and of Bao with He, for ordinary flag varieties. Applications follow for the double flag variety under diagonal action. Further links connect the double flag to canonical bases of tensor products. The result also settles the link of the identity in a reduced double Bruhat cell, answering an open question of Fomin and Zelevinsky.
arxiv-2602-09450:
Through-wall radar needs compact, wideband, high-gain antennas, but walls weaken signals, and raising power to compensate lets direct sender-to-receiver coupling swamp faint target reflections. Shobha Sundar Ram and Akanksha Sneh propose opposite circular antennas for sender and receiver in their 2026 paper. Opposite handedness cuts direct coupling while preserving the first bounce off the target.

The helical antenna emerges as a strong candidate: small, wideband, high-gain, and low in axial ratio across a wide field of view. The paper compares coupling reduction from oppositely handed helical antennas against common through-wall antennas, including Vivaldi and horn designs. Tests in through-wall settings confirm the approach, offering a practical antenna choice for seeing targets behind walls.
arxiv-2602-09550:
Generative AI may be reshaping how students seek physics knowledge, and Yossi Ben-Zion and two co-authors track that shift through search behavior. Their 2026 study analyzes Google Trends data for classical mechanics and electromagnetism across three academic years in more than twenty countries. Wikipedia page views in seven major languages check platform independence. Falling traditional search serves as a proxy for changing independent information-seeking.

The decline is substantial, systematic, and persistent across most topics, with mechanics falling more sharply and consistently than electromagnetism. English-speaking regions stay relatively stable or decline moderately, while non-English regions show much larger drops. Yet the seasonal rhythm of academic activity survives intact. The findings point to a redistribution of physics information-seeking toward generative tools rather than a collapse of curiosity itself.
arxiv-2602-09650:
Majid Rajabzadeh and Moein Khalighi focus on a bent flow-spread rule with space- and time-part Laplace ops in their 2026 paper. They develop local broken Galerkin methods, including Legendre basis functions, for solving this class of part spread problem, and prove staying power plus best-order closing in. The method turns the rule into a system of first-order rules and nears the answer by picking right basis functions.

Truth and staying power hinge on the basis functions, which greatly improve the method. Number results show the new scheme doing fast and well across varied cases, meeting the best order of closing in. The paper thus offers a tested, in-theory grounded solver for part flow-spread problems where classic methods fall short.
arxiv-2602-09750:
Triply repeat minimal surface forms are a new class of porous matter with varied shapes and good traits, hopeful for reactor insides in chem work. Timo Merbach and fourteen co-authors address limited lab data on internal flow in their 2026 paper. They probe printed forms with three-dim magnet echo speed scans in a large-bore upright system.

Three shapes are probed in tube columns under four cm wide, with match between compute flow sims and taken speed fields set through cross-check. Imaging yields fully three-dim speed fields with spread gap below six percent. The Gyroid form shows strong grooves, while the Schwarz-Diamond form shows merge-split behavior with nearly half more lateral mixing than the Gyroid. Sims remake the flow marks, checking speed scans for future heat, mass transfer, and reactive flow studies.
arxiv-2602-10050:
Picking one consensus string that sits closest to a whole set is a classic aggregation problem. A 2026 paper led by Diptarka Chakraborty, with three co-authors, asks for more: several near-optimal medians that are also diverse, giving decision makers flexibility and robustness. The study works with Hamming distance, where distance counts positions that differ.

The authors first give an exact algorithm for the diameter variant, finding pairs of near-optimal medians as far apart as possible. They then offer an approximation algorithm for sum dispersion and a bi-criteria approximation for the harder min dispersion case, producing more than two diverse medians. Structural insights into median space and code-construction techniques drive the results.
arxiv-2602-10150:
Turbulent flows strain both direct number methods, which cost far too much, and data-driven methods, which wobble on long rollouts. A 2026 paper led by Yilong Dai, with four co-authors, offers PEST, a physics-boosted Swin transformer for 3D turbulence. Window-based self-attention models local equation links while keeping compute cheap.

A scale-tuned adaptive loss stresses small-scale structures for faithful high-end dynamics. Navier-Stokes residual constraints and divergence-free smoothing enter the learning goal itself, keeping physics consistent. Tests on two typical turbulent setups show accurate, physically steady, stable long-term simulations that beat current data-driven baselines.
arxiv-2602-10250:
Upper-layer 5G security has hardened, but plaintext physical and MAC layers remain little studied as newer releases add lower-layer control messages. A 2026 paper led by Subangkar Karmaker Shanto, with two co-authors, explores lower-layer attacks on modern 5G with two practical exploits tested in a lab testbed. First, a reproduced SIB1 spoofing attack repeatedly changes one broadcast parameter. That forces user equipment to refresh system information, holding the radio active and draining battery.

Second, a new Timing Advance manipulation attack during random access injects an attacker-chosen offset in the random access response. Victims then apply wrong uplink timing. The result is uplink desync, link failures, and repeated reconnection loops amounting to denial of service. Tests with commercial smartphones and open-source 5G software show offsets beyond a small tolerance reliably trigger link failures, keeping devices stuck re-establishing while the rogue base station runs.
arxiv-2602-10350:
Middle layers in multilingual speech models often hold more phonetically exact pictures than final output layers. A 2026 paper led by Domenico De Cristofaro, with three co-authors, applies layer-wise decoding to a pretrained Wav2Vec2 model to trace phoneme-level guesses across encoder layers in Campidanese Sardinian, a low-resource language. Cutting upper transformer layers improves Phoneme Error Rates, with best performance two layers before the final layer.

Fine-grained alignment study shows middle predictions keep segmental identity better, curb overgeneration, and cut certain classes of phonological errors. The paper names regressive errors, cases where correct middle predictions are overwritten by final-layer errors. These regressions highlight limits of surface-level error scores and reveal how deeper layers may blur acoustic detail, supporting early-layer probing as a check tool for speech recognition in low-resource settings.
arxiv-2602-10650:
Anton Lutsenko and five co-authors report uneven spin-wave conduct in magnonic resonators in a 2026 paper. The devices pair yttrium iron garnet films with cobalt-iron-boron nanostripes in a Fabry-Perot shape. As stirring power rises, transmission gaps shift downward in rate, a systematic uneven effect.

The nonlinearity appears at low power, thanks to strong spatial concentration of spin waves inside the resonator. Power-dependent transmission yields neuron-like activation and rate-selective uneven absorption, two ingredients neuromorphic computing needs. The paper presents the resonators as compact, low-power uneven elements for magnonic neural systems, where waves rather than electrons carry the runs.
arxiv-2602-10850:
Can Hatipoğlu and Christian Lomp present a class of Hopf algebras in a 2026 paper. The algebras arise as two-step Ore extensions of a group algebra, parameterized by a group, characters, and extra data. The construction unifies and transfers known families, including broad Taft algebras and algebras related to the Lie algebra sl2.

The authors analyze ring-theoretic traits of the new algebras and classify all finite-sized simple modules over them. Tensor products of simple modules receive focus in the zero-derivation case. The work gives algebraists a unified system that places spread examples under one roof, with model theory worked out from the start.
arxiv-2602-11150:
Good mobile manipulators cost too much for most labs. Manan H Anjaria and thirteen co-authors present YOR, an open-source, low-cost mobile manipulator built from off-the-shelf parts. It joins an omnidirectional base, a telescopic lift, and two arms with grippers for whole-body work.

Modularity and easy assembly keep the bill of materials under ten thousand dollars, a fraction of rival platforms. YOR handles tasks needing coordinated whole-body control, two-handed handling, and self-guided navigation. The paper argues that form factor on a budget is still open, and offers YOR as a competitive research platform that more groups can build and adapt.
arxiv-2602-11350:
Estimating what an move will do over time is crucial in medicine. Tomer Meir and three co-authors propose a hybrid inner-data-driven model for time-dependent move outcomes. It splits a system's transition tool into parametric and nonparametric parts, separating move-related from unrelated motion.

Inner anchors give toughness, while learned residuals capture complex patterns. When inner settings are unknown, a two-stage procedure pre-trains an encoder on simulated data, then learns corrections from sights. Tests on a pendulum regime and on propofol bolus injections show the hybrid beats purely data-driven and purely inner models, especially out of spread. The work targets dosing and control where extrapolation matters.
arxiv-2602-11450:
Disk galaxies are chemically patchy on small scales, against well-mixed models. Benjamin Metha and two co-authors propose superbubbles as the cause: clusters of core-collapse supernovae, close in space and time, blow metal-enriched bubbles into the interstellar medium. Bubble size follows disk scale height, and metal content scales with star formation speed in bubble regions.

Geostatistical forward building of metallicity maps from the PHANGS-MUSE galaxy sample supports the picture, with bubble radii near three hundred parsecs and efficiencies in a plausible band. Small-scale settings track global galaxy properties, so local interstellar structure is not universal. Large galaxies thus look steady when averaged broadly, yet remain bursty on small scales like their smaller, distant cousins.
arxiv-2602-11550:
Large forecasting models trained on vast data can predict new time series without extra training, yet they often stumble when a new domain shifts away from what they saw before. Retraining their weights risks wiping out old skills, while looking up past cases at run time slows every forecast down. Sisuo Lyu and eight co-authors propose a middle path: a small memory add-on that leaves the base model frozen.

Their system, TS-Memory, first builds a careful lookup teacher that turns retrieved past outcomes into confidence-weighted targets, then distills that knowledge into the light add-on. At forecast time the memory and base predictions blend with only a fixed extra cost, so no lookup is needed live. Across several base models and test sets it improves both single-value and range forecasts, at speed close to the untouched base model.
arxiv-2602-11650:
Language models can now draft feedback for students, but nobody knows which feedback design actually helps different learners revise their answers. Momoka Furuhashi and five co-authors define six designs for multiple-choice biology questions, one baseline and five enriched variants, and test them with 321 high school students. They measure immediate revision success plus six subjective criteria, and compare reactions across personality profiles.

Presenting task-relevant information clearly stands out: it tracks better revision performance and earns favorable ratings across learner profiles. Other patterns differ more descriptively, especially around informational novelty and emotional framing, where learner profiles diverge. The study stops short of prescribing personalization, but it gives designers evidence that clarity is the safest first move, and a map of where tailored feedback might matter next.
arxiv-2602-11850:
Rectified-flow models learn a continuous flow field that turns simple noise into complex data, enabling high-quality generation plus training-free reverse mapping for reconstruction and editing. Chenru Wang and two co-authors tackle a weakness: existing reverse methods accumulate approximation errors across timesteps, shaking the flow field and hurting output quality. Their Proximal-Mean Inversion is a training-free gradient correction that steadies the field by guiding it toward a running average of past flows, constrained within a theory-based round Gaussian.

A second method, mimic-CFG, offers a lightweight speed correction for editing that blends the current speed and its projection onto the past average, balancing editing effectiveness with structural consistency. PIE-Bench tests show steadier reverse mapping, better reconstruction, and better editing accuracy, with fewer neural function evaluations. The approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the benchmark with enhanced efficiency and theoretical soundness.
arxiv-2602-11950:
Wireless radio maps are usually predicted assuming perfect knowledge of the environment. That premise breaks in real deployments through sensor limits, mapping errors, and change over time. Fabian Jaensch and three co-authors train neural nets with task-specific tweaks to geometry, materials, and transmitter spots, so the models learn to adjust for flawed inputs. On synthetic indoor scenes with noisy inputs, perturbed training cuts error by up to a quarter versus clean training.

Real-world measurements confirm the gain: about 2 dB RMSE with noisy inputs and about 1 dB with complete information, against over 2 dB for classical methods like ray-tracing and radial basis fitting. A second finding simplifies deployment: in single-room indoor scenes, binary presence maps perform at least as well as detailed material property data, so less scene detail is needed than often assumed.
arxiv-2602-12450:
Therapy research needs measures of what therapists do and how clients respond, at a scale human coding cannot reach. Angela Chen led this work with six co-authors, building a framework that uses large language model assessments to model therapist-client dynamics in therapy. Automated pipelines score therapist empathy and exploration, relational rapport, and client self-disclosure and emotional expression.

Scores were validated against human notes, then applied to about 2,000 hours of transcripts from the Alexander Street corpus, yielding 119,233 client utterances from 1,573 sessions with 37 clients. Agreement with humans ranged from good to excellent, with rapport highest. Models link empathy and exploration to more disclosure and more self-directed negative emotion, and to less enjoyment, while prior-session rapport showed no link to disclosure or negative emotion.
arxiv-2602-12950:
Unstable classes cost maintenance effort, and code smells are often blamed, yet most studies look only at smells inside the class itself. Zushuai Zhang and two co-authors ask whether smells in neighbouring classes matter too. A class can be forced to change because a class it depends on, an efferent neighbour, changes, and ripple effects may bite harder when that neighbour smells.

Smells also cluster: they co-occur within classes and across linked classes, a pattern called interrelation, and linked smells can interact through dependencies. The study mines one year of commits from 100 top-starred GitHub projects, detecting smells and dependencies, then models neighbour smells, interrelation, and interaction as predictors of stability. The design tests whether maintainability risk travels along dependency edges, not just within single classes.
arxiv-2602-13050:
Quantum phase transitions tied to Fermi surface topology form a special universality class, with the Fermi sea volume as order setting. Gennady Chitov advances that theory using the exactly solvable Hatsugai-Kohmoto model of interacting fermions in one, two, and three dimensions. He explores links among Lee-Yang zeros, the Luttinger theorem, and plateau theorems, confirming Luttinger validity in the model.

The order setting and universality class describe metal-to-band-insulator, metal-to-Mott-insulator, Lifshitz, and van Hove transitions alike, with gapless phases identified as Landau Fermi liquids. Beyond the usual continuous order setting picture, homology theory treats the transitions as critical points of a Morse function, quantified by Euler characteristics worked out for each phase. The claimed toughness of the universality class to interactions and model details, given non-degenerate critical points, is the paper's central thesis.
arxiv-2602-13350:
Brick kilns pollute the air and harbor forced labor across South Asia, yet monitoring them at scale is hampered by sparse, outdated ground data. This study turns to high-resolution satellite imagery, curating over 1.3 million tiles at zoom level 20 across five regions in South and Central Asia. It proposes ClimateGraph, a region-adaptive graph model that reads spatial and directional patterns in kiln layouts, tested against established graph baselines.

In parallel, a remote sensing pipeline is benchmarked against recent foundation models for satellite imagery. The comparison shows complementary strengths across graph, foundation, and remote sensing methods, offering practical guidance for large-scale kiln monitoring. Usman Nazir leads the work with seven co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13550:
Neural networks often fail badly on inputs outside their training range, giving unrealistic yet overconfident predictions. This paper names that problem out-of-support generalization and reframes it as sequence modeling in weight space: the training set is split into concentric shells that act as discrete sequential steps.
