The resulting WeightCaster framework yields plausible, readable predictions that flag doubt, without explicit inductive biases, while staying fast to run.

Validation on a synthetic cosine data set and real air quality sensor readings shows performance as good as or better than the state of the art. Reliable prediction beyond the training range matters most for safety-critical uses, where overconfident extrapolation can do real harm. Roussel Desmond Nzoyem is the sole author.
arxiv-2602-13750:
An odd spanning tree of a graph is a spanning tree in which every vertex has odd degree, a concept recently defined by Zheng and Wu. Feng, Chen, and Wu counted odd spanning trees in complete graphs using Prufer codes and exponential generating functions, in the spirit of Cayley's formula. This note gives a simple proof through a classical spanning tree enumeration formula and Boolean functions, and generalizes the result to complete bipartite graphs.

The proof's simplicity is its contribution: a classical enumeration formula plus Boolean function reasoning recovers and extends a recent counting result without heavy machinery. By moving from complete graphs to complete bipartite graphs, the note widens the class of graphs whose odd spanning trees are now counted. Jun Ge leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-13850:
Minku Kim and five co-authors present a 2026 arXiv paper on a humanoid robot that stacks boxes, Hanoi-style. The robot must chain pick-up, walking, and placement skills over long runs, in simulation and on real hardware. That simple task exposes a weak spot in modular robot design.

Most such systems stack learned skills on one shared whole-body controller, which may not be tough enough for long closed-loop runs. The team compared fixes, including tuning the controller per skill, adding a low-level correction, and pooling closed-loop data into shared training. The shared controller won on long-run robustness, and smoothing its handoffs removed much of the loss seen with separate controllers.
arxiv-2602-14150:
N. A. Khokhlov, writing alone, extends a 2026 arXiv method for the inverse scattering problem. Within Marchenko theory at fixed angular momentum, the author approximates an n-channel S-matrix as a function of first-channel momentum. Each matrix element becomes a rational term plus a truncated sinc series, with relativistic kinematics built in.

For energies where only some channels are open, the paper analyzes the S-matrix structure and shows the closed-channel submatrix near thresholds can be rebuilt from the open-channel part. Convergence is checked on data from a known potential, comparing the rebuilt potential with the original. The method is then applied to S31 pion-nucleon scattering data.
arxiv-2602-14450:
Issaku Kanamori and six co-authors test a 2026 arXiv mixed-precision solver for lattice QCD on the A64FX processor. Mixed-precision methods combining single and double precision are now standard, but half-precision FP16 remains less established. The paper adds rescaling steps in both the outer loop refinement and the inner BiCGStab solver to dodge number instability.

Tests with a simple Wilson kernel show improved stability, with extra iteration count versus the FP64 version staying within 20%. That margin indicates FP16 solvers are practical for lattice QCD use. The authors suggest the rescaling methods can also help other mixed-precision preconditioners avoid underflows, extending the benefit beyond the tested kernel.
arxiv-2602-14650:
Materials models often starve for data, yet small well-chosen sets can still teach a lot. Kati Asikainen, with three co-authors, predicts dopant formation energies in titanium dioxide monolayers from few examples. The models pair density functional theory with descriptors rooted in physics.

Tests start with platinum dopants in lepidocrocite sheets, where the chosen descriptors track stability well. Adding silver-doped cases then improves silver predictions while platinum stays robust. Accuracy grows steadily as more silver points join the training set. The work shows that compact, curated data can beat brute-force data hunger.
arxiv-2602-14950:
Maiani shows how gentle spatial twists in the magnetic order of altermagnets act on moving electrons like emergent gauge fields. These fields couple to a sublattice-odd channel. With a coplanar spin helix, that channel yields two effects that vanish without it. One is a momentum-resolved spectral pattern. The other is a net interband linear dichroism whose axes follow the helix wave vector.

The dichroism shifts regime with frequency. When frequencies are low, the absorption axis stays tied to the crystal axes; when they are high, it follows the helix instead. Anisotropic dc transport offers a second quantitative check, and the signatures survive weak spin-orbit coupling. The paper points to polarization-resolved optics, and to sublattice-sensitive spectroscopy, as ways to probe textured altermagnetic states directly, with possible direction-selective devices in view.
arxiv-2602-15150:
Sewell and Arakkal present bayesics, a single R toolkit for core stats methods via Bayesian inference. Bayesian stats anchors much of modern applied science, and it unifies syntax and output across routines from one- and two-sample tests to general mediation analysis. It leans away from needing sampling know-how, using closed-form answers when possible and auto-picking posterior sample counts when not.

The package reports key values: point values, credible ranges, which way an effect points, region of practical equivalence, and Bayes factors where apt. Model checks stay key, so it supplies check plots for model tests, including Bayesian p-values. Add-ons cover models from other R kits, with fixes to older builds.
arxiv-2602-15350:
Chehade and Zhu offer a proven, multi-stage line tuning an instruction-tuned LLM to make open-only fixing swapping plans from short PSPS case notes under a limit. Public Safety Power Shutoffs force rapid layout shifts that can make usual running points blocked, needing crews to spot fixing swapping moves cutting drops while keeping volt acts.

First, guided tuning boils a DC-OPF MILP sage into a rules set allowing reading and fit tests. Second, taste tuning tunes the plan using AC-scored taste pairs ordered by a volt fine score, adding sense beyond DC copying. Finally, best-of-N pick chooses the best option under the goal score. On IEEE 118-bus PSPS cases, tuning greatly lifts DC goal scores over zero-shot making, cuts AC power-flow flops from 50 points to single numbers, and lifts volt fine results on wins. Code and scripts are shared for reruns.
arxiv-2602-15850:
Liu and colleagues present EZCollegeApp, a large language model run system aiding high-school students with US college forms. Forms require handling scattered entry rules, repeated and if-then fields, and unclear questions demanding checking multiple sources. The system shapes form fields, grounds draft answers in official entry papers, and keeps full human control over final responses. A map-first method splits form reading from answer making, enabling steady thinking across varied form sites.

EZCollegeApp joins intake from official entry websites, search-based Q and A, and a human-checked chat panel showing drafts beside form fields without auto-send. The system design, data flow, inner forms, safety and privacy steps, and testing through auto checks and human review are told. Source code is released on GitHub to aid wider impact.
arxiv-2602-15950:
Levental runs a deliberately simple test on vision language models: copy a fifteen by fifteen grid of filled and empty cells. When cells are shown as text symbols, the models do well, but when the same grids appear as plain filled squares with no gridlines, their accuracy falls sharply. The catch is that both versions pass through the same visual encoder, since the symbols are images rather than tokenized text.

Across three frontier models, the gap in F1 score between text symbols and squares runs from roughly thirty to fifty points. Each model fails in its own way, undercounting, overcounting, or inventing a template, yet all share the same weakness in spatial localization for non textual marks. The result suggests these models lean on a strong text reading pathway for spatial tasks, while their native visual pathway for plain shapes lags far behind.
arxiv-2602-16050:
Amir Hosseinian leads a team of six researchers testing an evidence-grounded clinical reasoning system called January Mirror on endocrinology exam questions. Mirror draws on a curated endocrinology and cardiometabolic evidence corpus with a structured reasoning design, and it worked under a closed-evidence rule with no outside retrieval. Rival frontier models had live web access to guidelines and primary literature for comparison.

On a 120-question board-style exam, Mirror scored higher than both a human reference mark and the frontier models, including GPT-5.2, GPT-5, and Gemini-3-Pro. It also held up on the thirty hardest questions, where human accuracy fell below half. Most outputs cited at least one guideline-tier source, and manual checks found the citations accurate. The authors argue that curated evidence with clear provenance can beat open web retrieval for subspecialty reasoning.
arxiv-2602-16350:
Romain Dalidet leads a team of six coauthors reporting a direct demonstration of quantum-enhanced sensing in the Fourier domain. The team compares single-photon and two-photon interference in a fiber-based interferometer under strictly identical noise conditions. Capturing both signals at once supplies a common-mode reference, giving a fair and unambiguous benchmark of quantum advantage.

Spectral analysis shows that quantum correlations do not raise the height of the modulation peak. Instead they lower the associated noise floor, producing a three decibel improvement in signal-to-noise ratio. That gain holds in the sub-shot-noise regime, where the classical signal sinks into the spectral background while the two-photon contribution stays resolvable. The observations establish Fourier-domain quantum super-sensitivity as an operational resource for precision interferometric sensing, broadly applicable rather than tied to one setup.
arxiv-2602-16450:
Dario van den Berg and Isobel Kolbé study momentum broadening and jet transport in the quark-gluon plasma. They extend the Gyulassy-Levai-Vitev formalism with all-path-length and sub-Regge terms. Traditional calculations rely on large separation and formation time approximations, valid for large systems but failing for proton-proton and proton-nucleus collisions.

The authors derive expressions for broadening and transport to first order in opacity, with a numerical study of their impact. All-path-length correction suppresses low-momentum broadening. Its correction scales inversely with path length times transverse motion, dominating for small systems and matching the standard. The sub-Regge correction enhances high-momentum spread when transfer approaches the parton's light-cone component, vanishing when that ratio is small. Combined, the sub-Regge correction partly offsets all-path-length suppression, and the transport offset is complete. Sub-Regge corrections resolve large negative energy-loss contributions.
arxiv-2602-16950:
Kibon Ku and co-authors present HS-3D-NeRF, a stationary-camera multi-channel neural radiance field frame for hyperspectral 3D reconstruction of farm produce. Hyperspectral imaging and 3D reconstruction enable accurate, high-throughput characterization of produce quality and plant phenotypes, both essential for farm sustainability and breeding. Hyperspectral imaging captures biochemical traits, while 3D geometry improves morphological analysis, yet integrating the two at scale remains hard.

Conventional routes need complex hardware incompatible with automated phenotyping, and neural radiance fields typically need moving cameras, limiting throughput indoors. The new frame uses a stationary camera while the object rotates in a custom Teflon chamber with diffuse, uniform illumination. Object poses come from ArUco calibration markers. Postharvest inspectors get a high-throughput route to joint hyperspectral and 3D quality data.
arxiv-2602-17050:
Ziliang Zhao led a large team tackling a quiet flaw in large-scale recommendation systems: hash collisions in embedding tables. As the count of distinct user and item IDs grows, standard hash indexing maps different IDs to the same slot, which blurs their learned profiles and weakens personalization. The paper introduces Multi-Probe Zero Collision Hash, or MPZCH, an indexing scheme built on linear probing.

With sensible table sizes, MPZCH often wipes out collisions entirely while holding production speed, using helper tensors and fast CUDA kernels for probing and eviction. Old IDs are retired and their slots reset, so new features learn from scratch instead of inheriting stale profiles. Online tests showed zero collisions for user embeddings and fresher, better item embeddings, with training and serving speed close to prior methods. The code ships in the open-source TorchRec library.
arxiv-2602-17350:
Djordje Mihajlovic led a two-author team revealing shortcut learning in machine learning routes to knot sorting. Telling whether two embeddings of a closed curve match under ambient isotopy is central to low-dim topology, with uses from protein folding to polymer physics and magnetohydrodynamics. Neural networks excel at sorting, so asking whether they can sort knots is natural.

The paper probes generic shortcut methods in machine learning knot sorting. It finds hidden non-topological signals in training data built by atom motion runs of many-sided knots, signals the models exploit for good results. To ground future work, the authors release a dataset built to remove non-shape feature sorting plus code making knot shapes that truly explore a chosen shape state space at fixed knot type. The work aims to speed models that sort knots by shape done right, not by shortcuts.
arxiv-2602-17550:
Xiaoliang Fu led a ten-author team behind a 2026 arXiv paper on training language models to reason with verifiable rewards. Current methods in that family, GRPO included, use trust region mechanisms that are rigid, uniform, and symmetric. The authors argue those mechanisms fit large language model optimization poorly. They name three faults: hard clipping wastes gradient signal, uniform ratio limits ignore the token distribution, and positive and negative samples carry unevenly reliable credit.

The answer is MASPO, short for Mass-Adaptive Soft Policy Optimization, a unified framework that treats all three faults together. A differentiable soft Gaussian gating squeezes more use from gradients. A mass-adaptive limiter spreads exploration over the full probability range. An asymmetric risk controller matches update size to signal confidence. Broad evaluations present MASPO as a robust all-in-one solution that beats baselines by a wide margin.
arxiv-2602-17650:
Tyler Bonnen and team ask how humans infer three-dimensional shape from flat images, a feat decades of models failed to match. Their modeling frame predicts human shape inferences for arbitrary objects, straight from experimental stimuli. The key is a new class of neural nets trained with a visual-spatial objective over naturalistic sensory data.

Given images from distinct spots in a natural scene, the models learn to predict spatial facts such as camera location and visual depth, with no object-related biases built in. Those signals mirror cues humans already use. In zero-shot tests on a standard shape task, the models match human accuracy with no task-specific training. Model readouts even predict fine-grained human conduct, including error patterns and reaction times.
arxiv-2602-17850:
Erik Derner and team study how chatbot style shapes human-chatbot chat, in a between-subject study of a chatbot called NAVI. Chat agents mediate daily digital life, yet style effects on user feel and task success remain poorly understood. Users tried one of two NAVI versions in a live map-based 2D routing task, or a control setup with step-by-step steps and no chatbot.

One NAVI version used a friendly, warm tone. The other used a direct, task-focused tone. The friendly chatbot clearly raised user delight and task success against the direct one. Yet control users topped task success overall, suggesting chat adds overhead for tasks solvable with plain steps. Gender did not clearly shift style effects, though early split looks hinted at more. Word matching proved limited and spotty. Style choices, the authors argue, should be task-tuned, open and tested with care.
arxiv-2602-17950:
Jing Wang and team study the ground states of three-part rotating spin-orbit coupled spin-1 Bose-Einstein condensates, modeled by Gross-Pitaevskii equations. They prove the ground state exists and derive exact traits including the virial identity and below-zero spin-orbit energy.

They propose a fast preconditioned nonlinear gradient algorithm to compute the ground states. It cuts space to a bounded box domain and applies the Fourier spectral method to sketch the wave function. That method adapts step size control and preconditioner pick for a one-knob problem, with great accuracy. Number tests verify the existence and trait results. They confirm spatial spectral accuracy across common initial guesses for each component. Stepwise multi-grid and discrete Fast Fourier Transform use aids that work. The team also studies effects of local interaction, rotation, spin-orbit coupling and trapping potential, showing giant vortex and U-shape vortex line effects.
arxiv-2602-18250:
Yves Ruffenach proposes a neuron that carries uncertainty instead of a single number. His 2026 paper sketches a variational distributional neuron, a compute unit built as a variational autoencoder brick with its own prior, learned posterior, and local training objective. Computing then means shrinking a continuous space of possibilities under constraints, not passing scalars along.

Each unit parameterizes a posterior, passes a resampled draw onward, and is steadied by its local objective term, so its activation is itself a distribution. The amount of context it holds and how long that context lasts can be tuned locally. The paper frames a pointed question: if uncertainty is intrinsic to computing, why should the basic unit stay deterministic? It maps collapse modes, conditions for a living neuron, and extensions over time through autoregressive priors.
arxiv-2602-18350:
Qi Zhang and nine co-authors boost satellite image classification with quantum features. Their 2026 paper harnesses dynamics of many-body spin Hamiltonians to generate expressive quantum features, then pairs them with classical processing. The test is multi-class image classification for space applications against a strong ResNet50 baseline.

Classical accuracy peaks at eighty-three percent, or eighty-four with transfer learning, while the quantum-classical method reaches eighty-seven percent, a clear and reproducible gain. Run on several IBM quantum processors, the hybrid approach delivers steady gains of two to three points in absolute accuracy. The work shows current and near-term quantum hardware can already help high-stakes, data-driven fields like satellite imaging and remote sensing.
arxiv-2602-18450:
Faruk Alpay and Bugra Kilictas study how a dominant shared context can swallow individual meaning in multi-agent systems. Their 2026 paper names the failure mode Asymptotic Semantic Collapse in Hierarchical Optimization, in which repeated interaction with a dominant anchor node drives other agents toward near-uniform behavior.

The team models semantic states as points on a curved surface and analyzes the resulting dynamics. Two consequences follow. First, the final state ignores optimization history: smooth gradient-style updates and noisy stochastic updates converge to the same endpoint, showing path independence. Second, how much context matters controls information content: moving from atomic representations to fully entangled ones forces node entropy, read as range, to vanish. The theory links information quantities with geometric structure and suggests a fixed consensus rule binding agents to a shared semantic grammar. A small dataset-free benchmark on an RWKV-7 checkpoint backs the analysis.
arxiv-2602-18550:
Jane Castleman and four co-authors test whether language models rank job candidates fairly. Their 2026 paper notes resume screening seems well suited to language models, so many employers use general-purpose models without adapting them to the task. Earlier research showed some models favor certain demographics, but few studies measured whether their decisions are valid.

The team builds a large set of resumes tailored to particular jobs, directly comparable, with a known ranking of superiority. That solves the lack of a large resume corpus with known ground truth unused in training. They use it to measure ranking validity across models, finding many cannot consistently select more qualified candidates. Models also fail to abstain reliably when candidates are equally qualified, and select demographic groups at uneven rates, occasionally prioritizing historically marginalized candidates. Their framework offers a principled way to audit resume screeners without ground truth, aiding independent auditors and developers.
arxiv-2602-18950:
Digital computers face fundamental limits in speed and energy for massive data tasks. Johannes Maly, with two co-authors, investigates in 2026 whether linear photonic chips can accelerate a key linear algebra primitive, the singular value decomposition of a matrix.

The SVD underpins many modern data processing algorithms. The authors test hybrid systems that pair a digital controller with a photonic chip. Their main insights are twofold. First, hybrid systems asymptotically match large-scale CPU and GPU systems on runtime. Second, hybrid systems clearly beat digital systems on energy use. For specific applications, tailored analogue systems may thus offer a promising alternative to purely digital processors.
arxiv-2602-20050:
Cosmic strings and domain walls are defects left over from the early universe. Their imprint on the cosmic microwave background can test whether they exist. A 2026 arXiv paper by Luca Caloni and three co-authors combines full Planck 2018 data with BICEP/Keck 2018 B-mode measurements.

Defect patterns came from the Unconnected Segment Model for two string types and for stable domain walls, fitted jointly with standard cosmological parameters, the tensor-to-scalar ratio, and defect tension. No statistically significant evidence for defects emerged, though the data lean slightly toward non-zero cosmic string tension. The results tighten earlier limits for the cosmic string power spectrum. They also correct earlier domain-wall analyses that had overstated the limits. Forecasts say the Simons Observatory will improve string tension limits about threefold, while LiteBIRD improves domain-wall tension limits about fivefold. Nambu-Goto string loops are assessed too.
arxiv-2602-20250:
Millisecond pulsars are thought to form in close binaries, spun up by matter from a companion. Yet many millisecond pulsars in globular clusters sit alone, with no companion in sight. A 2026 arXiv paper by Raniere de Menezes, working alone, tests whether binary breakups explain the loners in clusters with uncollapsed cores.

The model joins two ideas: the Heggie-Hills rule for surviving encounters, and companion ablation, where a pulsar's wind eats its partner away. Together they predict the lone fraction as roughly forty-two percent divided by the square root of the ionization radius, give or take about one and a half points. That radius-dependent model beats a rival in which the lone fraction does not depend on radius at all, with a log Bayes factor above two and a half. The same model explains why NGC 5139, or Omega Centauri, holds so many lone millisecond pulsars.
arxiv-2602-20350:
Yibo Meng and three co-authors present Misty Forest, a virtual-reality game turning attention patterns linked to ADHD into shared play for young partners. ADHD still carries heavy stigma in many places, above all in China, where related acts are often judged as moral failings, not brain-based differences. The game uses uneven co-play, turning shifting focus and time blindness into matching roles that demand teamwork.

Rather than making up for shortfalls, the design treats thinking styles as a source of mutual need. In one study with mixed ADHD and non-ADHD pairs, Misty Forest raised task success, self-regard among ADHD people, ADHD facts, and empathy among others. The findings suggest design for different minds can foster insight, give-and-take, and open teamwork. The game treats gaps as things two players face side by side, not one player's problem to fix.
arxiv-2602-20450:
Federated learning lets many clients train one shared model without sharing sensitive local data, but accuracy often suffers because client data differ statistically. Nihal Balivada and three co-authors argue that prior selection methods fail twice over: model updates such as loss and bias misrepresent client heterogeneity, and selection itself is not deterministic. Their answer is Terraform, a client selection method that uses gradient updates plus a deterministic selection algorithm to pick heterogeneous clients for retraining.

The two-part approach lifts accuracy by up to forty-seven percent over prior work. Ablation studies and training-time analyses back the method's efficiency and robustness. Terraform thus offers a principled way to choose which clients retrain, turning client diversity from a liability into a source of accuracy gains.
arxiv-2602-20550:
Imaging forward models, from spectral cameras to MRI scanners, are usually built as bulky one-modality codes. Chengshuai Yang proves that every forward model in a broad, defined operator class admits a close match as a typed acyclic graph. Its nodes come from exactly eleven steps: Propagate, Modulate, Project, Encode, Convolve, Accumulate, Detect, Sample, Disperse, Scatter, and Transform. The paper calls this the Finite Primitive Basis Theorem.

The proof builds the graph by algorithm, with relative error at most epsilon and size within set bounds. The set is minimal: dropping any one step costs some modality its close match. Non-linear imaging physics sorts into two kinds: point-wise scalar maps handled by Transform, and self-consistent loops unrolled into linear steps. Checks on thirty-one linear modalities confirm error below one hundredth with at most five nodes and depth five, plus splits for nine more non-linear kinds.
arxiv-2602-20650:
Large image data sets drive deep learning, but their storage demands strain resource-limited use. Chenyue Yu and four co-authors note that most compression methods shrink data sets by dropping samples, missing the large overlap inside each image, above all in color space. Their method, Dataset Color Quantization, shrinks visual data sets by cutting color-space redundancy while keeping information crucial for training.

The method sets same palettes across similar images, keeps key colors guided by model sight, and maintains shape details needed for good feature learning. Broad tests across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet-1K show the method greatly improves training scores under aggressive compression. The paper presents dataset-level color quantization as a scalable and robust route to storage cuts.
arxiv-2602-20750:
Precision scanning has long tested the basics of physics. Early insights led to quantum rules, and later work proved quantum electrodynamics and found fundamental values. Today, gains in atomic and molecular scans allow fine searches for physics beyond the Standard Model.

A broad class of sound extensions predicts new light forms with weak links to electrons, muons, and nuclei. They give rise to tiny spin-free forces that can be probed at low energies. Cédric Delaunay and two co-authors present a single survey of scan searches for such forces. It discusses the working theoretical setup connecting fundamental forces to atomic and nuclear readings, lists key experimental and lab plans, and reviews atomic cases with the strongest sensitivity. The paper ends with updated scan limits on sample test models, highlighting the special and matching role of precision scans in exploring new fundamental forces.
arxiv-2602-21050:
Quantum networks need interference between photons from distant nodes, which usually demands tight optical synchronization. Baghdasar Baghdasaryan and thirteen co-authors develop a gentler route in this 2026 arXiv paper. It uses continuous-wave photon-pair sources, where indistinguishability comes from post-selecting detections within a coincidence window shorter than the photon coherence time. Their framework quantifies how time scales, visibility, and usable multi-photon rates relate.

Detector timing jitter, coherence time, and post-selection all enter the model, which four-photon Hong-Ou-Mandel measurements verify. With the framework now checked against experiment, it settles on the coincidence window giving the highest usable four-photon rates at a chosen visibility. Continuous-wave sources then match pulsed sources in rate under equal indistinguishability constraints, while relaxing synchronization demands.
arxiv-2602-21150:
Dengue burdens health systems worldwide, and age-aimed shots could change its course. Sourav Banerjee, Thomas Gotz, and Satyananda Panda model that problem in this 2026 arXiv paper via an age-grouped vector-host model. Humans are grouped by age, jabbed people further by time since the jab, and the insects are tied to host motion under a quasi-steady-state premise.

Adding up over jab age yields a bent rest-state form, with the endemic rest point as a fixed-point problem for sick insects. Lipschitz bounds plus a shrinking case prove one and only one rest point exists under a weak spread rule. The study highlights how age-tied shots shape long-term dengue motion.
arxiv-2602-21250:
The isotonic oscillator is a quantum system whose linked states reveal its build. Messan Medard Akouetegan, Isiaka Aremua, and Mahouton Norbert Hounkonnou build those states in this 2026 arXiv paper through the slant tool ranking trick. Both Barut-Girardello and Gazeau-Klauder linked states are built within that setup.

Their math traits are studied with copying kernels, and mean values of marking readouts are worked out. Classic dials are made discrete in the complex plane, and heat conduct in the built states is studied through mixed states from a standard density tool. A Glauber-Sudarshan P-picture rounds out the view. Readers get a full linked-state treatment of one oscillator.
arxiv-2602-21350:
When does quantum data coding give a true edge, and when does it merely restate a classic problem? Sebastian Zajac, Jacob Cybulski, Bartosz Dziewit, and Tomasz Kulpa answer with a match theorem in this 2026 arXiv paper. Any coding mapping classic data to real-valued sizes, then a stand-alone unitary and compute-basis reading, yields exactly the class of classic squared forms.

The shape engine is a dying Berry link forced by a limit to real values, dropping the complex phases needed for tied overlap. Coding checks for phase tangle and mutual facts link to a shape excess that dies exactly for real codings. Misreading such models as quantum compute power is termed the Inverse Born Rule Fallacy. Complex-phase structure emerges as strictly needed for data-driven quantum edge.
arxiv-2602-21450:
Felipe Bartelt and three co-authors develop a vector-field framework for path following on matrix Lie groups, with robot control as the target. Many robots control position and orientation independently, from omnidirectional aerial vehicles to manipulator end-effectors. Such systems often must follow a continuous sequence of poses, and path following beats trajectory tracking in practice.

The path-following problem is posed on the Lie group SE(3) for rigid bodies in three-dimensional space. Their guiding vector field guarantees convergence to a desired parametric curve from almost all starting conditions, with continuous motion along the path. The control input stays minimal in form and close to engineering practice, like the body twist for SE(3). Specialized to SE(3), the method yields an efficient real-time algorithm, validated on a manipulator tracking complex pose paths, with open-source code.
arxiv-2602-21550:
Zhao Yang and five co-authors challenge the idea that longer DNA sequences always improve gene expression prediction. Gene expression prediction forecasts mRNA levels from DNA sequences. Earlier work often extends input length to catch distal enhancers that may act from hundreds of kilobases away.

The team first shows that long sequence modeling can hurt current models. Even careful designs only soften the damage from long sequences. Proximal multimodal epigenomic signals near target genes prove more essential. Different signal types play distinct roles: some mark active regulatory elements directly, while others reflect background chromatin patterns that can confound models. Simple concatenation lets models form spurious links to background patterns. The proposed Prism framework learns multiple mixes of epigenomic features for distinct background states and uses backdoor adjustment to curb confounding, reaching leading performance with only short sequences.
arxiv-2602-21750:
Protein language models now serve as general tools for protein engineering and de novo design, trained as deep transformers on massive sequence corpora, scaled by adding depth. Recent work on autoregressive language models found a Curse of Depth: many later layers add little to final predictions. Aleena Siji and eleven co-authors ask whether the same depth inefficiency appears in protein models. Many are not autoregressive, and some take both sequence and structure as input.

Their depth analysis covers seven popular protein model families across scales, spanning autoregressive, masked, and diffusion objectives, using probing, perturbation, and downstream-evaluation measures. Across models, task-relevant computation concentrates in a subset of layers, while the rest mainly refine the final prediction incrementally. The pattern holds beyond sequence-only settings and in multimodal models, suggesting depth inefficiency is common in modern protein models and motivating more depth-efficient designs.
arxiv-2602-22050:
Young stars are born with disks of gas and dust that may form planets, but nearby starlight can erode those disks away. Jingyi Ping and three co-authors simulate whole populations of viscous disks under mild ultraviolet radiation from neighbors, tracking gas mass and size over ten million years. They compare the results with observed disks in Upper Scorpius, including targets from a large ALMA program.

Models that mix viscous spreading with external photoevaporation give disk lifetimes of a few million years, matching observed dispersal times. Low-mass stars lose their disks fastest, the authors find, since their weaker gravity holds gas less tightly: their share among surviving disks falls markedly over the simulated span. The study ties disk survival to stellar mass and neighborhood radiation in one consistent picture.
arxiv-2602-22150:
Unified image generators must juggle tasks that need different inner representations: some need concepts, others need precise locations. YuXin Song and eight co-authors argue that forcing one shared representation creates a concept-localization conflict. Their framework, CoLoGen, learns the two sides progressively instead, reconciling them for unified diffusion-based generation.

A staged curriculum first builds core concept and location skills, then adapts them to varied visual conditions, and finally refines their teamwork for complex instruction-driven tasks. A routing module sends features to specialized experts and blends their outputs steadily across stages. Experiments on editing, controllable generation, and customization show the staged design paying off.
arxiv-2602-22350:
Stock markets quote a National Best Bid and Offer as if prices across exchanges existed at one current moment, but Paul Borrill argues that moment is engineered, not found. He defines engineered simultaneity: a system that compares events at spacelike-separated places through an implicit simultaneity convention, then reports the result as objective measurement. The NBBO, he shows, is exactly such a system.

Special relativity proves the ordering of spacelike-separated price events depends on the reference frame: other frames would report a different NBBO than the official processor's value. The impossibility is exact, not approximate, within Minkowski spacetime, and general relativity compounds it. Market fairness rules thus rest on a convention physics cannot certify as unique.
arxiv-2602-22450:
AI agents that browse and call tools can be hijacked without any visible trace. Qianlong Lan and three co-authors demonstrate implicit prompt injection: adversarial instructions hidden in automatically generated URL previews, including titles, metadata, and snippets, can make an agent leak sensitive runtime context. The final answer shown to the user can look harmless while exfiltration proceeds.

In hundreds of experimental runs with a small open model in a fully local testbed, the attack succeeds nearly nine times in ten, and nearly all successful attacks escape output-based safety checks. A sharded variant splits stolen information across many requests to dodge detection, sharply reducing single-request leakage metrics. The paper names the threat silent egress, and shows why output checks alone cannot catch it.
arxiv-2602-22550:
Jianzhong Zhang and two co-authors prove that a damped model of compressible fluid flow behaves well for all time. The compressible Euler system describes gases and fluids whose density changes, and damping drains energy from the motion. Global well-posedness means solutions exist forever, stay unique, and change smoothly when starting conditions change slightly.

The result holds in critical Besov spaces of L^p type for p below 2, a setting that measures roughness of the flow at the borderline where standard tools break down. The key step is a new product estimate in hybrid L^2-L^p Besov spaces, which controls how interacting waves combine. For readers of fluid mathematics, it extends the safe zone for this damped system into rougher, more realistic regimes.
arxiv-2602-22650:
Xinxin Yang and five co-authors tackle auto-bidding across advertising channels. Budgets and limits must be split across channels that behave differently. Neither pure optimization nor pure reinforcement learning copes well: one is rigid in shifting markets, the other misses long-range history inside Markov-style frames.

AHBid joins a high-level generative planner with real-time control. A diffusion-based planner splits budgets and limits while reading historical context and time patterns. Constraint enforcement keeps spending inside its bounds, trajectory refinement adapts to change, and a control-based bidder blends history with live signals. Offline tests and live A/B trials showed about fourteen percent higher overall return than baselines.
arxiv-2602-22750:
Gaston Besanson and one co-author argue that large-scale inference has become cognitive infrastructure, a bottleneck input downstream apps need to compete. As generative AI commercializes, advantage shifts from one-time training to continuous inference, distribution, and routing, often controlled by firms that also compete downstream with assistants and developer tools.

Foreclosure need not work through price. It can run through latency, throughput, error rates, context limits, feature gating, or steering and default routing that is hard to see and harder to litigate. The essay defines cognitive infrastructure in testable terms and frames harm through raising-rivals'-costs logic. It proposes Neutral Inference: auditable quality parity, routing transparency, and FRAND-style non-discrimination for similarly placed buyers, triggered only by evidence of gatekeeper status.
arxiv-2602-22950:
Raphael M. Tromer and four co-authors benchmark a lean matter descriptor against a library giant. Choosing shape tags for machine-learning setups shapes both scores and clarity, yet richer tags cost compute and hide shape meaning. The Dynamic Collision Fingerprint probes atomic shapes in motion to produce concise, physics-true tags.

Tested on 120 two-dimensional carbon forms against the library, DCF easily matches library scores on every method. Tests used linear fitting, choice trees, and XGBoost across train-test splits from ten to ninety percent over many random seeds. It does so with far smaller tags, cutting compute load, and its accounts read far more physics-clear than the library's fussy ones. DCF thus stands as a flexible, grounded stand-in for heavy tag collections.
arxiv-2602-23350:
Sotiris Armeniakos and one co-author prove that a stronger form of the dimensional Brunn-Minkowski conjecture implies the (B)-conjecture for sufficiently regular even log-concave measures. The (B)-conjecture and the Brunn-Minkowski family concern how the sizes of sets and measures behave under averaging and interpolation, and links between them have been hard to establish.

The authors further show that hereditarily convex measures satisfy the strengthened form. That yields an alternative proof of a recent result by Cordero-Erausquin and Eskenazis, who showed that a hereditarily convex measure satisfies both conjectures. The paper thus ties the two conjectures together through a single stronger statement and gives the hereditarily convex case a new, shorter route.
arxiv-2602-23550:
Juan Angel Martin and four co-authors propose a clustering framework for pattern discovery in fluid flows. Clustering offers a powerful way to analyze complex flow dynamics and cut compute costs in large-scale simulations. Their method uses Vector Quantization Principal Component Analysis to find structural sensitivity zones, where flow responds most to change.

To the authors' knowledge, this is the first use of VQPCA for flow patterns and dynamically relevant regions. As a fully data-driven method, it needs no adjoint methods and costs little, since it uses only data from the direct problem. It groups the flow field into regions by their intrinsic dynamics, extracting dominant flow features. Tests on the wake behind a circular cylinder match previously known sensitivity regions, and the analysis extends to two planar synthetic jets.
arxiv-2602-23850:
Yifan Sun and two co-authors model magnetic flux tubes lit up by pulsar winds, to explain linear structures linking pulsars to gamma-ray halos. The 2026 paper considers fast electrons injected into the interstellar medium, traveling almost freely along large-scale magnetic fields with very slow spread across field lines.

The model treats a flux tube that leaves the pulsar and joins the ambient magnetic field. Particles in the tube show a skewed pitch-angle distribution, so their emission beams strongly in one direction. The model is applied to pulsar tails and filaments, including extended X-ray and gamma-ray emission near one pulsar and the misaligned jet of the Guitar Nebula. It constrains the particle populations and magnetic fields at work. It ties halo shapes to the geometry of field lines leaving the pulsar.
arxiv-2602-24050:
Takeshi Ikeda and two co-authors prove a Seidel product formula in torus-equivariant quantum K-theory for generalized flag varieties. The 2026 paper generalizes earlier results for cominuscule flag varieties, a special class where the formula was already known, to the broader generalized setting.

The proof rests on the K-theoretic Peterson isomorphism, together with a version of the K-theoretic nil-Hecke algebra for the extended affine Weyl group. Seidel-type formulas describe how certain symmetry operations multiply in quantum K-theory, which encodes curve-counting information on the variety. Extending the formula to generalized flag varieties widens the reach of quantum K-theoretic computations and ties the equivariant theory more closely to combinatorial algebra.
arxiv-2603-00250: Kozdon and colleagues present M-band spectra from the vast low-tilt disk of AB Aurigae, catching light from an off-centre, cool, compact source. Carbon monoxide line shapes and spectroastrometric signals place the source near an orbit of 65 au at angle 143 degrees. It sits well apart from protoplanet AB Aur b, which was not seen. If a disk orbits the planet, its peak heat would be about 550 K and its peak radius about 5 au. This hints at a previously unknown companion in the system.
arxiv-2603-00350: Leitão Filho and colleagues challenge the idea that AI progress means ever larger models on ever broader data. They introduce Monotropic Artificial Intelligence: models trading generality for precision within narrow domains, inspired by monotropism theory from autism research. The authors define such models and contrast them with polytropic designs. They test the idea with Mini-Enedina, a 37.5-million-parameter model near-perfect on Timoshenko beam analysis but deliberately incompetent elsewhere. Their work argues specialized and generalist systems can coexist, rather than general intelligence as the only legitimate goal.
arxiv-2603-00550: Wang and Zhao tackle weakly supervised video anomaly detection, where only video level labels exist and frame level truth is missing. Their LAS-VAD framework groups frames into semantic clusters with anomaly connected components, so segments in one group share meaning. An intention aware strategy then separates lookalike normal and abnormal acts, such as taking items versus stealing. Anomaly attribute cues like flames and thick smoke for explosions further guide detection. The team evaluates on the XD-Violence and UCF-Crime benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-00750: Pruss gives a simple integral representation for proper single event scoring rules, using no derivatives and no continuity assumptions. The result needs neither smoothness nor continuity from the scoring rule, making it unusually spare. Stripping away derivatives and continuity leaves a tool that applies wherever proper single event scores arise.
arxiv-2603-01450:
Jianfeng Liao, Yichen Wei, Raymond Chan Ching Bon, and colleagues wrote this 2026 study on how to spot fake face videos and images. Fake media made by AI now looks very real, and it can harm public trust and safety. Older tools often fail when a new kind of fake appears.

The team builds a system called DFA on top of CLIP, a large vision and language model, without changing CLIP itself. One part checks the whole image for odd signs, while a second part looks for small flaws in the face. A third part joins both views to make the final call. Tests on still frames and on video show strong results, with a clear gain on the hard DFDC test set.
arxiv-2603-02050:
Kihoon Son, Hyewon Lee, DaEun Choi, and colleagues design AI agents that collaborate with designers in real time. Their 2026 work notes that human partners coordinate through shared visibility of process and workspace. Agents, by contrast, usually deliver final outputs or read-only process views and ignore concurrent user moves.

A first study with professional designers shows process visibility helps, yet conflicts arise when agents misread feedback. Their system, Cleo, interprets collaborative intent from concurrent actions on shared artifacts and adapts live. A second two-day study analyzes hundreds of turns for action patterns and triggers. Designers split their work among delegation, direction, and concurrent co-work in shifting shares. A decision model with six interaction loops distills when to hand off and when to work together.
arxiv-2603-02350:
W Horowitz and A Rothkopf rebuild a classical action principle from quantum theory in this 2026 paper. Hamilton's principle derives motion from a single action quantity, usually for boundary value problems. Initial value problems, starting from a known state, need a different variational setup. The authors derive that setup as the classical limit of a quantum formalism.

The quantum starting point tracks expected values through forward and backward time paths. Both paths turn out to carry classical motion and fluctuations, contrary to common belief. Fluctuations on both paths prove essential for correct normalization of the limit. One path's unique classical solution is zero, and it runs backward in time. No hand-setting is needed. The authors note consequences for constrained systems and gauge theories.
arxiv-2603-02450:
Zheyu Wu, Hanyi Chen, Mengmeng Long, and colleagues report a switchable superconducting memory in this 2026 paper. Superconducting computers could beat ordinary electronics on energy use by far. Memory that can be written and read in such platforms has stayed elusive. Their material is uranium ditelluride, a candidate triplet superconductor in single crystal form.

A magnetic field tunes the crystal into a regime between two superconducting phases. There, direct current pulses push it into and out of a metastable state. That state carries an enhanced critical current, the most current it can bear without resistance. Pulse strength and duration control the switching. The material remembers which state it is in after the pulse ends. Such controllable memory is a missing piece for superconducting computing.
arxiv-2603-02550:
Mu-Tian Wang, Fei Dai, Hui-Gen Liu, and colleagues characterize a young planetary system in this 2026 paper. TOI-2076 is about two hundred million years old and hosts four sub-Neptune planets. Young multi-planet systems often sit in resonant chains set by disc migration. Those chains usually break apart over time, as in our solar system's story.

These four planets sit near resonance but not locked inside it, leaving the system fragile. Their cores weigh about the same, yet envelope shares rise steadily for cooler, outer planets. That gradient fits photoevaporation, where starlight strips the most irradiated envelopes first. Helium outflow detections rule out a pure water-world makeup. Reshaping of compact systems, both dynamic and atmospheric, clearly starts early. The system anchors models of long-term planet evolution.
arxiv-2603-02650:
Yuan Lu, Dongqi Han, Yansen Wang, and Dongsheng Li improve robot planners that learn from stored data. Their 2026 method, called SAGE, targets a known flaw in diffusion planners. Such planners can pick paths that score high yet clash with how the world really moves, so execution turns brittle.

SAGE scores each sampled plan with a learned check for physical consistency. A predictor trained on past state sequences flags plans whose next steps look unlikely, and that penalty joins the value score when choosing actions. The method needs no live trials and no retraining of the planner. Across locomotion, navigation, and manipulation tests, it made diffusion planners stronger and more robust.
arxiv-2603-02750:
Takuro Mochizuki studies whether families of flat connections stay bounded when their wildness is capped. A flat connection is a system of linked rate laws with a rigid shape. Its irregularity gauges how badly answers can blow up near singular points. His 2026 paper asks if a cap on that wildness bounds the whole family.

Bounded families can be charted by tidy parameter spaces, the base of any sorting scheme in this field. As a use case, Mochizuki turns to D-modules, a strong algebraic language for such rate laws. He studies bounded families whose cycle data, which track singular directions, stay held down in a precise sense. The work ties analytic control of equations to algebraic control of their families.
arxiv-2603-02850:
D. Katz, A. Gómez, E. Caffau, and a large team check whether the fastest stars in the Gaia catalog are real. The third Gaia release lists tens of millions of star speeds, but the faintest spectra are noisy. Noise spikes can fake extreme speeds, and true high-speed stars are rare enough that fakes could swamp them.

The team re-observed over one hundred candidate stars with sensitive ground spectrographs in France and Chile. About one hundred four speeds held up, while thirty were refuted as errors. Merging other major surveys let them chart the fake rate by signal strength and speed range. At the faintest levels, most extreme readings were false. The cleaned sample of truly fast stars then feeds orbit studies of the Milky Way.
arxiv-2603-02950:
Lingxiao Huang and Nisheeth Vishnoi trace how leaning on AI can quietly erode the skill it seems to support. Their 2026 paper models human skill and AI delegation as two quantities that evolve together. Delegation follows relative performance, skill grows with practice and decays with disuse, and both updates chase one shared error metric.

Despite that local alignment, the system gains a second stable resting point: a low-skill trap of permanent reliance, divided from the high-skill outcome by a sharp boundary. Early choices near that boundary become effectively irreversible. AI help can thus raise short-run scores while locking in long-run loss against the no-AI path. The authors show the trap survives noise and lopsided trust updates.
arxiv-2603-03250:
The CMS Collaboration hunts for a light new particle that decays into two photons at the Large Hadron Collider. Several theories predict a spin-zero particle below the electroweak scale, and photon pairs are a clean place to look. Their 2026 search uses proton-proton collisions recorded in 2018 at thirteen teraelectronvolts.

A new diphoton trigger opened the low-mass window, letting the team scan resonance masses from ten to seventy gigaelectronvolts in data made through gluon fusion. No significant excess appeared above the expected background. The team therefore sets upper limits on how strongly such a particle could be produced and decay to photons. The limits are also read as constraints on axion-like particles within an effective theory framework.
arxiv-2603-03450:
Christopher J Lindsay and four colleagues test how stellar modelers should handle a common chemical quirk in old stars. Metal-poor stars are often rich in alpha elements, oxygen and its kin, relative to iron. Modelers either build that enhancement in fully or fake it with a simple correction to total metal content. Their 2026 study models eight evolved metal-poor stars both ways, using spectroscopy plus individual oscillation frequencies from asteroseismology.

The two methods agree on the inferred stellar properties, and their uncertainties are comparable. That calm result disagrees qualitatively with earlier work based only on global oscillation summaries, where ages swung strongly with assumed chemistry. One warning stands out: the observed frequency of strongest oscillation exceeds scaling-relation predictions, especially at low metal content. Fixing that breakdown matters for dating hundreds of halo giants known only by global measures.
arxiv-2603-03550:
Zhiyu Cao and Peter G Wolynes study the stats of sudden shifts in driven glassy substances. Near instability, amorphous systems release stress in thermal avalanches, large grouped events rather than smooth flow. Working inside random first-order shift theory, the standard picture of glasses, their 2026 paper traces avalanches to stringy excited states, thread-like cooperative motions inside the material.

Those excitations produce waiting-time statistics that are not Poisson, so events remember each other. Embedding the stats in a general master formula captures the resulting non-Markovian, aging dynamics of avalanche clusters. The authors then analyze fingerprints under two driving styles, slow shear and random shaking: correlation functions and working temperatures. Full counting stats give complete distributions for avalanche sizes and counts, exposing the in-between-time conduct between single events and steady flow.
arxiv-2603-03650:
Felix Köster and Atsushi Uchida treat a physical system as a computer and learn where to read it. Dynamical systems preserve, transform, and scatter information as they evolve. Their 2026 framework learns not only from a system's data but how to measure the system itself. A trainable attention module decides both where to probe the state and how to combine the readings for the best prediction.

The demonstration system is a spatiotemporal field governed by a partial differential equation, though any samplable state qualifies. Adaptive spatial sensing improves prediction accuracy significantly on canonical chaotic benchmarks. The authors frame attention-enhanced reservoir computing, a known technique, as one special case of the broader paradigm. Their closing image is memorable: neural networks as trainable measurement devices for physical systems.
arxiv-2603-03750:
Sujoy Kumar Nath, Dipak Debnath, and Hsiang-Kuang Chang watch the echoes between X-ray colors during a black hole's awakening. The binary Swift J1727.8-1613 erupted in 2023 in an outburst lasting about ten months. China's Insight-HXMT telescope monitored the rising phase almost continuously for six weeks, catching strong type-C oscillations, the rhythmic flickers that track the inner accretion flow. Their 2026 paper measures the time lags between energy bands as the outburst climbs.

Both hard lags, where energetic light trails, and soft lags appear, with a clear transition from hard to soft as the outburst evolves. The lags anti-correlate strongly with oscillation frequency and with the spectrum's photon index, and correlate positively with the inferred shock location. The pattern supports the propagating oscillatory shock picture, in which a moving shock front orchestrates the coupled spectral and timing behavior.
arxiv-2603-04250: Ackerman and colleagues study long-lived metastable states in the 4f13 5d 6s configuration of Yb+. A co-trapped control ion sympathetically cools the spectroscopy ion, enabling accurate timing of its later decay. They record a strong decay signal, a weaker decay signal, and evidence for a much longer lifetime. These long-lived states open new opportunities for qubit and qudit state detection, plus optical clocks.
arxiv-2603-04350: Garai and Chamakuri parallelize parabolic equations in time with exponential integrators. Exp-ParaDiag builds on first and second order integrators, converging both on its own and inside GMRES. The form reaches sixth order temporal accuracy and extends to nonlinear problems with proven convergence. Numerical tests back the theory and show robust efficient methods. The method thus saves time on hard problems. Users get fast answers for long runs. Speed is the point.
arxiv-2603-04750: Bui, Li, and Liu offer HiMAP-Travel, a hierarchical multi-agent framework for constrained travel planning. Sequential LLM agents drift from global constraints as context grows, failing budgets and diversity. One lead agent splits resources by day, while day agents plan on their own in parallel. A transactional monitor enforces budget and uniqueness constraints, while bargaining lets agents reject bad sub-goals. One policy, trained with GRPO and conditioned by role, powers all agents. On TravelPlanner, HiMAP-Travel reaches 52.65 percent test Final Pass Rate, beating rivals while cutting latency.
arxiv-2603-04850: Murata and Tada model hybrid growth with a random lattice method across six cases. Multi-fall hybrid growth models produce various shape defects. Cases vary the number of fall fields and the inflaton curve form, Square or Cubic. Chance density functions and power spectra broadly match the random-delta-N rule. The Cubic case shows a special upper bound in the density function, curbing early black hole birth while shaping halo birth. Euler characteristic checks spot defect structures: domain walls, cosmic strings, and poles for one, two, and three fields.
arxiv-2603-04950: Denis Musinguzi and the rest of the team present place-aware early training for medical gap visual question answering, where models compare images to spot change that matters in medicine. Standard side-by-side or sorting training leaves vision encoders missing subtle changes that tell true disease course apart from capture shifts. Their method adds auto referring phrases, grounded labels, and linked auto referring phrases, building fine-grained forms grounded in space. Joined with a language model, it leads medical gap VQA on chest X-ray images.
arxiv-2603-05050: Enrico Bernardi and Alberto Lanconelli present a linear PDE whose Cauchy problem noise makes well-posed. A well-chosen multiplicative Stratonovich perturbation of Brownian type makes the operator well-posed in the smooth category, despite its double involutive traits and weak hyperbolicity. Its fixed counterpart reaches well-posedness only in Gevrey classes with s at least 1 and below 2. The example shows noise can regularize an otherwise ill-posed problem.
arxiv-2603-05150: Michael Hatzon and team model three microwave cavity resonators linked by thin metallic foils as coupled lumped circuits. The foils mediate energy exchange through mutual impedance, producing interference and a controllable antiresonance when the two input ones are balanced in amplitude and phase. Under balance, a sharp one appears with several-fold stronger phase sensitivity at the output cavity resonance. The seen coupling strengths fall inside the range predicted from the foil traits, confirming a route to control of it across a continuous metal interface.
arxiv-2603-05350: Issa Saddiq and the rest of the team present machine learning for automated XPS analysis, whose spectra challenge readers. A Spatial Transformer Network, quietly lining up spectra, sorts chemical settings. The model trained on 100,000 made spectra from 104 polymers. Random shifts and spread mimicked change. The network corrected electrostatic shifts reaching 3.0 eV, achieving around 82% functional-group accuracy. Neural networks can thus learn spectral-feature composition links when intrinsically accounting for variable shifts, advancing XPS analysis as an assistive tool.
arxiv-2603-05450: Yifan Zhu and the rest of the team present the Distributed Partial Information Puzzle. Establishing common ground, shared beliefs and mutually recognized facts, underpins collaboration, yet challenges current AI systems. The authors present a mixed data set, annotated and aligned across speech, gesture, and action. They test two common-ground models: large language models inferring shared beliefs, and an axiomatic Dynamic Epistemic Logic pipeline performing the same task incrementally. Annotated DPIP results challenge modern large language models tracking task progression and belief state.
arxiv-2603-05550: Andrade shows large odd integers, past a bound, split into one square plus fourteen prime fifth powers, in a Waring-Goldbach result. He also shows large even integers, past a bound, split into one square, one biquadrate, and twelve prime fifth powers. The work treats Waring-Goldbach problems for one square and higher powers.
arxiv-2603-05750: Gesese and team present NERdME, a named entity spotting data set for code-store items. Current pulling data sets focus on papers and miss building details in stores. README files describe data sets, code, and items, but free-form Markdown offers little structure, tangling pulling. NERdME holds 200 tagged README files with over 10,000 spans, 10 entity types. Base models using language models and transformer nets show paper versus building gaps, backing README entity types in benchmarks. A downstream entity-linking test shows README entities support finding and data-about-data joining.
arxiv-2603-05950: He and Chen propose E-AdaPrune, adaptive pruning setting image-specific budgets from feature spectra. Token reduction accelerates vision-language models, yet pipelines fix budgets across inputs. Preserving spectral energy, the method gives more tokens to dense scenes and fewer to redundant ones, without learnable parameters. Across backbones, selectors, and benchmarks under matched budgets, E-AdaPrune cuts redundant computation from simple cases and converts savings into gains. On SQA, it uses 35.8 percent fewer tokens for simple cases with under 1 percent decrease, while hard cases gain over 50 percent more tokens.
arxiv-2603-06150: Li and colleagues search for periodic radio signals from companions in double neutron star systems, most of which should be ordinary pulsars. They use the Fast Folding Algorithm, suited to long spin period pulsars, plus a time domain resampling code called PYSOLATOR that strips orbital modulation to lengthen usable data. From 272.2 hours of FAST observations across 13 systems, known pulsar signals sharpen clearly, including one faint signal visible only after folding. No companion signals emerge among 197962 candidates, though the authors note orbital geodetic precession could improve future detectability.
arxiv-2603-06350: Yu and colleagues present MoEless, a serverless MoE serving framework tackling expert load imbalance elastically. Sparse activation makes a few experts stragglers while others sit idle, inflating latency and cost. Static serverful deployments limit elasticity and force costly swapping. MoEless uses lightweight layer aware predictors to estimate expert load distributions and proactively identify stragglers. Optimized scaling and placement improve locality, GPU use, and cross expert load balance. On Megatron-LM across eight GPUs, MoEless cuts latency by 43 percent and cost by 84 percent against state of the art solutions.
arxiv-2603-06450: Yang and his team ask what demonstration data best enables transfer across robot setups, where rules train on robots, scenes, and views. Set experiments vary end-effector morphology, platform appearance, and camera perspective, testing data scaling against planned broadened diversity. View shifts benefit most from it, while shape shifts gain less from it and most from data matches: paired sets aligning scenes, tasks, or paths across bodies. Changing only data composition, guided by simulations, improves real-world cross-body gains by an average of 22.5 percent over unpaired datasets.
arxiv-2603-06950: Ouaari and colleagues ask how private DNA embeddings are, testing whether sequence representations can be inverted. DNA foundation models now shape bioinformatics and health care. Their embeddings, dense vectors capturing genomic detail, are shared through embedding services to support downstream tasks while supposedly shielding raw sequences. As sharing spreads, representation security is in question. They test resilience to model inversion attacks, where foes try to rebuild training data from model outputs. In their study, a zero-shot embedding feeds a decoder, and they test three DNA foundation models for privacy.
arxiv-2603-07150: Kumar and colleagues rework quadratic gravity's troubled extra spin-2 mode into a healthy inverted harmonic oscillator-like instability. Quadratic gravity is the unique renormalizable quantum gravity theory in four dimensions, but its massive tensor ghost has long blocked a clean reading. Quantized with direct-sum quantum field theory, the new mode has a well-defined quantum description yet no particle reading and no place in the asymptotic spectrum. It stays off shell and cut off from ordinary matter in effect.
arxiv-2603-07450: Wu and colleagues tame the Bessel landscape that governs antenna placement in fluid MIMO systems. Under rich scattering, spatial correlation follows a Bessel function of the adjustable positions, making capacity tuning highly non-convex. They derive a high-signal estimate splitting the goal into send and receive terms, plus a closed-form loss bound against ideal MIMO. Two alternating methods then search the landscape, one swarm-based and one using convex stand-ins for far faster convergence.
arxiv-2603-07850: Llorente-Saguer presents a fully graphics-chip-based design for checking Goldbach's conjecture at large scale. Moving the whole sieve onto the chip removes host-side build work and link delays. A lock-free counter spreads work across chips with near-linear gains. The setup checks the conjecture to a trillion in under three minutes and to ten trillion in under an hour on one top chip, with code and logs shared for repeat runs.
arxiv-2603-08250: Pokhrel and colleagues use a holographic approach to analyze transport properties of baryon-rich back-reacted thermal plasma with finite 't Hooft coupling correction. The dual bulk geometry is a charged AdS black hole with higher-derivative Gauss-Bonnet correction and string cloud. They study drag force, jet quenching parameter, screening length, radial profile, and energy loss across parameters. Drag force and jet quenching grow with Gauss-Bonnet coupling, baryon density, and flavor density, while screening length shrinks with those parameters.
arxiv-2603-08350: Silva develops a Barta-type form for the p-Laplacian on curved manifolds. It extends the approach of Cheung-Leung and Bessa-Montenegro from the linear to the nonlinear case. This framework yields sharp lower bounds for the p-tone with no boundary smoothness assumed. For use, the author obtains nonlinear versions of Cheng's eigenvalue contrast theorem and the Cheng-Li-Yau bound for p greater than or equal to 2. The context is minimal immersions.
arxiv-2603-08450: Kunz and colleagues build the first openly available English-to-Swedish dataset pairing translationese sentences with idiomatic alternatives. Each pair is tagged with the problems in the original translation. The set is designed to probe what language models prefer when translating. Tests on smaller Swedish and multilingual models find they often favor the translationese phrasing. Dropping the English source sentence makes models pick the human alternative more often, showing that seeing the source pushes models toward literal wording, though even without it they still often prefer translationese.
arxiv-2603-08550: Rajat Masiwal and colleagues trace how monsoon winds crossing the equator swap one boundary-layer regime for another. Near the equator, the usual Ekman balance fails as spin effects fade and flow from the south grows. Reanalysis plus a scaling test shows momentum control passing from friction to sideways transport, and model planet runs confirm the shift moves poleward when cross-equator push grows or spin slows.
arxiv-2603-08750: Benjamin Collins and colleagues test chemically polarized targets for nuclear and particle physics. Standard spin-polarized targets cost dearly and demand harsh cold and magnetic setups, limiting shapes and failing under intense radiation. Their SABRE method holds up in the beam at MAMI and survives high radiation doses, opening a path to such targets and sensor media.
arxiv-2603-08850: Guofeng Zhang and colleagues give video generation fine control over each object's path. Most models paint whole scenes at once, with no levers for composition. Their HECTOR pipeline mixes still-image and video references, lets users set each element's trajectory, place, size, and speed, and beats rivals on visual quality, reference faithfulness, and motion control.
arxiv-2603-09050: Adithya Pradeep and colleagues create, steer, and park single torons on demand with tailored electric fields. Torons are 3D double-twist lumps in chiral nematic liquid crystals, acting particle-like while keeping a fully reconfigurable optical response. Tuning cell thickness against twist pitch plus waveform settings yields robust birth and programmable motion with fine placement, plus scripted paths and microparticle transport.
arxiv-2603-09150: Johann Fernandes and colleagues offer a fast way to bound orbital eccentricity in binary black hole inspirals from time-frequency data. A decade of LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA events shows no firm eccentric signal, but better detectors raise the odds of catching one. Their method collects pixel energy across eccentric harmonics, forms a likelihood, and uses energy ratios between harmonics to sharpen the estimate. On 500 test systems it pins eccentricity close to the true value within minutes.
arxiv-2603-09450: Jiyuan Lyu reframes the transformation of values problem: instead of hunting one constant solution, characterize the allocation space under constraints from the physical production network. Building an input-output model, Lyu shows that when the macroeconomy has a physical surplus, the valid skilled-to-simple labor reduction vectors form a bounded value-feasible set. Inside that region the two classical macro equalities hold together for a reasonable range of profit rates. Value law and nominal prices can then be made consistent without breaking reproduction floors.
arxiv-2603-09950: Alberto Fernández-Hernández and coauthors look for early warning signs that a PPO training run has a bad learning rate. Such runs need costly searches, since too small a rate crawls and too large a rate collapses. Their overfitting underfitting indicator reads the balance of neuron activation patterns on a fixed probe batch. Measured at a tenth of training, it already separates rate regimes, with best critics and actors sitting in distinct bands.
arxiv-2603-10150: Simone Scaringi, Christian Knigge and Domitilla de Martino write an unreview of accreting white dwarfs that dwells on open questions. These nearby, bright, purely classical systems are prime laboratories for disk accretion physics. The authors ask what drives viscosity in largely neutral disks, how strong winds launch and feed back, and why retrograde precession and magnetic bursts persist. Each unknown is paired with suggested observational, numerical and theoretical ways forward.
arxiv-2603-10750: Didrik Bergström and Onur Günlü propose deep learning for randomized distributed function computation, a framework unifying many distributed applications. Their autoencoder is trained to shrink the gap between its outputs and a target whose form is unknown, using only data samples. The designs show strong performance, with load gains over data compression methods. The work shows neural channel simulation is a practical route when common randomness is limited.
arxiv-2603-10850: Gianluca Reali and Mauro Femminella model information flows in serverless platforms with topology. They ask which parts can be fixed locally, and which persist at every scale. With Hodge decomposition, they split the flows they observe. One part can be fixed locally. The rest are harmonic modes. They argue these flows arise from how functions interact, not from configuration errors. A step-by-step method points to practical remedies. These include dumping effects that contain the harmonic inefficiencies, not a full redesign.
arxiv-2603-10950: Mira Jürgens and coauthors ask when a machine's guess should be trusted. The guess is at a molecule's structure from its mass spectrum. They also ask when it should be held back for review. Their selective prediction framework sorts annotations by risk. It compares uncertainty scores at three levels: input, fingerprint, and retrieval. The tests use a standard benchmark. Retrieval-level uncertainty proves the strongest rejection signal. Cheap first-order confidence scores remain solid baselines. Distribution-free risk control lets users set a tolerable error rate in advance.
arxiv-2603-11050: Mohammad Hadi Shekarriz, Asef Nazari, and Dhananjay Thiruvady improve the search for soft happy colourings, which flag homophilic structure in networks: vertices whose neighbors mostly share their color. The problem is NP-hard. The cross-entropy method tends to stagnate in high dimensions, so they pair it with a structure-aware local search over local optima alone. Across 28,000 synthetic block-model graphs, the hybrid beats heuristics. It matches near-optimal results on real networks far faster than an exact solver, and holds up under constraints.
arxiv-2603-11450: Carosi and co-authors build a general way to measure time irreversibility in non-Hermitian Model A field theories. A non-Hermitian term drives the dynamics and breaks time-reversal symmetry. The team works in the stochastic path-integral picture and expands in small noise. That route yields the entropy production rate and tests of the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. Near steady states, the anti-Hermitian part alone sets the local entropy rate. As a test case, a non-reciprocal Ising model shows entropy piling up at interfaces.
arxiv-2603-11750: Cavus examines whether calibration can ease predictive multiplicity, where near-equal models give one applicant clashing outcomes. Using nine credit risk data sets, he asks where the clashes pile up and whether post-hoc calibration calms it. Minority class cases carry a lopsided share of the burden, with lower confidence. Platt Scaling, Isotonic Regression, and Temperature Scaling all link to less spread across the Rashomon set. Platt and Isotonic cuts run deepest. Calibration, he argues, can act as a consensus layer for fairness.
arxiv-2603-11950: Chen and co-authors introduce SLIP, a framework for sensor models that transfer across setups. Existing sensor-language models accept only fixed channel counts at fixed sampling rates, so new devices break them. SLIP pairs contrastive alignment with sensor-conditioned captioning, reusing a pretrained language model via cross-attention. A flexible patch embedder absorbs new channel counts and rates at test time, no retraining needed. Across 11 data sets it leads on retrieval, captioning, and question answering, with 77.14% average probing accuracy.
arxiv-2603-12050: Kunilovskaya tests whether translationese grows as a sane response to a harder task. Translated text differs in steady ways from text first written in the target language. A classifier scores each segment for how translated it looks. Difficulty comes from LLM surprisal plus syntax and meaning measures, in a two-way English-German corpus. Task difficulty explains the effect only in part. Cross-lingual transfer weighs more than source complexity, and surprisal helps in written text but not in speech.
arxiv-2603-12250: Zhang and a large team present DVD, a deterministic route to video depth from diffusion priors. Generative depth models invent geometry and drift in scale, while direct ones need huge labeled sets. DVD recasts a pretrained video diffusion model as a single-pass depth regressor. The diffusion timestep serves as a structural anchor for global stability and fine detail. A latent fix restores sharp boundaries, and affine coherence enables long-video inference in one pass. Zero-shot results lead the field while using far less task data.
arxiv-2603-12350: Tseng and Lee make text-aligned speech tokenization streamable for spoken language modeling. Speech unit sequences run far longer than text tokens, a mismatch that blocks joint modeling. The earlier TASTE method aligned speech token lengths with text but leaned on an external ASR system. Its non-causal decoder also barred real-time use in practice. TASTE-S builds an ASR module based on CTC into the encoder for instant dual encoding. A redesigned decoder works on the fly, matching TASTE quality with far lower latency.
arxiv-2603-12650: Sergey Astashkin and Per Nilsson study optimal upper and lower sequence spaces for Banach lattices.
