SDLLMFuzz integrates LLM-based structure-aware seeds with static crash analysis into a feedback loop refining test inputs, generating valid inputs.
arxiv-2604-17950: Chuhan Qiao revisits multi-agent delegation, arguing that capability varies with task context rather than staying fixed per skill. Static profiles average over unlike situations and can misassign work systematically. CADMAS-CTX keeps a Beta posterior per agent, skill, and context group, then delegates by a risk-aware score combining the posterior mean with an uncertainty penalty. On GAIA with GPT-4o agents it reaches 0.442 accuracy, beating a static baseline at 0.381, and it also lifts resolve rates on SWE-bench Lite.
arxiv-2604-18150: Macedo, Wuensche, and Miranda model why quasar absorption systems in the early universe show less carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen than older models predicted. They update the cosmic star-formation rate and add intermediate-mass black holes as permanent matter sinks. Black-hole sequestration plus primordial baryon inflow can then soak up the excess. That makes black-hole accretion rates a key target for refining chemical-evolution models.
arxiv-2604-18250: Liu and ten colleagues build a vision-language framework that predicts patient survival from 3D CT scans and clinical data. Radiologist readings carry rich signals, but turning images into text summaries loses information. Visual instruction tuning on large CT collections paired with radiology reports teaches the model clinical visual-text links. A survival head on top then beats baselines, most clearly when clinical data alone predicts poorly, while also answering preset clinical questions.
arxiv-2604-18350: Kişisel and Bayraktar study the shapes of Kostlan random real algebraic plane curves via a barrier method variant. They prove the expected count of long connected components grows without bound as degree rises, and likewise for deep nests. Adapting a norm bound of Shifmann and Zelditch to subspaces, they also bound below the chance that finitely many points land in distinct components of a large-degree curve's complement.
arxiv-2604-18450: Coeurdoux, Ferré, and Bouchaud model early stopping in gradient flow with random matrix theory. Trained models often show a window where signal is detectable before overfitting dominates. In a linear teacher-student model, learning happens as a lone eigenvalue pulls away from the noisy bulk. Anisotropy in input covariance creates fast and slow learning directions, yielding a transient Baik-Ben Arous-Péché transition: the teacher spike may never emerge, persist, or flash briefly before reabsorption. Phase diagrams map these regimes, validated against finite-size simulations.
arxiv-2604-18550: Rantzer derives an exact answer for the Bellman inequality matching minimax optimal dual control. The minimizing player picks control actions from past state readings and inputs, while the rival player selects shocks and model settings for the base linear fixed-time motion. The optimal cautious policy is a dual controller trading probing against cashing in. Once enough data has been gathered, the policy becomes a fixed sure-thing rule, but when data is thin, it adds a random term to improve probing.
arxiv-2604-18850: Wang, Berthouze, and Singh introduce the Triadic Loop, a framework for alignment in AI co-hosted livestreaming. Most frameworks treat interaction as dyadic, between one user and one AI system, but livestreaming plays out among streamers and audiences in real time. The Triadic Loop recasts alignment as bidirectional adaptation among three pairs: streamer and AI co-host, AI co-host and audience, and streamer and audience. Misalignment in any sub-loop can shake the broader system, and the authors propose strategic misalignment for sustaining community engagement.
arxiv-2604-18950: Laine and six colleagues use very long baseline interferometry to search for nuclear radio emission in the barred spiral galaxy NGC 7479. Earlier arrays had shown a jet like structure plus unresolved nuclear emission. New VLBA and EVN images resolve the nuclear source into two distinct regions about 30 milliarcseconds apart. The separation appears to change over ten years, suggesting relativistic jet motion or shifting shock illumination by a nuclear wind. They also measure spectral indices and brightness temperatures for both regions.
arxiv-2604-19250: Leontaris and Shukla review their recent work on assisted fibre inflation, a string-theory model of the early universe in which a fibre modulus drives rapid expansion. A single field would need to travel a very long trans-Planckian distance, but geometric limits on the compact space usually cut that journey short and spoil the expansion plateau. Sharing the distance among several fibre fields lets inflation succeed before any one field hits its own limit.
arxiv-2604-19750: Liu and five colleagues tackle a gap in code-writing agents: debugging graphical interfaces, where text-only feedback falls short. Current agents lean on command-line outputs for multi-round debugging, yet they cannot mimic user clicks that trigger interface logic, nor judge by text alone whether a rendered screen meets user needs. The authors introduce InteractGUI Bench, a testbed of 984 real-world desktop GUI applications built to probe visual debugging.
arxiv-2604-19950: Boulton and Evans give a method to decide when families of nonlinear trajectories are linearly complete in Hilbert spaces. Their tool is an analytic block Toeplitz operator formulation. Applied to Sobolev spaces, it proves completeness for dilated Weierstrass functions and for Gross-Pitaevskii eigenfunctions in a square well. The results link classical nonlinear analysis with linear approximation theory through a general method for this concept.
arxiv-2604-20050: Galanis asks whether AI agents in prediction markets can aggregate dispersed private information and read others' knowledge from price moves. In an experiment across four information structures of increasing complexity, median markets aggregate well when structures are easy but falter when harder. Accuracy does not improve with cheap talk, longer duration, or strategic prompting, and feedback on past performance does not help. Smarter agents do better and profit more, and a later wave with frontier models aggregates more often when easy but hedges near one-half when hardest.
arxiv-2604-20350: Wang and eight colleagues present X-PCR, a benchmark for step-by-step clinical reasoning in eye diagnosis across imaging types. One task chains six reasoning stages from image quality checks to clinical decisions, while a second task fuses six imaging types. The set holds 26,415 images and 177,868 expert-checked question-answer pairs from 51 public data sets, covering 52 eye diseases. Tests on 21 models reveal wide gaps in step-by-step reasoning and cross-type fusion, showing current models fall short of clinical practice needs.
arxiv-2604-20450: López-Vázquez and two colleagues test whether the simple macrospin approximation captures the true shape of soft magnetic nanoparticles, focusing on the well known mineral magnetite. Using a superellipsoidal shape formula moving smoothly from round to cubic shapes, they compare hysteresis loops that vary with angle from micromagnetic simulations against an extended Stoner-Wohlfarth model. That model adds an effective uniaxial term from particle stretch to the intrinsic cubic crystal anisotropy. It holds roughly from 10 to 60 nanometers for axial ratios above 1.5, and from 20 to 60 for ratios between 1.0 and 1.5.
arxiv-2604-20850: Dury presents Association-Augmented Retrieval, a lightweight re-ranking method that trains an MLP to learn relationships between texts using contrastive learning on co-occurrence tags. On HotpotQA, AAR lifts passage Recall@5 from about 83 percent to about 92 percent without tuning, with gains on hard questions. An inductive model trained on training links and tested on unseen links shows no significant gain, hinting the method captures corpus-only links rather than portable patterns. The method adds about 4 ms per query and needs under two minutes of single-GPU training.
arxiv-2604-21250: Fawzi Aly, Alex Kitt, and Luke Mohr derive closed-form cooling formulas for welding and additive manufacturing, where poor heat control leaves residual stress, warping, and cracks. Older Rosenthal solutions miss finite 3D geometry, cooling, and transient effects. Their framework adds Newton-cooling boundary rules and, via Laplace transforms and Fourier series proven equivalent, solves transient and steady heat patterns for Gaussian, ellipsoidal, and switching heat sources. The formulas match numerical results closely, cut compute and test costs, and can seed synthetic data for machine learning.
arxiv-2604-21750: Buhayh and three colleagues examine what happens when recommender users can take their profile with them and pick their own algorithm apart from the platform. Earlier work suggests such choice helps niche consumers and providers. The paper asks what happens to user models when people switch algorithms and their data moves too. The effects on user benefit differ across algorithms, raising policy questions for fair recommender design.
arxiv-2604-21950: McAndrews asks whether composing small language models into pipelines can recover capability on code tasks. He studies code pipelines with execution feedback. He tests whether complex pipeline structure helps beyond a simple refinement loop. On two benchmarks, run locally on one laptop, self-refinement with execution feedback improves generation by more than 4 standard deviations. Refinement fixes many runtime errors but rarely fixes logic errors. Generator matters less than refiner capability: a 1.5 billion generator with a 3 billion refiner matches a 3 billion model doing both.
arxiv-2604-22350: Kuczkowski and Ruotsalainen recast monocular visual odometry, camera motion from a single camera, as a generative task. Most deep methods regress a single motion estimate, giving no sense of uncertainty. Their PoseFM framework uses flow matching to model motion as a distribution, turning noise into pose predictions. That design gives uncertainty estimates and robust inference in poor structure or lighting. On TartanAir, KITTI and TUM-RGBD it posts the lowest trajectory error on some sequences and ranks with the best methods.
arxiv-2604-22450: Mazumdar, Malakar and Bhuyan test late-time Rényi entropic cosmology against DESI DR2 baryon waves, clocks, standard sirens, distortions and supernova sets. They tightly constrain the Rényi parameter to about 4 times 10 to the power minus 124. Across all sets the model gives Hubble constant about 68 and matter density about 0.29, with transition at redshift under 1. Its equation of state stays quintessence-like, without crossing the phantom boundary. The model modestly improves minimum chi-squared over Lambda-CDM, but the preference is competitive, not decisive.
arxiv-2604-22750: Bai and seven colleagues run the first systematic study of token spending by AI coding agents, tracking eight frontier models on SWE-bench Verified. Agentic tasks consume a thousand times more tokens than code reasoning or chat, driven by input tokens, and repeated runs on one task can vary thirtyfold in cost. Accuracy often peaks at middling cost, and models poorly predict their own spending beforehand.
arxiv-2604-22850: Güğül, Levi, and Acar present a few-shot generative framework that synthesizes defect images for factory visual inspection when new products arrive with almost no labeled defects. It separates defect shape from background look, learning defects by masked textual inversion, generating surface-aware examples, and blending them seamlessly. Synthetic data lifts detection accuracy in few-shot tests and sharply closes the gap when defects transfer to a new surface with no real target examples.
arxiv-2604-22950: Sigari and eight colleagues measure and control spatial coherence at the Canadian Light Source using X-ray double-slit interferometry with synchrotron radiation at 7 keV. Their findings match the predicted inverse link between fringe visibility and the storage-ring coupling factor: vertical coherence rises as coupling falls. A LOCO-tuned optics model tracks how vertical beam size varies at two source points with coupling. The coupling factor is set by the closest-tune approach, with bunch-by-bunch feedback confirming the trend in beam size and visibility.
arxiv-2604-23250: Nobili and Anselmi defend the Pound-Rebka measurement of gravitational redshift against a 2024 claim that it measured only a Doppler shift from reaction forces. They argue the claim rests on a misunderstanding of reference systems plus an unphysical reading of non-gravitational forces. Restoring the experiment to its place, they re-establish the physical bases of simple but fundamental questions in gravitational physics. The paper thus answers alleged inconsistencies in the literature with a careful re-examination of frames and forces.
arxiv-2604-23550: Karan and Jha report that orbital angular momentum is not conserved in Type-I parametric down-conversion, contrary to the standard assumption behind many high-dimensional entanglement techniques. Their high-sensitivity two-photon detector reveals the effect, which they trace to a spatial walk-off and prove without the usual phase-matching approximations. The finding reopens a foundational question that Type-I conservation had long seemed to settle.
arxiv-2604-24050: Gadbail and Bamba measure the Hubble constant without using the sound horizon scale, using baryon acoustic oscillations from DESI Data Release 2. Neural network reconstructions of distance, built only from data, combine supernovae, cosmic chronometers, and DESI data through the distance duality relation. Their result agrees with local TRGB and SH0ES measures, favors a higher value than the Planck inference, and adds independent support for a real Hubble tension.
arxiv-2604-24250: Louvin and colleagues describe the French Science Center infrastructure in the SVOM French ground segment. The cloud-based platform gives the French community single access to SVOM data and is the only ground link to the SVOM VHF network for near-time satellite communication. Pipelines in the platform automatically produce high-level data and broadcast alerts widely. Software running around the clock relies on micro-services, containerization, infrastructure-as-code, and continuous integration and deployment. The paper details design, ingestion, archiving, and processing, plus availability, volume, and speed.
arxiv-2604-24450: Fatima and five colleagues study reviewer-bot feedback on agentic pull requests in GitHub projects. Analyzing 7,416 bot comments on 4,532 pull requests, they find comments focus on bug fixes, testing, and documentation, are civil and prescriptive. Bots give clear, concise feedback, though relevance to code changes is moderate. Higher bot activity volume links to longer resolution times and lower feedback quality, as more comments dilute pertinence. Feedback quality shows no meaningful link to workflow outcomes, suggesting bots should favor targeted high-relevance feedback over sheer volume.
arxiv-2604-24650: Fuchs and Schönauer prove that no k-th power Diophantine triples of the form {a^k, b, c} exist. The result holds when k is at least 3 and the entries satisfy 1 < a^k < b < c. The result is a non-existence theorem for this restricted family. It rules out every candidate in the stated range, closing the case for triples whose first entry is a k-th power above one.
arxiv-2604-24750: Xie, Yu, Xiong and Xue seek spectral evidence for heavy nuclei in magnetar bursts, to probe the composition of a neutron star's outer crust. They build a framework for radiative transfer in a strongly magnetized electron-ion thermal plasma and apply it to observed X-ray burst spectra. The fits disfavor light-ion compositions, favoring instead plasmas whose effective charge numbers sit around 37. The results suggest heavy nuclei take part in magnetar bursts, constrain the baryonic content and fireball location, and point to a crustal origin for the heavy ions.
arxiv-2604-24850: Roy, Sen, Sen and Sengupta study a driven Rydberg atom chain. They identify drive protocols giving prethermal Bethe integrability at special values. They give a perturbative expression for its Floquet Hamiltonian at large amplitude. They show leading-term integrability at special values via the XXZ chain. Exact diagonalization on finite chains supports the analysis. Level statistics, entanglement entropy and magnetization show integrable nature at those values. It persists to a large prethermal time.
arxiv-2604-25050: Wang and six colleagues propose DiscreteRTC, discrete diffusion policies as natural async executors. Discrete diffusion policies make actions by unmasking. Inpainting is native to them, so no fine-tuning is needed, and early stopping adds adaptive help. DiscreteRTC replaces outside corrections with native unmasking. On dynamic simulated benchmarks and real handling tasks, it beats continuous chunking and other baselines. It needs no extra code. It uses about 0.7 times the compute of fresh generation. It raises success by 65 percent in a real-world hockey defend task.
arxiv-2604-25150: Sareen and four colleagues study how symmetry helps optimize networks with far more parameters than needed. Extra parameters add weight-space symmetries that help in two ways. First, they precondition the Hessian diagonally, so each class of functionally identical solutions holds a better-conditioned minimum. Second, they raise the share of global minima near typical starting points, so good solutions are easier to reach. Tests confirm wider networks converge faster with smaller condition numbers.
arxiv-2604-25250: Cheng and three colleagues study triangle packings in perturbed graphs. The Nash-Williams conjecture asserts triangle-divisible graphs of high minimum degree admit triangle decompositions; Frankl and Rödl showed random graphs contain near-perfect packings. They prove that for every positive density and every probability above a threshold, the union of a regular and a random graph contains a near-perfect packing with high probability. Moreover, this bound is best possible for small densities, settling the threshold. A new triangle-weighting lemma is a key ingredient.
arxiv-2604-25650: Mughees and five colleagues propose a human-in-the-loop approach for black-box testing of Functional Mock-up Units with language models. The approach feeds functional and interface specifications to a language model, which generates scenario goals in Given-When-Then form, plus input patterns and assertion oracles. The approach generates a full input time series, runs the FMU simulation, and evaluates assertions on outputs. Tests on a Lube Oil Cooling system suggest language-model-assisted generation can ease test design and verification.
arxiv-2604-26050: Arab, Khaleghi, and Aslansefat present a verification framework for evasive moves in autonomous cars. It unifies hazard-risk study, system-theoretic study, and state machine modeling. Hazard-loss mapping finds hazards and unsafe actions; a state layer captures the transitions neither method models. A T-junction study runs 1,880 cases across speed, time-to-collision, and friction. Steering reaches 81 percent avoidance and cuts mean impact speed from about 19 to 9 km per hour versus braking alone. Hazards, actions, and parameters are fully covered.
arxiv-2604-26250: Guo and six colleagues proposed Structured Qualitative Inference, a training-free method that steadies frozen vision-language models against optical illusions. It injects logical constraints, splits scenes into target and background, and checks claims against counterfactuals, curbing the shortcuts that make models trust words over what they see. The approach placed second in a 2026 illusion-understanding challenge.
arxiv-2604-26450: Tekden and three colleagues introduced phase-varying neural potential functions for robot learning from demonstration. First-order dynamical systems fail where paths cross, since one state must give one velocity, while second-order and phase methods each carry their own fragility. Their framework estimates phase from state progression rather than open-loop time, letting the system revisit states while a learned potential shapes local vector fields. It generalized across point-to-point, periodic, and full six-dimensional tasks and stayed robust under disturbances.
arxiv-2604-26550: Calandriello, Lazaric, and Valko introduced Sparse-HFS, a scalable algorithm for large-scale semi-supervised learning, where few labeled examples join many unlabeled ones. It solves such problems using only near-linear space and time, with polylogarithmic overhead factors. The method makes massive graph-based learning tractable without storing or processing the full dense graph. Its efficiency opens semi-supervised learning to web-scale problems.
arxiv-2604-26750: Otaki and six colleagues model early dust enrichment from core-collapse supernovae. JWST observations show flat ultraviolet curves and weak bumps in galaxies above redshift 7. They track grain sizes and dimming curves across parent stars, spins, metals, and densities. Dust-to-stellar mass ratio reaches about a thousandth at 30 million years before the reverse shock, but at most about a hundred-thousandth after it. The shock destroys grains under 10 nm, leaves glassy carbon on top, and flattens the dimming curve with a wide 2500-angstrom bump.
arxiv-2604-26850: Kühnle and fourteen colleagues present JWST spectra of COCONUTS-2b, one of the coldest known planet-mass companions, seen with the mid-infrared tool MIRI. They pair those spectra with old Gemini data and run air retrievals at full spectral detail to hunt faint molecular signs. They firmly detect three isotopologues, rare forms of ammonia and water, giving the first clear sign of oxygen isotopes in water on such a cold companion. The pinned-down element and isotope ratios open a path to tracing how the companion formed.
arxiv-2604-27250: Marripour and Abouie study early-time quasi-crystal-like order in a chain of non-interacting spin-1/2 particles driven by two parts. The drive switches disordered Ising interactions and a rotating transverse field on and off at a frequency whose ratio to the field frequency is irrational. That yields incommensurate frequencies and dynamics beyond Floquet theory. Exact diagonalization of time patterns, changing structure factors, and entanglement entropy reveals the quasi-crystal-like order in the early-time regime.
arxiv-2604-27450: Han, Lee, and Kang propose RAY-TOLD, a controller that helps mobile robots navigate dense, dynamic crowds where reactive planners stall in local minima. Their LiDAR-centred latent model compresses sensor data into a state, supporting a learned terminal value function and policy prior. A policy-mixture strategy adds trajectories from the policy to the planner's candidate set, guiding it toward the goal while keeping motion feasible. In tests with dense dynamic obstacles, the method beats the MPPI baseline and reduces collisions, showing that learned long horizon intent improves safety.
arxiv-2604-27750: Batista and six colleagues show steady, smooth control of harmonic helicity in solids using crafted light beams. Two crossed pulses with a set time delay drive each harmonic's shape from linear to circular, for any material. The effect holds across systems with distinct symmetry and form and comes from fast shifts of light-matter link through dipole action. The cross setup also breaks motion symmetry, making banned harmonics, so helicity becomes a field-set sign rather than a material mark.
arxiv-2604-27850: Ijurco and Lopez de Lacalle propose unimodal test-time reasoning letting language models reason over object metadata and dialogue history for coreference resolution. Results on SIMMC 2.1 show that LLMs can build step-by-step reasoning matching dialogue context to scene objects. Experiments show the models link chats and objects. Test-time reasoning under few-shot settings spreads to unseen scenarios and novel objects, beating supervised methods cross-domain. These findings stress the role of structured metadata and careful prompts in dialogue system robustness and generalization.
arxiv-2604-28050: Joshi and Mishra ask whether a smooth black hole horizon can hide its microstates. At fixed classical data, exterior distinguishability and departure from perfect infall obey a tight trade-off, and every point on its boundary can occur. Below maximal disruption, reaching the boundary requires measuring which state fell in, so the least a horizon can do to carry microstate hair is measure its infall.
arxiv-2604-28150: Lam and Nguyen map how long the SIRS epidemic process survives across network shapes. On finite sparse graphs they prove a regime of exponentially long survival, and on heavy-tailed networks survival stays exponential for all parameter ranges. For infinite trees they give conditions for strong survival, where the root is reinfected infinitely often even for light-tailed degree distributions such as Poisson.
arxiv-2605-00150:
Sergey Pirogov and Elena Zhizhina study non-local operators that arise in models of population growth and death in continuous space. They look at what happens when a steady birth-and-death process faces a repeating pattern of extra mortality. The birth pattern in their model may be uneven and may favor some directions over others.

The authors prove that any such negative, repeating disturbance pushes the operator's spectrum into the left half-plane. In the language of the model, that shift means the added mortality drives the population to extinction, in any spatial dimension. The result gives a clean test for when a periodic pattern of suppression is enough to end a population that would otherwise persist.
arxiv-2605-00250:
Yuhui Lu, Wenjing Liu, and Kun Zhan rethink how diffusion models for graphs choose their sampling steps. Standard samplers advance in uniform time steps, ignoring that a distribution can change fast at one stage and slowly at another. The authors view the sampling path as a curve on a curved statistical surface, where distance is measured by the Fisher-Rao metric.

From that geometry they derive the Drift Variation Score, which tracks how fast the distribution is changing at each moment. Their solver keeps the informational speed constant, so every step does an equal share of the work. Tests on molecule and social network generation show better structural fidelity and faster sampling than uniform stepping. The theory also confirms the score captures the local stiffness of the process.
arxiv-2605-01050:
Zach Shahn and Mats Stensrud examine when physician discretion can beat trial-average recommendations in medicine. Trials usually target average treatment effects, but decisions are made for individuals, so a treatment that helps on average may be wrong for a particular patient. The authors consider settings where randomized and observational data from the same population estimate average outcomes under treat all, treat none, and usual care.

They derive sharp bounds on the share of encounters where physicians' personal strategies outperform the better of treat all or treat none. The bound assumes no physician does worse than always choosing the worse of those two. The results clarify when clinical data support relying on physician discretion and when stronger justification is required.
arxiv-2605-01250:
Sai Ma and six co-authors present EO-Gym, an interactive environment for Earth observation agents that mirrors how analysts actually work. Real analysis often requires expanding a region, retrieving historical observations, and switching between optical and radar sensors, while most benchmarks collapse the process into fixed-input, single-turn tasks. EO-Gym formulates analysis as a local geospatial workspace backed by a large indexed file collection and dozens of specialized tools.

On that environment they build a benchmark dataset with thousands of trajectories and reasoning steps grounded in public datasets and satellite imagery. Ten vision-language models still struggle with interactive reasoning, especially temporal and cross-modal workflows. A fine-tuned small model improves the main pass rate substantially, providing a reference baseline.
arxiv-2605-01350:
Koshiro Saito, Ryuto Koike, Masahiro Kaneko, and Naoaki Okazaki ask whether machine-written text can be made easy to detect without making it worse. Watermarks can flag such text, but they often lower quality on real tasks.

Their framework, PUPPET, fine-tunes a model with feedback from two judges: a detector that scores how machine-like the text looks, and an evaluator that scores task quality. Like a watermark key, the detector is specific to the provider, who can then trace use of the model. On long answers, summaries, and essays, tuned models match watermark detection rates, even under strict false-alarm limits, while beating watermarks on task scores. The tuning needs only a few thousand samples and one to two hours of graphics time, and the gains survive new tasks, new detectors, and paraphrase attacks.
arxiv-2605-01450:
Panagiotis P Filntisis and five co-authors predict 3D face meshes from several camera views at once, with every point on the mesh meaning the same facial spot across people. Automated methods exist, but they learn from training faces that were registered by slow hand pipelines, the very cost they aim to cut.

Their framework, MOCHI, trains with no registered faces at all. A pseudo-linear solver keeps the mesh shape consistent, and dense keypoints from a landmark tool trained only on synthetic faces guide the match. The team also swap the usual point-to-surface loss for pointmap and normal losses, which train more smoothly and rebuild faces more cleanly in this setting. A short test-time tune of the network closes much of the gap to hand pipelines, and final scores beat the classic labor-heavy route on both accuracy and looks.
arxiv-2605-01950:
Siyuan Duan, Ke Zhang, and Xizhao Luo show how a world model used for planning can be attacked through the ranking of imagined futures. World models let agents look ahead by generating and scoring paths, but shallow attacks on single steps often fade inside that process. The authors find a deeper weakness in the long-tailed ranking of those imagined paths.

Their attack, TRAP, focuses loss on the few paths that matter most for a decision, aiming to reorder them and hijack the plan. It pairs that tail-aware loss with other steps described in the paper. The work frames ranking itself as a security surface that builders of planning agents need to guard.
arxiv-2605-02050:
Christopher Kelly and colleagues set out principles and guidelines for randomised controlled trials that evaluate artificial intelligence. Such trials, also called human uplift studies, test whether a tool truly helps people, but the field lacks shared standards. The authors draw on trial practice from software, economics, health, and psychology to build a common frame.

They synthesise five principles from validity and open-science standards on transparency, repeatability, and verification. Those principles support thirty-three actionable guidelines, each given as a requirement with a rationale, steps, and evidence. The set is meant as a design tool for new studies, a rubric for judging past work, and a blueprint as field norms settle.
arxiv-2605-02250:
Declan Frawley, Dmitri Vainchtein, Anton Artemyev, and Vassilis Angelopoulos work to recover full whistler-mode wave data from the THEMIS mission after a sensor fault. Whistler waves in Earth's magnetosphere accelerate and scatter energetic electrons, linking the magnetosphere and ionosphere. THEMIS gathered one of the longest near-equatorial records of such waves from 2008 onward.

After 2017, search-coil magnetometers on two THEMIS spacecraft lost the spin-axis component and could detect only spin-plane components. That cut the ability to find total wave amplitude. The authors reconstruct magnetic field spectra from electric field and plasma measurements instead. Restoring those years matters for studies that need long, consistent wave records across the outer radiation belt and magnetotail.
arxiv-2605-02450:
Luiz Carlos Pereira, Victor Barroso-Nascimento, and Elaine Pimentel revisit Glivenko's classic theorems, which link classical logic and intuitionistic logic. Those results showed that certain claims provable in one system map to claims provable in the other. The authors view the theorems through ecumenical logic, a frame that lets both styles of logic sit in one shared system.

Their study works through three such systems. One is Prawitz's natural deduction system, one is a close relative of a system by Krauss that was never published, and one is a newer system proposed by Barroso-Nascimento. For each, they trace how Glivenko's results extend or change. The paper serves readers in logic who track how old bridge theorems behave in mixed settings.
arxiv-2605-02650:
Yang Tian identifies a gap between what a transport model says and what thermodynamic measurements can reveal. Markovian transport is usually summed up by a master equation for the system's state. Yet experiments measure records resolved by reservoir: particle and heat currents, entropy production, and current noise. A state equation alone, Tian argues, may not fix those records.

The test system is a small quantum dot linked to several energy-filtered reservoirs. Different assignments of channels to reservoirs can produce the exact same state equation, with identical occupation behavior and linear response, while giving different heat currents, entropy, and noise. Tian states a completeness criterion: a quantity can be rebuilt from state dynamics only if it is unchanged under all such reassignments. The criterion doubles as a practical check on models.
arxiv-2605-02850:
Yixian Qiu and three co-authors introduce a new loss function for variational quantum algorithms, the near-term workhorse methods for quantum devices. Their known bottleneck is trainability: expressive circuits often hit barren plateaus, flat regions where training signals vanish. Standard goals, based on plain expectation values, do little to reshape that landscape.

The Quantum Tilted Loss generalizes a classical exponential tilting trick to the operator level. One continuous parameter sharpens the landscape, can amplify gradient signals in structured cases, and keeps the true best solutions in place. The theory unifies plain expectation goals with tunable heuristics already in use. A formal trade-off follows: stronger tilting moves the bottleneck from flatness to the cost of estimating nonlinear gradients from limited quantum measurements.
arxiv-2605-02950:
Mohit Kumar, Somayeh Kargaran, Bernhard A. Moser, and Manuela Geiß ask whether a heavy neural model still needs to encode every search query. Their Kernel Affine Hull Machine offers a much lighter encoder for cases where a strong teacher model and a fixed index already exist.

The method estimates the teacher vector from cheap word features, using cluster weights and refined prototype vectors, with no backpropagation. On an Austrian law test with five thousand queries, it gave the best retrieval among matched learned adapters and ran far faster per query than direct transformer encoding on the reported setup.
arxiv-2605-03050:
Rose Sathyanathan, Kinshuk Vasisht, and Danish Pruthi test whether reasoning models handle questions built on false assumptions better than standard models. Users often ask questions that presume something untrue, and models tend to go along instead of pushing back.

The team built queries with graded false premises across health, science, and general knowledge and tested widely used models. Reasoning models scored only slightly higher and still let a large share of false premises pass unchallenged, from about a quarter to over two fifths of cases. Stronger wording of the false premise also made models less likely to resist.
arxiv-2605-03450:
Brielen Madureira, Mariana Madruga de Brito, and Andreas Niekler test topic models as binary classifiers for finding news about extreme climate events in German media. Labeled data are often too scarce to train deep classifiers, while topic models are unsupervised and readable but normally used only to explore data.

Using topic posterior scores to select documents, without retraining the models, they refine retrieval for seven hazard types. Keyword probability information improved precision, and results were compared with an embedding classifier and an open language model, which had the lowest precision. Performance varied by hazard, arguing against one pooled climate category.
arxiv-2605-03650:
Zhiyuan Li and five co-authors rethink how video object-centric learning keeps track of objects over time. The standard approach trains dynamics modules to predict future object representations, called slots. The authors argue these predictors are costly approximations of a simpler discrete matching problem: matching objects between frames.

Modern self-supervised vision backbones already encode features that tell instances apart, so prediction can be replaced by matching. Their Grounded Correspondence framework starts slots from salient regions in frozen backbone features and keeps identity through Hungarian matching, with no learnable parameters for time modeling. It still achieves competitive performance on the MOVi-D, MOVi-E, and YouTube-VIS benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-03750:
Marco Mustafa Mohammed, Fatemeh Daneshfar, and Pietro Liò introduce Gated Evidential Mixtures, a family of models that estimates uncertainty in a single forward pass. Evidential deep learning predicts Dirichlet evidence to express uncertainty, but it can stay overconfident and miss multimodal uncertainty about what the model does not know. Their design adds an internal energy signal that gates the evidence.

GEM-CORE learns a feature-level energy and maps it to a bounded gate that suppresses evidence when support is low. GEM-MIX adds a mixture of evidential heads with learned routing, and GEM-FI stabilizes the mixture with a Fisher-informed regularizer. Across image classification and out-of-distribution detection, the models improved calibration and separation; on CIFAR-10 the full version raised accuracy and sharply lowered Brier score.
arxiv-2605-04050:
Clint Ehrlich and Theodore Blackman introduce Lossless Context Management, a deterministic architecture for language model memory aimed at long-context coding tasks. Their LCM-augmented coding agent, Volt, is benchmarked against Claude Code using Opus 4.6 on the OOLONG long-context evaluation. The authors report higher scores at every context length tested. The lengths run from thirty-two thousand to one million tokens.

LCM extends the recursive paradigm of Recursive Language Models. It splits symbolic recursion into two engine-managed mechanisms. The first is recursive context compression. A hierarchical summary graph compacts older messages while keeping lossless pointers to every original. The second is recursive task partitioning. Engine-managed parallel primitives replace model-written loops. The trade-off sacrifices maximal flexibility for termination guarantees, zero-cost continuity on short tasks, and lossless retrieval of earlier context.
arxiv-2605-04750:
Yasod Ginige and five co-authors tackle vehicle re-identification from thermal images, the task of recognising the same vehicle across cameras when only heat signatures are available. Thermal images lack colour, objects of a class look highly alike, texture is muted, and changing viewpoints alter which features are visible.

Their method builds feature vectors conditioned on viewpoint. It compares area-specific features in separate spaces. That lets them reuse powerful extractors pretrained on ordinary colour images, while adapting to heat imagery. The team tests on two data sets. One is a public infrared vehicle set. The other is a thermal maritime set they collected. On both, the system beat prior state-of-the-art results by large margins in average precision.
arxiv-2605-05150:
Halil Mutuk studies two predicted tetraquarks, exotic particles made of a heavy antiquark pair and a light quark pair, sitting near a key decay threshold. Working in the dynamical diquark model, he treats them as a heavy antidiquark bound to a light diquark through a potential taken from lattice calculations. Solving the radial Schrödinger equation then gives their masses and internal spacing.

Mutuk finds one state essentially at the threshold, allowing either a weakly decaying bound state or a narrow near-threshold structure. The other lies between two nearby thresholds, making it a natural resonance candidate whose shape should respond to the closer one. The spacing results support a compact diquark picture for both.
arxiv-2605-05250:
Yuan-Chi Li and four co-authors build a user simulator for testing chat-based recommender systems that pauses, the way real shoppers do. Testing sales agents needs such tools, but language-model versions process information far too well and almost never defer a decision, so yes rates come out too high. Their framework, Hesitator, models the inner choice process in detail.

A choice module separates choosing an item by utility from locking in under choice overload. Across test setups, domains, sales modes, and model families, adding the module curbed unreal behaviour as choice load grew. Hesitator also matched known patterns from psychological economics, backing its realism.
arxiv-2605-05550:
A defective coloring lets each vertex share its color with a few neighbors, relaxing the classic coloring rule. Shamil Asgarli, Tamsen Whitehead McGinley, and Nicholas Xue ask how much a graph's structure is fixed by counting such colorings at every defect level. The counts form a family of defective chromatic polynomials.

They prove a contraction formula that writes these counts through ordinary chromatic polynomials. For triangle-free graphs, the family determines the degree sequence. For trees it fixes short path counts but not longer ones, and they build pairs of distinct trees that share every defective polynomial.
arxiv-2605-05650:
Galaxies blow gas outward, and different spectral lines tell different stories about that wind. Antonia Fernández-Figueroa and four co-authors compare emission and absorption tracers in three clumpy star-forming galaxies. They used the LRIS spectrograph on Keck to map the galaxies region by region.

Magnesium absorption showed outflows moving near 560 kilometers per second, while hydrogen emission traced only about 124. Both tracers, though, rose and fell together with galaxy properties like star formation rate, offset by a roughly constant factor. The comparison clarifies what each tracer actually measures: fast diffuse gas versus slower dense gas.
arxiv-2605-06050:
Yingxu Wang and seven co-authors build brain network learning that survives a move to unseen scanning sites. Graph methods on brain imaging data often degrade across sites, since site effects can mask disease linked connection patterns. Static connectivity maps also miss informative variation within a single scan, the authors note.

Their framework, CORE, first estimates each site's confounder effects and combines corrections by cross source reliability. It extracts a shared scaffold of reproducible, label linked connections, then adds compact descriptors of how those links vary during a scan. Adaptive gating balances group priors with each subject's own pattern. In leave one site out tests on four data sets, CORE beat rival methods, with accuracy gains up to 10.3 percent.
arxiv-2605-06350:
Dylan Bouchard asks how deep a cascade of language models should go before escalation stops paying. Cascades let a cheap model defer hard queries to pricier ones, cutting inference cost, but practitioners must pick the pool size and every deferral threshold by feel. Bouchard derives first order optimality conditions showing that, at an optimum, the ratio of expected accuracy gain to expected downstream cost equalizes across every deferral boundary in the chain.

A local search on those conditions nearly matches exhaustive search. Experiments across five benchmarks, with thresholds optimized over pools of eight models, show two model cascades beating single model selection clearly. Adding a third or deeper model helped in almost none of the comparisons, and by a sliver when it did. Simulated scores show depth gains hinge on whether the confidence score reflects difficulty shared across models.
arxiv-2605-06650:
Mingwei Xu and Hao Fang propose POPO, a training method that improves language model reasoning by learning only from successful attempts. Standard verifiable-reward training also penalizes failed rollouts, but failures carry no grading of severity, and sampling a few negatives barely dents the vast space of wrong answers under sparse binary rewards. POPO therefore trains exclusively on positive rollouts.

Bounded importance sampling over the positive set lets implicit negative pressure emerge as good answers gain probability. A Siamese network with momentum updates and a bounded similarity penalty stabilizes training. Across math benchmarks POPO beats the GRPO baseline, including a clear margin on the AIME 2025 contest set.
arxiv-2605-06850:
Rui Zhu and five co-authors address a memory wall that hits reinforcement learning post-training of language models on long-context reasoning tasks. Online training must first generate exploratory rollouts, and the key-value cache for long contexts consumes enormous memory. Compressing that cache during rollouts helps, but it creates a mismatch: the sampler acts on a sparse context while the learner updates on the full one, and tiny errors amplify badly.

Standard fixes like importance reweighting suffer high variance and poor sample efficiency under that amplified bias. The paper proposes shadow mask distillation as its answer for memory-efficient alignment, targeting the sampler-learner gap directly rather than correcting it statistically after the fact.
arxiv-2605-07550:
Grzegorz Wilczynski and four co-authors take on three-dimensional reconstruction when the available photos do not overlap at all. Ordinary methods need shared views to align images, so crowd-sourced photos or robot swarm footage with disjoint viewpoints break them. The team defines this zero-overlap task, builds a dataset for it, and proposes scoring metrics.

Their framework, GLADOS, first uses generative models to synthesize in-between views that bridge the disjoint inputs. It then builds a coarse three-dimensional scaffold by global alignment, and finally expands and cleans the result for consistency. On their benchmarks, leading existing methods failed badly on this task. GLADOS is modular, so better generative or reconstruction parts can be swapped in later.
arxiv-2605-07750:
Yinrong Li and seven co-authors tackle the simulation problem behind designing many-core AI accelerators. Cycle-accurate hardware simulation is far too slow for systems like their TeraNoC target, with over a thousand cores and a shared scratchpad memory. Yet performance estimates must capture latency-sensitive interconnect behavior precisely.

Their approach tracks the timing of scratchpad reads across chip link scales while leaving out inessential detail. Against a cycle-accurate gold model it stayed within seven percent error across benchmarks while running up to one hundred fifteen times faster. Close tracking across cores and links guided two case studies: speeding up FlashAttention-2 to cut stalls, and moving network-on-chip routers to rebalance traffic. The framework supports both software work and hardware design search.
arxiv-2605-07850:
Ionut-Vlad Modoranu and two co-authors remove the rank-guessing problem from LoRA, the standard low-rank method for fine-tuning large models cheaply. LoRA's rank must be fixed in advance, and finding a good one takes exhaustive search. Rank-adaptive variants sample ranks during training but learn the high ranks poorly, because gradient signals are inconsistent across the hierarchy.

Their MatryoshkaLoRA inserts a fixed, carefully crafted diagonal matrix between the LoRA factors so every sub-rank receives the gradient information efficiently, nesting ranks like the dolls the method is named for. Rank can then be chosen dynamically with minimal accuracy loss. They also propose a metric, the area under the rank-accuracy curve, and show better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs than earlier adaptive methods.
arxiv-2605-08050:
Xinyan Ye, Jiankang Deng, and Abbas Edalat present a system for generating talking-head videos with fine control. A good result must match identity, head pose, expression, and mouth motion at once. Earlier systems handled only some of these factors and mixed control signals with fixed weights, which lets the signals interfere.

MoCoTalk is a video diffusion framework that combines a reference image, facial keypoints, rendered shading meshes, and speech audio. An adaptive router sets channel-wise gates that change with the noise level, so each signal leads where it helps most. A mouth-augmented mesh separates head, mouth, expression, and lighting, giving steady geometry for speech-driven motion.
arxiv-2605-08150:
Jonathan Bates releases a PyTorch library that turns Turing machine descriptions into neural networks. The built networks run the machines exactly, with no training at all. Given a transition function and a set of end states, the package builds a model. One forward pass of that model performs one machine step.

Two designs are included. One is a transformer based on a 2021 result by Wei, Chen, and Ma. The other is a recurrent network based on 1995 work by Siegelmann and Sontag. It hides its stack in a Cantor set. Bates builds the pieces from first principles. He shows how ReLU units form logic gates and adders. He also shows how hard attention looks up tape positions.
arxiv-2605-08250:
Xiaoce Wang, Sifan Zhou, Kaifei Wang, Leli Xu, and coauthors explain a slow failure. Repeated image edits with diffusion transformers drift over time. Each round adds a small semantic drift. After several turns, the picture no longer matches the user's intent. Single edits still look fine.

The authors split the pipeline into its VAE and transformer parts. The transformer injects mostly low-frequency drift in latent space. The VAE adds a steadier reconstruction bias. Their fix, VAE-LFA, needs no training. It low-pass filters the latent gap between rounds. It aligns low-frequency statistics to a moving average of past rounds. That damps the drift where it forms.
arxiv-2605-08450:
Maxwell Jacobson and Yexiang Xue teach agents new long tasks from demonstrations of other tasks. Imitation learning works when experts show the exact job, but collecting demonstrations for every task is unaffordable, and small errors snowball over long action sequences when the agent improvises.

Their ZALT method maps the demonstration set into a latent topology. It finds hub states where trajectories converge or split, learns local policies and a dynamics model for hub-to-hub hops, and then plans across that hub graph. An unseen start and goal can be connected through hubs the demonstrations did visit, which turns a fixed dataset into zero-shot solutions for long-horizon tasks beyond those shown.
arxiv-2605-08550:
Vincent Guan, Lazar Atanackovic, and Kirill Neklyudov propose learning how whole populations move by borrowing from classical mechanics. Flows that only lower free energy miss patterns like cycles, seen in molecules, cells, and animal groups. Their framework treats population motion as second order dynamics under a damped action principle, covering classical, quantum, and gradient systems in one view.

Their algorithm learns the hidden mechanics directly from snapshots over time, with no preset energy law. It forecasts and fills in unseen stages, beating flow based methods on vortex motion, embryo growth, and flocking tests. Population modeling gains a richer language for motion that loops, swings, and carries momentum.
arxiv-2605-08650:
Huiqian Lai and EunJeong Cheon study how Chinese women experience an AI boyfriend on the Soul social app. Millions of mostly young women form romantic ties with the companion called With-you. Through interviews with sixteen users, content review, and the researchers' own use, the study traces how these bonds form and strain.

Constant availability and freedom from judgment draw users in, yet three tensions follow. Instant confessions and pet names clash with cultural hopes for slow growing romance, memory slips and moderation breed doubt instead of safety, and keeping the bond alive demands repair work from women. Design lessons include consent aware pacing, user controlled memory, and clear moderation rules.
arxiv-2605-08750:
Emanuele Rossi and Emanuele Rodolà send sound through plain English. Words can prompt audio tools or talk about sound. Here words carry the sound itself. Their plan pairs two trained agents. The sender studies a wave and writes code for it. It uses a shared list of sound traits. The words it sends are the code. The receiver reads the words and builds the wave back. It refines the build in a loop.

The sent text is both a rich note and the truck that hauls the sound. Folks can read it and edit it. The plan trades list size, rate, and truth to source. Tests on short sounds and written music show real sound shape makes the trip.
arxiv-2605-08850:
Peter Richtárik, Kaja Gruntkowska, and Hanmin Li set out Broximal Gradient Descent, a bound task plan that needs no cast back step. The cast back step of its kin plan can cost a lot, or sit ill with hard bound sets. BroxGD swaps it for a brox step. Each step finds the best of a flat guess score. The hunt stays in the bound set, cut with a ball round the live point. The ball's size is set by rule.

The team builds a wide proof of its pace, cross many task kinds and size rules. Toy cases show how it moves. Bound work gains a plan whose steps stay in bounds by build.
arxiv-2605-08950:
Wicaksono Leksono Muhamad and four coauthors rate how hard words feel to folks who learn a new tongue. Their home tongues are not the same. Plain fit work grades with one score per word. It leaves the word space with no shape. Cross tongue links and the step like rank of hard are missed. Their plan pairs a ridge fit team with two match aims. One aim lines up views of a word across text. One aim keeps the soft rank of hard in place.

On three home tongue sets, the match aims lift cross tongue line up. They keep each tongue's own feel. The learned space holds the rank of hard. The team smooths each model's bent, for more firm scores at all grades.
arxiv-2605-09150:
Vlad Murgoci, Matthijs Spaan, and Yaniv Oren present AlphaExploitem, a poker agent built to profit from weak opponents rather than merely play a safe equilibrium strategy. Their 2026 system extends an earlier reinforcement learning agent, AlphaHoldem, with a layered transformer encoder that can reason over hands played earlier. Training also changes: the agent faces a diverse pool of opponents whose play can be exploited.

Poker is an imperfect information game, long used to test choices under uncertainty, and simply matching Nash equilibrium play caps how much an agent can win. The authors train and test on two standard benchmarks for such games. Their agent successfully exploits weak play from opponents both inside and outside its training pool, while holding its performance against equilibrium opponents. The result shows an agent can learn when to depart from safe play without giving up its footing against strong rivals.
arxiv-2605-09250:
Chen, Cao, and Jing compute gravitational wave fluxes for generic Kerr orbits, using a unified confluent Heun function setup. Extreme mass ratio inspiral modelling needs such fluxes, but standard frequency domain methods suffer costly parameter searches and failures in strong field or high frequency regimes. Angular and radial Teukolsky equations, recast with confluent Heun functions, plus hybrid analytic continuation for coefficients, remove auxiliary parameter dependence, yielding globally convergent solutions and scattering amplitudes.

An adaptive bi-power mapping quadrature handles highly oscillatory source terms for generic orbits. Standard tests show errors near 10 to the minus 11 for total flux over 168 low order modes, with costs cut 3 to 13 fold against GeneralizedSasakiNakamura and pybhpt. For highly oscillatory modes, the setup speeds up to 60 times over special oscillatory integrators, giving a solid tool for strong field theory, high order self force work, and rapid waveform generation.
arxiv-2605-09650:
Sarafian and four colleagues ask what stays trainable when an agent on a frontier model cannot change its weights. Their answer is the workspace, the structured outside store the agent reads, writes, and tests. Its evolution is called workspace optimization. It targets hard multi turn tasks where a strong model cannot solve in one shot. The method mirrors weight training. Artifacts stand in for parameters, evidence for data, counterexamples for losses, and text feedback for gradients.

They build the idea in DreamTeam, a multi agent testbed for ARC-AGI-3. Its roles build a runnable world model, plan, probe, and route failures. On the 25 game public set under official scoring, averaged over two runs, DreamTeam lifts the matched state of the art score from 36 percent to about 38 percent. It uses 31 percent fewer environment actions per game. Workspace evolution offers a principled path to agentic learning with no weight access.
arxiv-2605-09950:
Li and four co-authors speed up Boruta, a feature-picking method that ranks which factors matter in wide data. Wrapper methods like Boruta are accurate but slow on CPUs, which limits them on large data sets. The paper offers two graphics-processor versions: Boruta-Permut, based on permutation importance, and Boruta-TreeImp, based on impurity reduction in trees.

Tests on a self-built data set and several public ones show large efficiency gains with selection hit rate close to the first Boruta. One caution emerged: the impurity-reduction version can overstate the importance of some features. Overall, the authors present GPU Boruta as an effective, cost-efficient route to feature selection at large scale, especially for scientific data with many correlated variables.
arxiv-2605-10350:
Qihao Peng and colleagues model a subtle noise source in a new kind of wireless receiver. Rydberg atomic receivers turn radio signals into optical responses via atomic energy levels, promising high sensitivity, broad tuning, and compact front ends. Their 2026 paper builds a complex baseband model for superheterodyne Rydberg receivers, capturing signal-dependent shot noise from photodetection.

The model covers both direct incoherent optical detection and balanced coherent detection. It shows that the optical setting jointly sets receive gain and noise floor. Ignoring that noise, the authors warn, can mislead operating-point design. Extending to MIMO systems, they derive a lower bound on achievable rate with that noise included. Simulations back the analysis and yield closed-form design rules, revealing regimes where Rydberg MIMO beats conventional radio systems.
arxiv-2605-10450:
Julian Britten and Jan Henry Belz make the case for repair as a central topic in personal fabrication research. Through the right-to-repair movement and supporting legislation, attitudes are shifting in favor of repairing. Yet fabrication research rarely makes repair its main focus. Their 2026 CHI workshop paper argues that repair-centered research is timely, relevant, and impactful.

The authors define repair as a five-step process: identifying the issue, exploring solutions, acquiring materials, performing the repair, and testing. For each step they discuss challenges and opportunities researchers could pursue. The backdrop is stark: products grow more complex, spare parts are often unavailable, and designs sometimes actively discourage repair, from planned obsolescence to proprietary screws. Household electronics are used on average 2.3 years less than their designed lifetimes. In a 2020 study, 78 percent of EU citizens favored manufacturer repair duties. The moment for repair research, the authors argue, is now.
arxiv-2605-10750: Jun-ichi Inoguchi and Marian Ioan Munteanu prove a result about magnetic geodesics in the three-dimensional Heisenberg group. These are paths traced by charged particles under a magnetic field, taken from the group's canonical contact structure. The authors show the paths are homogeneous, which means they look the same under the group's own symmetries. Both authors contributed equally to this short piece of geometry.
arxiv-2605-10850:
Ruinan Jin and four colleagues warn that asking a medical vision-language model to check its own answers is far weaker protection than it looks. Self-verification reuses the same model in a fresh context, and teams increasingly treat it as a default safety layer for medical visual question answering.

Their diagnostic tool, VeriMap, splits verifier behavior into discrimination skill and agreement bias. Tests across six open models, five datasets, and seven tasks show the verifier often agrees with wrong answers, creating a mirage of accuracy deepest in knowledge-heavy clinical tasks. Hospitals and builders learn that self-checks are no substitute for independent verification.
arxiv-2605-10950:
Usman Nazir, Disha Gomathinayagam, Muhammad Kamran, and Sara Khalid build a continuous flood-nowcasting system for Pakistan, where the 2025 monsoon season ran from June to December with cascading damage. Existing flood products give episode snapshots, but rarely continuous, near-real-time inundation maps within the country.

Their ensemble fuses Sentinel-1 radar with Landsat-Sentinel, MODIS, and VIIRS imagery on a harmonized grid, preferring high-resolution sensors and falling back to coarser ones to keep daily coverage. A day-by-day track of the late-August super-flood shows the footprint evolving in near real time, checked against discharge and rainfall data. Disaster responders get maps that keep up with the water, not just summaries after it.
arxiv-2605-11150:
Xhek Turkeshi presents lecture notes on replica tensor networks for random quantum circuits. The notes are a pedagogical, hands-on tutorial tied to a course at the Les Houches School on Computational Quantum Physics in June 2026. The method turns circuit-averaged observables on multiple copies of a system into the contraction of a classical tensor network, which is also the partition function of a statistical-mechanics model.

Changing the observable or initial state touches just the replica boundary conditions, while a different ensemble changes the bulk tensors. The notes show the approach through quantum-information diagnostics, from wavefunction spreading metrics to entanglement quantifiers, in clean and noisy random unitary circuits, then extend it to orthogonal and Clifford circuits. A self-contained C++ and Python library, ReplicaTN, with pedagogical notebooks accompanies the notes. Quantum information students get a working tutorial plus code.
arxiv-2605-11250:
Marco Mantovanelli introduces a family of averaged meta-Fibonacci recursions and studies critical slow growth. Unlike classical Hofstadter-type cases, the averaging yields highly regular large-scale patterns.

Mantovanelli proves the sequence is well-defined everywhere at the critical point alpha equals 1, derives exact block structures, and shows the sequence asymptotically grows like the square root of two n. He further discusses the phase transition at alpha equals 1, numerical evidence for linear growth when alpha exceeds 1, and the link to Golomb-type sequences. Number theorists get a fully mapped averaged recursion family with regular behavior there.
arxiv-2605-11950: Dustin Clausen builds the Weil-Moore anima, a refined object for number theory. The Weil group refines a number field's absolute Galois group through class field theory, and the Galois-to-Weil step matters in several places. From the Galois view, a number field looks like a K(π,1), but from the Weil view it does not. Clausen therefore builds an object with the Weil group as fundamental group, yet with nontrivial higher homotopy groups. Its cohomology behaves more nicely than that of the Weil or Galois groups in several ways.
arxiv-2605-12050: Anouar Bahrouni and three colleagues present the fractional logarithmic p-Laplacian, a new nonlocal tool. Defined as the first rate of change in a setting of its parent, it admits a sum form. That form shows it is log-type, a nonlinear cousin of the logarithmic Laplacian. The authors build its setup on whole space and Lipschitz domains, proving Pohozaev-type rules, Díaz-Saa bounds, and compact fitting at the key power. They close by solving the Dirichlet eigen problem, proving solutions exist, are unique, and stay bounded.
arxiv-2605-12250: In 2026, Useong Shin examines a pricing gap in SPX and RUT index options. Parity links puts and calls at expiry, yet making parity hold costs money. Listed parity looks tight, but the traded forward route leaves a steady gap, which Shin reads as a premium for limited arbitrage funds. Adding a drift-preserving GBM term improves fits both in-sample and out-of-sample by year, mainly for SPX. The takeaway: real-world drift shapes not payoffs, but the machinery that enforces parity at risk-neutral values.
arxiv-2605-12350: Ghosh, Das and Chakrabarti propose FAMeX, a new way to explain what drives an AI classifier's decisions. The method builds a Feature Association Map, a graph that captures how features relate to one another, and uses it to rank feature importance in context. Across eight benchmark tests, FAMeX gauges importance for classification better than permutation importance and SHAP, two widely used explanation tools. The authors present it as a promising route to more trustworthy AI in high-stakes settings.
arxiv-2605-12550: Zhang and six colleagues adapt large vision models to time-series forecasting by closing two gaps between rendered series images and natural images. Rendered series show a markedly shallower power spectrum, and reshaping one-dimensional sequences into two-dimensional grids invents false spatial neighbours while breaking true temporal links. Their SSDA network adapts on both fronts at once, with one branch for spectral mismatch and one for structural mismatch. The dual adaptation unlocks more of the pretrained vision knowledge, improving forecasts over plain image-based transfer.
arxiv-2605-12650: Chung and five colleagues adapt diffusion models to medical imaging with medical reward fit. Base models generate real-looking images, yet the medical move suffers limited tagged data and false making. Metrics like FID miss per-image medical fit. Their Clinical Alignment Score rates made images along matching sides beyond look, using a base model as proxy. Building on it, Clinical Reward-Aligned Finetuning (CRAFT) transfers medical knowledge from language and vision models through prompt boost, medical checklists and smooth reward tuning. It lifts fit and sorting across four types.
arxiv-2605-12750: Yang and eight colleagues quantify transport effects on permeability guessing in FLiBe molten salt systems. Hydrogen isotope passage is often read from passage tests using simple 1D readings, which may miss coupled pathways in real systems. Their movement setup in FESTIM is checked against HYPERION data at MIT. The model tracks movement across molten salt and nickel parts plus outside edge settings, giving full reading of seen fluxes over heat from 773 to 973 kelvin.
arxiv-2605-12850: Costa and Vicente investigate emergent misalignment, the broad misbehaviour that appears when language models are fine-tuned on narrow harmful data. They argue the failure reflects persona-model collapse: a weakened ability to simulate and distinguish characters. Testing four frontier models with new measures of moral flexibility and consistency, they find insecure-code fine-tuning sharply raises flexibility and cuts consistency, while a secure-code control largely preserves both.
arxiv-2605-13050: Huang and six co-authors equip context optimizers for language models with Wikipedia search and browser tools for active information seeking. Naively adding tools to a standard step-by-step pipeline degrades performance. But paired with a search-based training procedure that keeps and prunes multiple candidate contexts, active seeking brings steady, large gains. Gains span low-resource translation, health scenarios and reasoning-heavy tasks, while the method stays data-thrifty and carries over across models.
arxiv-2605-13150: Reich, Messineo and Huber model nearly periodic time series, as produced by automated factory and cyber-physical processes. Each repeat follows a shared path but differs in length, size and fine detail. Strictly periodic models squash repeat-to-repeat differences, while non-periodic models miss the strong shared patterns. Their random generative model uses a Gaussian process with a novel kernel-tuned posterior, splitting within-repeat shape from between-repeat variation while keeping the mean curve the same across repeats.
arxiv-2605-13250: Wang and colleagues show how to read spin analysing powers from collision data at electron positron colliders. They prove the trace of the spin correlation matrix stays fixed under rotations of the measurement basis. That invariant lets them recover the full correlation matrix and the product of analysing powers for two fermion production. Applying a Bell test criterion, they probe quantum nonlocality in lambda baryon pairs at BESIII and gain a new probe of physics beyond the Standard Model.
arxiv-2605-13450: Samuel Schapiro and three colleagues run the first large study of whether human creativity tests predict the feats of large language models. Human creativity tests are often given to language models, yet their value for models was not shown. The Divergent Association Task best predicts writing. The Conditional DAT best predicts divergent thinking, but no single test predicts all three well. No existing test predicts scientific ideation well. The authors introduce the Divergent Remote Association Test, which tests focused and divergent thinking at once and first predicts scientific ideation.
arxiv-2605-13550: Shreya Prakash, Fan Xia and Elena Erosheva present Causal Discovery via Statistical Power, linking causal direction calls to statistical power. Working causal discovery methods use structural asymmetries but rest on strong model assumptions and give few uncertainty tools. CDSP treats two-way data, using power-like and effect-size quantities to judge when data favour one direction. Its effect-size asymmetry assumption marks when correct detection beats reverse error. Tests on 100 cause-effect pairs show it cuts false discovery rates by about 18 percent against a common method.
arxiv-2605-13650: Abdelhakim Necir, Nour Elhouda Guesmia and Djamel Meraghni introduce a weighted and cut Nelson-Aalen tail data process for extreme value index gauging under random gaps. Their class of total gauges, indexed by a tuning knob above one, brings a plain limit shape across the full gaps range. Under steady change rules, they prove a uniform Gaussian fit with trust and limit bell shape at any gaps level. Tests and real data show improved calm and closeness, most under mid and strong gaps.
arxiv-2605-13950: Faroughy and four colleagues present Collider-Bench, a test of whether language-model agents can reproduce real Large Hadron Collider analyses from public papers and open software alone. Reproduction is hard because public tools only approximate the collaborations' internal software, and papers omit implementation details a faithful rebuild requires. Agents must therefore lean on physical reasoning, domain knowledge and trial and error to turn each published analysis into a working reproduction.
arxiv-2605-14050: Forget, Paranjape and Yajnik weigh whether a graviton laser could be built in a lab. Past work deems Earth-based graviton lasers infeasible, since no known trick reflects gravitons to pass them again through a lasing medium. Astrophysical lasing stays possible, as circular graviton orbits around black holes allow very long paths through ultra-light dark matter. The essay picks gravitating systems as candidate media, gives three examples, and calculates whether gravitons can be reflected via conversion, the Gertsenshtein route.
arxiv-2605-14250: Ye, Xiong, Kavokin and Ghosh show coupled exciton-polariton condensates can host time crystals without periodic driving. This comes from incoherent gain and loss channels in semiconductor microcavities. A full quantum account recovers the known effective theory. The mean-field phase diagram is worked out in closed form: the time-crystal phase needs the Kerr-nonlinearity-to-nonlinear-loss ratio above the square root of 5 over 4. Periodic swings in particle numbers form an attractor blind to where it starts, and quantum effects stay periodic and far smaller.
arxiv-2605-14350: Corrado, Huang and Hanna introduce Distributionally Robust Adaptive Task Sampling, prioritizing unsolved tasks. Jointly optimizing all tasks yields imbalanced learning. Prior work blames conflicting gradients, but this paper focuses on imbalanced allocation. Standard MTRL gives each task equal interactions, over-allocating to easy tasks and starving hard tasks. DRATS comes from framing MTRL as a feasibility problem, yielding a minimax worst-case return gap objective. On MetaWorld-MT10 and MT50, DRATS lifts data efficiency and worst-task returns.
arxiv-2605-14850: A. R. Balasubramanian and Franzisco Schmidt extend nested counter systems, which stack counters inside counters like trees, with reset operations. Coverability asks whether a target tree can be reached from a start tree. The pair proves coverability for order-k reset systems is complete for the fast-growing class F of omega-tower height k. That gives a first natural ladder of complete problems for these classes, and it tightens bounds for XML, graph rewriting, and parameterized verification problems.
arxiv-2605-15250: Fanxu Meng and Zhixin Pan introduce Group-Query Latent Attention, a decoding design balancing KV-cache traffic, math, and parallelism. Multi-head latent attention offers absorbed and expanded forms, but head-specific projections block grouped KV sharing. Group-shared up-projections keep a joint latent and allow a shardable expanded cache, with the same weights supporting MQA-absorb and GQA execution. Converted DeepSeek-V3.1-Base nearly matches its source accuracy without gradient updates, and the GQA path lifts throughput 22 to 35 percent on eight GPUs.
arxiv-2605-15350: El Mahdi Chayti and Mohamad Fakhouri propose a hybrid momentum Frank-Wolfe method for stochastic compositional optimization. It minimizes a composition of functions over a compact convex set from noisy samples alone. The projection-free method tracks the inner map's Jacobian and value with momentum, correcting the value by a Taylor term. It feeds the linearization to a generalized linear oracle. It reaches a Frank-Wolfe gap of order K to the minus one quarter for non-convex objectives, and faster rates when linearized models minorize the objective.
arxiv-2605-15650: Cheryl Wang and twenty-three colleagues report MyoChallenge 2025, a NeurIPS test bed for athletic motor skill built on lifelike muscle simulation. Two tracks test upper-limb table tennis rallies and lower-limb soccer penalty kicks with true-to-life arm, leg, and trunk models. Almost seventy teams filed over 560 entries. The contest pushed control methods spanning motion planners, behavior cloning, hierarchical planning, and muscle synergies. It leaves a reusable open test bed for machine learning, biomechanics, and sports science.
arxiv-2605-15950: Liu and four colleagues extend generalized nearest neighbor decoding to channels whose memory stays inside each block. The original receiver design was built for memoryless channels. Their vectorized version gives exact optimality rules for Gaussian codebooks and a joint design for codebook shape and decoding rule. Tests on noisy channels show steady gains over older scaling methods.
arxiv-2605-16050: Borbolato and seven colleagues hunt the low-alpha Splash, old metal-rich stars on halo-like orbits with thin-disk chemistry. The known high-alpha Splash shares those orbits but has thick-disk chemistry. Using APOGEE spectra and galaxy simulations, they find only models with an early clumpy phase scatter such stars onto halo orbits. A merger alone, without clumps, cannot produce them.
arxiv-2605-16150: Salasnich works out the odds that a closed universe tunnels into being, in the Euclidean path-integral picture. The formula keeps both the exponential suppression and the exact Gaussian prefactor from small wiggles around the instanton. In a fixed-interval minisuperspace setup, he imposes the Hamiltonian constraint at the classical instanton level. The result sharpens past work and gives a clear estimate of the nucleation rate.
arxiv-2605-16350: Chen and six colleagues report a federated system that keeps inference memory flat while staying competitive on short-context reasoning. It strengthens long-context retrieval and streaming cross-entropy scores on non-IID MMLU tests. The trick is to stop treating federated learning as model fitting alone: clients jointly learn updating rules, not just models. Their framework, Federated Nested Learning, nests that learning on three levels and borrows Titans-based linear attention. Clients adapt at test time with no examples, reading a delta rule as one online gradient step.
arxiv-2605-16650: Shil and Samui propose SKG-Eval, a framework for judging multi-turn dialogue by tracking a growing knowledge graph of entities, relations, and commitments. It scores three things: fit to the current prompt, fit to past context, and logical coherence, the last via a geometric contradiction engine that needs no language-model judge. The three signals fuse into a session score that stays fair across lengths, with explicit contradiction certificates. Across benchmarks it matches human judgments better and catches long-range inconsistencies more reliably than flat evaluators.
arxiv-2605-16950: Yousofzadeh introduces quasi-Poisson modules over Lie-Rinehart pairs. She proves a one-to-one correspondence between simple cuspidal quasi-Poisson modules over one pair and simple cuspidal Harish-Chandra modules for an extended algebra. She also classifies the simple cuspidal quasi-Poisson modules over that pair, showing each is a tensor module built from an admissible general-linear module via a prescribed action.
arxiv-2605-17250: Haochun Wang and colleagues bring order to test-time adaptation for time-series forecasting, where models adjust as new data arrives. They propose a clean protocol that adapts only on matured ground truth, then examine existing adapters in frequency space and find their corrections weak and unstructured. Their frequency-aware calibration fixes predictions directly in that domain, matching rivals with far fewer trainable parameters.
