arxiv-2605-17850: Chenyang Wang and four colleagues introduce URGE, a derivative-free scaling method for diffusion models. Current guidance adds drift terms or reweights experts, but needs repeated score evaluations. URGE reweights each trajectory with a multiplicative weight from a Girsanov change of measure, then resamples periodically. No score, Hessian, or PDE evaluation is needed. Path-wise and particle-wise Monte Carlo prove equivalent, since the Girsanov weight recovers particle weights in expectation. Tests show URGE beats guidance baselines on synthetic and diffusion benchmarks with better quality and simpler code.
arxiv-2605-18350: Amrita Sain and four colleagues compute gravitational form factors for the pion and kaon, describing how mass and mechanical stress spread inside these mesons. Using light-front wave functions in their 2026 calculation, within Basis Light-Front Quantization, they find one form factor matches lattice and dispersive results, while the other runs high at low momentum. From these they derive mass and mechanical radii plus pressure and shear-force distributions.
arxiv-2605-18650: Isaac Carcacía-Campos, Enrique Macías-Virgós, and David Mosquera-Lois build, in 2026, a homotopical setup for small categories, extending topology invariants to them. A genuine path category built from localization lets them define strong and weak fibrations for functors. They set out basic properties, add a fibrant replacement for functors, and extend the Svarc genus and sectional category to that setting. It applies to motion planning there, giving analogues of Farber's topological complexity without finite size limits.
arxiv-2605-18950: Benedikt Gottstein, Gabriel-Dominique Marleau and Christoph Mordasini extend the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram from stars to forming planets. Using the Bern model coupled to radiation-hydro simulations, they track how accretion, cooling and migration shape brightness-temperature tracks. Shock heating that changes over time bears on whether planets start cold or hot. Tracks show three branches: rising during solid growth, near-flat after detachment when gas intake hits disk limits, and falling as cooling planets hold mass. The tracks match synthetic populations and broadly fit directly imaged planets.
arxiv-2605-19150: Aleksandar Terzić and six colleagues propose Flash PD-SSM, a state-space model matching unstructured expressivity at structured efficiency. It uses a trainable set of structured sparse matrices, one discretely chosen per step, giving finite-state automaton expressiveness at scale. On synthetic mechanistic and state-tracking tasks its expressivity holds in practice. On time-series tasks beyond 17,000 steps it sets a best accuracy among state-space methods. In hybrid language models it improves state tracking and language modelling, raising throughput and cutting memory use.
arxiv-2605-19350: Habib Slim and four colleagues present CompoSE, a method for building and editing 3D shapes part by part. It starts from primitives, such as boxes, arranged to mark each part's place, then synthesizes a part-separated object that supports local edits. A diffusion transformer alternates between handling each part alone and pooling context across parts, with conditioning that keeps outputs faithful to the user's layout. It infers part meaning and symmetry without part-level text prompts, and it beats rivals on guided synthesis by measured scores and model judgments.
arxiv-2605-19450: Foini, Kurchan and Pappalardi ask what classical hydrodynamics demands of a quantum system. Reading the quantum fluctuation-dissipation theorem in the time domain blurs fine correlation detail over a Planckian timescale. Tracking that blur along rays inside the light cone for diffusion, telegraph and mixed equations, they find the cone splits into classical and quantum regions where correlation and response part sharply. Keeping a finite classical region as temperature falls forces the relaxation rate to stay at least Planckian, bounding diffusivity, equilibration time and shear viscosity.
arxiv-2605-19550: Xu and team compare exotic hadron production of Tcc and X(3872) in proton-proton collisions at 7 TeV, using PACIAE with the DCPC coalescence model. Compact tetraquark states form at the partonic level while loose molecular states form at the hadronic level. Transverse momentum spectra show a significant gap between the compact state and the molecular states. The authors also probe the production asymmetry between the two Tcc charge states and extract coalescence parameters to characterize the emission source. These distributions offer criteria for telling the states apart in experiments.
arxiv-2605-19750: Li and colleagues give image generators that learn new concepts one after another without forgetting old ones. Visual autoregressive models, which build pictures step by step from text, usually handle only one fixed concept at a time. Their C2P-VAR framework picks concept-relevant settings by gradient size, protects shared settings from interference, and fuses several concepts in one picture with placed, separate features. Tests show stronger likeness to target subjects than rival methods, with little extra storage or delay.
arxiv-2605-19850: Jankovic characterises Starlink position error growth, comparing SGP4 with high fidelity propagation against operator truth. Across over twenty four thousand pairs, five hundred one satellites, three shells and generations in April 2026, error follows a power law with exponents between one and two. Pooled medians grow from about one kilometre at six hours to tens of kilometres at seven days. It does not beat SGP4 overall, winning only for newer satellites at long horizons, a result the author traces to operator residuals and truth alignment.
arxiv-2605-19950: Zhao and colleagues teach an emotion reader to guess where feelings head next. Past readers fuse full sight, sound, and text at once, leaving feeling shifts hidden. Their AffectVerse model dreams short range sight and sound futures and feeds them back for choice. Across nine benches it tops rivals by at least about two and a half percent.
arxiv-2605-20050: Calvin Yixiang Cheng, Dorian Quelle and Scott Hale track how conspiracy claims change wording over three years of posts on X. Claims with larger semantic mutations live substantially longer, and shifts in pronouns, social references, cognitive-process terms and risk- and health-related words all link to longer lifespans. Shifts in actor, action and target categories also extend lifespan, with simplification and assimilation as the two main mutation patterns. The authors argue moderation should weigh how mutable a claim is and target core claims that cover their likely variants.
arxiv-2605-20250: Rafał Topolnicki, Paweł Dłotko and Maciej Matyka present a framework predicting pore velocity fields from sample geometry. Flow simulation in porous media is hard, as pore shapes are complex and solvers converge slowly. Their convolutional encoder-decoder with skip connections preserves detail and extracts multiscale features. A loss mixes velocity rebuild with incompressibility, no-flow, periodicity, and the tortuosity index. Tests outside the training mix show generalization across obstacle shapes, boundaries, porosity, and structures. Fields warm-start Lattice-Boltzmann runs, cutting iterations in over ninety percent of cases.
arxiv-2605-20650: Hongsoo Kim and Se-Chan Lee prove a priori regularity estimates for degenerate fully nonlinear elliptic equations with integrable data. When the source term lies in L^p with p above the dimension, they obtain optimal interior C^{1,alpha} estimates. In the critical case, a log-Lipschitz modulus of continuity follows under a Lorentz rule. Sliding paraboloid and cusp methods give uniform Holder estimates, and an approximation lemma extends the results to Schauder-type estimates.
arxiv-2605-21050: Abdelhakim Benkrane and Giuseppe Gaetano Luciano constrain Kaniadakis cosmology using Starobinsky inflation and primordial tensor perturbations. They study a broad entropic cosmos from using the gravity-thermodynamics conjecture to the Universe edge using those stats, a relativistic extension of Boltzmann-Gibbs. That change in horizon entropy alters Friedmann motion and extends Lambda-CDM in a sound way. Within that design, they explore early-cosmos physics, on early gravitational waves and slow-roll Starobinsky-like expansion.
arxiv-2605-21150: Rowan Border and Margarita Chli introduce EllipseLIO, a real-time LiDAR inertial odometry system for robots that move without GPS. Its scan filtering and registration adapt to each sensor and setting, so one setup serves varied scenes with no per-scene tuning. On five diverse data sets it beat rival systems overall, cutting odometry error by thirty-five percent against the runner-up.
arxiv-2605-21950: Jiazheng Zhu and co-authors report a featureless tidal disruption event at redshift near 1, found by the Wide Field Survey Telescope as WFST250820mmsw, also called AT2025wet. A star torn apart by a supermassive black hole gives a blue flare peaking about 3 magnitudes above its host galaxy. A Keck spectrum near peak shows a blue continuum with no clear lines. Its redshift is still pinned down, letting the team test whether such events peak in extreme ultraviolet light and extend the black hole census to higher redshifts.
arxiv-2605-22050: Yuanmin Huang and co-authors identify a new signature of memorization in diffusion models: internal instability that surfaces as visibly broken flaws. This poses privacy and copyright risks, yet it was not previously linked to such instability. Inspired by stability analysis, they define empirical stability regions from latent update norms to measure the effect. Their on-the-fly framework then detects and mitigates it step by step, without changing prompts or guidance, keeping meaning and image quality intact. On Stable Diffusion 1.4 it reaches AUC above 0.999 with a 0.0 percent memorization rate.
arxiv-2605-22350: Morelli and Eckstein introduce partial fusion of neural networks, a middle path between ensembles and weight aggregation. Ensembles beat single networks but cost far more to run. Weight aggregation is cheap but less accurate. Partial fusion merges only the most similar neurons across networks, using partial optimal transport to find and match them. The idea also reads as generalised pruning, where neurons may be deleted or combined. Applied to one network alone, it gives a similar trade-off between isolating, deleting and combining neurons.
arxiv-2605-23050: Bergelson and Zelada study sets of large returns for polynomial multi-correlation functions, defined by near maximal overlap of a measurable set with its shifts under commuting transformations. They show every such set is syndetic exactly when the polynomials are linearly independent, answering a question of Frantzikinakis and Kuca. Linear independence further implies the stronger almost IP star property. Combinatorially, for positive density sets, return sets are almost IP star, and when dimension exceeds polynomial count by more than one, this result is sharp.
arxiv-2605-23150: Shi and three coauthors present HARDAT, an HDBSCAN based method for detecting and tracking active regions in magnetograms. Active regions drive storms and space weather, and follow-up matters for forecasts. Their DBSCAN based method had cutoffs, while HDBSCAN handles multi-density structures on the fly, finding diffuse regions well while keeping shape. A spin follow-up method with real motion models and Hamming distance likeness achieves multi-object follow-up. Tested on SOHO and SDO maps against NOAA and earlier lists, HARDAT wins on accuracy and stability.
arxiv-2605-23650: Pavlovic and colleagues study preference-only learning in episodic kernel Markov tasks, where feedback arrives as preferences, not numeric rewards. Each episode, the learner deploys two policies from a common start and gets one label for the favored path. A Bradley-Terry-Luce link on total unseen gaps models the label. Under kernel guesses on reward and transition functions, they develop preference-based value estimation and trust sets for episode match-ups. They prove high-odds regret bounds scaling slowly with episodes, implying the learned policy converges to optimal.
arxiv-2605-23750: Pan and colleagues probe whether cluster environment drives the Fanaroff-Riley dichotomy using a LoTSS DR2 catalogue. In the volume-limited sample, 48.6 percent of FRIs and 30.6 percent of FRIIs are cluster-associated. Yet cluster-associated FRIs and FRIIs occupy environments, with trends in luminosity and stellar mass with richness, and radial distributions peaking near half radius. FRIIs are less often found in clusters, at high luminosity, consistent with dense gas disrupting jets. Once inside clusters, FRIs and FRIIs inhabit similar environments, so cluster properties alone are unlikely drivers.
arxiv-2605-23850: Ali Zahir and colleagues chase energy savings in high performance computing without throttling science. Their AI assisted scheduler pairs fluid flow simulation with a physics informed variational autoencoder. That pairing makes lifelike synthetic workloads linking heat behavior to scheduling choices. Sorting workflows by resource profile, they test locality aware and speculative aware strategies. They find a sweet spot: trimming CPU speed by around fifteen percent yields up to ten percent energy savings. Turnaround grows only about five percent.
arxiv-2605-23950: Zhang and five colleagues argue that agent leaderboards mislead when they hide the harness, the layer managing context, tools, orchestration, and checks around a language model. Their Binding Constraint Thesis holds that, for long-horizon tasks on near-frontier models, harness setup drives performance variance more than model choice, sometimes flipping model rankings. Control theory, published benchmarks, and a variance split back the claim. They propose a harness-aware frame with a disclosure standard and a variance protocol, urging readers to treat undisclosed leaderboard comparisons as incomplete.
arxiv-2605-24250: Tian and five co-authors rebuild a time-varying phase object from a diffraction movie under a support constraint alone. A bounded temporal increment prior suffices under the thin-film approximation. Field evolution uses an update factor between frames, and a bound on its support caps the phase increment and enforces a passive amplitude constraint. Reconstruction becomes a feasibility problem with two projections: modulus and circular-sector. Tests with a spatial light modulator cover two phase patterns, both matching ground truth, and the same frame monitors 3D printing.
arxiv-2605-24550: Seokil Ham and three colleagues defend fine-tuning work against harmful attacks with a Buffer-and-Reinforce plan. A study shows temporary jailbreaking saturates harmful gradients while preserving benign task gradients. BufferLoRA induces temporary jailbreaking as an adapter that absorbs harmful updates while the user fine-tunes. After tuning, ReinforceLoRA restores refusal behavior and merges with the user adapter by QR decomposition, keeping safety intact without extra data.
arxiv-2605-24850: Kumiko Tanaka-Ishii proposes repeated subsequences as a diagnostic separating language models from natural language. Whether models capture language structure beyond local fluency remains open, since task scores reveal little about long-range organization. Analyzing how texts reuse earlier structure across scales, and relating reuse to Renyi entropies, probes finite-length organization. Power-law models fit restricted block-length ranges, but entropy growth is often better described by logarithmic-power forms. Natural language shows stable entropy-growth patterns, while GPT texts show clear, size-linked shifts in estimated exponents.
arxiv-2605-24950: Muhammad Naveed Riaz leads ARCANE-PedSynth, an open-source CARLA-based toolkit for building synthetic multi-pedestrian data. It trains crossing prediction for self-driving cars. CARLA on its own yields crossings in only a small share of cases. The toolkit mixes AI and manual pedestrian control to lift the crossing rate high. A twelve-state behavior machine with five character types drives varied crossing styles. Outputs sync color, LiDAR, and event-camera streams with per-frame crossing labels, behavior states, and pose points. Reproducible by command line..
arxiv-2605-25050: Mohamed Boussena and colleagues present Multimodality Stacking with Blockwise missing values, a late-fusion method for blockwise-missing data. Each source is modeled alone, then results are merged by stacking. Tested on PIONeeR: 443 patients, 378 markers, it predicts progression-free survival for late-stage NSCLC patients on immune therapy. It beats rivals on the C-index: linear models improve nearly sixteen percent, random forests five point four percent, and boosting two point one percent. It shrinks the linear-model gap from 0.380 to 0.055. Lab markers, signs, and PD-L1 levels drive results.
arxiv-2605-25150: Rutuja Sawant proves that the r-independence complex of any tree is vertex decomposable, for every positive integer r. Here a set of vertices counts as r-independent when each connected piece of the subgraph it induces has at most r vertices. The family of all such sets forms a simplicial complex. Her recursive proof describes shedding vertices through rooted subtrees, settling a conjecture of Abdelmalek and coauthors and clarifying the topology of these complexes.
arxiv-2605-25250: Leshu Li and colleagues coordinate a team of tuned language-model agents. The team designs fat-based delivery particles that are both potent and safe. In their LipoAgent system, toxicity acts as a gate: a candidate that fails safety never gets an efficiency score. Specialist agents check one another's work, with a person stepping in when they still disagree. Across several base models, the approach lifts predicted delivery success by about a third, and lab tests confirm the rankings carry over to real cells.
arxiv-2605-25450: Marek Rutkowski and Huansang Xu price equity protection swaps shielding variable-annuity holders from market falls, under jumps and default risk. Their frameworks use Merton jump-diffusion and a random-time default model, yielding closed-form values and put-call parity. Static hedging works without default, but counterparty default leaves residual losses that cannot be hedged. Those losses are quantified to define default-adjusted premiums in Black-Scholes and jump-diffusion settings alike. Numerical results show jump features and default intensity moving costs and premiums, underscoring crisis and credit risks.
arxiv-2605-25750: Seiffarth introduces structure-aware weight sharing for message-passing neural networks, which learn from graph data. Standard weights act on inputs only. His weights take their index from user-chosen graph invariants, functions preserved under node permutations, enabling reuse across equivalent subgraphs. ShareGNNs pair a simple encoder-decoder design with learnable adjacency and attention-style connectivity. Their expressivity matches the discriminative power of the chosen invariants, giving clear control over model complexity. Tests show steady gains.
arxiv-2605-26250: Ankit Gill and Anurag Sarkar study Krylov complexity for conformal field theories under periodic driving, plus lattice versions built from critical fermions. They compare a square-wave drive with a continuous sinusoidal drive, in a 2026 study. In the heating phase, Arnoldi coefficients approach unity exponentially, while in the non-heating phase they oscillate. On the lattice side, Krylov complexity, quasi-energy statistics, and the Floquet-operator graph differ sharply between drives, pointing to distinct mechanisms behind the heating transition.
arxiv-2605-26350: Chenghao Qiu and four colleagues reveal a correctness-utility gap in in-context learning: correct demonstrations can still reduce accuracy. Using task-preserving perturbations that change only exemplar inputs, they show changed examples can substantially degrade performance, hitting smaller models, tougher tasks, and higher perturbation ratios hardest. They formalize the failure as contextual evidence shift, where changes alter the effective mixture of evidence behind contextual inference. Robust in-context learning must therefore judge not only whether they are correct, but how they steer answers, in a 2026 paper.
arxiv-2605-26850: Yu and five colleagues propose spatiotemporal noise-contrastive estimation, a framework for learning energy-based models from stochastic interpolants. Earlier methods learn the joint density over data and time through spatial or temporal differences alone, and the authors identify distinct failure modes for each. Their joint spatiotemporal approach unifies many existing methods and yields new training objectives. Tests on images and molecules match state-of-the-art density estimation.
arxiv-2605-27750: Antonia Karamolegkou, Nicolas Angleraud, Benoit Sagot, and Thibault Clerice test whether vision-language models truly ground their Ancient Greek OCR in images or merely guess. Under character-level perturbations, vision models diverge sharply from perturbed truth while traditional OCR stays comparatively faithful. Token-level analysis shows prior reliance is model-specific: an OCR-specialist model leans little on the image, while general models stay visually conditioned even when wrong.
arxiv-2605-27850: Ding and colleagues argue that prompts and communication patterns for multi-agent systems must be designed together, not separately. Their TCP-MCP framework evolves both as one genome, probing the search landscape early and balancing task success against token cost and structural complexity. It topped graph-building rivals on three benchmarks while using far fewer tokens than debate-style systems.
arxiv-2605-27950: Li and colleagues ask whether wearable-camera images of meals can hint at a person's openness to changing eating habits. Using first-person eating photos paired with self-reports on awareness, capability, and motivation, they test a vision-language encoder plus a small classifier. Early results beat simple baselines, suggesting meal-scene images carry usable cues for timely health prompts.
arxiv-2605-28050: Daniel Carter and Jung Hon Yip prove Hadwiger's conjecture for two families of graphs defined by forbidden patterns. For graphs avoiding co-claw and co-gem patterns, and for those avoiding fork and antifork patterns, they build clique models with tightly bounded branch sets. The first case also settles the conjecture for complements of line graphs built from triangle-free multigraphs.
arxiv-2605-28150: Sakhi and colleagues explain why off-policy reasoning training works better than its textbook story suggests. Dropping importance weights, they argue, implicitly optimizes toward more conservative target policies than the nominal objective admits, a hidden pessimism that stabilizes learning. They then propose a principled tweak that steadies the induced distribution and improves off-policy learning further.
arxiv-2605-28350: Shahaf Ella Salach and Ron Shnapp test whether peristaltic pumping works in the brain's short annular fluid spaces. Their bench setup drives a pulse wave along a compliant inner tube inside a rigid outer tube, tracking flow by particle velocimetry. Despite back-and-forth sloshing, net transport follows the wave, with velocity profiles collapsing across deformation amplitudes.
arxiv-2605-28450: Jungwook Seo and three colleagues present BiasEdit, a training-free framework that finds and edits bias attributes in web image data. It first detects unknown bias attributes through statistical dependence in vision-language representations, then edits them with text-guided image editing to create realistic counterexamples. No manual annotations or known bias labels are needed, and off-the-shelf models suffice. Even on fully biased training data, the method reaches state-of-the-art debiasing for visual classifiers.
arxiv-2605-28750: Yueyang Zhang, Wei Wu, and Peifeng Su build an O(N3) framework for second-order perturbation from block tensor and canonical polyadic decompositions. Block tensor decomposition builds the kernel at O(N3) on a dual grid, and splits the exchange channel in two stages. A half-kernel design applies Coulomb to one vertex and averaged screening to the other, capturing the SOSEX part of renormalized theory without factoring. For MP2 the method matches canonical RI-MP2, and for renormalized theory on S66x8 the mean error is 0.36 kilocalories per mole.
arxiv-2605-28850: Weicheng Xue studies conduct fit and picture shifts of language agents in market settings. TradeArena, an open trading testbed with risk reports, trade play, memory, and saved runs, lets analysts trace reasons, positions, and nudges under stress. Pre-failure signs emerge: planning vectors drift from centroids, fused plan-risk pictures separate pre-drawdown states, and manifolds show effective-rank squeeze. Tests show squeeze can vanish without reasons, while intent-space signs stay useful, and risk feedback improves tuning for some models and returns for others without fine-tuning.
arxiv-2605-29350: Yilun Yao and colleagues present ConMoE, which splits mixture-of-experts compression into two decisions. The first builds a compact expert pool; the second assigns original experts' workloads to it. Existing methods couple the two steps, but the second can be optimized after the pool is fixed. ConMoE builds its pool with Anchor Coverage and optimizes the second step via a router-conditioned objective from a reconstruction bound. It uses unlabeled calibration inputs, with frozen router and weights. At half retention, ConMoE cuts peak GPU memory while improving accuracy.
arxiv-2605-29450: Zisis Tsiatsikas presents the first review of threats and defence tools for on device inference. Many defence tools exist, including secure runs, homomorphic encryption, hiding, and privacy. Past surveys focus on edge intelligence, which covers training, and miss issues in on device runs. The review finds the attack and defence uneven. About one quarter of papers focus on IP attacks, whereas half of fixes tackle it. Some attack groups have no paper, such as attacks at roughly one third of papers.
arxiv-2605-29550: Umesh Chandra Thuwal and four colleagues report a system that moves single nanoparticles inside a scanning electron microscope with a carbon-fiber tip. Etched carbon tips, rigid with apexes narrower than one hundred nanometers, cut adhesion and place particles about one hundred nanometers wide with similar precision. A piezo bimorph drives vertical motion, a four-quadrant piezo tube handles fine control, and a piezo walker covers coarse lateral moves. The team puts single magnetite particles on micron-scale superconducting sensors for best magnetic coupling and probes their magnetism.
arxiv-2605-29950: Berkay Kullukcu, Robin Pianowski, and Dina Hannebauer test a sound-and-shake method for loose bolts in rail vehicles. A shaker drives a rig while a sensor and mic listen, with one bolt at zero, one-fifth, two-fifths, and four-fifths preload. A pure tone near resonance makes the loose bolt sprout extra high-frequency peaks. Swept tones across a narrow band split the states further apart. Harmonic power ratios mark the loose state from the four-fifths state by a wide margin, growing wider at higher harmonics.
arxiv-2605-30150: Fares Nabil Ibrahim, Nafis Saami Azad and Raiyan Abdul Baten study how to widen idea pools from parallel model generation with no seed ideas. Across three creative task families, they test solo generation and semantic direction stratification against anchored baselines. Population-based divergence is a strong low-cost baseline, raising diversity while keeping quality scores. That method does better: one planning call spreads generations for the best diversity, quality and compute frontier. Anchored regeneration fades once full token costs are counted.
arxiv-2605-30250: Hoon-Gyu Chung and three co-authors present an ambient-robust inverse rendering method using active RGB-NIR imaging. Current methods often fail under ambient light. Near-infrared flash light, invisible to humans, gives stable point-light shading largely invariant to ambient light. Combining ambient-light RGB images with active-flash NIR images, a three-stage method exploits complementary RGB and NIR benefits. A RGB-NIR camera and flash system collected the first multi-view RGB-NIR dataset under varied ambient conditions, and tests show the method beats prior approaches.
arxiv-2605-30350: Jusuk Lee and eight co-authors introduce DynaFLIP, a way to teach motion sense into robot sight. They build image-language-flow triples from human and robot clips, using them to shape a sight net. The core idea: push the three senses to span a small simplex shape in shared sphere space, where a smaller shape means tighter match. Tests show DynaFLIP looks at spots that matter for handling, and its sight nets beat base nets on later tasks, with gains up to about 23 percent on new scenes.
arxiv-2605-30550: Kasumba, Barbour, and Ho ask whether early traces of how someone works can predict their later strategy on a new task. Outcome totals like scores blur distinct approaches, and modeling one task alone tangles personal habits with that task's layout. Their Process-Level Latent Variable Model fuses partial traces from two cleaning tasks in a game into one person-level profile, then predicts behavior on a held-out level. The model distinguishes steady zone planners from frequent zone hoppers, showing that cross-task traces can reveal transferable personal tendencies.
arxiv-2605-30650: Zeng and colleagues survey trustworthy AI in fintech, where AI drives choices across training and use. The scale behind finance AI systems opens attack surfaces, where small tweaks can snowball into broad harm. Old surveys treat AI as a defense tool or study adversarial learning in general, missing finance constraints like accounting plausibility and federated data. The authors sort seventeen attack subtypes into a lifecycle taxonomy spanning poisoning, boundary attacks, prompt injection, and deepfake ID tricks. They close by urging lifecycle-aware stress tests and finance-relevant benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-30850: Kim and colleagues review the quantum side of photonic time crystals, media whose traits repeat in time. One time edge can mix modes and spawn photon pairs; in bulk media, momentum rules split the field into paired parts with a squeezing form. Adding time repeats turns the problem into a Floquet band problem with momentum gaps. The review links these crystals to the dynamical Casimir effect and parametric gain, which share the pair-making step, and closes with light-matter cases and platforms.
arxiv-2605-30950: Milburn and Ringsmuth build a physical model of coordination without direct communication or optimization. Population size follows a birth-death process whose rates respond to a shared noisy signal linked to population state. Coordination emerges from feedback through imperfect common information, not from agents talking or optimizing. Geometric Brownian motion appears as a limiting case under suitable conditions. Varying signal traits yields diffusive and jump growth regimes, even as average growth stays exponential. In an appropriate limit, the framework recovers the Peters and Adamou growth model.
arxiv-2605-31150: Ujlayan and colleagues propose a single number, the Biofilm-Virulence Index, for gauging antifungal resistance in Candida albicans, a yeast behind thrush and vaginal infections. Combining stain-based biofilm mass with live cell counts, the index tracks how drugs slow early biofilm growth and then hold it steady. Most values stayed in the mild range, suggesting the drugs cut virulence, and the combined measure eases sample-to-sample comparison.
arxiv-2605-31450: Clarkson and Kontar present imaging spectroscopy of a noise storm observed by LOFAR between 30 and 40 MHz, with scattering simulations. The continuum forms a bright, compact source drifting across the disk. Across the band, its size is less than half that of typical type III burst sources. Type I bursts, S-bursts and spikes tucked inside share identical apparent sizes, suggesting a common mechanism. Simulations show compact sizes arise inside closed magnetic structures, where turbulence directs radiation away from the observer. Densities, gradients and turbulence matter only secondarily.
arxiv-2606-00050:
Magarshak presents Grokers, an architecture that moves language model comprehension from query time to write time, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Retrieval-augmented generation pays the cost of understanding material on every query. Grokers instead deploys autonomous agents that analyze nodes in a knowledge graph as data arrives. They extract structured attributes through governed model calls and compose meaning through dependency links. Those attributes then answer queries with no added model cost.

The paper proves three properties of the design. A byte-identity theorem shows assembled context stays identical between changes, enabling cache hit rates approaching 100 percent. A monotonicity theorem shows the share of queries resolved without model calls never decreases as the governed knowledge library grows. Another theorem fixes the traversal orders for generation and comprehension over dependency graphs. A deterministic alternative to embedding search, with a synonym cache whose fallback rate shrinks toward zero, rounds out the system.
arxiv-2606-00150:
Park and co-authors warn of a slow trick that can break the guard rails of chat models. Most past jailbreaks hit a model with one sharp prompt. Their method, Persona Attack, works step by step through chat memory. Small planted notes build up over turns.

As the planted notes pile up, the model heeds them more than its own safety rules. Tests span several well-known chat models. The team finds that success swings with how memory is built. It also swings with which note sets are paired. In the best case for the attack, success hits 95 percent. The work shows why chat memory needs guard checks of its own.
arxiv-2606-00350:
Houssaini and co-authors keep offline-learned plans near their data while they chase high value. Offline learning must grow a plan from fixed logs. Bold picks off the log can carry false worth. Spread and flow plans tame that risk but run slow at use time.

Their tool, DriftQL, pairs a drift-based pull with a critic-led push. The critic steers picks toward high-worth zones in the log. Pull and push keep picks close to logged acts. They also stop picks from piling on one mode. One net with one goal does the whole job. Picks come from a single fast pass at use. Tests on two bench sets beat spread and flow tools. Gains hold when log quality drops.
arxiv-2606-00450:
Ramlal, Hu, and Zelek weigh ways to seed 3D splat scenes with more points up front. Splat builds live or die by the worth of their seed points. Thin seeds leave soft spots in the end scene. The team test five ways to grow point clouds for that seed step.

Routes span straight fills, tri fills, curve skin builds, slide fits, and cell-based births. A depth-led lift adds points that keep the base build's shape. Tests use two known sets of wide and room scenes. Skin build routes win on rich, wild scenes. Plain fills suit smooth, part-wise scenes more. Depth-led points help most in blank zones with no grain. Picks should fit scene type and chip purse, they urge.
arxiv-2606-00550:
Tran and co-authors lay a four-tier talk stack for a free robot teach stage. Lab robot teach hits a wall twixt two poles. Paid twin tools cost much and bend in set ways. Free ROS tools pose steep walls of code for new hands.

Their stack is built to scale with green class plans. It bridges sight-based build rooms with real robot ends. The GOSP stage serves as the base build in the test. Their work tracks how data is packed, sent, and wrapped in the stack. 3D frame builds link to a firm ROS back end there. Sim-to-real tests on multi-axis paths check the bridge. The stack holds truth well and takes more than one gear type.
arxiv-2606-00950:
Luan and co-authors guide robots to learn useful skills without rewards in this 2026 paper. Unsupervised skill discovery teaches varied behavior with no reward function. Free exploration can waste time or turn hazardous. Guided variants add human intent, but they often need extra guidance models, fixed rules, or expert demos. Sparse online feedback breaks those crutches.

Their framework, COLLIE, builds a skill space from dense unsupervised data. The space is semantically coherent: near skills mean near things. That order lets sparse human feedback steer search with force. Guidance signals form with no extra model training, a training-free trick the authors justify in theory. Tests span state-based and pixel-based tasks. COLLIE learns skills that are varied and matched to human aims, they report. It dodges hazardous behavior and tops downstream scores with little feedback.
arxiv-2606-01050:
Zhang and co-authors test fake image detectors on fakes full of text in this 2026 paper. Detectors shine on natural images. But much misinformation rides on forged screenshots, documents, and news pages. Those text rich fakes had no benchmark of their own. The team built one to close the gap.

Their set, TextFake, holds 20,000 images across 28 languages, four topic classes, and two scene types. Fakes are made in four stages, with real images annotated on three controlled axes first. Counterparts are then generated to match the real spread, which blocks shortcut cues. Fourteen specialist detectors and three frontier vision APIs face the set cold. None breaks 80 percent accuracy, they report. Some fall over 60 points from their natural image scores. Three failure modes stand out. Dense glyphs swamp low level detectors. Clean rendering hides generative traces. And routine perturbations collapse thresholds toward chance.
arxiv-2606-01350:
Mohanty and co-authors probe how light scatters in a layered crystal. The crystal is bilayer 3R-MoS2, a van der Waals material. Raman scattering shows how light and lattice motion interact. The team vary temperature as they measure. They use Raman spectroscopy at several wavelengths. Photoluminescence and density functional theory add support.

Both zone-centre and finite-momentum phonons appear in the data. Stokes intensity falls sharply at low temperature, then levels off. Anti-Stokes scattering emerges above 130 K. The phonon temperature strays far from the lattice temperature. Resonance effects drive that gap, the team find. The work clarifies exciton-phonon coupling in such layered materials.
arxiv-2606-01550:
Fang and co-authors image single infrared photons with a silicon camera. Their system rests on two-photon absorption in a silicon EMCCD. A long-wavelength pump scheme uses mid-infrared pulsed excitation. It boosts the two-photon absorption coefficient. It also suppresses background noise from harmonic absorption of the pump. Photon-counting rates rise over 30-fold versus the degenerate scheme. Detection sensitivity approaches one photon per pixel per pulse. That enables true single-photon operation in the infrared.

No strict phase matching is needed, unlike parametric conversion. Spatial resolution reaches 13 micrometers in their setup. On-chip nonlinearity gives a broad spectral window and wide view. A 5-picosecond gate adds fine time resolution. Uses include low-light fluorescence microscopy and 3D time-of-flight imaging.
arxiv-2606-01650:
Pav estimates the true Sharpe ratio of a selected winning asset. The asset was picked for the highest in-sample Sharpe ratio among many. Its observed ratio overstates the true one by selection. He discusses several estimators for that bias problem. They rest on the polyhedral lemma and James Stein shrinkage. Debiasing the expected maximum and thresholding also appear. Empirical Bayes rounds out the estimator set. Simulations test them across sample sizes and asset counts.

Spread and shape of population Sharpe ratios vary in the tests. Rank correlation shows how the estimators compare team outputs. The James Stein estimator performs best across many realistic settings. The GMLEB estimator of Jiang and Zhang follows it. Results stay fairly robust to correlation of asset returns.
arxiv-2606-02050:
Di Gregorio and co-authors study private learning in trade between two agents. Bilateral trade is a core economic interaction. A seller and a buyer wish to trade a good. A middleman sets the terms of that trade. The learning version infers a mechanism from sampled values.

Known learning methods react strongly to single data points. The team view the task through differential privacy. Each data point should barely shift the learned outcome. They adopt the PAC-learning framework for the results. With high probability, the output is near optimal. That guarantee must hold in a private way too. Trade-offs between profit, efficiency, and privacy are mapped. The results give the first private bounds for this setting.
arxiv-2606-02550:
Loer and co-authors attribute heat extremes to climate change with a learning-based storyline method. Storyline attribution holds the air flow pattern fixed. It asks how the same event plays out under other climate states. Climate models cannot move such counterfactuals across forcing states directly. The team uses distributional autoencoders instead.

The autoencoders model full distributions of European temperature fields. Inputs are the circulation state and the global warming level. Conditional probability ratios follow from the distributions. Training uses coupled climate model simulations. Tests span factual and counterfactual simulation sets. A case study revisits the 2003 European heatwave. With 2003 air flow held fixed, peak intensity rises in the 2028 and 2053 versions. Probability ratios reach 2.1 and 3.2 against 2003. The method gives storyline studies a statistical engine.
arxiv-2606-02750:
Rizwan and co-authors show that word overlap steers language model representations more than meaning does. Representations from these models feed many downstream applications. Their structure often tracks lexical overlap over semantic content. The team quantifies that lexical pull against semantic signal. Adversarial semantic stress tests supply the probes. An information theory lens frames the findings.

Lexical influence spans the full depth of models. It holds across architectures, training regimes, and objective functions. Models trained for semantic similarity are not exempt. A mid-depth region stands out. There, lexical and semantic signals degrade together. That zone is transitional, poor for surface form and meaning alike. Downstream effects are shown through summarization and model editing case studies. The work warns that representation quality cannot be assumed from task scores alone.
arxiv-2606-03150:
He and Ji link lattice graphs to continuous grids to study limits and inequalities. As edge length shrinks to zero, its problems should tend to those on the full space. The team builds a shared frame for such singular limit problems and for Gagliardo-Nirenberg type inequalities on lattice graphs.

Restriction and extension estimates are the main tools. They let the authors compare variational problems on lattice graphs, metric grids, and the full space. Ground states of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation on lattice graphs converge strongly to the ground states on the full space as edges shrink. Fixed-mass critical points get multiplicity results as a side gain. The team also finds best constants for the inequalities in subcritical and critical cases. One new inequality settles an open problem posed by Dovetta. Supercritical cases are covered as well, for both action and energy ground states.
arxiv-2606-03250:
He, Frei, and Schmitt train German language models for clinical text. Digital healthcare makes vast clinical text that could power AI tools. German biomedical models lag, held back by old designs or thin training data. Their family, ChristBERT, is built on RoBERTa and tuned for clinical and healthcare topics.

The training corpus holds 13.5 gigabytes of text: science papers, clinical notes, health web content, and translated clinical sources. The team compares three paths: continued pretraining, training from scratch, and vocabulary adaptation. Tests cover three entity recognition tasks and two classification tasks in medicine. ChristBERT beat past general and medical German models on four of five benchmarks. It set a new state of the art for German clinical language work. The best path split by task. Training from scratch won on the most specialized texts. Continued pretraining won on more common medical writing. All models are released in public.
arxiv-2606-03750:
Trapote and co-authors extend the robust clustering method TCLUST to high dimensions. Outliers distort many standard clustering tools and can wreck the partitions they return. Trimming-based methods cut outlier influence and help flag real anomalies. TCLUST trims in the spirit of the MCD estimator, across unknown multiple clusters. It shines on low-dimensional data but strains in high dimensions, where parameter counts explode.

A rival method, RLG, assumes clusters lie near low-dimensional subspaces. It falters when subspaces cross and assumes plain isotropic errors. The new method, tHHDC, merges both lines inside the HDDC frame. Trimming and eigenvalue constraints are added with care. Theory for the method comes with a feasible algorithm. A simulation study and a real-data example show its value. Input parameter choice is discussed as part of the package. Statisticians get a robust option for high-dimensional grouping.
arxiv-2606-03950:
Rodionenko, Mazanov, and Gorlach study two-dimensional higher-order topological insulators. Such materials are classed as dipolar or quadrupolar by their key invariant. Past work treats those two classes as apart, with no overlap. A system could in principle host both types at once. That case had no clear example until now.

The team puts forward a system that shows both forms at the same time. They suggest a build with arrays of laser-written optical waveguides. Those guides couple to each other through fading field tails. Full-wave simulations support their claim, they report. Readers get a concrete route to test the merged class in the lab.
arxiv-2606-04050:
He and co-authors present LiftQuant, a way to set LLM bit-width on a smooth scale. Standard quantization locks width to whole numbers like two or three bits. That rigidity leaves a deployment gap for tight memory budgets. A model may not fit a given device at its best size. LiftQuant aims for true Pareto-optimal fitting instead.

Its core move lifts weight vectors into a higher-dimensional space. A simple one-bit lattice there is then projected back down. The width follows the ratio of lifted to original dimension. That ratio can be tuned in fine steps. Decoding still uses just linear maps and one-bit quantizers. A 70B model was squeezed to 2.4 bits for a 24GB GPU. It beat top two-bit models on that device, they report.
arxiv-2606-04350:
Daniel Amyot argues in 2026 that process mining should output Use Case Map models. Process mining rebuilds how an organization truly works from its system logs. Use Case Maps are a requirements notation that shows roles and scenarios at a glance.

He presents PM4Py-UCM, an open-source extension of a popular Python mining library. It adds a pipeline that emits Use Case Maps from logs. It also adds ways to nest the maps, and configurable mappings of who performs each step. An exporter to the standard notation tool survives round trips. Public and synthetic logs show how the same behavior renders under different groupings. The aim is evidence-grounded requirements work, not model-first guesswork.
arxiv-2606-04550:
Vestrum, Bergh, and Syrdal ask whether online shops can recommend greener products without losing customers, in a 2026 arXiv study of carbon-aware recommendation. Recommenders shape what shoppers buy. But product carbon footprints are almost never known at catalog scale. The authors first estimate footprints with a retrieval-augmented pipeline. It transfers labels from a small set of life-cycle-assessed products to a large unlabeled catalog. It uses semantic search, few-shot prompting, and a nearest-neighbor fallback.

They then re-rank recommendations from three established models. The re-ranking trades predicted engagement against estimated footprint through one tunable parameter. Amazon reviews serve as the engagement proxy. The test covers home and kitchen, sports and outdoors, and electronics. The authors map the Pareto frontier of trade-offs per model and category. Substantial carbon reductions proved achievable at minimal engagement cost everywhere. The headroom varied by model and category.
arxiv-2606-04650:
Fris and colleagues fine-tune how big language models teach small retrievers to handle conversational search, in a 2026 arXiv paper. In conversational search, each query depends on the chat history. Distilling a large model's query-rewriting skill into a learned sparse retriever avoids running the large model at search time. Recent work distills with Kullback-Leibler divergence. This is a softer alignment with the teacher than earlier methods. But its design choices were understudied for this task.

Gains are significant in precision-oriented ranking metrics. The contrastive sampling strategy matters and must be chosen carefully. More samples for estimating the divergence show diminishing returns, despite theory suggesting otherwise. They also fight the loss of sparsity in long conversations with a regularization loss. This substantially improved sparsity and inference efficiency at little cost to effectiveness. On TopiOCQA they halved the computation. Recall at 100 dropped by at most two percent.
arxiv-2606-04850:
Du, Huang, and Zardini unify the design of neural network chips into one framework that treats uncertainty, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Designing a processor is an end-to-end co-design problem: training budget set the workload. The stages are separate, and methodologies are welded to algorithms. Their framework composes four blocks covering training, chip mapping, wafer fabrication, and compute allocation.

Each block exposes only a functionality-resource interface. The central contribution is introducing Confidence as an optimizable resource alongside cost, time, and power. Three case studies validate the approach: Confidence behaves as a tunable knob.
arxiv-2606-04950:
Bernardi and Lanconelli solve a wave equation driven by pure noise, in a 2026 arXiv probability paper. The Tricomi equation changes type between hyperbolic and elliptic, and here it is studied in the hyperbolic half plane perturbed by space-time Gaussian white noise. The question is whether a well-defined random solution exists and what its paths look like. Using a Fourier transform approach, the authors obtain the solution's representation through certain integrals of Airy functions.

Careful asymptotic analysis of those integrals delivers the desired properties: the solution is square integrable, its sample paths are continuous, and it is stationary in the space variable. Notably, and contrary to a recent paper's findings for a related problem, the solution's properties match those derived for the wave operator. So the noise sets the regularity here. The result anchors stochastic Tricomi theory on the same footing as the stochastic wave equation.
arxiv-2606-05450:
Rodolfo Metulini proposes a spatial twist on matrix completion for filling gaps in air quality data, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Monitoring networks lose readings to malfunctions and calibration, and rebuilding the entries matters for exposure assessment and policy. Standard nuclear norm matrix completion exploits the data's low-rank structure to impute gaps, but it treats each monitoring station on its own and ignores the spatial dependence that air pollution has.

The new method, ESFNNMC, extends a fixed-effects filling model by replacing station-specific intercepts with eigenvector spatial filters. These are Moran-type eigenvectors, patterns extracted from the spatial weights matrix, that capture how readings link across space. In simulations varying the missingness pattern, autocorrelation levels, and matrix shapes, the method improved imputation accuracy whenever station differences had genuine spatial structure. It stayed competitive under mild departures from that assumption, and cost about the same.
arxiv-2606-05750:
Jessica Dai and colleagues read three years of the r/ChatGPT forum as a social sensor in a 2026 arXiv paper. The forum opened a day after ChatGPT launched in late 2022. Public adoption of chatbots has since exploded, but its texture is poorly tracked. The team proposes PuLSE, a method for watching social feeds for trends that matter to society. They run the first long-term study of the forum with it.

The broad story is normalization: posts treat ChatGPT as an everyday product, not a marvel. A sharper signal hides inside that calm. Posts seeking mental health support, and posts showing emotional attachment to the bot, rose steadily right after GPT-4o arrived in May 2024. PuLSE could have flagged the rise by October 2024. That was months before OpenAI publicly acknowledged the pattern. A live site updates the tracking daily.
arxiv-2606-05950:
Yuxiao Ye and colleagues train image editors to survive long, messy editing conversations in a 2026 arXiv paper. Real users refine pictures turn by turn, each instruction layered on earlier ones. Models falter two ways: old constraints dilute inside the growing image-text history, and early mistakes contaminate later turns. Edit-R2 attacks both with reinforcement learning on unified multimodal models.

Before each turn, the model reconstructs the session's operative intent as an explicit reasoning trace. Scattered constraints become one readable summary the editor can follow. Training optimizes text reasoning and image generation under a single objective. A trajectory filter discards corrupted rollouts so contamination cannot teach bad habits. The team also built MICE-Bench to score instruction following, content consistency, and global awareness across turns. Experiments showed substantial gains in multi-turn editing quality. Session memory, made explicit, is the paper's central trick.
arxiv-2606-06050:
Habermehl and Loulergue teach a machine to infer symbolic automata from examples alone in a 2026 arXiv paper. Symbolic automata label transitions with predicates, so they handle endless alphabets like numbers or signs. Passive learning means no oracle answers questions; a sample must suffice. Their method SAI targets monotonic algebras, where predicates are interval bounds on an ordered value.

SAI extends the classic RPNI state-merging framework to the symbolic setting. A splitting step, borrowed from a timed-automata learner, lets it refine transitions top-down while inferring predicates. Merging proposes broad guesses; splitting corrects overreach. SAI provably identifies the target automaton in the limit. Characteristic samples of polynomial size suffice to force the answer. Such guarantees matter for checking, where learned models feed safety checks. Software over endless data domains is the motivating use. It lifts a thirty-year-old learning framework into the symbolic world, keeping its speed.
arxiv-2606-06150:
Adrien Busnot Laurent and Sébastien Macé design numerical methods for sampling on curved spaces in this 2026 arXiv paper. A Riemannian manifold is a smooth curved space, like a sphere, where ordinary flat-space algorithms need rethinking. Ergodic dynamics wander such a space so that long-run averages settle on a target distribution, which is exactly what samplers such as Riemannian Langevin dynamics need. Accuracy of the long-run distribution matters more than tracking any single path.

Older methods embed the space in flat coordinates or project back onto it, adding cost and distortion. The new frozen-flow methods work intrinsically, using only geodesics, the shortest paths on the surface, and parallel transport to move vectors along them. The authors derive order conditions with a new algebraic operation on exotic Lie-Butcher series. Their experiments reach second-order accuracy for the invariant measure at reduced cost compared with earlier approaches.
arxiv-2606-06350:
Zhihao Wu and co-authors train language models to grade student answers by the rules in this 2026 arXiv paper. A trustworthy grader must tie every judgement to the mark scheme and to evidence in the answer, not just land near the right score. Existing training methods, built for self contained math reasoning, cannot spot which step of a grading chain went wrong, or how the model's belief about the final mark drifts.

Their framework, Edit, works in two phases. First it finds faulty steps using internal signals: the model's running belief over the final mark, and how grounded each step is in the input. It then rewrites only those steps against a rubric checklist. A reinforcement phase penalizes large harmful belief swings while allowing useful exploration. On two real multi subject grading benchmarks, Edit beat strong fine tuning and reinforcement baselines in and out of domain.
arxiv-2606-06450:
Jackson Butler and co-authors report a missing member of an exotic quantum family in this 2026 arXiv paper on condensed matter physics. The fractional quantum anomalous Hall effect appears in layered materials where electrons, driven by topology and mutual repulsion, form states at fractional fillings without any magnetic field. The one third filling state is the most robust of all in conventional quantum Hall systems, yet it had never been seen in its anomalous cousins. Its absence cast doubt on how the two effects relate.

In five layer rhombohedral graphene aligned to boron nitride, the team combined capacitance and transport measurements at thirty nine millikelvin. Tuning an electric displacement field revealed the one third fractional Chern insulator state, with gapless integer states nearby. A phase transition out of that state appeared as the field changed.
arxiv-2606-06550:
Shuanglin Li, Ruxiao Qian, and Siyang Song listen for feelings in the geometry of features in this 2026 arXiv paper on speech emotion recognition. Self supervised models turn speech into rich feature vectors. Summarizing an utterance usually means averaging them, which assumes the features vary on their own. They do not: how features move together carries emotional signatures. The authors' Second Order Correlation layer replaces averaging with covariance descriptors, matrices recording those joint movements.

Those descriptors live on a curved space, awkward for standard classifiers. A Log Euclidean mapping flattens them into a tangent space where plain linear learning works. Tests on the ESD and RAVDESS emotion datasets showed the layer recovers information that first order pooling throws away. It beat first order baselines again and again. Respecting feature geometry, the authors conclude, matters for solid emotion recognition from voice.
arxiv-2606-06750:
Brain tissue, hydrogels, and buried rock share one trait: they are sponges that bend. Barnafi, Rubiano, and Ruiz-Baier model such materials, called poroelastic media, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their focus is the case where the solid skeleton cannot change volume, an incompressibility condition that breaks some standard formulations of the theory and makes the equations inconsistent.

Starting from the fully nonlinear theory and simplifying it in a careful order, the authors derive a linear model that keeps the key couplings between fluid pressure and solid motion. The model tracks porosity and total pressure alongside displacement, and its tidy saddle point structure allows the simplest possible finite element spaces, the building blocks of computer simulation, while staying stable. They also build fast solvers on a Schur complement scheme and confirm the whole approach with numerical tests in two and three dimensions, aimed at brain mechanics.
arxiv-2606-06850:
Restoring a damaged face photo on a cheap phone chip is a tight squeeze. Li and co-authors present CFRNet in this 2026 arXiv paper. It is a small restorer built for consumer neural processing units. Big rival systems give fine quality but resist those chips. Their operators are hard to compile and quantize.

CFRNet has only two million parameters. Its trick is a new training scheme, not a bigger network. The scheme trains the model as a fixed point operator. Running a restored face through it again should change nothing. Three losses enforce that habit, plus steady supervision across cycles. On three hundred test images, it earned the best perceptual score. Its detail score at three cycles beat one cycle by about thirty one percent. It ran in about twenty three milliseconds per cycle on the target chip. Rival baselines could not compile there at all.
arxiv-2606-06950:
Fancier scans are not always better medicine. Hoq and co-authors test that idea for lung cancer screening in this 2026 arXiv paper. They compare image models fed two dimensional slices, small slice stacks, or full three dimensional volumes. Both convolutional networks and vision transformers enter the contest. All train under one fixed protocol.

The data came from a national lung screening cohort of nearly two thousand patients. Extra support came from a public nodule data set. The middle option won the balance contest. A 2.5D convolutional model, using thin slice stacks, discriminated most steadily. Full 3D models showed unstable decision thresholds. Transformers sometimes collapsed into predicting one class for everyone. Confidence ranges were wide and overlapped, so the authors avoid crown claims. They offer a resource performance frontier and a taxonomy of failure modes instead.
arxiv-2606-07150:
Encrypting what AI agents say still exposes who talks to whom, and that pattern can betray the mission. Dangol argues the real risk is workflow integrity in this 2026 arXiv paper. Agent protocols standardize messages but ride on address based transport. Endpoints are often labeled by capability, and workflows chain in recognizable shapes.

An observer watching only metadata can spot a recurring workflow from its opening moves. The task being assembled, and the action likely to follow, become predictable. Because agents act at machine speed, the observer can intervene before completion. The paper builds a threat model and defines privacy properties for transport layers. On real multi-agent traffic, a classifier recovered task classes six times above chance. It needed only the start of each interaction. Defense aware attackers barely dented the leakage. Only the full property set pushed recovery toward chance. Content protection, the author concludes, is half a defense.
arxiv-2606-07550:
Yang Fu and co-authors create the first standardized benchmark for learning fusion plasma controllers from data, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A tokamak's plasma cannot be tuned by trial and error on the machine, since experiments are costly and risky, so offline reinforcement learning from discharge records is attractive. Until now no benchmark existed for long-horizon plasma control. Their RL4F benchmark provides closed-loop evaluation environments whose dynamics are built from discharge data from the DIII-D tokamak in California.

4 tracking tasks structure the tests: controlling rotation, density, temperature, and pressure profiles. A suite of imitation learning and offline reinforcement learning baselines was compared under one protocol. Model-based offline methods, which learn a dynamics model and plan against it, achieved the best performance on most objectives. No method dominated every task, showing how much dynamics modeling matters for control. Code, data, and the framework are open-sourced.
arxiv-2606-07650:
Shaikh, Ni, and Dacier plant traps inside video games to catch a cheat anti-cheat software cannot see, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Aimbots aim by running detection on screen captures, never touching game memory, so kernel defenses detect nothing. Their system, PATCH, deploys patches as honeytokens to trigger the cheater's detector. A triggered patch exposes the cheat or floods the cheater's viewport with false targets until the game becomes unplayable, converting the cheat's vision model into the detection surface.

Testing in a game built on an engine, the patches detected cheaters at rates above 90 percent in white-box settings for all patch sizes. Across detector models the patches transferred, with detection in the 60 to 90 percent range by configuration, and scaling was checked across screen resolutions and cheat setups. The strategy is proactive: instead of hunting cheats after the fact, the game is seeded with bait a machine eye would bite.
arxiv-2606-07750:
The Euclid Collaboration, with Laloux as lead author, uses the Euclid telescope's first quick data release to catalogue active galactic nuclei and their host galaxies, in this 2026 arXiv paper. An active galactic nucleus is a bright galactic centre powered by an accreting black hole. Fitting spectral energy distributions, the pattern of light across wavelengths, yields their properties, but for such objects those fits are notoriously unreliable.

The team built mock spectra from observed quasars and galaxies to score how trustworthy each fitted property is. Applied to roughly one million candidate nuclei, a reliability cut at one half leaves eighty-eight percent of sources with robust stellar masses. Seventy-six percent keep reliable nucleus luminosities. A selection on the nucleus's share of mid-infrared light reached eighty-five percent completeness and purity together. Different identification methods probe quite different mass and brightness ranges, a warning against relying on any single one.
arxiv-2606-07850:
Adhikari, Noorsumar, and Jensen automate the full life of a finite element simulation through conversation, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their system, PDE-Agents, fields three specialist language-model agents, for simulation, analytics, and database work, under a supervisor graph. A knowledge graph with material properties, known failure patterns, and past runs gives the agents memory.

The claims are tested rather than asserted. A verification study confirms second-order spatial convergence for the heat-equation solver on all three benchmarks, the accuracy expected of a correct implementation. In a fifty-task ablation, smart use of the knowledge graph reached one hundred percent success, against lower rates with the graph off or always on. Its physics score was about ninety-three hundredths, versus eighty-five hundredths with the graph disabled. The authors also validate the model-agnostic design across two generations of open-source models on local hardware.
arxiv-2606-08150:
Bingxuan Dai, Hongsong Wang, and Jie Gui let engineers describe a material in words and receive its structure, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Three-dimensional metamaterial microstructures can be tuned for remarkable traits, but designing them takes skill, simulation loops, and manual adjustment. Automatic inverse design exists, yet its structures often lack diversity or feasibility.

Their diffusion model generates structures directly from text, using the prompt for both semantic guidance and property targets. To keep outputs faithful, they apply a dual matching strategy: contrastive text-structure matching in training, and test-time reward-guided matching while generating. Experiments show the model produces meaningful and plausible structures across many material types. The authors see it as a step toward interactive design, where a designer converses with the generator. You type what you want, and it drafts a small part for you to test.
arxiv-2606-08350:
Ruiyi Zhou and co-authors make an advanced equation for light absorption in materials tractable, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Bethe-Salpeter equation is the standard tool for computing how materials absorb light when electron-hole pairs, called excitons, interact strongly. Most past work uses a static approximation for the screened Coulomb interaction. But when excitons bind tightly, screening changes with time and that approximation is questionable. Solving the fully dynamical equation for crystals has been very expensive.

The authors formulate an all-electron version of the dynamical equation using an atom-centered orbital basis set. Electrons are described by functions tied to each atom rather than plane waves. Including all electrons, rather than freezing deep core states, matters for accuracy where dynamical effects are strongest. The aim is to make exciton physics usable for large systems at last.
arxiv-2606-08450:
Yanyan Wu and a large team use language models to design the inputs and rewards of a trading agent, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Financial portfolio trading is naturally a reinforcement learning problem: an agent sequentially rebalances assets under changing market conditions. In non-stationary markets, however, raw price-and-volume states under-specify the learning problem, leaving the agent to rediscover basic financial knowledge from sparse feedback. Their framework, GIFT, uses a large language model as a guided interface between the market and the learner.

The language model injects financial knowledge into both state representation and reward design. Richer states can encode regime information that raw price bars omit, and shaped rewards can penalize risk exposures that a simple return signal rewards by luck. The authors argue the interface, rather than the trading algorithm itself, is the bottleneck in financial reinforcement learning.
arxiv-2606-08550:
Jijun Huang, Bing Huang, and Song Li show that making diamond thinner can stabilize the quantum defects inside it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Group-IV vacancy centers in diamond, where a silicon, germanium, tin, or lead atom sits beside a missing carbon, are promising interfaces between electron spins and photons. Their neutral charge state is the useful one, but stabilizing it usually requires stringent Fermi-level engineering in high-purity boron-doped diamond, a serious materials-growth challenge.

Using first-principles calculations, the authors demonstrate that dimensional confinement in diamane, an ultrathin diamond film, offers an alternative route with no intentional doping. Quantum confinement and surface termination cooperate to tune the host band gap and push the occupied defect states upward. This enlarges the stability window of the neutral charge state. Varying film thickness and surface termination systematically tunes the electronic structure, giving growers two practical knobs.
arxiv-2606-08650:
Cheng Zhang and Zhifei Zhu bound how strongly a vibrating torus can concentrate on a smaller surface, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Toral eigenfunctions are the standing waves of the flat torus, built from lattice waves. Restriction estimates bound their size on a submanifold relative to their size on the whole space. Such estimates connect analysis to number theory, because the frequencies are lattice points in spherical regions. The authors establish new restriction estimates in the mean-square sense for toral eigenfunctions.

The estimates are sharp in certain cases. They prove a conjecture of Huang and Zhang for smooth submanifolds of large codimension, and give new progress toward a conjecture of Bourgain and Rudnick. The proof combines a slicing and packing method with approximation of the discrete spherical multiplier by tools developed by Magyar, Stein, and Wainger.
arxiv-2606-08950:
Ockerman and colleagues find that vector databases, workhorses of AI search, scale badly on supercomputers, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A vector database stores embeddings, numerical fingerprints of data, and answers similarity queries for tasks like molecular search. The leading systems were designed for cloud servers, not high-performance computing clusters. The team benchmarked Qdrant, Milvus, and Weaviate on two production supercomputers, scaling to 256 distributed workers across 64 nodes, with mixed read-write workloads and a real scientific dataset.

The results expose a scaling paradox. Adding cores could reduce query throughput by up to 30.67 percent, so more hardware sometimes meant slower service. Growing from 16 to 256 workers, a sixteenfold increase, yielded only a 5.46-fold improvement in throughput. Workload characteristics, not raw compute, capped the latency gains. The authors conclude that cloud-oriented designs fundamentally mismatch HPC systems, and they call for vector databases designed with supercomputers in mind from the start.
arxiv-2606-09150:
Xue and colleagues stream generated video at resolutions beyond today's real-time models, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Autoregressive video diffusion models produce video chunk by chunk for live streaming, but are stuck near 480p. UltraFlash cascades a super-resolution stage after a low-resolution generator, reaching about 30 FPS at 1K and 18 FPS at 2K on a single GPU.

Three contributions make the cascade work. First, training converts a text-to-video model into an upscaling model, preserving its generative ability, via a degradation pipeline mimicking AI-video artifacts. Second, a causal latent upsampler with a high-resolution decoder scales the latent representation, keeping frames coherent. Third, distillation compresses that model to single-step generation, with preference tuning and dynamic cache management. Experiments show state-of-the-art quality streaming, for live preview and game content creation.
arxiv-2606-09250:
Cao and colleagues restore blurry video to high quality by barely touching the giant model doing the work, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Video super-resolution adapts pretrained generators to enhance low-quality footage, but fine-tuning a huge diffusion transformer is computationally prohibitive. Shortcuts disappoint: direct low-to-high mapping demands extensive fine-tuning, and ControlNet-style adapters must duplicate the backbone, lacking an encoder-decoder split to exploit.

Flow matching predicts a constant velocity field across timesteps, so adaptation reduces to one fixed injection pattern, not time-varying transformations. The diffusion transformer stays completely frozen; only a lightweight state-aware adapter trains. Dual streams extract static cues from the low-quality input and dynamic cues from denoising states, cross-attention aligning them, shifting from structure to texture. Result: competitive quality with only 11.25 percent trainable parameters, 12 GPU-hours on one A100, and single-step sampling.
arxiv-2606-09550:
Shaoyang Cui introduces InquiTree, a test environment that checks whether AI agents can actually do science rather than recite it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Static benchmarks often reward rote recall, so Cui casts scientific inquiry as movement through a research tree. These directed graphs encode the logical dependencies among forming a hypothesis, designing a study, interpreting results, and updating beliefs, and are derived from real papers.

Agents were evaluated on a test pool of thirty papers, with an open subset of eighteen released publicly. Two flaws stood out. First, over long sessions the agents developed cognitive tunnelling: their critical judgement and anomaly detection eroded compared with their own baselines, a pattern Cui names the erosion of marginal capabilities. Second, performance dropped on papers published after the models' training cutoffs, exposing a boundary between interpolation and genuine extrapolation.
arxiv-2606-09650:
Animesh Sah, Mohamed Rameez, and Subir Sarkar argue that a known bias in supernova data flips a key cosmic verdict in this 2026 arXiv paper. Type Ia supernovae are standard candles used to track cosmic expansion. The headline result for decades has been speedup: the expansion is gaining pace. The team's past work found the signal mostly points one way, aligned with our local bulk flow.

Here they fix a bias in the Pantheon+ list. Older parent stars make these blasts shine a bit dimmer, and the mean age shifts with distance. Applying age fixes that grow with redshift moved the broad component of the slowing measure into positive ground. That reads as a universe that is slowing, not speeding. The local one-way part barely moved. Their claim strikes at the dark energy story built on these candles. It rests on how well the age fix can be trusted.
arxiv-2606-09850:
Aarush Sinha and his co-authors open up six alignment methods to see how each one rewires a language model inside in this 2026 arXiv paper. Alignment tuning is most often graded by outputs alone. That hides how the tuning reshapes inner computation. The team probe three open model families with layer-wise tests, sparse autoencoders, and crosscoders, tools that map where choice signals live.

Choice signals pooled in early-mid or mid-late layers across the board. The reshaping past that point split by method. KTO and GRPO sharpened the split between liked and disliked replies, by shared features and sparse, loud recruits. DPO and ORPO blurred that split, by turning the geometry and muting features. PPO and SimPO left the base layout near intact. The same method also bent unlike builds in unlike ways.
arxiv-2606-09950:
Lei draws a parallel between neural network theory and nuclear physics, in a 2026 arXiv paper on mathematical foundations. Averaging a network over random parameters, he argues, equals removing a sector from a physics problem, an operation algebra calls a Schur complement. For a closed sector, that returns a covariance and its inverse. The open case, where probability leaks away, is missing from network theory.

Nuclear reaction theory supplies the open case through the optical model, an effective description that tracks exactly what a system loses to unmodeled channels. Lei builds the full dictionary for the closed case, linking the neural tangent kernel to a sensitivity kernel and the infinite-width limit to a Gaussian-process emulator. He then tests the open export on attention maps, transfer operators, and expert routers, with a mostly negative result: useful uncertainty is epistemic, rooted in the closed half.
arxiv-2606-10050:
Salehi rethinks a stubborn step in three-dimensional graphics: assigning each surface point a flat map coordinate, called UV unwrapping, in a 2026 arXiv paper on geometry processing. Traditional solvers optimize distortion directly and can fail through bad starts, local minima, or foldovers where the map flips onto itself. His approach reparameterizes the problem continuously: an untrained neural network called a SIREN maps mesh features to UV coordinates, and its weights are tuned for a geometric objective instead.

The solver recipe combines spectral inputs, a warm-up stage, an injectivity barrier that penalizes foldovers, and validity-checked retries with fallbacks. On compact pre-cut charts it produced zero flips everywhere, and on a stratified forty-seven-chart benchmark it delivered forty-two valid zero-flip solves. A large run produced one thousand strictly valid atlases with zero flips after fallback routing.
arxiv-2606-10250:
