Chung and Lee dissect class imbalance in federated learning into three levels and design a remedy for each, in a 2026 arXiv paper on distributed machine learning. Class imbalance degrades deep learning in general and is a critical driver of non-identical data spreads across federated clients, where each client's data skews in its own way. They define inter-case imbalance within each class, inter-class imbalance between classes, and inter-client imbalance in how skewness differs across clients.

A Positive Negative Balanced loss addresses inter-case and inter-class imbalance during local training by weighting minority cases and classes more heavily. That improves reach on skewed client data for both multi-label and multi-class tasks. Client Balanced Reweighting then adjusts aggregation weights, favoring models trained on less skewed datasets. Experiments on X-ray and natural image datasets show FedBB outperforming other methods in scores and speed.
arxiv-2606-10950:
Boros and colleagues test a new way to read reactor fluctuations in this 2026 arXiv paper. Neutron noise methods extract kinetic parameters, like the prompt neutron decay constant, from random wiggles in neutron counts. At high rates, though, pulse counting suffers pile-up and dead time. The team instead analyzes the detector's continuous current, correcting pulse-shape distortions with detector pairs or deconvolution.

Simulations recover the decay constant accurately at rates where pulse counting fails, and reach far higher values than before. Experiments at the KUCA and BME TR research reactors confirm unbiased results despite dead time and electronic artifacts. The limits now sit in the acquisition hardware, not the method.
arxiv-2606-11050:
J. de Curtò and I. de Zarzà present a 2026 arXiv simulation of demand response in smart microgrids, small local power networks. Demand response means persuading households that both use and produce power, called prosumers, to cut use at peak times. They frame the choice as a repeated Prisoner's Dilemma, a game where cooperation pays but self-interest tempts defection, played across a network of unlike agents.

Their LLM Influence Compiler turns policy into structured directives for agents whose choices mix game-theoretic odds with a language model's reading of each message. Structured directives won demand-cutting cooperation in 33.3 percent of cases, against 27.0 percent for loose messaging and 28.0 percent with no intervention at all. Sending messages through well-connected hub members beat random targeting at every resistance level tested. Idealist agents were persuaded in about 85 percent of exchanges, while skeptics and opportunists yielded in fewer than 5 percent.
arxiv-2606-11150:
Liu and five co-authors present ABC-Bench in a 2026 arXiv paper, a benchmark measuring what AI agents can do in biology, for good and ill. Language model agents now perform computer-based biology tasks once needing experts. That skill promises faster discovery and shifts biosecurity risk, since the same abilities could help build harmful organisms.

The benchmark tests agents on benign and dual-use tasks. They write code to run liquid handling robots, design DNA fragments for lab assembly, and try evading DNA synthesis screening, the checks blocking dangerous orders. Every tested agent beat the median expert baseliner on all three tasks. Agents excelled on published-knowledge tasks and did worse where novel bioinformatics reasoning was needed. In three wet-lab experiments, scripts from OpenAI's o4-mini-high ran on an OpenTrons robot and assembled DNA with the expected sequences, proof the skill transfers to the physical lab.
arxiv-2606-11350:
Subedi, Abdelaty, and Sheshappanavar diagnose a scaling failure of retrieval-augmented generation in a 2026 arXiv paper. RAG degrades on large, mixed document collections, where dense similarity loses discriminative power and top-k retrieval returns chunks similar in meaning but wrong in context. They name this failure vector search dilution. They saw it firsthand in a deployed Wyoming Department of Transportation corpus, where scaling from 54 to 1,128 documents cut accuracy from 75 percent to below 40 percent.

Their fix, MASDR-RAG, scopes retrieval by domain using domain metadata. On 200 expert-validated queries across five backbones, six corpora, and two index stacks, domain scoping improved precision at ten from 0.77 to 0.86. Multi-agent setups, by contrast, gave highly varied results, a precision-faithfulness paradox. Their practical recommendation is simple: scope first, then make a single synthesis call. Full multi-agent orchestration should be reserved for genuinely multi-domain corpora paired with native-tool-call backbones.
arxiv-2606-11450:
Sun, Cheng, Zhang, Dong, Li, and Wang propose faster self-supervised learning for skeleton-based action recognition in a 2026 arXiv paper. Masked skeleton reconstruction models are strong representation learners, but must predict an exceedingly large number of spatiotemporal patches, prolonging training. Treating all regions equally distracts them from the critical motion patterns behind action semantics. Their Adaptive Masked Reconstruction framework attacks both problems.

First, they decouple the decoder from the encoder, enabling flexible prediction of larger patches and sharply reducing reconstruction complexity. Larger patches are harder to predict, so an adaptive guidance module identifies regions of high motion informativeness, focusing on the most discriminative parts of each patch. Experiments on NTU RGB+D 60, NTU RGB+D 120, and PKU-MMD show faster pre-training and better downstream recognition, surpassing current state-of-the-art approaches. The authors frame AMR as a simple yet efficient pre-training design for skeleton data.
arxiv-2606-11650:
Handi Zhang and four colleagues build fast stand-ins for physics simulations in this 2026 arXiv paper. A surrogate model mimics an expensive partial differential equation solver in near real time, but conventional simulators also offer error control that data-driven models usually lack. The team's surrogates preserve physical structure, especially conservation laws, by construction.

A lightweight transformer prescribes a reduced finite element space, the mesh-based blocks of standard simulation, using forms that respect conservation exactly. A Gaussian process, a probabilistic model giving uncertainty with its predictions, then learns how states map to fluxes between volumes. Training poses an optimal recovery problem with conservation as a hard constraint. The payoff is a Dirichlet-to-Neumann map, linking boundary values to boundary fluxes, with closed-form formulas for the uncertainty afterwards. Error bounds for the method are proved, and numerical experiments show the uncertainty estimates track the true errors well.
arxiv-2606-11950:
Antik Bhattacharya, Jürgen Horbach and Smarajit Karmakar chart a research programme for dense active matter in this 2026 arXiv perspective article. Active matter consists of particles that consume energy to move themselves. Dilute active systems are well understood, but dense ones, active glasses and solids, defy conventional theory.

Two puzzles stand out. Density fluctuations at long wavelengths look anomalously large, an apparent strengthening of a classic fluctuation effect. And shaking an active solid with oscillatory shear anneals it, improves its structure, much as activity itself does. The authors propose building equilibrium-style Hamiltonian models of active systems as reference frameworks, then mapping the route from those models to genuinely non-equilibrium behaviour. Comparative studies of shear in active and passive solids, plus work on chiral active matter, complete the roadmap. Establishing the activity-shear correspondence across systems would reveal universal large-scale physics and guide the design of adaptive materials.
arxiv-2606-12250:
Antoni Lasik and co-authors rebuild a medical exam benchmark to find out whether top language models really know medicine, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multiple-choice tests can flatter models, since options invite guessing and elimination tricks. The team expands Polish medical exams with over 15,000 new questions, two new domains, and four structural changes that strip away those artifacts. Twenty-one models then face the harder setup in both English and Polish versions.

Scores fall sharply. The best model, a Qwen system, drops by 28.4 points on the English exam and 31 points on the Polish one under the stricter design. Little sign of test contamination appears, so the gap is not cheating. Standard multiple-choice scores, the authors conclude, do not reliably reflect true medical competence. Exam design itself moves results as much as model quality. The benchmark is released publicly so other teams can test models under the tougher conditions.
arxiv-2606-12350:
Edwards and Togelius study what writers do when an AI offers words they are punished for taking, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Writing tools increasingly suggest the next word as people type. Whether users keep their own voice or drift toward the machine's is poorly understood. Their game, Nonslop, flips the usual assistant design: set in a dystopia where an AI harvests human individuality, it penalizes accepting AI suggestions. Seventy-four participants produced 214 responses under this inverted pressure.

Most players rarely touched the suggestions. In nearly three quarters of submissions, no transgression, no accepted AI word, occurred at all. Aggregated per user, the majority consistently protected their own phrasing despite the effort. Because the game punishes the lazy default, it reveals authentic preferences instead of mere convenience. The setup offers a reusable framework for studying human-AI creative tension: efficiency pulls one way, authenticity the other.
arxiv-2606-12650:
Ratnayaka and colleagues introduce nomp, a framework for building domain-specific compilers, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Programmers face a trade-off with graphics processors: low-level languages such as CUDA give fine control and speed but are hard to learn, while high-level tools are easier yet often slower. A domain-specific compiler targets one field, reusing optimisation patterns that recur there.

Nomp pairs a pragma-based model, where programmers annotate C code with directives, with a runtime that transforms and generates code from user-supplied metadata. The team demonstrates it on Nekbone, a fluid-dynamics mini-application, running on an AMD GPU in the Frontier supercomputer. Nomp reaches more than ninety percent of the hand-tuned version's performance across their cases, while needing notably fewer lines of code, evidence that productivity need not cost much speed.
arxiv-2606-13350:
Bézard and a team report an unidentified feature on Titan and Pluto in this 2026 arXiv paper. Titan, Saturn's largest moon, hides its surface beneath a nitrogen and methane atmosphere. The James Webb Space Telescope's sensitivity opens an atmospheric window near 5 micrometres where the surface can peek through. The team selected spectra from the centre of Titan's disk and compared them with a radiative transfer model, a calculation of how light travels through gas and haze. Pluto, with a thin Titan-like atmosphere, offers a comparison.

Both instruments on Webb detected an absorption dip centred at about 5.11 micrometres on Titan that the model does not explain. The feature is several percent deep and narrow, with a width given to high precision. A similar signature is investigated in Pluto's spectrum. Because the carrier of the absorption remains unidentified, the result poses a puzzle about the composition of both worlds.
arxiv-2606-13450:
Sathvik Udupa and colleagues propose predicting when a speaker is about to finish talking in this 2026 arXiv paper. Spoken dialogue systems usually work as a cascade: listen, think, speak. Their latency bottleneck is reactive turn-completion detection, which waits until the user has stopped before the system starts preparing a reply. Endpoint Anticipation instead forecasts the end of a turn in advance from the speech signal. The model can anticipate endpoints more than two seconds early, letting the language model and speech synthesiser start speculatively on partial context.

The authors introduce metrics that quantify the trade-off between realised latency reduction and wasted computation when a forecast proves wrong. Across conversational and task-oriented datasets, their model consistently beats baselines built on voice activity projection. Integrated with the Unmute dialogue framework, it cut average response latency by about half a second. Speculative computation rose by a quarter in exchange.
arxiv-2606-13550:
Jung and Wang present a retrieval framework for answering questions over long documents in this 2026 arXiv paper. Retrieval-augmented generation grounds language model answers in retrieved passages. The granularity of those passages is a dilemma. Large chunks preserve context but drag in irrelevant text that dilutes the evidence. Small chunks are compact yet often lack the lexical or semantic cues needed to be found. Their framework, UMG-RAG, treats chunk granularity as reliability estimated for each query. It is training-free and leaves the generator untouched.

Dense and sparse retrievers act as complementary experts across chunk sizes. For each query, every expert's score list becomes an evidence distribution, and its entropy, a measure of spread, estimates reliability. Candidates are fused according to semantic, lexical, and granularity confidence. The design targets long-document question answering, where the evidence may sit in a short passage that retrieval buries.
arxiv-2606-13850:
Patel and Damiano extend hidden Markov models so exact reasoning survives real-world path rules. These models infer hidden states from sequences, but their core assumption breaks under constraints spanning the whole path. Rules like required ordering, visit counts, or monotone progress create long-range links standard algorithms cannot handle exactly. Their 2026 arXiv paper compiles each constraint into a finite-state controller tracking the minimal history the rule needs.

Standard forward-backward and Viterbi algorithms then run on the enlarged chain, giving exact constrained answers in discrete and continuous time. Four guarantees are proved: exactness, monotone gains in constrained learning, cost linear in controller size, and a deviation bound under wrong constraints. A catalog covers eleven constraint families. Tests against six rival decoders on three real tasks reveal a clean split. Only controller augmentation recovers valid paths under cumulative constraints. Simpler decoders suffice for local ones.
arxiv-2606-13950:
Fiorentini explains how missing oxygen atoms change the charge state of vanadium inside a promising material. Hafnia, hafnium oxide, can be made ferroelectric, and doping it with vanadium may add magnetism, giving a rare multiferroic. Experiments show vanadium in both three-plus and four-plus states. His 2026 arXiv paper uses first-principles calculations on the doped material with oxygen vacancies.

Oxygen vacancies donate electrons to low-lying vanadium gap states. That lowers the cost of forming vacancies and converts nominal four-plus vanadium centers into three-plus ones. Computed local magnetization and core-level shifts match the measured signatures for both states. Yet vacancies alone match the seen three-plus to four-plus ratio, about two point eight near six percent doping, only under strongly reducing conditions. Extra electron sources likely act during growth. The same mechanism may explain magnetism in chromium-doped hafnia.
arxiv-2606-14050:
Yinjun-Wang and Udell ask whether suspicious battery bids really signal market power. Grid batteries submit stepwise buy and sell curves a day ahead; bids withholding energy can look strategic. Their 2026 arXiv paper models a price-taking battery choosing quantity-price pairs to maximize a mean-CVaR objective, balancing average profit against worst-case losses, under few price scenarios. A mixed-integer formulation has an exact linear reformulation, making analysis tractable.

Three findings follow. Withholding arises without market power: scarce stored energy plus uncertain prices raise the value of holding charge. Uncertainty cuts both ways: scarce stored energy raises sell prices; abundance can lower them. Risk management layers the bid curve, securing execution across scenarios while keeping exposure to rare spikes. In California data, discharge capability grew from about five hundred megawatts in 2020 to roughly thirteen thousand by late 2024. Monitors should separate risk-adjusted bidding from true market power.
arxiv-2606-14750:
Adarsh Arigala and co-authors make speech from text shown as pictures in a 2026 arXiv paper. Pixel-based language models show text as images. Look-alike letters then get like embeddings, even when their codes differ. That helps transfer across tongues and unseen letters. Usual token embeddings fail there. They need growth when adapted.

Pixel-TTS applies the idea to text-to-speech. Text is drawn as an image. A small two-dimensional filter layer turns it into embeddings for the speech maker. The design drops embedding growth during fine-tuning. It stands up better to unseen letters and odd spellings. Wide tests show scores on par with strong baselines. Training settles faster. Zero-shot transfer to new writing systems is robust. The authors suggest visual grounding is a practical base for speech tools in many tongues.
arxiv-2606-14950:
Pescuma and coauthors extend a wave solver called CHDG to a class of problems in a 2026 study. The solver uses a hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin method, which keeps only face variables in the global system. Standard versions put a numerical flux on each face, which slows iterative solution. CHDG instead uses a transmission variable tied to the physics of waves crossing each face.

The authors generalize the approach from the Helmholtz equation to time-harmonic wave problems with constant coefficients. They prove the hybridized system is well-posed and that a fixed-point iteration contracts toward the solution. The test case is the linearized Euler equations with a uniform subsonic mean flow, which carries both sound and vorticity waves. Two-dimensional benchmarks compare iterative schemes across settings. The fixed-point scheme always converges, runs nearly as fast as GMRES, and beats solving the discontinuous Galerkin system.
arxiv-2606-15150:
Chandra and coauthors re-examine the gravitational-wave event GW231123 in a 2026 astrophysics paper. The signal came from two black holes merging into the heaviest remnant yet detected. Standard analyses found both black holes spinning near the maximum possible rate. Such extreme spins strain formation theories. The catch is that standard waveform models ignore orbital eccentricity near merger. The authors test whether eccentricity could masquerade as extreme spin.

They re-analyze the event with eccentric templates from numerical relativity simulations. Eccentric signals with modest spins can be recovered as near-maximally spinning round-orbit systems. The missing eccentric features get absorbed into inflated spin estimates. A ringdown analysis, using only the remnant's vibrations, gives unbiased properties instead. For the real event, round-orbit templates still fit best. Yet the ringdown shows a second likelihood peak tied to large eccentricity. Better eccentric models are needed before the event's nature is settled.
arxiv-2606-15250:
Hu and coauthors automate lower-limb alignment measurement from knee radiographs in a 2026 medical imaging paper. Alignment angles guide joint health assessment and knee replacement planning. Manual measurement is slow, and learning methods hunt a fixed set of anatomical landmarks. Changing a clinical definition then forces costly re-annotation of training images. The authors instead encode each knee's shape into a compact latent code. Their implicit neural shape functions regress alignment angles from those codes.

The model trained on five hundred sixty-six radiographs with femur and tibia outlines. It matched landmark-based methods and human agreement levels on internal tests. On an external set of four hundred two cases, performance dipped. The authors link that dip to population differences between the cohorts. The latent codes correlated strongly with two of the three angles. Because no landmarks are hard-coded, new measurements can be added without rebuilding the model.
arxiv-2606-15650:
Kapelinski and colleagues present AnonShield in 2026, an on-premise system that strips identifying details from vulnerability scan data that security teams share. Such reports are laced with personal data, addresses, hostnames, and credentials, which collide with privacy law when data crosses organizations. AnonShield pseudonymizes reports where they sit, using GPU-accelerated entity recognition with streaming and caching.

On datasets up to five hundred fifty megabytes and seventy-one thousand records, it cuts processing from ninety-two hours to under ten minutes, a speedup of more than seven hundred times. Its best strategies reach an F1 score near ninety-four percent with recall near ninety-seven percent, so little analytical value is lost. Even on CPU-only hardware the speedup stays above five hundred times. The result makes compliant sharing practical in real response workflows, though formal privacy models still fit incident data better than raw vulnerability records.
arxiv-2606-15850:
Petkevičius proves a zero-one law for multifractal spectra in 2026, showing when the fractal fingerprint of a random process is not random at all. The spectrum records, for each roughness exponent, the fractal dimension of the times showing it. For fractional Brownian motion the spectrum is the same on every sample path, but no general theorem said when this happens.

The obstacle: the exponent is defined through infinitesimal behaviour, living in a germ sigma-algebra zero-one laws cannot reach. Kolmogorov's law needs tail events; Hewitt-Savage needs exchangeability. Petkevičius instead uses an accumulation integral over scales, built from a derivative, which concentrates almost surely under a decorrelation condition. The condition is sharp: it fails exactly for log-correlated fields, the boundary case. Fractional Brownian motion satisfies all conditions, and Lévy stable processes recover their known spectra. The result gives multifractal analysis a determinism criterion.
arxiv-2606-16350:
Charak and co-authors prove new tests in 2026 for when families of harmonic mappings behave normally, a core property in complex analysis. Harmonic mappings extend analytic functions to maps with both analytic and co-analytic parts. Working in the unit disk, the authors first establish a new condition for normality that involves extended spherical derivatives. They then prove a Zalcman-Pang type rescaling lemma adapted to phi-normal harmonic mappings.

Rescaling lemmas convert a failure of normality into a concrete limiting object, the standard engine behind such criteria. From the lemma, the team derives fresh phi-normality criteria as applications. They also introduce phi-normal families of harmonic mappings and obtain Lappan-type tests for them. One result stands out for its economy: for sense-preserving harmonic mappings, the relevant test set can consist of only three points.
arxiv-2606-17350:
Thennal and Hatzel present a 2026 arXiv paper asking whether language models tell the same stories over and over, using narrative similarity as the yardstick. High-quality machine prose is now routine, yet its diversity compared with human writing is disputed in the literature. The authors gather stories from ten representative models alongside human stories from a writing prompts community, then collect similarity judgements from human raters and three automatic annotation methods.

Across the comparisons, machine stories were consistently more similar to each other than human stories were to each other. Frontier models in particular converge on a generic mean narrative that resembles typical human stories but lacks the spread of the full human set. Common fixes did not help meaningfully in their tests. Neither negative prompting nor temperature scaling broke the sameness, leaving homogeneity as an open problem for creative generation.
arxiv-2606-17550:
Hussain and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on dark energy whose equation of state follows a damped harmonic oscillator, swinging toward an equilibrium value as the universe expands. Such motion can be underdamped, critically damped, or overdamped, giving the model distinct personalities to test against data. The Hubble tension, the mismatch between early- and late-universe expansion rates, is the prize: a good oscillator setting might ease it without wrecking the fit elsewhere in cosmology.

Fits combine microwave background, distance-scale, and age data with three supernova sets. The underdamped case raised the inferred expansion rate and cut the tension sharply with two of those sets. A third set instead favoured near-critical damping and a low rate, exposing real disagreement among the sets. Overall evidence versus the standard model stayed inconclusive, so the relief costs nothing statistically.
arxiv-2606-17850:
Wang and colleagues built a fast solver for chip heat simulations in a 2026 engineering paper. Three-dimensional stacked chips need fine-grained thermal maps to catch local hotspots, but fine grids create huge sparse linear systems that are slow to solve. General GPU solvers rarely exploit the regular patterns these systems have, so the team co-designed one for the task.

Their open-source CUTh-Solver condenses the diagonal storage format to cut waste and arranges sparse matrix operations so GPU memory reads stay aligned and efficient. A highly parallel Chebyshev preconditioner and an adaptive mixed-precision scheme speed the core conjugate gradient method further. In evaluations it beat both a leading commercial simulator and a range of native GPU sparse libraries by wide margins, targeting the banded systems that standard chip thermal models produce.
arxiv-2606-18050:
Xin builds the first semi-analytical theory for how often stars get torn apart by spinning black holes, in a 2026 dissertation-based work. A tidal disruption event fires when a star strays onto a near-radial orbit and the black hole's gravity shreds it. Relativistic tidal physics sets the angular momentum threshold, while ordinary stellar dynamics supplies the stars. A spinning hole breaks the symmetry, so survival depends on the orbit's tilt as well as its spin.

Using a new tidal tensor formalism, Xin computes tilt-dependent boundaries for disruption and for direct capture by the horizon. The classical one-dimensional loss cone problem gains nested boundaries and a closed-form capture fraction across all regimes. A two-dimensional Fokker-Planck treatment then follows diffusion in both angular momentum size and direction, showing how the spinning hole's lopsided boundary reshapes event rates.
arxiv-2606-18350:
Whitaker and colleagues announce the discovery of a stellar-mass black hole orbiting a visible star in Omega Centauri, in a 2026 astronomy paper. Simulations give black holes a central role in cluster dynamics, yet direct evidence for them in clusters has stayed scarce, and none had been found this way before.

Using Hubble data from the oMEGACat project plus JWST observations spanning twenty-three years, the team tracked the companion star's slow wobble and caught the pair near their closest approach. The orbit is wide and eccentric, lasting roughly ninety-four years. The unseen partner weighs about four and a half times the Sun's mass, making it a genuine black hole rather than a dense star. It is the first astrometric black hole discovery in a globular cluster and the longest-period black hole binary known, with future JWST epochs set to tighten the mass further.
arxiv-2606-18850:
Zhang and the team build a paper summarizer that mimics how a student drafts and a teacher corrects, in a 2026 natural language processing paper. Abstractive summarization of research articles demands fluency and factual faithfulness together. Extractive methods splice text rigidly, and break flow. Large language model tools write smoothly, but drift from the source's claims.

ScholarSum first sorts the document into a hierarchical knowledge graph of coherent units, whose community structure captures the global logic and themes. Guided by that structure, a student part drafts the summary. A teacher-like reviewer then examines the draft again and again, flags content that is not backed, and triggers re-retrieval and rewriting. It does so until the summary meets quality standards. Experiments on arXiv and PubMed papers showed the framework beat previous baselines, on both completeness and faithfulness. Ablations checked the graph guidance and the reflective polish loop.
arxiv-2606-18950:
Kim and colleagues introduce RTSGameBench in 2026, a benchmark that tests whether vision-language models can reason strategically in real-time strategy games. Such games require coordinating allies, adapting to opponents, and planning over long horizons with only partial information. Earlier benchmarks covered narrow scenarios and could not diagnose which specific strategic skill was failing when a model performed poorly overall.

Built on the large-scale game Beyond All Reason, the benchmark combines full matches in varied matchup structures with small diagnostic mini-games, each aimed at one competency. A self-evolving generator can turn free-form requests into new mini-games, widening coverage over successive cycles. An accompanying agent framework manages units through a finite-state machine with memory so models can operate at this scale. Tests of leading models show clear drops when coordination demands tighten, team coordination grows, or task scale increases, revealing limits that simpler tests miss.
arxiv-2606-19250:
Dai and colleagues prove local and global well-posedness for the extended Schrödinger-Benjamin-Ono system in 2026. The system couples a Schrödinger field with a Benjamin-Ono type field on the real line. A quadratic term in the second field makes the system quasilinear. As with the Benjamin-Ono equation itself, that term defeats solution by Picard iteration, so standard contraction arguments fail.

The authors prove the system is locally well-posed in a scale of Sobolev spaces for all nonnegative regularity. In particular the result covers the energy space. At that level they obtain global well-posedness, under a smallness assumption on the mass of the Schrödinger part of the initial data. Those guarantees license both analysis and numerical work on the coupled system. The proof extends methods built for Benjamin-Ono type dispersion to a genuinely coupled setting.
arxiv-2606-19350:
Sheth and colleagues propose causal attribution pruning in 2026, a training-free way to shrink language models while preserving reasoning. Large models reason well across many steps but cost a lot to run. Pruning by weight size or activation strength ignores what each part actually does. Cutting the wrong head silently damages reasoning.

The method masks each attention head during forward passes on a small set of reasoning problems. The measured performance drop becomes a causal score for that head. Scores convert into weight-level importance for the linked projection matrices, guiding fine-grained pruning. On a science question benchmark, the method gains up to sixty-one percent in relative accuracy over the Wanda baseline at moderate sparsity. Tests span math word problems, strategy questions, and science questions. Gains hold at low and moderate sparsity, while coarse attribution for other layers limits the method at high sparsity.
arxiv-2606-19450:
Siddhant Solanki, Jens Mahlmann, and Alexander Philippov study fast magnetosonic waves in fiercely magnetized plasma in this 2026 work. Fast magnetosonic waves are pressure waves that move through magnetized gas and fields together. The setting matters for fast radio bursts, brief bright radio flashes that may start inside magnetar magnetospheres.

Running relativistic force-free simulations, the trio confirm past theory and watch the waves decay on their own. A parametric decay instability turns the main wave into secondary magnetosonic and Alfvén waves. Energy keeps draining even after the two wave families reach rough balance. The excited spectrum spreads wide across the range of wave scales in the box. Bursts born deep inside a magnetar thus face heavy loss and smearing before they can escape to space.
arxiv-2606-19550:
Useong Shin asks in 2026 whether asset pricing factor models win or lose because of the test portfolios themselves. Factor models explain stock returns with a few shared drivers, and judges grade them on chosen test assets. Shin builds random portfolios with no characteristic sorting from a broad CRSP stock universe.

Stock choice, starting weights, holding style, and rebalancing rules all vary across the tests. Rankings shift in material ways as those choices change. Buy-and-hold designs favour the FF5 and FF6 models, while daily constant weighting favours FF3. FF3 also proves the most stable model across designs. The q5 model posts the highest maximum Sharpe ratio in spanning tests, yet leaves larger pricing errors on random portfolios. Those errors swing with construction choices as well. Test-asset construction thus counts as a design choice in model evaluation, not a neutral backdrop.
arxiv-2606-19650:
Mohamed Jleli and Bessem Samet prove no-go results for elliptic inequalities on weighted graphs in 2026. The setting is a connected, locally finite weighted graph with a graph Laplacian and a real potential. The inequality couples the Laplacian, a potential term, and a power nonlinearity.

A positive solution of the homogeneous equation transforms the operator into an H-Laplacian on a new weighted graph. That trick absorbs the potential into fresh weights. The main criterion then speaks through cut-off functions and where their H-Laplacian stays controlled. Unlike older metric criteria, no annulus volume estimates are needed. An example shows the criterion covering cases past methods miss. Sharpness is proven too: an example fails the condition by an arbitrarily small power while a positive solution exists. Such methods thus give fine control over when only the zero solution can survive.
arxiv-2606-19750:
Darrien McKenzie, Nicklas Hansen, and Xiaolong Wang rethink how reinforcement learning picks practice problems for language models in 2026. Training gains hinge on which problems get sampled during optimisation. Standard curriculum methods chase middling difficulty and treat each problem as an isolated bandit arm.

Problems actually relate through the model's latent representation space, a structured task manifold. Sampling choices also steer how learning signals evolve across that space. Their Bayesian Manifold Curriculum arranges problems in a hierarchical task tree. Bayesian learning over the tree then guides which problems to draw next. Experiments expose trade-offs among productivity, diversity of coverage, and evaluation relevance. Chasing difficulty alone fails to maximise downstream performance. Structure-aware sampling, the authors argue, should replace difficulty-only curricula for reasoning training.
arxiv-2606-19850:
Yasutoshi Kishimoto and three colleagues add feature selection to neural additive models in 2026. Neural additive models keep predictions readable by scoring each feature through its own small network. Feature interactions need two-input networks, which explode in cost on wide datasets.

A feature selection layer joins both the additive and basis variants. Selection weights update during training alongside the networks. Useless features fade out, shrinking compute and model size together. Two-input networks then stay feasible even for high-dimensional data. Interactions between feature pairs become learnable inside an interpretable frame. Experiments show clear efficiency gains over the plain models. Accuracy matches or beats leading generalised additive models at the same time. Readable models thus scale to wider tables without giving up their clarity.
arxiv-2606-20150:
James Fant-Male and Roel Pieters ask how a robot partner should track the state of a shared assembly task when all it sees is recognized human actions. Their 2026 paper notes that turning a stream of recognized actions into a reliable assembly state is not trivial in realistic noise. The authors compare five state-tracking approaches, spanning logic-based rules, hidden Markov models, and neural networks, across two datasets.

Tests used both simulated action streams with controlled noise and real output from an action recognition model. Neural and hidden Markov methods did well when task variability was limited. Logic-based approaches proved tougher in messier scenarios where learned models faltered. Modeling how long actions should last mattered greatly for tasks with repeated actions and no extra sensing. No single method won everywhere, so the authors map which tracker fits which kind of task.
arxiv-2606-20250:
Duc Nguyen and three colleagues simplify weakly supervised segmentation of tissue images by purifying features during training instead of repairing masks afterward. Their 2026 paper addresses a standard three-stage pipeline: generate class activation maps, refine pseudo-masks offline, then retrain with full supervision. That pipeline is expensive, and errors from shallow-layer texture bias propagate through every later stage. Their framework, SSHR, works in a single stage.

A rectification module uses deep global context to filter local anomalies out of shallow features while the forward pass runs, producing high-fidelity activation maps directly. On the LUAD-HistoSeg and BCSS datasets, SSHR beat state-of-the-art multi-stage methods. It also cut training time by a factor of two to five, a practical advance for pathology workflows where labeled data is scarce.
arxiv-2606-20350:
Lynne Hillenbrand, Kishalay De, Adolfo Carvalho, Dan Stern, Evan Portnoi, and Nicholas Earley announce a new FU Orionis outburst in the young star V7995 Sagittarii. Their 2026 paper reports an eruption that peaked in late 2024 after a steep 4.6-month rise of 2.85 magnitudes in the r band. A shallower infrared rise over the previous four years preceded it. The progenitor was an unstudied young stellar object with a flat-spectrum energy distribution and extended nebulosity.

FU Orionis events are the most extreme episodes of young-star accretion, thought to be disk instabilities dumping matter onto the star. Multi-wavelength light curves cover the quiet state, outburst, and early decline, and optical images show the surrounding nebula brightening in step. Spectroscopy taken a year and a half after peak confirms the type: a mixed-temperature absorption spectrum formed in an accretion disk, with blueshifted lines from a strong wind.
arxiv-2606-20450:
Mahmoud AlaaEldin, Amy Inwood, Xidong Mu, and Michail Matthaiou optimize fairness in pinching-antenna NOMA networks. Their 2026 paper studies antennas that slide along waveguides, repositioning radiating elements to create line-of-sight paths around blockages. Each waveguide is driven by a single radio-frequency chain, so non-orthogonal multiple access is the natural sharing scheme.

Antenna positions and base-station precoding are jointly optimized to maximize the minimum rate across users, the max-min fairness criterion. Lifting the worst-served user's rate matters more than boosting the average in blocked urban settings. Fairness-first design suits pinching antennas, whose whole point is serving users that blockages would otherwise strand. The joint problem couples continuous positions with precoding, making it a genuinely hard design task.
arxiv-2606-20550:
Vishal Verma presents Easy Reads, an open-source Python program that reformats arXiv papers for readability and accessibility. His 2026 paper describes the problem: dense layouts, small fonts, tight line spacing, double columns, and crammed figures strain readers and shut some out entirely.

Easy Reads fetches a paper from arXiv by URL and works from its source to produce a friendlier rendering, end to end and automatically. The tool targets the layout features that make papers compact but hard to read. Accessibility is treated as a formatting problem with a software fix. Researchers with visual or attention difficulties get a practical on-ramp to the literature.
arxiv-2606-20750:
Ali Elgindi introduces a new invariant for contact geometry in a solo 2026 mathematics paper on three-dimensional manifolds. The setting is a closed, orientable 3-manifold with a co-oriented contact structure. The invariant, written mu, takes values in the Picard group of complex line bundles over the manifold. Its construction uses an open book decomposition, a way of splitting the manifold into pages around a binding.

From a supporting open book, Elgindi embeds the manifold into complex three-space. The contact structure becomes a holomorphic line field along the binding. Stein theory extends the induced line bundle, and only its restriction to the manifold is kept. Using Giroux correspondence, the construction is shown not to depend on the chosen open book. As an application, two tight contact structures on the 3-torus are distinguished by different first Chern classes.
arxiv-2606-21050:
Kosuke Imai and three colleagues propose triage scores in 2026, a counterfactual upgrade to risk scores used in medicine and criminal justice. A risk score predicts a bad outcome if no one intervenes. High scores are read as calls to intervene. That logic ignores what would happen under intervention itself. Good decisions need outcomes under each available action.

Triage scores build on additive counterfactual utilities. Risk scores appear as a special case. Ethical and practical factors can enter the utility structure. The team illustrates triage scores with their own randomized trial of a pretrial risk score. Rich utility structures are captured in the analysis. The reframing matters wherever scores gate liberty or care. A person who would not benefit from intervention should not be treated like one who would.
arxiv-2606-21250:
Zhidan Li, Siyu Liu, and Kuan Yang study the anti-ferromagnetic Potts model in 2026, a statistical physics model where neighboring sites prefer different states, generalizing the Ising model. They work on random regular bipartite graphs at low temperature, in the regime where multiple phases coexist. The central object is the partition function, a weighted sum over all configurations whose approximation underlies both physics predictions and complexity theory.

On the negative side, the standard single-site Glauber dynamics mixes exponentially slowly at low temperature, extending a recent Ising result. On the positive side, they design a deterministic approximation algorithm built on abstract polymer models, a method that groups configurations into clusters. The pairing matters: random sampling fails here, but a carefully structured counting method still succeeds on these expander-like graphs.
arxiv-2606-21350:
Till Schmeil, Gunther Waxenegger-Wilfing, and Sebastian Schirmer connect robot task planning with reinforcement learning in 2026 through Temporal Behavior Trees. Behavior trees organize robot tasks as hierarchies of actions; the temporal version adds timing constraints written in Linear Temporal Logic at the leaf nodes. Reward design for such long, structured tasks is notoriously hard, since sparse rewards leave learning agents with almost no guidance.

The authors translate a Temporal Behavior Tree into a Petri net and assign rewards from its structure, producing a Reward-Petri-Net. In a series of harder and harder test environments, tree-derived rewards let agents learn where plain reinforcement learning fails, and improve how many trials learning takes. Different reward distribution schemes and tree shapes give users intuitive control over the learning process.
arxiv-2606-21450:
Eduardo Costa Martins and Tim Willemse study quotients for behavioral equivalences in 2026, the reduced versions of a system model that keep its observable behavior. Quotients were known only for a few equivalences in the linear time-branching time spectrum. The authors extend the theory to weak simulation equivalence and coupled similarity, two closely related notions built from simulation preorders, which compare how one system can mimic another's steps.

They give abstract procedures that turn any labeled transition system into a unique canonical representative of its class, and into an equivalent system minimal in both states and transitions. The minimization problem itself is shown to be NP-complete, so minimal forms are canonical but hard to compute in the worst case. The results complete a missing corner of the equivalence spectrum used in concurrency theory.
arxiv-2606-21550:
Daniel Halpern and five colleagues, listed alphabetically, survey in 2026 how social choice theory can improve the way AI systems learn from human feedback. Alignment methods train a scoring function on human judgments of model outputs, then steer the model toward high scores. When judges disagree about desirable behavior, that score quietly becomes an aggregate vote, and how the votes combine decides what the model learns to prefer.

Social choice, the mathematical study of collective decisions, offers tools for exactly this aggregation step. The survey shows how that lens exposes failure modes in current feedback pipelines, such as majority views swamping consistent minorities. It also maps a broader design space for handling disagreement openly and on principle, rather than by accident of the averaging rule.
arxiv-2606-21750:
William A. Sands, Pierson T. Guthrey, and Nathan V. Roberts bring multigrid thinking to high-dimensional equations compressed in tensor format in 2026. Kinetic-theory problems live in phase spaces too large for ordinary grids, the curse of dimensionality. Low-rank hierarchical Tucker forms tame the size, but solving systems in that format needs preconditioners as adaptive as the format itself.

Their contributions stack in three layers. A projection method extends to flexible preconditioning in low-rank formats. Multilevel preconditioners adapt geometric multigrid, serving as preconditioners rather than standalone solvers. An inexact Newton wrapper handles nonlinear systems. Model problems, linear and nonlinear, show robust, scalable convergence. For plasma and multiphase modelers, the payoff is solvers whose cost tracks the solution's true complexity, not the grid's.
arxiv-2606-22850:
Anna Elisabeth Riha and four colleagues question whether Bayesian model selection is needed at all, in this 2026 paper. Workflows often weigh several candidate models of differing complexity, picking a simpler one to protect generalization. The authors study when such selection is needless, or even harmful, for prediction with finite data, and find the answer can hinge on the prior.

They define predictively consistent priors, which keep a model's prior predictions stable as complexity grows. Across examples and tests, including adding covariates in regression, forward variable selection, and nonlinear modeling, flexible models with such priors typically matched or beat selected simpler models out of sample. When selection did help, it flagged poor prior choices, such as putting too much weight on implausible predictions. The authors propose replacing parsimony at the component level with priors that stay sensible in predictive space.
arxiv-2606-22950:
Yulin Wang and colleagues address online learning with delayed labels in a 2026 paper. Online learning updates a model as each new data point arrives. In many streams the true labels arrive late, because labeling is slow and costly. Meanwhile the data itself keeps changing, so old patterns stop working. Models that wait for labels fall behind the stream. The authors call their framework DT-GOL, short for dual-track geometric online learning.

Wang and colleagues treat the delay problem as partly a geometry problem. The shape of incoming data changes before labels catch up, and that shape can hint at concept change. Their system turns those hints into soft labels, which carry uncertainty instead of one hard guess. Two tracks run side by side. One stays anchored on confirmed labels, while the other adapts quickly using the soft labels, balancing stability against speed.
arxiv-2606-23050:
Baidu Inc. reports a document reading model called Unlimited OCR in a 2026 technical report. Optical character recognition turns page images into text. Recent systems pair a vision encoder with a large language model decoder, gaining accuracy from language knowledge. Long documents expose a weakness, though. The decoder's memory cache grows with output length, slowing generation page by page. Humans copying long texts show no such slowdown. Unlimited OCR aims to copy that steady working memory.

Baidu replaces every attention layer in the decoder with a reference sliding window design. The change holds the memory cache constant through the whole decoding run. Attention cost drops as well. Combined with a highly compressing encoder, the model transcribes dozens of pages in one forward pass within a standard length limit. Baidu notes the attention design should also suit speech recognition and translation.
arxiv-2606-23150:
Anna Bindler and colleagues ask whether a surge in hiring demand widens workforce diversity in a 2026 economics paper. Their setting is German academia after reunification. Nearly all social science professors in East Germany were replaced, while science and technology faculty stayed largely in place. That shock created many openings with no diversity policy attached. A simple framework predicts a trade-off between the demographic mix and the quality mix of new hires when demand jumps.

Bindler and colleagues use administrative data with a regional difference-in-differences design. New hires came from a wider spread of department quality, showing less selective origins. Female representation did not rise, despite qualified women waiting in the pipeline. East German hiring instead converged to West German gender patterns. Simulations suggest the marginal female hire was notably stronger than the marginal male hire, marking a missed opportunity.
arxiv-2606-23550:
Pacifico and colleagues use planted attractors to make neural differential equation models classify inputs, in a 2026 paper on interpretable machine learning. A neural ordinary differential equation treats an input as a starting point that flows through a learned landscape, and the ending point determines the answer. Earlier attractor methods fixed stable resting points, one per class, so the flow itself became the classifier, but those designs risked losing neural flexibility.

The team shows how to embed a chosen set of fixed points into the learned velocity field while keeping the model's universal approximation ability, its power to mimic essentially any smooth field. Each input then travels toward the attractor planted for its class, and the reached attractor serves directly as the prediction, with no separate classifier head. The basins of attraction, the regions flowing to each resting point, make the decision rule visible and explainable.
arxiv-2606-23750:
Mane derives new power series for the roots of a simple polynomial equation, in a 2026 mathematics note. The trinomial equation sets a power of the unknown plus a linear term plus a constant to zero. Its roots are known as hypergeometric series in powers of a combination of the coefficients. For the cubic case, the classic Kummer identities reshuffle such series into alternative forms. Whether similar reshuffles exist for higher order series was open.

Using Kummer's identities, Mane first rewrites the cubic's roots as series in powers of the discriminant. The discriminant measures how close the roots are to merging. Series also appear in powers of its reciprocal. New series of both kinds then follow for every degree from three upward. The resulting formulas suggest a family of identities like Kummer's, now for higher order hypergeometric series.
arxiv-2606-23950:
Wang, Li, Eldesokey, and Wonka train image generators to vary a subject's pose and setting boldly without losing who the subject is, in a 2026 paper on generative AI. Subject driven generation makes new pictures of a subject from a reference image. Models that guard the likeness tightly copy the reference pose, producing near duplicates. Models pushed for variety drift away from the subject instead. The authors call this the identity diversity paradox.

DivRL scores the two sides with separate measures drawn from a robust similarity model. One measure rewards structural variety among the outputs. The other scores how well the likeness is kept. The training plan lets the model roam freely, penalizing only samples whose likeness score falls below a set threshold. Identity thus becomes a constraint to meet, not a goal fighting variety. Experiments show variety rising while likeness stays on par with strong baselines.
arxiv-2606-24150:
Vakili proposes quantum bits built inside altermagnets, a recently recognised class of magnetic materials. Gate-defined spin qubits normally rely on spin-orbit coupling to steer spins electrically. Altermagnets offer another handle. Squeezing one into an elliptical quantum dot splits its low-energy states into a doublet. The two members carry opposite spin polarisation, forming a natural qubit.

Simulations over time show a phase-controlled quadrupolar gate drive performing standard single-qubit rotations. The drive wobbles the confinement shape around a fixed bias. The qubit splitting sits in the microwave range, while leakage to other states stays far away in energy, protecting operations. Vakili then pairs two dots. Their joint spectrum projects cleanly onto separate-dot states with a coupled two-qubit term. Wobbling the central barrier drives the pair close to a maximally entangled state.
arxiv-2606-24250:
Korotchenko and Aksenov design a lock that understands what operations actually conflict, instead of treating all writes as enemies. Concurrent programs coordinate through locks, and the classic read-write lock is blunt: writes block everything, reads block writes. Their SemanticLock, built in 2026 at ITMO University, generalises that design using a conflict graph between the operations a data structure offers, so only genuinely clashing operations exclude each other.

Two demonstrations show the payoff. A toy array supporting point queries and several kinds of range queries gains fine-grained synchronisation matched to its real conflict structure. More consequentially, the authors augment Java's ConcurrentHashMap, a heavily used concurrent hash table, with additional long-running operations that a coarse lock would serialise painfully. Korotchenko and Aksenov argue semantic knowledge about operations, not just read-versus-write labels, is the right basis for synchronisation, letting concurrent structures stay correct while running more work in parallel.
arxiv-2606-24450:
Patil, Das, Bhosale, and Roy teach a robot hand to feel contact without any touch sensors. Dexterous manipulation depends on knowing when fingers meet an object. Tactile hardware is costly, fragile, and awkward to integrate, though. Humans manage differently. They infer contact by fusing vision with proprioception, the sense of one's own body position. Their 2026 framework, NoContactNoWorries, asks whether a robot can learn the same trick.

A transformer-based model fuses RGB-D vision with the hand's proprioceptive signals. It predicts binary contact states, a pseudo tactile signal for hand object interaction. One model trains across multiple objects, rather than per object. The inferred signal then feeds reinforcement learning agents performing in hand object reorientation. It generalises to objects never seen in training. Experiments in simulation and on a real robot validate the approach. Patil's team presents vision plus proprioception as a scalable substitute for tactile sensing.
arxiv-2606-24650:
Nyoma stacks state space models into a hierarchy that reads at three speeds. Language models need long context, and attention's cost grows brutally with length. Harmonic, presented in 2026, stacks three recurrent levels that run at progressively slower timescales. Each level receives the prediction error from the level below, rather than its raw hidden state, so higher levels only process what lower levels failed to predict.

On a standard character level benchmark with equal token budgets, Harmonic beats a comparable transformer at every context length, and beats Mamba at every length too. The gap widens dramatically as sequences lengthen. At the longest setting, both rivals run out of memory on a large accelerator, while Harmonic, with linear memory, trains successfully. Scaling studies show the transformer winning at short context and small scale, but losing as length grows. Replacing all attention in a billion parameter model removes its positional encoding limit entirely.
arxiv-2606-24850:
Duong Trinh and Santiago Montoya-Blandón build a framework for peer effects when people choose their own networks. Outcomes spill over between peers, but responses differ from person to person. Links also form endogenously: unobserved traits drive both who connects and what outcomes follow. Ignoring that selection corrupts spillover estimates. Their model, called SCHSAR, jointly handles link formation and outcome determination. A finite mixture structure lets peer effects vary across latent types.

Estimation is fully Bayesian, using data augmentation to sidestep failures of standard methods. A simulation study validates the approach. The application studies an innovation network among United States firms. Peer effects on corporate research and development spending come out positive and significant, yet clearly heterogeneous. The correction for self chosen links is what makes the estimates credible. Policy shocks to research spending would therefore land unevenly across firms, which targeted policy design can exploit.
arxiv-2606-25050:
Ankur Verma and four colleagues show how high energy astrophysical neutrinos can probe scalar non standard neutrino interactions. Such interactions would modify the neutrino mass matrix and, through matter effects from the cosmic neutrino background, split active and sterile states slightly. Neutrinos would then behave in a pseudo Dirac way, with oscillation effects over cosmic distances. The splittings leave two fingerprints on the astrophysical flux: they change its flavour composition, and they distort its energy distribution. The authors analyse the channels.

Predicted flavour ratios are confronted with IceCube measurements and the projected reach of IceCube Gen2. The spectral analysis uses IceCube's diffuse flux datasets, tracks and cascades, plus spectral shapes of neutrino bright sources. Regions of parameters excluded by the analyses become limits on the interaction: on its Yukawa couplings and on the scalar mediator's mass. The strongest gains are for ultra light mediators, where other probes are weak.
arxiv-2606-25750:
Judging chatbot safety by reading answers is slow and pricey. It is also hostage to whichever judge grades them. Chang-Chieh Huang, Yan-Lun Chen, Chia-Mu Yu, and Wei-Bin Lee propose measuring safety inside the model instead, in 2026. Their SafeVec procedure starts from a safety aligned reference model. It extracts refusal directions, the patterns active when that model declines a request. A target model is scored by how strongly its hidden states line up with those directions. The prompts are unsafe and jailbreak ones. The result is a calibrated score from zero to one hundred.

Across the Llama, Gemma, and Qwen families, the score separated aligned models from uncensored ones. It flagged de-aligned variants too. It tracked attack success rates measured the slow way, and ran far faster than judge based evaluation. Refusal alignment, the authors conclude, is an efficient white box signal for safety screening.
arxiv-2606-25850:
Ferroelectrics hold a switchable electric polarisation, normally flipped by applying voltage. Cameron Scott, Xabier Diaz de Cerio, and Jorge Íñiguez-González explore a thermal lever in 2026. A temperature change alters polarisation through the pyroelectric effect, and the uneven polarisation creates bound charges whose depolarising field fights back. That fight, the authors show, can be harnessed. Using scale free Landau potentials and predictive atomistic simulations, they map how temperature modulations steer the ferroelectric state by working through its own electrostatics.

The headline prediction is poling without electrodes: temperature patterns alone rotate dipoles into a chosen state by letting them flee the bound charge. Adding strain to temperature gradients opens another route. Persistent polar textures form, including multidomain states that stay after the stimulus ends. Thermal control could suit devices where wiring every element is impractical.
arxiv-2606-25950:
Sebastian Neef, Cenk Schlunke, and Anne Hennig survey how Germany's largest listed companies handle coordinated vulnerability disclosure, the practice of giving outside security researchers a clear channel for reporting flaws. Their longitudinal study covers all forty firms on the DAX index. Adoption is tracked through public program pages and security.txt files, and through questionnaires sent by email and post in two waves, which drew replies from about a fifth of the firms.

Adoption jumped sharply between the two waves. Half the firms had a disclosure program in the first wave, and more than nine in ten had one by the second, alongside many new security.txt files. Legal duties under the new European NIS2 and Cyber Resilience rules drive much of the growth. Firms still complain about scarce staff and uneven report quality, a pairing that smaller companies will also face.
arxiv-2606-26050:
Juliana Li and Diya Sreedhar report a strange training phenomenon they call natural ungrokking. A small language model learns a pronoun-gender rule early in pretraining. Cued with a girl's name, it picks the matching pronoun on held-out probes. A few thousand steps later, the skill vanishes. The rule's evidence never left the training data. Loss curves show no sign of the reversal.

One corpus statistic predicts which rules survive. Rules live or die by how often the training stream shows them winning. Data volume only deepens the fall of doomed rules. A rival surface pattern out-competes the rule inside the model. Their internal margin crosses zero within a hundred steps of the visible collapse. Public Pythia checkpoints show the same dynamics at several scales. Control turns out lopsided. Flooding the data with counter-evidence kills a rule on demand. Flooding it with support cannot revive one.
arxiv-2606-26250:
M. Kornbleuth and M. Opher predict what the IMAP mission should see at the edge of the solar system. The heliosphere's tail, the heliotail, is shaped by the solar wind's fast and slow streams. The Sun's magnetic field may also actively squeeze the wind into two jets, challenging the old passive picture. Energetic neutral atom maps are how spacecraft image this frontier. Earlier IBEX maps showed high-latitude lobes whose origin is disputed.

Simulations run with and without the solar field settle the energy split. Below ten kiloelectronvolts, the fast-slow wind pattern organizes the atom maps on its own. Higher energies hand control to magnetic collimation, which builds the two tail lobes. At eighty kiloelectronvolts the lobe brightness doubles the low-latitude region in the split-tail model. IMAP's sharper eyes should decide whether the field truly collimates the wind, and reveal the deep tail's shape.
arxiv-2606-26350:
Kaicheng Zhang and colleagues open OpenFinGym, a testing ground where AI agents do quantitative finance under supervision. Finance agents are usually graded one task at a time. Real desk work chains tasks: forecast, build a strategy, manage risk, then trade. Single-task scores flatter agents and hide generalization failures. OpenFinGym unifies the chain under one execution and verification interface. Forecasting, market generation, live trading, and fraud detection all live inside it.

Automation widens the task supply. A pipeline converts published quant research into runnable task packages. A containerized runtime with a host-side verifier blocks train-test leakage during rollouts. A paper trading engine streams market data at low latency. Long-horizon and event-market forecasts resolve later, on schedule. Hooks for fine-tuning and reinforcement learning post-training are built in. Financial meaning, not just task completion, is the grading standard.
arxiv-2606-26550:
Shengwen Gan, Cheng Zhang, and Zhifei Zhu prove sharp bounds for oscillatory integrals and spectral clusters. Oscillatory integrals model wave-like behaviour and link Fourier analysis to the vibration patterns of shapes. Spectral clusters group vibrations with nearby frequencies. Estimating their size in various norms is central to harmonic analysis. The endpoint cases, at the extremes of the norm range, are the hardest.

The authors prove sharp multi-linear estimates for Carleson-Sjölin operators at all frequency scales and exponents. Endpoint logarithmic behaviour is included and shown unavoidable in general. For spectral clusters on any closed three-dimensional shape, though, they remove the logarithm entirely. That resolves a problem posed by Burq, Gérard, and Tzvetkov. Sharp multi-linear spectral cluster estimates for every order follow as a consequence.
arxiv-2606-27050:
Roethig and colleagues ask how large a data burst can grow in future all-optical satellite networks. In optical burst switching, a ground station gathers data into one burst and sends it along a reserved light path. The team studies bufferless multi-channel versions, where bursts cannot wait in memory along the way. Realistic end-to-end delay limits, roughly thirty to sixty thousandths of a second, cap how long gathering may take during their 2026 analysis.

Simulations cover real planned constellations, including Starlink, Telesat, and Amazon LEO, with many ground stations and low-orbit satellites. Bursts of a few hundred megabytes meet the delay target in those runs. Growing bursts within that range also adds little extra burst loss for a given traffic load. The results give planners a concrete size window for burst assembly at ground stations.
arxiv-2606-27350:
Cui leads a large team presenting CHIA, an open-source framework for agentic artificial intelligence in chip design. Hardware and software co-design is slow because tools, simulators, and evaluation steps sit in disconnected silos. CHIA represents each design flow as a directed cyclic graph, called a CHIA loop, looping over tools from chip generators to architecture simulators. Agents operate inside those loops with isolation, profiling, and fault tolerance built in. The framework targets reliable, reproducible automation of long design campaigns in this systems paper of 2026.

Five case studies exercise the machinery on real design problems. Agent-written register-transfer-level code runs more than twenty-five trillion instructions of the SPEC CPU2006 benchmark suite. Performance gains follow from closing the loop between code generation and measured feedback. The authors release the framework openly, inviting community extension. Co-design automation gains a common, auditable home.
arxiv-2606-27550:
Chen speeds up language model inference, in a machine learning paper published in 2026, by letting speculation depth follow the local entropy of the text being generated. Multi-token prediction heads draft several future tokens at once for parallel verification, but existing systems fix one tree-shaped drafting pattern for the whole sequence. Natural language is uneven: predictable stretches support deep drafting, while uncertain stretches need caution. EntMTP, a training-free scheduler, switches among a set of task-specific Pareto-optimal drafting trees using a running estimate of generation entropy. No retraining of the underlying model is required.

Across code, chat, mathematics, and literary benchmarks, the scheduler consistently beats a leading tree-based baseline by a factor between about one point one and one point one five in the reported speedups. Against an earlier drafting method the peak speedup reaches about one point three six times in the same evaluation.
arxiv-2606-28250:
Nicholas J. Ossi, Barbara Prinari, Theodoros P. Horikis, and Dimitrios J. Frantzeskakis study kinks, wave fronts that hold their shape, in the defocusing modified Korteweg-de Vries equation, a model of weakly nonlinear waves. Real systems always add small disturbances, so the team wanted a perturbation theory predicting how a kink responds.

Ossi and colleagues expand the disturbed wave in squared eigenfunctions, special functions tied to the equation's hidden scattering problem. They prove the expansion is complete for a kink background, work out the adjoint structure needed for both smooth and bound components, and derive equations for how the kink itself drifts. At first order, disturbances typically grow a radiative shelf ahead of the kink, and the forecasts for physical cases matched direct runs.
arxiv-2606-28550:
Susobhan Mandal and Sambuddha Sanyal show that a mismatch usually blamed on unequal ingredients can create itself. When two fermion species pair into a superfluid, their Fermi surfaces, the boundaries of their filled momentum states, may not coincide. Textbooks treat that mismatch as built in, a fixed inequivalence between the species.

In a massless Dirac theory with two components and exact flavor symmetry, Mandal and Sanyal find a self-interacting vector boson that condenses and splits the Fermi surfaces spontaneously, while preserving time reversal. Pairing across the self-made mismatch still yields a stable relativistic superfluid. The famous Chandrasekhar-Clogston limit, normally a line, widens into a surface in coupling space, because the mismatch is no longer a free parameter but is set self-consistently by the symmetry-breaking coupling itself.
arxiv-2606-28650:
Athmouni, Brahmia and Hachani work out the energy cost of controlling a chain from one end. Their model is the Aubry-Andre lattice, a chain whose spacing pattern almost repeats. They ask how fast the needed energy grows when the target sits far from the single boundary control knob. The answer is an exponential rate, a steady multiplying factor per step of distance.

They prove that this rate equals a quantity from the chain's transfer mathematics. It is judged at a reflected band edge. That edge is a mirrored point outside the allowed energy band. The identity holds for almost every phase of the pattern across the metallic and critical ranges, and in the localized range under stated conditions. Their proof uses an exact change of basis, a positive sum with no cancelling terms, and a three-distance argument to close the remaining gap.
arxiv-2606-28750:
Li, Yang and Lin propose deciding which quantum phase a material is in without first preparing its ground state accurately. Preparing ground states, the lowest-energy configurations, is usually the expensive step. Instead they prepare a typical state of a candidate phase. Then they cool it briefly with dissipative dynamics, meaning evolution that sheds energy. The cooling is tuned to the target Hamiltonian, the rule governing the system's energy.

Cooling quickly suppresses high-energy parts and pushes the system into a low-energy manifold, a family of states whose measurable properties already reveal the underlying phase. This worked before the system settled to its steady state. They demonstrate the strategy on three standard models, covering topological transitions as well. Coarse filters and short times sufficed to recover key quantities such as the Luttinger parameter. For free-particle systems they justify the method rigorously. They also probe interacting fermions.
arxiv-2606-28950:
Nakamura, Hagino and Kondo review progress on dineutron clusters, pairs of neutrons bound tightly together inside neutron-rich nuclei. Such clusters are expected in the low-density outskirts of nuclei, and interest has grown fast with studies of rare isotopes. The review gathers experimental and theoretical evidence for where dineutrons appear and how they shape nuclear behaviour.

Experiments on two-neutron halo nuclei, such as lithium-11, found evidence through quasi-free proton scattering, Coulomb breakup and charge radius measurements. Certain unbound nuclei past the neutron drip line, decaying by two-neutron emission, are also candidates; beryllium-16's decay into a core plus two neutrons has been studied closely. Theory shows the dineutron partly arises from mixing configurations of opposite parity for the two outer neutrons. The review also covers four-neutron clusters, recent tetraneutron experiments, and the observation of oxygen-28, closing with future prospects.
arxiv-2606-29150:
Helbling, Bryutkin, Martino, Dehmamy and Strobelt introduce Flow Reasoning Models, which turn flow-based text generators into strong puzzle solvers. Flow models generate in few steps, but applied naively to structured reasoning like Sudoku and Zebra puzzles, the models converge confidently to wrong answers, solving only about a third of Sudoku puzzles. The key observation is that these models can act as their own verifiers.

At test time, the models propose many candidates and keep the dynamically stable ones. That search alone reached perfect Sudoku scores and about ninety-six percent on Zebra puzzles. It generalised to harder out-of-distribution Sudoku variants. To cut wasted computation, a training recipe improves the base model. A self-conditioning channel teaches refinement of past predictions, and preference training teaches it to avoid its own failed generations. The improved model solved Sudoku in just seven forward passes, far fewer than the strongest baseline.
arxiv-2606-29550:
Mockus releases a deforking map covering the World of Code, a vast collection of open-source repositories. A fork copies a project's git history, so one commit surfaces in many repositories at once. Any popularity or spread measure counted over raw repositories is therefore inflated, sometimes by orders of magnitude. Platform fork graphs also miss families that span several hosting services.

His map collapses each raw repository into the deforked project it belongs to, using tens of millions of shared-commit groups. Simple merging over-connects unrelated software into giant clusters, so capped variants bound cluster size and remove boilerplate hub bridges. Validated against GitHub's declared fork graph rebuilt from archive events, the map agrees on nearly all shared edges. The disagreements expose fork families that GitHub's graph cannot represent, including families that span several hosts.
arxiv-2606-29750:
Purja Pun, Obst, Basilakis, and Ginige tackle the automatic mapping between disease classification systems, the International Classification of Diseases among them. Mapping codes between versions is essential for integrating health data. Embedding-based methods focus mainly on one-to-one mappings. 

Their method borrows the blocking-and-matching pipeline from entity resolution. A blocking stage uses embeddings to gather candidate matches for each code. A matching stage then asks a large language model, through a multiple-choice format, to pick all valid mappings inside each block. Across several ICD version pairs, the method achieves higher precision than existing approaches, with comparable recall and broader coverage. The authors release their code and dataset.
arxiv-2606-30050:
Kansei Ushiyama and Shun Sato design faster algorithms for minimizing nonconvex functions, without any restart tricks. Many optimization methods rely on restarts to hit the best known speed. Restarts complicate implementation and break some useful properties. Their two first-order methods reach an approximate stationary point efficiently. Neither method needs the target accuracy as an input.

Both methods come from discretizing one continuous-time model. That model is an ordinary differential equation with momentum-like dynamics. The first method is simple, and its last iterate stays differentiable. That smoothness in the starting point helps when inputs are varied. The second method estimates the needed Lipschitz constants adaptively. It therefore needs no prior knowledge of those constants. Its numerical results beat existing parameter-free methods on some problems. Continuous and discrete convergence proofs run in parallel throughout.
arxiv-2606-30150:
Berkin Ulukutlu and seventeen colleagues test silicon pixel sensors bent into curves for a major detector upgrade. The ALICE experiment at CERN plans to replace its innermost tracking layers. The new sensors are wafer-scale CMOS chips bent to small radii. This study uses ALPIDE chips, the current generation, in bent form. Proton beams at three energies probe their behavior.

The beams scatter elastically off a polypropylene fiber target. Two tracker arms, with sensors bent at three radii, reconstruct the protons. The team studies clustering in events with high energy loss. Bending shows no significant impact on cluster size. Alignment strategies are checked against simulations using track benchmarks. Distance of closest approach and opening angle both serve as tests. The achieved resolution matches simulation expectations closely. Bent sensors look suitable for future high-energy physics detectors.
arxiv-2606-30250:
Yuqia Wu, Yue Wang, and Yaohua Hu pin down the exact convergence speed of a regularized Newton method for problems with several goals. Multiobjective optimization balances competing criteria without fixing weights in advance. Their method minimizes a regularized max-envelope of local quadratic models each step. A Tanabe-type merit function measures progress toward Pareto optimality. The question is how fast that merit can decay globally.

Under a compactness assumption on the starting level set, they prove the rate. The merit decays at a global asymptotic rate slightly faster than one over k squared. The single-objective case falls out as a special case. A constructed family of one-dimensional convex bi-objective problems shows sharpness. No uniform rate with a higher exponent can hold in general. The exponent two is thus essentially best possible uniformly. Per-trajectory decay can still beat any fixed polynomial bound slightly.
arxiv-2606-30650:
Carlos Sanoja and Oscar Moreno Mayz model a staffing puzzle in student support services. The scarce resource is staff time that is both free and qualified. Qualification decays with disuse, new needs appear that nobody is trained for, and training itself eats the hours current students need.
