The protein, lactoferrin, was known to rally immune cells against the virus, but a direct blocking effect was untested. Using a harmless stand-in virus carrying the SARS entry spike, they dosed human cells fitted with the virus's receptor.

The protein stopped infection in proportion to dose, acting at the attachment step before entry. It did not disturb the spike's grip on its main receptor, though. Instead it coated sugary chains on the cell surface that the virus uses as first landing pads. Stripping those chains, or flooding them with a similar sugar, copied the effect. The findings name those chains as essential entry helpers and suggest the milk protein as a defence lead.
europmc-pmc3198950:
Noel O'Boyle and colleagues presented Open Babel in this 2011 paper in the Journal of Cheminformatics. Chemists store molecular structures in many incompatible file formats, and converting between them is a constant chore in computer modeling. Open Babel is a free, open-source toolbox built to translate between those formats, handling more than one hundred and ten of them in the version described.

Beyond conversion, the toolbox supplies algorithms chemists need daily, such as assigning partial charges, detecting aromatic rings, perceiving bond orders, and producing canonical forms of a structure. The paper details the design of the new release and shows uses from conformer searching and two-dimensional drawing to filtering, batch conversion, and similarity searching. Developers can also embed it as a library in their own software.
europmc-pmc3207950:
Paul Magwene, John Willis, and John Kelly built a statistical framework for bulk segregant analysis with modern sequencing in this 2011 paper in PLoS Computational Biology. The technique hunts for genes behind a trait by pooling offspring that show the trait and sequencing the pool, looking for regions where allele frequencies shift.

Their method smooths the standard test statistic and accounts for two sources of noise: sampling when the pools are formed, and sampling during sequencing itself. Simulations explored how pool size and sequencing depth affect the power to detect trait-linked regions. Surprisingly, larger pools worked best, even though they dilute the signal. The authors show the approach can find even weak-effect loci, and they demonstrate it on a yeast experiment.
europmc-pmc3291550:
Snelders and co-authors asked whether farm fungicides could train a mold to resist medical drugs, in a 2012 study. The mold Aspergillus fumigatus causes serious lung disease, and doctors treat it with a small set of triazole drugs. Resistant strains carrying a paired genetic change had begun appearing in patients, including some who never took the drugs.

The team compared dozens of farm chemicals approved in the Netherlands over past decades with the medical drugs. Five farm triazoles matched the medicines closely in shape and in how they dock onto the target protein, and they produced the strongest cross resistance. Those five entered use just before the first resistant patient strain appeared, and lab tests showed spray pressure alone could push the genetic change further.
europmc-pmc3314950:
Mischo and colleagues showed that a yeast protein guards the genome while genes are being read, in a 2011 study. The protein, named Sen1, was known for helping to end the copying of certain RNA messages. When a fresh RNA strand sticks back onto the DNA it came from, it forms a loop that leaves one DNA strand exposed and fragile.

Without working Sen1, these loops pile up in baker's yeast and trigger unwanted swapping between DNA regions during gene reading. The protein's unwinding action normally clears the loops away. Genes for DNA repair also interact with Sen1, suggesting repair crews finish the cleanup. The authors argue that loop formation happens often during normal gene activity, and that stopping it is a core part of Sen1's job.
europmc-pmc3324550:
Bhullar and co-authors found widespread antibiotic resistance in bacteria from a cave cut off from the surface for millions of years, reporting in 2012. The cave, Lechuguilla Cave in New Mexico, holds microbial communities isolated for over four million years, untouched by human medicine. If resistance were mainly a product of modern drug use, these bacteria should have shown little of it.

Instead, many cave strains resisted a wide range of modern antibiotics, and some shrugged off fourteen different drugs. Resistance even covered a last resort drug used against stubborn infections. The team uncovered enzyme based tricks the bacteria use to disable drugs, including one gene closely related to resistance genes now circulating in hospitals. The authors argue that resistance is ancient and natural, built into microbial life long before pharmacies existed.
europmc-pmc3334750:
Gonçalves-Pereira and Póvoa reviewed how the body handles a major class of antibiotics in intensive care patients, in a 2011 paper. Beta lactam antibiotics kill bacteria only while their level stays above a threshold, so dosing depends on predictable drug handling. Critically ill patients, the authors suspected, break the predictions borrowed from healthy volunteers.

Surveying fifty seven studies covering six widely used drugs, they found striking variation from patient to patient. The space the drug spreads into and the speed the body clears it each varied more than two fold, tied partly to kidney function. Half lives and time above the killing threshold were nearly impossible to predict, especially in patients whose kidneys looked normal. Slow, prolonged infusions usually gave better coverage, and drug entry into infected tissues faltered in septic shock. The authors urge dosing guided by drug level monitoring.
europmc-pmc3367650:
Dumler and co-authors reviewed human granulocytic anaplasmosis in 2005, a tick-borne illness first recognized in 1990. The sickness is caused by a bacterium that lives inside neutrophils, the white blood cells that normally fight infection. Cases had been climbing in the United States since the disease was first described.

The review traces how the germ was separated from a related ehrlichiosis and renamed Anaplasma phagocytophilum. It describes the usual picture of fever, headache, muscle pain, low white cell counts, and mild liver injury. Dumler also explains how the bacterium changes the cells it infects. That grounding helps doctors spot, treat, and prevent a severe illness that is easy to miss.
europmc-pmc3383750:
Stuckler, McKee, Ebrahim, and Basu examined in 2012 how global producers drive rising use of unhealthy goods in poorer countries. The goods include soft drinks, salty and fatty processed foods, alcohol, and tobacco. Consumption was climbing fastest in low- and middle-income countries, while rich countries had largely leveled off.

Growth in poorer countries, they report, is running even faster than it once did in rich ones. Multinational firms have penetrated middle-income food markets about as deeply as rich-country ones. Sales of unhealthy foods track closely with tobacco and alcohol sales, hinting at shared industry tactics. Rising income alone does not doom a country; trade and investment deals shape the outcome.
europmc-pmc3431850:
Singh and Li reviewed in 2012 how two plastic chemicals, bisphenol A and phthalates, rewrite the chemical tags that control genes. Such epigenetic marks, on DNA and its packaging proteins, can change gene activity for life after exposure in the womb. The review gathers evidence from cell and animal studies.

In yellow mice, bisphenol A stripped tags near a coat-color gene, and feeding mothers folate or a plant estrogen blocked the effect. The chemical also altered tags in human breast and placental cells and shifted tiny regulatory RNAs. A phthalate loosened tags on the estrogen receptor gene in breast cancer cells, while another raised tag-writing enzymes in mouse testis. Some effects in rats passed to later generations.
europmc-pmc3497250:
When separate populations evolve the same trait, do they reuse the same genes? Gina L. Conte, Matthew E. Arnegard, Catherine L. Peichel, and Dolph Schluter estimate the odds from published studies in 2012, separating parallel evolution from shared ancestors and convergence from distant ones.

Reuse is surprisingly common. Genetic mapping studies give a mean probability of 0.32, and candidate gene studies 0.55. The chance falls as the common ancestor ages, from about 0.8 for young splits to 0.1 to 0.4 for the oldest. Reuse runs higher when populations start from the same ancestor. Evolution, at the gene level, looks more predictable than chance would suggest.
europmc-pmc3504050:
Draft genomes are full of holes, and Adam C. English and twelve colleagues present PBJelly in 2012, a tool that patches them with long reads from the Pacific Biosciences RS sequencer. Short-read assemblies stumble on repeats, biases, and variation, and manual finishing with older Sanger methods is slow and costly.

PBJelly guides long reads onto a draft assembly, filling gaps automatically. It also produces coordinate tables that carry existing annotations from the old draft onto the upgraded sequence, protecting years of prior work. The software is public, and the authors show the approach on real genomes. Long reads, they argue, turn finishing from a craft project into a routine automated step.
europmc-pmc3506950:
Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis reshape gut microbes, and Xochitl C. Morgan leads a fifteen-author team asking what those microbes stop doing properly in 2012. They sequence microbes from intestinal biopsies and stool of 231 patients and healthy subjects, then follow a subset with shotgun metagenomics to read function directly.

Which microbes are present shifts less than what they do: 12 percent of pathways change against only 2 percent of genera. Oxidative stress pathways rise, while carbohydrate use and amino acid building fall in favor of nutrient transport and uptake. Disease status, treatment, and personal traits all leave marks. Treating the microbiome, the results hint, means fixing metabolism, not just membership.
europmc-pmc3584150:
Min Kwon and colleagues built and tested a smartphone addiction scale in PLoS ONE in 2013. Heavy phone use was already raising clinical concern, but no standard self-test existed for it. Their scale adapts a Korean internet addiction questionnaire to features unique to smartphones. One hundred ninety-seven adults in South Korea, aged eighteen to fifty-three, filled in the new scale plus established addiction and mood questionnaires between late 2011 and early 2012.

Statistical pruning cut the draft to six factors, dropping one subscale about losing touch with reality. The final scale hung together strongly, with an internal consistency score of 0.967, and its scores moved in step with the internet addiction measures and with how hooked people said they felt. Scores also differed by job and schooling. The authors present the instrument as a first reliable screen that clinics and researchers can use to flag problem phone use.
europmc-pmc3598250:
Anne-Claire Haury and colleagues presented a network-finding method called TIGRESS in BMC Systems Biology in 2012. Gene regulatory networks map which genes switch which others on and off, guiding everything from basic cell biology to drug target hunts. Rebuilding those maps from gene activity data is notoriously error-prone, and many methods exist with modest accuracy. TIGRESS recasts the job as picking a few strong predictors for each gene from a crowd of candidates.

The method pairs least angle regression, a stepwise fitting technique, with stability selection, which reruns the fit on many data samples and keeps only links that recur. A new scoring rule sharpens that selection. In the DREAM5 challenge, a blind community contest, TIGRESS ranked among the best overall and first among regression-based methods. Tests on computer-made networks and on real bacteria and yeast data fill out the paper, and code is offered online.
europmc-pmc3616050:
Matthew Strain and colleagues applied a new counting method to HIV DNA in PLoS ONE in 2013. The DNA copies of HIV lodged in a patient's cells are the most sensitive gauge of leftover infection during treatment, and the reservoir they form is what a cure must erase. Droplet digital PCR splits a sample into thousands of droplets and counts positive ones, promising exact counts without a reference standard. Its performance on targets as rare as HIV had never been shown.

Over three hundred patient samples, more than one hundred fifty assayed three times by both methods, made the comparison. The droplet method cut measurement scatter about five fold for the main viral gene count and improved accuracy over twenty fold for a rare circular DNA form. It also shrugged off small mismatches between test primers and virus sequence. For reservoir studies and cure trials, that precision is the offer.
europmc-pmc3760650:
Olivier de Jong and eight co-authors reported a study in the Journal of Extracellular Vesicles in 2012 on exosomes from the cells lining blood vessels. Those lining cells answer stress, such as low oxygen or inflammation, by adapting and sending out signals. Exosomes, small vesicles carrying RNA and protein from their source cell, are strong carriers of such signals.

The team exposed cultured lining cells to low oxygen, an inflammation activator, or high sugar, then compared the RNA and protein cargo of the exosomes they released. They catalogued 1,354 proteins and 1,992 RNA messages. Low oxygen and inflammation left clear marks on both cargo types. High sugar changed the protein cargo only slightly and left the RNA cargo alone. The authors conclude that cell stress is reflected in exosome content.
europmc-pmc3761350:
Amy DiMarino, Arnold Caplan, and Tracey Bonfield wrote a review in Frontiers in Immunology in 2013 on mesenchymal stem cells in tissue repair. Stem cell therapies built on these cells excite interest for diseases involving inflammation and tissue damage. Their promise is clouded by hard questions about how to measure a cell batch's potency and what the cells do after treatment.

The review covers lab and animal assays for MSC function and how they carry into clinical use. Results vary with cell source: a patient's own cells avoid matching problems but may carry the disease's own defects, while donor cells raise immune questions once thought settled. The authors stress that judging efficacy requires grasping the disease model and standard outcome measures, and that preparation and quality control are only as good as the assays behind them.
europmc-pmc3773450:
Giovanni De Pergola and Franco Silvestris wrote a review in the Journal of Obesity in 2013 on obesity as a major risk factor for cancer. About 20 percent of cancer cases are estimated to be caused by excess weight. International agency reports find the strongest evidence for cancers of the womb lining, esophagus, colon, breast after menopause, prostate, and kidney.

The review works through the systems that may link fat to cancer: insulin and a related growth factor, sex steroids, and fat-tissue signals called adipokines. Newer candidate mechanisms include chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, cross-talk between tumor cells and nearby fat cells, low oxygen inside expanding fat, shared genes, and weakened immune defense. The authors argue that understanding these links must come before better prevention and treatment.
europmc-pmc3778950:
David Cooper, Michael Krawczak, Constantin Polychronakos, Chris Tyler-Smith, and Hildegard Kehrer-Sawatzki wrote a review in Human Genetics in 2013 on reduced penetrance. Penetrance is the share of people carrying a disease mutation who actually show the disease. When some carriers stay healthy, penetrance is reduced, and the phenomenon is common.

Reduced penetrance explains why genetic diseases can pass through unaffected parents, and why healthy people can carry many risky variants without harm. It can stem from the mutation itself, from gene dose, from uneven expression of the two gene copies, or from copy number changes. Modifier genes, epigenetic marks, environment, age, and sex can all tune it. The review gathers the evidence that reduced penetrance is widespread and works through the molecular mechanisms proposed to explain it.
europmc-pmc3810850:
Zhang, Kapli, Pavlidis, and Stamatakis presented in Bioinformatics in 2013 a new method for drawing species boundaries from DNA data. The task matters for DNA barcoding, microbe surveys, and metabarcoding studies. Their Poisson tree processes model, PTP for short, reads the branching pattern of a phylogenetic tree to judge where one species ends and the next begins.

Unlike threshold methods, PTP needs no preset similarity cutoff, and unlike coalescent models it needs no ultrametric tree and runs fast enough for large data sets. In tests it beat the popular GMYC model and OTU picking when species were close kin. A paired tool, EPA-PTP, counts species among sequences placed onto a reference tree, aimed at high-throughput survey data.
europmc-pmc395750:
Stefan Kurtz and colleagues present MUMmer, software for comparing whole genomes, in Genome Biology in 2004. Comparing one gene against a database was routine by then, but lining up two entire genomes against each other had become a new and pressing task as genome sequences piled up. Earlier tools were too slow or too limited for the largest chromosomes. MUMmer was written to close that gap, and this paper describes its newest version.

The open-source system finds exact matches between genomes quickly, then builds alignments from them, handling large eukaryotic genomes at a range of evolutionary distances. The authors demonstrate it on several genome pairs, from microbes to much larger species. The paper became a standard reference for whole-genome comparison, a basic operation in reading gene function and tracing how genomes evolve.
europmc-pmc3995050:
Camillo Porta, Chiara Paglino, and Alessandra Mosca review drugs that target a key growth pathway in cancer, in Frontiers in Oncology in 2014. The pathway links three named parts, PI3K, Akt, and mTOR, and steers cell growth and survival. The parts are so tightly linked that the authors treat them as one route.

Tumours live under stress, with low food and low oxygen, so control of this route matters for their growth. Faults in its genes are common across many cancers. The review first lays out the route and its main parts, then surveys drugs that block each part. Some are already approved for use, such as temsirolimus and everolimus, while others are new compounds just leaving the lab. The survey gives a snapshot of where this drug family stood and what was coming next.
europmc-pmc4017650:
William W. Wheaton and eleven co-authors pin down how the diabetes drug metformin slows cancer, in eLife in 2014. Reports from patient records and lab work had linked metformin to slower tumour growth. Two routes were on the table: a whole-body route through lower insulin, and a direct route inside cancer cells.

In human cancer cells, metformin blocked complex I, the first step of the power chain in mitochondria, and cut cell breathing. Cells still grew while sugar was present, by leaning on sugar breakdown alone, but died when sugar was withdrawn. A stress sensor that helps tumours in low oxygen also quieted. Adding a yeast version of the blocked step, immune to the drug, undid all these effects. In mice, metformin slowed grafted human tumours unless the grafts carried that yeast rescue. The proof shows the anti-cancer action runs through complex I inside the cancer cells themselves.
europmc-pmc4057750:
William Peverill, Lawrie W. Powell, and Richard Skoien reviewed how non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, or NASH, develops and worsens. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2014. NASH combines fat buildup and swelling in the liver, and in some people it leads to scarring and cirrhosis.

The authors argue that fat overload, insulin resistance, and excess free fatty acids injure liver cells through oxidative stress. Dying or aging liver cells then trigger signals that switch on scarring. They also discuss a ductular reaction, growth of liver progenitor cells, and a T-cell response that may drive progress. Readers get a map of the many linked steps behind liver scarring, beyond fat and swelling alone.
europmc-pmc4066750:
Xiaobei Zhou, Helen Lindsay, and Mark D. Robinson tackled a weakness in RNA sequencing studies: single outlier samples can distort comparisons of gene activity. Their methods paper appeared in Nucleic Acids Research in 2014. Count-based tools compare read counts between conditions, often sharing information across genes to help small samples.

The authors showed that outliers can sway a whole analysis, not just the gene where they occur. They propose giving each observation a weight, so odd counts count for less, inside existing analysis frameworks. Tests on real and simulated data kept strong detection power while resisting outliers. An implementation for the edgeR package is provided, and the weighting idea can travel to other tools.
europmc-pmc4075450:
Eunkyoo Oh, Jia-Ying Zhu, Ming-Yi Bai, Rafael Augusto Arenhart, Yu Sun, and Zhi-Yong Wang mapped a central control circuit for cell elongation in the young stem of Arabidopsis, a small model plant. Their study appeared in eLife in 2014. Growth signals from hormones, light, and temperature must be coordinated for a coherent response.

Three transcription factors, one each answering to auxin, light and temperature, and brassinosteroid signals, bind each other and jointly control many shared target genes. A gibberellin-sensitive repressor can block their DNA binding. A further three-part module feeds back on the system, tuning auxin sensitivity to growth stage and conditions. The circuit shows how a plant merges hormone, environment, and development signals into one growth decision.
europmc-pmc4076250:
Marten Boetzer and Walter Pirovano presented SSPACE-LongRead, software that uses long DNA reads to order and join the pieces of a draft bacterial genome. Their paper appeared in BMC Bioinformatics in 2014. A new single-molecule sequencing machine produced very long reads, offering a cheap way to improve rough assemblies built from short reads.

The method works step by step, using the long reads as a backbone to scaffold pre-assembled fragments. On six bacterial draft genomes, even moderate coverage of raw, uncorrected long reads sharply cut the number of separate pieces. Compared with a rival scaffolder, the approach more often produced nearly complete genomes. The authors note the program needs only modest computing power, so genome finishing becomes fast and reliable.
europmc-pmc4095950:
David W. Green and Jubin Abutalebi proposed the adaptive control hypothesis, a theory of how bilingual speakers manage two languages. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Cognitive Psychology in 2013. Speaking the right language at the right moment takes control processes that keep goals in mind and suppress interference.

Earlier work showed people raise control effort to meet a goal. Green and Abutalebi go further: control processes themselves adapt to the setting a speaker habitually faces. They distinguish eight control processes and three settings, single language, dual language, and dense code-switching. Each setting, they predict, tunes specific brain circuits in lasting ways. They concede the predictions may fail, but set out tests linking everyday language habits to brain adaptation.
europmc-pmc4203350:
Isabel Delany, Rino Rappuoli, and Ennio De Gregorio surveyed the state of vaccines in EMBO Molecular Medicine in 2014. Vaccination has been the most effective medical step against infectious disease, saving an estimated two to three million lives a year and wiping out smallpox. Yet big targets remain unmet.

The review reports on trials for vaccines against HIV, malaria, tuberculosis, and cancer, all still unsolved. It also notes under-served groups, such as the elderly and pregnant women, for whom existing vaccines work less well or are little used. New tools get a tour: stronger adjuvants that wake the immune system, carrier vectors, nucleic acid vaccines, and antigens designed from protein structures. The authors hope these methods will bring diseases once thought out of reach under vaccine control this century.
europmc-pmc4204150:
Daniela Berg, Anthony E. Lang, and ten co-authors opened a debate on redefining Parkinson's disease in Movement Disorders in 2014. The statement introduces a task force of the Movement Disorder Society charged with rethinking the definition. Better knowledge had begun to strain the old rules for who counts as having the disease.

Several fault lines are named. Some genetic cases lack the Lewy body deposits long treated as the gold standard, while many healthy brains hold such deposits. Dementia, once grounds to exclude the diagnosis, is now seen as a common part of the disease. Early warning years, when only nonmotor signs such as lost smell appear, call for criteria for prodromal disease. The group also weighs naming formal subtypes, and lays out what new criteria must do.
europmc-pmc4287950:
Simon Anders, Paul Theodor Pyl, and Wolfgang Huber present HTSeq, a Python library for handling high throughput sequencing data. Their paper appeared in Bioinformatics in 2015. Many standard analysis steps have ready tools, but projects that leave the standard path need custom scripts, and writing parsers for each data format wastes time.

HTSeq supplies parsers for the common formats plus objects for reads, alignments, gene models, and variant calls, all searchable by genome position. A companion tool, htseq-count, counts reads per gene to prepare RNA sequencing data for expression analysis. Released as free open source software, the library became a building block in many genomics pipelines.
europmc-pmc4381250:
Sara Reed and Dawn Quelle reviewed a chemical tweak to the famous tumor suppressor p53, in Cancers in 2014. Proteins gain small tags after they are built, and those tags steer what they do. For p53, one tag type, ubiquitin, controls its stability and location. A second, acetylation, is less understood. It has been shown to steer which genes p53 switches on, and whether cells pause growth or die after damage. The review asks how much that steering really matters in living animals.

Mouse studies complicate the story, casting doubt on whether acetylation at certain sites is needed for tumor suppression at all. The review covers the enzymes that add the tags, what controls those enzymes, and how other tags interact with acetylation. The authors conclude that single tags fine-tune p53 rather than switch it on or off.
europmc-pmc4396150:
Panteha Hayati Rezvan, Katherine Lee, and Julie Simpson reviewed how medical papers report a missing-data method, in BMC Medical Research Methodology in 2015. Missing data are routine in medical studies and can bias results if mishandled. Multiple imputation fills gaps with plausible values several times over and pools the results, and journals increasingly demand clear reporting of it. The team systematically reviewed papers in two top journals, The Lancet and the New England Journal of Medicine, from 2008 to 2013.

They found 103 papers using the method, rising from 11 in 2008 to 26 in 2013. Most named the variables imputed, but only 37 percent stated the imputation method used, and just 9 percent said how they handled skewed variables. Sensitivity analyses appeared in a minority. Adoption is racing ahead of reporting quality, the review concludes, leaving readers unable to judge many analyses.
europmc-pmc4419550:
Joseph Phillips, Doaa Hewedi, Abeer Eissa, and Ahmed Moustafa reviewed evidence in Frontiers in Public Health in 2015 linking the cerebellum to mental illness. Long treated as a center for balance and movement alone, the cerebellum is now also tied to thought, feeling, attention, and working memory.

Studies covered here connect cerebellar faults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, autism, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depression, and anxiety. Damage to parts of the cerebellum can shape movement, thinking, and mood, the authors note, because its paths reach many brain areas. They close by pointing to open questions and to the kind of work needed to test how strong these links are.
europmc-pmc4429650:
Ananda Prasad, writing alone in Frontiers in Nutrition in 2014, reviewed zinc as a guard against oxidation and inflammation in human health. Zinc was recognized as essential only about fifty years before the article. Prasad's own trials in older adults found far fewer infections in those given zinc. They also found lower markers of oxidative stress and inflammation.

In zinc-poor human cells, a key inflammatory message and its gene activity rose. Adding zinc raised a protein called A20, which in turn damped a master inflammation switch known as NF-kB, cutting inflammatory signals. Prasad links this chemistry to diseases of aging, including artery disease, cancer, brain decline, and immune disorders, and argues that correcting zinc shortage is a simple, low-cost way to cut that risk.
europmc-pmc4430650:
Alicia Thorp and Markus Schlaich reviewed the role of the sympathetic nervous system in obesity and metabolic syndrome in the Journal of Diabetes Research in 2015. This nerve system is best known for controlling blood pressure and heart action. It also governs energy use, and evidence from animals and humans suggests long-term overactivity helps cause the cluster of problems called metabolic syndrome.

Several drivers are proposed, including insulin excess, faulty pressure sensors in blood vessels, and signals from fat tissue. In turn, overactive sympathetic nerves may worsen two core features of the syndrome, fat carried around the waist and poor response to insulin. Because the syndrome raises risk of diabetes, heart disease, and early death, the authors argue that calming this nerve activity deserves more attention in care and research.
europmc-pmc4448150:
Alex Ritter and a team of co-authors filmed killer T cells preparing to strike, in Immunity in 2015. Cytotoxic T lymphocytes destroy infected and tumor cells by releasing poison granules in a focused burst at the contact point, called the immunological synapse. The order of the steps leading to that burst was still unclear, despite its speed.

With sharp four-dimensional imaging, the team timed each step. The T cell first arrived with actin-rich fingers and a dense actin mesh at the contact. Within about a minute the mesh thinned across the synapse, receptor clusters gathered at the center, and the cell's organizing center began to move. Granules clustered around it and reached the contact minutes later, arriving where actin and a key membrane lipid were sparse. Actin clearing, they conclude, opens the gate for secretion.
europmc-pmc4464350:
Heonjong Han and a large team of co-authors built TRRUST, a database of human gene control links, in Scientific Reports in 2015. Rebuilding the networks by which transcription factors switch target genes on or off is a long-standing goal in genetics. Computer methods that guess such links from large data sets need a trusted set of known links to be judged against, and hand-checked collections were small.

TRRUST was assembled by mining sentences in millions of medical abstracts and then curating the extracted claims by hand. It records thousands of interactions between hundreds of transcription factor genes and their targets, along with whether each factor activates or represses its target. Tools in the database test whether a factor's targets form modules, whether factors cooperate on a target, and which associations deserve priority. The authors present it as the largest public hand-curated set of its kind then available.
europmc-pmc4530250:
Ramu Adela and Sanjay K. Banerjee review a stress signal protein tied to diabetes and heart disease, in the Journal of Diabetes Research in 2015. The protein, GDF-15, is made by heart, fat, vessel, and immune cells, and its blood level climbs with tissue injury and inflammation. High levels track with heart thickening, heart failure, vessel plaque, obesity, insulin resistance, and kidney damage in diabetes.

The review asks whether GDF-15 is a culprit, a marker, or a guard. Most studies cast it as protective: it calms several damage pathways in heart, fat, and vessel lining cells. Yet a few reports find that lacking it helps against vessel injury. Age and smoking also raise levels, complicating its use as a test.
europmc-pmc4564950:
D. Baumeister and four co-authors pool studies on whether childhood trauma leaves inflammation switched on in adults, in Molecular Psychiatry. Trauma in childhood raises the risk of later physical and mental illness, and a smoldering immune system is one suspected bridge. The team searched five databases for studies measuring blood inflammation markers in adults with and without early trauma.

Twenty-five papers qualified. Three markers were pooled separately: C-reactive protein from 18 studies with 16,870 people, interleukin-6 from 15 studies with 3,751 people, and tumor necrosis factor from 10 studies with 881 people. All three ran significantly higher in adults who had suffered childhood trauma. Breakdowns by abuse type refined the pattern, supporting inflammation as one path from early harm to later disease.
europmc-pmc4598350:
A 2015 literature review from Caridad Figueroa and colleagues centres on attitudes toward HIV self-testing among key populations. Self-testing could help groups who face the highest HIV risk and the poorest access to clinics. The review covers men who have sex with men, sex workers, people who inject drugs, transgender people, and prisoners.

Most studies came from rich countries and focused on men who have sex with men, who generally found self-testing acceptable. Privacy and convenience were the main draws. Concerns included missing counselling, user error, and test accuracy. Evidence for the other groups was thin, and the authors call that gap a research priority as self-testing spreads to poorer settings.
europmc-pmc4598750:
Mark S. Paget wrote a solo 2015 review of bacterial sigma factors and the anti-sigma factors that control them. Sigma factors are parts of the bacterial RNA polymerase machine that find gene start sites and open them for reading. The review focuses on the large sigma-70 family. It appeared in Biomolecular Concepts.

Housekeeping sigma factors drive most gene reading during fast growth, while related alternative factors switch on stress and development programs. Anti-sigma factors hold sigmas inactive until needed. Release happens by three main routes: cutting up the anti-sigma, partner switching between proteins, and direct sensing of a signal. The review maps these control tricks and shows how bacteria blend several signals before turning genes on.
europmc-pmc4599250:
A team led by Chia-Yi Liu published a 2015 study on vimentin, a structural protein that rises as cancer cells turn more mobile. That shift, called EMT, helps breast cancer spread. Data from patients linked high vimentin after drug treatment to poor outcomes. The team used two breast cancer cell lines.

Lowering vimentin slowed cell growth, wound closing, and directed movement, and it made cells less stiff. Raising vimentin in the other line did the reverse and added spread-linked traits. Vimentin also shaped focal adhesions, the grips cells use to pull on their surroundings, and it swayed a gene switch called slug. The authors say vimentin keeps cancer cells sound in body and form while they take on their mobile state.
europmc-pmc4650350:
How resistance to drugs, germ killers, and metals travels as a set is the subject of a 2015 gene study by Chandan Pal and colleagues. Germ killers and metals can pick out drug resistance by chance when the genes sit side by side. Hard data on the scale of this were scarce. The team mined more than two thousand five hundred full germ genomes and more than four thousand plasmids.

On plasmids, only mercury resistance genes and one gene for soap-like killers sat often beside drug resistance genes. New links showed up between cadmium or zinc resistance and resistance to two drug groups. Genes for metal or killer resistance sat in most genomes, and they shared space with drug resistance in about one case in six. Some germ groups of note in clinics were prone to carry both kinds.
europmc-pmc4675850:
Thomas D. Parsons wrote a solo 2015 review of virtual reality for neuroscience research that feels more like real life. Laboratory tasks are controlled but often use flat, simple stimuli unlike everyday experience. Virtual environments can embed tasks in rich, dynamic scenes while keeping experimental control. The review appeared in Frontiers in Psychology.

Parsons argues that virtual scenarios with visual, spoken, and story context let researchers measure how people integrate cues about others' feelings and intentions over time. That matters for clinical testing, emotion research, and social neuroscience, where sterile tests generalise poorly. He surveys assessment designs that use emotionally engaging narratives and social interaction inside virtual worlds. The review makes the case for virtual reality as a bridge between rigour and realism.
europmc-pmc4687950:
Penny Whiting, Jelena Savović, Julian P. T. Higgins, and colleagues built a tool named ROBIS, described in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology in 2016. Systematic reviews guide medical decisions, yet a review itself can be biased by poor design. No tool existed to judge bias in the review rather than in the studies it collects. ROBIS was developed in four stages, from scoping and evidence checks to a face-to-face meeting and pilot testing.

The finished tool runs in three phases. Users first check relevance, then probe four areas where bias can creep in, from study selection to how findings are combined. A final phase gives an overall judgment, guided by signaling questions at each step. ROBIS is aimed at guideline makers and at authors of reviews of reviews. It is the first rigorously built tool of its kind.
europmc-pmc4740350:
Guney, Menche, Vidal, and Barábasi build a network measure of how close a drug's protein targets sit to a disease's gene module in the human interactome. The measure corrects for biases that make well-studied proteins look artificially central. Testing it on 238 drugs across 78 diseases shows a pattern: drugs that truly treat a disease cluster in its network neighbourhood.

Drugs used only for symptom relief sit farther away, and the measure flags weak efficacy for some Parkinson's and inflammatory-disease drugs. The same proximity score predicts new drug-disease pairings, pointing to repurposing candidates and possible side effects before either shows up in the clinic.
europmc-pmc4754750:
Zhongyang Liu and eleven colleagues present an online analysis tool in Scientific Reports in 2016. The tool, BATMAN-TCM, aims to show how traditional Chinese herbal formulas act inside the body at the molecular level. Such formulas mix many plant chemicals at once, so their paths of action stay hard to trace by lab work alone.

The site predicts which human proteins each herb chemical may hit. It then maps those hits onto pathways, gene roles, and disease links, and draws the web for the user. Users can also compare several formulas side by side. The team tested it on a heart pill formula and, with lab checks, tied its benefit to a hormone system that controls blood pressure.
europmc-pmc4772450:
Jack Cuzick and six colleagues report long-term results from the IBIS-I trial in The Lancet Oncology in 2015. The trial tested whether tamoxifen, a hormone-blocking drug, can prevent breast cancer in women at raised risk. Earlier trials showed benefit over ten years; this report follows women far longer to see if the shield lasts.

Over 7,000 women in eight countries took tamoxifen or a dummy pill for five years. At a median of sixteen years of follow-up, the tamoxifen group had clearly fewer breast cancers, about seven in a hundred against nearly ten. The protection held steady in the second decade, well past the end of dosing, and was strongest for the hormone-sensitive cancer type. No clear gain in survival appeared, but the lasting prevention case is firm.
europmc-pmc4779150:
Giovanni Pezzulo, Francesco Rigoli, and Karl Friston set out a unified account of behavior control in Progress in Neurobiology in 2015. Animals keep their inner state steady, a task called homeostasis, while also acting on the world. Psychology describes that control with three systems: reflex-like Pavlovian responses, habits, and plan-driven goal seeking. The three are usually modeled apart.

The authors fold all three into one frame called active inference, in which the brain acts to make the world match its expectations. Reflexes, habits, and plans then fall out as settings of a single system, tuned by how much weight each signal carries. The paper also sketches an evolutionary path from simple controllers to layered ones, and maps the scheme onto brain regions.
europmc-pmc4791150:
Jolyon Troscianko, Martin Stevens, and Sean Rands present a free imaging toolbox in Methods in Ecology and Evolution in 2015. Biologists increasingly measure animal color and pattern from photos, but consumer cameras are built to please human eyes, not to record light faithfully. Uncalibrated shots can quietly ruin a study, and many researchers lack tools to fix them.

The toolbox, an add-on to the free ImageJ program, straightens camera files into true light measures and scales them against grey standards shot in the same light. It folds in ultraviolet channels and can re-render a scene as a chosen animal's eyes would catch it. Tests showed a straight-line response in every camera tried, and animal-view conversions matched lab instruments closely. The tools also pull brightness, color, and pattern measures from the cleaned images.
europmc-pmc4816150:
Hong Ruan and Lily Q. Dong review adiponectin in the Journal of Molecular Cell Biology in 2016. Adiponectin is a hormone poured out by fat cells. It does the opposite of what its source suggests. It makes muscle and liver answer insulin better. It calms swelling. It steadies energy use. Its fall in obesity sits close to the root of type 2 diabetes. That makes its pathways prime drug territory.

The review maps how the hormone signals inside insulin target tissues. It names the receptors and relay proteins that carry the message. It shows where the path crosses other metabolic circuits. It also weighs why the hormone itself has not become a drug. It asks what a drug would need to copy. The authors call for sharper mechanism work joined with trials.
europmc-pmc4816350:
A. C. Day, P. H. J. Donachie, J. M. Sparrow, and R. L. Johnston report United Kingdom cataract surgery outcomes in Eye in 2015, from a national eye database. Cataract removal is the most common operation in the national health service. The audit drew on over 180,000 eyes from nearly 128,000 patients, operated between 2006 and 2010 at 28 sites.

Sight after surgery was strong: among eyes with no other eye disease, over nine in ten reached the standard acuity line or better. A tear in the lens capsule, the main surgical mishap, occurred in just under two percent of cases and sharply raised the odds of retinal detachment surgery and inner-eye infection soon after. Outcomes and mishap rates matched the previous decade, giving surgeons a steady benchmark.
europmc-pmc4817050:
Tal Galili, writing alone in Bioinformatics in 2015, presents dendextend, an R software package for working with cluster trees. Statisticians group items with hierarchical clustering and draw the result as a branching tree called a dendrogram. R, the field's common language, computes such trees well, but restyling them or comparing two trees was clumsy, since each tree carries its own display settings inside it.

The package supplies tools to recolor, reshape, and relabel tree parts freely, and methods to compare trees by eye and by number. It plugs into R's existing cluster ecosystem rather than replacing it. Worked examples in the package's guides show the tools on real data. The software is free under an open license from the standard R archive.
europmc-pmc4835650:
Letteria Minutoli leads a twelve-author review in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity in 2016 on a damaging sequence in restored blood flow. When an organ's blood supply is cut and then returns, the return itself injures the tissue: reactive oxygen species surge, ion balance breaks, and inflammation follows cell death. A key amplifier is the NLRP3 inflammasome, an alarm complex the oxygen surge helps switch on.

The review traces that alarm's role organ by organ, in brain, heart, kidney, and testis, and the routes by which oxygen species trip it, directly or through signals from strained mitochondria. No proven therapy yet blocks this injury, which carries heavy death and disability. The authors close with the state of new treatment attempts aimed at the alarm and its triggers.
europmc-pmc4864250:
Francesca Cordella and co-authors reviewed what users of upper limb prostheses need, in work from 2016. Losing a hand cuts autonomy in daily tasks, work, and social life. Current prosthetic hands help less than hoped: control links are clumsy, and the hand sends back no grip force or touch signals, so grasp stays weak and many devices end up abandoned.

Users rank tasks they wish they could do and rate their satisfaction with present devices. From those needs the review builds a requirement list for next designs: better control, feedback, comfort, and looks. Designing from user need, rather than from parts alone, aims to raise daily use and cut abandonment.
europmc-pmc4887650:
Monica Molteni, Sabrina Gemma, and Cristina Rossetti reviewed Toll-like receptor 4, a first-line alarm sensor, in infection and sterile inflammation in 2016. The receptor spots lipopolysaccharide, a coat piece of gram-negative bacteria, and triggers a pro-inflammatory response. It also binds the body's own molecules freed by tissue injury, so germs and damage converge on the same alarm.

That dual role makes the receptor an amplifier in many acute and chronic diseases, from sepsis to metabolic ills. Blocking or tuning it is a live drug aim, but care is needed: the same alarm guards against real infection. The review tracks the signal path and disease links, and weighs where therapy might safely intervene.
europmc-pmc4908950:
Amy O'Callaghan and Douwe van Sinderen reviewed bifidobacteria as members of the human gut community in 2016. These bacteria rank among the first to settle a newborn's gut and are credited with health gains, which is why food makers add them to yogurts and supplements. They also live in mouths, insect guts, and sewage.

Genome reads reveal their survival kit: sugar tools tuned to milk and plant fibers, ways to dodge host immunity, and surface appendages for gripping the gut wall. Gene editing in these bacteria lags, which slows firm proof of each trick. Knowing the kit helps makers pick strains that truly survive the gut trip.
europmc-pmc4972250:
Sonja Oberbeckmann, A. Mark Osborn, and Melissa B. Duhaime study the microbes that colonize plastic bottles in the sea. Their study appeared in PLoS ONE in 2016. Plastic debris fills oceans and fresh waters, and microbes coat it fast. Those biofilms may hold pathogens or plastic eating species, yet what shapes them was unclear. The team sank PET drinking bottles at three North Sea stations for five to six weeks in three seasons, alongside glass and seawater controls.

Communities on plastic varied with season and station. Many abundant members came from the Bacteroidetes group. Plastic communities differed from both seawater and glass communities, which shows the surface itself selects its settlers. Season and geography, though, rivaled material as drivers. The authors argue that judging plastic's ecological role needs this context, since a bottle hosts a shifting crew, not a fixed plastic biome.
europmc-pmc4973350:
S. Ma, E. S. Henson, Y. Chen, and S. B. Gibson show that two drugs together kill breast cancer cells by ferroptosis. Their study appeared in Cell Death and Disease in 2016. Ferroptosis is an iron dependent form of cell death driven by oxidative damage, distinct from apoptosis. The team treated four breast cancer cell lines with siramesine, a lysosome disrupting agent, and lapatinib, a kinase inhibitor. Alone each drug was modest; together they killed strongly within a day and raised reactive oxygen species.

An iron chelator drug cut both the oxidative surge and the death, which points to iron at the core. A known ferroptosis blocker also saved the cells. Treated cells took up more iron, since the iron importer transferrin rose after treatment. Removing transferrin protected the cells. The authors propose the pair as a way to force a death route that resistant breast cancers cannot easily dodge.
europmc-pmc4977650:
Glyn Elwyn, Dominick L. Frosch, and Sarah Kobrin argue that shared decision-making in medicine must be judged by its full range of consequences. Their article appeared in Implementation Science in 2016. Shared decision-making joins clinicians and patients in choosing care. Ethics alone, the authors say, will not change how care is organized; cost, quality, and efficiency govern practice. Yet studies of the approach have mostly measured short term effects on patients, such as knowledge gained or conflict felt about a choice.

Most research so far tests patient decision aids rather than the wider practice. The authors map a broader set of possible effects across conversations, teams, organizations, and whole systems, over longer spans. Some effects may be unintended, for good or ill. They call for research that tracks this wider ledger. Only then, they argue, can health systems decide how far to invest in the approach.
europmc-pmc5010150:
Rick M. Maizels and Henry J. McSorley review how parasitic worms tune the host immune system, in The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology in 2016. Helminths are worm parasites that live in the gut and tissues, often for years. To stay in place, they must calm the immune attacks that would expel them, and they have evolved many ways to do so.

Their tactics include blunting the cells that present foreign material, changing T cell and B cell behavior, and coaxing out regulator cells that enforce calm. This broad damping can spare the host damage and ease allergy, autoimmune, and swelling disorders. It can also weaken vaccine responses, raise the risk of other infections, and perhaps cut watchfulness against tumors. The authors weigh whether worm molecules could be turned into drugs for immune disease.
europmc-pmc5150650:
Saravana K. Ramasamy and eleven co-authors showed that blood flow steers bone growth, reporting in Nature Communications in 2016. Bone is laced with blood vessels, and new bone forms close to a special capillary type, yet how flow itself shapes the vessel network was poorly understood.

Imaging living mouse long bones, they watched vessel buds extend and fuse into loops in a distinctive flow pattern. Choking off flow broke both vessel growth and bone formation and dimmed Notch signaling in vessel cells. Old mice showed the same decline, but switching Notch back on restored vessel and bone growth, and a common osteoporosis drug, a bisphosphonate, also raised flow and growth in aged bone. The work casts flow as a master control on skeletal aging.
europmc-pmc5177050:
Clayton Lane announced a new human hookworm in The Indian Medical Gazette in June 1913. In 1911, Looss had described Agchylostoma ceylanicum from a civet cat sent from Colombo and guessed it might also live in tame cats and dogs and so reach experimenters.

Lane, a major in the Indian Medical Service, found the worm constantly in dogs and cats around Berhampore in Bengal, and in a lion born and dead in the Calcutta zoo. Routine stool checks of prisoners at Berhampore jail turned up hookworm eggs. After treatment, three men from a Mymensingh jail batch passed worms. The worms were shorter and thinner than the common human hookworm. Under the microscope they matched ceylanicum, making it a confirmed, if overlooked, parasite of people.
europmc-pmc5210650:
Konrad J. Karczewski and colleagues, with the Exome Aggregation Consortium, presented the ExAC browser in Nucleic Acids Research in 2017. Knowing how common a gene variant is in the general population helps clinicians judge whether it causes disease or is harmless. The browser displays reference variation data drawn from the exomes, the protein-coding parts of the genome, of 60,706 people.

Views are organized by gene and by transcript, which suits clinical work, and a variant view adds population frequency, functional notes, and the short reads that support each call. The software is light, flexible, and open source, and any group can reuse the framework for other large population data sets. Clinical laboratories around the world already use it to weigh variants found in patients against this broad reference.
europmc-pmc5244550:
Lindsay M. Kindinger and nine colleagues studied vaginal bacteria, cervical length, and progesterone treatment in women at risk of preterm birth, in Microbiome in 2017. Early birth is the leading cause of infant death worldwide. A short cervix in mid-pregnancy raises the risk, and vaginal progesterone lowers it for some women. The study followed 161 at-risk women with gene sequencing of vaginal samples.

At sixteen weeks, women whose vaginal community was dominated by the bacterium Lactobacillus iners were more likely to have a short cervix and to deliver before 34 weeks. Dominance by Lactobacillus crispatus pointed the other way, predicting full-term birth with high accuracy. A disordered vaginal mix by itself showed no such link. In women given progesterone, the treatment did not change the bacterial community or cancel the early-birth risk tied to L. iners, which also reassures patients using a vaginal pessary.
europmc-pmc5289450:
Charlotte Glinge and eleven colleagues tested how handling of blood samples affects circulating microRNAs in PLoS ONE in 2017. These tiny RNA strands are being studied as painless markers and possible treatment targets, but labs prepare and store samples in differing ways. The team drew blood from 12 healthy donors into tubes with different anticoagulants. They stored samples at room temperature or minus 80 degrees for up to nine months, shook them, and froze and thawed them repeatedly.

Results were reassuring on some points: most tubes gave similar levels of the three measured microRNAs, though lithium-heparin tubes proved unusable. Whole blood kept microRNAs steady for at least 24 hours at room temperature, but levels shifted significantly by 72 hours, and separated fractions changed sooner. Deep storage preserved plasma well for nine months, while four freeze-thaw cycles cut concentrations in plasma and serum. The message: collection and storage must be standardized.
europmc-pmc5304550:
Steffen E. Petersen and a large group of co-authors published heart scan norms in the Journal of Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance in 2017. The source is the UK Biobank, a large health study of adults. Heart scans need clear normal ranges so doctors can tell a healthy heart from a sick one.

More than five thousand adults had heart scans. After the team removed people with heart disease and other risks, eight hundred and four healthy adults aged forty-five to seventy-four set the ranges. Men had larger heart chamber volumes than women. Volumes shrank with age in both sexes. The pumping share was higher in women than in men. The tables cover all four heart chambers for clinic and research use.
europmc-pmc5367550:
Samuel J. Jackson led a large team that surveyed rodent ages in lab studies, in Laboratory Animals in 2017. Rats and mice back much of drug testing, yet their results too often fail to carry into people. Age is one design point that shapes results, but it is often poorly told and easily skipped. The team asked hundreds of researchers which ages they use, and why.

Close to three hundred people gave more than six hundred answers. Most used young animals of six to twenty weeks, no matter what biology was at stake. The word adult meant anything from six to twenty weeks across labs. Cost of older animals and the wish to match past data drove the picks more than the science did. The authors warn that sloppy age choice can weaken claims and waste animals. In some fields, older animals would fit the human state far better.
europmc-pmc5376950:
Gopal K. Singh and Ahmedin Jemal traced cancer gaps by class and race in the United States in the Journal of Environmental and Public Health in 2017. Their span is wide: from 1950 to 2014, more than six decades. They linked census want scores to national death and cancer records, and used a long death study for person-level checks on schooling and income.

The gaps in death and new case rates ran deep and, in key ways, grew. Poorer areas and lower schooling and income groups bore higher death and case rates. The excess was sharpest for lung, bowel, cervix, stomach, and liver cancers. As deaths fell, they fell more slowly in poor groups, so gaps in schooling and income widened. Black patients had the highest death rates, while Asian, Pacific, and Hispanic groups sat below white rates. Survival after diagnosis was also lower in poor areas.
europmc-pmc5422350:
Ferguson presents a simpler design for the forceps used to help deliver babies. The paper was read to the Edinburgh Obstetrical Society. He opens with a warning against hasty forceps use. In skilled hands the tool can save mother and child. Used too early or too often, it can tear the mother and harm the baby. Good teaching of its use matters greatly, he argues.

His target is the design, not the indications. Axis-traction was the great recent advance in forceps design. Rods added to Simpson's forceps achieved that pull. But the rods came at a cost. They spoiled the fine curves of Simpson's original instrument. Those curves protected the baby's head. Ferguson proposes a modification that keeps the traction gain. It also restores the safer shape. The paper preserves period views on obstetric practice and instrument craft.
europmc-pmc5427250:
Latulippe and co-authors review whether eHealth tools narrow or widen social health inequalities. Their literature review appeared in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. Digital health promises fairer access to care. It can also shut out the people most at risk. The team set three goals. They mapped who faces health inequality. They sought design rules that avoid deepening it. They modeled how at-risk people actually use such tools.

They kept 73 articles from two databases. Ten were theoretical and seven were reviews. The rest were empirical studies. Most used quantitative methods. Few involved at-risk users in the research. The digital divide stood out as a major barrier. Ethnicity and low income most often marked risk. Four actions looked most promising. Aim for universal access to the tool. Match the tool to users' literacy levels. Respect users' cultural traits in design. Involve at-risk people in building it.
europmc-pmc5436850:
Chowdhary and co-authors profile a drug-resistant yeast that is spreading through hospitals around the world. Their review appeared in PLoS Pathogens. The yeast is called Candida auris. It was first described in Japan in 2009. It came from a patient's ear canal. Within seven years it had reached five continents. It resists fluconazole, the standard drug for such infections. Response to other drug classes varies widely.

Many labs miss this yeast entirely. Common test systems give it the wrong name. They label it as a related species instead. One Indian study rechecked 102 stored samples by gene sequencing. About 88 percent of them proved to be this yeast. The test databases simply lacked the species. A mass spectrometry method names it far more reliably. Candida blood infections total about 400,000 a year worldwide. A hidden share may belong to this species. The authors urge close watch in intensive care units.
europmc-pmc5447450:
Stavropoulos and co-authors test whole-genome sequencing as a first test for sick children. Their prospective study appeared in NPJ Genomic Medicine. Standard care starts with a chromosome microarray. It hunts large copy-number changes. Targeted gene tests often follow. Most children still leave without a diagnosis. One genome scan could catch all variant types at once. The team enrolled 100 children at a paediatric genetics service.

Genome sequencing gave a firm diagnosis in 34 percent of cases. The microarray alone reached only 8 percent. Microarray plus targeted tests reached 13 percent. The genome scan caught every key copy-number change the array found. It added small insertions, deletions, and single-letter changes. Four children carried faults in two genes at once. Counting useful secondary findings, 38 percent could gain from genetic counselling. The authors back genome sequencing as a primary test. It finds more answers and may shorten the search.
europmc-pmc5485950:
Fransen, Lismont, and Walton present a review in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. It covers the ties between two cell organelles, peroxisomes and mitochondria. Both handle fats and reactive oxygen in the cell. Neither works alone; each shapes the other's numbers and health. Faults in one often drag down the other.

Shared control factors set how many of each organelle a cell keeps. The review traces how they swap signals and metabolites. Joint work spans fat burning, redox balance, and immune signaling. Diseases from rare genetic faults to diabetes show the cost of a broken link. Keeping the partnership healthy matters for the whole cell.
europmc-pmc5516350:
Hung and Fu present a review in the Journal of Biomedical Science on Alzheimer's drug candidates in clinical trials. Alzheimer's is the commonest cause of dementia worldwide. Current drugs ease symptoms but cannot cure the disease. No new drug had won approval since 2003 when this review appeared. Trials now chase five hallmarks of the disease, from amyloid plaques to inflamed brain tissue.

Antibodies that clear amyloid lead the late-stage pipeline, they report. Crenezumab, gantenerumab, and aducanumab were all in phase III trials. Other candidates block the enzyme that builds amyloid. Some target tau tangles or a serotonin receptor instead. Results will decide the field's direction.
europmc-pmc5520850:
Yang and co-authors report a molecular biology study in Cell Research on circular RNAs. These loop-shaped RNAs were long thought to make no proteins. They lack the usual start signals for translation. A common chemical mark on RNA, called m6A, changes that picture. The mark is thick on circular RNAs in human cells.

A single m6A site can launch protein building from a circle, they report. The process needs the reader protein YTHDF3 and factor eIF4G2. Heat shock turns the output up. Hundreds of natural circular RNAs show signs of being translated. The coding map of the human genome grows wider.
europmc-pmc5579350:
Sasaguri and co-authors review mouse models of Alzheimer's disease in The EMBO Journal. Good animal models are vital for testing drugs before human trials. Many past drug candidates failed, and poor model choice is one suspect. The review focuses on mice built around the amyloid precursor protein gene.

First-generation mice overproduce that protein or its partner proteins. They show disease signs, but excess output can add traits that are not part of the disease. Second-generation mice carry human-like sequences in their own gene. They build up amyloid without the excess-output side effects. They still fall short of the full human disease. The authors weigh each model's strengths for a given study goal. Readers get a sober guide to picking the right mouse.
europmc-pmc5698050:
Peng and co-authors report a plant study in Plant Biotechnology Journal. It engineers citrus trees that resist canker disease. Citrus canker is caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas citri. The germ exploits a host gene called CsLOB1. Its effector binds the gene's promoter and switches it on. The team used CRISPR/Cas9 to edit that promoter spot. Five guide constructs targeted the binding element. The work used Wanjincheng orange as the host variety.

Editing rates ranged widely across the constructs. Sixteen lines carried changes in the binding element. Four lines blocked the gene's response to infection. Those lines showed stronger canker resistance than wild type. Two lines showed no canker symptoms at all.
europmc-pmc5733050:
Schulz-Bohm, Martín-Sánchez, and Garbeva review gases given off by microbes in soil. These small compounds, called microbial volatiles, travel far through air and water gaps. Work once focused on plants and insects above ground. Far less was known about talks between microbes below ground.

The review sums up effects on other microbes and on plant roots. Some volatiles block rival bacteria or fungi. Others spur plant growth or warn of attack. Terpenes stand out as a large, little studied group. The authors note hard parts of this work and uses in farm biocontrol.
europmc-pmc5746550:
Frost and Li review the part astrocytes play in making amyloid in Alzheimer disease. Astrocytes are support cells that help keep the brain stable. Amyloid beta, the protein that clumps in this disease, is usually tied to nerve cells. The review asks how much of it astrocytes themselves produce.

The survey draws on work about amyloid precursor protein and its cutting enzymes. Cited studies cover secretases, astrocyte amyloid plaques, and signals that raise amyloid output. The review places astrocytes inside the amyloid hypothesis, not outside it. It offers a base for judging astrocytes as a treatment target.
europmc-pmc5794850:
Trockel and co-authors test a brief survey that scores doctor burnout and professional fulfillment together. The 16 item index was built to sense change from well-being efforts. A sample of 250 resident and practicing doctors filled it in. They also took older, trusted measures and reported their own medical errors.

The index split cleanly into fulfillment, exhaustion, and disengagement scales, they report. Scores held steady on retest weeks later. Its burnout scales matched the classic inventory closely. Doctors flagged as burned out also reported more errors. The tool tracked sleep and mood scores as expected.
europmc-pmc5870550:
Gel and Serra present karyoploteR, an R package for genome plots. Their article appeared in Bioinformatics. The package draws linear maps of whole genomes. Any species can be plotted, not just standard models. Notes and experiment data sit along the chromosomes. Earlier tools forced circular layouts or fixed data types. Custom options were often narrow, the authors note.

Plot building follows the style of base R graphics. A first call draws the bare genome map. Later calls add data and graphic elements step by step. Users can even plug in their own plotting functions. That gives full freedom over position and style. The package is free through Bioconductor, with a tutorial online.
europmc-pmc5900450:
Rea and co-authors review inflammation, cytokines, and ageing. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Older immune systems often lose fine control of inflammation. That slow shift toward a pro-inflammatory state is called inflamm-ageing. It is linked to heart disease, diabetes, and Alzheimer's disease. Cancer and arthritis also sit on that list.

The review traces triggers such as worn redox balance and senescent cells. Senescent cells release signals that feed inflammation. Declining cell cleanup can also spark the inflammasome. Long-lived groups offer clues to healthier ageing. The authors suggest timely calming of inflammation may delay disease. Readers get the main pathways and open questions.
europmc-pmc5976950:
Sprigg and co-authors report the TICH-2 trial of tranexamic acid for hyperacute intracerebral haemorrhage. Their phase 3 trial report appeared in The Lancet. Tranexamic acid prevents bleeding deaths after trauma and childbirth. The team asked if it limits haematoma growth after brain haemorrhage. The trial ran at 124 hospitals in 12 countries. It enrolled 2,325 adults within eight hours of symptom onset.

Half received tranexamic acid and half received placebo. Functional status at day 90 did not differ significantly, they report. Deaths by day 7 were fewer with the drug. By day 90, death rates were the same. Serious adverse events were fewer after tranexamic acid.
europmc-pmc5988750:
Zhou and co-authors link cardiac ischemia reperfusion injury to CK2 alpha disturbing mitochondrial balance via FUNDC1 mitophagy. Their study appeared in Cell Death and Differentiation. Faulty mitochondria help drive injury when blood flow returns. The team found the kinase CK2 alpha rises after acute injury. More of it meant worse damage, cell death, and heart function. Mice lacking it in the heart were protected instead.

CK2 alpha switches FUNDC1 off by phosphorylation, they report. That block stops mitophagy from clearing damaged mitochondria. Energy chains then fail and oxidative stress climbs. Mice lacking both proteins lost the protection. The pathway marks a target for limiting reperfusion harm.
europmc-pmc5990650:
Campbell and Tait review how BCL-2 regulated apoptosis can be targeted in cancer. Their review appeared in Open Biology. A cell's path to mitochondrial apoptosis is set by BCL-2 family proteins. Pro-death and pro-survival members hold a careful balance. That balance guards development and everyday health. When it tips, cells resist death and tumours can grow. Treatment resistance often follows the same tip.

New drugs can now hit single family members, the authors note. Early results in blood cancers look promising. The review covers how the pathway is controlled. It then covers how cancers distort that control. Drug development against these proteins is surveyed.
europmc-pmc6095650:
Okoro and co-authors report disability rates and health care access among United States adults. Their CDC report appeared in Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. It analyzes 2016 survey data from all states. Six disability types were tracked. They span hearing, vision, thinking, mobility, self-care, and independent living.

One in four adults reported some disability. That equals about 61.4 million people. Mobility problems were most common overall. Cognitive disability led among young adults. Rates ran higher for women, Native Americans, and poorer adults. Access gaps hit young and middle-aged adults hardest. Insurance, regular providers, and checkups all lagged. Readers get a baseline for closing care gaps by disability type.
europmc-pmc6111450:
Neag and co-authors wrote a review in Frontiers in Pharmacology on berberine, a plant compound with a long history in folk medicine. Plants that hold it have been used for fevers, wounds, gut ills, and infections. Use in Asia goes back more than 3,000 years. It still draws strong interest from drug researchers.

The review covers where berberine occurs in plants and how labs extract and detect it. It then sums up studies of its effects on the body. Reported actions include guarding the heart, liver, and kidneys. Others involve blood sugar and immune control. Readers get one broad survey of both old uses and new lab work.
europmc-pmc6146950:
Dahlhamer and co-authors report a study in Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report on chronic pain among adults in the United States. Chronic pain is a top reason adults seek medical care. Past estimates of its reach ranged from 11 to 40 percent. The team used the 2016 National Health Interview Survey for a sharper count.

They estimate 20.4 percent of U.S. adults had chronic pain. That is about 50 million people. Another 8 percent, near 19.6 million, had high-impact pain. Such pain often limits life or work. Rates ran higher for women, older adults, and rural residents. The authors say the counts can guide pain services.
europmc-pmc6198850:
Nembrini and co-authors present a methods article in Bioinformatics asking whether the Gini importance can be revived. Random forests are a fast, robust way to analyse high-dimensional data. Their variable importance scores help pick the features that matter. The popular Gini measure is quick but biased.

It favors variables with many possible split points and common genetic variants. The team built a fast correction that debiases impurity-based importance. The fix works for classification, regression, and survival forests. The corrected score stays unbiased for category counts and allele frequency, at nearly the old speed. Their verdict is that the measure can be trusted again, reopening a simple tool for feature selection.
europmc-pmc6319250:
Mehanna and co-authors test a gentler drug swap in HPV-linked throat cancer. The phase 3 trial appeared in The Lancet. The cancer affects younger patients and is rising fast. Standard care pairs radiotherapy with cisplatin. Cetuximab was proposed to cut toxicity. No randomized proof backed that swap. The trial ran at 32 centers in three countries.

It enrolled 334 patients with low-risk disease. Severe side effects proved equal in both groups. All-grade toxicity also matched closely. Survival, though, clearly favored cisplatin at two years. Recurrence was far higher with cetuximab. The authors conclude the swap offers no benefit. Cisplatin should stay the standard partner for radiotherapy.
europmc-pmc6340950:
Xu and co-authors review apoptosis and the vesicles dying cells leave behind. Their review appeared in Bioscience Reports. Apoptosis is programmed cell death without inflammation. It clears damaged cells from tissues. Two main paths drive it from inside and outside the cell. Drugs that trigger it already treat some diseases.

Small-molecule inducers help remove harmful cells. Engineered proteins and antibodies add sharper tools. Dying cells also release sealed sacs called apoptotic bodies. These carry proteins, RNAs, and other signals. Other cells read those signals and respond. The review weighs their promise as drug carriers. It also weighs their use as disease markers. Both paths turn cell death into a useful tool.
europmc-pmc6387150:
Yasuda and co-authors review interleukin-18 in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. IL-18 is a signal protein first found for raising interferon-gamma output. It helps drive type 1 immune responses, the kind that fight germs inside cells.

Its effects reach far beyond that one role, the review shows. With other signals present, IL-18 can also drive allergy-type responses. It acts on T cells, natural killer cells, mast cells, and more. That breadth links it to many diseases. The authors trace its healthy roles and its part in illness, step by step.
europmc-pmc6399450:
Milanese and co-authors present a software update in Nature Communications. Profiling microbes from DNA samples usually needs reference genomes. Many species lack one, which skews counts of who is present.

Their tool, mOTUs2, uses universal marker genes instead of full genomes. It can profile more than 7,700 microbial species. Over thirty percent of them could not be measured this finely before. The tool also reads which microbes are active, not just present. Tests show more exact counts than rival methods. It is aimed at gut, ocean, and environmental studies alike.
europmc-pmc6403250:
Yang and co-authors report a liver repair study in Nature Communications. After liver injury, immune cells must shift from attack to repair. The team shows neutrophils, the first cells on scene, drive that shift.

Neutrophils release reactive oxygen species into the injured liver. Those chemicals push incoming macrophages toward a repair form. Removing neutrophils blocked the shift and slowed repair. So did blocking the reactive oxygen. The study reframes neutrophils as repair organizers, not just germ fighters. It suggests care in wiping them out after liver damage. Their finding rests on mouse and tissue tests.
europmc-pmc6417250:
Sohn and Oh review bone grafts and substitutes in Biomaterials Research. A graft from the patient's own bone is still the gold standard. Supply is limited, though, and taking it can harm the donor site.

Synthetic substitutes use minerals like hydroxyapatite and tricalcium phosphate. They offer endless supply and easy storage and sterilization. They are also brittle and resorb at uneven rates. Newer materials aim to coax bone to grow, like demineralized bone matrix. The review compares each option for fracture surgery, where strength and healing both matter. Surgeons gain a clear trade-off table.
europmc-pmc6441150:
Yi and co-authors review the case for pairing immune checkpoint blockade with anti-angiogenesis drugs in cancer treatment. Checkpoint inhibitors free T cells to attack tumors, but response rates stay low and resistance is common. Blocking blood-vessel growth does more than starve a tumor; it also reshapes the immune environment around it.

In animal studies the combination beat either therapy alone, raising the share of anti-tumor immune cells and cutting expression of several checkpoints besides PD-1. Clinical trials built on those results were reporting promising outcomes as the review was written. Biomarkers such as PD-L1 and lymphocyte infiltration still guide patient selection, and the pairing offers one route past monotherapy resistance.
europmc-pmc6532150:
Gong and co-authors review necroptosis in cancer biology and therapy. Their review appeared in Molecular Cancer. Necroptosis is a regulated form of necrotic cell death. It runs without caspases. RIP1, RIP3 and MLKL mediate the pathway. It offers a route around apoptosis resistance, a major cause of chemotherapy failure.

Its role in cancer is two-sided. Many cancers lower key pathway regulators to evade it. In some cancers, those mediators are raised instead. Necroptosis can spark strong antitumour immunity. Yet its inflammation may also aid growth and spread. The authors cover mechanism, crosstalk with other death modes, and detection. Drugs that target this pathway close the review.
europmc-pmc6542350:
Pedersen and co-authors introduce hierarchical generalized additive models for ecology, writing in PeerJ. Ecologists often face curves that bend — say, how fish size tracks water temperature — where each group bends its own way. Plain additive models force one shared curve, while hierarchical models vary straight lines but not curves.

The new models let each group keep its own smooth curve, pulled toward a common shape so sparse groups borrow strength. The paper links the math to both parent methods, sets out model variants for different sharing assumptions, and shows the fitting in R's mgcv package. Worked examples, plus computing and statistics pitfalls, round it out. All code and data are posted openly.
europmc-pmc6603150:
Huang and co-authors review how reactive oxygen species guide plant life. Their article appears in Frontiers in Plant Science. These molecules arise as by-products of plant metabolism. At low levels they act as signals for growth. At high levels they damage DNA and kill cells.
