The review covers where plants make and remove these species. Chloroplasts, mitochondria, and peroxisomes all play a part. The authors trace roles in shoot meristem growth and organ formation. They also cover responses to drought, salt, and other stresses. A special focus falls on links with epigenetic marks. Those links help tune gene expression under stress. Plants, the authors conclude, weave these signals with hormones to adapt.
europmc-pmc6650350:
Aldape and co-authors lay out the challenges blocking cures for primary brain tumours. Their position paper appears in Nature Reviews Clinical Oncology. Brain tumours remain among the deadliest cancers. Most adults with glioblastoma die within two years. These tumours infiltrate vital tissue beyond surgical reach. The blood-brain barrier blocks many drugs as well. Their biology also resists conventional and novel treatments. Cancer Research UK convened an international expert panel.

The panel named seven key challenges for the field. They span the whole research pipeline. Better models, deeper biology, and smarter trials all feature. The rarity of these cancers fragments effort and funding. The authors intend the list as a call to arms. Future investment should focus on these fronts.
europmc-pmc6710350:
Rashid and co-authors review the role of microglia in retinal degeneration. Microglia are the resident immune cells of the retina, the light-sensing tissue at the back of the eye. They patrol the retina and guard it against harm. The review gathers recent work on what these cells do in eye disease.

In short bursts, microglia protect nerve cells. Under lasting stress, their responses can turn harmful and speed up sight loss. The authors survey diseases marked by slow degeneration and chronic immune activity. They also cover new treatments that calm microglia down, with the aim of slowing disease and saving vision.
europmc-pmc6744450:
Griss and co-authors show that B cells sustain inflammation in human melanoma. Tumor inflammation predicts who responds to checkpoint blockade drugs. Most theories credit T cells for that inflammation. This study puts B cells at the center instead. Human B cells exposed to melanoma secretions turned into plasmablast-like cells in the dish.

Those cells make both calming and provoking factors. In real melanomas, they also produce signals that recruit T cells. When patients received a B cell-depleting drug, tumor inflammation and T cell numbers fell. Before therapy, more of these cells meant better response and survival on checkpoint blockade. B cells may thus predict and shape treatment success.
europmc-pmc6761150:
Yu and co-authors studied how macrophage polarization toward the M2 state is fine-tuned. A signal protein, Stat6, drives macrophages into this calming, repair-minded state. Too much of it can help tumors by quieting immunity. The team found a brake built into the same system. Stat6 gets an acetyl tag during activation, and that tag restrains it.

A ligase called Trim24 helps attach the tag, by way of another protein, CBP. Losing Trim24 removed the brake and raised M2 polarization in mouse and human cells. That could weaken anti-tumor responses. In tumors, Stat6 also suppresses Trim24 itself. The loop shapes the immune niche that cancers exploit.
europmc-pmc6813250:
Yang and co-authors review plant hormones in Frontiers in Plant Science, with jasmonic acid at the centre. Plants use hormones to guide growth. They also use them to answer attack by insects and germs, and stress from heat or drought. Jasmonic acid is a key defence signal. It rarely acts alone.

The review explains how jasmonic acid talks with other hormones such as salicylic acid and ethylene. Proteins called JAZ repressors help switch the signal on and off. These links let a plant weigh growth against defence when food and energy are limited. The authors frame jasmonic acid as a core hub in that balance.
europmc-pmc6815950:
Zhu and co-authors report a study in Theranostics on nicotine and clogged arteries. Smoking is a known driver of atherosclerosis, the build-up of fatty plaques in artery walls. Macrophages, immune cells inside plaques, shed tiny vesicles called exosomes. Those vesicles carry messages to the muscle cells of the vessel wall. The team asked whether nicotine changes those messages.

Macrophages exposed to nicotine released more exosomes, loaded with a small RNA called miR-21-3p. That RNA lowered PTEN, a brake protein, in vessel muscle cells. The cells then moved and multiplied more, steps that grow plaques. In mice fed a high-fat diet for 12 weeks, nicotine sped up lesion growth along this same path.
europmc-pmc6825150:
Reyman and co-authors report a study in Nature Communications on babies' gut microbes. Birth by caesarean section seeds a baby's gut differently from vaginal birth. Antibiotics given to mothers around delivery can blur that effect. The team separated the two by delaying routine antibiotics until after the cord was clamped.

They followed 74 vaginally born and 46 caesarean-born infants through the first year of life. Gut microbes differed between the groups all year. Vaginally born babies carried more Bifidobacterium and less Enterococcus and Klebsiella. The mix at one week of age also tracked with how many chest infections a baby later had. Delivery mode, the authors conclude, shapes early health through microbes.
europmc-pmc7069050:
Baumann and Cabassa argue for an equity lens in implementation science in BMC Health Services Research. Research has produced strong knowledge about healthcare inequities and good interventions against them. Yet the inequities persist, because proven programs are rarely adopted in routine practice, especially for vulnerable populations. Implementation science studies how programs get taken up and sustained, and the authors propose merging the two fields.

Using a well-known framework as a case study, they reframe five elements. Studies should focus on reach from the very beginning, design interventions for vulnerable and low-resource communities with implementation in mind, and implement what works in ways that shrink gaps in care. A science of adaptations should be developed, and implementation outcomes should be judged through equity. The paper continues a dialogue rather than closing one: its goal is research that reduces inequities on purpose, not by accident.
europmc-pmc7072450:
Condrat and co-authors review microRNAs as disease biomarkers in the journal Cells. MicroRNAs are small non-coding RNAs that fine-tune protein production by marking messenger RNAs for destruction. Progress in tracing their origins and jobs has raised a practical hope: measuring them could diagnose disease and forecast its course. The authors analysed the literature across major medical databases to judge that hope.

The evidence is promising. MicroRNAs meet most tests of an ideal biomarker: they are accessible in body fluids, and they show high specificity and sensitivity for particular conditions. Standard protocols for using them in the clinic do not yet exist, which is the main limitation. As techniques improve, the authors expect microRNA profiles to become routine, sharpening each patient's personal profile and guiding more specific treatment. The review covers both diagnosis and prognosis, and where the molecules stand for conditions from cancer to heart disease.
europmc-pmc7141850:
Tareen and Kinney introduce Logomaker, a Python tool for drawing sequence logos, in Bioinformatics. Sequence logos stack letters above each position in a DNA, RNA, or protein sequence, with letter height showing biological importance. They are widely used but were hard to produce and customise inside Python.

Logomaker builds publication-quality logos from a table of numbers or from a multiple-sequence alignment. The figures are native matplotlib objects, so they can be styled freely and dropped into multi-panel figures. The package installs through pip and works with Python 2.7 and 3.6. Examples range from splice site patterns in the human genome to mutation effects in yeast experiments.
europmc-pmc7247050:
Xiao and Loscalzo review reductive stress, the lesser-known mirror of oxidative stress. Their article appeared in Antioxidants & Redox Signaling. Cells need reducing power, carried by molecules such as NADH, NADPH, and glutathione, to stay in balance. Too much of that reducing power is itself harmful. It is implicated in many disease processes, the authors note.

These redox couples are kept in separate pools within the cell's compartments. Coordinating the pools under stress is a core challenge for the cell. Recent work shows defense switches can flip on through different routes under reductive stress. Heart studies in mice link excess reducing power to cardiac damage. The review gathers the critical open questions. It argues the field must treat balance, not just oxidation, as the goal.
europmc-pmc7281250:
Obotey Ezugbe and Rathilal review membrane technologies for treating wastewater so the water can be used again. Their review appeared in Membranes. Fresh water is scarce, while industry, farming, and homes produce ever more wastewater. Older treatment methods clean effluent well enough for discharge but not always for reuse.

Membranes filter water to a quality fit for industrial, agricultural, and household purposes. The authors survey the membrane types now in use, weighing the strengths and weaknesses of each. Two practical problems get close attention: fouling, where dirt builds up on the membrane, and cleaning methods that restore performance. They also explain membrane module designs and close with recommendations for future research in the field.
europmc-pmc7293650:
Larrazabal and co-authors demonstrate that gender imbalance in medical image datasets produces biased diagnostic AI. Their study appeared in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Artificial intelligence systems for reading scans are being adopted worldwide. The team tested what happens when training data contain far more images from one sex than the other.

Using three deep neural network designs and two public chest X-ray datasets for thoracic diseases, they varied the gender balance systematically. Performance consistently dropped for the underrepresented gender when a minimum balance was not met. The same algorithm could thus diagnose one sex worse than the other purely because of the data. The authors urge regulators to require gender balance and diversity checks before approving computer-aided diagnosis systems.
europmc-pmc7314750:
Buonanno and co-authors test a kind of ultraviolet light that may kill airborne coronaviruses while people are in the room. Their study uses far-UVC light at 222 nm. Plain germ-killing UV at 254 nm harms skin and eyes. Far-UVC is thought to kill germs with no such harm to bare tissue.

Two human coronaviruses, 229E and OC43, were sprayed into air and lit. Small doses killed 99.9% of the virus. All human coronaviruses are alike in genome size, so the team expects SARS-CoV-2 to fall the same way. At the dose limit now in force, steady far-UVC in a public hall would kill about 90% of airborne virus in about 8 minutes. Near all of it would fall in about 25 minutes.
europmc-pmc7362150:
Taylor and co-authors define a COVID stress syndrome in Depression and Anxiety, using a representative survey of 6,854 adults in the United States and Canada. Early in the pandemic they measured five linked fears: danger of the virus, money and supply worries, blaming foreigners, traumatic stress symptoms, and compulsive checking for reassurance.

Network analysis puts worry about dangerousness at the center, holding the other fears together. People fell into five classes by severity, and 16 percent landed in the worst class, possibly needing mental health services. Severity tracked earlier mental illness, avoidance, panic buying, and trouble coping in isolation. The authors frame the five fears as one syndrome rather than separate problems, measurable with their scales.
europmc-pmc7392450:
Park and co-authors describe a COVID-19 outbreak in a South Korean call center in Emerging Infectious Diseases. Crowded, air-conditioned floors made the site a natural test of workplace spread. Investigators traced contacts with standard forms and tested 1,143 people linked to the building.

In total, 97 people, 8.5 percent, were confirmed infected. Nearly all of them, 94, worked on the 11th floor, where 216 employees sat together, an attack rate of 43.5 percent. Household spread from symptomatic cases ran at 16.2 percent. Only a handful of cases stayed symptom-free through quarantine. Tracing everyone, testing all contacts, and quarantining early stopped the chain, the authors conclude. Dense offices, they warn, can amplify a single introduction fast.
europmc-pmc7464350:
Bibi Sadeer and co-authors review antioxidant assays used in food science and safety. Interest in natural antioxidants is growing fast. Assays offer a quick, cheap way to screen plant and food samples.

Yet many researchers doubt how well lab assays match effects in the body. Results can also be hard to repeat. Each assay rests on its own chemistry, with its own strengths and flaws. The review explains the reactions behind each test, why assays show color, and why each uses a set wavelength. It asks what makes a color appear in these reactions. The authors close with critique and ideas for a better, more universal assay.
europmc-pmc7496150:
Menter and co-authors report autopsy findings in 21 COVID-19 patients from two Swiss hospitals in Basel. The full reach of organ harm was not yet clear. Autopsies offer a direct route to those answers.

Respiratory failure was the main cause of death. Lungs showed exudative diffuse alveolar damage with heavy capillary congestion. Small clots sat in lung vessels in spite of anticoagulation drugs. Ten cases had added bronchopneumonia in the lungs at the time of death. Other finds included pulmonary embolism, alveolar bleeding, and vasculitis. Most harm in other organs traced to shock. Most patients were male, many had blood group A, and most carried other illnesses such as hypertension and obesity. The picture points to vessel dysfunction at the core.
europmc-pmc7512150:
Malberg Tetzschner and co-authors test in silico genotyping of E. coli virulence genes from genome data. Extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli, or ExPEC, leads as a cause of urinary tract infection and bacteremia in humans. Fast typing aids care and tracking.

The web tool VirulenceFinder reads whole-genome sequencing data for this task. It lets researchers and clinical staff pull virulence facts from sequence data fast. The study checks how well such in silico genotyping works on real isolates. Computer typing can replace slow lab assays when it proves sound. It also speeds outbreak work and surveillance of harmful strains. The authors frame the tool as a practical aid for clinics and labs. Genome-based typing keeps growing as sequencing gets cheaper and faster worldwide.
europmc-pmc7555650:
Maida and co-authors review neuroinflammation in ischemic stroke, with a focus on cardioembolic stroke. Ischemic stroke is a major cause of death and disability. Immune activity shapes damage after blood flow is blocked.

Inflammation after ischemia can kill more brain cells. It can also help start repair processes in tissue. Immune signals draw many cell types into the lesion. These include T cells, monocytes and neutrophils. Cardioembolic stroke tends to cause severe damage. It is linked to worse disability and higher death rates. The review covers both brain and whole-body inflammation. It also sets out treatment ideas tied to these pathways.
europmc-pmc7790550:
Yang and co-authors review quercetin, a plant flavonoid with wide biological activity. Quercetin occurs in many plants. Lab work shows promise for medical use.

The authors explain how quercetin acts as an antioxidant. They cover its broad action against bacteria and parasites. Possible roles in cancer care are summed up. Heart protection and relief of immune suppression are also discussed. Quercetin can soften the harm of fungal toxins in feed and food. The review gathers the science behind these claims. It aims to guide further study and sound clinical use.
europmc-pmc7835650:
Sencio and co-authors review the lung-gut axis during viral lung infections. Gut bacteria are vital for good health. They also help the lungs fight viral infection. Infections themselves can disturb the gut mix. Those shifts can make the illness worse.

The authors explain how gut microbes arm the lung. Signals from a healthy gut tune lung defenses. They then trace how viral infections reshape gut bacteria. Loss of balance can stir gut disorders. It can also open the door to second bacterial infections. The last section weighs the axis in COVID-19. The message is that lung care may need gut care too.
europmc-pmc7857950:
Suarez-Lledo and Alvarez-Galvez review how much health falsehood spreads on social media. Experts agree the problem needs control. Its true scale was still unknown. The team set out to measure it. They also sought the topics and platforms hit hardest.

The authors screened studies that counted false health claims. Vaccines, drugs, and smoking were hot topics. Platform rates of false posts varied widely. Some studies found low shares, and others found very high ones. Methods differed enough to blur a single answer. The review calls for shared ways to count the problem. Knowing the scale is step one to fighting it.
europmc-pmc7859450:
Vaiserman and Krasnienkov review telomere length as a marker of biological age. Telomeres cap the ends of chromosomes. They shrink as cells divide and years pass. Fast shrinkage marks many age-related diseases. Length has long been sold as a top aging marker.

Newer work tempers that claim. Length alone gives only a rough rate of aging. It predicts illness and death weakly by itself. Other gauges, like epigenetic clocks, can do better. Telomere length still helps inside a marker panel. Frailty scores and balance measures pair well with it. The authors weigh the disputes in the field. They set out where the measure truly earns its keep.
europmc-pmc7945550:
Wiese presents a biographical study of Dominique Jean Larrey, Napoleon's chief surgeon. Books on Napoleon fill a library, Wiese notes. Yet the men who made his rise possible are little written about. Even most doctors do not know the chief surgeon's name. Larrey served with Napoleon from Italy to Waterloo. Wiese sets out to give him his due.

Larrey is widely held to be the greatest military surgeon in history, he writes. Only Ambroise Paré can stand beside him. Both men had strong self-reliance and tested every method for themselves. Neither bowed to custom just because it was old. Wiese resists splitting their merits into surgery versus administration. Greatness, for him, lay in picking the best method and opening new fields. The study restores a giant of army medicine to view.
europmc-pmc8196750:
Dresser and co-authors give a full account of myasthenia gravis, from spread to signs. The disease is an autoimmune fault at the junction between nerve and muscle. Signals fade there, and muscles tire fast.

Incidence runs from 4.1 to 30 cases per million person-years. Prevalence sits between 150 and 200 cases per million. Most patients carry antibodies against acetylcholine receptors. Others target MuSK, Lrp4, or agrin instead. The review covers how these antibodies break signal transfer. It then walks through the clinical picture doctors should expect. The article serves as a compact reference on the disease.
europmc-pmc8263750:
Greaney and co-authors map which spike mutations let SARS-CoV-2 escape antibodies. Antibodies from past infection target many spots on the spike. Which classes carry the shared response was unclear.

A yeast-display system tested every mutation of the receptor-binding domain. Three classes of strong neutralising antibodies got full escape maps. The team compared those maps with maps for whole convalescent plasma. Plasma binding suffered from mutations across many sites. No single class explained the whole plasma response. The maps guide vaccine updates and antibody drug choices. Escape maps for plasma from the same donors were included.
europmc-pmc8292450:
Lüönd, Tiede, and Christofori use breast cancer to show tumour diversity and cell plasticity at work. Diversity inside a tumour helps it adapt to change. It also worsens outlook and treatment response.

Outside factors from the tumour setting mix with traits inside cells. Genetic, epigenetic, and gene activity traits all vary. So do growth, movement, and stem-like states. Plasticity lets cancer cells rewrite their gene programmes fast. Cells can shift identity to meet new pressures. The review traces how diversity and plasticity feed each other. Together they drive the cancer's advance.
europmc-pmc8354850:
Legius and co-authors issue revised diagnostic criteria for neurofibromatosis type 1 and Legius syndrome. The two conditions overlap in young patients with pigmentary signs. Telling them apart early matters for care.

An international group ran a multistep consensus process. A Delphi round with global experts came first. Patients, foundations, and outside experts then weighed in. Genetics, eye, skin, and imaging advances were folded in. Minimal clinical and genetic criteria define each condition. Mosaic forms received criteria as well. The update replaces older rules that predated gene testing. Differentiating the two syndromes in childhood is the practical aim.
europmc-pmc8377850:
Liu and co-authors study how a circular RNA helps lung cancer hide from the immune system. The work centers on non-small cell lung cancer and a molecule named circIGF2BP3. Such circular RNAs had been linked to cancer growth, but their role in immune escape was unclear.

The team found that circIGF2BP3 levels rose in this cancer and tracked with low CD8 T cell entry into tumors. Tests in cells and in mice showed the molecule weakens T cell killing. It acts through two small RNAs and the protein PKP3, which raises PD-L1 levels. PD-L1 helps tumors avoid attack. The findings point to a new target for treatment.
europmc-pmc8381650:
Barnabei and co-authors review NF-kappaB, a key switch for immune and inflammatory responses. This transcription factor helps control both innate and adaptive immunity. The first half of the review covers what turns it on, its signaling paths, and its controls.

The authors then show where NF-kappaB guards self-tolerance. It shapes the growth of thymic cells that teach T cells to spare the body. It also helps switch off or remove self-reactive T and B cells. The second half turns to disease. Faults and mutations in the pathway drive autoimmunity and autoinflammation. These finds have already shaped new treatment ideas.
europmc-pmc8431850:
Stirling and co-authors describe CellProfiler 4, a new release of the free image analysis program. Microscope images hold rich data that eyes alone cannot judge well. High-throughput imaging now makes data sets too large for hand review. Automated pipelines turn those images into clear measurements.

The team reshaped the interface based on user feedback, to make the tool easier to run. New modules widen what the software can do. Speed tests guided fixes that cut the time and cost of large jobs. The authors report clear gains on complex workflows over past versions. The release aims to keep this open tool useful for years.
europmc-pmc8516650:
Kyriazopoulou and co-authors test early anakinra treatment for COVID-19 patients flagged by a blood marker. High levels of soluble urokinase plasminogen activator receptor, or suPAR, mark risk of breathing failure. The SAVE-MORE trial used that marker to pick patients for the drug.

The double-blind trial enrolled 594 patients with suPAR at the set risk level. Most were also getting dexamethasone. By day 28, patients on anakinra had clearly better clinical status than those on placebo. Death rates at 28 days fell as well. Organ failure scores improved faster in the drug group. The trial shows the worth of marker-guided early treatment.
europmc-pmc8550750:
Markiewicz and co-authors describe OpenNeuro, a resource for sharing neuroscience data. Shared data let others repeat work and raise the value of public research funds. OpenNeuro is a BRAIN Initiative archive built on FAIR sharing principles. Data must be findable, accessible, and reusable to count.

The archive holds more than 600 data sets from over 20,000 participants. They span many species, scan types, and health traits. A shared brain imaging structure standard makes curation and reuse work. Over 150 publications have already reused the shared data. The authors close with plans to grow the archive and link it to wider open science.
europmc-pmc8761750:
Zhu and co-authors review the ketogenic diet as a treatment for human diseases beyond epilepsy. The diet is high in fat, very low in carbohydrate, and rich enough in protein. It mimics fasting and pushes the body to make ketone bodies. It has long controlled hard-to-treat epilepsy with success.

Evidence now hints at value in obesity, cancer, and other diseases. The review sums up lab and clinical results for each. It also weighs the diet's safety record. Cell and molecular work suggests the diet acts through several routes. Those routes are not yet fully mapped. The authors call for randomized trials to ground clinical use.
europmc-pmc8809250:
Banskota and co-authors engineer virus-like particles that deliver therapeutic proteins into living tissue with high efficiency. Delivering gene editors as ready-made protein complexes could be safer than sending in their genes. The team reworked DNA-free particles to fix packing, release, and targeting faults. Their fourth-generation design edited several primary cell types well.

Changing the particle coat shifted which cells it entered. Single injections in mice edited multiple tissues at useful levels. One treatment cut a blood lipid protein level by 78 percent. Another partly restored sight in mice with genetic blindness. Off-target editing was near zero, beating virus and plasmid routes.
europmc-pmc8855550:
Yu and co-authors review exosomes as a new frontier for cancer liquid biopsy. Liquid biopsy reads cancer signals from blood or other fluids. Exosomes are tiny vesicles cells release into those fluids. They carry molecular cargo from cell to cell. Tumors shed them in large amounts. That makes them promising markers for diagnosis and prognosis.

The review first explains how exosomes form and what they carry. It then covers old and new ways to isolate them. Enrichment methods get a careful comparison. Sections follow on reading exosome contents. Protein and nucleic acid detection both feature. Machine learning methods appear as well. The authors weigh exosomes for diagnosis, treatment tracking, and prognosis. They close with the hurdles to clinical use. Separation quality is the chief one.
europmc-pmc9438950:
Formenti and co-authors introduce gfastats, a software tool for genome assembly work. Reference genomes now arrive at a fast pace. Teams need sound ways to sum up and check each assembly. They also need ways to fix and reshape assemblies as new data types appear.

Gfastats computes assembly summary statistics from one program. It reads and writes FASTA, FASTQ, and GFA files, with compression support. Inside, it stores sequences in a GFA-like form. That lets it build an assembly graph from the data. Users can edit sequences through the graph by set instructions. New metrics come out with each edited set. The tool was built for the Vertebrate Genomes Project. It is written in C++ and shared under the MIT licence.
europmc-pmc9549250:
Afzaal and co-authors unveil the links between human gut microbiota, health, and disease. The gut hosts a dense microbial community of many species. Writers have called the community a vital extra organ. It talks with other organs along several axes at once.

Signals run through neural, hormone, and immune routes. A balanced community guards against invading pathogens. It also supports metabolism and immune steadiness. When balance breaks, disease risk climbs across the body. The review ties such breaks to anxiety and depression. Heart disease, obesity, and diabetes are also linked. Bowel inflammation and cancer close the disease list. Food shapes the balance in daily life, they note. The final part lists what must be tamed to hold health. Clear mechanism maps are still missing in many spots.
europmc-pmc9730250:
Tang, Xiong, Fang, and Li review how weaning stress harms the gut health of piglets. Weaning is among the most fraught stages in pig farming. Piglets face sudden parting from the sow at that point. Diet, housing, and pen mates all change at once.

The stress reshapes the small gut in form and work. Digestion and uptake of feed both drop after weaning. The gut wall's guard job weakens across several layers. Its shape, chemical shield, and immune shield all suffer. Gut microbes shift as the barrier thins out. Feed intake falls and diarrhea rates climb in herds. Growth slows as a direct cost of the strain. The review gathers these effects into one account. It offers the picture as a base for feed based fixes. The authors aim to guide care for young mammals broadly.
europmc-pmc9825450:
Paysan-Lafosse and co-authors report InterPro in 2022, the protein family classification resource. InterPro sorts protein sequences into families in one place. It flags domains and conserved sites that matter for function. Thirteen signature databases feed into its single frame.

Recent work updated both content and the website. Coverage kept pace with the fast growth of UniProtKB. A junk family filter called AntiFam joined the member set. Old entries were revised as knowledge moved on. Structure predictions from two AI systems were integrated. The Pfam website's features moved into InterPro's pages. That shift came as the Pfam site faced retirement. Search and the protein viewer both got faster. A card game was built to reach lay audiences. The authors discuss AI structure tools' gains and strains.
europmc-pmc9992450:
Hoeft and co-authors show that platelets instruct macrophages that drive fibrosis after organ injury. Fibrosis is the common end stage of chronic organ damage. It destroys tissue structure and drives organ failure. The team found a profibrotic macrophage group marked by Spp1, Fn1, and Arg1.

This group expanded after injury in their models. A broad search flagged the chemokine CXCL4 as a top rising gene in its formation. Loss of Cxcl4 blocked the macrophage shift and eased fibrosis. Gains appeared after both heart and kidney injury. Platelets, the richest CXCL4 source, drove the shift. Macrophages then activated fibroblasts through Spp1, Fn1, and Sema3 signals. The group also expanded in human kidney disease and heart failure.
everard-divine-pymander-1650:
John Everard Englished the Divine Pymander of Hermes Trismegistus in 1650, the first rendering of the Corpus Hermeticum into English. Hermes, sage and god in one, discourses on God, mind, and the making of the world. English readers gained a door into Renaissance magic and hidden wisdom through Everard's vigorous Civil War prose.

The dialogues claim an age older than Moses in their own telling. Everard, a clergyman with mystical leanings, gives them plain, strong English. Seekers of secret lore treasured the book for generations afterward here. It carried strange old wisdom into a land at war with itself, and its influence ran through English occult thought for centuries.
fasciculus-chemicus-or-chymical-collecti:
Dee's Fasciculus Chemicus collects the secret Hermetick science from famous older authors. Arthur Dee gathered and ordered the chymical pieces. James Hasolle made them English, the title page says. The record dates the book to 1650, printed in London.

Its full title promises the ingress, progress, and egress of the science. The order aims to aid beginners and proficients alike, the title claims. No earlier work had disposed the art in this method, it adds. The Arcanum, or grand secret of Hermetick philosophy, is joined to the collection. A motto from Ventur states the whole mastery in one thing: Mercury. The scan's early pages are rough, but the title page reads clean.
fbi-vault-16th-street-church-bombing-16t:
Part one of 50 in the Federal Bureau of Investigation Vault release covers the Sixteenth Street Baptist Church bombing. The attack struck Birmingham, Alabama, on September 15, 1963. An internal FOIPA cover sheet inside labels this section Part 1 of 11. The Bureau warns that some pages are blurred or light from the originals.

Sampled pages open with an urgent teletype from the Birmingham SAC. It went to the Director and to Atlanta, Knoxville, Jacksonville, Memphis, Mobile, New Orleans, and Savannah. A later sampled letter bears J. Edgar Hoover's name as Director. It concerns paying an informant if he delivers information. The pages mix routing slips, teletypes, and letters from the first days.

Part eleven of 50 in the Federal Bureau of Investigation Vault release continues the church bombing file. Its internal cover sheet reads Part 3 of 11 under the FOIPA heading. The subject line names Birmingham, Alabama, and the September 15, 1963 bombing. Deleted page information sheets appear at the start.

A sampled memorandum from A. Rosen reports a call from SAC Roy Moore. Moore asked authority for three listed steps in the case. One step was to afford a polygraph examination to a named person. The bottom line records that Moore was authorized to proceed with items 1-3. Importance of the matter is stressed in the memo. The rest of the sample returns to deletion sheets and routing marks.

Part twelve of 50 in the Federal Bureau of Investigation release on the Sixteenth Street bombing opens with withheld pages. FOIPA deleted page sheets explain pages kept back under exemptions. A teletype to the SAC at Indianapolis follows in the sample. It directs that office to contact informants at once for case information.

A later sampled page reports friction with a local department head. He offered his investigators to work alongside FBI agents. Personal jealousies, animosities, and political overtones had made the rift, he felt. A meeting could remove those thorns, he argued. The page confirms this word reached SAC Roy K. Moore at Birmingham that day. Deletion sheets recur through the part.

Part thirteen of 50 in the Federal Bureau of Investigation Vault file on the Birmingham bombing is heavy with redactions. Its head pages are FOIPA deleted page information sheets. A garbled authorization page names suspects in rough OCR. The text layer here is hard to read in places.

A clearer sampled passage covers the Knoxville Division's leads. Liaison with local officers chased a dynamite theft in Walker County, Georgia. The theft hit an E. I. DuPont Company storage magazine on September 18 and 19, 1963. That check met with negative results, the report says. At Chattanooga, the office would keep contact with RAC informants. Bureau copies went to Birmingham and Atlanta for follow-up.

Part fourteen of 50 in the Federal Bureau of Investigation release carries an internal cover sheet marked Part 4 of 11. The subject is the Sixteenth Street Baptist Church bombing of September 15, 1963. A sampled memorandum from Birmingham concerns the San Antonio office. It notes that all auxiliary offices handle bomb suspects or Klan members in their own territories.

That division of labor was meant to cut the volume of Birmingham's reports. The same memo opens this file section in the sample. Middle sampled pages in this part are garbled OCR of printed matter. Their text cannot be tied to the case with confidence from this copy. The part thus mixes clear Bureau routing with poorly legible pages.

Part fifteen of 50 in the Federal Bureau of Investigation Vault release shares its opening with the preceding chunk. Its cover sheet also reads Part 4 of 11 for the Birmingham bombing file. The same Birmingham memorandum begins the sampled pages. It assigns bomb suspects and Klan members to the auxiliary offices over them.

That plan aimed to decrease the reports Birmingham had to prepare. Beyond that memo, the sampled middle is mostly process paper. FOIPA deleted page sheets list pages withheld under exemptions. They note third-party material and matter sent to other agencies. Little case narrative survives in the pages sampled here. The part is best read as file housekeeping around the investigation.

Part seventeen of 50 in the Federal Bureau of Investigation release holds a headquarters memorandum dated October 29, 1963. A. Rosen wrote to Mr. Belmont on unknown subjects in the church bombing. Birmingham informants reported a meeting of Eastview Klavern Number 13. That United Klans group would meet at Woodlawn Meeting Hall on October 30.

At the meeting, men would allegedly get Robert Chambliss and things straightened out. The memo says the meeting will be covered. Klansmen interviewed on October 28 gave no pertinent information. A sampled teletype adds surveillance of Chambliss on a delivery trip. A Tallassee parts dealer recalled a Hudson clutch assembly tied to his route. Its later disposal was unknown to the dealer.

Part eighteen of 50 in the Federal Bureau of Investigation file turns to press fallout in November 1963. A memorandum to Mr. Belmont quotes Birmingham newspaper articles and editorials. Papers of November 6 and 7 were extremely critical of the Justice Department. Their target was an incident with Reverend Martin Luther King Jr. and a Department rented automobile.

Departmental Attorney Thelton Henderson resigned over the affair, the memo notes. One editorial asked what certainty existed that the Department knew others' doings. It could not rely on its own personnel, the paper charged. Another warned that one rolled head would not silence questioning. Later sampled pages concern legal moves tied to the NSRP. The part shows the Bureau tracking its own public damage.

frus-1861-d150:
A letter of 5 September 1861 went from William H. Seward to William Dayton in Paris. The letter is document 150 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

September letters from Seward turn to trade, ships, and the fine print of neutrality. The grand pleas of spring gave way to detail. This note to Paris shows high policy becoming clerk's work, which is where it was won or lost. Detail, Seward knew, was where neutral pledges were kept or quietly broken. Neutral pledges live or die in details, and Seward never forgot that truth. Fine print was where pledges lived or died.
frus-1861-d250:
Writing on 4 September 1861, James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands sent his report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 250 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d50:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 June 1861. The dispatch is document 50 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Adams wrote in a spare, exact style that Seward learned to trust. His June reports cover talks, notes, and the mood of the British press. For readers, they are a model of how a skilled envoy turns daily talk into clear word for his chief. Seward read Adams's reports with close care and often shared them with the cabinet. Cabinet eyes on his pages made Adams the best read envoy of the war.
frus-1862-d150:
Circular No. 24, dated 25 September 1862, is Document 150 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. A circular was not a private letter but a single set of orders sent at the same time to many American envoys and consuls abroad. So that all of them spoke with one voice.

Seward used circulars when Washington needed the same line taken in every capital at once. This one went out three days after Lincoln announced his emancipation plan, in a week when foreign governments were reassessing the war. It shows the State Department managing its whole foreign service as one body, not post by post.
frus-1862-d250:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 21 January 1862 in a letter printed as Document 250 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward, though it stands in the file after a later Seward letter.

The printers grouped some papers out of date order, so this report follows the dispatch it may have crossed at sea. Dayton's mail gave Washington its best read on Napoleon III's court, where policy could shift with one man's mood. Reports from his hand shaped how the Union handled France all year. The Paris mail sailed from Le Havre and took about two weeks to reach Washington.
frus-1862-d350:
Henri Mercier, the French minister in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 23 December 1861, in a letter printed as Document 350 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Mercier wrote two days before Washington settled the Trent affair by freeing the seized envoys. French diplomacy had counseled calm in that crisis, which Washington noted with gratitude. His letter belongs to the closing days of the year's worst foreign scare, when the French channel proved one of the steadiest Seward had. The French legation's notes were written in French and printed here in the Department's English. Cases in this channel often mixed the war at home with French designs in Mexico.
frus-1862-d450:
John Lothrop Motley, the American minister in Vienna, received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 January 1862. It is Document 450 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, opening the Austrian file.

Motley was already famous as the historian of the Dutch republic when Lincoln sent him to Austria. Vienna was a conservative court, cool toward republics, and its view of the American war was shaped by its fear of revolution at home. Seward's opening order for the year armed Motley with the Union's case. The dispatch begins a file written by one of the most literary men ever to hold an American post abroad.
frus-1862-d50:
Seward wrote again on 19 April 1862, this time to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It was printed as Document 50 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It belongs to the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d550:
A second note of 30 September 1862 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Roest van Limburg. It stands as Document 550 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, beside its same-day companion.

Paired notes on one day meant separate subjects, each answered in its own letter under the Department's standing practice. The Dutch file had run that way since June, and the habit gives the modern reader a clean record: no mixed paragraphs, no buried answers. Van Limburg's government got from Seward that day two distinct statements it could file and quote. The pair closes the September Dutch exchange, one of the most orderly in a volume full of harder and hotter correspondence.
frus-1862-d650:
Dated 17 May 1862, this dispatch from Robert H. Pruyn reached Secretary of State William H. Seward as part of the regular mail from Japan. Pruyn was the American minister there, in the first weeks of his time in the post. The letter is document 650 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Note the dates around it: Pruyn wrote again and again that May, a sign of how much a new envoy had to report. His letters told Washington about the legation's talks and troubles in a land the United States had known for less than a decade. Each one adds a page to that early record.
frus-1863p1-d150:
On 9 April 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 150 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, carrying a round number in the count.

The middle sheet of Adams's 9 April set holds its own head of the brief, as his sets always did. That spring the heads were ships and the law that might hold them. This letter is the second of the three. With its mates, it rounds out a day on which the London post worked the full width of the Union's case in Britain.
frus-1863p1-d250: Document 250 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume is an untitled paper dated 28 July 1863. It sits inside the long run of letters between Secretary of State William H. Seward and Charles Francis Adams in London, the channel that handled relations with Britain during the Civil War. The catalog gives it no title or author, so its place in that correspondence is what the record shows.
frus-1863p1-d350: On 3 January 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 350 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the formal exchange through which the two governments handled Civil War disputes. Notes on this route dealt with neutral rights, stopped ships, and British complaints.
frus-1863p1-d450:
William H. Seward, Secretary of State took up his pen on 7 April 1863 and wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail.

A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d50: This untitled paper is dated 25 October 1862 and printed as document 50 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It sits inside the group of Confederate letters in that part, between papers of Mallory and Memminger. The evidence gives its date and place in the run, but no title, writer, or name addressed.
frus-1863p1-d550:
William H. Seward took up his pen on 5 June 1863 and wrote to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d650:
On 29 October 1863, the American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams in London was the Union's front line in Britain, pressing its case with the British government week after week. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863.

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d150: The Joint Chiefs of Staff wrote to Ambassador Harriman in Moscow on November 20, 1943, and the letter is Document 150 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. A message from the chiefs as a body to an ambassador was a weighty channel, used when military and diplomatic lines had to meet. The record gives the senders, the receiver, and the date. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d250:
A dinner meeting at Cairo involving President Roosevelt and Prime Minister Churchill is covered by an editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume. The fact of the meeting and the names of those present come from the President's Log, and no record of what was discussed at the dinner has been found.

The editors add one careful pointer. Later documents in the volume show that Roosevelt raised the future status of Hong Kong with Churchill at Cairo. There is, however, no sign showing whether that subject came up at this particular dinner or at some other meeting between the two men during the conference.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d350:
Steve Early, the President's secretary, telegraphed Harry Hopkins from Washington on 2 December 1943 with the American reaction to the Cairo communiqué. Sent by military channels, the message mixes celebration at the statement's reception with anger at how its secrecy was broken.

The communiqué, Early reports, was received with enthusiasm across the country, with great praise and jubilation in all quarters. That came despite Reuters' Lisbon dispatch. The dispatch printed virtually the whole Cairo story almost twenty-four hours before the release. It cut the statement's force. It also let German and Japanese propagandists broadcast their versions in the gap. Early urges shorter intervals between distribution and publication for any future communiqués, and a strict ban on sending their contents abroad before the release date.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d450: Document 450 is a short piece of editorial writing, not a 1943 dispatch. Historians in the Office of the Historian prepared notes like it for the Cairo-Tehran volume. They use the notes to add context the wartime papers lack. Sometimes they point to documents printed elsewhere in the series. The conferences covered here shaped Allied plans for 1944 and beyond. A reader gets orientation before returning to the primary papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d50: Roosevelt answered Hull on October 21, 1943, the same day the secretary's letter in this series was written. The reply is Document 50 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. With his secretary of state in Moscow and the Tehran summit five weeks away, the president kept a close hand on the talks. The record gives the date and the two men. The exchange is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d550:
President Roosevelt wrote to Secretary of State Cordell Hull on January 24, 1944, answering the flow of department business with a presidential message of his own. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

The Roosevelt-Hull channel ran both ways all winter: reports and requests went up, decisions and instructions came down. January 1944 was a month of consolidation, when the Tehran and Cairo results were being turned into policy on Poland's future, Germany's treatment, and the coming invasion. For readers, this message shows the President working the machinery of his own government between summits, in writing.
frus-1944-quebec-d150:
Eisenhower sent the Combined Chiefs his recommendations on taking command of the Dragoon forces on September 9, 1944. The southern France armies were racing north, and by September 15 they would be strong around Dijon. At that point, he proposed, operational control should pass to him, with directives going directly to General Devers.

Air arrangements fill much of the message: the Ninth Air Force would take over the tactical air command supporting Seventh Army, while the Twelfth Air Force kept helping until relieved. Supply, though, should keep flowing from the Mediterranean while American stocks there exceeded local needs. Eisenhower asked that the end of that arrangement be settled by agreement between Wilson and Devers.
frus-1944-quebec-d250:
Stalin answered Roosevelt's message on the Dumbarton Oaks discussions on September 14, 1944, in a secret, personal letter printed here in translation. He hoped the talks on a world organization would end successfully. But he laid down the Soviet condition: the order of voting in the proposed Security Council would decide whether the organization could work at all.

The Council, Stalin argued, must proceed on coordination and unanimity of the four leading powers on all questions, including those directly relating to one of them. That principle, he said, underlay the agreement reached at Tehran for the future struggle against aggression. Without unanimity among the leading powers, the consequences would be grave. He also complained of absurd prejudices that hindered an objective attitude toward the Soviet Union.
frus-1944-quebec-d50:
On September 2, 1944, Churchill wrote again to Roosevelt. The Quebec Conference would open ten days later. The State Department placed the message in the Quebec 1944 volume.

Churchill crossed the Atlantic that week aboard the Queen Mary. He wrote ahead to the President as he traveled. His September letters fixed the British agenda. They covered finishing the war in Europe. They covered settling Germany's treatment after defeat. They also covered Britain's part in the Pacific war. American aid formed part of that case too. For readers, the message shows a case argued in advance. Churchill then argued it in person.
frus-1945-50-intel-d150:
On 9 May 1946, the President’s Chief of Staff (Leahy) sent a memorandum to President Truman. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 150 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The postwar system was still new: the National Intelligence Authority gave the orders, and the Central Intelligence Group carried them out.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d250:
A text titled "Memorandum of Discussion at the 2d Meeting of the National Security Council" bears the date 14 November 1947. It stands as document 250 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. By law the CIA now stood where the Central Intelligence Group had stood, and the National Security Council sat above it.

Where no stenographer sat in, a memcon is the meeting. It holds the talk in the words of the man who wrote it up. So the talk could guide later work, each point is set down while its weight is still clear. The Council was still new, and its early meetings worked out how the president's top advisers would handle defense and foreign policy together.
frus-1945-50-intel-d350:
A memorandum from Robert G. Barnes reached William J. McWilliams of the Executive Secretariat on 25 August 1948. The State Department prints it as document 350 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. It was a season of stock-taking: the CIA was a year old, and its friends and critics were both writing things down.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d50:
Minutes of the 170th meeting of the Secretary of State's Staff Committee are dated 27 November 1945. Two numbered meetings within a week point to a heavy agenda at the department. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

The staff committee was Secretary Byrnes's inner council on department business. Its minutes for late November belong to the weeks when the intelligence plans of State, War. The Budget Bureau were being forced into one shape. Readers should note the pace: the 168th meeting on the 20th, the 170th on the 27th. Institutions meet this often when a decision is near and the details will not settle themselves.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d150:
A new Polish cabinet in London leads the items in this 1 December 1944 briefing for the President. Titled “Special Information for the President,” the memorandum from Secretary Stettinius collects the notable foreign developments of the past few days. The excerpts are printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Schoenfeld reports from London that the new Polish government is generally seen as the anti-Russian wing of the exile Poles. Against that, the Lublin Committee's chairman, Osobka-Morawski, has told the Soviet press that his organization will cooperate with Mikolajczyk. But the offer holds only on the platform the Lublin Committee itself supports. Two rival Polish authorities were thus hardening, weeks before the Big Three met.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d250:
Detailed staff talks, not more general talk, are what the Far East now needs, Harriman warned on 10 October 1944. This excerpt from his report to the President, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, looks past Churchill's Moscow visit to the planning that must follow.

Stalin has given full agreement, Harriman writes, not only to join the Pacific war but to enter it with full effort. What remains unknown is what Russia can actually do in the East. The limiting factors are logistics, about which the allies know very little. Churchill's talks with Stalin should therefore stress the weight of the detailed discussions agreed between General Deane and the Red Army Staff. Harriman adds that he has General Ismay's agreement on this line.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d350:
Roosevelt and Churchill lunched together at Livadia Palace at 1 p.m. on February 6, 1945, away from the full table. The record preserved here gives the setting and the company. Harry Hopkins, James Byrnes, and Ambassador Harriman sat on the American side. Sir Alexander Cadogan, the Foreign Office chief, joined Churchill.

No topics are listed in the portion that survives, so the lunch must be read by its place in the week. It fell on the third day of plenary bargaining, between sessions on Germany and the world body. Private talks like this one let the two Western leaders align before facing Stalin again.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d450:
Ambassador Harriman's memorandum gathers his three conversations of February 10, 1945, into one record. At 2 p.m. he called on Molotov at Koreis, at Molotov's request. Molotov handed him, in English translation, the draft of Stalin's political conditions for Russia's entry into the war against Japan. The terms had been discussed with the President on February 8.

Harriman told Molotov there were three amendments he believed the President would wish to make before accepting. Two more conversations followed at Livadia Palace, the last at 4:30 p.m. with Stalin and the President present. The subject was the Far East, on its political side. The secret price of Soviet entry enters the record here.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d50: Churchill sent Roosevelt a further message on 10 January 1945, his third letter in three days. Filed as document 50 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on Malta and Yalta, it keeps the January sequence intact. The full text appears as the editors printed it, one link in the chain of cables that preceded the Malta meetings by three weeks.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d150:
President Truman set his staff a string of homework questions in a memorandum dated June 9, 1945. The memo to Acting Secretary Grew is document 150 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It responds to the British list of suggested subjects for the summit.

Truman asks for a brief, informal statement of the State Department's position on each British point, plus any subjects the Department thinks should be added. He also asks how the peace terms for Europe should be worked out. Should there be one conference like Dumbarton Oaks, with steady talks until proposals are agreed? Or should there be a series of meetings in different places? Last, he asks the Department's view of a 25-year treaty among the great powers to keep Germany disarmed, along lines Senator Vandenberg had proposed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d250:
Naval aide George Elsey traced the Korea trusteeship idea in an undated memorandum printed as document 250 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. The note, prepared for the President's staff, pulls together what the Map Room files held on Korea before the conference.

The Cairo Declaration of 1943 had promised that Korea, enslaved by Japan, would in due course become free and independent. At Yalta, Roosevelt told Stalin he had in mind a trusteeship for Korea of Soviet, American, and Chinese representatives, lasting perhaps twenty to thirty years, with no foreign troops stationed there. Stalin said the shorter the better. By May 1945 Stalin had agreed to a four-power trusteeship adding Britain, and Truman so informed Chiang Kai-shek on June 15.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d350:
Willard Thorp answered MacLeish's draft on the aims of the German occupation in a note dated July 14, 1945. Thorp, deputy to the Assistant Secretary for Economic Affairs, wrote because he could not attend the Staff Committee meeting on Monday. He put his reactions on paper instead, and a copy went to Clayton at Babelsberg.

Present directives, Thorp argues, recognize no single basic objective. The government instead chases a series of aims, some immediate and some long-run, which can clash with each other. His list begins with the reform aim MacLeish stressed, then turns to the removal or destruction of much of Germany's war-making plant.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d450:
The British reply on Greek elections is relayed to Athens in Grew's urgent cable to MacVeagh of July 11, 1945. The Foreign Office telegram of July 9, Grew reports, answers the Department's aide-mémoire favorably. Britain accepts the proposal that invitations to supervise the Greek elections go to the Soviet and French governments from Washington and London, not from Athens.

That procedure departs from the strict letter of the Varkiza Agreement, both sides admit. Britain remains strongly opposed, though, to advising Athens to hold elections before the plebiscite, calling the order a matter of Greek internal politics. London deems it essential the invitations go out this week, so the matter can reach the Big Three talks.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d50:
Churchill laid out his fears about Soviet power in an extract from telegram number 72 to President Truman, sent June 4, 1945. It is document 50 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Much of the telegram is omitted in print, but the surviving passages show a Prime Minister deeply worried about the American army pulling back in Germany.

Churchill dreads the retreat of American troops to their agreed line, which would bring Soviet power into the heart of Western Europe behind what he calls an iron curtain. He still hopes the meeting date can be moved up, though he accepts July 15 if it cannot. He also says he must bring Labour leader Clement Attlee, so the other powers know they deal with the whole of Britain.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d550:
Britain's chiefs of staff set out a top secret memo at Babelsberg on July 15, 1945. It is document 550 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The paper asks what should happen to the Combined Chiefs of Staff system after Japan falls.

The British chiefs say the joint system has worked well since 1941. They warn that the world will stay troubled for years, and joint work will still be needed. Shared facts, common weapon design, and common training could all help both states. They ask both governments to keep the framework and the habit of consulting. They add that it need not clash with the new world security body's military staff.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d650:
London ambassador Winant reported British thinking on Palestine once more on July 14, 1945. His secret wire is document 650 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It gives the views of the Foreign Office's Eastern Department head, Charles Baxter.

Baxter named two outstanding points. First, it had always been understood that nothing definite would be done on Palestine until the war in Europe ended. That point was now reached, and the next step was being asked for. Second, the immigration quotas would run out by November. Before then, London must make what he called a very important decision. Trouble would almost surely follow either way, since Jews or Arabs would be roused. Baxter expected a short-term plan on immigration, with the big questions deferred to the post-election government.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1050:
Richard Miles, a secretary at the British Embassy in Washington, wrote to John deWilde on July 30, 1945. His short letter passes on an aide-mémoire about the draft directive on coal production in Germany. Miles presumes deWilde will hear from Potsdam about the talks held there.

The enclosure restates London's position. Britain has weighed the revised directive meant for the American commander in Europe. The Foreign Secretary has told Secretary Byrnes that Britain agrees with its terms. A directive in the same words will go to Field Marshal Montgomery as interim instructions for the British zone.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1150:
The Polish team at Potsdam spoke as a body in this memorandum of 28 July 1945. Earlier Polish papers had come from one man, Deputy Premier Mikolajczyk. A paper from the whole team carried a different weight: it was the joint stand of Warsaw's envoys at the summit.

By the last week, the choices on Poland were taking final shape. The team's paper made its shared case once more, on borders, on the vote, and on Poland's place in the new order. It is Warsaw's group effort in the home stretch of the talks. Read beside the solo papers, it shows the Poles closing ranks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1250:
The White House Map Room wrote to Ambassador Hurley in China on 25 July 1945. The Map Room was the president's own message center, the small staff that handled his secret traffic with posts and commanders around the world. Its cables spoke with his authority.

A Map Room message to an envoy carried the president's word without the forms of a department letter. Hurley in China received it as direct guidance from the top. This note shows that swift, private channel at work during the summit. It linked the president's traveling court to a distant post in a single step.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1350:
J. Rives Childs, the American representative in the talks about Tangier, reported to the acting secretary of state on 18 July 1945. Tangier, the port city at the mouth of the Mediterranean, had a special status shared by several powers. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Tangier was a small place with an outsized diplomatic file, since its rule had been shared before the war and seized by Spain during it. Childs took part in the talks meant to settle the city's future. His report shows a side negotiation running beside the Potsdam summit. Such quiet work filled most of the department's days, even in historic weeks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-150:
Formal State Department minutes record a meeting of July 31, 1945, the Potsdam Conference's last full day. The next day the leaders would adopt the final protocol. Minutes from this date sit near the summit of the second Potsdam volume's record. They state the business in the ordered form the Department favored.

End-of-conference minutes are thick with settled points. Readers watch topics close one by one. The plain record also shows what stayed open past the deadline. That mix of done and undone is honest history. The minutes give later disputes about Potsdam a firm text to argue from.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-50:
A rapporteur's report sums up the foreign ministers' meeting of July 21, 1945, at noon. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Three heads of business are reported in turn.

On the Council of Foreign Ministers, the ministers agreed it should be set up not later than September 1. Invitations to join its work would go to China and to France's provisional government before any public announcement. The drafting committee was asked to make a few minor changes to the proposal's text. German economic questions were put off until tomorrow, since the subcommittee's report had only just arrived. On Poland, the subcommittee chairman presented his report to the ministers. Its points of disagreement, the report signals, would have to go up to the heads of government.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d750:
The Soviet delegation tabled this proposal at Potsdam on July 26, 1945, as document 750. It came in the conference's second week, when the hardest trades were live. Soviet drafts tended to hold firm lines. This one joined the numbered record of the second Potsdam volume, beside rival American and British texts.

A late Soviet proposal shows Moscow's hand near the endgame. Readers can test what it asked against what the final protocol gave. The gaps and matches tell the story of the bargaining. The document keeps the volume's balance: the settlement was written by all three sides, each in its own words.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d850:
Donald Heath, director of political affairs for the American group on the Control Council for Germany, wrote to Robert Murphy on July 17, 1945. Document 850 comes from the occupation machine in Germany itself. Murphy was the political adviser to the American command there. The letter joined the second Potsdam volume.

Letters from the Control Council staff show the settlement being run, not just debated. Heath's office handled Germany's daily political facts. Readers see the layer where summit lines met German streets. The document ties Potsdam to the occupation it governed. The men in Germany had to make the protocol work, and their mail shows them bracing for it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d950:
Marshal Zhukov, commander of Soviet occupation forces in Germany, reported to Stalin in this undated message, filed with the July 29, 1945 papers. He charges that American and British troops, while pulling back from land later assigned to the Soviet zone, took railway rolling stock without Soviet agreement.

His tables list 10,413 loaded goods cars, 2,139 empty cars, and 600 passenger cars removed. The Erfurt board alone lost 9,722 loaded cars to the Americans. Zhukov also counts 102 locomotives of all types. He asks Stalin to press the Allies for the stock's return. His zone, he says, faces an acute shortage of cars and engines.
frus-1950v01-d150: An editorial note in the 1950 national security volume records the start of a national emergency. On December 16, 1950, President Truman issued Proclamation 2914. It cited the menace of communist aggression and asked citizens to put national needs first. The same day, Executive Order 10193 created the Office of Defense Mobilization. Charles Wilson of General Electric became its director. The note also recalls the December 13 meeting with congressional leaders and the President's December 15 radio address.
frus-1955-57v16-d150:
A memorandum of conversation at the State Department on August 30, 1956, records the Egyptian Ambassador's call on Secretary Dulles. Ambassador Hussein carried a message from President Nasser. Nasser objected to the word internationalized for the Suez Canal.

Hussein said the 1888 Convention kept Egypt's ownership while it kept passage free. Dulles replied that the term meant use by all nations, not ownership. He offered to clarify the point in public. The talk shows both sides testing words as the crisis deepened, with each phrase weighed for its effect abroad. The meeting's record is short, and each side kept its own copy.
gao-gaoreports-b-299150:
ITT Electronic Systems, Radar Systems--Gilfillan protested an Army sole-source award to Raytheon Company. The Aviation and Missile Command ran the buy. The work covered air traffic and radar gear, spares, and site services. GAO acted in the B-299150 series on February 2, 2007.

The firm claimed the agency's needs had shifted since the award. On its view, those shifts broke the base for a sole-source path. GAO found the claim too early. The agency had not yet fixed any change to its needs. No contract change yet showed the claimed shifts. A claim built on shifts not yet made cannot be heard. GAO dismissed the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-306050:
Contract rules tucked into spending laws are surveyed in this GAO report, B-306050, dated April 28, 2006. The House Government Reform Committee voiced a worry. Such rules may clash with the aim of one shared contract system. GAO agreed to list and sum up the rules in recent laws. The review spans fiscal years 2001 through 2005.

The review covers 30 spending acts or parts of joint acts. The acts fund six broad areas of government. They run from defense and foreign aid to homeland security. GAO counts a rule if it guides buys of goods or services with public funds. Grant rules and land buys sit outside the count. The report gives lawmakers a map of where spending laws add their own contract terms.
gao-gaoreports-b-308150:
Embassy housing costs in Cairo may be shared in this GAO decision, B-308150, dated March 9, 2007. The Office of Military Cooperation sits at the U.S. Embassy in Cairo. Embassy homes form a shared pool for staff of many agencies. The office asked if its funds could pay leases for homes used by staff of other agencies.

GAO held that they may. Pool payments count as a proper use of funds when they match the office's own share of pool use. If the office paid less than its share, it would gain at the cost of others. That gain would swell its funds in an improper way. The ruling blesses fair-share cost pools abroad.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-250:
Social Security Administration, GAO-05-250 of February 28, 2005, checks pacts that let workers pool credits earned in two lands. Since 1977, the United States has signed such pacts with 20 foreign states. In fiscal year 2004, it paid about $206 million to 102,000 people in those states. Pacts with Mexico and Japan wait in the wings and would grow both sums.

GAO asks how the agency tests the truth of foreign pay data when a pact is made. It asks how staff check that each paid person still counts as due the cash. A more formal path would firm up both tasks, the title holds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-650:
Job training under the Workforce Investment Act is measured in GAO-05-650, dated June 29, 2005. Local boards held about $2.4 billion for adults and laid-off workers in program year 2003. They spent an estimated $929 million, near 40 percent, on training. Some 416,000 people got training, mostly classroom courses bought with personal training accounts. Boards cap those accounts and set tasks before study starts.

Two strains recur: boards lack good data on which schools deliver, and rural areas lack schools nearby. At the national level, almost nothing is known about results after training. The Labor Department disputes some estimates; GAO defends its count.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1050:
Interior land appraisals get an efficiency audit in GAO-06-1050, issued September 28, 2006. In 2003, the department pulled appraisals from its land agencies into one directorate. The move aimed to cure decades of problems. Congress and client agencies now say service has grown less efficient. GAO used expert appraisers to test compliance with standards. It also judged customer service and oversight reach.

Headings list the flaws. Policies do not fully ensure that appraisals meet recognized standards. No system sets realistic delivery times or negotiates them with clients. No system ranks work in progress. Roles for sharing information are unclear. Contract and billing steps add drag. Finding contract appraisers with federal land skill is hard. The directorate even appraises lands that yield little revenue, GAO found. Some appraisals under department grants sit outside its oversight entirely.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-150:
Chemical plant security after the September 11 attacks is reviewed in GAO-06-150, dated January 27, 2006. An attack on a chemical site could harm public health and the economy. The Department of Homeland Security now leads federal work on this risk. It took that role from the Environmental Protection Agency. GAO reviewed the department's strategy work, its aid to industry, and its legal powers. It also studied industry steps and the hurdles firms face.

The department has named 3,400 sites that pose the greatest hazard if attacked. It runs aid programs, such as one that hardens areas around plants. Its sector plan, though, has no set finish date. Industry groups require some firms to assess and fix weak points, with outside checks. Costs and thin guidance slow other firms. The department cannot order plants to add security, so GAO says added authority is needed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-250:
The business cases behind federal tech spending are tested in GAO-06-250, a report issued on January 12, 2006. Each year agencies send the budget office a Capital Asset Plan, called the exhibit 300, for each big tech project. The form should prove sound management and set cost, schedule, and performance goals. Budget officials lean on its facts to spot weak projects. GAO tested the backing behind fiscal year 2006 exhibits.

Too many exhibits rested on thin or shaky support, GAO found. If the facts wobble, the whole oversight chain wobbles with them. GAO urged the budget office to sharpen its guidance and training on the forms. It also urged that known limits on the data be flagged and eased. The budget office accepted the findings. It noted that agencies, not the budget office, own the accuracy of their data. GAO agreed, and aimed part of its advice through the office to them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-450:
New voting rules met their first presidential test in 2004. GAO's GAO-06-450 report, issued June 6, 2006, reviews the nation's election system in the November 2004 general election. States had made big changes since the 2000 election. Some changes were required by the Help America Vote Act of 2002. That law touched people, processes, and technology in elections.
