GAO surveyed all 50 states and the District of Columbia. It sent a questionnaire to a sample of 788 local election areas. It visited 28 local areas in 14 states. For each stage, GAO describes changes and problems met. Readers get a national picture grounded in local practice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-750:
A key health data network's defenses are faulted in GAO-06-750, the GAO report of August 30, 2006. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services runs Medicare and Medicaid, which serve about one in four Americans. It relies on a contractor-owned network to move data with its partners. GAO tested the security controls that guard that network. The review covered both the design of the controls and how well they worked in practice.

GAO found that security controls over the network were ineffective. They failed to protect the privacy and availability of the data that crosses it. Many controls were in place, but key ones were missing. Others had not been applied in an effective way. GAO said the agency needs to improve controls over this vital link.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-850:
Screening of foreign forces for rights abuses is faulted in GAO-06-850, released on July 31, 2006. Algeria, Morocco, and Tunisia are valued United States allies in the war on terrorism. The United States gives them security assistance, including training. Congress bars funding when credible evidence shows a unit committed gross human rights violations. GAO described the goals of the aid and checked how the screening, called vetting, was done.

GAO found lapses in the human rights vetting of foreign trainees. Unclear procedures caused many of the failures. So did a lack of monitoring to ensure that embassies followed State Department policy. GAO also noted that Morocco and Tunisia held no United States defense articles needing certain end-use checks. GAO said further oversight is needed to keep aid within the law.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-150:
Public television runs on a patchwork of local stations, member fees, and federal aid. GAO mapped that system in report GAO-07-150, issued January 19, 2007. The report covers how public TV is organized and what it broadcasts. It reviews where the money comes from today. It also asks how stations raise nonfederal funds and profit from program ventures. GAO gathered data from all 173 licensees.

The system holds 349 stations that reach 98 percent of TV households, GAO found. Universities, local governments, and community groups own the stations. The Corporation for Public Broadcasting passes federal funds to the system. The Public Broadcasting Service supplies much of the prime-time and children's fare. Children's shows fill 16 percent of all broadcast hours. On program spinoffs, royalties were a small slice of retail sales. A $20 item might return $0.50 to $1.50 to the producer.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-50:
Unpaid import duties top at least $480 million since 2003, and GAO-07-50, a GAO report issued October 18, 2006, reviews the bond fix. U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) collects antidumping and countervailing duties on unfairly priced imports. In July 2004 it raised the bonds importers must post, sharply for some goods. Shrimp imports served as the test case. Importers and trade partners sued to stop the policy.

GAO traced why the agency rewrote the rule and how it rolled the change out. The new bonds did shield revenue better. Yet outreach to importers was weak, and shrimp traders called the costs heavy. Uneven use across ports added doubt. The report draws lessons from the test case before the policy spreads to more goods, weighing revenue safety against fair burden on trade.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-650:
A plan to share weather office work stalled for lack of proof, and GAO-07-650, issued June 8, 2007, tells why. The National Weather Service runs 122 forecast offices. In November 2006 it approved a 2-year prototype in which offices would share set tasks. The aim was leaner work and faster backup in severe weather. The prototype was later suspended.

GAO found the goal sound but the groundwork thin. No cost-benefit study backed the launch. Goals and measures existed, but no full plan tied them to a baseline for fair judging. Staff inside the agency were consulted; forecast users outside were not. No plan guarded service quality during the test either. GAO's advice is to do the homework first if the idea returns. A prototype judged on flawed data, it warns, can kill a good idea or bless a bad one.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-750:
Oversight of the federal student loan program is faulted in GAO-07-750, dated July 31, 2007. The Federal Family Education Loan Program is the largest federal student loan effort. Banks lend the money, and schools certify the loans. Reports of gifts and perks from lenders to schools raised concern. GAO read the Education Department's rules and case files. It asked how the department uses its oversight and enforcement powers.

GAO found the department's tools dated and largely reactive. It urged the Secretary to refresh ways to spot improper inducements. It also urged faster probes when signs of abuse appear. New guidance should guide lenders and schools until fresh rules take effect. The department needs a scale for how hard to respond to each breach. The aim is to guard borrower choice in the loan market. Students should pick loans on price and service, not on perks to schools.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-350:
Defense Department reporting on industry security clearances is assessed in GAO report GAO-08-350, released February 13, 2008. The clearance program has long faced delays and backlogs. Congress in 2006 ordered yearly reports from the department and asked GAO to judge the first one.

GAO found the report hit the mandated topics but left out key facts on hand about funding needs, phase-by-phase timing, and quality. Older data were too weak to report counts and costs for fiscal years 2000 through 2004. In fiscal year 2006, the Office of Personnel Management ran 138,769 investigations of industry staff. GAO recommended richer future reports, and the department agreed with each point.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-50:
Adult coverage in the State Children's Health Insurance Program is described in GAO report GAO-08-50, dated November 26, 2007. Congress built the program to cut the ranks of low-income uninsured children, funding about $40 billion from 1998 through 2007. Some states may also cover adults; about 349,000 were enrolled in June 2006.

GAO studied 10 states that cover adults. Five covered parents only, 1 covered childless adults only, and 4 covered both. All 10 made adults share the cost. Adults were about 40 percent of those covered in these states in 2006 and about 54 percent of program spending in the 9 states with data. Shares swung widely by state. States reached eligible people through three outreach paths, detailed in the report.
gregory-great-morals-on-job-vol-3-part-1:
The first half of volume three of Gregory the Great's Morals on the Book of Job came out in 1850, in the Rev. James Bliss translation. The Moralia, written in the late 500s, is Gregory's verse-by-verse reading of Job and the largest work he ever produced. This part opens the final stretch of that reading.

Gregory is now deep into Job's long speeches and God's reply from the storm. His method stays the same: history first, then the teaching hidden in the words, then the moral for daily life. He lingers on pride, hidden sin, and the limits of human judgment. The volume carries the commentary toward its close in the following part.
gregory-great-morals-on-job-vol-3-part-2:
Volume three, part two of Gregory the Great's Morals on the Book of Job, published in 1850, closes the Rev. James Bliss English translation. It covers Books Thirty through Thirty-five of the Moralia, the commentary Gregory wrote in the late 500s, and it adds the indexes for the whole set.

In these last books Gregory works through the end of Job: the great speeches on God's power in nature, Job's humble reply, and his restoration. Leviathan and Behemoth become figures for evil and pride. Gregory sums up his lifelong theme, that suffering rightly borne purges the soul. The ending completes the most widely read Bible commentary of the early Middle Ages.
grimoire-pape-honorius-1850:
Spirits are summoned in the Grimoire of Pope Honorius, in this 1850 reprint of the 1760 Rome edition. Circles, prayers, seals, and commands promise power over demons. The classic French grimoire bears the name of a medieval pope, Honorius the Third, as its supposed and most unlikely author of all.

Priests were said to guard copies as tools of their office. Feared, banned, and endlessly reprinted, the book spread through rural France. Its rites mix church Latin with folk daring in equal parts. Few ritual magic books in French match its dark fame, and collectors of grimoires still rank it among the essential texts.
hawthorne-scarlet-letter-1850:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published The Scarlet Letter in 1850, his great novel of guilt and Puritan conscience. The book is the founding text of American psychological fiction in the judgment of many critics since. Hawthorne claimed to find the letter and tale in the Salem custom house attic papers there.

Hester Prynne stands on a Boston scaffold with her baby and a scarlet A for adultery. Her husband, presumed lost, returns as Chillingworth and vows to find and torment her secret lover. Dimmesdale, the young minister, hides his guilt while his health and mind waste in secret shame. Pearl, the wild child, links them all and demands the truth her elders will not speak. Hawthorne's symbols and gloom shaped how America writes about sin, shame, and hidden selves.
hermes-pymander-everard-1650:
John Everard put the Pymander of Hermes into English in 1650, the first English Hermetica. The text speaks as Hermes Trismegistus, the sage linked with Egypt and Greece. Its talks claim great age, and early readers prized them as ancient wisdom.

In these books, Mind speaks to Hermes and shows how the world was made. Soul, stars, fate, and man's fall and rise fill the talks. Good readers, the text says, can know God and be born anew. Everard's version fed English occult thought for two hundred years. The sample text shows spellings and speech of that age.
his-last-bow-pg2350: His Last Bow: Holmes comes out of retirement on the eve of war to catch a German spy. "There's an east wind coming." The great detective's farewell, patriotic and moving. The end of an era.
hohman-long-lost-friend-1850:
John George Hohman was a German settler in Pennsylvania who collected the charms and remedies printed as The Long-Lost Friend, in this 1850 edition. The book is a pow-wow manual: pow-wow here means German-American folk healing by prayer, charm, and rite. It became the foundational text of American folk magic.

Its short entries tell how to stop bleeding, cure burns, break fevers, protect cattle, and guard a house from fire and thieves. Most cures join a spoken charm in the name of the Trinity to a small rite or herb. Families kept the book in kitchens and barns for everyday emergencies.
holy-bible-wycliffe-forshall-madden-1850:
Long before print, John Wycliffe's followers put the whole Bible into English by hand, in the 1380s. The Wycliffe Translation presented here comes from the 1850 edition prepared by Forshall and Madden. It was the first complete English Bible, made a century and a half before Tyndale's famous version.

Owning or reading the translation could draw persecution, yet copies spread widely among ordinary believers. The language is the English of Chaucer's age, demanding but rewarding. Scholars use this edition to study how scripture first sounded in the mother tongue. The pioneer of all English Bibles deserves its place in any library of translations. Its survival through bans and burnings is a story in itself.
hottel-memo-1950:
An FBI field chief sent Washington a saucer tale in March 1950, and it became the bureau's most read file. Guy Hottel's memo of March 22 tells of three downed saucers and small dead crews, as told to an agent at third hand. The bureau never worked the claim and stands off from it now.

The tale came from a man in New Mexico by way of an Air Force contact, links too weak to hold weight. Hottel's crisp memo outlived its proof by far once the file came out. It is famed less for what it shows than for what it cannot. Students of Roswell lore meet it at every turn.
hutcheson-reflections-upon-laughter-1750:
Hutcheson's Reflections upon Laughter appeared first as essays in the 1720s and were reprinted in 1750 with remarks on the Fable of the Bees. The laughter essays take up a puzzle from Hobbes, who had called laughter a sudden glory at another's weakness. Hutcheson thought that account both false and unkind.

He shows that we laugh at incongruity, at odd pairings of dignity and meanness, often with no scorn at all. The remarks on Mandeville's Fable answer the cynical claim that private vice brings public benefit. Hutcheson defends a warmer view of human nature, the same benevolence his moral-sense theory requires. The piece is the lightest of his works, philosophy with a smile. It still reads as a model of how to correct a great thinker with good humor.
in-the-fire-of-the-forge-a-romance-of-ol:
Volume 8 of In the Fire of the Forge, by Georg Ebers, counts a silent week at Schweinau. Ebers reports that no word has come from Heinz Schorlin or from Katterle, and the waiting itself becomes the story. Heinz is besieging the castles of the Siebenburg brothers and their robber knight allies, work that has proved slow and hard in this late volume.

Chapter XV collects the news that does arrive: a strong mountain fortress has fallen, and the allied knights lost a fight that began as a sortie. A sortie is a sudden rush out of a besieged place. Still Heinz sends no line for his servant Biberli, whose loyalty now faces ruin in Nuremberg. Even the emperor, asked to shield the man, refuses to interfere in city justice. Faithful service meets cold law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-ben-jacob: Aaron ben Jacob of Karlin, known among the Hasidim as Rabbi Aaron the Great, fills this Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. Born in 1738, he died in 1771. He was one of the early great rabbis who helped Hasidism spread fast in eastern Europe. His fiery eloquence in exhortation set him apart, the entry says. He died one year before his master, Rabbi Baer of Mezhirich. His son Asher of Karlin succeeded him. Aaron wrote a Sabbath hymn still used in Hasidic liturgy, plus an ethical will.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abba-mari-ben-i:
Abba Mari ben Isaac of St. Gilles flourished about the middle of the twelfth century, at St. Gilles, near Lunel, in Languedoc. Benjamin of Tudela, who visited the town's Jewish community, reports a rare fact. About 1165 Abba Mari held the office of bailli, or magistrate there. Raymond V, who was friendly to the Jews, had appointed him.

The entry treats that post as a sign of the place Jews held in southern France before the war with the Albigenses. Some scholars took Abba Mari to be the father of Isaac ben Abba Mari, author of the "'Iṭṭur." The entry notes that Gross has set that claim aside in full.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aberle-rabel-ab: Abraham Aberle was a Moravian Hebraist who lived at Austerlitz in the third decade of the nineteenth century. All of his writing in print appeared in one journal. Poems, verse translations, notes on Scripture, and riddles by him fill parts of volumes nine and ten of "Bikkure ha-'Ittim." That journal record is the ground of his notice here. The entry adds no named book of his, no post he held, and no year of birth or of death for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-isa:
Liturgical poet Abraham ben Isaac Auerbach lived in the seventeenth century. Born at Kosfeld, he became rabbi at Münster. On a visit to Amsterdam in 1675 he learned of charges against the Jews spread by a clergyman, Christopher Bernard.

The charges were fully disproved. During the danger Abraham wrote selihot, or penitential hymns. After it passed he wrote pizmonim, odes of triumph. Joseph Athias printed them at Amsterdam in 1677 in a pamphlet now very rare. Many rabbinic leaders signed their approval of his poems, among them Isaac Aboab of the Portuguese congregation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-philip-: Philip Abraham was an English and Hebrew author born in 1803. He died in London on Dec. 17, 1890. His books include The Autobiography of a Jewish Gentleman, from 1860, and Autumn Gatherings, a prose and poetry collection printed at London in 1866. He also wrote Ha-Nistarot weha-Niglot, the Secret and Revealed Things. His Curiosities of Judaism, printed at London in 1879, gathers facts, opinions, anecdotes, and remarks on the Hebrew nation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abu-650:
Abu is an Arabic word that means father. It opens many compound names. Its case forms are aba and abi, and its short form is bu. Steinschneider sorts the link between Abu and the next name in three ways. The link can be by birth, by past story, or by a trait a man shows.

By birth, Abu named the real father of a son. A man called Ibrahim with a son Isḥaḳ became Abu Isḥaḳ. By story, the name points to a famed bearer of old. By trait, it joins with words for good traits, as in Abu al-Kheir, Father of the Good. The entry lists eight paired names of this kind. It also lists the trait words most used by Judæo-Arabic writers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-acrostics-750:
Acrostics are works in which set letters form a name or a line. The letters are most often the first or last of each verse line. Read in order, they spell the hid word. The Hebrew Bible holds verse acrostics built on the alphabet. Psalms, Proverbs, and Lamentations hold most of them. Psalm cxix. gives eight verses to each letter.

Scholars have hunted for name acrostics in the Bible with less luck. Claims for the name of God in Esther rest on weak ground. Two finds have some strength: Pedahel at the end of Psalm xxv., and Simon in Psalm cx. The entry lists the alphabet psalms with care. It notes lost or moved lines in each. Later Hebrew use ran to prayer, charms, and short forms. One tour de force by Abraham ibn Ezra reads the same four ways.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adoni-zedek-zed: Adoni-zedek ruled Jerusalem when the Hebrews came into Palestine. Joshua x. 1 and 3 name him. He led a pact of five Amorite towns to block the advance. The pact was beat at Gibeon and at Beth-horon. A great hail storm struck the fleeing host as well. The five kings hid in a cave at Makkedah. Joshua had them brought out, shamed, and put to death. The entry notes that his name may be warped into Adoni-bezek in Judges i.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aha-ahai-of-sha:
Aha of Shabha was a leading Babylonian Talmudist. He lived in the eighth century. He was the first rabbinical author known after the Talmud closed. The gaon of Pumbedita had died. All agreed Aha was the fittest successor. The exilarch Solomon bar Hasdai held a grudge against him. He passed Aha over for the post. He picked Natronai, Aha's own secretary, instead.

Angered by the slight, Aha left Babylonia. He settled in Palestine about 752-753. He stayed there until his death. In Palestine he wrote the "Sheiltot." The work holds 190 or 191 treatises. They follow the weekly readings from the Law. They were written for thoughtful laymen, not scholars alone. They stress duties like benevolence and respect for parents. Later works copied them freely. The "Halakot Gedolot" took about one hundred and fifty passages from them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aksai-tashkicha: Aksai, also called Tashkicha, is a village in the Tersk province of the Caucasus. About 1,000 Jews live there. They claim descent from the exiles taken by Shalmaneser. Their forebears came early from Persia to Daghestan. In the seventeenth century they moved on to the village of Andrei. Their old burial-grounds still lie on the Dzuhot-tuba, the hill of the Jews. Suffering under Muslim persecution, they moved to Aksai in 1844. Most of them work as merchants, butchers, and tanners.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-sende: Alexander Sender ben Mordecai was an associate rabbi of Prague. He lived in the second half of the seventeenth century. His one named work is "Shehitot u-Bedikot." It appeared at Amsterdam in 1667, in Hebrew and in Judaeo-German. As its title says, it treats the rules for slaughtering cattle. It also covers the inspection of the inner organs. The entry gives no dates for his birth or death, and names no other writing of his.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alkan-charles-h:
Charles Henri Valentin Alkan was a French pianist and composer. He was born in Paris on Nov. 30, 1813. He died there on March 29, 1888. He entered the Paris school of music at age six. At age seven he won a first prize. He took first prizes in harmony and in composition as well.

He wrote seventy-two works for the piano and more. His sets of twelve studies pushed piano skill to its edge. The entry quotes Grove on those studies. They hold feats of skill found nowhere else. Yet they lack the beauty of the studies by Chopin and Liszt. A long list of his chief works follows.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amador-de-los-r:
Jose Amador de los Rios wrote on the past of Spanish Jews. He was born in 1818. He died at Seville in 1878. He served as head of public teaching in Spain. He wrote many works on old remains and digs. Two of his books bear on Jewish life. The first came out in Madrid in 1848.

That book was turned into French in 1861. He later grew it into a three-volume work. That set came out in 1875-76. His strength lay in the legal place of Jews. His weak side was Hebrew, which he lacked. For Jewish letters he leaned on notes by De Castro. The entry flags that lack with care.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anagram-greek-o:
Anagram is a word with its letters turned about. The shift makes a fresh word or phrase from the old. Jews used such turns from the most old times. Some stand in the Bible, the entry holds. One pairs the name Noah with a word for grace. Both words share the same letters in Hebrew.

Rabbis built a whole method on such turns. They called that method inversions of letters. Poets of the Arabic age took up the game with zest. The golden age of the form came with the Cabala. Cabalists sought hid forces in the turns of names. Most charms rest on turns of that kind.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anna-1550: Anna was a learned woman of Champagne, in France, in the middle of the twelfth century. She was a daughter of Rabbi Meir of Ramerupt. Her brothers were Rabbenu Tam and Rashbam, and her grandfather was Rashi. The short entry gives her one distinction of her own. She taught women in the Jewish religion. It names no writings by her and gives no dates for her birth or death, pointing readers to Kayserling's book on Jewish women.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-apocalyptic-lit:
Apocalyptic literature, in its Neo-Hebraic branch, is one limb of a large family of writings. The entry traces an unbroken chain of such works from the Maccabean war to the close of the Middle Ages. From the start, this writing refused to stay in its native Palestine.

It reached Alexandria at once, dressed as the heathen Sibyl in Greek dress. At Christianity's rise, the Church took the form over whole from the Synagogue, a fact the entry says all modern critics admit. Jewish and Christian apocalyptic then flowed into each other for some fifteen centuries. The entry maps that long exchange and the Hebrew works it produced in the later ages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-apollos-1650:
Apollos was a learned Jew of Alexandria and a coworker of Paul. Acts, chapter 18, tells that he came to Ephesus about the year 56, an eloquent man mighty in the Scriptures. He preached boldly in the synagogue, though he knew only the baptism of John.

Aquila and Priscilla, Jews who had joined the new Christian faith, taught him the way of God more fully. He then went to Achaia and won Jews to belief in Jesus by arguments from Scripture. The entry links him to a circle of John the Baptist's followers at Ephesus. Paul rebaptized about twelve of them, and the entry reads the two stories as one picture of that Baptist sect.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arens-louis-175: Louis Arens was an operatic singer, a tenor, born in Mitau, Russia, on March 23, 1865. He was schooled at the Riga Gymnasium. He studied music at the Imperial Conservatory of Moscow under Tchaikovsky and graduated in 1890. He sang at the Imperial Opera of Moscow and in Berlin, Milan, Naples, and Turin. In 1894 he sang at the Theater Royal, Covent Garden, in London, where he later gave many concerts. He also wrote The Quartet, a children's pantomime for orchestra, and a song for tenor, Die Erinnerung.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenasy-eugen: Eugene Ashkenasy was a student of plants, born at Odessa on May 5, 1845. He died on July 24, 1903. He held a post as honorary teacher of botany at the University of Heidelberg in Germany. In 1871 he put out a work that weighed the worth of Darwin's theory. His short papers ran in plant journals and in the reports of the University of Geneva.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-astrakhan-2050:
Astrakhan is the capital of a Russian province of the same name. It stands on the left bank of the Volga, about sixty miles from the Caspian Sea. The entry thinks it rose near Atel, the old capital of the Chazars. Of its Jews, little is known between 969 and 1804, except that Jewish merchants traded there in size.

In 1804 Alexander I. let Jewish farmers and craftsmen settle in the province. Nicholas I. repealed that right in 1825. In 1883 local officers limited visiting Jewish merchants to three days in the city. Christian merchants protested, since Jewish fish sales topped five million rubles a year. The limit was stretched to a month, but many Jews had left and fish prices fell by half. In 1899 the city held 1,575 Jews in a total of 117,772 people. The entry closes with its two synagogues, one Ashkenazic and one Sephardic.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-austerlitz-2150:
Austerlitz is also a Jewish family name, taken from the Moravian town of that name. The entry warns that a name drawn from a place does not prove that all who bear it form one family. The name appears on Prague gravestones after 1620. It also appears among the Jews driven out of Vienna in 1670, and in towns across Austria and Hungary.

Four members of the name get notices here. Aaron Austerlitz was secretary to the rabbinate of Berlin in 1775. Baruch Austerlitz preached at Prague and wrote approvals for printed books in the early seventeen hundreds. Hirschel Austerlitz, exiled from Vienna in 1670, signed a petition five years later asking that Jews be allowed back into the city. Moses Austerlitz kept a house in Nikolsburg that sheltered scholars, and after the Prague fire of 1689 he supported several writers of cabalistic works there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bagi-2350:
Bagi is the name of a noted Karaite family of Constantinople in the fifteenth, sixteenth, and seventeenth centuries. The entry says the name is also written Badschi, Pegi, or Poki, and may come from a Turkish word. It then treats the best known members one by one, giving each man's town, dates in broad terms, and books.

Joseph ben Moses ha-Kohen Bagi gets the fullest notice, with six works, among them a defense of Karaism against the charge that Karaites descend from Sadducees. Elijah Bagi is listed with three works, and Moses Bagi with two, one on the calendar and one on the precepts of the Pentateuch. Isaac and Samuel Bagi receive only a line or two each, as men named by other writers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-banu-aus-2450: Banu Aus was an Arab tribe that came to Medina with the Banu Khazraj, about the year 300, and settled among the Jewish inhabitants of the place. The entry tells the story in a few lines. For a time the newcomers lived under Jewish protection and married into Jewish families. As they grew stronger, they slowly made themselves masters of the town and oppressed the Jews. In the end they invited Mohammed to live in Medina, and the Jews there were overthrown, some driven out and some massacred.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barrios-simon-l: Simon Levi de Barrios was the son of Daniel Levi de Barrios, the Amsterdam poet. He was born on March 17, 1665, at Amsterdam and died on May 16, 1688, at Barbados. He belonged to the Eẓ Ḥayyim congregation and to several poetical academies of Amsterdam. The entry is a short notice of four lines. It gives his parentage, both dates, and his memberships, but names no work of his own and tells nothing of why he was in Barbados when he died.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bass-shabbethai:
Shabbethai Bass, called Bassista, is named here as the founder of Jewish bibliography. Born at Kalisz in 1641, he lost his parents in attacks there in 1655 and went to Prague. He sang bass in the Altneuschule choir, which gave him his name.

Bass learned the book trade in Amsterdam, then set up a Hebrew press at Dyhernfurth near Breslau. The entry follows his press, his time in prison over a book charge, and his books for young readers. He died on July 21, 1718, at Krotoschin. After his release he spent his last years on a larger second edition, which he did not live to finish.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bat-2650: Bat names the winged mammal listed among unclean creatures in Leviticus, Deuteronomy, and Isaiah. The Hebrews counted it among the birds. Ancient writers in general treated it as part bird and part mammal. Like other night birds it was held unclean. The entry adds that caves and ruins in Palestine shelter vast swarms of bats. Tristram counted no less than seventeen kinds native to that country. Some of those kinds are also found in Europe and America.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beer-wilhelm-27:
Wilhelm Beer was an astronomer born in Berlin on Jan. 4, 1797. He was a brother of the composer Meyerbeer and the poet Michael Beer. At sixteen he fought as a volunteer against Napoleon, then entered his father's banking house and headed it from 1826.

With his friend Mädler, Beer built a fine private observatory at his Berlin villa. Their map of the moon, in four sheets from 1834 to 1836, set a new standard for its care. They measured hundreds of lunar spots and the heights of its mountains. He died in Berlin on March 27, 1850. Mars studies with his partner came first, across the years 1828 to 1837, before the moon work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-ben-aa: Benjamin ben Aaron was a Ḥasidic writer who lived toward the end of the eighteenth century. He learned under Israel Ba'al Shem-Ṭob and under Baer of Meseritz. Later, in 1790, he preached at Zlazitz. Four books bear his name. They give sermons on the Pentateuch, on Lamentations and Esther, and on the Song of Songs, plus a work on Ecclesiastes and a commentary on the Passover Haggadah. The entry gives their Hebrew titles and the towns and years where each was printed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berenice-3050:
Berenice, daughter of Herod Agrippa the First, was born in 28. Twice widowed young, she came to live with her brother Agrippa the Second, amid whispered scandal. In 66 she was in Jerusalem to fulfil a vow when the governor Florus sparked a riot. On her knees she begged him to stop the bloodshed, in vain.

She and her brother then sided openly with Rome. She backed the Flavian cause and won high esteem from Vespasian. Her plea alone saved Justus of Tiberias from beheading. The entry closes with her long bond with Titus, the Roman commander.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernstein-natha:
Nathan Osipovich Bernstein was a Russian physiologist. He was born at Brody in Galicia in 1836. He died at Odessa on February 9, 1891. He studied medicine at the University of Moscow. A gold medal honored his 1857 treatise. From 1865 he taught anatomy and physiology at Odessa.

The entry lists his many civic roles. He served as alderman and hospital director. He led the Odessa Society of Physicians for fourteen years. His articles appeared in Russian and French medical journals. He also published a two-part manual of physiology in 1868. Earlier he edited the periodical "Sion" until its suppression in 1862.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-biach-alois-325:
Alois Biach was an Austrian physician and medical writer. He was born in Lettowitz, Moravia, on May 1, 1849. He studied at Brünn and at Vienna's university. He took his medical degree in 1873. He then settled in Vienna. He joined the board of health there. In 1883 he became a privat-docent of medicine.

The entry lists his many medical essays. One treats aneurysms of the heart valves. Another studies jaborandi and its alkaloids. A third tests the effects of quinoline. Later papers cover liver cirrhosis and stomach cancer. His book on newer fever drugs appeared in 1889.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blanc-piotr-335: Piotr Blanc was a Polish financier of the eighteenth century. His birth date and place are unknown. He died at Warsaw in 1797. He served as court banker to King Stanislaus Augustus. With Dekert and Raffalowitsh he formed the tobacco monopoly. That was in 1776. He also helped form the government lottery in 1781. In 1790 he was raised to the nobility. In 1792 a plan arose to better Polish Jews' condition. Blanc guaranteed five million rubles for it. The sum would amortize the king's debts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bochart-samuel-:
Samuel Bochart was a French scholar born at Rouen in 1599. He died in Caen on May 16, 1667. He studied theology and Oriental languages in France, England, and Holland and served as pastor at Caen.

Bochart won fame in a nine-day debate with the Jesuit Véron. His Geographia Sacra of 1646 treats the nations of Genesis and the Phoenicians. His Hierozoicon of 1663 gathers lore on the animals of the Bible. The entry calls him one of the great scholars of the seventeenth century. A report of that long debate was printed at Saumur in 1630. His learning grew out of the notes he made while preparing his weekly sermons.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bonsenyor-judah:
Judah Bonsenyor, called Jaffuda, was notary-general of Aragon and a translator from Arabic. He was a son of the elder Astruc and served as interpreter to Alfonso III. and then to Jaime II. He died about 1334.

Judah rode with Alfonso against Minorca in 1287. In 1294 he became notary-general for the kingdom. Merchants who knew only Arabic had to bring their papers to him. Royal favor freed him from the Barcelona community's taxes in 1310. At the king's order he gathered Arabic maxims into Catalan. The sayings number 753 in 67 chapters and are still quoted in Majorca and Catalonia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-braudo-alexande: Alexander Braudo was a Russian author born in 1864. From 1889 to 1892 he reviewed books on Russian history for two St. Petersburg journals. He translated old sources on Russian history into Russian as well. His articles appeared in a Russian biographical dictionary from that city. In Voskhod for 1896 he reviewed Bershadski on Jewish history. As secretary of a society for Jewish education, he steered its work toward elementary schooling. He later advised the Jewish Colonization Association.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-browning-robert:
Robert Browning was an English poet born in Clerkenwell, London, in 1812. He died at Venice on Dec. 12, 1889. His knowledge of Hebrew and sympathy with Jews long led people to think him of Jewish descent. The entry says genealogy work by Dr. Furnivall disproved that idea. His father's Bank of England post came through Rothschild influence.

Several poems take up Jewish subjects. Holy Cross Day voices a Jew of the Roman ghetto resisting forced sermons. Rabbi Ben Ezra gives the life philosophy of a Jewish sage, perhaps Abraham ibn Ezra. Jochanan Hakkadosh tells of a rabbi granted extra months of life by his pupils. Browning also signed an 1881 protest against persecution of Jews in Russia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bush-busch-isid:
Isidor Bush was a writer, publicist, and grape grower born in Prague on Jan. 15, 1822. Burns suffered at age seven marked his life, yet he rose above them by will. He entered a Vienna printing house at fifteen and edited a calendar and yearbook for Israelites from 1842 to 1847. The failed Revolution of 1848 forced him to flee to New York.

In America Bush published the first Jewish weekly in the United States, though it lasted three months. He settled in St. Louis, ran a store, and led a savings bank. During the Civil War he served as a captain and aide, and he helped frame a plan for a huge government loan. Later he aided B'nai B'rith and an orphan asylum. His Bushberg grape catalogue won readers in several languages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-camp-3950:
Camp means a set of tents, booths, or huts that shelters shepherds, travelers, or soldiers. A stay might last one night or many months. The entry says water supply and safety fixed the choice of site. Camps often sat beside a ravine for cover. Night watches ran in three shifts, and a guard stayed behind when the main body marched out.

The camp seems usually laid out in a circle, though one Hebrew word may instead point to a ring of wagons. Numbers describes the tribes grouped by flags around the tabernacle. Later, herders built fixed enclosures near caves to hold flocks at night. The entry calls those stockades the first step away from wandering life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-catechumens-hou:
Catechumens, House of, was a Roman institution for converting Jews to Catholicism. Jews were forced, through taxes, to support it. The Vatican founded the house on March 21, 1548. A decree of Jan. 1, 1565, assigned it certain revenues and the fines levied on Jews for money lending and other acts.

Under Pius V, forced conversions grew common. Gregory XIII kept the house going and ordered church leaders to aid converts with gifts and recommendations. The cost then shifted onto the Jews themselves. The house served as retreat and prison for converts in transition. Later, when funds fell low, Jews had to attend sermons against Judaism three times a year. In 1604 Rome's chief rabbi and his four children were forced into the house, and the children were baptized.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-charlemagne-425:
Charlemagne, king of the Franks and emperor of the West, was born in April 742 and died on Jan. 28, 814. His stance toward Jews was that of a clever politician, the entry judges, not a liberal mind. He saw the gain their business skill brought the country. He gave them full freedom in trade.

Some Jews held high places at his court. One named Ferragut served as his physician. A Hebrew named Isaac joined an embassy to Harun al-Rashid, likely as interpreter. Political status, though, barely changed. His capitularies set hard rules: a Jew charging a Christian needed more witnesses than a Christian needed. No Jew could hire a Christian workman on Sunday. Church property could not be taken in pledge. A Jew swearing an oath had to hold a copy of the Pentateuch.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-china-11550:
China receives one of the longest treatments in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, split into two large parts on history and on religious customs. The opening asks whether China was known to Bible writers at all. Most commentators cited link it to the land of the Sinim in Isaiah. Early ties ran through Persia and the silk trade.

From there the entry traces Jewish settlement, the Chinese name for Jews, and the community at K'ai-Fung-Foo. It weighs Arabic writers, synagogue records, and reports from modern visitors. A closing stretch follows Jews in Shanghai and Hongkong and efforts to aid the old colony. Readers get a full survey built from many named sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chor-ashan-r-v-: Chor-ashan, named in I Samuel xxx. 30, may be better read as Bor-ashan. The entry rests that spelling on earlier manuscripts edited by Baer. The Septuagint supports it too, though one reading there gives Beersheba instead. The place is probably the town known simply as Ashan. Nothing more is claimed, and the brief entry leaves the identification as likely rather than certain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-coen-raffaelo-d: Raffaelo del fu Vitale Coen, an Austrian physician, was born at Spalato, Dalmatia, on Jan. 19, 1839. He studied at the University of Vienna and took his medical degree there in 1872. He then practiced in Vienna, focusing on speech impediments. In 1882 he opened a private clinic and hospital for stammerers. The entry lists four of his books. They treat speech disorders, deaf-mutism, and stammering care.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cologne-german-:
Cologne, chief city of Rhenish Prussia, shows signs of a Jewish community from very early times. Its first firm document is a decree of Constantine dated Dec. 11, 321, ending the Jews' exemption from heavy civic offices. Later emperors cut their rights further. Under Frankish rule from 462, a long stretch of freedom and prosperity followed.

Norman invaders burned the city in 881 and ended the community for a time. It rose again in the tenth century under the archbishops, growing rich and learned, with a synagogue built in 1010 and a hospital raised by a benefactor. The long entry then follows crusade-era dangers, the plague year 1349, when elders chose death by fire over forced baptism, and the community's later fate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cordova-joshua-: Joshua Hezekiah de Cordova was a rabbi and preacher in Amsterdam. He worked there about the middle of the eighteenth century. The entry is very short. Its one named work is a moral sermon. He preached it in the Talmud Torah congregation on the Sabbath of Bamidbar, 5 Siwan, 5504. The sermon was printed at Amsterdam in 1744. Its title is given in Portuguese form. No birth or death dates are stated. Readers learn where he preached and what he published, and nothing more.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cremona-4750:
Cremona is an Italian city in the plain of Lombardy. Its Jewish community seems to date from the middle of the twelfth century. The first firm notice comes in 1420, when the city renewed older Jewish privileges. Jews lived on the Via Giudecca, near a large synagogue. Francesco Sforza took them under his protection in 1456. By 1466-68 citizens were asking that no more Jews be let in.

Under Spanish rule their lot hardened. In 1553 the burning of Talmudic works ordered by Pope Julius III. was enforced there. Charges over taxes cost the Jews state protection. An expulsion order arrived in 1596, but war kept them until 1597. A fresh royal decree then forced them out at once.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dainow-zebi-hir:
Ẓebi Hirsch Dainow, known as the Slutzker Maggid, was a Russian preacher. He was born at Slutzk, in the government of Minsk, in 1832. He died in London on March 6, 1877. His oratory was of a high order. He urged secular knowledge, industry, patriotism, and progress on Russian Jews. In him the modern haskalah, or progressive movement, found its pulpit voice. Its writers at first backed him in every way.

His break with custom stirred the other camp. He dropped the traditional dress and manners of the maggid, and suspicion grew. Government favor deepened the hostility toward him. Gordon warned that he mistook opposition for persecution. In 1874 he left Russia for good. In London he preached to a congregation of Russian and Polish Jews and lectured at a synagogue there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-ben-jacob: A Turkish Talmudist named David ben Jacob ha-Kohen flourished about 1550 in Salonica. He wrote essays, called shiṭṭot, on three orders of the Talmud: Mo'ed, Nashim, and Neziḳin. Only the part on Giṭṭin was published after his death, under the title "Migdal Dawid" (The Tower of David), at Salonica in 1597. Other scholars cite him in their responsa, and Ghirondi praised his profound knowledge as a Talmudist. Azulai supposed that David had been a pupil of Solomon ben Jehiel Luria, the noted Polish scholar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-deutz-elijah-be: Isaac's son Elijah Deutz was a rabbinical author who lived at Hamburg in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and the entry about him is only two lines long. His one known work is "Pi Eliyahu" (Mouth of Elijah), printed at Altona in 1735. It is a commentary on "Pereḳ Shirah," the Chapter of Song, a short old hymn of praise by the creatures of nature. The entry cites Steinschneider and Zedner and gives no dates or further details of his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dodai-dudai-ben: Dodai, also written Dudai, ben Nahman was a Babylonian scholar of the eighth century. He served as gaon of the academy at Pumbedita from 761 to 764. The entry says little is known of his life. His brother Judah b. Nahman was gaon at Sura from 759 to 762. Together the brothers blocked Anan b. David, the future founder of Karaism, from the exilarchate left open by his uncle Solomon b. Hasdai.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dubrovna-5350:
Dubrovna is a village on both banks of the Dnieper, in the government of Mohilev. Its people in 1898 numbered 8,687, and 4,559 of them were Jews. The place is famed as nearly the only maker of woolen tallits. A factory for them stood there in 1750.

About 600 families weave tallits at home, wives and children helping. Dyers earn eight to ten rubles a month, more than the weavers. Work goes on in foul air, and dealers who supply the wool squeeze the makers. Machine-made tallits now push Dubrovna's out. A new stock company, backed by the Jewish Colonization Association, aims to improve the trade.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eglah-heifer-54: Eglah was the mother of Ithream, David's sixth son. The entry is three lines long. It notes that Scripture calls her David's wife, and takes that phrase to mean his favorite wife. The Targum, it adds, identifies Eglah with Michal, Saul's daughter. Whether the two were one woman the entry does not settle. It gives no dates, no family beyond the names above, and no deeds of hers at all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliezer-b-natha:
Eliezer ben Nathan of Mayence was a halakist and prayer poet. He lived in the first half of the twelfth century. Men called him by the short name Raban. He was a fellow student of Rashi at school. Through his four daughters he founded learned lines of note. One great-grandson was Asher ben Jehiel, a famed rabbinic name. Eliezer wrote letters to Rabbi Tam and Rashbam.

His chief book bears a title made from his initials. In it he gives grounds for old customs and solves hard points of law. The first part answers questions from pupils and peers. The book holds names, tales, and notes on custom. That mix makes it a store for the history of his age. Eliezer ruled with care but little self-trust. What the old rabbis banned, he held, no one may allow. He also wrote prayers for the liturgy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elijah-of-ferra: Elijah of Ferrara was an Italian Talmudist and traveler. He lived in the early fifteenth century. In 1437 he took a post as teacher in Jerusalem. The voyage there was stormy and cost him dear. He lost his son and his grandson on the way. He wrote letters home to his wife and children. Only one letter, dated 1438, has come down to us. In it he describes Jerusalem for his family. Signs in the letter hint he worked as a doctor too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-endingen-5750: Endingen is a town of Baden near Freiburg. Its name is grim in the annals of the Jews. In 1470 three Jews were burned at the stake there. The charge was the blood charge, a claim of ritual murder. The claim told of a Christian family slain eight years prior. Under torture the accused owned to the crime. The bones of the said victims are kept in a church still. Jews were banned from the town for that act. It fell at last in the year 1785.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-escudero-lorenc: Lorenco Escudero, also called Abraham Israel, was a Spanish poet born at Cordova of Marrano parentage. He died about 1683. After turning to Judaism, he lived in deep poverty at Amsterdam. The Marquis of Caracena, governor of Flanders, pressed him to return to Christianity. Rewards were offered, but he refused each time. De Barrios praised him in verse after his death. The entry credits him, with some doubt, as author of Fortaleza del Judaismo, a defense of Judaism surviving in Italian and Hebrew manuscript versions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ezekiel-5950:
Ezekiel was a priest of Jerusalem, son of Buzi, carried to Babylonia when Nebuchadnezzar first took the city in 597 B.C. He lived among fellow exiles at Tel-abib on the river Chebar. He was married and kept his own house. In the fifth year of his exile, 592 B.C., he saw the glory of the Lord by the Chebar and was made a prophet. His last dated word falls in 570.

His hearers came in crowds, the entry says, but treated his speech as a fine show and did not act on it. He calls them a rebellious house. Ezekiel stands between two ages, the entry argues. The fall of city and Temple broke Israel's old life in two. His book draws lessons from the age before and points the path for the age after. Of his death nothing is known.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fee-6050:
A fee is pay for work done or to be done, most often for skilled or special service, with the sum set by law or custom. The entry opens with Temple pay: Levites lived on Israel's tithes, and priests took a tithe of that plus twenty-four priestly gifts. Samuel took nothing from any man's hand. Elisha refused Naaman's gift for a cure and cursed Gehazi for taking one.

On teachers, the rule is strict: no pay may be demanded for teaching the Law. Moses taught free, as God commanded him, and all must copy that. A small-child minder or a chant teacher may charge, since the pay covers care, not Torah. Maimonides allows the going rate for Scripture teaching only. The pupil, though, must hire a teacher if none will teach free.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fischer-moritz-:
Moritz von Fischer was a Hungarian porcelain maker born at Totis in 1800. He died there on Feb. 25, 1900. His factory at Herend, near Veszprim, won him fame in Hungarian industry and art. He founded a small works there in 1839. He met many hardships before it grew.

In time it became a true art institute, the entry says. It stood comparison with Sèvres, Meissen, and Berlin. Its exhibits took first prizes at many world fairs. In 1869 Francis Joseph I raised him to the Hungarian nobility. A grandson ran the works in 1903.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fould-achille-6:
Achille Fould was a French statesman and financier born at Paris on November 17, 1800. He died at Tarbes on October 5, 1867. A wealthy banker's son, he studied banking and traveled widely. In 1847 he was chosen deputy for Tarbes. After the Revolution of 1848 he wrote three pamphlets on finance that drew wide comment. His sharp attacks on the finance ministry of the day made his name.

On October 31, 1849, Fould became minister of finance under Louis Napoleon. He ended the income tax and set up the Algerian Bank. He also provided pensions for the aged. He was twice dismissed and recalled in the crises of 1851. Later he served as senator and minister of state. He organized the great Paris exposition of 1855. In 1861 he took the finance post again to face a growing deficit. He retired for good in January 1867.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-freudenthal-ber:
Berthold Freudenthal was a professor of law at the academy of Frankfort-on-the-Main. He was born at Breslau on August 23, 1872, a son of Jacob Freudenthal. He was schooled at the Breslau gymnasium and at four universities. In 1898 he joined the law court of his home town. The next year he began to lecture at its university.

In 1901 he was called to the same duties at Frankfort. In 1903 he was made a professor at the Frankfort academy of social and business studies. His books are studies in criminal law. One treats bribery at elections, printed in 1896. Two more treat crimes that need more than one person to commit them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gabriel-man-of-:
Gabriel, named with Michael in the Book of Daniel, explains visions to Daniel there. In Luke he comes to Zacharias and then to Mary. He tells Mary she will bear a son named Jesus. Gabriel ranks among four angels who stand at the four sides of God throne. The four guard the four parts of the world.

In Jewish lore Michael stands at God right hand and Gabriel at his left. Gabriel stands for fire, yet he is sent to save men from a fiery furnace. As God messenger he does God will on earth. Tales credit him with the fall of Sodom, the saving of Lot, and war on the leviathan in days to come.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gedaliah-judah-: Don Judah Gedaliah, a Portuguese printer born in Lisbon, worked as foreman in the print house of Eliezer Toledano. Driven from Portugal at an advanced age, he settled in Salonica. About 1515 he set up the first Hebrew press in that city. He used in part type he had brought from Lisbon. Early works from the press include Jacob ibn Habib En Yaakob. Gedaliah died about 1526. His sons kept the press going.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ghazali-abu-ham:
Abu Hamid Mohammed al-Ghazali, an Arabian theologian and moralist born at Tuz in Khorasan in 1058, died there in 1111. His works bore hard on Jewish thought in the Middle Ages. Friend and foe of philosophy alike drew rich stuff from them. His Makasid sets out logic, physics, and higher thought after Aristotle. Many Jewish pupils learned sound facts from that book.

His Tahafut then turns on the thinkers and picks out twenty weak points. Its sharpest stroke hits the claim that cause must bind events in a set order. Judah ha-Levi and Hasdai Crescas both took fire from it. Yet his ethics won him his chief rank among Jews. Writers such as Abraham ibn Ezra borrowed from his works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goldman-bernard: Bernard Goldman was an Austrian deputy. He was born at Warsaw on Feb. 20, 1842. He died at Lemberg on March 23, 1901. His father owned a Hebrew printing house there. Bernard attended the Warsaw rabbinical school. In 1863 the Polish rising brought his arrest in a synagogue. A court sentenced him to banishment in Siberia. He escaped, paused in Paris, and settled at Lemberg in 1870. In 1876 voters sent him to the Galician Landtag. He worked there for Galician Jewish welfare and schooling. The emperor decorated him in 1894.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-graes-ortuin-de:
Ortuin de Graes, also called Ortuinus Gratius, was an anti-Jewish writer of the sixteenth century. He was born at Holtwick in Westphalia in 1491. He died at Cologne on May 21, 1542. He was a priest's son and a leader of Cologne's Dominican party. He sided with Pfefferkorn against Reuchlin.

With Victor von Karben, a baptized Jew, he wrote "De Vita et Moribus Judæorum" in 1504. He then translated it into German himself. The entry calls the book a fanatical diatribe against Jews and Judaism. He also put Pfefferkorn's anti-Jewish writings into Latin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gunzburg-horace:
Horace Günzburg, Baron, was a Russian philanthropist. He was born on Feb. 8, 1833, in Zvenigorodka, in the government of Kiev. After the Crimean war his father Joseph, a rich merchant and army contractor, settled the family in St. Petersburg. In 1863 Horace helped found the Society for the Promotion of Culture Among the Jews of Russia. After his father's death in 1878 he led it. His great work was pressing the Russian government to better the Jews' legal standing.

He advised official commissions on the Jewish question in 1870 and 1887. He chaired the St. Petersburg Jewish congress of 1882. He led bodies that pushed Jews toward farming and trades. The baron title came in 1871 from the Grand Duke of Hesse-Darmstadt. His seventieth birthday was marked across Europe and in New York.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hai-ben-nahshon: Hai ben Nahshon was gaon of Sura from 889 to 896 and president of the school of Nehardea. His father Nahshon and his grandfather Zadok were geonim before him. A Vatican manuscript makes him the author of views on many Talmudic tractates. He is known here chiefly for one stand: he protested against the reciting of "Kol Nidre." The entry rests on the sources listed in its bibliography and adds no dates for his birth or death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hammurabi-7150:
Hammurabi was king of Shinar, sixth king of Babylon's first dynasty, and perhaps the Amraphel of Genesis xiv. 9. He founded the united Babylonian empire. By beating Rim-Sin of Larsa he joined the northern and southern kingdoms and set the capital at Babylon. Later Babylonians looked back on his age as a golden age. The entry gives his reign as 2267 to 2213.

He dug a great canal, named "Hammurabi Is the Blessing of the People," and enriched temples at Ur, Larsa, Sippar, Babylon, and Borsippa. His lasting monument is his code of laws, found at Susa in 1901-02 on a black diorite block 2.25 meters high. A relief shows the sun-god Samas teaching him the law. The entry sets his rules of retaliation and payment beside the laws of Moses, case by case.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-harden-maximili: Maximilian Harden was a German author born at Berlin on Oct. 20, 1861. He wrote political and social pieces for papers such as the "Nation" and the "Frankfurter Zeitung." Many appeared under the pen name "Apostata" and were later gathered into a book. In 1892 he founded the "Zukunft," a leading German journal that he still edited in 1903. The entry also notes his arrest on a charge of lese-majesty, and that his birth name was Witkowski.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hemerdinger-mic: Michel Hemerdinger, born at Colmar in Alsace on May 1, 1809, was a French jurist. He took a letters degree at Strasburg, then entered the rabbinical school at Metz. In 1830 he went to Paris to read law and joined the bar in 1833. He served the courts, led the attorneys' society, and joined the Central Jewish Consistory in 1845. In 1848 he acted as prosecutor and as a special envoy to settle disputes among Alsace Jews. From 1870 to 1879 he was a justice of the peace in Paris.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hessberg-albert: Albert Hessberg, born at Albany, New York, on Dec. 13, 1856, was an American lawyer. He studied law in the office of Rufus W. Peckham and later became his partner. He served as assistant corporation counsel from 1883 to 1886. In 1887 he helped revise Albany's laws and ordinances. Elected recorder in 1888, he served until 1896. The entry also lists posts with a Jewish home, a hospital, a railway, and the state bar group, where he was treasurer for ten years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-honigsmann-oswa:
Oswald Hönigsmann, born in Rzeszow, Austrian Galicia, on Dec. 2, 1824, was an Austrian deputy. Educated at Lemberg, he graduated as a doctor of law there. His democratic leanings delayed his entry to the Lemberg bar for several years. He sat on city and communal councils.

Hönigsmann defended a later minister accused over the Polish rising of 1863. He represented Brody in the Galician Diet. On Oct. 8, 1868, he gave a strong speech for Jewish emancipation that helped win the day. In 1872 he settled in Vienna. After a hard campaign in 1873, Galician voters sent him to the Austrian Parliament. He died on Oct. 24, 1880.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hurwitz-lazar-l: Lazar Lipman Hurwitz was a Russian scholar born in 1815 who died at Wilna on October 21, 1852. He taught privately at Wilna for years, then taught in a public school at Riga. The government later made him head master of the Wilna rabbinical school. With Fuenn he issued a journal on Jewish history, letters, and Bible study. Its numbers appeared in 1841 and 1844. His own works treat the book of Job and the history of ancient Jewish poetry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-idi-8050: Idi is the name of several Babylonian teachers who lived from the middle of the second century to the middle of the fifth. The entry is a note on the name itself. In the Talmud Idi is sometimes swapped with Ada. The swap follows a shift in speech between eastern and western Syriac. The same shift pairs Abba with Iba, Ami with Imi, Asi with Isi, and Hasda with Hisda. No deeds or sayings of any single Idi are given here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-b-abba-ma:
Isaac ben Abba Mari, French codifier, was born in Provence about 1122 and died after 1193, perhaps at Marseilles. His father, a leading rabbinical authority, was his teacher. He began writing at seventeen with rules on slaughtering and on zizit. His great work, the "'Ittur," occupied him about twenty-three years, from 1170 to 1193, and covers nearly the whole code of law in three parts.

The "'Ittur" became a classic of French rabbinical literature. Isaac knew both Talmuds as almost no one else of his time did, and he criticized even the Geonim and Alfasi freely. After the "Tur" spread, the work fell into disuse until Joseph Caro drew on it for his "Bet Yosef."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ish-bosheth-lit:
Ish-bosheth was the fourth and youngest son of Saul and, as the last male of the direct line, his lawful successor. His first name was Esh-baal. The entry explains that later religious feeling objected to the ba'al element, so scribes swapped in bosheth, a word of contempt. Under his uncle Abner's guard he became king at Mahanaim, east of the Jordan, safe from the Philistines.

Abner's skill won him every tribe west of the Jordan except Judah, and he is credited with a two-year reign. David's power grew against the house of Saul all the while. Ish-bosheth then accused Abner of intrigue with Rizpah, Saul's concubine, and lost his protector. After Abner's murder, two captains, Baanah and Rechab, killed Ish-bosheth in his bed and carried his head to David. David, far from rewarding them, put both men to a shameful death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-itzig-sometimes:
Itzig is the name of a wealthy German family that did much for modern culture among the Jews in the eighteenth century. Its center here is Daniel Itzig, a Berlin banker born in 1722 who died on May 21, 1799. He headed Prussia's Jewish communities from 1764 to 1799. His firm, Itzig, Ephraim & Son, banked Frederick the Great through his wars. The king made him mint-master in 1756 and again in 1758, a rare opening for a Jew.

In 1797 he became court banker under Frederick William II. Named a general delegate to the royal commission on Jewish grievances, he and his son-in-law David Friedländer spoke out boldly. They laid bare the cruel laws of Frederick's reign and refused the small reforms on offer. The family won equal rights with Christians. Leah Itzig, the entry adds, married Abraham Mendelssohn and became Felix Mendelssohn Bartholdy's mother.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-of-orlean:
Jacob of Orleans was a French tosafist who died a martyr in London on Sept. 3, 1189. He was among the most distinguished pupils of Rabbenu Tam, so much so that he is often called by his teacher's name. He was still at Orleans in 1171. Later he went to London, probably answering a call to teach there. He was killed in the anti-Jewish riots at the coronation of Richard I.

His tosafot are quoted across many tractates, from Berakot to Zebahim. He also glossed the Pentateuch, filling his notes with number readings, gematriot. Those glosses sit inside Isaac ben Judah ha-Levi's "Pa'aneah Raza." Gross holds that Jacob also wrote the tosafot to Rashi's Pentateuch commentary that went out under Rabbenu Tam's name. Few English Jews of his century left a larger trace in French learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jonah-8750:
Jonah was a prophet in the days of Jeroboam the Second, a son of Amittai of Gath-hepher. He stands as a real man of history, the entry argues, because Second Kings credits him with a word from God on how far that king would restore the northern kingdom's borders. With him the line of prophets that began with Elijah may have closed, just before Amos opened a new, writing line.

The book that bears Jonah's name does not prove to be his own writing. It tells his story from outside, as the Books of Kings tell of Elijah and Elisha. The entry holds that its Jonah is the same man as the Jonah of Kings, against a recent claim that split them in two, a claim its own maker later took back.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-ben-joha: Joseph ben Johanan was a French rabbi of the fourteenth century, a native of Treves. He seems to have been the first to take Treves as a family name, and his learning earned him the title the Great. He moved to France in 1306. By 1343 he was rabbi of Marseilles, where he stood out in a ruling on marriage law. His wife was also deeply learned in the Talmud, and one of her rulings has been kept. As a widow in Paris in 1363, she was excused from wearing the Jewish badge.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judo-greek-and-:
Judaeo-Greek and Judaeo-Italian are labels for the Greek and Italian dialects spoken and written by Jews. The Greek of Balkan Jews hardly differs from their neighbors' speech, the entry says. The Italian side means the Venetian and Apulian dialects. Corfu stands as the meeting point of the two worlds.

Greek-speaking Jewish towns are listed across the Balkans, from Constantinople and Salonica to Crete. For those Jews, parts of the Bible were rendered into modern Greek, a Pentateuch at Constantinople in 1547 among them. The entry traces mixed speech forms, such as Hebrew plurals bent to Italian sound laws. It closes with a map in words of which tongue Jews speak in each town today.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kalisch-david-9:
David Kalisch, born at Breslau on Feb. 23, 1820, became the leading German farce writer of his day. He died at Berlin on Aug. 21, 1872. His father died when the boy was seven. The family was left without support. So young Kalisch went to work for a dealer in small wares. Later he ran a branch shop at Ratibor. A move to Paris in 1844 put him among poets and socialists. At Leipsic he began writing farces.

Settled in Berlin from 1846, Kalisch still worked in trade while his stage pieces caught on. After a breakthrough hit in 1847, the big comedy houses of Germany staged little else for years. In 1848 he founded the comic paper "Kladderadatsch," whose stock figures became proverbial. The entry closes by listing his printed farces and his celebrated song verses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kawwanah-plural:
Kawwanah is a Hebrew word whose broad sense is devotion. In the plural, kawwanot, cabalists use it for the ideas hidden in letters and words of prayer. Some prayer books print these notes in the margin. Others set them in the text itself. They are traced in the main to Rabbi Isaac Luria, of the sixteenth century.

The entry also treats kawwanah as intent in doing a command. A question runs through the sources. If a man hears the shofar by chance, with no thought of the command, has he met the law? Talmudic voices split on the point. All agree that intent is to be sought. So a set form of words took hold. Before a blessing, a man declares himself ready to do the command.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kishinef-kishin:
Kishinef, capital of the government of Bessarabia, had 147,962 people in 1904. About 50,000 of them were Jews. The entry describes Jews as central to the city's trade. They handled much of its commerce in grain, wine, and tobacco. It counts 6,837 Jewish artisans, 2,115 of them masters. Many Jews worked as day-laborers, in vineyards, and in tobacco growing. Jewish poverty was growing year by year.

The entry then gives a long account of the riots of April 19-20, 1903. In them 47 Jews were killed and hundreds injured. Seven hundred houses were destroyed, and 600 stores were pillaged. Some 2,000 families were utterly ruined. The entry blames years of incitement by the paper "Bessarabetz." It also blames officials who let the riots run their course. The trials that followed ended mostly in light sentences.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kuna-9550:
Kuna is the Polish name for the pillory, a tool of shame and pain used by Polish and Lithuanian Jews in the eighteenth century. They seem to have taken it from Christian neighbors. It stood in a corner of the ḳahal office by the synagogue. The offender was placed in it before morning or evening service. Each worshiper could spit at, beat, and insult the person held there.

Three cases show the tool at work. In 1770 a freethinker at Wilna got forty lashes, then the kuna, then banishment from town. In 1772 elders refused a wish to place a Ḥasidic man in it and used lashes and a ban instead. In 1782 at Minsk, men who charged elders with misuse of funds were put in the kuna.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lasker-emanuel-:
Emanuel Lasker, chess champion of the world, was born on Dec. 24, 1868, at Berlinchen in Germany. He studied at Berlin, Göttingen, and Heidelberg and took a doctorate at Erlangen. First prizes at Breslau in 1889 and in England in 1892 built his name. In 1893 he won every game against thirteen leading players in New York.

The world title came in 1894, when Lasker beat Steinitz at New York by 10 games to 5. A Moscow return match in 1896 ended 10 wins to 2 losses. First prizes at St. Petersburg, Nuremberg, London, and Paris followed. The entry also credits him as a mathematician of ability with papers on curved lines and measures.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lentils-hebr-ad:
Lentils are edible seeds first named in the Old Testament story of Jacob and Esau. Jacob gave Esau bread and lentil stew for his birthright, in Genesis chapter twenty-five. Lentils also appear among the food Barzillai brought to David in exile. In hard times, Ezekiel shows them ground with other grains into bread.

De Candolle held that the lentil came first from western Asia. The red kind was prized most, and the lentils of Pelusium won fame in Egypt. In Talmudic times lentils were a staple food in Palestine and even a feast-day dish. The rabbis read the round, mouthless seed as a fit dish for mourners.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levin-moritz-98: Moritz Levin, a German rabbi, was born in 1843 at Wongrowitz, Posen. He studied at the University of Berlin and trained for the rabbinate with private teachers. He served a short time as rabbi at Zurich. In 1872 he took a like post at Nuremberg. Since 1884 he has been preacher of the Reform congregation in Berlin. His books include a prayer book in two volumes, texts on Bible history and Jewish history, and plays and studies on Iberia and Bar Kochba. He also wrote a festschrift for the Berlin Reform congregation in 1895.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-libya-9950:
Libya is a district in the north of Africa. The ancients used the name loosely, the entry says. At times it meant all of north Africa except Egypt. At times it meant one province west of Egypt. Josephus says Libya was founded by Phut, and another tale links its name to a hero from Egypt.

The Bible data are firmer. Libyans marched in Shishak's army and fought against King Asa. In the Greco-Roman age Libya matched Cyrene and its land. Jews lived there, and Augustus granted them rights. The Jewish war of the year 70 had an echo in Libya. Its Jews also joined the revolts under Trajan and Hadrian.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-loans-jacob-ben: Jacob ben Jehiel Loans was physician to the German emperor Frederick III and Hebrew teacher of Johann Reuchlin. He died at Linz about 1506 after long, faithful service to the emperor, who knighted him. Reuchlin met him at Linz in 1492, when Reuchlin had been sent to the court. Loans became his first teacher in Hebrew grammar. Reuchlin praised him warmly in print as a learned and kind teacher. One scholar thinks Reuchlin used Loans as the model for a Jewish scholar in a later book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowenstein-bern:
Bernhard Löwenstein (1821–1889) was an Austrian rabbi born at Meseritz, in the province of Posen, and he is profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Gotthard Deutsch. Recommended by Ludwig Philippson, he was elected preacher at Szent Miklos in Hungary in 1845. There he became known as a pioneer of the modern synagogue service in Hungary.

In 1857 Löwenstein left Szent Miklos for the rabbinate of Butschowitz in Moravia, and soon afterward he was called as rabbi to Lemberg, where he died. The article describes him as an impressive preacher and a tireless communal worker who was twice decorated by the Emperor of Austria. It also notes his sermons and a volume of poems, “Jüdische Klänge,” published at Brünn in 1862, making the entry a useful short record of a reforming rabbi’s career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mandel-paul-103:
Paul Mandel, a Hungarian jurist and deputy, receives an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Nyirbator on January 6, 1839, he studied law at Budapest and Vienna. In 1875 his native city elected him to the Hungarian Parliament. He was still holding that seat in 1904.

The article follows his work inside the legislature. He joined the law committee in 1881 and helped frame laws on guardianship and copyright. The office of royal notary public also bears his hand. His speeches won wide attention more than once. In 1878 he spoke against capital punishment. In 1884 he argued for religious freedom, and in 1885 against the anti-Semites. The short entry preserves a lawyer who used a long parliamentary career to defend civil and religious liberty in Hungary.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marx-david-1045:
David Marx was chief rabbi of Bordeaux. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. He was born at Landau, in Bavaria, in 1807. He trained at the rabbinical school at Metz and led a Jewish school at Nancy. Bordeaux chose him as chief rabbi in June 1837, ahead of the usual age for the office, and he died in February 1864.

The entry describes a reforming and much-loved rabbi. In 1841 he proposed bringing confirmation to Bordeaux, when the rite still looked like a dangerous novelty. He founded a nursery and an infirmary. He also stepped in for Jewish children kidnapped by Catholic proselytizers. Napoleon III gave him the Legion of Honor in 1852, and at his funeral the cardinal archbishop ordered every church bell in Bordeaux tolled.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-media-latin-med:
Media, the ancient land south and west of the Caspian Sea, is surveyed for its place in Jewish history in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906 by Richard Gottheil and A. V. W. Jackson. Its territory matches roughly modern Azerbaijan and the Persian districts toward Kurdistan. Scripture names the Medes more than a dozen times: Madai son of Japheth stands as their ancestor, and Shalmaneser planted the exiles of Samaria in Median cities.

Other threads follow. The "laws of the Medes and Persians" became a byword for rules that cannot be changed. Isaiah foresaw Media helping to overthrow Babylon. At Ecbatana, Media's capital, the scroll of Cyrus's decree for rebuilding the Temple was found, and the Median city Rhages carries much of the story of Tobit. The article then turns to Greek accounts of Median antiquity, beginning with fragments of Berosus and Ctesias.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-megiddo-once-me:
Megiddo was the fortress town of the plain of Esdraelon. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn survey it in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. It was the capital of a Canaanite king beaten by Joshua and was assigned to Manasseh, though its people were taxed rather than expelled. Solomon restored its ancient fortifications, and one of his twelve provision officers drew supplies from it. Kings died there: Ahaziah died fleeing Jehu, though Chronicles tells the story differently, as the article notes.

The great day of the city was its worst. At Megiddo, Pharaoh Nechoh met King Josiah in battle, and Josiah was killed. The “mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddon” in Zechariah is read as its echo. Herodotus records the same fight under a garbled name. The article closes by weighing the rival identifications of the site, Al-Lajjun among them, the choice of Robinson.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-zion-be:
Menahem Zion ben Solomon, generally called Menahem Ziyyon, was a Polish rabbi and preacher. He died at Altona in 1681. Herman Rosenthal and M. Seligsohn give him a brief notice in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He served first as rabbi of Vladislav. Vladislav lay in the government of Suwalki in Russian Poland. Afterward he served as dayyan, or judge, at Cracow.

His one book is the "Nehamot Ziyyon," Consolations of Zion. It is a collection of twenty-two sermons. It was printed at Frankfort-on-the-Main in 1677. That was four years before his death. The entry rests on Wolf's Bibliotheca Hebræa. It rests on Steinschneider's Bodleian catalogue too. It records nothing else of him. There are two posts and one volume of preaching. There is a death far from both his congregations, in the community at Altona.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-arthur-10:
Arthur Meyer, born at Havre in 1846, became one of the most powerful French journalists of his generation, as a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman records. As a young man in Paris he bought and edited the Revue de Paris, though it soon folded. He then reported for nearly twenty years for Le Gaulois and the Paris Journal.

In 1868 Meyer became part owner of Le Gaulois and made it the voice of the Bonapartists. After 1879 he bought the Paris Journal, Le Gaulois, and the Clairon, merging all three under the Gaulois name as the chief organ of the Clerical-Monarchic party. The entry ends on a sharp note: Meyer was one of the most vehement opponents of Captain Dreyfus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mines-and-minin:
Mines and mining barely existed in ancient Israel, and a Jewish Encyclopedia article by Emil G. Hirsch and Wilhelm Nowack, published in 1906, starts by saying so. Deuteronomy's hills that yield iron and brass probably mean stones hard as iron, the writers argue. Only surface iron ore and old copper-works in the Lebanon offer real evidence nearby.

Real mining knowledge shows up instead in the book of Job, chapter twenty-eight, whose author knew shafts that twist after the vein and lamps worn on miners' foreheads. The article matches verse to verse against Diodorus's account of Egyptian mines, where fire-setting cracked the rock. Its picture is of Israelites who knew mining as neighbors practiced it, not as an industry of their own.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-monotheism-1095:
Monotheism, the belief in one God, gets a careful Jewish Encyclopedia article from Joseph Jacobs and David Philipson in 1906, beginning by refusing an easy compliment. Renan had called the monotheistic instinct a Semitic trait; later research, the writers say, will not bear it out. Robertson Smith traced Semitic religion's ethical turn instead to its alliance with monarchy.

The Hebrews alone among Semitic peoples reached pure monotheism, and they reached it slowly — through the prophets' teaching, over centuries, before every trace of idolatry disappeared even among them. Hebrew tradition roots the belief in Abraham's religious awakening, and the article follows the legends that grew around that beginning. A theological entry that insists on history rather than essence.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-of-smolen:
Moses of Smolensk was a Russian engraver known from a single document of 1284. Herman Rosenthal and George D. Rosenthal wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. The document, published by Professor Kunik, records a court decision in a suit about a bell. Under the signature of Duke Feodor of Smolensk it adds: Moses, engraver of Feodor, made this seal.

The document never calls Moses a Jew, and the entry argues the point. The name Moses was not in use among Russian Christians of that time. The Russians of the day also knew nothing of engraving seals and coins. On those two grounds the scholars conclude that the duke's seal maker was a Jew, a lone craftsman at a Russian court.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-myers-walter-11:
