Walter Myers was an English physician and toxicologist born at Birmingham in 1871. Joseph Jacobs wrote his short Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He studied at Cambridge and at St. Thomas' Hospital, taking his medical degree in 1897. He then worked under Ziegler at Freiburg, Koch at Berlin, and Ehrlich at Frankfort.

Myers translated Ehrlich's work on the blood and won a Cambridge scholarship for research in pathology. With the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine he sailed to Brazil to study the causes of yellow fever. There he caught the disease himself and died at Para in January 1901. The entry calls him a martyr to science.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-elias-sa:
Elias Salomon Nathan was a German doctor with a second life in letters. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Eutin about 1806. He took his medical degree at Kiel in 1830. After a Polish campaign, he settled in Hamburg as a doctor.

Nathan died at Hamburg on July 5, 1862. Beside medicine, he gave his time to Jewish learning. Under the pen name Essenna, he translated a French history. Salvador's book on Moses and the Hebrew people became three German volumes. G. Riesser wrote the introduction for that edition. Nathan also published thoughts from a Jew's diary in 1837.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-netherlands-114:
The Netherlands became a great refuge for persecuted Jews. Joseph Jacobs and E. Slijper wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews appear in its provinces well before Holland itself. Nimeguen, its oldest settlement, had Jews by 1404. A cemetery came in 1382, a synagogue by 1426.

Utrecht expelled its Jews in 1444 for good. Till 1789 no Jew might sleep a night there. Spain's rule brought edicts against Jews and lax Christians. Freedom came with independence from Spain in 1581. Maranos reached Amsterdam in 1593, turned away elsewhere. Their trade tied Holland to Morocco and Brazil. Six hundred Jews sailed for Brazil in 1642. Amsterdam's Jewish quarter grew, but it was no forced ghetto.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ocana-11650:
Ocaña was a town in Castile, in Spain. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A Jewish group lived there from an early date. At first its members held full rights in the town. In time the Christian folk began to curb those rights.

King Fernando the Fourth told the town board to stop. He said the Jews must keep the rights past kings gave them. A false charge of child murder was laid on them there. A Christian had killed a boy and hid the body. He put it in a Jewish house to cast blame. The plot failed, and the truth came out. In 1391 many Jews were killed at Ocaña. Others were forced to take baptism against their will.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oral-law-11750:
The Oral Law is the body of laws and teachings said to have been given to Moses by word of mouth, alongside the written Torah. Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stands next to the written law of Moses. Rabbis teach that God gave both to Moses. The written part is the five books of Moses.

The oral part held laws, rules, and plain sense of texts. Moses was told not to write this part down. He was to pass it on by mouth to the folk. In a wide sense it holds much more than that. It holds all sense drawn from the written Torah by scribes. It holds the rules those scribes set in place too. So it takes in the Mishnah and the Tosefta. It takes in the law tracts of the Midrash as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paggi-angelo-11:
Angelo Paggi was an Italian scholar of the Hebrew tongue. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Sienna on May 4, 1789. He died at Florence on June 7, 1867. Leon Vita Monseles trained him in Hebrew in his youth.

Angelo read the books of Italy and of Rome as well. For a short time he worked in trade for his bread. He soon left trade to open a school of his own. In that school he brought in a clear, sound way to teach. From 1836 to 1846 he led the Jewish school at Florence. Ill health then forced him to give up that post. He still wrote and taught in private for years. He wrote grammars of Hebrew and of the Chaldee tongue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paul-de-burgos-:
Paul de Burgos was born Solomon ha-Levi, the leading Jew of Burgos. He was born about 1351 and died in 1435. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He served as rabbi of Burgos before his baptism.

In 1390 he was baptized and took the name Paul de Santa Maria. His wife Joanna refused and stayed in her faith. Paul rose fast in the Church and the court. He became Bishop of Cartagena, then Archbishop of Burgos. He also turned hard against his former people. As chancellor he drafted an edict that cut Jewish rights.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pharisees-arama:
The Pharisees were the popular religious party of the Second Temple age. Kaufmann Kohler wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They stood against the priestly Sadducees. Their name means those who separate themselves for holiness. They spoke for the heart of the Jewish people.

Pharisees kept the Law as the scribes read it. Tradition, not the letter alone, guided their reading. They formed a brotherhood with strict entry pledges. Members swore purity, full tithes, and care for others' goods. The New Testament paints them with hostile strokes. Josephus, writing for Romans, softens them into philosophers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pillar-12150:
The English word pillar covers several Hebrew terms. The Executive Committee and J. F. McLaughlin wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. One term means the door-posts of a gate. The chief term, mazebah, means a standing stone. Excavators found eight such stones in a row at Gezer.

Such stones marked graves, like Rachel's tomb stone. They witnessed treaties and marked the borders of land. Some served as rough altars for poured offerings. Moses set twelve pillars at Sinai for the tribes. Baal shrines and Tyre had pillars as well. Later law codes banned them as idolatry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pollak-ludwig-1:
Ludwig Pollak was an Austrian scholar of old art, born at Prague in 1868. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He took his doctorate at Vienna in 1893. The Austrian state then sent him for a year to Italy and Greece. He settled in Rome and lived there from that time.

Pollak made a long study tour in 1900. It took him through Egypt, Syria, and Asia Minor. In 1898 he joined the German institutes for old art as a member. His book of 1900 treats two vases from one Greek workshop. His book of 1903 lists classical gold work owned by a Russian envoy. Both books came out at Leipsic.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-press-moses-ale: Moses Alexandrovich Press was a Russian engineer born in 1861. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He trained at the Institute of Technology in St. Petersburg. He wrote for a journal on roads and travel there. He wrote for journals of the city's engineers as well. At his death in 1901 he was at work on a book. It treated the share of Jews in trades in western Russia. He died at Sankt Blasien that year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-purims-special-:
Special Purims are local feasts kept by single towns or families. Gotthard Deutsch, M. Franco, and Henry Malter wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Each marks a rescue from some past danger. The danger may have threatened a whole town. It may have threatened one family alone. The feast copies the great Purim in its form.

On the set day a scroll is read aloud. It tells the tale of the event in full. The reading takes place in the synagogue or at home. Set prayers are said for the day as well. Some of these days join fasting with feasting. The article lists known cases town by town and house by house.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ramathaim-zophi:
Ramathaim-Zophim is named as Samuel's birthplace in First Samuel. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The article warns that the present text is corrupt. The usual reading breaks Hebrew usage, it argues.

The writers propose reading the verse in a different way. A man of Ramathaim was a Zophite of Mount Ephraim. Zuph was a district south of Ephraim, near Benjamin. No clear details fix the town's exact site. Still, Samuel's home city lay in that district. The short entry is a lesson in careful Bible reading. One small wording change shifts the whole sense.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rehumai-iii-126: Rehumai III was one of the early saboraim. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this short Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He died in 505, in the month of Nisan. In Erubin 11a he appears with his peer R. Jose. Each man explains an earlier authority's words differently. Sherira, Halevy, and Grätz are the cited sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ries-elias-elka:
Elias Elkan Ries was an American electrical engineer born on January 16, 1862. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Randegg in Baden, Germany. His parents brought him to America at age three.

The article says he schooled in Baltimore and New York. He also attended lectures at Johns Hopkins University. In 1876 he became a telegraph operator. He worked for the Edison Company and other firms. Back in Baltimore he developed his own inventions. He founded the Ries Electric Specialty Company in 1891. Since 1896 he has lived in New York City. His patents number about one hundred fifty. They cover telephones, lamps, rail welding, and motor controllers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenfeld-morri:
Morris Rosenfeld was a Yiddish poet born at Boksha, in Russian Poland, on December 28, 1862. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He worked as a tailor in New York and London, and cut diamonds in Amsterdam.

Rosenfeld settled in New York in 1886 and joined the staffs of Jewish papers. He later edited the New Yorker Morgenblatt and spoke at the Fourth Zionist Congress. His first book, Die Glocke, held revolutionary poems he later tried to destroy. Das Lieder Buch, from 1897, made his name in many lands. Leo Wiener's English version, Songs from the Ghetto, appeared in Boston in 1899.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saadia-12950:
Saadia, without more, names a Bible commentator whose land and age stay uncertain. Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Rapoport first showed he is not the famous Saadia Gaon.

The Daniel commentary long ascribed to the Gaon belongs to this Saadia instead. Matthews held that the Ezra and Nehemiah commentary is his as well. Saadia knew both Talmuds and the Targum in great depth. He quotes earlier interpreters under one general term, seldom by name. His readings often rest on swapping letters of like sound or class.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salvador-joseph:
Joseph Salvador, also Joseph Jeshurun Rodrigues, was an English philanthropist flourishing about 1753. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His family came from Holland with money invested in commerce.

Salvador ranked among the merchant princes of England's Jews in his day. His firm negotiated loans for the British government after Sampson Gideon's death. He was elected a director of the Dutch East India Company, a first for a Jew. He presided over London's Portuguese congregation and its deputies' committee. Lisbon earthquake losses and the company's failure ruined him late in life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schapiro-moses-:
Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Moses ben Phinehas Schapiro. He was a Russian rabbi and printer. Schapiro was born probably at Koretz, in Volhynia, about 1758. He died at Slavuta in 1838. His father was the Ḥasidic rabbi Phinehas of Koretz. Moses became rabbi of Slavuta in 1808.

That year Schapiro began a new edition of the Talmud. It far surpassed earlier editions and sold out fast. Rival printers at Kopys broke the rabbis' twenty-five-year ban to compete. Schapiro answered with a second edition from 1817 to 1822. A bitter feud with the Romm press of Wilna followed. His sons began a third edition at Slavuta. Then a bookbinder's suicide in their shop brought a murder charge. After a harsh trial the sons were flogged and sent to Siberia. The press was closed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-scopus-13350:
Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Scopus. Scopus is a height seven stadia north of Jerusalem. Tradition says the high priest welcomed Alexander the Great there. Josephus gives its name as Saphein, rendered in Greek as Skopos. The Greek word means prospect. From that height one can see Jerusalem and the Temple.

The Talmud places the Alexander meeting at Antipatris instead. Grätz blamed a confusion between similar names. The article finds Josephus more plausible. Scopus later hosted Roman camps in the war on Rome. Cestius Gallus camped there first. Titus then leveled the ground from Scopus toward the city. In Jewish law Scopus counts as a boundary of Jerusalem. In 1889 diggers found a rock-cut canal at the hill's foot. It may be the Temple's water conduit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-set-off-sometim:
Set-off, sometimes called a counter-claim, lets a defendant answer a claim with one of his own. Wilhelm Bacher and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Roman law called the idea compensatio. The goal is one judgment that settles both sides at once.

Talmudic law allows the idea, though it gives it no name. When two men beat each other, damages can cancel out. The court then awards only the difference. Beyond that case, the entry finds just hints in the Talmud. One passage in Bava Kamma is the main text later writers cite. Readers see a fair legal tool traced through sparse early sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shemaiah-13550:
Shemaiah was a prophet who served during the reign of King Rehoboam. Emil G. Hirsch and Isaac Broydé wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. God sent him to stop Rehoboam from making war. The northern tribes had just revolted and formed their own kingdom.

Shemaiah told the king that split was God's own will. Israel would stand as a separate state, he said. Later, Egypt's King Shishak invaded Judah and besieged Jerusalem. Shemaiah spoke again when the princes humbled themselves. God would not pour out wrath through Shishak, he promised. Twice this prophet's words spared Jerusalem, the entry shows. Once they stopped a civil war, and once they softened an invasion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simon-lady-rach:
Lady Rachel Simon was an English author born in London on August 1, 1823. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. She was the daughter of Simeon K Salaman and Alice Cowen. Her home drew many noted guests. In 1843 she married John Simon.

From age seventeen she kept a diary called Records and Reflections. In 1893 she published fifty years of it, from 1840 to 1890. She also wrote a work on the Psalms called Beside the Still Waters. The entry adds a note on her son Oswald John Simon. He was a communal worker and author in his own right.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-abr:
Solomon ben Abraham ben Jehiel was an Italian rabbi at Rome. Isidore Singer and M Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He flourished in the eleventh century there. He was nephew of Nathan ben Jehiel, author of the Aruk. A generation after Nathan's death he joined the rabbinate of Rome.

For a time Solomon presided over that rabbinate himself. He also headed the high school founded by Nathan. His authority shows in the questions put to him by others. He explained why the Eighteen Benedictions are not said on Sabbaths. He also answered questions from Menahem ben Solomon repeatedly. One responsum from Rome to Paris bears his signature first.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sperling-jacob-:
Jacob Hirsch Sperling was an Austrian teacher of religion at Lemberg. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Lemberg in 1837. He taught at the Jewish school and the German gymnasium there. He backed the Haskalah movement in Galicia with energy.

Sperling was also a gifted Neo-Hebrew poet of his time. He wrote for many Hebrew and German Jewish periodicals. He coedited the Jüdische Presse and the Neuzeit in Lemberg. He founded the societies Ahawah we-Haskalah and Shomer Yisrael there. His poems include a life of Rapoport in verse. He also wrote an epic poem in five cantos, Horodot.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stier-josef-140:
Josef Stier was a Hungarian rabbi born on April 12, 1844. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Neustadt-on-the-Waag in Hungary. He studied at Presburg, Vienna, and Breslau. He earned his doctorate in 1869 and ordination in 1872.

In 1872 Stier became chief rabbi at Stein-am-Anger in Hungary. He also taught Jewish religion at the local gymnasium. Later he moved to Berlin for a rabbinate. He has held that Berlin post since 1890. His books include a work on Ferenc Deák from 1875. Others treat priests and prophets, and honor in the Bible. One 1896 book weighs theism against natural science. The entry lists a rabbi active in print and pulpit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sword-hereb-bar:
The sword was the standard blade weapon of ancient Israel. Emil G. Hirsch and Wilhelm Nowack wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Its Hebrew name is hereb, with barak as a poetic form. Men wore it at the hip on a belt. A sheath guarded the blade when at rest.

Some swords were double-edged for cutting and thrusting. Ehud's short dagger-like sword fills one famous story. He drove it, haft and all, into Eglon's belly. Blades were usually iron, rarely bronze, in Israel. Israelite swords likely matched Assyrian and Egyptian shapes. Some ran straight, others curved like daggers. The Bible gives no full descriptions of types. The entry rebuilds the weapon from scattered verses and phrases.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tarnow-14250:
Tarnow is a town of Austrian Galicia with an old Jewish community. Isidore Singer and Ignaz Schipper wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. An organized community existed by the mid-1500s. The town belonged hereditarily to the lords of Tarnow. Jews lived under those lords' jurisdiction.

In 1637 a privilege placed Jews under castle protection. It let them trade on equal footing with citizens. Popular jealousy and magistrates killed that privilege in 1654. Plague, fires, and Swedish attacks then ruined the town. Its overlord restored the Jewish privilege in 1670. The town's survival required the Jews' return. A deal set Jews' share of town taxes at thirty percent. Later lords confirmed the privilege repeatedly. The entry shows rights traded against a town's needs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-texas-14350:
Jewish settlers in Texas, from republic days to statehood, fill this long article. Cyrus Adler and Henry Cohen wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia, published in 1906. Texas was an independent republic from 1836 to 1845. It joined the Union in 1845, left in 1861, and returned in 1870.

Samuel Isaacs arrived with Austin's first colonists in 1821. He earned 320 acres by serving the republic's army. Other pioneers traded, farmed, and held town office. Michael Seeligson became mayor of Galveston in 1853. Jewish soldiers fought at Goliad and the Alamo. One Jewish surgeon served in Sam Houston's army. The article names dozens of these early Texans.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-toronto-14450:
Toronto, capital of Ontario in Canada, had four organized Jewish congregations in 1905. Cyrus Adler and Clarence I. de Sola wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Holy Blossom was the oldest, begun in 1845. It organized formally in 1852 and dedicated a synagogue in 1857.

Goel Tsedek dated from 1880, and Shomerei Shabbas from 1891. Chevra Tillim followed in 1895. Smaller new congregations kept growing in importance. Aid work flourished alongside the synagogues. The city had benevolent societies, a burial society, and a Talmud Torah. Zionist groups numbered four, and a YMHA served the young. About 7,000 Jews lived among 207,971 residents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tushiyyah-lit-s:
Tushiyyah was a Warsaw publishing house founded in 1896 for Hebrew books. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Its name means sound knowledge in Hebrew. Though a private business, it worked like a publication society. Its aim was to spread new Hebrew literature widely.

Ben-Avigdor founded the house and served as first editor. Its program promised good and useful Hebrew books. Youth would gain knowledge, morality, and civilization from them. Scientific books in all branches were also planned. Novels, biographies, poems, and histories all appeared. Its textbooks taught Hebrew by modern methods to children. Authors like Frischman, Brainin, and Berdyczewski published with it. The house much encouraged young Hebrew talent.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vatke-johann-ka:
Johann Karl Wilhelm Vatke was a Christian scholar of the Hebrew Bible. Crawford Howell Toy wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Vatke was born in Saxony on March 14, 1806. He died in Berlin on April 19, 1882. He taught at the University of Berlin from 1830 onward.

Vatke's key book appeared in Berlin in 1835. It dealt with the religion of the Old Testament. On the Pentateuch, he took the boldest view of his day. He denied that Moses wrote any of it. He also treated Deuteronomy as the earliest of its books. Critics attacked him, yet his teaching shaped later scholars. He is counted a forerunner of Graf, Kuenen, and Wellhausen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wahl-moritz-cal:
Moritz Callmann Wahl was a German writer on language. He was born on March 28, 1829, at Sondershausen. Isidore Singer and W. Salzberger wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died on October 15, 1887. He studied Oriental languages at Leipsic. His teachers were Julius Fürst and H. L. Fleischer.

Wahl taught in England, then worked in business at Lyons. He finally settled at Erfurt. There he founded a business academy. His research focused on proverbs across languages. He wrote on proverbs in Hebrew and Aramaic writing. He also studied English proverbs before Shakespeare. Proverbs in Shakespeare's own plays drew a book as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weiss-wilhelm-1:
Wilhelm Weiss was an Austrian mathematician. He was born at Ridka, Bohemia, on February 3, 1859. Isidore Singer and Alexander Kisch wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died at Prague on June 18, 1904. His father, a village teacher, taught him first. He studied at Prague, Leipsic, and Erlangen.

Weiss took his doctorate in 1887. He taught math at Prague's German technical school. He climbed its ranks year by year. In 1900 he became a full professor there. From 1901 to 1902 he served as dean of engineering. The brief entry marks a steady academic rise.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wisdom-hebr-gre:
Wisdom, in Hebrew hokmah, joins insight with skill. Kaufmann Kohler wrote this long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Wisdom means grasping the nature of things deeply. It also means performing hard tasks with craft. The word is both a human and divine trait. Scripture traces all wisdom back to God.

God's spirit made Joseph wise before Pharaoh. It filled Bezalel with skill for the Tabernacle. Solomon's wisdom came as God's direct gift. The wise formed a class beside priests and prophets. Kings sought their counsel on hard matters. Wisdom grows by watching nature and history. It also grows by study and wise company. The entry surveys wisdom across Bible and rabbinic thought.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zeror-raphael-j:
Raphael Jedidiah Solomon Zeror (1681-1737) was an Algerian rabbi of note. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Algiers, he died in that same port town. He came of a house of great Talmud men of old.

His grandsire was chief rabbi of Algiers in his day. With the rabbis of his town he signed a ban writ. That writ was the ban on Nehemiah Hayyun of ill fame. He read world books with care all his life long. Logic, the frame of things, and earth lore drew him most. He gave time to verse craft in those years as well. He won fame as a deft healer of the sick in town. He ran a wide trade by sea and by land at once. His pupil bound his replies and notes as one book.
keyhoe-flying-saucers-are-real-1950:
Donald Keyhoe, a retired Marine Corps major, published The Flying Saucers Are Real in 1950. The book grew out of his hit article in True magazine the year before. It was the first major book of civilian UFO research and launched a movement.

Keyhoe gathers pilot reports, radar cases, and his talks with Air Force men. He argues the saucers are craft from other worlds and that the Air Force hides what it knows. His charges set the tone for decades of UFO writing: keen sightings, official silence, public doubt. Later UFO books followed the path Keyhoe cut here.
king-richard-ii-pg2250:
William Shakespeare's history play King Richard II follows a king who loses his crown. Richard rules England with weak judgment and heavy taxes. His cousin Bolingbroke returns from exile, gathers support, and forces him to give up the throne.

Alone in prison, Richard looks back on his fall. He breaks a mirror and says he has no name and no title left. A quiet garden scene adds a moral lesson about careless rule. Readers value the play for its rich verse and its sad picture of power lost. The play asks what a king is once his crown is gone. Its speeches give that question a sad, musical force.
long-lost-friend-hohman-1850:
John George Hohman, a German immigrant healer in Pennsylvania, first published The Long-Lost Friend in 1820. This edition of 1850 carried his collection of charms and cures through German America. The book became the classic grimoire of Pennsylvania Dutch pow-wow, the folk healing tradition of that region.

Its pages give words to say over burns, bleeding, toothache, and sick cattle. Bible verses, short prayers, and folk recipes stand side by side. Pow-wow practitioners treated the book as a license and a toolbox in one. Families kept copies for daily use across generations. Everyday magic for farm and family is here in its most durable American form, still consulted today.
mellon-ms-12-a-collection-of-alchemical-:
Mellon MS 12 is a paper manuscript of about 1450, held at Yale. The Beinecke Library in New Haven keeps the book today. Its texts are alchemical works ascribed to Ramon Llull, with extra matter.

The works came into English from French and Catalan forms. A later hand added leaves on thin paper in the 1500s. Wheels, tables, a tree of the art, flasks, and a furnace are drawn inside. Denis Duveen held the book once, and the Mellons gave it to Yale in 1965. Headings in red and slight pen work mark the text breaks. Such books show how the art passed from hand to hand.
mellon-ms-2-alchemical-miscellany-1350:
Mellon MS 2 is a parchment manuscript of about 1350. Yale's Beinecke Library holds the book, with 88 leaves. The record calls it the first such practical book in the Mellon set.

Its texts came in part from Arabic sources, with European adds. Works by Geber, Avicenna, and Rasis stand in the contents list. Richard de Fournival's work on the art stands there too. Three scribes wrote the book in a clear gothic hand, in Latin. Leaves from a German song book serve as its pastedowns. That reuse shows how old parchment was prized and kept.
mellon-ms-33-alchemical-miscellany-1550:
Mellon MS 33 is an English paper manuscript of about 1550. Yale's Beinecke Library holds the book, with 128 leaves. Brown calf covers it, though the back strip is now lost.

Most texts inside are alchemy turned into English by Robert Freelove. Jean de Meung's book on the mineral stone is one such work. The Radix Mundi, turned in 1550, stands in the list too. Khalid ibn Yazid's secrets of the philosophers close the named set. At least three scribes shared the work of this copy. Their hands shift from neat script to rougher forms as it goes.
mellon-ms-36-alchemical-miscellany-1550:
Mellon MS 36 is a paper manuscript from Italy, dated about 1550. Its maker wrote Lapis Philosophalis, the philosopher's stone, on its back. The parchment cover is home made, from a used deed sheet.

One Johannes Baptista F. compiled the book of Latin alchemy texts. The record calls his copies corrupt, as was common for such sets. Practical steps and poems in the vernacular stand among the texts. Small ink drawings of flasks, furnaces, and a Bain-Marie fill the front leaves. The book is worn and wormed, and loose in its cover. Its gear drawings still show the tools of the old art.
notes-and-queries-number-11-january-12-1:
Number eleven, dated Saturday, January 12, 1850, returns to Sir E. Dering's household book. E. Rimbault handles that note this time. Bayswater and its origin, Eva daughter of MacMurrough, and Billingsgate follow. Plagiarisms, or parallel passages, get a note on borrowed lines. Fly leaves yield a fourth set of notes.

Opinions on English historians reach Lord Clarendon in a second part. Miscellanies treat books by the yard, the thistle of Scotland, and humble pie. By hook or by crook, the origin of grog, and Dr Faustus all appear. Queries ask about catacombs and bone houses, and contradictions in Don Quixote. Colonel Blood's house also draws a question.
notes-and-queries-number-12-january-19-1:
Hudibras leads number twelve, dated Saturday, January 19, 1850, with a passage explained by E. F. Rimbault. The Field of the Brothers' Footsteps and the receipts of the Beggar's Opera follow as notes. Bolton Corney continues on books and authors, and Rimbault adds more notes on Cunningham's London. Sewerage in Etruria sits oddly among them.

R. Monckton Milnes asks about St Thomas of Lancaster, and J. R. Planché about the Black Prince's shield. M. A. Lower asks for the origin of the name Shylock. Minor queries hunt the origin of snob, of cannibal, and of the word poghele. Pictures in churches and flaying for sacrilege draw graver questions.
notes-and-queries-number-13-january-26-1:
Domingo Lomelyn, jester to Henry the Eighth, opens the notes in number thirteen, for Saturday, January 26, 1850. Edward Rimbault writes that piece. Marlowe and the old Taming of a Shrew, beetle mythology, and old painted glass follow. Churchwardens' accounts for St Margaret's, Westminster, give local colour.

Lord Braybrooke asks after Catherine Pegge, and J. P. Collier after William Basse and his poems. Minor queries touch a Christmas hymn, the circulation of the blood, and Lord Bacon's psalms. Luther and Erasmus reappear as a query. Answers in the miscellanies settle the etymology of muffins and the seal of Killigrew. Defoe also gets a word.
notes-and-queries-number-14-february-2-1:
Reprints of old books, by J. P. Collier, lead number fourteen, dated Saturday, February 2, 1850. Catacombs and bone houses get a note in answer to an earlier query. Lines attributed to Hudibras and fly leaf notes, in their fifth part, follow. The Pursuits of Literature closes the notes.

The Reverend J. Jebb sends nine queries at once, and Barryana gets one more. Minor queries chase Norman pedigrees, Dr Johnson's library, and the derivation of calamity. Replies settle the Field of Forty Footsteps and the meaning of pokership. The etymology of Armagh and matters of the Revels also come in. Gray's Elegy and Shylock fill the miscellanies.
notes-and-queries-number-15-february-9-1:
Wages in the seventeenth and nineteenth centuries open number fifteen, for Saturday, February 9, 1850. The Reverend L. B. Larking compares those wages. Marlowe and the old Taming of a Shrew return, from S. Hickson. Shakespeare's use of monosyllables gets a note from C. Forbes. Fly leaf notes reach part six.

William J. Thoms asks for folk lore, in the form of metrical charms. Allusions in the Homilies draw a second query. Minor queries touch Pope's translations of Horace, Arabic numerals, and dog Latin. The cuckoo as Welsh ambassador charms the list. Replies settle Selago and Samolus, and portraits of Luther and Erasmus.
notes-and-queries-number-16-february-16-:
Daniel Defoe and his ghost stories lead the notes in number sixteen, dated Saturday, February 16, 1850. Pet names follow, from the Reverend B. H. Kennedy. Lacedæmonian black broth gets a note, plus a hint to intending editors. Folk lore notes cover Easter eggs, buns, and a Gloucestershire custom.

C. H. Cooper asks about the White Hart Inn at Scole, and others about passages in Pope. Belvoir Castle draws a query of its own. Minor queries hunt French leave, Cromwell relics, and a Kentish ballad. A monumental brass and the symbolism of the fir cone appear. Replies settle Aelfric's colloquy and the origin of snob.
notes-and-queries-number-17-february-23-:
Alfred's Orosius opens number seventeen, for Saturday, February 23, 1850, in R. T. Hampson's hands. Folk lore follows: omens from cattle, a horse's head, and rush bearings. Bolton Corney's notes on authors and books reach a fifth part. Parallel passages, or plagiarisms, continue in a second part. St Antholin's gets a short note.

The Reverend Dr Maitland asks about college salting, a student custom. H. E. Strickland sends a few dodo queries, about the lost bird. Coleridge's Christabel and Byron's Lara share a query with a tablet to Napoleon. Replies give the etymology of Armagh and the poems of William Hasse. Beaver hats also earn a reply.
notes-and-queries-number-18-march-2-1850:
An unpublished letter of Horace Walpole leads number eighteen, dated Saturday, March 2, 1850. S. Hall presents that letter. Lady Arabella Stuart follows, from R. Cole, and W. Robson treats the name Martel. Only three notes fill the front of this number, fewer than usual.

Junius, the mystery letter writer, draws a query from J. Sudlow. A new edition of Dr Owen's works gets another. Minor queries chase a manuscript Book of Hours, Bess of Hardwick, and Cromwell's estates. Replies settle the origin of the Jew's harp and Arabic numerals. Chaucer's night charm and the Fraternity of Christian Doctrine appear among them.
notes-and-queries-number-19-march-9-1850:
Our Progress opens number nineteen, for Saturday, March 9, 1850, before the notes begin. The captivity of the Queen of Bruce leads those notes, from W. B. Rye. A note on Robert Herrick and the meaning of the word lærig follow. Folk lore fills a long run in this number.

St Valentine in Norwich, cook eels, and old charms head the folk list. Superstitions in the north of England and decking churches with yew follow. Welsh folk lore brings the Cron Annwn and a hag of the mist. William Basse, John Stowe, and an unpublished poem by Burns also appear. Ten queries on poets and poetry close the sampled contents.
notes-and-queries-number-20-march-16-185:
Alfred's Geography of Europe, handled by S. W. Singer, leads number twenty, dated Saturday, March 16, 1850. E. F. Rimbault writes on the first coffee houses in England. The True Tragedy of Richard the Third and a passage in Milton's L'Allegro follow. Folk lore notes treat the Merry Lwyd and deathbed superstition.

Rimbault also notes the use of beaver hats in England, and R. Cole prints extracts from old records. Queries ask about old songs once popular at Christ's Hospital. Watching the sepulchre draws another. Minor queries hunt cromlechs, the meaning of grummett, and the use of coffins. Replies settle a letter attributed to Sir Robert Walpole.
notes-and-queries-number-21-march-23-185:
Early statistics from a Kent chart open number twenty-one, for Saturday, March 23, 1850. A Latin tag, bis dat qui cito dat, gets a note on giving twice by giving fast. Parallel passages, errors corrected, and direct and indirect etymology follow. An error in Pope's Homer's Odyssey is pointed out.

Proverbial sayings and their origins fill a full note. The Reverend A. Gatty asks what a chapel is, and Rimbault who translated the Turkish Spy. Minor queries hunt smelling of the lamp and paying through the nose. Replies settle portraits of Ulrich of Hutten and a letter attributed to Walpole. Bolton Corney answers queries in a sixth set.
notes-and-queries-number-22-march-30-185:
Samuel Hickson writes on The Taming of the Shrew in number twenty-two, dated Saturday, March 30, 1850. Proverbial sayings and William Basse's poems continue from earlier numbers. Folk lore adds more about salting, a Norfolk weather proverb, and Irish medical charms. Dean Swift gets a note on Herodotus.

J. M. Gutch treats Herrick's Hesperides among the notes. Queries chase the Bristol riots, the Inquisition in Mexico, and the etymology of Dalston. Brown study and coal brandy also puzzle readers. Replies take up the dodo, from S. W. Singer, and watching the sepulchre. A poem by Sir E. Dyer is printed in reply.
notes-and-queries-number-23-april-6-1850:
R. T. Hampson opens number twenty-three, for Saturday, April 6, 1850, with the Periplus of Hanno. Pope Vindicated and The Supper of the Lorde follow as notes. Folk lore treats Palm Sunday wind, a curious symbolical custom, and the Wild Huntsman. Bolton Corney's notes on authors and books reach part six.

J. P. Collier asks about Nicholas Breton's Crossing of Proverbs. Rimbault asks about a sword called Curtana. George Munford asks if the Dombec is Alfred's Domesday. Minor queries chase Milton's pedigree and Wycliffite versions of the Scriptures. Replies settle the Arabic numerals and cipher, and the derivation of the word news.
notes-and-queries-number-24-april-13-185:
Skinner's Life of Monk, by W. D. Christie, leads the notes in number twenty-four, dated Saturday, April 13, 1850. Cunningham's lives of Whitgift and Cartwright follow. An unpublished letter of the Duke of Monmouth is printed. Rimbault writes on Lydgate and Coverdale, two early English authors.

Queries ask about the Speculum Exemplorum and the second Duke of Ormonde. C. Forbes asks about Quevedo and Spanish bull fights. Mayors get a query about their correct prefix. Minor queries chase an earwig called a coach bell, and Marylebone Gardens. Replies catch a blunder in Malone's Shakespeare and offer hints to intending editors.
notes-and-queries-number-25-april-20-185:
Our Further Progress opens number twenty-five, for Saturday, April 20, 1850. Roger Bacon follows, with hints for a new edition of his works. Craik's Romance of the Peerage gets a note, and Rimbault returns to Cunningham's London. Pope's revision of Spence is treated by W. S. Singer.

Folk lore offers a charm for toothache, Easter eggs, and a cure for hooping cough. The Duke of Monmouth's pocket book is described by C. Ross. Queries ask about Luther's translation of the New Testament. Minor queries chase buccaneers, travelling in 1590, and Locke's manuscripts. Replies settle the Scala Coeli and watching the sepulchre.
notes-and-queries-number-26-april-27-185:
Nicholas Breton opens number twenty-six, dated Saturday, April 27, 1850, in the Reverend T. Corser's hands. Rimbault adds notes on Cunningham's London and on the dodo, the latter from H. E. Strickland. The derivation of sterling and penny gets a note. Hanno's Periplus returns in S. W. Singer's treatment.

Folk lore covers cook eels and divination by Bible and key, plus a weather proverb. Rimbault asks when umbrellas were introduced into England. Minor queries chase the song of the bees and swords worn in public. The emblem and national motto of Ireland also puzzle a reader. Replies settle Gray's Alcaic ode and Sterne's Koran.
notes-and-queries-number-27-may-4-1850:
The Mosquito Country leads the notes in number twenty-seven, for Saturday, May 4, 1850. Notes on Bacon and Jeremy Taylor follow, then the Duke of Monmouth's correspondence. Peter Cunningham presents a poem by Parnell. Early English and early German literature are compared by S. Hickson.

Folk lore lists a charm for toothache, the evil eye, and a roasted mouse cure. The Anglo-Saxon word unlæd is weighed by Singer. Arabic numerals and Roman numerals each get notes, as does an anecdote of Charles the First. Queries ask about the words esquire and gentleman, and lines by Suckling. Replies take up early statistics.
notes-and-queries-number-28-may-11-1850:
Etymology of the word penniel leads number twenty-eight, dated Saturday, May 11, 1850. Rimbault continues his notes on Cunningham's London. An original letter of Peter Le Neve is printed by E. Hailstone. Folk lore treats superstitions of the middle counties and a rainbow in the morning. An error in Johnson's Life of Selden is caught.

Sir F. Madden asks about a Purvey of the Apocalypse and Bonner on the seven sacraments. Replies settle Luther's translation, through Singer, and lines on London dissenting ministers. Other replies explain coal brandy, howkey or horkey, and a frog he would a-wooing go. The symbolism of flowers also gets an answer.
notes-and-queries-number-29-may-18-1850:
Oliver Cromwell appears in number twenty-nine, for Saturday, May 18, 1850, as a feoffee of Parson's Charity at Ely. Dr Parr and Dr John Taylor share a note. Provincial words get a list of their own. Folk lore turns dark: deathbed superstition, May marriages, and throwing old shoes.

Sir Thomas Boleyn's spectre and Shuck, the dog fiend, haunt the folk list. Numismatic queries ask about coins, and Bolton Corney proposes a second set of queries. Rimbault asks about authors who printed privately. Replies give Dr Percy on the poems of the Earl of Surrey, through Collier. Symbols of the four evangelists also come in.
notes-and-queries-number-30-may-25-1850:
Dr Johnson and Dr Warton open number thirty, dated Saturday, May 25, 1850, in F. H. Markland's note. Spenser's monument and borrowed thoughts follow. Folk lore offers Easter eggs, a cure for warts, and a charm for wounds. Bartholomew Legate, the martyr, gets a note of his own.

Bohn's edition of Milton's prose works and a reprint of Jeremy Taylor are announced as notes. Queries ask about Dr Richard Holsworth and Thomas Fuller, and a passage in Macbeth. Replies return to the dodo queries, through Singer. The Abbey of St Wandrille and the origin of the word news also get settled here.
notes-and-queries-number-31-june-1-1850:
Number thirty-one, dated Saturday, June 1, 1850, restarts its paging at one for a new volume. Parish registers and their statistics lead the notes. Singer treats the Hudibrastic verse, and James Crosby the custom of presenting gloves. Folk lore warns that exhuming a body is ominous to the dead person's family.

Suffolk folk lore, a cure for fits, and divination by Bible and key follow. Unpublished epigrams from the British Museum are printed. Queries ask about death by burning as a punishment, and about Cornelis Drebble. Martello towers, guineas, and members for Calais draw minor queries. Replies settle feast and fast, and Charles Martel.
notes-and-queries-number-32-june-8-1850:
Strangers in the House of Commons open the notes in number thirty-two, for Saturday, June 8, 1850. The Agapemone follows, from Richard Greene, and London Irish registers from Robert Cole. Folk lore offers divination by Bible and key, a charm for warts, and a charm for learning a child's sex.

Poet laureates draw a query of their own. Minor queries chase wood paper, Roman roads, and the language of Queen Mary's days. Hanging out the broom and clerical costume also puzzle readers. Replies give Samuel Hickson on the derivation of news and noise. Strickland returns to the dodo, and umbrellas get an answer at last.
notes-and-queries-number-36-july-6-1850:
Further notes on the derivation of the word news open number thirty-six, dated Saturday, July 6, 1850. Samuel Hickson writes them. More borrowed thoughts follow from Singer, and strangers in the House of Commons return through C. Ross. Folk lore warns that high spirits can presage coming calamity.

A hydro-incubator is described by H. Kersley among the notes. The etymology of parliament gets a short piece. Queries ask about James Carkasse's Lucida Intervalla. Minor queries chase Lammas Day, Jewish music, ventriloquism, and the plant haemony. The family of Love and Sir Gammer Vans also appear. Replies settle death by burning as punishment.
notes-and-queries-number-37-july-13-1850:
The author of the Characteristics is identified in number thirty-seven, for Saturday, July 13, 1850, by W. D. Christie. Caxton's printing office follows, from R. F. Rimbault, plus sanatory laws in other days. Folk lore treats midsummer fires. Minor notes include borrowed thoughts and an infant prodigy in 1659.

Queries ask for letters of Queen Elizabeth and Philip the Second of Spain. Minor queries chase mildew in books and George Herbert's burial place. The Lass of Richmond Hill and the curfew also appear. Replies print a French poem by Malherbe, through Singer. The Dies Irae gets a reply, and Dr Samuel Ogden a note.
notes-and-queries-number-38-july-20-1850:
Shakespeare's use of the word delighted opens number thirty-eight, dated Saturday, July 20, 1850, through S. Hickson. Lord Braybrooke names the authors of The Rolliad. Notes on Milton and the derivation of Easter follow. Dr Guest collects folk passages of death, and divination at marriages is added.

Dr Rimbault writes on Francis Lenton the poet among the notes. Queries ask about Nicholas Ferrar of Little Gidding, from John Miland. Stukeley's Stonehenge draws a query from Henry Cunliffe. Minor queries chase smoke money and Michael Scott the wizard. Replies settle Caxton's printing office and the New Temple question.
notes-and-queries-number-39-july-27-1850:
Etymology of Whitsuntide and Mass opens number thirty-nine, dated Saturday, July 27, 1850. Folk lore follows with sympathetic cures, a cure for ague, and eating snakes as a charm for growing young. Long Meg of Westminster gets a note from Rimbault. Spelling, sanatory against connection, is also weighed.

Minor notes include Shakespeare as a brass rubber and a mayor of misrule. A story of three men and their bag of money draws a query. A. De Morgan asks about the geometrical foot. notes-and-queries-number-40-august-3-185:

phrenology-explained-and-exemplified-185:
Eneas Mackenzie's Phrenology Explained and Exemplified, published by the author in London, begins by defining its word. Phrenology, from the Greek for mind and discourse, means that our intellectual faculties, moral virtues, base urges, and animal emotions may be known by bumps on the skull. These correspond to organs of the brain beneath, strong in proportion to their size.

Mackenzie credits Dr. Gall, a physician from Tiefenbrunn in Swabia, as the science's discoverer and champion. He adds the caution that exercise and education shape the faculties, so actions cannot be positively predicted. The little book is a mid-century primer of the system.
phrenology-proved-illustrated-and-applie: A hosted sample showing only the Google Books digital-copy notice pages that precede this scan, with no page of the work itself visible. The catalogue record names the book Phrenology Proved, Illustrated, and Applied, accompanied by a chart, and credits O. S. Fowler, dating this edition 1850. Its long title promises the location of the phrenological organs in the head and a view of the moral and intellectual powers.
plos-pbio-0020050:
Haoxing Xu, Jie Jin, Louis J. DeFelice, and their team reported a surprise about metal transport in PLOS Biology in 2004. A protein called DMT1 is the main route for iron to enter mammalian cells. A mutation that keeps turning up in the protein revealed something extra: a path for calcium entry.

Mutations that appear again and again often mark a spot a protein cannot do without. Here, studying that spot exposed a hidden side of DMT1's work. The finding widens the picture of how cells handle metals, where iron and calcium traffic may cross. It may also help explain odd symptoms in people and animals with faults in this transporter.
plos-pone-0000050:
Karla Eger, Mark Sundrud, Alison Motsinger, and co-authors showed in 2006 that one class of immune cells is far from uniform. Natural killer T cells patrol for abnormal cells and can release signals that steer the whole immune response. A key question was whether they can reprogram those effector functions, switching the kind of signal they send.

The team found human natural killer T cells are heterogeneous in that capacity: some can reprogram, others are more fixed. A mixed population changes how doctors should think about using these cells in therapy, since the helpful subset may need to be picked out. The study maps variety where earlier work had assumed sameness.
plos-pone-0000150:
Roman H. Khonsari and Vincent Calvez published this theory paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It addresses concentric demyelination, a striking pattern seen in some brain lesions where myelin, the insulation around nerve fibers, is lost in rings. The authors model how such rings could arise through self-organization in the human brain.

Ring-shaped damage is hard to explain by simple spreading. A self-organization model shows how local interactions can build the pattern without a ring-shaped cause. The work offers neurologists a new way to think about an unusual lesion pattern. It also shows how maths can suggest mechanisms for diseases that are hard to study directly.
plos-pone-0000250:
Sagi Levy, Jan Ihmels, Miri Carmi, and colleagues published this yeast genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Budding yeast is a single-celled fungus and a workhorse of genetics. The authors lay out the strategy of transcription regulation in this yeast. It is the overall logic by which the yeast decides which genes to switch on and when.

A strategy-level view shows design principles: how one regulator can serve many conditions, and how the system stays flexible. The authors draw that logic from genome-wide data. Understanding yeast regulation guides work in more complex cells, where the same principles apply with more parts.
plos-pone-0000350:
Gianfranco Diretto, Salim Al-Babili, Raffaela Tavazza, and colleagues published this plant engineering paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Carotenoids are the pigments that make carrots orange and supply vitamin A. The authors use metabolic engineering to raise potato carotenoid content, switching on a bacterial mini-pathway only in the tuber, the part people eat.

Potatoes are a staple for millions, so enriching them could fight vitamin A deficiency at scale. A tuber-specific pathway avoids burdening the rest of the plant. The paper reports the engineered potatoes' carotenoid gains, a step in the biofortification program for staple crops.
plos-pone-0000450:
Hu-Hui Lee and Richard R. Behringer switched a developmental gene on during cartilage formation and watched the result, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The gene is Wnt4, a signal that guides building in the embryo. Using conditional expression, a method that turns the gene on only in chosen tissue and time, they activated it during chondrogenesis in mice.

The outcome was dwarfism: the mice grew up short-limbed. Cartilage is the template that bone later replaces, so a signal that disturbs cartilage growth reshapes the whole skeleton. The experiment shows Wnt4's dose and timing must be tightly controlled for normal bone length, a lesson relevant to human skeletal disorders.
plos-pone-0000550:
A. D. McNaghten and colleagues argued for a fairer way to watch the HIV epidemic in the United States, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Existing behavioral and clinical surveillance drew on convenience samples that may not represent all persons with HIV. The authors set out the rationale for developing a population-based approach to improve representativeness.

If surveillance misses whole groups, programs aim at the wrong targets and disparities stay hidden. A population-based design samples so that every group counts in proportion. Methods papers like this one do quiet but durable work: they change the data every later decision depends on.
plos-pone-0000650:
Mike M. Moradian, Denis Beglaryan, Jill M. Skozylas and colleagues sequenced the full mitochondrial genomes of three Tetrahymena species for PLOS ONE in 2007. Tetrahymena is a single-celled ciliate used widely as a model organism. Its mitochondrial genome is divergent and unusual. Half of its 44 genes still lacked a definite function.

Those genes fall into known protein-coding genes and a group called Ymf genes. The title reports mutation hot spots and faster nonsynonymous change in the Ymf group. Nonsynonymous changes alter the protein a gene encodes, so their speed says something about evolutionary pressure. Comparative sequences like these help untangle how this odd genome evolved.
plos-pone-0000750:
Delphine Hu, Stefano M. Bertozzi, Emmanuela Gakidou and colleagues weighed what it costs to keep mothers alive in Mexico. Writing in PLOS ONE in 2007, they give Mexico's lifetime risk of dying from maternal causes as 1 in 370. The United States figure was 1 in 2,500. National efforts had improved maternal services over the prior decade, but progress toward Millennium Development Goal 5 was unclear.

The team assessed costs, benefits, and cost-effectiveness of interventions against maternal illness and death. Money spent on the wrong mix of services saves fewer mothers. Their accounting gives policymakers a ranked case for where the next peso does the most good.
plos-pone-0000850:
Allan Saul and Michael P. Fay analyzed how human immunity should shape vaccines that bundle several components against one target. Including multiple immunogens against one organism is a strategy pursued for many trial vaccines. It helps most where one immunogen alone cannot raise a strongly protective response. Many existing human vaccines already contain multiple components.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE question is design logic: given how human immunity actually responds, when do extra components help, and when do they compete? Immune responses can focus on a few dominant targets, wasting the rest. Sound design rules save vaccine developers from bloated formulas, and they matter most for hard targets like malaria and HIV.
plos-pone-0000950:
Marco Salemi, Brant Burkhardt, Rebecca Gray and colleagues traced how HIV changes inside different tissues, in PLOS ONE in 2007. As HIV infection advances, the virus often switches which cell door it uses, from CCR5 to CXCR4. The CXCR4 forms are especially deadly to young thymus cells.

Almost no work had checked which virus forms live inside the thymus itself. The team compare viral populations in lymphoid and other tissues. Their analysis gives the thymus a central role in the emergence of the CXCR4 forms. That finding ties a turning point in disease to one small organ where T cells mature.
plos-pone-0001050:
Yulei Wang, Catalin Barbacioru, Dov Shiffman and colleagues found a blood gene signature for a hidden artery swelling, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Thoracic aortic aneurysm is a bulge in the main artery near the heart. It usually gives no symptoms, yet it kills at high rates when it bursts. Surgery can prevent that, but finding who is at risk is hard.

The team hypothesized that gene expression patterns in peripheral blood could betray the aneurysm. A blood test for a silent, deadly swelling would change screening entirely. Their signature work is a first step: show the signal exists in an easy sample before building a clinic ready test.
plos-pone-0001150:
When a broken bone heals, the body rebuilds it using two routes: one that first lays down cartilage, and one that forms bone directly. Danielle Behonick and colleagues examined an enzyme's part in both routes, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The enzyme is matrix metalloproteinase 13, also called collagenase-3, which cuts collagen.

The enzyme was already known to matter in long bone development. The authors found it is expressed during adult skeletal repair and tested its role in regeneration after injury. Their work links the reshaping of the matrix around cells to successful bone healing in adults.
plos-pone-0001250:
The brain rewires itself as it adapts, but how its own activity changes the strength of its connections is largely unknown. Masako Tsukamoto-Yasui and colleagues report observations from the hippocampus, a region central to memory, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They describe active hippocampal networks undergoing spontaneous synaptic modification.

In their experiments, synapses changed strength without an external lesson driving them, following the network's own activity. The brain, in their phrase, is self-writable. Findings like these bear on how memories form and how networks stay stable while remaining flexible.
plos-pone-0001350:
Thousands of systematic reviews summarize health care evidence. Such reviews sit near the top of the evidence ladder in medicine. But their quality varies, and it should routinely be appraised. Beverley Shea and colleagues externally validated AMSTAR, a measurement tool for assessing systematic reviews, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They used the tool to appraise 42 reviews.

External validation asks whether a tool works in hands other than its makers'. AMSTAR has since become a standard checklist for review quality. The paper helped establish whether its scores are reliable and meaningful for judging the reviews on which clinical guidelines rest.
plos-pone-0001450:
Zhuofei Xu and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study that reads the full genome of a pig germ. The germ causes a lung ill in pigs that costs farms a great deal world wide. The strain they read is a type common in China. Its full gene code gives a base for all later work on this germ.

The full code lets labs compare this strain with kin strains from other lands, gene by gene. That base lets them spot vaccine and drug targets with far more care than before. It also lets vets track how strains spread and change. That is key for a disease that moves with the pig trade.
plos-pone-0001550:
Joseph Lemire, Ryan Mailloux, and Vasu Appanna wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on lactate use in human brain tumor cells. Lactate was long seen as a waste end of energy work without air. Its fate in brain chemistry was not pinned down. The team tested a human astrocytoma cell line, a model of a common brain tumor cell.

They show, for the first time in this line, that the cells can take in and burn lactate for energy. An enzyme inside the cell power units drives that use. The result recasts lactate as a fuel, not just waste. It may shape how brain tumors are fed and fought.
plos-pone-0001650:
Mikhail M. Pooggin, Johannes Fütterer, and Thomas Hohn compared a protein-making trick used by two plant viruses in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Cauliflower mosaic virus infects broad-leaf plants, while rice tungro bacilliform virus infects rice. Both are pararetroviruses, and both pack several genes onto one RNA strand. To read the later genes, ribosomes shunt: they start, then jump past a section to the next start point.

The authors asked whether the shunt parts from one virus work in the other, across the wide gap between the plant groups they infect. The full text gives the swap tests and how much protein each version made. Shared function across such different viruses hints that this jump mechanism is old and sturdy. It also gives plant science a tested tool for making several proteins from one gene strand.
plos-pone-0001750:
Henry Haeberle, Leigh A. Bryan, Tegy J. Vadakkan, and their co-authors studied touch sensor cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Merkel cell-neurite complexes are among the most sensitive touch receptors in skin, pairing epidermal Merkel cells with sensory nerve endings. Merkel cells are proposed to be the sensing cells that signal nerves chemically, but functional proof was thin.

The team reports that swelling-activated calcium channels trigger calcium signals in Merkel cells. Calcium signals are how such cells would pass the touch message onward. The full text gives the cell recordings and channel tests. Pinning a channel to the first step of touch helps explain fine fingertip sensitivity and may guide work on touch loss.
plos-pone-0001850:
Anandharaman Veerapathran, Rajnish Joshi, Kalyan Goswami, and their co-authors set cut-off values for tuberculosis blood tests in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Blood tests called IGRAs are a promising alternative to the tuberculin skin test. Reading repeated tests is hampered by lack of evidence on the best cut-offs for flips. A flip is the point where a result counts as newly positive or back to negative.

Using repeat testing data, the team derived cut-offs from how much one person's T-cell assay results vary. The full text gives the spread of results and the proposed thresholds. Health workers screened again and again, such as hospital staff, need such thresholds to avoid chasing noise as if it were new infection.
plos-pone-0001950:
Caroline Charlier and co-authors matched brain scans to illness severity in a fungal brain infection, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The infection, cryptococcal meningoencephalitis, strikes people with HIV and kills about one in five despite antifungal drugs. Doctors lacked a sharp way to grade how bad a case is.

The team studied brain images from sixty-two HIV-positive patients treated in the era of strong HIV therapy. They report that the brain lesions seen on scans correlate with how severe the illness is. If scan patterns grade a case well, doctors could sort who needs the most urgent and intense care.
plos-pone-0002050:
Toru Nakamura and co-authors compared the pattern of behavior in mice and men, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Mental functions, and how psychiatric illness warps them, are hard to reach with molecular tools, since objective measures of behavior in animals were lacking. The team instead studied laws of behavioral organization, the math shape of how acts are timed.

As the title states, they report a universality in that organization across mice and humans, and its breakdown in illness. If the timing laws match, a mouse's act stream can stand in for aspects of human mental state that genes alone cannot show.
plos-pone-0002150:
Tal Arnon, Gal Markel, Ahuva Bar-Ilan, and co-authors explored a new way to aim the immune system at cancer, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Natural killer cells are immune cells that can kill tumor cells and infected cells. On their surface sit natural cytotoxicity receptors, including NKp46, NKp44, and NKp30, which help them pick out targets.

These receptors also exist in a loose, soluble form that floats free of the cell. The team worked on using those free forms to build new cancer immune therapies. If a receptor can be turned into a drug-like molecule, the killer cell's own targeting skill might be borrowed for treatment.
plos-pone-0002250:
Evelyne Derelle and co-authors described the life cycle and genome of a virus that infects a marine alga, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Large DNA viruses infect hosts from algae to humans and descend from an ancient common ancestor. In the oceans, algal viruses shape plankton blooms and steer the evolution of the tiny plants at the food web's base.

Their subject, OtV5, infects Ostreococcus tauri, a unicellular green alga of the open sea. The team charted how the virus grows and read its genome. Each such genome sharpens the picture of how giant viruses evolved and rule marine microbes.
plos-pone-0002350:
Ma-Li Wong, Chuanhui Dong, Karin Esposito, and co-authors analyzed blood thickening in depression and its response to treatment, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Major depressive disorder raises the risk of cardiovascular disease on its own, and depressed patients who suffer a heart attack face more cardiac complications afterward. One suspect link is stress-hemoconcentration, where stress squeezes fluid from the blood, leaving it thicker.

Using data from a randomized, double-blind trial, the team found stress-hemoconcentration was elevated in major depression and normalized with antidepressant treatment. A measurable blood change that tracks with mood treatment gives the depression-heart link a concrete, testable form.
plos-pone-0002450:
Work from Guerreiro and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Rita J. Guerreiro, Jennifer C. Schymick, Cynthia Crews, and others. Its subject is tDP-43 Is Not a Common Cause of Sporadic Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis. TAR DNA binding protein, encoded by TARDBP, was shown to be a central component of ubiquitin-positive.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002550:
In 2008, Park and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Sungsu Park, Hyejin Hwang, Seong-Won Nam, and others. Its subject is enhanced Caenorhabditis elegans Locomotion in a Structured Microfluidic Environment. Behavioral studies of Caenorhabditis elegans traditionally are done on the smooth surface of agar plates, but the natural habitat of C.

elegans and other nematodes is the soil, a complex and structured environment. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002650:
Published in PLOS ONE in 2008, research by Stefan Koelsch and colleagues addresses cognitive components of regularity processing in the auditory domain. The catalog record names Stefan Koelsch first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Music-syntactic irregularities often co-occur with the processing of physical irregularities. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002750:
Bronwen Martin led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was iTRAQ analysis of complex proteome alterations in 3xTgAD alzheimer's mice: understanding the interface between physiology and disease. Authorship is credited in the record to Bronwen Martin and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by progressive cognitive impairment associated with accumulation of amyloid β-peptide. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002850:
Published in PLOS ONE in 2008, research by Lihui Liu and colleagues addresses K-ras/PI3K-Akt signaling is essential for zebrafish hematopoiesis and angiogenesis. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Lihui Liu, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The RAS small GTPases orchestrate multiple cellular processes. The summary also notes a further point. Studies on knock-out mice showed the essential and sufficient role of K-RAS, but not N-RAS and H-RAS in embryonic development. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002950:
Huaiqing Chen, Yueyun Ma, Jun Yang and co-authors hunted genes needed for pneumococcal ear infection in 2008. Ear infection, or otitis media, causes most bacterial respiratory infections in children worldwide. Streptococcus pneumoniae is one of its three major causes, alongside two other bacteria named in the paper.

Little was known about which pneumococcal genes the infection itself requires. The PLOS ONE study screens for that genetic requirement, separating genes the germ needs in the ear from those it can lose. Such a list can guide vaccine and drug work aimed at a very common childhood disease.
plos-pone-0003050:
Pamella Wang, Gabriela Campanholle, Marcos Cenedeze and co-authors tested blocking the bradykinin B1 receptor in kidney injury in 2008. The team had earlier shown mice lacking that receptor were protected against renal ischemia-reperfusion injury, damage when blood returns after a cutoff. A drug blocker could offer the same gain without gene deletion.

Here they analyze the effect of B1 antagonism on that injury and whether blocking or deleting the receptor shifts the response. The title states antagonism is beneficial. Published in PLOS ONE, the work supports a drug route to protect kidneys after transplant or shock.
plos-pone-0003150:
David Pickar, Jessie Vinik and John J. Bartko survey drug treatment for schizophrenia in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Patients are often prescribed combinations from several drug classes, even though single antipsychotic use matches official labelling and the science behind combinations varies widely. The authors set out to gain current data on real drug treatment practice.

The title reports their main finding: off-label drug use was preponderant among schizophrenic patients in the data studied. Readers get a snapshot of how far practice can drift from labelled use. That gap matters for safety checks, cost, and for judging whether combined prescribing helps or harms.
plos-pone-0003250: Patrick S. Sullivan and colleagues published a PLOS ONE study in 2008 comparing HIV care in two kinds of clinics. The title states the comparison: care quality in sites backed by the Ryan White Program versus sites not backed by it. No abstract beyond the title was supplied, so this record does not state which group gave better care.
plos-pone-0003350:
Julien Sérandour, Stéphane Reynaud, John Willison and colleagues study insect attraction to aquatic plants in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Plants produce semiochemicals that sway insect attraction and repulsion. Generally, this attraction is closely associated with herbivory and has been studied mainly in air. The link between aquatic plants and insects was less explored.

The title reports ubiquitous water-soluble molecules in aquatic plant exudates determine specific insect attraction. Readers see chemical cues working through water rather than air. Those cues may guide insects to host plants for egg laying, with effects on aquatic food webs.
plos-pone-0003450:
Sergio Lizano and co-authors studied swapped genes in a strep germ for this 2008 paper. Streptococcus pyogenes causes strep throat and worse diseases. Its history suggests some genes came from another species wholesale. The swapped gene replaced the germ's own matching copy.

One such swap involved genes for pili, hair-like strands on the cell surface. The team tested how the foreign copy changed pilus gene control. Imported DNA had rewired the circuitry that turns those genes on. The study shows gene theft can reprogram a pathogen's surface. Pili help the germ grip host cells, so their control matters for infection.
plos-pone-0003550:
Jason G. Bragg and Sallie W. Chisholm modeled a stolen gene's payoff in this 2008 paper. Viruses of sea bacteria often carry a gene called psbA. That gene encodes D1, a core protein of photosynthesis. The host's own D1 decays during infection in the light.

A virus-carried copy may keep photosynthesis running while the virus replicates. Their model weighs the fitness gain of carrying that gene. Keeping the host's energy plant alive could yield more virus offspring. The math explains a strange case of genetic piracy in the ocean. Sea microbes drive much of Earth's oxygen output, so their viruses matter globally.
plos-pone-0003650:
Francesca Martinato, Matteo Cesaroni, Bruno Amati, and colleagues published this gene study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Myc is a protein that switches genes on and drives cell growth. It binds a large share of gene promoters across the genome. The team asked what it does to chromatin there.

They measured the chemical marks on histones, the spool proteins DNA wraps around, at Myc's target sites. The pattern of marks changed where Myc landed on the DNA. Those changes help explain how one growth switch can reset the activity of many genes at once, a process that goes wrong in cancer.
plos-pone-0003750:
Amets Sáenz, Margarita Azpitarte, Rubén Armañanzas, and colleagues published this muscle disease study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2A is an inherited disorder caused by faults in the calpain 3 gene. What calpain 3 does inside muscle cells was still little known.

The team profiled gene expression in tissue from patients with the disease. The portrait shows which genes change their activity when calpain 3 fails. That map gives researchers leads on the protein's real jobs in muscle and on how its loss leads to wasting.
plos-pone-0003850:
M. Mar González-Barroso, Irina Giurgea, Fredéric Bouillaud, and colleagues published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Congenital hyperinsulinism makes newborns release too much insulin, driving blood sugar dangerously low. Faults in the pancreas's potassium channel explain many cases, but more than half had no known cause.

Mice lacking the protein UCP2 also mishandle insulin secretion. The team therefore searched patients for mutations in UCP2 and found them. The finding reveals a role for UCP2 in regulating insulin release and adds a fresh genetic cause to this infant condition.
plos-pone-0003950:
Nicolas Bréchot, Elisa Gomez, Marine Bignon, and co-authors studied limb blood loss in mice lacking a protein in 2008. Critical limb ischemia starves leg tissue of blood and can end in amputation. Macrophages, immune cells that guide healing, flood such tissue. Yet inflammation markers track with worse disease in patients.

Their PLOS ONE article used mice without thrombospondin-1 to test macrophage tuning. Shifting macrophage activation state protected tissue from necrosis in those mice. The result suggests calming one immune mode can save ischemic limbs. It points to immune tuning as a treatment angle for patients.
plos-pone-0004050:
Bernard A. Okech, Isaac K. Mwobobia, Anthony Kamau, and co-authors documented falling malaria in Kenya in 2008. Their team was surveying insects ahead of planned malaria control in Mwea. Meanwhile, cases at Kimbimbi sub-district hospital kept declining steadily. Why cases fell before interventions began was unknown.

Their PLOS ONE article credits integrated malaria management for the reduction. Integrated programs combine several control tools at once. Identifying what drove the decline mattered before adding new measures. The lesson helps other districts copy what already works. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004150:
Ricardo Palacios and colleagues published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Most genes exist in two copies, one from each parent, and the two copies are not always used equally. This uneven use, called allele-specific gene expression, may shape many human traits and diseases.

To map how common the pattern is, the team combined genotyping with gene activity measures across the human genome. They report that allele-specific expression is widespread, touching many genes and many biological processes. The result means that which copy of a gene came from which parent can matter far more often than once thought.
plos-pone-0004250:
Brian Fink and colleagues published this cell energy study in PLOS ONE in 2009. MitoQ is a version of the antioxidant coenzyme Q engineered to enter mitochondria, the cell's power plants. The team had earlier found that, surprisingly, it increased superoxide production in cow artery endothelial cell mitochondria fed certain fuels but not others.

Here they dig into that puzzle: how a mitochondria-targeted antioxidant, plus the choice of fuel, changes superoxide output. Fuel selectivity, which food molecules the mitochondria burn, turns out to shape the result. The findings warn that antioxidant drugs can behave as pro-oxidants depending on the cell's diet.
plos-pone-0004350:
Danuta Martuszewska and colleagues published this kidney cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The tensin family of proteins is thought to link the extracellular matrix to the cytoskeleton, mediating signals for cell shape and motility. Dysregulation of tensin expression had previously been implicated in cancer.

The team report that tensin3 is a negative regulator of cell migration, a brake on cell movement. They also found all four tensin family members downregulated in human kidney cancer. Losing brakes on movement fits a cancer that spreads, which is why the family matters. All four were turned down, not just one.
plos-pone-0004450:
A small enzyme called PRL-3 helps melanoma cells spread, show Ran Song, Feng Qian, Yu-Pei Li, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. PRL-3 belongs to a family of enzymes named for the regenerating liver, where they were first found. Many studies had hinted that it aids the spread of cancers, called metastasis, but the proof was thin.

The team worked with B16F1 melanoma cells, in dishes and in animals. They found PRL-3 sits at the cell membrane, and that the cells need it to spread. Removing its effect cut the cancer's ability to move and invade. Pinpointing a needed helper of metastasis gives drug hunters a concrete target, and gives doctors a possible marker of cancers most likely to spread.
plos-pone-0004550:
A red tide coated seabirds in a slimy film and killed them in large numbers in Monterey Bay, documented by David Jessup, Melissa Miller, John Ryan, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. In November and December 2007 a widespread seabird mortality event struck the bay in California. It coincided with a massive red tide of the dinoflagellate Akashiwo sanguinea, a single-celled alga.

Affected birds had a slimy yellow-green material on feathers that were saturated and lost their waterproofing. The team links the deaths to a surfactant, a soap-like substance, produced by the bloom. Surf-like foam can strip the oils that keep seabirds dry and warm. Naming this mechanism matters, because such blooms are not poisonous in the usual way, yet can still kill at scale.
plos-pone-0004650:
A bacterium best known for harming newborns is turning up in the lungs of cystic fibrosis patients, report Vera Eickel, Barbara Kahl, Beatrice Reinisch, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Streptococcus agalactiae is a well-known pathogen for neonates and for adults with weakened immunity. Beyond the newborn period, it is rarely found in the respiratory tract.

Between 2002 and 2008 the team noticed it in respiratory secretions of a notable share of their cystic fibrosis patients. They describe this emergence of respiratory isolates. Cystic fibrosis lungs are a special environment where unusual microbes can settle. A new regular in that environment changes what doctors should test for when a patient's condition worsens without explanation.
plos-pone-0004750:
