Lin and colleagues built a computer method to predict which drugs will bind which body proteins in a 2026 study. Lab testing of every drug and protein pair is slow and costly, so good predictions narrow the search. Their method reads drug shapes with a graph network that weighs the most telling parts, and reads proteins with a pre-trained language-style model.

Tests on three standard data sets beat older prediction methods, the authors report. Fuller reading of both drug structure and protein sequence drove the gain. Better shortlists mean chemists spend lab time on pairs most likely to work. The approach adds a fresh route for early drug discovery work.
plos-pone-0352350:
Zhengxiu Sun and five colleagues examine this 2026 PLOS One study of how being schedulable at any hour through apps like WeChat relates to job satisfaction in China. Using a nationally representative 2021 social survey, they asked whether workers whose shifts and tasks can be arranged anytime through messaging tools feel worse about their jobs, and why.

Always-on scheduling was indeed tied to lower satisfaction, and the link ran largely through two channels: more conflict between work and family life, and a stronger sense of pressure at work. The negative pattern concentrated among highly educated workers and professionals. The authors argue the findings show how communication tools quietly stretch the working day, with costs that fall unevenly across the workforce.
plos-pone-0352450:
Ruining Jin and co-authors examined how gender links to physical bullying among teenagers in India, and whether that link shifts with age. Bullying research leans heavily on Western samples, so they reanalyzed open survey data from a hundred sixty-nine school students. Students were grouped into early, middle, and late adolescence for the comparison.

Boys reported both more bullying of others and more being bullied themselves than girls did. The gap in doing the bullying grew wider in the later teen years. Because the pattern changes across adolescence, the authors argue that prevention work should not treat all teens alike: what fits a twelve-year-old may miss the point for a seventeen-year-old. The sample was small, so the findings are a starting point rather than a final word.
plos-pone-0353350:
Wen and colleagues, in a 2026 study, compare the chemistry inside the pulp of three citrus varieties grown in China. Flavor and nutrition live in that chemistry, yet varieties had rarely been dissected side by side. Using a scanning method that catches hundreds of compounds at once, the team profiled a mandarin type, a sour orange hybrid, and a yuzu relative.

The three pulps formed clearly separate chemical clusters. More than three hundred compounds differed between them, from the flavonoids tied to health claims to acids, aromatics, and bitter limonoids. The mandarin leaned into flavonoid pathways. The yuzu relative piled up organic and amino acids. The hybrid showed its own blend, rich in fatty acid and purine activity. Networks of linked compounds confirmed whole pathways shift together. The authors offer the maps to breeders chasing better flavor and to makers of citrus health products.
plos-pone-0353550:
Ahmad and colleagues, in a 2026 study, fine-tune a fast vision model to find defects in fabric as it is made. Flawed cloth is wasted money, and human inspection is slow and tiring. Mills also make plain and printed textiles side by side, so one detector must handle both. The team trained on cloth from a Pakistani mill and checked the model on three public data sets.

Their customized model, built on the twelfth version of the YOLO detector family, learned features aimed at varied defect shapes and used adaptive tricks to enrich training images. On the home mill's cloth it scored well across seven defect types, balancing catches and false alarms. On the public sets it again beat comparison methods, staying light enough for cheap computing. The authors present it as a universal inspector for mixed textile lines, ready for the factory floor rather than only the lab.
plos-pone-0353750:
Vinicius Oliveira and co-authors compare in 2026 how older adults in Brazil and Europe manage daily life, using a World Health Organization framework for care in ageing. Large ageing surveys from both places supplied measures of basic and tool based daily tasks, plus five areas of built in ability such as movement, memory, and senses.

Risk patterns differed by place: grip strength protected more in Europe, while walking speed mattered only in Brazil for basic tasks. Depression carried more risk in Europe, and hearing loss more in Brazil. Overall, decline began about ten years earlier in Brazil, which the authors tie to social and economic gaps.
plos-pone-0353850:
Tomioka and colleagues, in a 2026 study, link social life to oral frailty in older Japanese adults. Oral frailty means weakening of chewing, swallowing, and the mouth's overall function, and it predicts wider decline. Japan has universal dental care, yet gaps by income persist. The team asked whether social capital, meaning trust, reciprocity, and taking part in community life, protects the mouth.

Data came from a large national aging study, with more than thirty thousand people followed from 2019 to 2022. About one in five developed oral frailty risk over three years, more among poorer participants. People with richer social ties and stronger trust in neighbors had lower odds of oral frailty, at every income level. Joining in community activities also protected, and it helped poorer participants most. The authors suggest that building social connection is a health policy in itself, one that can narrow oral health gaps.
plos-pone-0354150:
Zhanyan Li and colleagues study in 2026 how people in China reacted online just after the first imported mpox case reached the mainland. They gathered comments under popular posts on a major social platform during the first two days. Language tools scored feeling in each comment and grouped the main topics of concern.

Comment volume peaked within two hours and faded fast after four. Most comments carried negative feeling, and concern centred on how the illness spreads and on attitudes toward it. High activity posts also drew stronger feeling. The authors argue that fast, place aware official messaging matters most in those early hours.
plos-pone-0354350:
Freihat and colleagues, in a 2026 global study, chart the burden of lung cancer from 2010 to 2050. Lung cancer kills more people than any other cancer, yet counts of cases and deaths alone do not say how hard the disease hits each patient. The team combined three global data sources covering nearly two hundred countries, and added two severity measures.

In 2022 the world saw roughly two and a half million new cases and close to two million deaths, with tens of millions of healthy years lost. Men and richer regions bore more, by their measures. Two forward views were built: one holding 2022 rates fixed so only population change acts, and one extending each country's recent trend. Their severity frame pairs the share who die with healthy years lost per case, a fairer way to compare countries.
plos-pone-0354450:
Shanshan Hu, Chaxiang Li, and Wei Zhang explore in 2026 how older adults living with type two diabetes experience being cut off from others. Fourteen patients from a hospital clinic in Yichang, China, took part in face to face interviews. The team sorted what they heard into patterns at personal, family, and wider levels.

Many described pulling back after losses linked to illness and fear of decline. Others felt held back by overprotective families, shrinking friend circles, and brief talks with doctors. Poorly matched local services, hard to reach public spaces, and stigma added to the problem. The authors call for stronger family and local support.
plos-pone-0354750:
Kyuhyung Choi and co-authors published this 2026 study of immune activity inside the human dorsal root ganglion, the cluster of sensory nerve cells targeted by many pain treatments. Using public single-nucleus gene data, they asked whether immune activity there follows one pattern or several distinct ones.

Choi's group sorted a curated set of immune nuclei into seven recurring gene programs. Some programs clustered in particular spots instead of spreading evenly through the tissue. That patchy layout points to small immune niches rather than uniform swelling. Knowing where these programs sit could help doctors aim local pain treatments at the exact tissue zones involved.
plos-pone-0355550:
Kady D Waggle and colleagues describe how a hospital system runs routine genome sequencing of germs to catch outbreaks early and cheaply. Standard infection control often misses silent spread between patients. Their program sequences samples from high-risk germs every week, compares genomes to spot hidden clusters, and reports back to infection teams. The paper lays out staffing, workflow, and costs across two phases over three years.

In a typical week the team sequenced dozens of samples, with per-sample cost falling below a round threshold in the later phase once staff pay and supplies were counted. Results reached infection teams in a little over a week on average. Waggle and colleagues argue the routine is feasible for other hospitals and can pay for itself by stopping outbreaks sooner.
plos-pone-0355650:
Judith Legrand and fellow doctors test whether texture patterns on chest CT scans can tell whether chest lymph nodes in lung cancer patients truly hold cancer. Node status decides treatment, and scans alone often mislead. The study looked back at about one hundred ten surgical patients whose nodes looked suspect. Up to three nodes per patient were outlined in three dimensions. Texture features were extracted. Two machine learning models were trained across many repeated splits.

The stronger model sorted malignant from harmless nodes modestly well, far from perfect but better than chance. Three texture features recurred in the winning signatures, all capturing how uneven the node tissue looks. Legrand and colleagues present scan texture as a supporting signal for staging, not a replacement for tissue proof.
plos-pone-0355850:
Nicholas Dietrich and David McShannon test a popular fix for scarce medical images in this 2026 study: making synthetic training data. Their task was classifying emphysema subtypes in lung CT scans, where only a small set of real image patches was available. They compared three modern generative models, which learn to invent new scans, against simple geometric tricks like rotating and flipping real images.

None of the methods, alone or combined, improved the classifier's accuracy in a statistically reliable way over training on real images only. The best single result came from one generative model at an equal mix of real and synthetic data, but the gain was not significant. How realistic the fake images looked did not predict how much they helped. The authors say generative augmentation in tiny, texture-driven datasets needs better methods before it can be trusted.
plos-pone-0355950:
Chuanyin Liu and seven colleagues trace how microbes in shrimp pond mud break down a cyanobacterial toxin without oxygen, in this 2026 study. The toxin, microcystin-RR, threatens aquaculture and water safety, and knowing its fate in oxygen-free sediment matters for pond management. The team enriched a microbial community from pond sediment, fed it toxin labeled with heavy nitrogen, and tracked the chemistry and gene activity as degradation proceeded.

Three breakdown products were identified, pointing to a path that opens the toxin's ring, then strips pieces away step by step into short fragments and amino acids. One bacterium dominated the community, while a scarcer genus stayed unusually active. The enzymes doing the cutting appear to be an unconventional set, not the classic microcystin pathway, and nitrogen-cycling genes switched on alongside. The authors offer the map as a basis for building toxin-eating communities.
plos-pone-0356250:
Juan Ge and three colleagues study the link between sleep quality and type 2 diabetes in Chinese community patients who already live with chronic disease, reporting in 2026. More than nine hundred patients answered questionnaires, and the team scored their sleep with a standard index where higher scores mean worse sleep. Nearly two thirds of the group had diabetes.

Worse sleep went together with a higher share of diabetes, but the relationship was not a straight line. Once sleep scores passed a certain point, the odds of diabetes climbed steeply, then leveled off at still worse scores. The authors suggest that community health workers treat sleep checks as a useful extra tool. Helping the worst sleepers in this high-risk group, they add, could be a practical way to fight diabetes.
plos-pone-0356550:
Berna Dizer and three colleagues survey nurses about wounds caused by the medical devices attached to their patients, in this 2026 study from a Turkish state hospital. Tubes, masks, and monitors can press into skin and cause injuries that lengthen stays and raise costs. One hundred fifty nurses in intensive care and surgical units completed a questionnaire on their knowledge of, and attitudes toward, preventing such injuries.

Average scores suggested moderate knowledge and generally positive attitudes, yet only about a third of nurses reached the study's threshold for adequate knowledge paired with positive attitudes. Item-by-item results exposed stubborn misconceptions about prevention and healing, and knowledge did not line up neatly with attitudes. Because the study covered a single hospital, the authors are cautious, but they argue for structured, device-injury-focused training in nursing education and hospital programs.
plos-pone-0356650:
June Labbancz and three colleagues issued this correction in 2026 to their study of tomato plants under aphid attack. The original paper compared tomatoes grown with conventional and organic fertilizer and found that fruit quality held up under an uncontrolled infestation by green peach aphids. Meanwhile gene activity in the plants shifted toward breaking down stored resources. In the published version, the captions were correct but the eleven figures appeared in the wrong order.

The notice republishes the figures in their proper sequence. They cover gene co-expression networks in leaves and fruit, and links between gene modules and aphid presence or fertilizer type. They also cover enrichment analyses of the biological processes involved. Readers using the study's transcriptomic results should match each analysis to the corrected figure rather than relying on the original layout.
plos-pone-0357050:
Signe Nilssen Stafne and coauthors published a 2026 cohort study in PLOS ONE on physical activity in Norwegian women. Their pregnancies were complicated by gestational diabetes, blood pressure disorders, early birth, or a small baby. Such histories raise later heart disease and diabetes risk, making activity especially valuable, yet nobody knew if these women move less. Drawing on the large HUNT study linked to the birth registry, the team measured activity with accelerometers worn for several days.

About a quarter of the nearly four thousand women had adverse pregnancy histories, and they were less active than the others on total and vigorous activity. However, the gap largely faded once postpartum health and lifestyle factors were taken into account. This is hopeful, they say: lower activity is not fixed by pregnancy history itself but travels with health and habits support programs can target. Pregnancy complications should trigger activity support, not resignation.
plos-pone-0357450:
Azar Taheri Tayebi and colleagues compared in 2026 three ways to predict angler pressure: how many people will fish a lake or river, and where. Managers need such forecasts to guard fish stocks and to plan docks, parking, and wardens. The team tested three routes side by side.

One model was guided by what past studies in the field advise. A second was built with the help of a large language model. A third was purely data driven, fitted to records of past fishing. The head to head test shows what each route gains and what it misses. Agencies far beyond this study face the same forecast problem with thin data, and now have better grounds for picking a tool.
plos-pone-0357950:
Richard W. Nauman and colleagues published a 2026 immunology study in PLOS ONE comparing two strains of BCG, the vaccine bacteria also used as a bladder cancer treatment. North American treatment has relied on one strain, but supply problems have pushed interest in an alternative strain produced in Russia. Because much of BCG's benefit is thought to come from trained immunity, a lasting priming of the innate immune system. The team gave mice one dose of each strain and examined bone marrow weeks later.

Both strains expanded the blood-forming stem cells that seed immune responses. The long-used strain, however, produced stronger trained immunity, with immune cells releasing more inflammatory signals when challenged again, and it switched on more inflammation-related genes. The Russian strain primed the system more weakly. Such strain differences, the authors say, could matter for how well bladder cancer immunotherapy works if supplies force a switch.
plos-pone-0358250:
Raffa Mubeen led a team of six authors building a questionnaire on swallowing problems for nurses, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Dysphagia, trouble swallowing, puts patients at risk of choking and lung infection. Nurses are the front line for spotting it, but their knowledge varies. The team developed and validated a tool that measures both knowledge and self-rated competence.

Mubeen's questionnaire reveals training gaps clearly, before patients pay the price for them. Hospitals can aim teaching at the exact weak points instead of generic refreshers. Validating the tool matters: a questionnaire that does not measure truly is worse than none. With sound measurement, nurse training on swallowing safety can improve where it counts, at the bedside.
plos-pone-0358550:
Kristina Fuentes led a team of eight authors setting out a photovoice protocol centered on caregivers, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Caregivers know the flaws of health systems firsthand, yet they are rarely given a real voice in fixing them. Photovoice hands participants cameras, so their own photographs become the evidence.

Fuentes's protocol aims to strengthen health systems by working alongside caregivers, treating them as co-researchers rather than subjects. Photos can show barriers that surveys miss, from confusing signage to exhausting routines. Health leaders presented with images from daily caregiving find them hard to wave away. The protocol's care in design should make its later findings hard to ignore as well.
plos-pone-0358750:
Karin Johnson leads a team of seven studying how birth teams actually involve women in decisions during labor, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their setting is the Swedish rollout of TeamBirth, a care process built around team huddles meant to share decisions with the woman and her partner. The researchers observed twenty-three births, covering seventy-nine huddles, and interviewed sixty-five care providers across two labor wards during 2022 and 2023.

They found four rungs of engagement. At the bottom, staff simply instructed without explaining. Higher up came brief information, then genuine involvement in discussion, the most common pattern, though staff still decided. True partnership, with joint decisions, appeared least often. Limited Swedish skills, heavy workload, and emergencies pushed engagement down. The study shows a well designed process still bends under ward pressure, and names where support should aim.
plos-pone-0358950:
Mario Tudela-Petit and three colleagues test game design in gym class in PLOS ONE in 2026, comparing points and prizes against story and choice. Two hundred nine Spanish secondary students spent eight physical education sessions in one of three setups. One group got ordinary teaching. One got gamification built on outer rewards. The last got gamification built on inner drivers such as narrative and autonomy. Questionnaires before and after measured motivation, competence, and plans to be active later.

Both gamified groups trended toward feeling more capable, and that interaction with time was statistically real. Intention to stay active in the future rose only in the inner driven group. Other motivation measures stayed flat everywhere, and head to head comparisons between groups fell short of firm significance. The authors read the pattern as a nudge: playful design helps modestly, and meaning based elements may outlast rewards for keeping teenagers moving.
plos-pone-0359550: Drost and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study that asks a direct question about athletes and identity. When injury or illness leaves athletes unable to compete, does that loss track with how strongly they see themselves as athletes? A strong athletic identity can aid drive, yet it may deepen distress when sport stops. The study speaks to coaches and counselors who support sidelined players.
plos-pone-0359650:
Saba Karimi and five colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on diet and health. It assesses how much red meat adults with high blood pressure eat in excess, and then decomposes that excess, breaking it down into the parts explained by different factors. The method is a Wagstaff decomposition analysis.

Decomposition shows whether high meat intake in this group tracks income, education, place, or other influences, and by how much. Hypertension advice almost always includes eating less red meat, so knowing who over-consumes and why sharpens that advice. Nutrition policy researchers are the audience for this anatomy of a dietary pattern.
pmc-10654550:
Jie Wang and eight colleagues published a national survey study in two thousand twenty-three on lifestyle and suboptimal health in China. Suboptimal health means feeling unwell without a diagnosable disease. The team asked which daily habits push people toward that grey zone.

The survey covered one hundred forty-eight cities and kept nearly twenty-three thousand participants. Just over half reported suboptimal health. Current smokers and drinkers faced higher risk than people who never did either. Eating takeaway food more often raised risk step by step. Eating breakfast more often and doing mild exercise lowered it. Short sleep also raised risk compared with sleeping over seven hours. The authors argue daily habits are a lever for prevention.
pmc-10655850:
Anatoly Belostotskii, a solo author, presents a study from twenty twenty-three that maps how electron clouds spread in a set of nitro and azide anions. These ions sit at the heart of some cheap, strong explosives. Where the cloud sits sets how the ion reacts and how it breaks. He uses a bond analysis method on quantum sums to chart the spread on each frame.

In the two pernitro ions, the top cloud hugs the center atom. In kin ions it hugs the oxygen ends, which flips which end takes new groups. One bond in the key explosive ion breaks with ease since stretching it fills a star orbital that fights the bond. A pyramid azide ion holds its charge tight.
pmc-10657350:
Alessia Sarica, Federica Aracri, and colleagues explain a survival model that predicts which patients with mild cognitive impairment will progress to Alzheimer's disease in a 2023 medical study. Random survival forests had already beaten the classic proportional hazards model on this conversion risk task. A black box that outpredicts but cannot explain itself, though, is hard for clinicians to act on.

The authors open the forest up, ranking which patient features drive its risk estimates. Data come from a major Alzheimer's neuroimaging initiative. Explainable risk scores could help doctors counsel patients and enrich prevention trials with those most likely to decline.
pmc-10691650:
Renée Joosen, Johannes Breur, Jeroen Wessels, and a wider team wrote this case series, published in 2023. It argues that a measure of how well the heart's right side matches its load beats simple pressure readings when watching patients whose tetralogy of Fallot was repaired in childhood.

Two patients kept a narrowed outflow path after repair. Doctors combined catheter measurements with heart scans to compute the coupling between the right ventricle and the lung artery. The first patient had no symptoms despite very high pressures, and coupling was preserved; after a widening procedure, function held up over years. The second was breathless despite milder pressures. The authors say gradient numbers alone can mislead in both directions. Coupling, which weighs the pump against what it pumps into, may time repeat procedures better.
pmc-10693150:
Aleš Kvasnička and ten colleagues published a lipid study in two thousand twenty-three on gout and high uric acid. Doctors cannot yet tell which people with high uric acid will progress to painful gout. Blood fat patterns might separate the stages.

The team measured over six hundred fats in blood from healthy controls, people with silent high uric acid, and gout patients, split by early or later onset. Both patient groups showed shifted fat patterns. One fat family rose while a protective group fell. Changes ran deepest in early-onset patients not yet on urate-lowering drugs. Combined patterns separated early-onset groups from controls with high accuracy. Treatment partly corrected the imbalance.
pmc-10694150:
John Ng'ombe and four colleagues use machine learning to find what makes people buy earthquake insurance, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. Oklahoma went through a decade of injection-linked earthquakes. That raised the stakes for coverage. Yet uptake is patchy, and no one could say why.

Eight hundred twelve Oklahoma residents answered a survey for the team. Five supervised learning methods, from logistic regression to random forests, modeled who buys coverage and who does not. Age, gender, race, and ethnicity came out as key drivers of the choice. The models also aimed to pick out the people most apt to buy, so outreach can find them. Tools for environmental risk work just when households take them up in fact. The team frames its findings as guidance for insurers and policymakers. They can use it to close the protection gap before the next quake hits.
pmc-10694950:
Moran, Suhrcke, and Nolte ask what drives first-line care efficiency in Europe. First-line care is a core part of strong health systems. How well it uses funds and staff is poorly mapped. Diabetes care gives a clear tracer for system performance.

The team used data for 18 European states from 2010 to 2016. A two-stage method first scored care efficiency for each state. The next stage linked scores to health system traits. Traits held funds, staff mix, and care gate rules. Results show which traits track with lean, high-value care. Leaders can use those links to shape reform.
pmc-10695950:
Saina Beitari leads a team that tests a nose and muscle vaccine route. Their study from twenty twenty-three uses a virus shell to carry a spike part. The spike comes from the virus that caused COVID.

Mice got two doses by nose, by muscle, or by a mix of both. Blood and cell tests checked the strength of defense. Mix plans that used both routes gave strong results. Nose doses twice also did well in their tests. Route choice shapes both local and whole body defense. The work guides how such shots are given.
pmc-10696850:
Danni Liu leads a team of twelve authors surveying Helicobacter pylori infection household by household across Hainan Province, China, because this stomach bacterium spreads within families. Four hundred twenty-one families, over thirteen hundred people in five cities, were tested between twenty twenty-one and twenty twenty-two, alongside questionnaires on shared living and eating habits.

Individually, about forty-seven percent were infected; risk rose with age over twenty, marriage, and more schooling. At household level the picture was starker: eighty percent of families had at least one infection. Larger households carried sharply higher odds, while higher income and drinking boiled tap water appeared protective. The authors aim the findings at household-level prevention rather than individual treatment alone.
pmc-10699050:
Jiye Yang, Youngnim Shin, Hwee-Jin Kim, Hyo-Eun Kim, and Jang-Soo Chun show that a protein called prokineticin 2 drives cartilage breakdown in osteoarthritic joints. Their mouse study was published in twenty twenty-three.

A low-oxygen switch already known in arthritis raised the protein's levels in joint cartilage cells of mice and humans. Forcing extra protein into cells and cartilage samples boosted two enzymes that chew up cartilage. Injecting the protein into joints had the same effect, while silencing it protected the tissue. Arthritis was triggered in mice by a standard joint surgery to test these moves. Blood tests hinted the protein could also serve as a disease marker. The work names a fresh target for slowing joint decay.
pmc-10701450:
Mirindra R Ratsifandrihamanana and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-three protocol for filming brain activity in awake mouse pups. Calcium imaging with two-photon microscopy reveals how circuits behave during development. Doing it in unanesthetized young pups is technically hard.

The steps cover injecting tracer into the brain fluid spaces of pups. Surgery to install a viewing window comes next. Imaging sessions then record the hippocampus region tied to memory. An analysis pipeline for handling and sharing the data is included. Developmental neuroscientists get a tested recipe, with pointers to the studies that first used it.
pmc-10712050:
Meng-Yuan Jiang and a team of co-authors traced how a fat tissue signal guards the heart in diabetes. Their study, from twenty twenty-three, deals with diabetic cardiomyopathy. In this state the heart leans on fat burning for fuel. Fat build up in heart muscle then poisons it and weakens its work. The signal, adipsin, may play a guard role. The team bred mice with extra adipsin in fat tissue and fed them a high fat diet to spark diabetes.

They found adipsin blocks a partner protein from moving to the cell's power plants. That block lifts fat burning in a clean way and cuts the poison load. Compound reads and cell tests back the path. Readers get a fresh target for a heart ill tied to diabetes.
pmc-10715850:
Dong Shim and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-three on recycling a patient's own cartilage to fix ankle bone lesions. Such lesions in the talus bone cause chronic ankle pain. Many repair routes exist, each with flaws. Their route grinds the lesion's own cartilage into chips and plants them back in the hole. Just over thirty patients took part, with at least a year of follow up.

Nearly all lesions were of the worst grade at the start. Repair scores on scans rose a lot at one year in those checked. Scope looks in a few showed near normal new cartilage. Pain and foot function scores all improved in a clear way. The team calls the route safe and sound for short term gains.
pmc-10729150:
Kurt Jenkins, Miso Park, Magali Pederzoli-Ribeil, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2023. It reports early tests of XTX101, a cancer antibody drug built to switch on only inside tumors, aiming at the benefits of an existing drug class with fewer body-wide side effects.

Drugs that block the CTLA-4 checkpoint can shrink tumors but often trigger harsh immune reactions elsewhere. XTX101 wears a mask: extra peptides block its gripping ends until enzymes common in tumors snip them off. Its tail is also tuned to grip immune cells harder once active. Lab and cell tests confirmed the drug works only after unmasking. In mice carrying the human target gene, the drug alone slowed tumor growth strongly, in some cases clearing tumors. Effects stayed concentrated in the tumor, as the design intends.
pmc-10733450:
Qingchun Ji, Chenglin Zhou, and Yingying Wang published a sports cognition study in twenty twenty-three on how expectations bend a goalkeeper's anticipation. Semi-elite keepers and non-athletes were told how likely a kick was to go each way, then judged videos cut just before, or slightly before, foot met ball. Brain waves were recorded throughout.

Prior information swayed judgments, but the timing differed between groups, pinpointing when expectation hijacks perception. A second experiment with fresh goalkeepers probed the adaptive behavior at that critical moment. The design separates what the eyes see from what the mind presumes. For training, the message is double-edged: scouting reports sharpen anticipation until the opponent breaks the pattern on purpose.
pmc-10736450:
Ling Xu and Lingya Zhao systematically review technology help for dementia care in this two thousand twenty-three paper. Most people with dementia live at home, cared for by informal caregivers, usually family. A wave of technology interventions, from monitoring systems to support apps, aims to help both parties. The authors searched fourteen online databases plus Google Scholar for studies from January two thousand five to January two thousand twenty, screening over three hundred articles down to twenty-three meeting their criteria.

Most included studies found benefits on both sides. Caregivers' psychological condition improved and they received practical help with care tasks. People with dementia performed better, felt better mentally, and stayed safer at home, potentially delaying institutionalization and saving costs. The authors recommend technologies people with dementia can use independently, matched to disease stage, and call for more randomized controlled trials to firm up the evidence.
pmc-10737450:
Shangang Zhao reports laboratory research on leptin and the aging effects of visceral fat. Visceral adiposity is a hallmark of aging and is tied to shorter healthspan and lifespan. Zhao's work tests whether leptin, a hormone produced in fat tissue, drives those harmful effects.

Raising leptin levels in fat tissue sped up diet-induced obesity and glucose intolerance in the experiments. It also promoted inflammation and pushed cells toward senescence, the state where aged cells release inflammatory signals. Removing leptin from visceral fat depots reduced both visceral adiposity and those senescence signals. Zhao concludes that targeting leptin could become a new approach against aging-related metabolic syndromes.
pmc-10738450:
Edmund Duthie and seven co-authors adapted one short lesson on dementia caregiver referrals for students in three health professions. Their report came out in 2023. Family caregivers give most of the care for Americans living with dementia, yet clinicians rarely connect them to community help.

The fifteen-minute lesson teaches a referral program run by a national association and shows students how to promote it in clinics. Students in medicine, nursing, and pharmacy all rated the lesson as highly relevant. Nursing students rated it highest and said they were most likely to make referrals. Most students in each group said they would probably use the program in practice.
pmc-10738550:
Nadine Sikora and co-authors study how the timing of adversity shapes stress hormones in a 2023 paper. Hardship is thought to flatten the daily rhythm of cortisol, a pattern tied to heart and metabolic risk. The team merged two cohort studies with matching measures.

The combined sample held 175 adults with an average age near sixty-one. Childhood trauma reports and adult stressor records were set against saliva cortisol slopes. Overall childhood adversity showed no link to later slopes, though emotional abuse did. The number of adult stressful events, and recent ones especially, also tracked with slopes. Adult stress stayed significant when all measures competed.
pmc-10738950:
Tania Rodriguez and Rachel Wu asked in 2023 what stops low-income Latino older adults from learning new skills. Latino seniors in the United States face higher risks of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias than White older adults, and learning new skills is one way to stimulate cognitive and functional growth. Yet learning opportunities assume resources this population may not have.

The researchers interviewed twenty low-income Latino older adults, in Spanish, by phone, about the obstacles they face when trying to learn something new. Their answers give a first-person catalog of impediments, from cost and transport to health, language, and confidence. Naming those barriers matters for anyone designing classes or interventions for this fast-growing group. Programs that ignore the obstacles will keep enrolling everyone except the people they most hope to reach.
pmc-10739150:
Paola Sosa-Sarmiento, Jose Ocampo-Chaparro, and Carlos Reyes-Ortiz studied heart and blood vessel disease and frailty in Colombia, in a paper from twenty twenty-three. They used a national survey of adults aged sixty and older. Frailty was judged by weakness, slow walking, low activity, tiredness, and weight loss.

About six in ten adults in the sample had some form of cardiovascular disease, and one in five was frail. People with one such disease had higher odds of frailty. People with two or more had higher odds still. The authors suggest that preventing heart and vessel disease may also help prevent frailty in older adults.
pmc-10740150:
Johanna Lemons and nine co-authors test how extracts of three herbs used in traditional Chinese medicine affect the human gut microbiome, the community of microbes living in the gut. Their study came out in 2023. The three plants have long histories of use for gut illness, epidemics, and mental health.

The team used a laboratory fermentation system that mimics the human gut, with samples from several donors. Two extracts shifted the microbe community in similar ways, raising beneficial bacteria and short chain fatty acids, which are helpful products of fermentation. The third extract caused larger changes, raising several species linked to mental health benefits. It also raised a bacterial family that can be harmful for some people, so the tested dose may not suit everyone.
pmc-10742150:
Julie Bergeron and others wrote Canadian consensus guidance on leukemia testing in 2023. One gene fault appears in many myeloid leukemia cases. That fault signals worse results for patients. Testing now shapes first treatment choices. Practice still varied across Canadian centres. A uniform approach was the goal.

Six care questions framed the joint guidance. Topics covered testing at first finding. Relapse testing was also covered. Leftover disease tracking raised further questions. Fault burden and write-ups were covered. Evidence and Canadian know-how were joined. Labs and clinics both get guidance. Steady care across regions should follow.
pmc-10754550:
Chaoyu Huang and four colleagues report brain surgery in a man whose blood lacks clotting factor VII. Congenital factor VII deficiency is the most common of the rare bleeding disorders. Its severity varies widely between patients. The fifty-five-year-old patient had never bled abnormally and had no family history. He needed a craniotomy to remove a papillary tumor near the pituitary region. Bleeding into the brain is a feared complication of such surgery.

Doctors gave eight doses of recombinant activated factor VII plus one dose of plasma around the operation. Dosing was steered by drug-response evaluation, lab tests, and imaging. No excessive surgical bleeding occurred. The twenty twenty-three case report, paired with a literature review, offers a worked perioperative plan for similarly risky patients.
pmc-10811250:
Goncalves-Garcia and Hamilton published a review of how alcohol exposure before birth affects learning and memory. Drinking during pregnancy can alter brain growth and later thinking. Their focus is the hippocampus, a brain area central to memory. They examine long-term potentiation, a lasting strengthening of nerve links tied to learning. Many studies link prenatal alcohol to changes in that process.

The review weighs why results vary so much between studies. Sex, dose patterns, and timing of exposure all seem to matter. It also surveys possible treatments, both drug-based and non-drug approaches. Some show promise for easing harm to thinking skills. The authors say more work is needed on exact mechanisms. Clearer science could lead to better help for affected people.
pmc-10834750:
Chao Zhong and twelve co-authors published a plant genetics study on trehalose-making genes in cultivated peanut. Trehalose supports plant metabolism, growth, and stress tolerance, and two gene families build it. Little was known about those families in peanut, so the team searched the whole genome.

They found sixteen TPS genes and seventeen TPP genes, closely related to those of wild diploid peanuts. Segmental duplication and strong purifying selection shaped the families' evolution. Expression patterns differed across tissues, stages, and treatments, hinting at roles in growth and stress response. Experiments on one gene, AhTPS9, confirmed it helps the plant tolerate cold.
pmc-11534250:
Usman Ali and colleagues analyse depressive symptoms among people living with HIV in Pakistan using national stigma study data. Their 2024 secondary analysis screens nearly fifteen hundred participants with a standard Urdu questionnaire.

About forty percent had no depressive symptoms, while roughly a quarter had mild symptoms. Smaller shares fell into moderate, moderately severe, and severe categories, together covering over a third of participants. Worry about meeting basic needs like food and shelter predicted stronger symptoms. Female sex and substance use also predicted higher scores. Employment predicted lower symptom levels in the regression model. The authors also explored whether stigma in health services moderated symptom patterns.
pmc-11535250:
Jun Shimizu and colleagues report a laboratory study, published in 2024, on how fluid from activated human CD4 T cells affects SARS-CoV-2. The work asks what soluble mediators from those immune cells do to viral spread, and which mediator matters most.

The fluid inhibited viral propagation, but the effect depended on viral strain and host cell type. The original wild-type virus was most susceptible, while the Delta variant resisted in a human monocyte cell line. The fluid also abolished antibody-dependent enhancement for the original strain. The authors attribute most inhibition to interferon-gamma in the fluid, and they argue that new variants should be tested for sensitivity to it.
pmc-11536950:
Yilan Guo leads a team of eleven authors chilling a valuable tropical fish to watch its blood-brain barrier respond. The leopard coral grouper is prized commercially but cold-sensitive, and its low-temperature biology is little studied. Six-month-old fish were cooled from twenty-five to thirteen degrees within a day, then allowed to rewarm naturally.

Serum hormones, enzyme activity, and brain gene expression were tracked through the cycle. The fish first coped by quieting their activity. Changed genes clustered in blood-brain barrier, inflammation, and blood-clotting pathways. A barrier gene, claudin 15a, was confirmed by tissue staining to respond to the cold. The work maps an early molecular alarm system relevant to aquaculture in variable climates.
pmc-11572650:
Metalia Puspitasari and three colleagues catalogued biopsy-proven kidney diseases at their Yogyakarta hospital, including how the pandemic years changed the picture. Biopsy remains the gold standard for classifying glomerular disease. The retrospective review covered seventy-five adults biopsied between twenty seventeen and twenty twenty-two. Mean age was about thirty-two, and fifty-seven percent were women.

Lupus nephritis led the diagnoses at one-third of cases, followed by minimal change disease at about twenty-seven percent. Lupus dominated in women; minimal change led in men. The commonest cause of nephritic syndrome was lupus, and of nephrotic syndrome, minimal change disease. Regional biopsy registries like this twenty twenty-four report guide Indonesian nephrology planning, because imported disease patterns from Western cohorts do not match local reality.
pmc-11583050:
Laurine Choisez and four co-authors examine impurities in iron powder burned as a clean fuel in a two thousand twenty-four paper. Iron powder stores energy in dense form and can be recycled, so it may serve as a sustainable fuel. Yet burning it can release nanoparticles, cause tiny explosions, or leave cavities in the grains. The team ran thermodynamic simulations to screen how the usual impurities in iron sources affect those problems.

Flame temperature and iron evaporation rose with the specific energy of the fuel. Several impurities were also expected to evaporate strongly. Most of them cut cavity formation, with two exceptions. Two mineral additions, magnesia and lime, looked best at cutting nanoparticles and porosity. They also sped the hydrogen based recycling of burnt powder. Well chosen ones could make an already promising fuel still better.
pmc-11586450: Xie and three co-authors reported a single case in twenty twenty-four of a forty-six-year-old woman with chronic heart failure treated with a fifth-generation cardiac contractility modulation device. She had come to the hospital with chest tightness and shortness of breath lasting over a month. Scans showed an enlarged left ventricle, and her heart tracing showed a slow rhythm with a narrow signal width. After the device was implanted, her chest tightness and breathlessness cleared, and her exercise tolerance and quality of life improved markedly.
pmc-11590850:
Hulter, Weggelaar-Jansen, Ahaus, and Pluut read in twenty twenty-four how Dutch patients talk about seeing test results at once on ward portals. Instant access frees folks from waits but hands them a hard pick. Talks with twenty-eight patients, half with portal use, fed the read.

Three talk frames came out of the chats. One frames access as a stress source, from hard words and check urges. One frames it as calm, since waits shrink. One frames it as self-care, with folks set for their doctor talks. Mixed frames call for mixed aid plans, they find.
pmc-11596750:
Dominguez and coauthors track real-world use of a skin repair matrix in head surgery. The matrix helps rebuild soft tissue in head and neck work. Few real-world studies log how much care such patients use. Claims data can fill that gap at large scale.

The team used two large United States claims databases. Records ran from late 2015 to early 2022. Adults had head or neck surgery with the matrix on the same day. All had at least 30 days of cover before and after. The team logged surgery types and return visits. Thirty-day re-do rates were a key outcome of interest.
pmc-11600650:
Gebeyehu and four co-authors review clean delivery kit use in poorer countries, in work from twenty twenty-four. Clean delivery kits hold sterile basics for a safe birth: soap, gloves, a blade, and cord ties. Their use promotes healthy outcomes where births occur at home.

Representative data across low and middle income countries were lacking. The systematic review and meta analysis searched five databases to pool an overall use estimate. Knowing how many mothers actually use kits, not just receive them, helps programs target supply and education. Birth hygiene is among the cheapest ways to cut newborn infection deaths.
pmc-11602750:
Wu, Luo, Wang, and Sang wrote a commentary in twenty twenty-four on how human egg cells build a spindle, the structure that sorts chromosomes during cell division. Getting two clean poles is vital. Faults in this step can leave eggs with the wrong number of chromosomes.

Unlike most cells, human eggs lack the usual pole-forming centers, so they build poles in a distinct way. Small early poles form first and linger through a long phase of division. The authors review work on twenty-one proteins tied to this process. Only three proved essential, each guiding a different phase: growth of the spindle fibers, lengthening, and steady upkeep.
pmc-11606150:
Nobuhiro Goi and four colleagues published a drug study in two thousand twenty-four on eye drops for a rare disease called cystinosis. In this disease, cystine crystals build up in the cornea and make light painful. The study tested cysteamine drops over a year in Japanese patients.

Six patients used the drops for about fourteen months on average. Microscope scores for crystal load trended downward in every cornea layer. Most patients reported at least one step of relief from light sensitivity. Side effects were common but mild, with a tingling feeling reported most often. No serious side effects or deaths occurred. The authors judge the drops effective and well tolerated for this tiny group.
pmc-11608250:
Rasoul Karimi and Behrang Golmohammadi simulate a cleaner ship fuel process in a 2024 paper. New world rules cap sulfur in marine fuel, and the usual removal method needs hydrogen and harsh conditions. Their method, oxidative desulfurization, runs gently without hydrogen: sulfur compounds are oxidized into forms that can be washed out.

The simulation uses acetic acid as catalyst and hydrogen peroxide as oxidant, followed by absorption and distillation steps to separate products and recover materials. The process ran at modest heat and low pressure. Sulfur content fell from three and a half percent to under half a percent by weight. The authors present the design as a viable route to low sulfur marine fuel.
pmc-11608350:
Anil Kumar Vadathya and a large team of colleagues validated FLASH-TV, a system that passively measures how much television children watch. Self-reported viewing is imprecise, so the team built a machine learning pipeline using computer vision. Three validation studies in twenty twenty-four covered a lab pilot, a lab validation, and a home validation. Trained staff labeled observation videos every five seconds to create a gold standard.

Across fifty-nine children with valid data, FLASH-TV 3.0 reached a mean accuracy of eighty-five percent. Its sensitivity was eighty percent and its specificity eighty-six percent. Agreement on total viewing duration was strong, with an intra-class correlation of 0.86. Performance varied more for some children. The system offers researchers a less burdensome, more objective measure of children's screen exposure.
pmc-11611750:
Wesley Stansberry and three co-authors study a mouse model of ALS in a 2024 paper. The disease slowly paralyzes patients, and many gene faults are now linked to it. Their mice carry one such fault, in a gene tied to protein cleanup. The team read which genes were active in motor neurons as the disease progressed.

At one year old, the mice had lost motor neurons and nerve-muscle links, and moved poorly. Gene readings showed pathways for signaling and metabolism shifting in opposite directions. A surprise was that motor neurons normally use several muscle genes, which fell sharply in sick mice. The authors suggest those genes may help neurons support muscle.
pmc-11613350:
Kulakova and eight colleagues link testosterone levels to symptoms in women with borderline personality disorder in twenty twenty-four. Women with this disorder often show raised baseline testosterone. The team asked whether hormone levels track specific symptoms. They expected links to aggressive or impulsive behaviour, based on ties to dominance.

Saliva samples came from ninety-eight women with the disorder, aged eighteen to forty-six. Self rating scales measured borderline and depressive symptom severity. Higher testosterone linked to higher total scores on both scales. Item level analysis tied it to self dislike, senselessness, and pessimism. A sense of being a failure also rose with testosterone. The pattern points inward, not outward, contrary to the team's expectation. The authors note this cluster reflects a harsh view of the self.
pmc-11614150:
Patrick, Terry-McElrath, Arterberry, and Miech report a survey study from twenty twenty-four on why teens in the United States vape. Vaping can lead to nicotine habit and harm the lungs, heart, and brain. The team used school survey data from twenty twenty-one to twenty twenty-three. They asked students in three grades who had vaped in the past year to name their main reasons.

Near-daily vaping rose with age, from a small share in the youngest group to a larger share in the oldest. Students picked from a list of thirteen reasons for vaping. The study sorts those reasons by grade and by how often students vape. The results can help schools and health staff plan steps to cut teen vaping.
pmc-11615350:
Rinako Nakagawa and colleagues show how a small RNA rescues antibody-making cells from lack of oxygen inside germinal centers. To raise affinity, B cells picked in the light zone must divide there, in a low-oxygen zone hostile to cell cycling. From there, high-affinity clones move to the dark zone to multiply using oxidative phosphorylation. How they adjust their metabolism was unknown.

The team shows microRNA-155 drives metabolic reprogramming during positive selection, protecting such clones. It represses a histone demethylase that rises under hypoxia, and so controls a histone methylation mark. That epigenetic control tunes gene expression in the nucleus for mitochondria, keeping oxidative phosphorylation going while holding back excess reactive oxygen species and cell death. The study names an epi-microRNA circuit: a tiny RNA tuning chromatin to keep the energy supply of the immune system's best antibody factories running.
pmc-11618350:
Andrea Pedroni and eight co-authors published a neuroscience study in twenty twenty-four mapping the nervous system inside the zebrafish heart. The brain's control of the heart is well studied, but the heart's own local network was largely uncharted. The team combined single-cell RNA sequencing, anatomy, and electrical recordings to classify its neurons.

They found far more neuronal variety than expected. One group resembled pacemaker neurons known from central pattern generator circuits in the brain. That suggests the heart carries its own rhythm-shaping circuitry, not just relays from above. The taxonomy gives cardiac researchers a reference for studying how this hidden network keeps the beat and how it fails in disease.
pmc-11620450:
Xavier Gasparutto and five co-authors published a biomechanics study in twenty twenty-four on how the whole body walks before and after knee replacement, not just the knee. One hundred osteoarthritis patients and thirty-two healthy controls underwent full gait analysis, repeated a year after surgery. Clustering patients by whole-body movement, deliberately excluding the knee itself, sorted them into three functional groups.

The groups differed in posture, limb motion, and walking parameters, and in how they reported their own recovery. The design asks whether deviations elsewhere in the body persist after the joint is fixed, and whether they explain why a fifth of patients stay dissatisfied. Phenotyping gait this way could let rehabilitation target the pattern, not only the prosthesis.
pmc-11623450:
Noda and co-authors test phone app coaching for diet in Japanese health guidance. Japan runs checkups and guidance to curb lifestyle disease. Dropout and fading gains plague the standard program. The team added app-based diet help for one group. The other group got standard human coaching alone.

They tracked 109 people in 3-month and 6-month cohorts. The main target was change in non-HDL cholesterol. Lipid panels and metabolic marks were tracked as well. App login counts showed how much the tool was used. Early results point to a clear shift in the main cholesterol mark for app users.
pmc-11625250:
Karthik and three co-authors built a step-by-step chart to guide Ayurvedic treatment of anemia in children, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Ayurveda, the traditional Indian medical system, has its own rich ways of naming diseases and picking remedies. Those ways can be hard to learn and apply quickly.

The chart focuses on bhasmas, specially prepared mineral remedies used to treat the anemia condition called Pandu. Classic texts on the disease's causes and signs were gathered and sorted into groups. Each group is matched with the remedies that suit it. The chart was tested and tuned at one center. The authors say wider trials across centers, with later fixes, are still needed.
pmc-11626750:
Khalil, Issa, and Kamal measured a developmental gene's protein in thyroid tumors in twenty twenty-four. Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the commonest thyroid cancer and usually curable, yet about ten percent of patients die within ten years, mainly from spread to neck lymph nodes. The SIX1 protein helps build tissues in the embryo and may mark aggressive tumors.

Using antibody staining on one hundred twenty-five tumors, the team compared the classic subtype with the follicular variant. High SIX1 levels tracked with larger tumors, multiple tumor foci, lymph node spread, higher grade and stage, and invasion beyond the thyroid. The exact partners differed by subtype: size and grade in classic tumors, nodal spread and invasion in the variant. The authors propose SIX1 as a prognostic marker guiding subtype-specific strategies.
pmc-11629250:
Junya Ebina and colleagues compare tracer uptake in the major salivary glands between Lewy body diseases and a look-alike movement disorder. Their 2024 imaging study tests whether gland scans help separate Parkinson's disease from progressive supranuclear palsy.

Heart nerve loss is specific to Lewy body disease, and salivary glands show similar nerve loss in Parkinson's. Over one hundred patients and controls underwent the scan in glands and heart. Gland uptake in the delayed phase was significantly lower in Parkinson's and Lewy body dementia than in the palsy group and controls. Gland scanning showed higher diagnostic specificity than smell testing between Parkinson's and palsy, with sensitivity comparable in one gland group.
pmc-11632350:
Gularte and co-authors describe a new species of bone-eating worm from the deep South Atlantic. Osedax worms colonize sunken bones on the sea floor. Divers found this one on cow bones set out at 550 meters off Brazil. It is only the second Osedax known from the Southwest Atlantic. Five gene markers placed it firmly in Osedax Clade V. Its nearest kin live in the Pacific, though that link is weak.

The new species, named nataliae, differs from every known relative by at least 13.9% in a key gene. Within the species, variation stayed under 2.5%. Body traits complete the formal description. Haplotype maps show the population's structure.
pmc-11633650:
Weitong Wang, Ya Zhu, Monika Osterberg, and Bruno Mattos refine plant tannins by split steps for use in Pickering emulsions. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Works tannins from black wattle are rich but mixed, which clouds fine use. A soak-based split gave clean cuts with low spread, read by magnet and mass tools.

Cuts of distinct weights were used to brace oil drops with chitin fibrils. Drop size and traits tuned with cut weight, through how tannin and chitin meet at the oil face. Tannin adds firm, spring traits, and strain guard to the drops. The team backs the split as a cheap way to fit tannins to top goods.
pmc-11638750:
Rhyu wrote an essay in twenty twenty-four on the rise of smart writing tools in science. These tools can now draft text, build ideas, and even list sources from a short prompt. Rhyu notes that journals must now check if a sudden burst of papers hides misuse of such tools. The essay asks who should steer the work, the author or the tool.

Rhyu warns that these tools can invent false claims that slip past busy authors. Fake or unchecked text could then mislead readers who trust the journal. The essay also notes how hard it grows to tell machine text from human text. It urges authors to check every line and own the final work.
pmc-11640250:
Nadya Kagansky and colleagues published a 2024 study of chest pain decisions in emergency departments. Chest pain brings huge numbers to emergency care. Many cases remain unclear after first tests. Doctors must choose admission or discharge. The team reviewed four hundred patient records.

Most patients had been referred by primary care. About three in five went home. Admitted patients were notably older. Night-shift arrivals were admitted more often. High blood fats predicted admission strongly. Risk scores and lab results also mattered. Knowing decision drivers can standardize triage. It may also reveal where caution outweighs the evidence.
pmc-11642650:
Mari-Roig and seven co-authors review airway care for severe face fractures, in work from twenty twenty-four. Panfacial fractures break many parts of the face skeleton at once. They often come with other trauma and need several surgeries in a short time.

Keeping the airway open is hard. Doctors must check how the teeth meet, and the nose and skull base may be too harmed for standard tubes through mouth or nose. A tube through the chin area is used more often to avoid a neck opening and its risks. The review compares all options and proposes a step by step plan to guide surgical teams.
pmc-11644350:
Perakis, Gikas, and Retscher sharpen indoor positioning from phone radio signals in twenty twenty-four. Ultra wideband and Wi-Fi round trip timing can locate walkers where satellite signals fail. Error models for each radio type were built and tested on real and simulated runs. A shared mode lets walkers' devices help locate each other.

Fusion of the two radios cut position error sharply for both types. The peer mode helped most when fixed anchors dropped out for short spells. With anchors live, gains were modest but real. The engine targets group navigation on foot. Phone based services stand to gain accuracy from the scheme.
pmc-11644950:
Ráfales-Perucha and a team including Bravo-Viñuales and Molina-Molina checked in twenty twenty-four a shoe-top step tool for walk traits in a large group. Shoe tools can give live walk news and spot gait flaws, but many lack proof. They had more than four hundred folks walk on a belt at a set pace.

The shoe tool was read next to a light-gate tool for step rate, length, and times. Most traits matched with strong links and small shifts between the tools. Touch time and swing time matched less well than the rest. The team backs the shoe tool for walk checks at large.
pmc-11647550:
Alidadi, Rabiei, Akbari, Emami, and Laal Mousavi review mobile apps for breast cancer aftercare, in work from twenty twenty-four. App use in postoperative care has risen fast in recent years. What features those apps offer, and which needs they meet, needed a synthesis.

The scoping review searched five databases for all articles up to mid twenty twenty-four. A classic scoping framework guided selection and charting. Features were grouped to show the state of the field. Such a map helps developers avoid rebuilding what exists and focus on gaps in recovery support, from wound checks to mood tracking.
pmc-11648550:
Guangdi Li, Guiwen Zhou, Qiang Fu, and Minliang Chen report deep harm to a belly wall after liposuction care went wrong. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Liposuction sucks fat out through low pressure to shape the body. It is seen as a safe act, but poor judgement by some clinics has raised its harms.

A patient has fluid under the skin after waist and belly liposuction. Shots of a hardening agent and two rounds of dead tissue removal follow. Scans then show defects through many layers of the right lower belly wall, with a tear in the inner lining. The case is a warning on the use of such shots.
pmc-11651950:
Pengzhi Nan and colleagues build a model that combines two kinds of brain imaging information to diagnose Alzheimer's disease. Their 2024 study uses structural magnetic resonance imaging, which shows brain structural abnormalities with high contrast and resolution.

Most earlier work used only image-space information from disease-related regions, ignoring network relationships between regions. The new model adds a graph channel representing those connections alongside a multiscale image channel. Each participant's grey-matter volume feeds the combined representation. The authors aim to improve early diagnosis by joining both spatial views. Node aggregation mechanisms in the graph network help capture how brain regions interact.
pmc-11653050:
Miyakoshi and co-authors tie blood sugar reads to body and food facts from polls. Wrist gear can grab more than one body fact at one time. Such gear feeds find, guess, and care picks for ills. Food and moves sway blood sugar, yet live links stayed loose. The team mines a free bank, PhysioNet, for those links. Bank facts join wrist reads with food poll facts per host.

Three read ways drive the work in the bank sets. First, pair ties test if mean or spread of body facts tracks sugar. Lag reads shift facts in time to catch lead and trail ties. Next, post-meal sugar rise and fall get set next to facts. Food scores join the same post-meal checks in the bank. The aim is a live map of what moves sugar.
pmc-11653850:
Osman Savran, Klaus Bønnelykke, and Charlotte Ulrik follow severe childhood asthma into adult lung disease, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. Their Danish cohort held 232 adults who had spent months at a childhood asthma center. The team sorted those with fixed airflow limits by smoking history.

Thirty people fit the asthma-origin COPD type and twenty-three the smoking type. Both groups had more flare-ups than peers with clear airways. The smoking group breathed harder and carried more of one inflammation cell. The asthma group kept better lung volume and higher breath nitric oxide.
pmc-11653950:
Chi-Tung Chen, Mao-Wang Ho, and Wei-Hsin Chung published a case report in two thousand twenty-four on a rare fungal infection spread through the body. A healthy sixty-one-year-old farmer came in with blurred vision, double vision, low fever, and headache. He also had a year of back pain after a fall.

Scans found masses near his spine and several ring-shaped lesions in his brain. Tissue tests confirmed Cryptococcus gattii, a fungus that usually strikes people with weak immunity. Blood work revealed the hidden cause: his own antibodies were blocking a key immune growth factor. Antifungal drugs followed, first a strong infusion then a milder pill. Within a month his symptoms eased, and scans a year later showed the lesions gone.
pmc-11654350:
Bachmann and a large team of colleagues agree a core set of gut checks for the most ill adults in this twenty twenty-four study. Gut failure is rife in such patients and ties to poor fates, yet wards check it in unlike ways. A shared set would let future studies speak to each other.

Inside, ward staff, lab staff, and patient voices rated a long list of gut traits in two rounds. From scores of first picks, the group kept just over a dozen core checks. The set spans belly swell, gut bleed, stool pass, and food pipe use, each with a fixed sense. The authors give the set as a frame for all new gut work in sick wards.
pmc-11655650:
Fu-Der Chen and a large team build a silicon brain probe that shines a steerable beam of light from inside the brain, in a twenty twenty-four paper. Shining patterned light on single brain cells lets scientists switch those cells on and study their roles. Brain tissue scatters light, so the light source must sit deep inside. Their probe carries tiny light circuits that form one clean beam without lenses.

The design pairs phased light emitters with grating structures to cut stray side beams, tuned for blue or amber light. In mice, the probe gave enough light power to switch brain cells on. Scattering in tissue widened the beam and the steering range proved narrow. Still, the work shows a path toward compact probes for precise light-based brain studies.
pmc-11655850:
Soaad Soboh and colleagues show that heparanase-two, a protein long overlooked, suppresses tumour growth in cervical carcinoma. Their 2024 study links higher levels of the protein to better patient outcomes.

High protein levels correlated with prolonged survival and lower tumour grade in patients. Overexpressing it in cervical cancer cells produced tumours half the size of controls in animal grafts. Two patient-derived mutant forms produced even smaller tumours. The protein interacts with another protein that moves into the cell nucleus in mutant tumours. Experiments in engineered mice further showed the protein shapes macrophage polarisation, since its absence shifted macrophages toward a pro-tumour state.
pmc-11657350:
Yong Ng and six co-authors map how middle-aged adults use health care and what drives those patterns. Their scoping review was published in twenty twenty-four. People aged forty-five to sixty-four use services heavily yet are rarely studied as their own group.

The team searched three databases through mid twenty twenty-three for original studies in English. Cohort, case-control, and cross-sectional designs all qualified. Findings were grouped with a classic model that sorts drivers into predisposing traits, enabling resources, and need. Income, insurance, illness burden, and habits each shaped use in their own way. The map shows where midlife care reaches people and where it quietly misses them.
pmc-11663250:
Darrian Talamantes, Caitlin Kirkpatrick, and Jason Wallace develop measurement tools for a grass and its fungal partner in a 2024 paper. Tall fescue owes much of its toughness to a fungus living inside it, which shields the grass from stress. Existing tests only check whether the fungus is present, not how much of it there is.

The team compared several primer sets, the short DNA anchors used in quantitative PCR, for both the grass and the fungus. They report standard curves, fit quality, and efficiency for every candidate. The best sets allow side by side biomass estimates of host and partner. Such measurement matters for breeding and managing fescue pastures where the fungus's benefits and risks both scale with its amount.
pmc-11665850:
Giulia Pisegna, Suropriya Saha, and Ramin Golestanian study order in active matter in this two thousand twenty-four physics paper. Active matter is made of units that move on their own, like bacteria or tiny motors. Here the units are not polar; none has a built-in head or tail. Their interactions are nonreciprocal, meaning the pull between two units need not be mutual. Standard rules would not predict flocking from such parts.

The authors show that true long-range polar order still arises in two dimensions and up. They map their mixture theory onto a classic theory of flocking. A well-chosen order measure makes the mapping exact. Checks at linear level and beyond confirm the result. The paper expands what kinds of matter can organize into directed motion.
pmc-11666550:
Cinzia Bussè and co-authors review how Lewy body disease harms sight-based skills and memory, from its earliest stage to full dementia. Dementia with Lewy bodies stands out for weak attention and executive function and poor visual processing, while memory stays fairly spared at first. That pattern is the key to telling it apart from Alzheimer disease, where memory fails early. The review sums up studies that use targeted tasks to sharpen the contrast.

The evidence shows deep faults in visual-spatial and visual-construction skills in the prodromal stage, when impairment is still mild. In the same stage, patients do fairly well on memory tasks that rest on the hippocampus. Spotting these early signs through clinic and cognitive tests is the first step. It guides which scans and lab work-ups to order.
pmc-11668350:
Hans-Christoph Nothdurft reports, published in 2024, that people judging whether two textures look alike barely weigh the direction of the pattern. Texture research has long chased how the eye splits scenes into regions. Judging sameness between two fields is a different skill. In his experiments, observers compared patches that varied in two traits at once. In one series the traits were color and line angle. In another, both were spatial: grain size and angle. Again and again, angle was shrugged off.

Patches were grouped as similar when they matched in color or in grain, even with crossing angles. Orientation ranked lowest among the traits tested. Nothdurft reads the result as a weighting fact about similarity judgment, not about seeing angle itself. Designers of texture studies should not assume all visible differences count equally. Some plainly visible traits float to the top of a sameness call, and direction sinks.
pmc-11669950:
Li and four co-authors show how a growth call throttles breast cell sac flow in this twenty twenty-four study. Cells shed tiny sacs that bear news to kin cells near a growth. The call aids growth spread through those sacs in ways still dim.

Inside, the call mutes one haul gene through a mid switch in the cell. With that gene low, sac flow out of the cells drops hard. Sac loads then grow rich and shift mix in the same runs. Sacs so re-mixed blunt kill-cell strikes on the growth in tests. The pair of call and gene thus steers growth fate by sacs.
pmc-11672650:
Seyed Hossein Hoseinifar and colleagues update the search for probiotic microbes to keep farmed fish and shellfish healthy. Dense fish farming invites disease outbreaks at larval and adult stages. Vaccines and antibiotics have limits, so focus has shifted to helpful microbes and related products. Most probiotic research has reused the same two bacterial groups, Bacillus and lactic acid bacteria. The review widens the field to bacteria tied to the host, outside those groups.

Genera such as Bifidobacterium, Clostridium, and Micrococcus have of late shown benefits in aquatic animals. The authors survey evidence for these newer candidates and how they work. Lasting fish farming needs disease control that does not breed antibiotic resistance. A broader probiotic bench gives farmers more living tools matched to their species and systems.
pmc-11673050:
Zsuzsanna Piros and a large team study whether ringing in the ears may flag hidden fat trouble in the blood. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Past work on tinnitus and lipid levels gave mixed results. They compare a clinic group in Hungary with official rates for the whole adult population.

Patients with long-term tinnitus of no known cause have far higher rates of lipid disorder than the public rate. The gap holds when age bands are split, which rules out age as the sole cause, since both ills rise with age. The authors urge a lipid check for each tinnitus patient, which could catch heart risk early.
pmc-11673150:
Vicenta Martinez-Corcoles and seven co-authors test shoe insoles for balance in older adults in a 2024 trial. Falls are a major risk after sixty five, partly because the sense of foot position fades with age. One hundred fifty healthy adults, average age about sixty nine, stood barefoot and with hard and soft insoles while balance was measured.

Soft insoles gave the worst postural control in all conditions, with eyes open and closed. Hard insoles also failed to improve on barefoot standing. The authors conclude insole density matters for standing balance, and soft insoles may actually impair it in healthy older adults. The findings caution against assuming cushioned insoles help balance.
pmc-11676950:
Jiang and co-authors test low doses of spinetoram on the tomato leaf miner. The moth is a major pest of tomato crops in many lands. Lab tests dipped leaves for third-stage larvae. Two low doses, LC10 and LC20, were the focus. Growth, breeding output, and enzyme shifts were tracked.

Low doses stretched larval and pupal stages and the egg-laying span. Pupal weight, pupation rate, and egg hatch all fell. Female share and total eggs laid dropped as well. Two antioxidant enzymes rose sharply in the first two days. Detox enzymes fell by up to half in the same span.
pmc-11677450:
Filipe Pinheiro and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-four mouse study of sulfur amino acid restriction and heart remodelling on a high-fat diet. Cutting these amino acids brings broad health gains, some via the hormone FGF21. Heart effects were mixed and poorly mapped.

Normal and FGF21-deficient mice ate four diet combinations for five weeks. Restriction trimmed weight and belly fat while raising FGF21. Heart tissue shifted toward burning fat, taking up glucose, and building mitochondria. Stress, inflammation, and cell-death gene signals from the fatty diet were blunted. Most heart benefits persisted without FGF21, widening diet-based options.
pmc-11678450:
Bruna Chwal and colleagues followed Brazilian adults with diabetes in two thousand twenty-four. Guidelines push bad cholesterol very low for most patients. These patients were not at high heart risk. Trial evidence for mortality benefit stays inconclusive here. Real-world data hinted at greater deaths instead. The cohort was tracked for about a decade.

People at guideline target levels died more often. The lowest group showed the highest adjusted risk. Risk was greatest for cancer deaths specifically. Older participants showed stronger excess risk. Early deaths did not explain the pattern. Frailty checks also failed to explain it. The findings challenge one-size cholesterol targets.
pmc-11678550:
Michael Wang, Jonathan Sussman, Jessica Xu, and a wider team wrote this narrative review, published in 2024. It surveys drugs that target PRC2, a gene-silencing complex that cancer can hijack in either direction, sometimes driving tumors and sometimes restraining them.

Because the complex can help or hinder cancer, therapy must be selective. The review gathers the leading inhibitors. Tazemetostat and GSK126 block the complex's engine subunit, including lymphoma-linked mutant forms. Valemetostat and UNC1999 hit both engine variants at once and can be swallowed, a guard against resistance. Other drugs aim at the complex's supporting subunits instead. The authors compare promise and risk across lymphomas and solid tumors. Their aim is one unified map of a crowded, fast-moving field, so clinicians and developers can see which lever each drug pulls.
pmc-11680250:
Sarah Jensen, Alexandra Kehl, and Urs Giger survey a genetic blood and muscle disease in spaniels. Their genotyping survey from twenty twenty-four covers English springer spaniels across Europe. The syndrome causes anaemia, muscle weakness, and newborn losses. A frameshift variant in one gene causes the recessive disorder.

Over eight hundred samples arrived from eighteen European countries. A targeted DNA test separated normal and variant gene copies. The variant allele appeared in roughly one in ten gene copies. A few dogs carried two copies and would be affected. Many more carried one copy silently as carriers. Breeders can now test before mating to avoid affected puppies.
pmc-11683650:
Brenda Velázquez-Dodge and colleagues studied a human protein that ferries a sugar acid into the cell's Golgi compartment, where it is attached to other molecules. They focused on a shortened form of the carrier, missing a chunk of fifty-nine building blocks. A known disease-causing change was tested in both the full and shortened forms.
