The change did far less harm in the shortened form than in the full one. A computer model, built from mouse and maize versions of the protein, helped explain why. The work is the first to map how this shortened form works. It shows that splice variants can soften the blow of a harmful gene change.
pmc-11690150:
Charles Hoy-Ellis and four co-authors study, in twenty twenty-four, partner violence among transgender older adults. This group faces more violence and abuse than peers of the same age. That raises risk of poor health, disability, low mood, and stress. The team uses survey data on more than two thousand five hundred lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender adults. Ages ran from fifty to ninety-five. Transgender respondents numbered one hundred sixty-seven.

Transgender adults faced partner violence at more than twice the rate of their peers in the survey. Among them, such violence linked strongly to more victim blaming and hidden shame. It also predicted worse mental quality of life and more low mood signs.
pmc-11690550:
Jacqueline Eaton and five co-authors assess age inclusion in a nursing college, in twenty twenty-four. Their site is the research-heavy College of Nursing at the University of Utah. Split age groups, they note, can leave students less ready to work with older adults. The team ran a campus climate survey in late twenty twenty-three and shared it by email and code scans.

Two hundred forty-seven people replied, most of them students. More than half did not know the age-friendly campus push. Most saw age bias as a big social problem, but far fewer saw it as a problem at their own college. The results point to gaps the college can act on.
pmc-11690950:
Joann Montepare gave a presentation in 2024 on how to become more dementia-inclusive in and beyond the classroom. The number of people living with the illness is set to rise sharply as people age. Calls for action have emphasized stigma, knowledge, diagnosis, and caregiving, but have often overlooked teaching young adults.

Montepare shares a survey of 106 students across diverse classes. More than half had experience with someone living with dementia or Alzheimer's disease. Their knowledge was low, yet they expressed strong concern about developing the condition and interest in learning activities. She supports adding such work to age-friendly university programs. It also describes practical tools, such as narrative work in class and a buddy scheme in the wider community, that let students learn by doing.
pmc-11691150:
Barbara King and Linsey Steege interview older patients about what walking during a hospital stay means to them. Their study came out in 2024. Older adults often lose the ability to walk independently in hospital, and that loss is the biggest threat to living independently after discharge.

Fifteen patients were interviewed in depth three months after going home. Patients described walking as valuable in four connected ways. It helped them manage illness, filled empty time, showed them whether they were ready to go home, and kept them connected with other patients and staff. Walking also limited loneliness and boredom. The authors argue that care built around the patient's own view of walking could protect function better.
pmc-11692650:
Angela Gutierrez and four co-authors published a study in 2024 on allostatic load among Latinx adults in the United States. Allostatic load is the wear and tear on the body that builds up from long-term stress, and it is a sign of faster physical aging. The researchers asked how neighborhood conditions and social life together shape it.

The study drew on data for 319 adults aged fifty or older, followed across three waves over a span of years. People who felt lonelier had higher allostatic load at the start. When social support was added to the analysis, the link with loneliness became weaker and was no longer statistically significant. Perceived disorder in the neighborhood mattered less. The authors suggest that efforts to build social support, designed for this group, could help protect health as people age.
pmc-11692750:
Evan Plys, Makenna Law, Morgan Seward, and Ana-Maria Vranceanu report a 2024 qualitative study of staff views in nursing homes. Short nursing home stays after a hospital visit are a stressful time for patients and their caregivers. The authors asked what a joint support program for patient and caregiver should contain, and how it should run.

Five focus groups with 28 staff members, from leaders to clinical and office workers, named the main needs. Staff said they need help responding to psychological concerns, and that services for short-stay pairs are lacking. Themes covered fear of declining health, reactions to lost independence, and effects on rehabilitation and discharge. The findings shaped a program called BRISK, to be tested in a pilot study. Programs built with staff input are more likely to fit real care settings.
pmc-11693050:
Jiaying Li and three co-authors map how everyday tasks and thinking skills connect in older adults without dementia, to find which links matter most. Their study came out in 2024. The analysis covered more than two thousand Americans over sixty-five.

Network analysis placed meal preparation at the center of the daily-task web, and visual attention at the center of the cognitive web. Shopping bridged the two webs, linking tasks to thinking. In women, laundry and meal preparation were tied more strongly than in men, and meal work sat even more centrally. The authors suggest that training meal preparation, visual attention, and shopping gives the most benefit per effort. They warn that meal-based programs may need redesign for men.
pmc-11694050:
Debra Jones, Anne Marie Sowerbutts, and Sorrel Burden gathered health professionals' views on a mobile app for malnutrition screening. The Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool, called MUST, is standard in United Kingdom care settings. Paper versions invite calculation errors, and web versions need internet access. A phone app with simple navigation could screen more accurately in more places. The twenty twenty-four qualitative study ran online focus groups with potential users.

Participants reacted to the app's content, design, functionality, and usefulness while it ran in demonstration mode. Their feedback was analyzed with deductive and inductive framework methods. Malnutrition is a huge global problem, with hundreds of millions of adults underweight. The study shows what front-line staff need before a screening app can work in daily practice.
pmc-11699250:
Xiaofeng Zhang, Jian Hu, and ten co-authors studied a fat-tissue signal in Crohn's disease, in work from twenty twenty-four. In Crohn's, fat near the gut swells and sends out signals that may shape the disease. One such signal, SFRP5, is known to shield cells. The team measured it in patient tissue and tested its effects in gut cell models and mice.

The signal ran high in the swollen fat of Crohn's patients and pooled near gut lining cells. In lab and mouse tests, it eased harm to the gut wall. It did so in part by blocking a path that pushes gut cells to die. The work points to the fat-gut route as a drug target.
pmc-11709750:
Dorota Kossowska-Kuhn, Gillian Gouveia, and Neil Charness published a 2025 meta-analysis of spatial navigation in mild cognitive impairment. Losing one’s way is one of the earliest signs of Alzheimer’s disease. The authors combined earlier studies comparing people with mild impairment against healthy older adults on navigation tasks.

Across 47 studies with 2,916 participants, the impairment group performed worse by a large margin. The team then tested what changed the size of that gap. Age and the type of task both mattered: maze tests, route tasks, and map tests did not perform alike. The authors call for agreement on how navigation skill should be measured. A standard test could become an early warning tool for dementia.
pmc-11713050:
Shreya Harikrishnan and a large team of co-authors published this study in two thousand twenty-five on a test made for people with severe dementia. Common screens like the MoCA bottom out in this group: too many people score at the floor, so real differences are lost.

The team checked the English form of the Severe Cognitive Impairment Rating Scale against the MoCA in one hundred forty-one people with dementia. Scores on the two tests tracked each other well, which backs the new scale as a true measure. The floor problem was much smaller on the new scale than on the MoCA. Many people who scored at the MoCA floor still spread out across the new scale. The authors say the scale can track thinking in severe dementia where older screens go blind.
pmc-11715750:
Emilie Reas and co-authors investigated in 2025 whether lingering problems after COVID-19 leave measurable traces in the brain's barrier and wiring. Some older adults develop persistent neurological symptoms after illness, and the fear is that the virus accelerates the processes of Alzheimer's disease. A leading suspect is the blood-brain barrier, the selective wall between blood and brain. Its breakdown is implicated in Alzheimer's. It is known to vary with sex and with the APOE4 gene variant.

The team studied older adults between fifty and ninety. One group was small, with post-COVID mental impairment, and the other was larger, without it. Both were studied using psychological testing plus two magnetic resonance methods. One method, contrast-enhanced imaging, measures barrier leakiness. The other, multi-shell diffusion imaging, probes tissue microstructure. Their study asked whether the groups differed, and whether sex and APOE4 status changed the gaps, as the title announces.
pmc-11728450:
Valeria Daniele and three colleagues published a materials study in two thousand twenty-four on a greener way to make tiny zinc-based particles. Simonkolleite nanoparticles have layered hexagonal shapes and can turn into zinc oxide. Older routes need more steps or high heat.

Their one-step process works in water at room temperature and pressure. It yields nearly ten kilograms a week of pure, crystal-grade particles in eight minutes of reaction. Each flake is built from very small grains only a few nanometres wide. The particles reached the highest surface area reported for this material. They can also convert to zinc oxide without heating. The authors stress the low environmental cost.
pmc-11788150:
Knez, Narat, and Ogorevc study an immune sensor in lung cells, in work dated twenty twenty-four. Sensors called Toll like receptors spot virus parts and start innate defense. The role of one sensor, TLR10, in COVID infection was poorly known.

The team raised TLR10 levels in human lung cells in the lab. They then exposed the cells to two viral proteins from the COVID virus. Extra TLR10 mostly lowered swelling signals and interferons. It also changed gene activity in immune cells grown alongside. The authors suggest TLR10 may dampen the response, a hint that tuning it could one day affect care.
pmc-11805250:
Vinaykumar Suryavanshi and colleagues compare leakage of root-end fillings boosted with chitosan gel. Their dental study from twenty twenty-four uses extracted premolar teeth. A poor tip seal is a top cause of root surgery failure. Fillings must block contaminants from reaching surrounding tissue.

Sixty single-rooted teeth were prepared and sealed for the test. Two standard cements were tested with and without chitosan. Dye uptake measured how much each filling leaked. Chitosan cut leakage in both cement types. The gain reached significance for one cement pairing. Natural chitosan may upgrade common dental materials cheaply. Bench results need clinical follow-up before routine use.
pmc-12514950:
Seiji Nakagame and colleagues demonstrate a 2024 process for making a key polyester ingredient from wood waste instead of oil. Terephthalic acid is the backbone of common polyester, and making it from fossil fuels adds to warming. Earlier biomass routes leaned on energy-hungry chemistry. This team built a gentler route run by microbes.

They tested six underused plant waste materials and chose hardwood, rich in cellulose. A hot alkaline wash stripped away the lignin, and enzymes then broke the fibers into sugars. Two microbes finished the job in relay: one turned the sugars into an intermediate compound, and the other oxidized it into terephthalic acid. Only small amounts were produced, but the full chain worked. The authors offer the result as proof that polyester's base can come from renewable plant matter.
pmc-12690150:
Taha, Zaher, and Shehata tested in twenty twenty-five a layered mineral mix that can clean a common drug from waste water in two ways. The drug, a germ killer, lingers in water and can harm life and health. Their mix both soaks the drug up and breaks it with sun light.

In lab tests the mix took up the drug fast at a set dose and pH. Sun runs broke down near four-fifths of the drug in one hour. Form reads backed the mix's high pull for the drug. A green wash with plant aids can renew the mix for reuse, they add.
pmc-12699550:
Manandi and six co-authors review how cardiac rehab gains vary with a person's social and money position, in a review from twenty twenty-five. Rehab after a heart event cuts death and return to hospital on the whole. Whether the gains differ by social position was not clear. Six studies that cover over five hundred fifty thousand people are included.

People who take part die and go back to hospital less than those who do not. Some of the largest gains show up in poor areas. Schooling shows no clear gap for the combined count of deaths. Return to work and knowledge favor the better-off more. Rehab shaped to fit people's lives and reading skills could even out the gains.
pmc-12703050:
Maryam Alikamali and four colleagues review how the vaginal germ mix links to early breaking of the waters in pregnancy, in a twenty twenty-five article. This event, called PPROM, affects about four to five percent of pregnancies and is a top cause of early birth. A healthy vaginal mix is ruled by Lactobacillus germs; a shifted mix is suspect. The team searched three databases for studies on the germ mix and this complication.

The gathered proof sketches a chain: harmful germs climb upward and trigger swelling signals. That swelling attacks the fetal membranes in three ways at once: enzymes chew their fibers, cells die on cue, and oxygen stress damages tissue. Standard antibiotics show limits, so the authors discuss newer care ideas.
pmc-12711950:
Sarah Le Diagon, Jean-Baptiste Van der Henst, and Jérôme Prado followed up a Montessori experiment in 2025 and found a benefit that arrived five years late. In an earlier randomized trial in France, an adapted Montessori kindergarten curriculum produced larger reading gains than conventional schooling. Such early gains often fade, so the researchers recovered the children five years later, when they were ten or eleven and studying in ordinary classrooms. Ninety-seven children were retested on academic, cognitive, and social skills.

The reading advantage had vanished, matching the usual fadeout pattern. But the Montessori group now clearly outperformed peers on mathematical problem-solving, an effect that had not been present in kindergarten. A delayed effect is scientifically provocative: some educational seeds may germinate only when later schooling gives them something to build on. The finding argues for judging early programs over years, not months.
pmc-12716250: This record documents a sixty-two-minute webcast conversation about heart transplantation, published in twenty twenty-five as a companion to a journal issue devoted to the topic. Led by the issue's editor, the discussion brings the issue's authors together to draw out new themes and the lessons they took from researching and writing their articles. It serves readers who want the field's current debates in spoken form.
pmc-12717050:
Ahtisham Fazeel Abbasi and four co-authors run a bake-off of thirty-five AI classifiers that sort cancers into molecular subtypes, because the field's mixed setups make published results hard to compare. How subtypes are sorted guides prognosis and targeted therapy in precision oncology. Their test spans one hundred fifty-three datasets, eight kinds of molecular data, and twenty cancers, built around six research questions.

Certain dataset configurations performed best again and again for five of the eight data types. RNA sequencing, microRNA, copy-number, and exon data for the most part sorted cancers better than methylation, array, mutation, and protein data, the last two also proving prone to quirks. The authors distill which mixes deserve trust. To redo such work, they argue, starts with standard setups and scoring.
pmc-12723850:
Xinrong Li and nine co-authors test if daratumumab, a myeloma drug, cuts bone breaks and like harms in new patients. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. The drug hits a mark on tumor cells and works well, but its bone role was thinly known. Past cases of more than one hundred sixty new patients from many hubs were weighed, some on the drug and some not.

Bone harms hit near one fifth in all, less in the drug group but not by a firm span. In folks with sound blood calcium at start, the drug cut harm risk by a lot. A like edge showed in mid-risk folks. The team calls for more proof of a bone guard role.
pmc-12727750:
Kwan Kyu Park and colleagues published a 2025 study of hip fractures during COVID distancing in South Korea. Older adults stayed home far more during distancing. Intuition suggests indoor falls should rise. The team checked hospital records across both periods. One large hospital provided the data.

Over two thousand fracture patients were included. Matched groups allowed a fair comparison. The indoor share of falls actually fell during distancing. The drop surprised the authors. Outdoor falls did not simply move indoors. Other behavior changes may explain the pattern. The study warns against assuming pandemic effects without data.
pmc-12732250:
Florin Tovirnac and a team of co-authors unpack risk patterns for early birth in teen and adult mothers, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. Their Romanian hospital records covered deliveries from twenty twenty to twenty twenty-one. Three groups were compared: teen early births, adult early births, and adult full-term births.

A pattern-finding method drew three hidden risk dimensions in each group. In teens, mother complications, outside behaviors, and birth tract factors clustered together. Adult groups split the pieces differently, with behavior and social factors leading at term. The profiles argue for care tuned to each group's risk shape.
pmc-12736250:
Caiyun Zhang and co-authors pull in 2025 a new compound from a folk diabetes plant and then build it in the lab. The plant, Cassytha filiformis, is used traditionally for type 2 diabetes. The compound, named filiforidine, is an oxidized aporphine alkaloid with a novel structure.

Spectroscopy pinned down its shape. The team then achieved its first total synthesis, with key steps including a light-driven ring closure and a copper-catalyzed finishing step. They also cut purification work with a salt trick. In liver cells the compound boosted glucose use at low doses without killing cells. The authors propose it as a promising diabetes drug candidate.
pmc-12738550:
Neshat, Imami, and Honnery build a model to predict burn timing in methane engines. Their target is the HCCI engine, which burns a uniform fuel mix under compression. Knowing when burning starts, called combustion phasing, is key to running such engines well.

Starting from a large known chemistry set, they trimmed it to 22 species and 48 reactions. Ion reactions were then added, giving 27 species and 54 reactions in total. The scheme uses ion current signals inside the cylinder to track the burn. It was built into a multi-zone engine model for testing.
pmc-12739450:
Shivani Thakre and co-authors published a trial protocol in twenty twenty-five for comparing two ways to preserve the jaw ridge after a tooth is pulled. Without help, the socket shrinks and complicates later implants. Both arms of the planned trial add titanium platelet-rich fibrin, a blood-derived scaffold, to a graft material.

One group receives freeze-dried donor bone; the other receives a graft made from the patient's own extracted tooth dentin. The trial will compare the two clinically, on scans, and under the microscope, counting new bone inside healed sockets. Ridge width and height changes are secondary measures. As a protocol, the paper fixes the design in public before results exist, guarding against selective reporting.
pmc-12740950:
Raja Murugan, Anant Dubey, Navdeep Dhami, and Abhijit Mukherjee grow biocement from limestone with a bacterium's help, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. The method copies how nature builds beach rock and stromatolites. Acetobacter aceti was mixed with ethanol and limestone powder.

The acid from the bacteria dissolved the stone into calcium acetate. Once the ethanol ran out, the pH rose and calcite crystals formed anew. Checks confirmed the new cement is mostly calcite. The route skips urea and added chemicals and uses stone as its own calcium source, cutting the carbon cost of cement.
pmc-12746450:
Guiying He, Sihan Chen, and Rongchao Jin survey how to control triplet-state formation in gold nanoclusters of exact atom counts, in a perspective from twenty twenty-five. Such clusters make triplet excited states with striking efficiency. That promises materials with room-temperature phosphorescence and delayed fluorescence. Steering the triplets is still hard, though.

The authors first outline the light marks by which the triplet state is known. Time-resolved and temperature-dependent glow methods get explained. Transient absorption spectroscopy joins the toolkit. What is newly known about cluster triplet states is then summed up. Ways to steer intersystem crossing follow. Open challenges and future paths close the piece. The goal is star materials for optoelectronics, photocatalysis, and solar upconversion. Better triplet control would serve all three.
pmc-12749950:
Ruiqiang Liu and co-authors build a cobalt catalyst in 2025 that pulls hydrogen off propane to make propylene, a key feedstock for plastics. Cobalt catalysts for this job tend to be either weak when the cobalt is caged in a crystal, or short-lived when it sits loose. Their design tries to get both strength and staying power.

They anchored single cobalt atoms in the rings of a silica crystal and grew tiny cobalt oxide clusters right next to them. Fine imaging confirmed the pairing. The combo hit high output rates and faded very slowly over three days of hot running. The authors credit teamwork between the lone atoms and the clusters for the balance.
pmc-12750750:
Naama Rotem-Kohavi and a large team set out a protocol for a Canadian spinal injury image library. Their protocol paper from twenty twenty-five covers acute traumatic injuries. MRI scans can help predict recovery after spinal cord injury. Promising scan markers still need accuracy and practicality improvements.

The library will gather scans from centres across Canada. Patients had neck-level injuries within a defined recent period. All were already enrolled in a national injury registry. Stored images will support shared analysis across research teams. Better markers could guide early care and family counselling. A national repository also ends wasteful duplication between centres. The protocol fixes consent, storage, and access rules in advance.
pmc-12751250:
Gloria Grace Akurut and a large team of colleagues evaluate a multi-pathogen test card for diagnosing fevers in patients first suspected of viral hemorrhagic fever. The card detects twenty-six pathogens within about two hours of extracting nucleic acids. They ran it on 182 stored samples, all hemorrhagic-fever negative, from surveillance in Uganda and neighboring countries.

Seven pathogens turned up in about a third of samples. Malaria parasites dominated, followed by salmonella species, yellow fever virus, and a few others. Assay positivity was significantly tied to whether patients lived or died. The authors conclude the card is a feasible, readily adoptable tool for national testing algorithms during fever outbreaks in sub-Saharan Africa.
pmc-12751450:
Sentayehu Oljira Bekele and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-five qualitative study of women who survived wartime sexual assault in North Wollo, Ethiopia. War brought mass sexual violence and destroyed health facilities. Survivors who became socially isolated carry a double burden.

Twenty-five women took part through focus groups and deep interviews. Their accounts were coded and grouped into themes. Survivors described abuse, shunning, and loss of dignity and confidence. Helplessness and isolation ran through the stories. Coping strategies also emerged from the interviews. The study gives voice to experiences that policy often leaves unheard.
pmc-12756250:
Marcin Machalski and five co-authors confirm that some ammonites lived past the asteroid impact that ended the dinosaurs. Their fossil study was published in twenty twenty-five. Shells found above the boundary layer were long dismissed as reworked older fossils.

New specimens came from a limestone bed at Stevns Klint in Denmark. Three ammonite genera were identified. Close study of the rock fabric and fossil wear showed most shells were buried where the animals died, in early post-impact seas. Only one shell, from the bed's base, looked truly reworked. The survivors add a chapter to ammonite history: the group did not vanish in a single day.
pmc-12763950:
Yen-Ling Chen and six co-authors shared a study protocol in twenty twenty-five. It brings early psychosis care into ordinary community clinics. Young people at clinical high risk for psychosis have varied outcomes. Specialty clinics are scarce. They cost a lot, and some feel unwelcoming. The program screens all young people instead. It screens where young people already seek care, in their own towns.

Clinicians in community mental health centers give stepped care. They start with low-intensity cognitive behavioral case management for general distress. They step up only as signs specify. The protocol takes on the known barriers head-on. Those are workforce limits, community awareness, and engagement. The long-term design will show one thing. It will show if detection and first treatment in community settings reach youth that specialty pipelines miss.
pmc-12766950:
Jaehun Lee, Soomin Kim, Youngchul Oh, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It shows how young stomach cancers break free of their neighborhood: instead of waiting for growth signals from nearby support cells, tumor cells learn to secrete the signal themselves.

Healthy stomach lining depends on WNT signals supplied by fibroblasts next door. Colorectal cancers escape by mutation, but stomach cancers rarely carry those mutations, leaving their escape route mysterious. Working with mouse stomach organoids carrying cancer mutations, plus patient-derived organoids, the team withdrew growth factors and blocked signal secretion. Tumors that turned on their own WNT production kept growing unaided. Genome-wide single-cell maps showed the rewiring in transcription and chromatin. Checks in human cancer cell lines broadened the claim. The authors name self-secreted WNT as the niche escape hatch to target.
pmc-12780450:
Gao leads a large team comparing two drug coated balloons for heart artery branches, in work from twenty twenty-five. When a heart artery splits, the main branch often gets a stent and the side branch gets a drug balloon. Two drug types are in common use.

The prospective randomized trial was held at many centers. Patients with fresh, non left main split lesions were split evenly between sirolimus and paclitaxel balloons for the side branch. The main check was narrowing of the treated spot on angiogram nine months later. A non inferiority design asks whether the newer drug is no worse than the standard by a set margin.
pmc-12782050:
Shearin and Surdell give a how-to note for a nerve bite in the low arm. Nerve bites are a oft ask for brain and nerve docs in wards. Calls for a bite span vessel flare, dim nerve ills, and scar ills. The sural nerve in the leg is the top pick in most wards. A top arm nerve, SSRN, is picked when ills sit in the arms. That nerve is most oft bared in the high arm in past work.

It sits twixt two cords there in the high arm frame. Their note moves the bite to the low arm in full steps. There the nerve sits close to the skin in plain reach. Steps spell the cut, the find, and the pull of the bit. The note aims to give docs a safe, plain path there.
pmc-12783750:
Elsa Bunz, Daniel Haeufle, Syn Schmitt, and Thomas Geijtenbeek show that a stripped-down spinal reflex network can produce a whole menu of two-legged gaits in simulation. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Proprioception, the body's sense of its own limbs, feeds reflexes that textbooks often sideline. Earlier reflex controllers were hand-tuned for one gait each.

Their controller uses only same-muscle and opposing-muscle length and force feedback, at fixed gains. No rhythm generator or gait switcher sits on top. Yet the simulated legs walked and hopped, forward and backward. They also ran in several styles and speeds. The variety surprised even the authors, given the controller's simplicity. The work argues reflexes deserve a bigger role in locomotion theory. It also offers a base for richer neuromuscular models.
pmc-12789450:
Wangsheng Jiang, Bita Badehnoosh, and Wenfeng Ruan reviewed food-grade nano carriers for a health compound in twenty twenty-five. The compound, astaxanthin, is a pigment found in nature with strong anti-oxidant and anti-swelling traits. It is held back by poor mixing with water, weak stability, and low uptake from the gut when taken by mouth.

The review covers tiny carriers made from food-safe stuff, such as fat-based bits, liposomes, protein carriers, and plant-based gels like chitosan and alginate. It weighs how they are made, how much compound they hold, how stable they stay, how they release their load, and how the gut takes them up. It also sums up gains seen for stress damage, long-term swelling, brain decline, metabolic ills, and cancer, and it notes safety rules and the hard steps in scaling up to factory size.
pmc-12808750:
Trivedi, Srivastava, and Mahajan share Macretina, a public dataset for spotting eye disease in preterm babies. The disease, retinopathy of prematurity, can blind a child if missed early. AI tools could help screen for it, but good labeled data are scarce.

Macretina holds 1,432 retina images from 112 babies at a hospital in Indore, India. Images came from a wide-field camera used for routine screening. Experts labeled the images, which are split into three sets. Each set targets a distinct retinal trait that guides diagnosis and care for these infants. The team presents the set as a base for building and testing such screening tools.
pmc-12816150:
Natsanet Woldesenbet Rayya and four co-authors make tiny zinc oxide materials with a plant root extract. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Copper is added to some of the material to boost its work. The aims span clean water, killing germs, and keeping fruit fresh for longer.

The green method uses the root extract to form and steady the grains. Tests with light, X-rays, and scans check the build of each form. The copper form breaks down dye in water far better than the plain form, and it stays stable over time. It also fights common germs more strongly. The study links low copper use to gains across all three uses.
pmc-12816450:
Xiao-Jie Liu and his team show that a strike at an enzyme that makes harsh air goods holds back growth of a flat-cell tumour of the food pipe. It works by a shift in a path that holds tumours back. Their 2025 study makes clear the role of the enzyme that drives this throat tumour on.

When the enzyme was made still in tumour cell lines, cell growth was held back, cell death was pushed up, and the cell round stopped early. The hold-back gene rose in a marked way. In flesh from sixty-six sick folk, the enzyme was more high in tumours and the hold-back good more low. High grades of the enzyme told of a poor path for the sick folk. High grades of the hold-back good told of good ends. Both marks told of life span on their own.
pmc-12816750:
Won-Jung Oh and three co-authors report progress on printing pure copper parts in a 2025 study. Copper carries power and heat very well, so demand for it is high. Printing it with a laser is hard, because copper reflects much of the beam and spreads heat fast, which can spoil melting.

Using a strong infrared laser, the team found the settings where melting stays stable. At high power and modest scan speeds, parts came out nearly fully dense. The best parts carried power as well as standard worked copper, with no heat treatment after printing. Crystal patterns inside the metal also mattered: fewer grain borders meant less scattering and better flow.
pmc-12822150:
Juszczak and three co-authors sort gene name clashes in man and three beast kinds in this twenty twenty-five study. Each gene bears a stock tag plus a crowd of past names. Shared tags can pin one name to two genes, which traps data joins.

Inside, tag banks from a globe genome hub gave the full tag lists. Name loads ran from low in pigs to vast in mice in the count. Near one in five man's genes wore a tag shared with a kin gene. Firm bank IDs, not names, form the team's core fix for the trap. Their free script cleans name lists and flags each clash it finds.
pmc-12829050:
Moath Hattab and colleagues tested whether richer patient teaching improves bowel cleansing before colonoscopy, in a randomized trial published in twenty twenty-five. A poorly cleaned bowel undermines the exam, and standard leaflets often fail. Adults booked for elective colonoscopy were assigned to the usual leaflet or to a light-touch package: a face-to-face talk, a short video, an illustrated booklet, and phone app reminders. Preparation quality was scored on a standard scale for the whole colon and each segment, alongside procedure times, side effects, anxiety, and satisfaction.

By the strict definition requiring every segment to pass, four fifths of the taught group were adequately prepared versus about two thirds of controls. The gap needs roughly seven patients taught per extra success. Looser definitions narrowed the edge. The authors present the package as cheap and worth adopting.
pmc-12837450:
Yaradua compares leaf gene sets of Nigerian spice plants in the ginger family. The genus holds plants of high ecological and market value. Past leaf gene work focused on Asian kin of the family. African lines had been left out of that work.

Five Nigerian species gave full leaf gene sets for contrast. Fast gene reads built and labeled each set in full. Checks covered form, code use, repeats, and gene pressure. Tree methods inferred kin ties and split times. The sets show how the African line diverged over time. Facts may aid crop breeding and wild stock care.
pmc-12841850:
Henny Thanki and Suril Vithalani described a misleading bleeding case in two thousand twenty-five. A teenage boy had repeated dark stools and belly pain. A scope found only mild stomach erosions. His colon check looked normal. Doctors treated stomach irritation, and symptoms settled briefly.

Ten months later, heavy bleeding brought him back. Scans pointed to an inflamed pouch on his small intestine. Surgeons confirmed a Meckel's pouch during the operation. They removed the affected bowel segment and his appendix. Lab study showed stomach-like tissue inside the pouch. The case warns against stopping at a mild first finding. Persistent bleeding deserves a small bowel search.
pmc-12849150:
Yi Zeng and colleagues surveyed university students in Shanghai in two thousand twenty-five. Below-threshold depression affects many undergraduates quietly. The team explored its links to thinking biases. They also studied how students read others' minds. Classes were sampled across academic years. Thousands of students completed online questionnaires.

About two in five students met subthreshold criteria. Over-reading others' minds linked to lower depression odds. Under-reading minds linked to higher odds instead. Stronger thinking bias independently raised the odds. Patterns held broadly across student subgroups. One link varied by self-rated health status. Campus screening could target these thinking patterns.
pmc-12849550:
Bohong Long and five co-authors test electric pulses to the pelvic floor in rats with stress urine leakage. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Such leakage, where a cough or strain lets urine out, often follows birth. A tiny implanted device can pulse the pelvic muscles, but which pulse rate works best was not known.

Rats are given a birth-like stretch that brings on leakage, then pulsed at one of four rates for two weeks. Leak pressure, a gauge of control, falls with the injury and rises back with pulses at each rate. No rate beats the rest. Bladder size does not shift. More work on rates and long-term gain is called for.
pmc-12875550:
Sandeep Yadav and four co-authors report a case where MRI untangled a parasitic brain infection alongside degenerative spine disease, in a two thousand twenty-five case report. The patient was a forty-year-old man with chronic headache, dizziness, and a recent seizure.

Brain imaging showed multiple ring-enhancing lesions with the eccentric scolex typical of neurocysticercosis, the larval tapeworm infection that is a leading cause of acquired epilepsy. Lesions also appeared in eye, face, and tongue muscles. Spine scans separately showed cervical disc bulges and lumbar disc pathology without cord compression. Treatment combined antiparasitic drugs, corticosteroids, and antiepileptic medication, with conservative care for the discs. The case argues for whole-system evaluation.
pmc-12892850:
Danilov and colleagues review in twenty twenty-five how well image-based machine learning can read the genetics of glial brain tumours from scans. These tumours are the most common growths of brain tissue, and biopsy-free subtyping would help care. The team pooled over forty studies that used scan features and learning models to predict gene markers.

Overall accuracy was high, near nine in ten correct. Markers covered several key mutations, a chromosome change, and a growth index. Yet methods varied widely, above all in how the region of interest on scans was chosen, which blocks repeat testing in clinics. The authors call for standard rules so results can travel into practice.
pmc-12918050:
Desheng Yan and three colleagues published a youth study in two thousand twenty-five on internet use and teen behaviour. They split behaviour into helpful, goal-driven acts and harmful acts that hold a young person back. The question was which side drives the other over time.

The team analysed data from more than nine thousand students measured twice, about a year apart. Heavier internet use went with less helpful behaviour and more harmful behaviour at both time points. The cross-time analysis suggested the influence runs both ways. Problem internet use can slow healthy growth. In turn, active and healthy behaviour can pull teens away from problem use. The authors back school and family efforts on both fronts.
pmc-12985850:
Pengliang He, Yucheng Jie, Yi Zeng, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It studies how coix, a grain used as both food and medicine, copes with cadmium, a toxic metal that can build up in farm soil.

The team grew one coix strain in soil with no cadmium and with two added levels. The plants took up and moved little cadmium, and higher cadmium slowed their water loss and food-making from light. The authors then read the plants' gene activity in roots, stems, leaves, and grain. Thousands of genes changed activity under cadmium stress, with the leaf showing the most change. The work maps genes and paths that may help breed crops that handle polluted soil.
pmc-13093250:
Tomer Babu, Matthew Levine, Bingsong Zeng, and Jonathan Sessler report a single molecule that carries three cancer-fighting payloads at once. The construct links a platinum drug precursor, a gold compound, and the chemotherapy drug gemcitabine, and it splits apart inside cells to release all three. Writing in twenty twenty-six, the team compares the combined prodrug with its separate parts in cell tests. They measure how well it kills cancer cells, how much metal enters the cells, and whether the death it causes alerts the immune system, judged by cell surface and release signals.

The combined molecule beat its constituents on potency and metal uptake, and it triggered a stronger immune-style death response in the dish. Gene activity profiles after treatment had a distinct signature. The authors pitch multi-metal prodrugs as a way to combine complementary attack modes while dodging the dosing problems of loose drug mixtures.
pmc-13117750:
Saule Bukanova and colleagues refine road bitumen out of fuel oil leftovers, in this study from twenty twenty-six. The question is how deeply to strip the lighter gas-oil fraction before oxidizing the residue into binder. Too light a feed and the bitumen ages fast; too heavy and it fails specification.

A viscosity window solved it. Feedstock with the stated flow time, corresponding to fractions boiling across the mid-four-hundreds Celsius, yielded bitumen meeting three standard systems at once: American, European, and Kazakh. The team tied the seven-component chemical makeup of the residues to how fast they oxidize, explaining the window mechanistically. The authors pitch the range as a recipe for turning non-standard heavy feedstock into specification binder with better resistance to heat and oxygen aging.
pmc-13130750:
Haryati Ahmad Hairi and colleagues reviewed plant phenolic compounds as a possible aid against osteoporosis. Osteoporosis thins bone and weakens its structure, raising fracture risk. It develops when bone removal outruns bone building, driven by oxidative stress, long-term inflammation, cell-death pathways, and hormone change, especially loss of estrogen.

Sections explain those disease mechanisms first, with stress and hormone problems given special weight. Evidence on phenolic compounds follows, including recent clinical observations and delivery methods meant to make the compounds work better. The authors judge these plant-based compounds promising for preventing and managing weak bones, while presenting them as a strategy still being developed.
pmc-13156550:
Aaryan R Jadhav and colleagues describe a two thousand twenty-six case report of a rare stromal tumour in the vulva. Such tumours usually grow in the gut. Ones outside it are uncommon, and vulvar cases are exceptionally rare.

Their patient was a fifty-three-year-old woman with a returning labial mass. She also had a history of breast cancer. Removal showed a spindle cell tumour with marker patterns matching gut stromal tumours. Gene testing found a mutation that guided management. Margins were positive, and scans showed local return without spread. Gut checks found no hidden primary tumour.
pmc-13174950:
Jiang and a large team compare two fixes for a burst brain aneurysm in twenty twenty-six. An aneurysm is a weak bulge in a blood vessel that can leak blood into the brain. Days later, low blood flow can harm the brain further, a harm called delayed ischemia. Doctors fix the bulge by clipping it shut or by filling it with coils.

The team pooled twenty-one studies with more than five thousand patients. Harm from low blood flow was more common after clipping than after coiling. Grades of bleed severity helped predict the harm in both groups. Age also helped predict it in the coiling group. The authors urge more high quality studies to confirm the gap.
pmc-13179750:
Gyarteng Mensah and colleagues published in twenty twenty-six a study of intestinal parasites shared among people, primates, and dogs near Ghana's protected areas. Parasites that jump between species threaten all three groups. The team collected stool samples and questionnaires at three sites. Sites included Boabeng Fiema, Mole National Park, and Shai Hills. Lab tests identified parasite types in each host group. Dogs and primates carried far heavier parasite burdens than people at most sites.

Hookworms and roundworms appeared in all three hosts. Human prevalence varied widely by site, from about eleven to fifty-eight percent. One site held the richest mix of parasite species overall. Poor dog confinement and open defecation helped sustain transmission. Inconsistent footwear, hygiene, and deworming added to the risk. The authors urge a One Health response joining human and animal measures.
pmc-13183550:
Napolitano and six co-authors report a lab study from twenty twenty-six on fluid made by stem cells from birth cord tissue. The fluid holds the helpful goods those cells release, with no cells in it. That cell-free mix may heal wounds while dodging risks of live cell care. The team tested the fluid on skin cells stressed by a harsh chemical. They also tested it on germs and checked its germ-fighting parts.

Treated skin cells coped better with stress and raised their own defense systems. The fluid held clear levels of germ-fighting proteins. It slowed one common germ that infects skin wounds. The authors back the fluid as a safe, cell-free aid for tissue repair.
pmc-13185650:
Rajbanshi, Brentari, Denti, Cummings, and Guruacharya wrote a review in twenty twenty-six on RNA-based therapies for Alzheimer's disease and kin tau diseases. These diseases feature buildup of a protein called tau in the brain. Antibody and small-molecule drugs have failed in many trials so far. RNA therapies can target tau at its molecular source instead. The review surveys forms like messenger RNA, antisense strands, and splicing switches. Each form carries distinct promises for tau control. Shared hurdles include delivery to the brain and durability.

The authors outline molecular targets now in play. They track clinical trials and patent trends in the young field. Translational barriers get a full treatment in the review. The piece maps a nascent route to disease-modifying care.
pmc-13194150:
Fan Yang and colleagues studied family background and exercise in China in 2026. Health gaps are drawing wider public attention. The team asked whether family resources shape adult exercise habits. They used a large national social survey from twenty twenty-three. The sample held well over two thousand adults of working age. Family capital was split into money, culture, and social ties. Models tested direct links and one indirect path. That path ran through the children's own schooling.

Money and cultural resources both linked to more exercise. The cultural link proved the steadier one. Social ties showed no clear direct link. Children's schooling carried part of the family effect. That carrying role was larger for cultural resources. Money mattered more in rural and low-income groups. Culture mattered more for city residents and women. The authors urge policy that builds schooling and health awareness together.
pmc-13197450:
Valentina Parra Rodríguez and co-authors test two plant compounds and a known antibiotic, alone and mixed, against Pseudomonas aeruginosa. This germ haunts hospitals and resists many drugs; the World Health Organization lists it as a critical priority. Its staying power rests in part on biofilms, slime cities it builds, steered by quorum sensing, a census that tells the germ when to attack.

The team measured the lowest dose that stops growth for quercetin, baicalein, and azithromycin. They then gauged biofilm growth, three virulence products, and the activity of two quorum sensing genes. Quercetin alone left the least biofilm, about a third of the untreated level. The best pair was azithromycin with baicalein, near 35%. Azithromycin and that pair also curbed the virulence products most. The hope is anti-virulence therapy: strip its weapons, so immune systems and old drugs can finish the job.
pmc-13198050:
Steven Dodd and colleagues evaluated a public involvement network for health research in a 2026 study. Public involvement means patients and community members help shape research, not just take part in it. Many such efforts fade fast and grant little real say, so the team studied a long-running network in northwest England.

The network, called CoREN, has linked researchers and community groups since 2019. Interviews and group talks showed it brokers ties, lifts community voices, and builds research skills in local groups. Power gaps between researchers and residents narrowed. Hurdles included a fuzzy role, slow bureaucracy, and thin reach into poorer and more diverse areas. Lasting funding is the key lesson.
pmc-13198450:
Costanza Spadini and colleagues tested a cobra-derived peptide against dog ear germs in a 2026 lab study. Canine ear infection is common and often involves drug-resistant bacteria and yeast. The peptide, called NCP-3, comes from Chinese cobra venom protein and kills germs with low cell harm in past work.

The team tested it on reference strains and field strains from dogs with ear disease. It killed all reference strains but one. Against a key staph germ, including resistant forms, it acted fast and at low doses, wiping out growth within five minutes. Higher doses were needed for other germ groups. It failed to reach kill levels for gut-type germs and the ear yeast. Gram-positive germs remain the best target.
pmc-13198550:
Safinaz M Elhadad and colleagues tested houseplants as indoor air filters in a 2026 study. Labs that handle chemicals can hold harmful vapors in their air. The team placed four ornamental species in a real drug-lab setting, as pots and as a green wall, and tracked vapor levels plus plant health.

One species, Cordyline fruticosa, cleared the most vapors, carbon monoxide, and carbon dioxide. It also scored highest on a pollution tolerance index and leaf traits. A second species cleared all fine dust particles in tests and cut gases well. Plants with tougher leaves and more complex surfaces cleaned best, per math models. Plant filters look like a cheap, green aid for indoor air.
pmc-13199650:
Tapas Paul and Sua Myong present a 2026 protocol for viewing single protein clusters. Biomolecular condensates are droplet-like protein clumps that organize cell work. Their earliest tiny forms are hard to catch with bulk tests, so the protocol pins single clusters down for close imaging.

Steps cover preparing a coated surface, forming clusters in a flow chamber, and catching them with antibodies for fluorescence imaging. The method tracks how fast clusters form, their relative size, and how molecules swap in and out. A worked example uses FUS, a protein tied to nerve disease. As a protocol, it reports no new findings; its value is a recipe other labs can repeat. Details point to a prior paper for full use.
pmc-13200050:
Haozhi Zhang and a large team build a layered artificial ligament that heals better after knee reconstruction in rats, in a proof-of-concept study from twenty twenty-six. Hundreds of thousands of anterior cruciate ligament reconstructions happen yearly, yet return to prior activity stays limited. Artificial grafts risk chronic fluid, inflammation, and failure.

Their graft weaves magnesium and recombinant spider silk protein into a dual core-shell structure spanning nano to macro scales. At the graft-bone junction it sparked early bone, nerve, and adhesion markers and sped new bone mineralization around the tunnel. Rats receiving it healed better after reconstruction. The authors see strong clinical potential for future knee applications.
pmc-13200350: Jingyi Zhao and colleagues are authors of a trial corrected in a 2026 note in the Journal of NeuroEngineering and Rehabilitation. The trial tested whether repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, magnetic pulses through the scalp, improves combined thinking-and-moving task performance in children with cerebral palsy. The note fixes a methods sentence about randomization and stimulation timing. It also corrects a results sentence, giving day-by-day test values that show group differences on days two and three but not day one. The original article has been corrected.
pmc-13200850:
João Pedro de Melo and colleagues synthesize evidence on kneecap lower-pole fractures in adults in a 2026 review. The patella is the kneecap, and its lower pole anchors the tendon that straightens the knee. Breaks there strain the whole straightening system and stir debate on best repair, so the team reviewed recent literature.

Their search of one database over five years found twenty-two studies, of which sixteen entered the review. Stable fixation methods favored bone healing and early return to movement. No single method won outright: choice still hinges on fracture pattern, surgeon experience, and cutting complications such as repeat surgery. The evidence base is case series, the weakest tier, so firm guidance awaits stronger trials.
pmc-13202650:
A calcareous tubeworm from the Sea of Japan gets its first complete mitochondrial genome in a 2026 study headed by Qinghua Bao. The research article sequences Serpula uschakovi, filling a gap for the genus Serpula, whose family is known for scrambled mitochondrial gene orders.

The circular genome runs just over twenty thousand bases and holds the standard thirteen protein-coding genes, two ribosomal RNA genes, and twenty-two transfer RNA genes. Its gene arrangement is heavily rearranged compared with the presumed ancestral pattern, yet it keeps a conserved block shared with the genus Hydroides. Family tree analysis placed the species as sister to Hydroides, informing tubeworm evolution studies.
pmc-13203150:
Han Zhang and co-authors design virtual reality scenes for public speaking, and test how avatar realism and natural scenes shape user comfort. Their 2026 study puts one hundred thirty-two people in a two-by-two experiment.

Those who took part spoke in front of avatars that were realistic or stylised, in a scene that was natural or indoors. Questionnaires caught how they saw the event. Skin conductance and heart rate variability gauged stress in the body. Natural scenes lifted satisfaction and how users saw the event as a whole, by a share that counts. Style of avatar most of all shaped the body, with stylised avatars that gave lower arousal than realistic ones. No effects showed in which scene and avatar factors acted on each other. Talks after the test hinted that vague feedback from the audience held back how users judged how they were seen.
pmc-13207250:
Tselebis and five co-authors surveyed in twenty twenty-six how anger, distrust, bad dreams, and poor sleep hang together in nurses. Nurse work is high strain, and that strain can follow staff home at night. They ran an online survey in late twenty twenty-five with four scale forms.

Four hundred forty-one hospital nurses took part in the survey. Poor sleep was the most common strain, hitting more than six in ten nurses. Anger was next, at more than four in ten. In their model, anger linked to poor sleep both straight and through distrust and bad dreams in a chain. Care that calms anger may aid sleep, they say.
pmc-13210250:
Zsálig and co-authors test whether a gut bacterium linked to leanness changes body weight in mice when given rectally. Christensenella minuta is a candidate next-generation probiotic. It has been tied to lower weight and better metabolism. How strong and lasting those effects are under varied diets stayed unclear. The team used 180 mice, split evenly by sex, in nine groups. Groups differed by diet, bacterium dose, and antibiotic pretreatment.

The team tracked weight gain, food intake, and calorie use during and after dosing. Interactions among diet, antibiotics, and the bacterium were the focus. Rectal delivery puts the microbe straight into the lower gut. The study tests whether diet background decides the benefit.
pmc-13210750:
Plastic antibodies molded around a protein can fish it from mixtures, and a 2026 study headed by Nan Zhang improves the molding with multiple anchors. The research article imprints cytochrome C onto dendritic mesoporous silica nanospheres using a custom poly(ionic liquid) macromonomer that grips the protein at several points at once.

The support particles averaged about eighty nanometers with channels that let proteins move freely in and out. A thin imprinted skin formed on their surface, keeping the target's shape stable during capture according to simulations and spectroscopy. The material bound large amounts of cytochrome C selectively, kept most of its capacity after repeated reuse, and modeled well on standard adsorption equations.
pmc-13212150:
Giacomo Moraglia, Mohamed Aboelnour, and Paola Crippa published a climate modelling study in two thousand twenty-six on cities, rain, and floods in Texas. The Texas Triangle of big metros is growing fast and flooding more. The team asked how city growth itself worsens extreme rain and flood risk.

A weather-and-chemistry model simulated a winter frontal storm and a long summer event. Present-day city maps were compared with an end-of-century growth scenario, holding weather patterns fixed. Growth strengthened updrafts and raised rain over San Antonio and Austin in the winter case. The summer case mixed gains and losses across Dallas-Fort Worth. Flood risk zones spread under growth in both frameworks tested. The authors back the model as a first-order risk guide.
pmc-13212650:
Orapa Suteerojntrakool and colleagues run a 2026 trial in Thailand on whether a nutritional drink helps undernourished young children grow. Children aged one to six whose weight lagged for their height were assigned to dietary advice alone or advice plus a daily fortified milk-based drink.

Among 159 children treated for three months, the drink group gained more weight and height than the advice-only group. Measures of lean body tissue also rose more in the drink group at both check points. The authors conclude that supplements paired with counselling support healthier body composition, not just heavier bodies, in children at risk of malnutrition.
pmc-13213550:
Julia Sophie Böke leads a large team presenting in 2026 a single-chip platform that runs many kinds of droplet-based laboratory tests. Most existing devices serve one assay family and need several separate handling steps, which limits flexible use.

Their disposable chip makes, stores, incubates, and reads droplets on one device, running test and control experiments side by side with hundreds of thousands of uniform droplets each. Computer simulations and bench checks confirmed the droplet-forming unit works as predicted. Demonstration assays covering biochemical signals and microbial growth showed the readout works with several optical methods. pmc-13226650:

pmc-13230550:

pmc-13230850:

pmc-13249750:

pmc-13275750:

pmc-13276450:

pmc-13276950:

pmc-13277350:

pmc-13279550:

pmc-13289050:
