pmc-13289750:
Saki Hasegawa-Tamba and colleagues present a 2026 autopsy case of pulmonary veno-occlusive disease after cancer immune therapy. That rare condition blocks small lung veins and raises lung pressure. An 80-year-old man with lung disease, high blood pressure, and heavy smoking history had lung cancer surgery first, with no sign of the vein disease in tissue at that time.

After cancer returned, he got nivolumab plus ipilimumab, developed breathing and kidney immune problems, then improved on steroids. Ipilimumab stopped, and nivolumab alone ran for 22 months until worsening breathlessness and severe low oxygen appeared. Heart tests confirmed lung hypertension, but breathing failed fast and he died on hospital day 53 overall. Autopsy showed vein wall thickening.
pmc-13289850:
Nazila Dalir, Glenn S Parker, Rachel Amanda Masia, and Patricia Torres share a 2026 case series on two fiercely aggressive signet ring cell cancers of the colon. This rare subtype makes up under one percent of colon cancers and often spreads before discovery. Both patients arrived with blocking tumors needing major surgery, illustrating how fast and wide the disease can move.

One case was a 58-year-old woman with a rectal tumor invading the pelvis and spreading to nearby reproductive organs. The other was a 45-year-old man with a tumor at the splenic bend, spread across the belly lining, unstable microsatellites, and several cancer gene changes. Tailored, multi-pronged care is urged for such cases.
pmc-13290150:
Christine A Heisler and colleagues survey surgeons about microaggressions and career harm in a 2026 study. Microaggressions are small slights that signal bias at work. The survey ran through American College of Surgeons community channels in late 2022 and early 2023. Of 377 respondents, two thirds said they had faced such treatment. More than half of those had taken some action in response.

Who committed the slight shaped what happened next. When a supervisor was responsible, escalation and job changes with demotion grew more likely. Women who acted saw resolution far less often than men did, at about 13 percent versus 39 percent. Retaliation and employer silence also fell harder on women and younger surgeons. Surgeons hit in job after job were more likely to say they would not pick surgery again. The authors link fixing this climate to keeping the surgical workforce intact.
pmc-13290450:
Chronic pelvic pain in men leaves marks on the brain's wiring, Huipeng Ren and colleagues report in 2026. They studied men with chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome, comparing their cortical structure with healthy volunteers.

Thirty-one patients and 28 controls underwent high-resolution MRI, and cortical thickness was mapped across the Destrieux atlas. Patients showed thinning in several temporal, frontal, and occipital areas and thickening in a few others, and two regional measures tracked symptom and quality-of-life scores. Network analysis told a matching story: patients' structural covariance networks were more clustered and less globally efficient, suggesting more segregation and weaker integration. Ren and colleagues read the pattern as multi-level brain change accompanying a pain condition long treated as purely local.
pmc-13290650:
Old livestock pens keep feeding the savanna long after herders move on, Dennis Kipng'etich and colleagues show in a field study from 2026 in Kenya's Maasai Mara. In the Olare Motorogi Conservancy, they compared grass near corrals abandoned five years earlier with grass farther away.

Plots 5 to 55 meters from a corral held more standing grass biomass than plots 150 to 200 meters out, in both wet and dry seasons, with nutrient-loving decreaser grasses thriving closest. Diversity ran the other way: far plots held 18 species against 14 near plots, since a few strong competitors dominate the rich soil. Wildlife dung, a sign of use, piled up near corrals, especially in the dry season. The authors cast abandoned corrals as nutrient hotspots that managers can work with.
pmc-13290850:
Two of three women get too cold during keyhole gynecology surgery, Yingbo Ren and colleagues find in a prediction study from 2026. Cooling during surgery worsens outcomes, yet risk tools for this surgery type have been scarce, so the team built a simple scoring chart from routine data.

The study covered 424 patients at one center, operated on between January 2019 and February 2024, of whom 65.8% dropped below 36 degrees. Split-sample modeling kept just three risk factors: age, body mass index, and how long surgery lasted. The chart sorted high-risk from low-risk patients well in training, with an AUC of 0.788, and checks of accuracy and clinical value backed its use. Ren and colleagues propose flagging high-risk patients early so warming can start before body temperature falls.
pmc-13292450:
David O Ehizibolo and a large team investigate a 2026 blind spot in Nigerian foot-and-mouth disease control: the part sheep and goats play. Cattle usually serve as the indicator species, leaving small ruminants understudied. On Plateau State farms where the animals mix, the team sampled 138 sheep and 39 goats across nine local government areas, taking blood, oral swabs, and tissue from suspected cases.

Most animals, 71.2 percent of those tested, had antibodies showing past exposure, with sheep at 77.5 percent and goats at 48.7 percent in the results. Viral RNA appeared in 36.6 percent of oral swabs, and serotypes O and A were identified. Gene trees tied the sheep and goat viruses closely to cattle viruses on the same farms. The authors urge planners to count small ruminants in surveillance.
pmc-13292550:
Haymanti Bhanot compiles a 2026 question-and-answer installment in the STAR Protocols series, this time on organoids. These lab-grown tissue models mimic their organs of origin and open questions animal models cannot reach. Reproducibility, though, plagues the field, with results swinging between organoids and between batches.

Protocol authors and advisory board members answer practical questions from the bench. On batch variation, contributors blame timing, handling, and lot-to-lot differences in matrix gels and growth proteins, advising fixed passaging rhythms, gentle and consistent dissociation, and checking certificates of analysis when lots change. Another answer tackles uneven seeding: because organoids sink, tubes should be inverted gently so suspensions spread evenly across wells. The piece collects craft knowledge aimed at steadier, more comparable organoid experiments.
pmc-13292650:
Joyce R Mbwana and a large team trace a 2026 drug-resistance thread through children and chickens in Tanzania's rural Korogwe District. They collected Klebsiella pneumoniae complex isolates from children with and without diarrhea and from commercial and smallholder chicken farms, then sequenced the extended-spectrum beta-lactamase producers among them. The question was how closely the human and poultry germs relate.

Resistant isolates appeared in 14 percent of children with diarrhea and 7 percent without, and on 10 percent of commercial and 5 percent of smallholder farm samples in the survey. Sequencing found mostly true K. pneumoniae plus two sister species, spread across many sequence and capsule types. Fifteen clonal clusters turned up, chiefly among chickens on one farm. The gene blaCTX-M-15 dominated. The authors warn of possible cross-species spread and urge One Health action.
pmc-13292850:
Ibrahim Untan and Volkan Sabur ask, in a 2026 study, whether a simple blood ratio can flag severe illness in emergency patients with flank pain. The ratio compares albumin to globulin and reflects both nutrition and body-wide inflammation.

Charts covered 291 adults who had an ultrasound scan between August 2022 and May 2023, and 59 met the study mark for a severe visit. That mark needed at least two of four signs, such as kidney swelling or high inflammation. Patients in the severe group had lower ratio values on average. The ratio predicted severity on its own, yet added nothing beyond standard CRP and creatinine tests.
pmc-13293450:
Sian Calvert and co-authors set out, in a 2026 protocol, an updated review of ways to help adults use hearing aids more steadily. Hearing aids improve talk and quality of life, yet many owners wear them rarely or not at all.

The planned review will gather trials of support programs for adults fitted with at least one aid and pool results where fitting. A behavior framework sorting capability, opportunity, and motivation will guide how each program is classed. Knowing which strategies work, and which behavior levers they pull, should steer future research and clinic practice. No results are reported yet in this protocol.
pmc-13293650:
Rebecca K Simmons and co-authors warn, in a 2026 article, that gene-based low-oxygen scores are often misread in brain tumor research. Computer tools tag gene patterns as hypoxia signals, yet brain tissue normally lives at far lower oxygen than lab air.

Adult brain oxygen sits in the range of 1 to 7 percent, values the authors give, which should count as normal for brain, not oxygen-starved. No single gene pattern marks low oxygen in all cell types, so scores built in one cell may mislead in another. Careful experiments in each cell type are needed before such scores guide claims.
pmc-13293750:
Sudip Kunwar and co-authors join, in a 2026 study, drone-based light scans with gene mapping to find wheat genes behind yield traits. Gene hunts are limited by slow, low-volume trait measures, and light signatures may offer a fast stand-in for yield.

The team grew 341 diverse soft wheat lines over three years, with 273 light bands recorded by a drone sensor. Bands tied most to grain yield, grain weight, and grain count were folded into one score per trait. Gene mapping found 31 linked markers across both hand and light measures. One marker on chromosome 1A sat in a photosynthesis gene and linked to all three light scores.
pmc-13294050:
Liyan Zhang and coauthors build a 2026 prediction model for whether an ovarian-adnexal mass is cancerous, using clinic details plus ultrasound features. Records covered 930 patients with 1,380 masses confirmed by pathology between January 2020 and December 2025. Two senior sonographers, blinded to pathology, re-read every scan and settled disagreements by discussion.

Masses split into a training set of 966 and a validation set of 414. Screening, multivariable models, and Lasso selection fed a nomogram, while four machine learning methods gave comparison classifiers. A simple chart that flags risk before surgery could help triage referrals and spare benign cases from major operations.
pmc-13294150:
Shun Muroga and coauthors fuse many measurement types with machine learning in a 2026 study of carbon nanotube films. Film behavior swings with tiny structural shifts, and no single test captures the whole picture. Shape measures from electron microscope images, covering curl, alignment, junctions, and voids, were merged with Raman crystal signals, surface area, and electrical resistance.

Visual maps grouped films cleanly by crystallinity and tangling. Nonlinear models, led by XGBoost, predicted properties best under leave-one-out checks. Resistance hinged on junction spacing, crystal quality, and network links, while surface area hinged on junction density and void size. The interpretable setup offers a template for other complex materials.
pmc-13294850:
Sara Zekri, Esperanza Navarro-Pardo, and Francisco Alcantud-Marín review links between autism, gender identity, and gender dysphoria in a 2026 article. Some earlier work hints that autistic adults show gender diversity more often than the general population. The review limits itself to adults without cognitive impairment.

Searches of five major databases for work since 2013 yielded only 12 suitable articles, mostly small studies from Western countries. Findings point to a real connection between autism and varied gender identity, with some positive link to dysphoria as well. The authors urge larger, more balanced samples and better recognition of gender diversity when supporting autistic adults.
pmc-13295050:
Suiyang Liu and colleagues teach a neural network to predict how strongly a surfactant will loosen the boundary between oil and water, in a 2026 study aimed at enhanced oil recovery. That tension decides how easily trapped crude lets go, yet it depends jointly on the surfactant's molecular shape and on conditions like temperature and salinity, a pairing older models handle clumsily. Their network reads the molecule as a graph and fuses that reading with environmental features through an attention mechanism.

Two gates steer how messages pass between atoms, and a loss function built for data spanning many orders of magnitude keeps wild values from wrecking training. The model beat random forests, gradient boosting, and two rival graph networks on accuracy. Removing the gates or the attention fusion measurably hurt performance, confirming each part earns its place. The authors report sturdy behavior even when fed abnormal tension values.
pmc-13295250:
Shengjie Wang and colleagues study tiny drifting animals in two nearshore systems of China's Beibu Gulf in a 2026 article. Zooplankton pass energy up food chains to young fish, yet nutrient pollution reshapes their communities. Surveys in Qinzhou Bay and the Beilun River mouth traced water quality gradients from inner to outer waters.

Salinity rose seaward while nutrients and pollution fell along the same line. Small copepods dominated, led by one species whose grip had tightened compared with older records. Modelling split pollution harm into direct effects, poorer food quality, and community narrowing, which together dragged total plankton biomass downward in enriched waters.
pmc-13295450:
Victória Ribeiro Silvestre and colleagues survey public views on antimicrobial resistance in Brazil in a 2026 study. Resistance threatens health, farming, and the environment together, yet public understanding in Brazil was poorly measured. An online questionnaire shared through social media between April and August 2025 fed the work.

After cleaning, 945 valid answers remained for analysis. Schooling level predicted knowledge and attitude scores most strongly, while age and gender effects wavered. Fewer than half correctly spotted antibiotics among common medicines, and only about a quarter disposed of packaging properly. Health worry drove interest in antibiotic-free goods, guiding calls for sharper public teaching.
pmc-13295650:
Sandro La Vignera and Rosita A Condorelli review falling sperm counts and testosterone in a 2026 article. Male reproductive measures have dropped markedly over five decades in many countries. The review gathers trend data, body mechanisms, and environmental drivers behind the slide.

Sperm concentration fell by roughly half worldwide between 1973 and 2018, with the pace quickening after 2000. Testosterone slipped steadily with age held aside, by about one to two percent yearly in several groups. Hormone-disrupting chemicals, weight gain, sitting habits, smoking, and heat all share blame. The authors favour combined care plus prevention through cleaner environments as the strongest long-term answer.
pmc-13295850:
Mohamed Abdeldayem and colleagues report a 2026 prospective study of dental implant repair after injury-related jaw bone loss. Twenty adults had defects rebuilt with bone taken from the hip crest, then received implants six months later once the graft had settled.

Thirty implants were placed and all but one survived, while graft width and height both grew markedly over six months. Implant firmness rose, bone loss at the edges stayed modest, and most patients said they were satisfied. One person had a hip wound that opened. The authors see hip bone grafting as a promising route to delayed implant repair.
pmc-13297150:
Sophie Lehner and colleagues review adding immunotherapy to chemotherapy around lung cancer surgery in a 2026 systematic review. The cancers are non-small cell tumours that surgeons can remove. Earlier studies hinted at substantial survival gains from the combination, with mixed safety reports.

Every included study favoured the combination for survival and for tumour shrinkage seen under the microscope. Safety findings varied more, with a trend toward more frequent and more severe side effects under combined treatment. Reporting quality also differed between studies. Careful patient selection therefore matters, the authors say, and more research should clarify who gains enough to justify the added risk.
pmc-13297250:
Mitsuki Ikeda and colleagues test a Japanese version of a behaviour-based pain scale for children on breathing machines in intensive care in a 2026 study. Such children cannot say where it hurts, so staff judge pain from behaviour. Seventy scoring rounds from thirty-seven patients were rated by three watchers and checked against two known scales.

Scores tracked the known scales well, and the three watchers agreed fairly with each other. Deep sedation, present in most rounds, flattened behaviour so much that even painful care barely showed. Fine hand-movement scoring proved shaky under deep sedation. The authors warn that low scores in sedated children may hide pain rather than prove comfort.
pmc-13297750:
Phillip Müter, Vandita Verma, and Jörg Hinrichs ask how much of the crust that fouls hot surfaces in oat drink making comes from oat protein, in a 2026 study. Oat drinks need heat treatment for shelf life, yet crust forms fast and cuts efficiency. The team raised protein levels by membrane filtering and ran heating trials at 140 degrees for one hour.

Crust stayed negligible at low protein shares, then rose sharply across a middle band and levelled off. The protein share of the crust tracked the feed closely, but capped at a level that left most crust as carbohydrate instead. Only heavily enriched feeds gave protein-led crusts. Makers can use the pattern to set protein targets that spare their heaters.
pmc-13298550:
Women whose clotting disease also hurt their pregnancies show a more fired-up immune profile, Paula David and a large team report in 2026. From 663 people with steadfast antiphospholipid marks and proven clots, they picked 295 women with the clot form of the disease and a past pregnancy.

Of those, 115 women, or 39.0%, also met the pregnancy form's rules. That group showed more ANA marks, more triple-mark blood tests, and more low platelet counts. With other traits weighed, ANA stayed tied to the group, at an odds ratio of 1.94. Clot type and new clots, though, matched the rest. High blood pressure, not pregnancy past, flagged artery clots. The team say immune traits may help sort risk.
pmc-13298850:
Kaustubh Wagh and Gerardo Chowell compare pre-pandemic forecasts of diabetes deaths with newer global burden data, in a 2026 perspective. Earlier projections expected large rises by 2030 yet could not include pandemic disruption to health systems and chronic care. Fresh estimates covering the period through 2023 now allow a direct check.

Global diabetes deaths had already passed the upper forecast bound for 2030 several years early. Type 2 diabetes drove almost all of that total, and the authors stress that the two main diabetes types carry distinct causes and pandemic vulnerabilities. They urge stronger prevention and management as systems recover from disrupted care.
pmc-13299250:
Yu Zhou and a large team catalogue a family of ubiquitin ligase genes in a medicinal plant famed for its alkaloids, in a 2026 genome study. Abscisic acid, a stress hormone, shifts production of four medically important compounds in Uncaria rhynchophylla. Seventy-three family genes were identified and characterised from the genome.

Expression analysis found five ligase genes whose activity moved opposite to two alkaloid-regulating transcription factors under hormone treatment. The authors hypothesise those ligases tag the factors for destruction, thereby tuning alkaloid output. Direct proof is openly lacking, since no interaction or degradation experiments were done. The model is offered as a testable idea for follow-up work.
pmc-13300150:
Fat makes up about half the dry weight of the brain, and Wei Shao and five colleagues argue in a 2026 review that drifting lipid balance helps drive age-related brain disease. The authors place glial cells at the center of the story, with neurons as partners rather than sole actors.

They trace APOE-linked faults in cholesterol transport, lipid droplets that strain microglia, and ceramide paths that push neurons toward death. The same networks are then mapped onto Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and demyelinating disorders. Closing sections weigh food-based steps, LXR and RXR agonist drugs, nanoparticle delivery past the blood–brain barrier, and lipid profiling as an early warning tool.
pmc-13301250:
B Petrazzini and co-authors build an artificial intelligence tool that spots sudden cardiac death inside electronic health records, reported in 2026. Registries miss these deaths because whether a death was sudden and cardiac is rarely recorded cleanly. The transformer model trained on diagnostic and procedural codes from over seven million people in a UK primary care database, then fine tuned on 1,084 confirmed cases and 6,142 curated controls.

In testing it reached an area under the curve of about 0.95 with a positive predictive value near eighty-six percent, a large gain over the previous phenotype's fifty-five percent. Scores ran higher for sudden than expected deaths, and the model's reasoning leaned on cardiovascular codes as it should. Applied nationally it flagged 138,387 UK cases, exposed mismatches between sudden death incidence and defibrillator density, recovered most known QT prolonging drug risks, and tracked established risk markers across two more datasets.
pmc-13302450:
G Manzo and colleagues compare, in a 2026 multicentre study, leadless pacemaker implants at hospitals with and without on-site heart surgery. Guidelines often insist on surgical backup because the device can pierce the heart and cause bleeding around it. The authors gathered real-world results from thirty Italian centres.

The series held 2,612 consecutive Micra implants, split between fifteen centres with surgery and fifteen without. Success reached nearly ninety-nine point eight percent overall. Bleeding around the heart occurred eight times, at closely similar rates in both settings, and no patient died. Drainage through a needle handled most events, with one transfer for surgery after stabilisation. Training and a clear emergency protocol are credited for the safety.
pmc-13303150:
Most patients on nintedanib for progressive lung scarring held their ground for a year, Vanesa Vicens-Zygmunt and colleagues report in a 2026 real-world cohort from a single center. Fifty-five people with non-IPF fibrotic lung disease who started the drug as their fibrosis advanced had lung function compared against their own pre-treatment year. Breathlessness, side effects, and survival were tracked alongside.

After twelve months, 63.4 percent had stable or improved breathing capacity and 82.5 percent on the gas-transfer measure. Decline slopes flattened compared with the prior year, though not significantly. Three quarters reported side effects, diarrhea leading, and fifteen paused or stopped treatment. The authors read everyday practice as broadly matching trial expectations.
pmc-13303350:
Skin's hidden weave, not just its fibers, explains its springy stretch curve, Jia Li and colleagues show in a 2026 computer study. Block-face electron microscopy mapped collagen layout in fresh human skin, and a tensor method read fiber direction voxel by voxel. Those maps fed tissue models, set against versions that assume one even fiber layout throughout.

At the same stretch, the true-to-life model bore about four times the stress of the even-layout versions. It also gained its steep late stiffening from structure alone, with no need for nonlinear fibers. The method, the authors note, transfers to cornea, cartilage, arteries, and lungs.
pmc-13304450:
Alessandra-Madalina Matei-Man and co-authors report, in a 2026 real-world study, a gene variant that predicts how fast psoriasis patients respond to biologic drugs. Ninety-two Romanian patients with moderate-to-severe disease received their first biologic, spanning three drug classes. Two variants in the interleukin-23 inflammatory pathway were tested against skin scores tracked for a year.

Carriers of the T form of one IL12B variant cleared their skin far better by week twelve than patients with two C copies, reaching strong improvement in ninety percent of cases. The genetic effect faded at later visits, and the second variant showed no link at all. Quality-of-life scores improved for everyone regardless of genotype. The authors suggest early genotyping could guide personalization, while urging validation in larger cohorts from underrepresented populations.
pmc-13304650:
Ruoxuan Huang and co-authors profile the tissue under two mouth lining types in a 2026 study of what makes gums tough and cheek lining soft. The deep connective layer likely sets each surface's character and healing strength.

Human gum and loose cheek lining samples underwent gene sequencing plus protein and staining checks. Gum tissue carried more collagen-building gene activity and fewer attack-ready immune cells, with quieter defense cascades. Its inner chemistry also showed drained levels of a vitamin A product that guides surface growth. Such maps may steer graft design for lasting gum repairs.
pmc-13305250:
Keliang Zheng and colleagues use gene-based analysis to hunt changeable causes of tinnitus, the perception of ringing without outside sound, in a 2026 study. Aging, noise, smoking, and hearing loss are linked, but firm causal factors stay murky.

Thirteen lifestyle factors were tested with Mendelian randomization in a British biobank, then checked in a Finnish biobank. Belly size measures and blood sugar markers tied to tinnitus in the first group, and smoking tied in the second. When both groups pooled, only waist size kept a clear link. Trimming waistlines may be one lever worth testing in clinics.
pmc-13306050:
Xiaojun Zhang made a yellow pigment that also kills bacteria under light in a 2026 study using one-step combustion. Carbon was added to bismuth vanadate with citric acid serving as both fuel and carbon source.

At a citric acid ratio of 1.2, colour strength peaked with a reported b* value of 79.71 in the authors' measures. Light tests cleared 96.63% of a test dye and inactivated 99.99% of E. coli bacteria, far above the plain pigment. The powder also mixed well into plastic and glass, stayed stable with heat, and passed skin safety checks.
pmc-13306450:
Yugui Liu built a heat-reversible network inside recycled PET plastic in a 2026 materials study. Furan groups were grafted onto recycled chains, then linked with a partner compound through Diels–Alder bonds that break and reform with heat.

Higher linker shares raised gel content and crosslink density while swelling fell, with one mix showing the strongest network in reported checks. Heating traces showed bond opening near 143 °C and reforming near 124 °C in the given figures. The best mix kept strength after three re-pressing cycles and could heal damage, lifting recycled plastic performance.
pmc-13306650:
Syeda Sitara Waseem fused sound and video checks to catch deepfakes on small edge devices in a 2026 study. Single-mode detectors fail when an attack targets only one channel, so the design weighs each stream by quality in real time.

Benchmarks held 5472 audio and 1842 video samples, where fusion reached 96.7% accuracy and a 0.988 area score in reported results. Attack tests kept accuracy at 92.3% under a standard gradient method in the given figures. The model fits in 30.3 MB and runs at 20 frames per second on edge hardware. Such checks may help shield phones and ID tools from fake face and voice tricks.
pmc-13306850:
Martín Carballo-Pacheco optimised a plastic moulded to catch the antibacterial triclosan in a 2026 design study. Three recipe factors, two building acids and solvent share, were varied through a Box–Behnken plan to tune recognition strength.

The best mix gave a strong imprinting factor showing efficient target recognition in reported checks. Infrared scans confirmed the expected bond types, and microscopy showed a porous, clumped texture that opens moulded cavities to the target. Release ran in two phases over 48 hours, fitting a diffusion model with a score of 0.9754 in the given figures.
pmc-13307050:
Bo Wang tested how a clonal bamboo shares resources across uneven phosphorus patches in a 2026 pot study. Fragments joined a mother shoot, rhizome and daughter shoot, with phosphorus given evenly or placed at one end, and rhizomes left linked or cut.

Placed phosphorus raised growth of shoots sitting in rich patches and lifted total system mass over even feeding in reported results. Linked rhizomes boosted daughter mass and phosphorus stores against cut controls under every feeding pattern. Root shape shifts and sugar allocation patterns completed the picture of sharing at work.
pmc-13307650:
Miao An and co-authors mine in 2026 published herbal prescriptions for bovine viral diarrhea, a cattle disease with gut, lung, and breeding harms. They gathered 391 records from 2004 to 2024, covering 189 herbs used 2031 times in total across those records.

Data tools sorted herb traits, tastes, and pairings that showed up often, while network methods linked herb compounds to body targets and pathways. Docking runs added early guesses about how those links might work in the body. The map gives a tidy base for lab tests, yet the authors stress that real proof of benefit in cattle still lies ahead of any farm use.
pmc-13308550:
Belinda Cochrane and co-authors assess in 2026 a home based, team run service for lasting breathlessness in Australians with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The Macarthur clinic enrolled 89 patients with at least fairly severe lung block, gave each a nine week tailored plan, and scored breath, mind, and life quality over a year.

Mastery scores on a chest questionnaire rose by 0.5 points at nine weeks and by 0.8 points at 52 weeks in the cohort. Confidence, symptom load, and breath burden also held their gains at the late check in this study. Gains looked more like stronger coping and trust than like weaker breathlessness itself, which still marks real value.
pmc-13308750:
Jiaying Li and co-authors survey in 2026 how adults in China view immersive extended reality for health care, a field with scant public side data until now. Their poll ran from June to September 2024 and drew 35,861 adults across 33 top level regions and 800 towns with staged sampling.

Mean acceptance scored 63.11 on a 100 point scale, with wide swings by province and a fall with rising age. Richer social standing, past digital health use, and strong web health skill all tracked with warmer views of the tech. Past abuse, many siblings, and some health states tracked the other way. A short tree model spotted likely refusers far better than likely fans.
pmc-13310650:
Anna Piscone and co-authors study what happens when a DNA repair scaffold protein goes missing in breast cells in a 2026 article. Oxygen-driven DNA damage constantly threatens the genome, and the base excision repair path fixes the most common lesions. Two of its factors, APE1 and XRCC1, also steady the copying machinery.

Matched breast cell models lacking each factor were compared at rest and under oxidative stress. XRCC1 loss, more than APE1 loss, raised damage signaling and pushed chromatin fragments, rich in telomere DNA, into the cell body. Those cells also switched on an internal alarm path, inflammatory signaling, and aging traits. The authors name XRCC1 a key guard against stray DNA and float it as a treatment lever.
pmc-13310750:
Adriana Krenz and colleagues compare B cell clearing drugs for multiple sclerosis in a 2026 blood study. Drugs that remove B cells help many patients, and they can be given by vein drip or by skin injection. Whether the route changes the immune effect was unclear, so the team profiled blood cells in detail.

Groups held 25 patients on each of three drug plans, plus 20 healthy controls. All drugs cut B cells sharply. Patients on skin injections kept a higher share of memory B cells than those on vein drip. People who switched routes also gained memory share over eight weeks. Route may shape long term immune balance.
pmc-13310950: A short 2026 correction notice fixes swapped author names on a case report about complete androgen insensitivity syndrome. First and last names had been reversed for all authors of the genetic study. The correct lead name is Maria Francesca Astorino, followed by nine co-authors in full. The online version has been updated to match. The notice itself adds no new clinical data, results, or conclusions beyond the corrected byline.
pmc-13311450:
Hyun Bin Kim and co-authors detail a 2026 field test of a records-based tool that flags patients likely to carry drug-resistant gut bacteria on hospital entry. The bacteria, called CRE, resist carbapenem antibiotics.

The tool scored every admission at two Atlanta hospitals from June 2024 to March 2025 using current and past stay data. Of 853 patients approached, 342 agreed to stool or swab testing, and 11 carried CRE. Carriers had higher median risk scores than non-carriers, and the model's accuracy was modest. The team priced a screening program at the best cutoff to inform hospital policy.
pmc-13311750:
Meilan Chen and co-authors give their 2026 trial protocol on when to give dexmedetomidine to cut delirium after surgery in older patients with leg fractures. The drug may protect the brain, but the best timing is unknown.

Patients aged 65 and over having fracture surgery under spinal anesthesia will be split into three groups. One gets the drug before the spinal, one during surgery, and one gets salt water both times, using a double-dummy design. The main outcome is delirium in the first three days after surgery. Thinking scores, sleep quality, and pain are also tracked for later care guidance.
pmc-13311950:
Nicole Zhang writes a 2025 commentary on a qualitative study of pelvic floor problems among women living with multiple sclerosis. The discussed study found the problem common, distressing, and largely unmet by services.

Within ten years of diagnosis, most women with the disease face some pelvic floor trouble, on the cited evidence. The study's title quotes a clinician dismissing a patient with weight advice, capturing how concerns get silenced. Zhang argues nurses need knowledge of how these symptoms shake identity, autonomy, and control. She urges care shaped with patients, reaching beyond mobility to continence and sexuality.
pmc-13312050:
Wen Yu and colleagues report a 2026 randomized, double-blind trial of a long-acting local anesthetic for pain control after open heart surgery through the breastbone. They tested whether liposomal bupivacaine, placed in a superficial parasternal block, could beat the standard drug ropivacaine on pain and stress after surgery.

Forty-four patients having elective surgery with a heart-lung machine were assigned to one of the two drugs. The liposomal bupivacaine group reported lower pain scores from 18 to 72 hours after surgery, had lower levels of the stress markers angiotensin II and interleukin-6, and needed fewer extra pain doses. They also left intensive care sooner and recovered better, with no block-related complications in either group.
pmc-13312450:
Vinita Lal and colleagues report a 2026 surface science study of methanol oxidation on copper and on a copper surface dotted with single platinum atoms. Turning methanol selectively into formaldehyde on copper is an important industrial reaction. How product choice shifts with the amount of oxygen pre-loaded on the surface had never been mapped systematically on these single-atom alloys.

Using deuterated methanol with desorption and photoelectron measurements, the team found the lone platinum atoms slow the surface's own initial oxidation at low oxygen doses. Product choice, though, barely moved: formaldehyde stayed the main product on both surfaces across a wide oxygen range, peaking near a third of a monolayer. The platinum atoms did open a small oxygen-free route by splitting the molecule's O-H bond at very low temperature. Calculations agreed, showing platinum raises the barrier to oxygen splitting.
pmc-13313250:
Ying Wang and a large team report a 2026 antibody study aimed at Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a germ that more and more often shrugs off antibiotics. They sought a treatment that works no matter the drug resistance, by aiming at flagellin, the protein of the tail the germ swims with.

From a panel of 20 antibodies against flagellin FliC, they picked 16G10 as the lead for its strong binding. Mapping showed it grips a short stretch in the D1 domain, from Gly71 to Ile88, a site kept across types and key to building the tail. In lab tests the antibody clumped the germs, slowed swimming, cut entry into lung cells, and shrank biofilms. In mouse lung infection, even against a drug-proof strain, it raised survival, lowered germ counts, and calmed inflammation.
pmc-13314350:
Ragil Angga Prastiya and co-authors use, in a 2026 study, stray female cats as living sensors for lead pollution in Jakarta and Surabaya. Rapid urbanization has loaded both Indonesian megacities with lead, and strays accumulate what their neighborhoods contain. The team measured blood lead in strays from both cities and examined ovarian weight and follicle size, testing whether city of residence or exposure level left a mark on breeding structures.

Neither city stood out. Lead levels and reproductive measures did not differ between Jakarta and Surabaya cats, and ovarian structure showed no damage, suggesting exposure sits at chronic, sub-toxic levels rather than poisoning. The authors are careful not to call that reassuring: endocrine and reproductive effects can hide below visible change, so they ask for surveillance and cell-level studies. The work frames urban strays as a warning system whose quiet readings still argue for cleaner city policy.
pmc-13314450:
Yehui Han and colleagues show how maize roots call in helpful microbes to beat salty, alkaline soil in a 2026 study. Carbonate-type salt-alkali stress cuts maize yields badly on the Songnen Plain of northeast China, and the joint answer of roots and microbes was not clear.

Field tests paired soil chemistry with microbe sequencing and broad chemical mapping of the root zone. Stress raised soil pH and salt readings and lowered organic matter and key nutrients, yet the thin soil layer around roots buffered the blow and kept a high capacity to hold nutrients. Microbe variety near roots even rose under stress, per the report. Root chemicals acted as signals that drew in helpful microbes and built a working web. The finds may guide ways to farm harsh soils.
pmc-13315150:
Adina F. Turcu and co-authors survey, in a 2026 study, why American doctors so rarely screen for secondary hypertension. The curable causes hide behind fewer than two percent of high blood pressure cases. Guidelines urge screening in resistant hypertension, yet it almost never happens. The team surveyed selected primary care physicians, cardiologists, nephrologists, and endocrinologists from the national medical association. Drawing 425 responses from 633 doctors, they reached a 67 percent response rate.

Time was the top barrier, cited by 43.5 percent, followed by poor ancillary support at 29.4 percent and testing logistics at 27.5 percent in the responses. Private practice doctors reported more reimbursement worry yet better specialist access. The authors prescribe longer visits, support staff, education, and specialist pathways as the fix.
pmc-13315450:
Gerda Deveikienė and colleagues report a rare case in 2026 of granulomatosis with polyangiitis starting during pregnancy. A 26-year-old first-time mother in her second trimester had worsening nose and sinus disease treated as severe bacterial infection, with repeated antibiotics and ear, nose, and throat procedures.

Her state worsened with coughing of blood and hollow lung lesions. Tissue tests showed dead, inflamed tissue with granulomas, and blood tests found anti-PR3 antibodies, confirming the disease near 22 weeks. Care was hard due to fast multi-organ spread, possible kidney harm, a fungal lung infection, and few pregnancy-safe drugs. Steroids, immunoglobulin, and azathioprine brought control.
pmc-13315750:
Adel Mahmoud Negm and co-authors mapped an oil reservoir in 2026 in the I and R fields of Libya's Murzuq Basin. The Upper Ordovician Mamuniyat Formation is the main reservoir there, shaped by glacial deposits and complex structure, so the team combined well data, seismic imaging, and 3D modeling.

Eleven wells showed quartz-rich sandstones with shale under 25 percent, effective pore space near 12 to 15 percent, and water share from about 20 to 55 percent. Seismic traits revealed a northwest to southeast fault system splitting the reservoir, and amplitude patterns marked sand-rich fairways with better quality rock.
pmc-13316250:
Diana R. Tamondong-Lachica and the Philippine Periodic Health Examination task force issue 2026 guidance on lifestyle advice for adults and teens. Smoking, inactivity and poor diet drive much of the burden from heart disease, cancer, lung disease and diabetes. Clinic-based advice is one practical way to lower that burden.

The group used the GRADE approach, reviewing current guidance before a broad expert panel reached consensus. For diet and physical activity questions they adapted World Health Organization guidance after checking the source texts with a standard quality tool. External review followed. The panel made nineteen recommendations, weighing prevention of new disease alongside outcomes for people who already live with chronic conditions, and noting conflicts linked to wellness and tobacco interests.
pmc-13316650:
Daniel Marcano Zamora and a global team report a 2026 demonstration study that extends the World Health Organization GLASS surveillance system to Candida yeasts in the bloodstream. Drug resistance in these fungi is a rising threat, yet tracking had no shared global method.

Twenty-four laboratories were invited to collect cases under one protocol with shared software, covering infections confirmed between January 2017 and July 2021. Fourteen labs in 13 countries sent data, building a set of 3,447 cases for shared counting of species and drug resistance patterns. Sites also fed back on the tools through forms and meetings. The pilot shows standardized fungal tracking can work across very different health systems.
pmc-13316950:
Khaoula M'Rabt and colleagues present a 2026 case report on two sisters, aged 12.5 and 8 years, seen at a dental center in Rabat with pycnodysostosis, a rare inherited bone disorder also called Toulouse-Lautrec syndrome. Their parents are related by blood, matching the disorder's recessive pattern.

The report lingers on face and tooth features, since dentists may be the first to spot the pattern and steer families toward diagnosis. Bone hardening from faulty bone-eating cells drives the syndrome, which affects roughly one to two people per million worldwide.
pmc-13317050:
Motunrayo T Ojo-Rowland and colleagues review, in 2026, depression after childbirth in the United States, covering how common it is, who is at risk and how care is changing. The condition harms mothers and infants and remains a major public health concern. A systematic search gathered 25 eligible studies published between 2010 and 2026.

Rates stay substantial, with gaps tied to race, income and access to care. Risk rises with earlier mental illness, weak social support, unplanned pregnancy and stressful life circumstances, and genetic factors may also contribute. Symptoms can appear at varied times, so repeated screening matters more than a single check. Talk therapy and antidepressants remain central, while telehealth, phone apps and wearables show promise for earlier detection.
pmc-13317850:
Marcel Falis and his team compare, in 2026, a commercial insecticide with its pure active ingredient in a small aquatic crustacean. Pesticide residues persist in surface water and move through food webs. Artemia franciscana, a brine shrimp, serves as a test species for such effects.

The team measured lethal levels over several days for the made-up product Mospilan SP and for acetamiprid alone, then tracked body length and width at lower doses. The shop product strongly suppressed both growth measures after ten days, with clear statistical gaps. Effects of the pure ingredient did not match the product over the same spans, so the added ingredients appear to matter. The authors argue that growth measures at sublethal doses give a more sensitive warning than death alone.
pmc-13318650:
Raphael Groß and colleagues compare, in a 2026 retrospective study, two operations for sinus venosus atrial septal defects, a heart hole near the sinus node, looking mainly at rhythm problems afterwards. Records covered 110 adults and children treated in northern Bavaria between 2000 and 2025.

Seventy patients had the standard patch repair and forty the newer rotational Z-flap. Operations ran shorter with the flap, yet rhythm trouble appeared in 54.5 percent of all patients afterwards, and one pattern, sinoatrial block with junctional rhythm, was clearly commoner after the flap at 17.5 percent against 4.3 percent in the comparison. No one needed a permanent pacemaker, and leftover shunts or vein narrowing did not differ between the techniques.
pmc-13318750:
Giorgia Coratti leads a large consortium reporting, in 2026, on updating disease registries for spinal muscular atrophy. New disease-modifying treatments and newborn screening have reshaped the illness. Old centre spreadsheets and mismatched databases cannot track these changes. Registries must measure treated and untreated patients comparably over time.

Their group helped build the international ISMAR registry across the United States, United Kingdom, and Italy. It uses shared definitions, standard scoring, and trained examiners. Over seven years it has gathered natural history and real-world treatment data. The account describes why the registry scope is now being redefined again. Highly specialised centres led the first phase. Wider, harmonised monitoring is the next challenge for this fast-changing field.
pmc-13319050:
Ping Li and colleagues present a 2026 field experiment on cutting chemical fertiliser use for lettuce. Four treatments kept total nutrients equal. They ranged from chemical fertiliser alone to half replaced by organic manure, with biochar added in two arms. Yield, soil properties, and leaf chemistry were compared.

All three other mixes improved soil organic matter, pH, and available nutrients over chemical fertiliser alone. Lettuce yield and nutrient uptake also rose. The full mix of manure swap plus biochar did best overall. Leaf analysis showed richer phenolic acids and flavonoids under the new mixes. Manure mainly shifted tyrosine pathways, while biochar shifted nitrogen pathways. Leaf chemistry tracked soil organic matter, pH, and potassium most closely when links were checked.
pmc-13319650:
Sena Kaşıkçı and Ebru Şirinoğlu test ways to clear drug paste from young teeth with open tips in a 2026 lab study. Pastes placed inside a tooth to calm infection must come out cleanly before the final fill, and any paste pushed past the tip can cause harm. Sound based rinsing at two pulse types was put to the test.

Thirty two pulled lower canine teeth were shaped to mimic open tips and filled with one of two pastes. Fast pulse rinsing left far less paste behind than slow sonic rinsing for both pastes. Amounts pushed past the tip were alike across all groups. The newer paste cleared at least as well as the standard one, which supports it as a sound choice.
pmc-13319950:
Menglan Zhai and co-authors compare longer use of electric field therapy for a fast brain tumor in a 2026 study across many centers. The wearable therapy uses mild electric fields to jam tumor cell splitting and is given with drug and beam care at first. Whether keeping it on into the later drug phase adds gain was unclear, so records for two paths were set side by side.

One group of 68 people kept the fields into the later phase, while 32 stopped after beam care. Time without tumor growth was alike in both groups, near a year in each. Length of life ran longer in the kept on group by a few months on median counts, but the gap could reflect chance in this non random split. Scalp harm did not rise with longer use.
pmc-13320250:
Jennifer Hutchings and co-authors check whether a full body radiation shield slows heart attack care in a 2026 records study. Fast opening of a blocked heart artery is a core quality mark in heart attack care, with a goal of ninety minutes or less from door to balloon. A new shield system guards staff far better than aprons, but any setup delay would be a real cost.

Records for 133 straight heart attack cases at one center split 71 shield room cases from 62 standard room cases across a year and a half span. Door to balloon times ran close in both rooms, near fifty minutes in each, with no clear gap in any time slice. Better staff safety came with no loss of speed for patients.
pmc-13320550:
B Kaiser and colleagues release a 2026 data set on shock waves driven by high explosives through layered materials. Fast computer models that stand in for full physics runs need good training data, and no public set existed for this problem. The set, called HEAT, was built with a multi-material shock code from Los Alamos National Laboratory.

Two families of two-dimensional runs are included, one with an expanding shock cylinder and one with a rippled layered boundary. Each run tracks how shocks move through several materials at once, a task that needs rules for pressure, bending, phase change, and damage. The release lets machine learning teams train, test, and check fast surrogate models openly.
pmc-13321250:
Tolulope Popoola and colleagues report, in 2026, a drug-coated balloon treatment for a narrowed heart transplant artery. Cardiac allograft vasculopathy, a diffuse narrowing of the transplanted heart's vessels, is among the top causes of late graft failure. Stents themselves often narrow again, leaving few good options.

Their patient was a 33-year-old man transplanted as a child for a weakened heart muscle. His course included rhythm problems, a pacemaker and rejection episodes. Disease progressed despite stents in the right coronary artery and later bypass surgery. When the stent narrowed again, doctors inflated a paclitaxel-coated balloon inside it without adding another stent layer. Angiography at three and nine months showed open vessels and preserved graft function. The authors call for larger studies of this stent-free approach.
pmc-13322150:
Joyce O'Shaughnessy and co-authors test whether a 70 gene signature predicts who gains from stronger chemotherapy in a 2026 breast cancer analysis. Anthracycline drugs have shown no clear average benefit in hormone sensitive, HER2-negative early breast cancer. Data came from the FLEX study of high risk tumours classed by the MammaPrint signature.

Among 1106 patients in the lower high risk group, three year disease free survival matched between drug regimens, both at 95.9 percent in the study. In the highest risk group of 153 patients, the anthracycline regimen reached 100 percent against 94.8 percent without it, a 5.2 point gain. Benefit grew with genomic risk.
pmc-13322950:
Jing Ning and co-authors pool trial evidence on deep brain stimulation and thinking in Parkinson's disease, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. They searched four databases for randomised trials that set stimulation against best medical treatment, judging bias with a standard Cochrane tool.

Ten trials with 1,274 patients qualified. Stimulation groups fell more on verbal fluency and on a Stroop colour-word task than medical groups in the pooled results. Overall cognition, mental flexibility, depression and anxiety measures showed no clear difference between groups. The authors frame stimulation as a strong motor therapy with a narrow cost to word-finding speed, and they call for longer and more uniform mental testing in future trials.
pmc-13323250:
Alex Gittelman proposes a unified framework for rhythm coordination across brain, body and social life, in a 2026 theory article. Brains coordinate behaviour from milliseconds to days through cross-frequency coupling, where slow waves shape the timing and strength of faster ones.

The framework, called Temporal-Oscillatory Entrainment, sorts nine frequency bands into neural, biological and social groups. Hearing and movement form a privileged path, since coupling appears in the auditory brainstem near a natural rhythm band. Music training, breathing rhythms and social rhythm therapy give supporting cases across scales. The author argues that one nesting principle links neural timing with daily routines and group coordination.
pmc-13323950:
Kah and co-authors review immune based treatments for hepatocellular carcinoma in this 2026 article. This is the most common form of liver cancer, and it kills many patients worldwide. Drugs that release the brakes on the immune system have widened the options for advanced disease. Yet only a minority of patients gain lasting benefit from them.

The review blames the liver tumour environment, which is shaped by chronic viral hepatitis and fatty liver disease. Suppressor cells, exhausted T cells and natural killer cells, and blocking signals such as HLA G all help tumours escape. Kah surveys newer targets such as TIGIT and Tim 3, cell therapies aimed at glypican 3, natural killer cell treatments, and blood tests that track response. The authors argue that matching patients to treatments through biomarkers is the way to lift response rates.
pmc-13324450:
Laura H. H. Winkens and colleagues tested whether people welcome just-in-time digital prompts for healthier food choices, and when. Their 2026 mixed-methods study gave 14 adults, averaging 27 years old, a researcher-built app for one week after each chose a nutrition goal. The app prompted healthy choices near food outlets and at preset times, and the team measured receptivity, usability, privacy views, and perceived effectiveness.

Usability suffered from technical issues and battery drain, and participants with less schooling reported more installation trouble, less favorable views of prompt tone, and smaller gains in food choices. pmc-13325150:
Bahriyenur Arabacı, Aslı Yüksel, and Canan Varlıklı turn sugar beet pulp into a light-driven catalyst for cleaning sugar factory wastewater in a 2026 study. The loop is neat: solid waste from the industry treats its own liquid waste.

Hydrothermal cooking made hydrochar from the pulp, which then supported graphitic carbon nitride. Best char yield, 36.74 percent, came at 200 °C for 60 minutes with 20 g of biomass. Under tuned conditions the pair removed 14.02 percent of total organic carbon from real effluent. That share looks low until the starting load, above 7000 mg per liter, is weighed. The char also made the catalyst sturdier for reuse.
pmc-13326050:
Alejandra Pedraza and six co-authors report a nine-year-old boy whose weak heart turned out to hide a rare coronary defect present from birth. Their case report appeared in two thousand twenty-six. In the defect, the left coronary artery springs from the lung artery instead of the aorta. Left unseen, it can scar the heart muscle beyond repair.

Oddly, the usual ultrasound clues of the defect were missing. Heart MRI and catheter studies finally confirmed it. Surgeons moved the artery to its proper root and repaired the valve. Recovery went well. The authors urge doctors to check the coronary origins in every child with a weak heart.
pmc-13326350:
Yichao Liu and co-authors compare five drying routes for the medicinal herb Atractylodes chinensis in a 2026 study. Drying shapes both the active compounds and the prized aroma of the roots.

Volatile profiles centered on terpenoids, esters, phenols, and ketones. The freeze-dried batch stood out for atractylodin, atractylone, and bornyl acetate, which carry woody and camphor notes. Terpenoid building pathways dominated the chemistry shifts.
pmc-13326450:
Veronika Papon, Uwe Siebert, Ursula Rochau, and colleagues publish the protocol for judging whether prescribing nature against loneliness is worth its cost. The RECETAS project runs trials in Barcelona, Prague, and Helsinki. The trials refer lonely people to group outings in natural settings, backed by a menu of nearby nature-based community assets.

Outcomes include quality of life, loneliness scores, and personal capability. Direct, indirect, and informal costs all count, over twelve months. Publishing the design in advance, the authors argue, keeps the economic verdict open and repeatable. That serves decision makers weighing nature-based social prescribing.
pmc-13326950:
Sameer Dal and a large team profile epileptic spasms that begin after infancy in a 2026 cohort study. Late-onset spasms are often missed, and older series left most causes unknown.

Steroid treatment stopped spasms in 29 percent, and vigabatrin in 35 percent, each favoring different cause groups.
pmc-13327950:
YuQi Ren and co-authors run a pilot causal study of an added drainage cut in glaucoma surgery in a 2026 article. Records covered 102 eyes, 54 with the standard operation and 48 with the added cut.

pmc-13328250:
Rulan Shangguan, Jiajing Xie, and Xiaofen Hamilton develop a scale for physical activity awareness in college students in a 2026 study. Campuses could use the scale to find which awareness gap keeps each student inactive.
pmc-13328450:
Ragini Bodade and fellow editors introduce a collection on extremophiles in biotechnology in a 2026 editorial. The editors survey what the gathered studies offer for greener industry.

One thread traces extremophile origins toward early Earth life and catalogs survival gear, from tough enzymes to protective solutes, with uses in clean production, pollution cleanup, and climate work. Another covers CRISPR systems in tough bacteria and archaea, including TnpB from a radiation-proof species, as next-generation editing tools. Genome comparisons show how these organisms trim energy use to thrive where little else can.
pmc-13328650:
Shaoying Li and co-authors published a 2026 study of night light in the bedroom and hepatic encephalopathy, a grave clouding of the brain, in patients with liver cancer. Light at night is tied to liver harm in past studies. The brain condition comes when the liver fails to clear its waste. The team asks whether a lit bedroom raises its risk.

Sleep quality scores came with the measurements. All were followed for a year for adverse outcomes. Bright bedrooms, above a set mark, were tied to higher odds of both the overt and the hidden form of the brain condition. They were tied to worse liver function, gut bleeding, and more deaths too. Age and tumor stage modified the ties somewhat.
pmc-13329750:

Three days after his second cycle of adebrelimab, alongside other cancer drugs, he developed chest tightness, weak muscles, eye movement loss, and breath trouble.

The drug was stopped and strong immune calming care was given, yet his state worsened and cardiac arrest came on day 9. The authors urge baseline checks, fast spotting, and team care for such events.
pmc-13330450:
Rongchao Ma and team surveyed circulating biomarkers of carotid plaque vulnerability. The team calls for large prospective multicenter studies and standard methods to advance early risk stratification.
pmc-13330550:

One method found 76 volatile compounds, with 31 key markers splitting the types. A second method found 60 compounds. Semi-sweet wine held the richest mix. Joined tools can grade and track wine flavour, the authors conclude.
pmc-13331050:
Yanni Zhang and colleagues map world clinical trials of cytokine-induced killer cell therapy in a 2026 analysis. The team pulled trial records from Informa, current to February 2026, yielding 199 interventional trials across cancers and some immune disorders. Killer cells grown with cytokines blend T cell targeting with natural killer style killing.

Early-phase work dominates the field, with China leading translation and academic centres as top sponsors in the reported landscape. Lung cancer, leukaemia, and liver cell cancer trials are most frequent. Pairings with dendritic cells or checkpoint drugs are rising, mostly in added or maintenance care. The authors urge better patient sorting, standard making, and marker-guided design.
pmc-13332050:

Sequencing found clear zones: Burkholderia and Pseudomonas up front, Paenibacillus in the middle, and genera that shun oxygen in the hindgut. Gene data showed the hindgut bacteria actively run nitrogen cycling chemistry. Knowing this inner fertilizer factory could expose weak points for pest control. This twenty twenty-six study gives the pest's hidden partners their first detailed census.
pmc-13332550:
Astrid Grouls and colleagues survey 2026 how embedding palliative care clinicians in ALS teams changes ALS clinicians' confidence. A total of 141 ALS clinicians responded, mainly from neurology, nursing, and therapy. Those with an embedded specialist felt surer handling pain, breathlessness, and end-of-life needs, with the pain gap largest. They also reported fewer referral blocks and referred for different reasons. The study suggests that placing that expertise inside the team, rather than only on referral, strengthens day-to-day ALS care and clinician confidence.
pmc-13332750:
Divya Garg and colleagues test 2026 whether the Tisdale risk score can guide heart-rhythm drug safety in primary care. The score is validated for predicting drug-induced QT interval prolongation in cardiac care, but its use in general practice is less clear. Eighty-five patients with heart tracings before and after drug therapy formed the case group.

A control group of 184 patients not on QT-prolonging drugs was assessed for comparison. Psychotropic drugs were the most common QT-prolonging medicines prescribed. Most cases fell in the low-risk band, with about a quarter moderate and under five percent high.
pmc-13333350:
Monica Pomaville and Jessica B Foster argue in a 2026 commentary that making CAR T cells from short-lived mRNA, rather than a lasting virus, could make brain tumor therapy safer for children. The authors present the format as a way to keep the anti-tumor punch while lowering early and late brain risks.
pmc-13333450:
Xiaogang Jin and colleagues compare students in China and Kazakhstan in a 2026 cross-cultural survey. For Chinese youth, economic capital was the main family resource tied to career self-determination, a pattern the authors link to involutionary competition. For Kazakhstani youth, social capital, the family's network, mattered most. In both countries, how students perceived their social class mediated the link between family resources and self-determination, translating wealth into confidence. Traditional values pulled against self-determination in both cultures but did not change the resource effect. The authors draw lessons for career counseling policy along the Belt and Road.
pmc-13333750:
In New Hampshire and Vermont, César Alas-Pineda and co-authors surveyed cancer survivors about alcohol use in a 2026 study. The study measured drinking patterns, awareness that alcohol raises cancer risk, and survivors' wishes and obstacles around cutting down.

The cross-sectional survey drew 471 survivors aged 21 and older from two statewide online panels, and about a third had an alcohol-related cancer. Two-thirds currently drank alcohol, yet only about half knew alcohol increases cancer risk. Among current drinkers, 26.5 percent wanted to cut down within six months, and many in that group drank around seven drinks a week. Heart and memory worries motivated change, while socializing and stress relief held people back. The authors call for targeted education and support.
pmc-13334050:
Lukas Blumrich and seven colleagues track maternal cortisol across pregnancy and the months after birth in a São Paulo birth cohort, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Prenatal stress is suspected of reshaping the stress-hormone axis of the mother. Hair cortisol sums up months of hormone exposure. One hundred eighty-five women reported violence exposure, anxiety, and depression in late pregnancy.

Cortisol fell a lot from pregnancy into the postpartum months. Most stressors showed no link to hair cortisol at any point. Psychological partner violence, anxiety, and depression were all without a link. Acute physical or sexual partner violence was the exception. It tracked with lower cortisol at specific prepartum points and lower average levels overall. The pattern complicates simple stories of stress raising cortisol. Timing and stressor type, the authors suggest, shape the biology.
pmc-13335150:

No design erased the twist penalty, so care is urged for large turned moves.
pmc-13406950:

pmc-13407950:

pmc-13408050:

pmc-13408350:

The authors read the flattened rhythm as a weaker time signal reaching the circadian clock. pmc-13408450:

pmc-13408850:

pmc-13410550:

pmc-13410950:

pmc-13411150:

pmc-13412050:

pmc-13412550:

pmc-13412850:

pmc-13415550:

pmc-13416150:

pmc-13416750:

pmc-13417350:

pmc-13417850:

pmc-13418050:

pmc-13418450:

pmc-13418850:

pmc-13420650:

pmc-13420850:

pmc-13424750:

pmc-13426150:

pmc-13426350:

pmc-13426850:

pmc-13426950:

pmc-13427250:

pmc-13427650:

pmc-13427750:

pmc-13427950:

pmc-13428350:

pmc-13428450:

pmc-13428550:

pmc-13428750:

pmc-13431750:

pmc-13432850:
Jens Bedke and co-authors mapped real-world care in 2026 for bladder cancer that has not yet dug into the muscle wall, drawing charts from North America, Europe, and Japan. Such cases form three quarters of new finds. Guides sort patients by risk and urge scope surgery plus up to three years of a bladder-wash germ therapy for high-risk cases.

No patient in the set had the bladder cut out at first, though guides urge that step for the worst risk or for returns after wash care. Second rounds echoed first ones. The authors flag a wide gap between guide care and real care.
pmc-13433550:
Heike Klepetko and colleagues validate a machine-learning algorithm that measures facial first impressions, judgments formed within milliseconds that colour social interaction. Traditional ratings of such impressions are subjective and vary between observers, while aesthetic face treatments can shift how a face is read.

Clinicians and researchers get a reproducible, scalable yardstick for first impressions, useful for judging whether a treatment changes how a face is perceived.
pmc-13434350:
Songfan He and colleagues weigh the carbon balance of bays along the Antarctic Peninsula in 2026. Warming is moving old carbon from land to sea, where some is buried and some is lost as gas. Two bays with unlike bedrock were compared with heat based lab tests and isotope models.

The bay cut in soft rock buried ten fold more rock derived carbon than the bay cut in volcanic rock. Across the region, burial of living source carbon likely beats loss of rock carbon. Models suggest burial could rise two to four fold as change goes on. Rock type must enter forecasts of polar carbon storage.
pmc-13434550:
Hamidullah Yaşar and Nihal Ekmekci study spark machining of medical-grade Ti6Al4V titanium in pure water, for surface quality and wear in medical use. Titanium suits dentistry and bone surgery through low density, rust resistance, and kindness to living tissue.

Research linking wear acts to surface quality was thin, motivating tuning of machining settings for medical parts. Implant makers get a study of how water-based spark machining trades cell-friendly roughness against wear strength.
pmc-13434650:

Packed into a porous block, the clusters ran without pause in a flow reactor. Flow models guided the block design. Making and using peroxide in one unit trims waste and hazard.
pmc-13435050:
Euna Oh and coauthors coat surfaces with a wood based dye that sterilizes itself in room light in 2026. Lignin from plants is tied firm to a pink xanthene dye, then locked into a spray cured film. Leaching is blocked because the dye is bound, not blended.

pmc-13435950:

pmc-13436650:
Brian Chen and coauthors clear false penicillin allergy labels in a veterans emergency ward in 2026. Pharmacists reviewed 144 patients with allergy labels over one year. Low risk patients headed for admission got a test dose of amoxicillin by mouth, then an hour of watch.

Twenty patients took the test dose, while 124 did not. Groups looked alike at baseline on the counts given. Ward stays for tested patients ran a non significant thirty six minutes longer. pmc-13436950:

pmc-13438450:

pmc-13439050:
Adrienne Henderson's team tested carbon fiber deformable foot orthoses in 2026 to see how stiffness reshapes foot and ankle work during walking. pmc-13439250:

pmc-13439850:

pmc-13441250:

pmc-13441750:

pmc-13442850:

pmc-13443050:

pmc-13443150:

pmc-13443750:

pmc-13444250:

pmc-13446350:

pmc-13447150:

pmc-13448050:

pmc-13448250:

pmc-13448350:

pmc-13449250:

pmc-13449350:

pmc-13449850:

pmc-13450250:

pmc-13451250:

pmc-13452250:

pmc-13453050:

pmc-13453250:

For Brazil, they weigh crop output by town to price the risk. The map can guide watch lists and border checks.
pmc-13453650:
