Patients averaged 59 years of age and 84 percent were women in this surgical series. Enlargement let surgeons implant prostheses two to three sizes larger than the native ring allowed, with tissue valves in 12 patients and mechanical valves in seven. No one died in hospital, and scans showed the sinus widening by 7.0 millimeters and the junction above it by 6.9 millimeters after repair. The trade-offs were electrical: the heart's conduction interval lengthened from 90 to 114 milliseconds, and right heart function dipped, warranting surveillance.
pmc-13453750:
Luocheng Zhang and five co-authors report three patients whose dangerous immune overreaction hid an aggressive lymphoma in the liver. The syndrome, shortened to HLH, floods the body with inflammation and can mask the cancer driving it. Their 2026 case series covers adults whose platelet counts had crashed and kept falling despite transfusions, which made a standard needle biopsy too risky.

A biopsy taken through the jugular vein into the liver, a route that contains bleeding, proved B cell lymphoma in all three patients. Chemotherapy aimed at the lymphoma could then start without delay. In two patients, platelet counts returned to normal within two to four weeks, and the inflammation settled. The authors show the low platelet counts had several stacked causes, from immune attack to trapping in the liver.
pmc-13453850:
Frankel and colleagues describe a 67-year-old woman with hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy. Her planned mitral valve repair took a surprise turn. Surgeons found a perforation in the front leaflet pointing to infective endocarditis. Testing showed the cause was Borrelia burgdorferi, the Lyme disease bacterium. That is a rare source of heart valve infection.

Her outflow tract gradients measured 66 millimeters of mercury at rest and 102 on provocation before surgery, with severe mitral leakage jetting through the leaflet hole. The team did a complex repair guided by the valve's anatomy plus a limited septal muscle shave, easing the obstruction without replacing the valve in this patient. Avoiding a prosthesis counted doubly because implanting artificial material into an infected field invites persistent, hard-to-treat infection around the device. The authors highlight repair-first techniques as protective in exactly this incidental-infection scenario.
pmc-13453950:
Daniel Camprubí–Ferrer and others studied dengue vaccine safety in travelers in 2026, in a real-world Spanish pharmacovigilance cohort. TAK-003 is the first dengue vaccine approved for endemic and non-endemic regions, but safety data in non-endemic travelers, especially older adults and people with comorbidities, were scarce.

Travelers from non-endemic areas receiving TAK-003 were followed prospectively across multiple Spanish centers, with adverse events recorded and factors associated with events analyzed. The cohort design captures events as they occur in routine travel clinics, rather than trial settings. Travel medicine clinicians gain real-world safety data to counsel travelers considering dengue vaccination.
pmc-13454650:
Takashi Kido and eight colleagues examine, in a 2026 study, whether stiff filling of the right heart predicts trouble after a valve operation in people born with a heart defect. Patients with repaired tetralogy of Fallot often need a pulmonary valve replacement later in life, and the best timing is debated. The team reviewed all such operations at the University of Osaka from 2002 to 2022.

Poor right-heart filling was defined by high end-diastolic pressure or an enlarged right atrium on standard cutoffs. The study asks whether that stiffness forecasts a combined risk of bad outcomes after surgery. It also probes which patient traits travel with stiff filling. A final question splits patients by filling pattern to test whether age 35 or older at surgery is risky for everyone, or only for some. The framing treats filling stiffness as a summary signal for timing decisions.
pmc-13454750:
Lizhi Huang and Yangshun Zhang pool, in a 2026 meta-analysis, trials of lung cancer surgery done without a breathing tube. Standard keyhole lobectomy uses full anesthesia with a tube in the windpipe. The no-tube approach keeps patients breathing on their own. The team gathered 18 studies covering 2,313 patients, 1,082 of them in the no-tube group.

Operations without intubation ran shorter, and waking, feeding, and chest drain times all shrank. Hospital stays shortened by about a day. Overall complications fell, with sore throat and pneumonia notably rarer. About four percent of no-tube patients needed a tube placed mid-operation. Survival also favored the no-tube group in the pooled data. The authors still caution that most studies were not randomized, so patient selection may flatter the newer method.
pmc-13454950:
Li and colleagues report a 2026 case in which a heart attack hid a rare adrenal tumor called a pheochromocytoma, a growth that floods the body with stress hormones. Their patient was a 51 year old man admitted with chest tightness and raised troponin, a blood marker of heart damage. Scans of his heart arteries showed blocked vessels, so doctors first treated him for a heart attack without artery raising on the tracing.

During a procedure to open the blocked artery, his blood pressure shot up, fell sharply with a standard drug, then rose again, with no clear link to the drug dose. Blood tests showed very high stress hormone levels, and imaging found a mass near his left kidney that surgeons removed. Tissue tests confirmed the tumor, and after surgery his blood pressure stayed stable with no drugs at all.
pmc-13455550: Mohammad Al-Harbi and seven colleagues published a 2026 correction to their study linking muscle and fat makeup on scans with knee arthritis severity. The notice is a correction only, replacing a wrong funding statement and changing nothing else in the study. The corrected wording states that the work was in fact funded, naming a university researchers project in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, with its grant number. The record now shows the support the authors received.
pmc-13456850:
Zhao, Li, and Yu test a simple blood based ratio as a warning sign for death in very ill patients with diabetes. The ratio divides blood glucose, a sugar measure, by platelet count, a clotting cell measure. Their 2026 study draws on the MIMIC-IV database of intensive care patients and covers 21,145 adults with diabetes. Patients fell into four groups by ratio level, and the team tracked deaths at 28 days and 360 days.

Death rates rose steadily from the lowest ratio group to the highest at both checks. In adjusted models, the highest group's risk of death by 28 days ran about a third higher than the lowest group's. Risk climbed in a bent, not straight, pattern as the ratio rose. The link held across age, sex, and sepsis subgroups. The authors present the ratio as a cheap risk flag that still needs testing in care.
pmc-13457050:
P. V. Varshini leads a ten-author review, from 2026, of tiny RNA parcels in the blood that may sharpen the diagnosis of acute coronary syndrome, the family of sudden heart artery crises. Current blood tests center on troponin, a heart protein that rises after damage. Its timing and precision leave gaps, especially in the first hours.

The parcels are exosomes, bubbles shed by cells, carrying microRNAs that survive the trip intact. Heart cells release them early in an attack, often before troponin climbs. Different parcel signatures mark inflammation, cell death, vessel growth, and scarring, and some can tell crisis subtypes apart or predict recovery. The review also imagines therapy: blocking a harmful microRNA with a designed antidote. Practical hurdles remain, from messy isolation methods to small, varied study groups. The authors call for standard protocols and large validation cohorts.
pmc-13457650:
Valeria Loise and fellow editors introduce a 2026 set of studies on the chemistry and physics of bitumen, the sticky petroleum binder that glues asphalt roads together. Pavements must last longer while using less virgin oil. The editors argue that every gain, from polymers and fibers to nanoparticles and bio-based additives, stands or falls on what molecules do inside the binder.

One highlighted study tackles recycled asphalt pavement, whose old asphalt film weakens bonding with fresh mineral binder. Coating the recycled aggregate interface with a mineral paste improved compaction, tensile strength, and shrinkage. At 28 percent recycled content the mix also cut carbon emissions per unit volume by up to 54.3 percent against cement-stabilized crushed stone. The editorial frames bitumen as a colloidal system whose road performance at full scale can only be engineered well once chemistry, physics, modeling, and nanotechnology insights are combined, pointing toward greener roads.
pmc-13457950:
Ana M. Valencia-Palacios and colleagues show that tiny feather angles steer hummingbird shine in a 2026 optics study. Hummingbird shine comes from layered pigment packs inside feather barbules, yet most light measures assume barbules lie flat in the feather plane. The team paired angle-based light tests with layered light models for Coeligena hummingbirds, predicting peak shine angles and inferring barbule tilt from fine structure.

Ignoring tilt can misread spectra, and reanalysis of published data across species suggested many measures fit tilted-barbule shape better than flat-feather shape, within model limits. Barbule tilt thus links fine structure to signal direction, and the authors offer a plan for standard light measures. Biologists gain a caution that colour comparisons need shape stated, not just wavelength reported.
pmc-13458350:
Yuanpeng Wu and colleagues rebuild medical record quality control around an AI engine at a large Chinese tertiary hospital. Manual checking samples only a sliver of records, applies standards unevenly, and feeds back too late. Their 2026 development study encodes record-writing rules into a database, trains deep learning and natural language processing to screen every chart, and wraps the machine in a four-level human-machine review process.

Automated first-pass screening reached 100 percent of electronic records, a coverage manual teams cannot approach. Human reviewers then handle the upper three levels, exchanging findings with clinical departments in a closed loop that pushes corrections back to the writers. After implementation, completeness, timeliness, consistency, and accuracy all improved significantly, and the shares of grade-A and excellent records kept climbing, each trend significant beyond the 0.001 level. The authors offer the tiered model as a transferable reference for hospitals drowning in digital paperwork.
pmc-13459550:
Eralp Dogu and co-authors present MSstatsQC-ML, a machine-learning system for quality control in mass spectrometry proteomics. Instruments drift and technical artefacts creep in, so laboratories run standard mixtures and watch many metrics at once, a task that scales poorly by eye. Their 2026 paper adds supervised classifiers to an existing open-source quality package.

The method trains classifiers on features drawn from quality metrics and uses experimental design ideas to simulate suboptimal runs that have not yet been observed, so the system can recognise them later. Tracking each feature over time also helps pinpoint why performance degraded and what preventive action to take. On quality data from both discovery and targeted proteomics experiments, the approach cut error rates in detecting suboptimal performance and beat traditional monitoring methods. The tool is released within the open-source MSstatsQC package.
pmc-13459750:
Sun and colleagues study how yaks adapt their blood to life at high altitude in this 2026 genomics paper. Thin air demands better oxygen transport, and yaks have lived on the Qinghai-Xizang plateau for millennia. The team measured blood traits in 1,244 plateau yaks and 154 lowland cattle. They then scanned the genomes for variants tied to those traits. They also looked for signs of natural selection.

Yaks showed higher hemoglobin and red cell concentration than cattle, but lower platelet counts, the opposite strategy from the hemoglobin damping seen in many high-altitude species. The scans found 6,485 selection-linked variants across 43 blood traits and 172 genes favored in yaks. Thirty-eight genes affected several traits at once, and six overlapped with genes under selection in Tibetan highlanders, hinting at shared solutions to thin air.
pmc-13460150:
Javardo H. McIntosh and Jeffrey H. Jennings tracked in 2026 how prescribing of dual long-acting bronchodilators changed around the GOLD 2023 guideline for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The guideline urges two long-acting inhaled drugs together after a hospital flare. Their Henry Ford Hospital cohort held 2,537 patients hospitalized between December 2017 and July 2024, split at the guideline's publication into earlier and later periods.

Discharge prescribing of dual therapy rose from 38 percent before the guideline to a little over 56 percent after it. Trend analysis showed prescribing was already climbing before publication, with the steepest gains among patients not previously on dual therapy. Admission under a pulmonary service also predicted receiving the combination. Longer follow-up should show whether the trend holds.
pmc-13460650:
Chad C. Andersen and Michael J. Stark argue that early lung form should guide lung fault treatment in a 2026 story-style review. Lung fault is defined at 36 weeks by treatment needs, reflecting practice rather than body workings, yet infants diverge much earlier. Published trials of after-birth steroids serve as the main example of how form shapes response.

Some very preterm infants settle with helping care alone, while others develop lasting lung disease, and broad early treatment dilutes apparent benefit from babies who get better on their own. As age rises and groups enrich for lasting disease, treatment effects grow larger and more steady. Trial designers and newborn doctors gain a case for matching therapy and sign-up with early clinical form.
pmc-13460950:
Pratisma Wagle and colleagues present in 2026 a 48-year-old woman whose two years of abdominal pain after meals finally traced to median arcuate ligament syndrome. In this rare condition, a fibrous band near the diaphragm squeezes the celiac artery. She had cycled through multiple specialties without an answer. The syndrome mimics common gut complaints, and its signs shift with anatomy and breathing.

Contrast CT eventually showed a pinched celiac artery with widening just beyond the pinch, plus a well-developed detour network of collateral vessels linking the liver's artery to the intestinal artery. The authors argue that such prominent collaterals may mark the cases that actually produce symptoms when they appear alongside significant narrowing. That would help separate harmless anatomy from true disease when planning care with a multidisciplinary team.
pmc-13461550:
Xue and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how the cancer drug doxorubicin harms the heart through failing mitochondria, the cell's energy factories. Use of this wide-spectrum drug is capped by dose-linked heart damage, and no effective clinical remedy exists. The review traces how the drug breaks mitochondrial quality control and rewires their metabolism, sparking excess reactive oxygen and leaked mitochondrial DNA.

Xue explains that this damage ends in PANoptosis, a newly defined form of inflammatory cell death that blends features of three older death paths. The review covers faults in protein upkeep, shape balance, new mitochondria building, and cleanup of worn ones. It then surveys countermeasures: targeted antioxidants, cleanup activators, mitochondria transplant, PANoptosis blockers, nano-scale delivery, and gene or cell therapy. The goal is keeping the drug's anti-cancer power while shielding the heart.
pmc-13462150:
Jieyang Wang and co-authors report, in a 2026 study, that the signaling enzyme ADCY4 holds back lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. The enzyme's job in this cancer was not known. Large gene data first flagged ADCY4 as reduced in tumors. The team measured it in tissue and cell lines and boosted its levels to watch effects on cancer cell behavior.

Low ADCY4 went with worse patient outlook and more advanced stage. Restoring the enzyme in cancer cells slowed growth, movement, and invasion in dish tests. The mechanism ran through a partner protein, PRKCB: ADCY4 binds it and raises its amount. Blocking the partner removed the benefit, showing the suppression depends on that link. Tumors grown in animals shrank when ADCY4 was restored, through the same partner route. The authors name ADCY4 a tumor suppressor in this lung cancer, and a possible marker and target.
pmc-13462450:
Andreia Pimenta and colleagues tested a symptom-checking computer aid in 2026 inside a large private health network, where patients answer questions before seeing a doctor. Such digital front doors are spreading, yet proof of how they fit daily care is thin. Adults filled in a structured symptom form, and both patients and doctors later rated the advice and report it produced.

Doctors mostly judged the urgency advice and reports apt, and felt better prepared and faster when they had read the report first. Patients mostly said their symptoms were fully captured and that they felt readier for the visit. The work offers real-world backing for such aids in routine care, while leaving open how far they can ease queues and staff strain across wider health systems.
pmc-13462550:
Jinhua Huang and colleagues build, in a 2026 records study, a model to tell apart two kinds of lung tumors in women with breast cancer. One is spread from the breast, the other a new lung cancer. The call changes treatment, yet the two can look alike. The team reviewed 158 patients seen between 2013 and 2023, using clinical traits plus radiomics, which mines patterns from CT scans inside and around the tumor.

100 patients had new lung cancers and 58 had breast spread. The spread group showed higher stage, more node spread, and higher levels of markers. A clinical model alone sorted the groups fairly. Scan-pattern models did better, with the tumor-interior model strongest. Joining traits with scan patterns gave the best sorting, in building and testing groups. The authors say the model can sharpen diagnosis and guide treatment for breast cancer patients with lung lesions.
pmc-13462850:
Liangzhao Wu and colleagues examine, in a 2026 database study, whether a blood inflammation index predicts kidney injury in newborns with jaundice. Kidney injury is a serious complication in these babies, and inflammation sits at its core. The index, SII, combines three blood cell counts and predicts kidney injury in adults, yet its role in jaundiced newborns was unknown. Records came from an intensive care database holding 2,326 jaundiced newborns.

 Higher values independently went with higher kidney injury risk, in a straight-line pattern with no bend. The link held across clinical subgroups and survived robustness checks, including methods testing how strong hidden bias would need to be to erase it. Oddly, higher values also went with shorter intensive care stays, a puzzle the authors flag for study. They present the index, cheap to compute from routine blood counts, as a candidate early risk flag for kidney injury.
pmc-13463650:
Golmohammadi and colleagues reviewed in 2026 whether the MIND diet is linked to calmer mental health. The MIND diet blends Mediterranean and blood-pressure-friendly foods. It was designed to protect the aging brain. The team searched four databases through August 2025. They sought studies connecting how closely people followed the diet with depression, anxiety, or stress symptoms.

Twenty-one studies qualified, and eleven were cross-sectional snapshots taken at one point in time. Twelve studies tied closer adherence to fewer depression symptoms. Seven found a similar pattern for anxiety, and three for stress. The picture was far from uniform, though. The studies used different designs, questionnaires, and populations. Most could show association rather than cause. The authors conclude the diet may help mood. Only long-term follow-up studies and proper trials can settle whether the benefit is real.
pmc-13463750:
Kristensen and co-authors use Norway's national stroke registry to test clot-busting treatment in mild strokes in this 2026 study. Intravenous thrombolysis dissolves the clot causing a stroke, but recent trials did not prove it helps patients whose symptoms are mild. The team studied registry patients from 2016 to 2022 with low stroke severity scores and matched 1,736 treated patients with 1,736 similar untreated controls.

Ninety days later, treated patients had an excellent recovery in 68.4 percent of cases, with little or no disability. The matched controls reached 61.2 percent in the same registry period. The benefit appeared in patients with mild-to-moderate symptoms but not in the very mildest group, whose scores were zero or one. Death rates did not differ, while 3.7 percent of treated patients suffered a symptomatic brain bleed, a known risk of the therapy.
pmc-13464150:
Li Rong and colleagues showed in 2026 that one dose of a therapeutic Salmonella bacterium can train natural killer cells in mice to guard against cancer spread. Spread causes about 90% of cancer deaths, yet most therapies are judged on shrinking the first tumour rather than blocking later spread. The team used functional tests and multi-layer molecular profiling to trace how trained killer cells change.

Trained cells rewired their gene control for survival and attack, releasing more interferon-gamma and killing more strongly on a second challenge. Training needed a brief pulse of IL-12 plus steady IL-18 signalling, and trained cells beat PD-1 and TIGIT checkpoint blockers at stopping spread. Bacterial vaccines or trained killer cells may thus offer lasting spread prevention, pending human safety trials.
pmc-13465550:
Manal Saleh Moustafa Saleh leads a team that surveys 117 mental health nurses in Egypt on toxic leadership and its fallout. Abusive, authoritarian bosses can wound staff well-being in high-pressure wards. Four standard scales fed a structural model joining leadership, distress, body symptoms, drive, and extra-mile behavior.

Toxic leadership tied clearly to psychological distress among the nurses. Distress, in turn, tied strongly to physical symptoms such as aches and fatigue. Inner drive lifted extra-mile behavior on its own track, yet it failed to carry any leadership effect across, against the team's guess. No direct line ran from toxic leadership to extra-mile behavior. Leadership training and staff mental health support head the authors' remedies.
pmc-13465650:
Ercengiz and colleagues grouped university students in 2026 by how mindfulness and experiential avoidance mix with social media use disorder. Mindfulness means present-moment awareness. Experiential avoidance means dodging feelings one dislikes. The sample held 826 students aged 18 to 25, most of them women. Links among the measures came first. A latent profile analysis then sorted people into types.

The links pointed the way theory suggests. More mindful students reported less social media disorder and less avoidance. Social media disorder itself rose together with avoidance. The profile step distilled four student types. Each type pairs its own level of disorder with a distinct mix of awareness and avoidance. The authors argue the types describe students better than single scores do. They urge testing whether the same four profiles appear in other age groups and school levels.
pmc-13466250:
Andrew Hearn and colleagues lay out a diagnostic path for a throat problem that often hides inside difficult asthma, in a 2026 clinical article. The problem, inducible laryngeal obstruction, narrows the voice box briefly and reversibly, mostly while breathing in. Around a tenth of asthma patients stay hard to treat despite standard care, and this hidden contributor is one reason.

Asthma itself affects roughly seven percent of adults, with cough, wheeze, and breathlessness that come and go. Mistaking laryngeal episodes for asthma flares can push inhaler doses up and even trigger biologic therapy without benefit. The article gives clinicians an ordered way to suspect, test for, and confirm the throat condition alongside asthma.
pmc-13466650:
Zhang and a multicenter team randomized 698 colonoscopy patients in 2026, comparing a spectral imaging mode against standard white light. The spectral mode uses narrow color bands to make the bowel lining stand out. Small or flat growths, called adenomas, are easy to miss with white light. Eight endoscopy centers took part. Patients aged 45 to 85 split evenly between modes. The main measure was the share of patients with at least one adenoma found.

Spectral imaging won clearly. Adenomas appeared in about 38 percent of its patients against about 30 percent with white light. Polyp detection and advanced adenoma detection also rose. Adenomas per exam climbed from about half to about three quarters on average. The advantage concentrated where misses hurt most: the right side of the colon, growths under five millimeters, and flat lesions. The authors recommend the mode for routine use to lift colonoscopy quality.
pmc-13467150:
Julien Jost and colleagues ask whether robot-guided spine screw placement stays accurate during night and weekend emergencies at a teaching hospital, in a 2026 analysis. The dataset held 146 operations and just over a thousand screws into the spine and pelvis. Sixteen procedures, covering 150 screws, ran off-hours, and all of them were emergencies.

Off-hours cases carried more trauma, needed repeat imaging or re-registration more often, and used intensive care more, with longer stays. Screw accuracy stayed close between shifts, with top-grade placements in the mid-nineties percent off-hours against slightly higher in regular hours. A fairer comparison against daytime emergencies only was also run. The authors call the approach feasible under strain.
pmc-13467750:
Gomes and co-authors review in this 2026 systematic review whether bacteriophages, viruses that infect and kill bacteria, can control Campylobacter on food after harvest. Campylobacter is the world's leading bacterial cause of foodborne stomach illness, and poultry meat is its main route to people, so a safe spray-on treatment would matter.

Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, the team gathered 14 original studies applying phages to food products. Twelve of the 14 studies reported significant bacterial reductions, ranging from 0.2 to at least 5 log units, meaning up to a hundred-thousand-fold drop in counts. Refrigeration alone gave modest gains, while combining phages with physical treatments passed the 2-log reduction benchmark European regulators reference. Screening confirmed the candidate phages carried no toxin, resistance, or dormancy genes, supporting their genomic safety.
pmc-13467950:
Fu and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how liquid chromatography with high-resolution mass spectrometry can hunt unknown contaminants in cosmetics. Such contaminants sneak in through illegal additions, impure raw materials, or packaging leaks, and standard targeted tests miss anything not on their lists. The newer approach scans everything in a sample, flags thousands of chemical features, and uses molecular networking, which groups look-alike spectra, to spot relatives of known hazards.

Fu argues this pairing lets regulators move from reacting to known dangers toward early warning of new ones. It speeds the tentative naming of hidden risk substances and whole families of related chemicals from a single known starting point. The review also covers workflow design and the regulatory hurdles that remain, such as proving identity without reference standards. The authors present the method as core support for proactive cosmetic safety control.
pmc-13468150:
Florian Wilhelm and colleagues watched, molecule by molecule, how a cell switch called arrestin locks onto an adrenaline receptor in the cell membrane. The receptor, named beta-2 adrenergic, helps control heart and airway responses, and arrestin turns its signal down.

Using a tool that pulls single molecules and computer simulations, the team timed how fast each part of the pair joins. Arrestin grabbed the receptor's tail within thousandths of a second, far faster than it engaged the receptor's core. A membrane fat called PIP2 steadied the core grip but blocked arrestin from holding tail and core at once. Wilhelm shows this fat acts as a third control on signalling, beside the drug-like trigger and chemical tagging.
pmc-13468750:
Haas and colleagues in Germany tracked in 2026 the step counts of bone break patients with wrist worn counters, to see how arm and leg breaks split the road back. Leg breaks chain a patient to bed and crutch, while arm breaks leave the legs free. Their pilot drew 38 arm break and 55 leg break patients, all fixed with surgery. Steps were logged each day, and health forms and work state were checked at three months.

Leg break patients walked far less in the first weeks, as the team had guessed. The gap then shrank as bones knit. Work told the split in full: near nine in ten arm break patients were back at their jobs by three months. Just half the leg group had made it back. The authors warn that shop bought wearables vary, so the marks are first hints, fit to shape a bigger, tighter trial.
pmc-13469050:
Feng and Dongre reviewed in 2026 how a shape-shifting program in cancer cells, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, doubles as an immune evasion strategy. The program normally serves embryo development and wound healing; cancer hijacks it for movement, stem-like traits, and drug resistance. The review assembles evidence the same program mutes immune attack inside tumors, walking through effects on innate and adaptive immune cells and each step of spread.

Four master switches drive the program: SNAIL, SLUG, ZEB1, TWIST1. These switches also dial up immune-blocking molecules on the cell surface, including PD-L1, the target of major immunotherapy drugs. Cells in half-shifted states seem especially adept at surviving travel through blood and seeding new sites, a pattern documented across many cancer types. Their message is direct: blocking the shape-shift program may be required before immunotherapy works in tumors using it most.
pmc-13469650:
Hunseok Kang and three colleagues published this 2026 study on classifying dementia from brain-wave recordings. They ask whether messy, inconsistent EEG patterns can still carry real diagnostic signal. Standard methods assume stable disease markers. Yet the patterns models use may be fragmented. The authors built a method called Clustered Pattern Projection, which groups recurring pattern fragments into prototypes. They tested it on a public EEG dataset covering Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal dementia and healthy people, under strict validation.

The method performed competitively. It did best on the harder frontotemporal dementia versus control task, where signatures are usually weakly preserved. The team also examined the margins, a measure of how confidently each person was classified. Margins varied by task. They argue that loose EEG fragments can still form a recurrent discriminative structure. Margin analysis, they say, helps judge how reliable a learned EEG representation is.
pmc-13470250:
Zohra Zahir studied cattle effects in 2026 on pond microbes in the Prairie Pothole Region of the North American Great Plains. Farm ponds water cows, yet how cattle stirring reshapes germ worlds was little-known. Gene reads plus water makeup compared ponds with and without cattle across the region.

Calm ponds showed makeup-driven niches, with carbon and sulphur experts ruling under mixed-in organic carbon and sulphate shifts. Cattle manure and tramping raised within-pond patchwork yet cut mix and flattened groups across ponds, dulling water control. Sulphur-cycling Thiobacillus fell under cattle pressure, showing cows can override earth makeup in pond makeup.
pmc-13470350:
Sridhar and colleagues in India ran in 2026 a four way trial for frozen shoulder, a stiff, sore joint that locks arm motion. Care can use the patient's own blood goods, rich in growth cues, or a steroid shot. No trial had set three blood goods against the steroid at once. Sixty four patients drew one of four single shots: two forms of platelet rich plasma, one low in white cells and one rich, a soft fibrin form, or the steroid.

All four groups eased over the year. The steroid won the first month, with the least pain and best arm scores. From six months on, the blood goods pulled ahead and held the lead. At one year, the soft fibrin form scored best, with the low white cell plasma next. The steroid group slid back to near its start. Side effects were brief in all arms.
pmc-13470450:
Dewei Hu built tiny disease maps in 2026 by mixing omics data with protein network maps. Omics studies usually score genes one by one, missing system-level teamwork in teams and pathways. Disease-own genes, RNA reads, gene changes, and protein reads data were fused with the STRING working link network through node2vec maps.

Maps for seven swelling, cancer, brain, and blood-vessel ills found two to four times as many known disease-linked proteins as omics alone at equal strictness. Grouping showed shared modules such as swelling pathways and cancer hallmarks, plus disease-own ones like skin hardening in atopic skin rash and matrix rebuild in aortic bulge. Network maps thus sharpen disease biology and target hunt.
pmc-13470550:
Dane Mauer-Vakil and colleagues map in 2026 what is known about substance use care inside forensic hospitals. These secure hospitals treat people with mental illness who have entered the justice system, and substance use disorders are common among them. Care for addiction is widely seen as something forensic hospitals should provide, yet practice knowledge stays thin.

Following standard scoping methods, the team searched four databases for peer reviewed studies in English through May 2025. Forty nine articles qualified, most from Europe and most observational. Reported substance use burden ran high, though estimates swung with the detection method used. Treatment studies were mostly small and uncontrolled, centered on group based talking therapies. Patients found them acceptable and intermediate outcomes improved, but effects on substance use itself were mixed.
pmc-13470650:
Rudd and Hansen review a little-known protein called FLOWER in this 2026 cell biology paper. In humans the gene produces several small protein versions that sit in cell membranes. First spotted helping nerve endings recycle tiny packets, the protein is now known to steer traffic of lysosome-related organelles, storage and recycling compartments found in many cell types.

The review gathers evidence from immune killer cells, skin cells, and nerve cells. A shared pattern emerges. FLOWER seems to raise calcium levels inside the cell, which then moves the compartments. How it raises calcium is still unknown, so the authors offer new ideas that fit the protein's known shape and suggest experiments to test them. They also map where the less-studied protein versions sit and what each might do.
pmc-13471250:
Liu and a cell therapy team asked in 2026 whether the immune mix in blood before CAR-T therapy predicts how engineered cells behave in relapsed B-cell lymphoma. The study followed 33 patients receiving a dual-target CAR-T product at one center, profiling blood immune subsets before treatment. The cells' growth inside each patient was tracked and grouped into patterns, and survival compared across patterns.

Two growth patterns appeared: eighteen patients showed low expansion, fifteen high expansion with a stronger, later peak, cresting around day 14 instead of day 10. The high group started with more naive and helper T cells, a higher CD4-to-CD8 ratio, and fewer activated regulatory T cells, the immune system's brakes. A higher starting ratio meant longer freedom from progression, risk cut by more than half, though the authors stress the small exploratory sample: these are hypotheses for prospective trials, not clinical rules.
pmc-13471350:
Wu and colleagues introduce a new body measure, the Fat-Muscle-BMI Index, built by multiplying the fat-to-muscle ratio by body mass index. Their 2026 cross-sectional study asked whether this combined score tracks fatty liver disease and heart risk in 1,592 Chinese adults aged 40 to 79.

pmc-13471550:

pmc-13472850:

pmc-13473150:

pmc-13473250:

pmc-13474150:
Sun and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how failing mitochondria help shut down the immune system in sepsis, the body's extreme response to infection. After the first storm of sepsis, many patients slip into immunoparalysis, where defenses weaken and new infections take hold. The review places mitochondria, the cell's power plants, at the center of that decline.

The review ties these faults to energy failure, chemical imbalance, leaked danger signals from damaged mitochondria, and poor quality control of the organelles. It proposes pairing mitochondria-based blood readouts with standard immune markers to spot high-risk patients early, and lists repair strategies aimed at restoring immune strength.
pmc-13474350:
Nantapat Soontornnon and five colleagues built in 2026 a solid polymer electrolyte for safer lithium-ion batteries, replacing flammable liquids. pmc-13474550:

pmc-13474750:

pmc-13476250:
S. Shreyas Thanthri and co-authors study interface traps in 2026 for tree-shaped stacked transistors aimed at sub-three-nanometer chips. pmc-13478050:

pmc-13478150:

pmc-13478750:

pmc-13479450:

pmc-13479550:

pmc-13480250:

pmc-13481250:

pmc-13481650:

pmc-13482150:

pmc-13482850:

pmc-13483450:

pmc-13483750:

pmc-13483850:

pmc-13485350:

pmc-13486050:

pmc-13487150:

pmc-13487450:

pmc-13488250:

pmc-13490450:

pmc-13493050:

pmc-13493950:

pmc-13494550:

pmc-13494750:

pmc-13495150:

pmc-13495250:

pmc-13495450:

pmc-13495950:

pmc-13499850:

pmc-13500150:

pmc-13501550:

pmc-13501850:

pmc-13502050:

pmc-13503650:
Wenya Cai, Qingshan Yan, and Yong Guo report a 2026 study of body makeup and immune signals in young children. They asked how muscle and fat measures link to six signaling proteins in the blood. The work took place in Guangzhou, China, with children aged four to six.

The team tested 171 children with a body scan that uses a mild electric signal, and they measured blood proteins with flow tools. Boys scored higher than girls on most body measures. Higher body scores mostly went with lower levels of one protein, IL-10. Grouped body factors tied to IL-6 and IL-4 in distinct ways. The links held even though weight class alone showed no clear pattern.
pmc-13503750:
Masoumeh Ebrahimi and others publish a data set of levee erosion and wave-front speed from full-scale wave spillover tests. In 2026, the data paper gathers readings from four campaigns testing erosion toughness of current and newly built clay covers under set spillover loads. The campaigns were built under the EU Interreg North-West Europe Bonsai project. Spillover waves impose severe water loads on landside slopes.

The data set covers soil traits, water loading plans, spillover traits, wave-front speeds, and erosion advance, plus small-sample erosion-function guesses for transfer to other clays and sites. It supports side-by-side analysis across levee types and gives a redoable base for model tuning, erosion review, and flood defence design.
pmc-13504250:
Saadi and co-authors make a water-based transistor channel free of PSS polymer. Organic electrochemical transistors amplify ion signals at low voltage. Most top devices rely on PEDOT:PSS, which is acidic. Its excess insulator can slow charge flow and raise safety doubts. The new colloid uses PEDOT with nitrate and PVA in water.

The mix forms smooth, conductive films from water alone. Films ran as transistor channels in water-based tests. Peak transconductance passed 10 millisiemens in those runs. The authors call it the first PVA-held PEDOT colloid to run this way. The route suits bioelectronic and sensor uses.
pmc-13505050:
Yichen Luo and others compare a novel customized distalizer with cervical headgear for upper molar distalization. In 2026, the preliminary forward-looking cohort enrolls fifteen patients with the fully customized intraorally cemented individual distalizer and thirteen with headgear, adding finite element analysis of stress and displacement. Standard headgear depends heavily on patient compliance and can extrude molars.

Distalization took about sixty-five days with the distalizer versus about 181 days with headgear, at similar distances, with monthly rates of 1.97 versus 0.57 mm. The distalizer trended toward molar intrusion while headgear extruded molars, and models corroborated medical movement. The device offers a fast, compliance-independent option, mainly for high-angle patients, with anterior anchorage tracking advised.
pmc-13505150:
Guannan Liu and co-authors compared three ways of performing endoscopic submucosal dissection, a technique that removes early gut tumours through an endoscope. The standard method was set against a version using traction to lift tissue and a version done under water. Their network meta-analysis pooled nine randomised trials with 919 participants, weighing speed, completeness of removal, and harm.

Traction-assisted and underwater procedures both ran faster than the standard method, with shorter typical procedure times. Complete and margin-clear removal rates were high and close across all three approaches. Harm rates were lowest for the underwater method and highest for the standard one. Rankings favoured traction for speed and completeness, and the underwater route for safety, though several comparisons stayed uncertain. Operators get a balanced map of trade-offs rather than a single winner.
pmc-13505750:
Ruifang Su and co-authors built a nanoprobe that can measure six different DNA targets from one small sample at once. Their probe pairs semiconductor quantum dots, which glow brightly in tunable colours, with a terbium donor that passes energy to them. By loading several DNA strands per dot and fine-tuning the energy transfer, they created six signals that differ by colour and by glow duration.

A single light wavelength excites the whole system, keeping the test simple. In their demonstration assay, the probe measured all six DNA targets at picomolar levels, amounts of only a few femtomoles in a standard sample volume. Because the recognition chemistry and the signal scheme sit independently on the same particle, the design should extend to other biomarkers. The authors argue that such probes can turn complex multi-target testing into a routine, quick measurement.
pmc-13506550:
Nasera Rizwana, Poorvi Shivakumar, Vipul Agarwal, and Manasa Nune describe 2026 lab work on a printable ink for repair of injured peripheral nerves. The ink blends alginate gel with matrix stripped of cells from rat Schwann cells, the cells that support nerve fibers. Tests showed the matrix kept key proteins while DNA fell sharply.

The team also used two crosslinking steps, one before printing and one after, to hold printed shapes. Schwann cells mixed into the ink stayed alive and active in the printed structures. The approach offers a lab-made option for bridging nerve gaps that are too wide to heal alone.
pmc-13508350:
Shasha Chen and eight co-authors report two-year results for a catheter-based heart valve used in patients too frail for open surgery, in 2026 work. The valve system, VitaFlow Liberty, treats severe narrowing of the aortic valve. The trial ran at 22 Chinese sites and treated 163 patients, with regular follow-up planned out to five years. Average age was near 77, and nearly half had a two-leaflet valve, a harder anatomy. Main measures covered death, stroke, pacemaker need, and valve flow.

At two years, about one in seven patients had died and a smaller share had suffered stroke. Roughly one in five needed a new pacemaker. Valve flow improved greatly, with pressure drops falling to a fraction of starting values and the valve opening tripling in size. Moderate leakage beside the valve stayed uncommon. The authors judge the system's performance durable in this high-risk group.
pmc-13508550:
Yanan Zhang and six co-authors test whether electric brain stimulation can restore a brain-fluid rhythm weakened in insomnia with anxiety, in 2026 work. The rhythm links brain blood flow signals to spinal fluid movement, a pairing tied to the brain's waste clearing. Sixty patients joined a two-week, double-blind trial with real or sham stimulation. Sessions ran twenty minutes for fourteen days, aimed at forehead sites. Sleep, anxiety, and mood scales plus sleep lab tests were gathered.

At the start, patients showed weaker blood-fluid coupling than controls. Weaker coupling tracked with worse insomnia, poorer sleep quality, and higher anxiety scores, and with more broken sleep in lab measures. After treatment, patients were rescanned and rescored to judge change in the coupling and in symptoms. The authors frame the coupling measure as a window on how brain stimulation may work in this pairing of sleeplessness and anxiety.
pmc-13509250:
Valerie Schütz and six co-authors test whether heart rhythm wobble can help predict a delayed brain blood shortage after a burst brain aneurysm, in 2026 work. This delayed ischemia is a major cause of harm after the bleed, and it is hard to foresee, above all in comatose patients. The study followed patients admitted to a specialist intensive unit between 2016 and 2024. Heart tracings were recorded continuously and turned into rhythm variability features in real time. Four forecast models were compared: fixed clinical facts, lab and blood gas data, rhythm features, and all combined.

Of 101 patients, thirty-five developed the delayed shortage. Rhythm features alone forecast it modestly, about matching lab data. The combined model did best overall, though its edge was moderate, and rhythm features carried over half of its decision weight. The authors argue live rhythm data add a moving signal that static scores miss.
pmc-13510550:
Ping Huang, Yiqiong Yin, Ziqiang Wang, and Zechuan Jin explore whether routine blood scores taken before surgery can refine survival outlook in early rectal cancer, in 2026 work. Stage one patients usually do well after removal surgery, yet outcomes still vary. The team built several survival models from blood measures tied to inflammation and nutrition, then used an explanation method to show what drove the chosen model.

Age carried the most weight in the final model, and four blood ratios added further signal. Only thirty deaths occurred in the group, which limits how firm any pattern can be. The model was checked only inside its own dataset, with no outside group for proof. The authors label the work exploratory and call for multi-center studies before any clinical use.
pmc-13510750:
José Cozain-Hernández, Josué Aarón López-Leyva, Miguel Angel Ponce-Camacho, and Víctor Manuel Ramos-García build a decision framework for greener innovation in Mexico's medical device industry, in 2026 work. The sector leans on low-value assembly and plays a small part in research and design stages, which threatens its future standing. The team reviewed the literature and studied multi-criteria decision methods that weigh many factors at once under uncertainty.

Their taxonomy groups the problem under governance, technology innovation, and human capital. Findings stress a shift toward circular economy habits and additive manufacturing, where parts are built layer by layer. Blended methods that rank options and map cause links can steady strategic choices under doubt. The main output is an innovation flow tied to global standards and staged readiness levels, offered as a roadmap for moving the industry toward richer global roles.
pmc-13512050:
David Bienjonetti-Boudreau and colleagues report a 15-year-old boy carrying harmful variants in two heart rhythm genes at once, SCN5A and KCNH2. Each gene alone is tied to a known rhythm disorder, Brugada syndrome or long QT syndrome type 2.

His illness looked like neither disorder: it mixed upper-chamber rhythm faults, faulty signal relay, wide fast rhythms, and a failing heart pacemaker node. Because sudden dangerous blocks could strike without warning, doctors implanted a defibrillator that can shock the heart back to rhythm. Family testing found the two variants travelling separately in relatives, each with mild or no symptoms. The team judges the SCN5A variant the main driver, Bienjonetti-Boudreau writes, and urges care guided by the patient, not the gene list alone.
pmc-13512150:
Diego I. Álvarez-López and seven co-authors estimate excess deaths in Sonora, a northern Mexican state, during the COVID-19 pandemic, in 2026 work. Excess mortality counts deaths above what normal patterns predict and captures crisis impact when cause records lag or miss cases. The team modeled deaths from 2015 to 2022 across 28 cause groups, fitting expectations on the five pre-pandemic years with trend and seasonal terms.

About fourteen and a half thousand excess deaths occurred between March 2020 and July 2022, roughly a thirty-one percent rise over expected levels. Four clear peaks matched the major pandemic waves. The virus itself explained most of the excess, yet among other major causes only ischemic heart disease and diabetes showed significant extra deaths. The authors offer the method as a workable routine for public health watch where full investigations are impractical.
pmc-13514750:
Zainab Alknery and Ali Arab report an engineering study, published in 2026, on how the inner diameter of hollow, nature-inspired scaffolds affects their strength. The scaffolds use Voronoi patterns, irregular cell-like networks copied from biology, and are meant as biodegradable supports for regrowing bone after large injuries.

The pair printed scaffolds with different inner radii using stereolithography, a light-based printing method, and a plant-based resin, then crushed them to test performance. Widening the inner radius significantly weakened the structures, while smaller inner diameters resisted compression better and absorbed more energy. The results guide designs that balance the open space bone growth needs against mechanical strength.
pmc-13518250:
Jing Shen and five colleagues pin a splicing kinase as a guardian of tumours' oxygen sensor in a 2026 study. Tumours grow blood vessels under the command of HIF1α, a protein that senses low oxygen and normally gets shredded when oxygen returns. In colorectal cancer data, the kinase CLK3 rose alongside vessel-growth programmes. Lab and animal tests agreed: extra CLK3 boosted tumour vessel growth, and deleting it stalled the process.

The mechanism is protective custody. CLK3 binds HIF1α directly and blocks the tagging that sends it to the shredder, while also adding its own phosphate marks to the protein. Without HIF1α, CLK3's vessel promotion collapsed, proving the partnership essential. Shen's team proposes CLK3 as both a drug target and a marker for colorectal cancers leaning on this pathway, in a field hungry for options after standard vessel blockers fail.
pmc-13518650:
Dun Jack Fu and seven colleagues present 2026 real-world results for faricimab injections in polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy, an eye disease that can bleed under the retina and harm sight. Their single-center review covered 159 eyes, with 40 never treated before and 119 switched after earlier drugs stopped working well.

After 12 months, untreated eyes gained an average of 6.8 letters on eye charts, while retinal thickness fell in both groups. Previously treated eyes held their vision steady rather than gaining. Fu and co-authors note that ethnic subgroups were too small for firm comparisons. Readers see practical evidence from a mixed United Kingdom cohort, where trial data had mostly come from Asian populations.
pmc-13518850:
Shihui Zhang and colleagues report in 2026 an electrically driven route to turn propane into propylene, a basic building block for plastics and chemicals. Oxidative methods promise easier conversion, yet oxygen often burns the product too far into carbon oxides. Their design runs inside solid oxide electrolysis cells, which split carbon dioxide with electric current.

A cobalt oxide coating on a mixed ceramic anode kept surface oxygen activity moderate through continuous replenishment from the cathode side. At the best current setting, olefin selectivity reached 92.6 percent with 14.2 percent single-pass conversion, and propylene yield rose 18.5-fold over the no-current baseline. A 120-hour run showed good stability, suggesting a robust process.
pmc-13518950:
Keren Peng and a large team attack chemotherapy resistance in acute myeloid leukemia in 2026 by targeting STAT3, a signaling protein that rewires fat metabolism. Resistant leukemia cells switched on many lipid-handling programs, with STAT3 activity and its targets SREBP1 and CPT2 raised. The team also found W1307, a selective STAT3 blocker.

Blocking STAT3, by gene or drug, choked both fat making and fat burning, leaving lipids piled up, reactive oxygen rising, and cell power plants faltering. STAT3 directly switched on the genes for SREBP1 and CPT2 in their tests. W1307 also made resistant cells sensitive again to the standard drug Ara-C, in dishes and in animals. Peng and colleagues nominate W1307 for development.
pmc-13520150:
Kaitlyn Brown, Sofia Sirocchi, and William Frank Willett report a 2026 case of anorectal melanoma, a rare and aggressive cancer that is usually advanced when found. A 71-year-old man was sent in after noticing more frequent bright red rectal bleeding. A scope exam revealed a darkly pigmented, irregular mass of 1.5 centimeters in the anorectal region.

The cut-out tissue showed highly malignant spindle and rounded cells making abundant brown pigment, and stains for S-100, HMB45, and Melan-A confirmed melanoma. Scans found no spread. A transanal resection of the tumor site then showed no residual cancer. About two years of follow-up found no recurrence. The authors credit the prompt scope exam and plead for standard treatment protocols for this rare disease.
pmc-13520250:
Hongyan Zhang leads an eight-author analysis in 2026 of which allergens children in Suzhou, China test sensitive to, and how age, sex, season, and disease shape those patterns. Blood antibody tests for 17 airborne and food allergens were run on 2,434 symptomatic children at a district hospital.

Airborne allergens dominated, especially the two house dust mite species, while milk and egg led among foods. Airborne sensitization climbed with age as food sensitization fell, patterns holding at stricter positivity cutoffs. Boys showed higher odds, particularly for mites, whose positivity peaked in humid summer and autumn. Zhang and colleagues advise mite-focused checks from school age and early milk and egg testing in young children.
pmc-13522050:
Yamini Vig, Yohannes Gebreegziabher, Charlotte Hanlon and Matteo Cella review in 2026 thinking-skills therapy for psychosis in low and middle income lands. Thinking trouble drives poor daily function in psychosis. Most trial proof came from rich lands until now.

Fourteen studies from Africa, Asia and South America made the cut. Delivery varied a lot across sites. Some care ran at home. Some ran through caregivers or health workers. Thirteen studies found thinking gains, from small to large. Nine found function gains, from small to mid size. Care looked safe and well liked. No single delivery style won out. Local fits may guide fair scale-up.
pmc-13522350:
Hang Zhang, Yujie Wu and Zhiyi Fu search in 2026 for exercise-linked gene flags of spine disc wear. Long-term running seems to help discs. Flag-guided care is the long goal. Public gene sets and exercise gene lists fed a chain of screens.

Two flags stood out, named TNFAIP6 and CHI3L1. Both ran high in worn disc samples. Lab gene checks backed the split. A risk chart built on both flags scored well in tests. Shared path study flagged the spliceosome route. Drug hunts named one compound per flag, with good docking scores. Single-cell data place flag action inside disc tissue.
pmc-13522450:
Francesca Ascenzi, Giovanni Blandino, Gennaro Ciliberto, and Rita Mancini review, in 2026, how a fat-processing enzyme helps cancers resist a form of cell death called ferroptosis. That death process depends on iron and on damage to fats in cell membranes. The enzyme, known as SCD1, converts saturated fats into a less damage-prone form, which helps tumor cells keep their membranes intact under stress.

Across many cancer types, tumors raise SCD1 through different routes shaped by tissue, oxygen, nutrients, and nearby immune signals. Blocking the enzyme in laboratory studies increased fat damage and made tumor cells easier to kill, often boosting chemotherapy, radiation, or immune treatment. The review closes with delivery and dosing challenges that must be solved before this strategy reaches patients.
pmc-13523050:
Qiaoyi Shen and Yibo Gao published a 2026 review of nanotechnology paths to wake the immune guard in esophageal cancer, a grave cancer of the food pipe. This cancer kills fast and often. Immune therapy has changed the field, but here it fails for most patients. The block is the environment around the tumor: low oxygen, acidic fluid, a dense weave, and crowds of immune-damping cells. That environment keeps the tumor cold to the immune system.

Tiny particles can be built to crack those barriers. The review walks through how they ease the low oxygen and the acidity, how they flip damping immune cells to fighting mode, and how they wake the presenting cells. Some particles make tumor cells die in a way that calls the immune guard in. Pairings of particles with immune therapy are examined as well. The aim is a hot tumor the immune system can hit.
pmc-13523150:
Karol A Sadowski and colleagues examine how a replacement heart valve deforms inside a calcified two-leaflet aortic valve in a 2026 laboratory case. A fifty-three-year-old man's severely narrowed bicuspid valve was removed during surgery, and a catheter valve was deployed inside the excised specimen without balloon preparation, preserving the natural calcium constraints. Ultrasound imaging from inside the vessel scanned the frame during pullback.

The frame's inflow section was severely squeezed, reaching only about two fifths of full expansion, while expansion at the leaflet levels stayed above one hundred percent. Caliper measurements matched the ultrasound values closely. The case gives direct evidence that a rigid calcified ridge can decouple the inflow frame from the working leaflet section, a pattern previously inferred from clinical scans.
pmc-13523250:
Simona Szabóová and co-authors compare blood fats and insulin resistance in episodic migraine in a 2026 case-control study. Forty-five adults with episodic migraine and forty-five healthy controls, all aged eighteen to fifty, gave fasting blood samples between attacks under standardized conditions. Measures included an insulin resistance index and several derived lipid ratios linked to artery disease risk.

After adjustment for age, sex, body mass, and smoking, migraine was tied to a more artery-unfriendly lipid profile, including a higher cholesterol ratio, a higher atherogenic index, and lower protective cholesterol. No adjusted link appeared for insulin resistance or fasting insulin. Migraine frequency and attack intensity did not track the metabolic measures. The authors call for larger longitudinal studies to confirm the lipid pattern and its meaning.
pmc-13523450:
Francesca Licata and colleagues report a 2026 cross-sectional survey on how well adolescents in southern Italy followed the recommended vaccine schedule. National guidance covers HPV, meningococcal ACWY, and a diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, and polio booster during adolescence. The team asked university students to recall their own vaccination history and attitudes.

Among 527 students aged 18 to 29, under one third reported the meningococcal vaccine, about two thirds reported HPV vaccination, and nearly nine in ten reported the booster. Missing advice from a health worker was the leading barrier for the meningococcal vaccine. Higher parental education, female sex, and younger age were linked with HPV uptake. About one third said a health worker had discouraged vaccination, a finding the authors say targeted efforts must address.
pmc-13524350:
Chand, Chand, Lal, Sharma, and Kumar design controllers for a swarm of self balancing scooters in twenty twenty-six. Segway like robots could move people and goods in smart cities. A swarm must reach targets, hold formation, and dodge obstacles together. Their controllers are distributed, so each robot computes its own moves.

A Lyapunov based scheme shapes a potential function for the swarm. It pulls robots to targets, keeps them together, and prevents collisions. Static obstacles are modelled as disks and lines, and moving ones are evaded. Stability and convergence are proven mathematically. Simulations in four scenarios showed reactive behaviour around moving entities. The work lays theory for future prototypes, the authors say.
pmc-13524450:
Rao and colleagues present a 2026 population study of alpha-gal syndrome, an allergy to a sugar found in red meat, usually triggered by lone star tick bites. Some patients get hives or dangerous allergic attacks; others get only gut symptoms hours after eating meat, which are easy to misread. 

Symptoms typically begin hours after a meat meal, not minutes. Gut-only patients formed a distinct phenotype, meaning a recognizable separate presentation of the same disease. Because their pain, nausea, and diarrhea point doctors toward the gut itself, these patients underwent endoscopy, camera inspection of the digestive tract, at high rates while the allergy went unrecognized.  Naming this pattern could spare patients repeated invasive tests.
pmc-13524650:
Shumin Nie and co-authors track in this 2026 study how groups of symptoms shift after surgery for oral squamous cell carcinoma, a mouth cancer often requiring tissue flap repair. Two hundred fifty-one patients rated their symptoms on days one, three, seven, and thirty after the operation.

Statistical networks grouped the symptoms into clusters that grew more complex over time, from three groups on day one to five by day thirty. Different symptoms held the network together at each stage: choking cough early on, then drowsiness, mucus problems, and finally vomiting and distress as key bridges. Overall network tightness changed between the middle time points. The authors say care should match each recovery stage, while noting the patterns are descriptive, not proof of causes.
pmc-13525350:
Ferreira and colleagues reported in 2026 a case of lung abscess, a pocket of dead infected tissue inside the lung, that spread into the chest wall of a healthy young woman. The patient was a 21-year-old veterinary student with fever and a painful swelling below her left collarbone that bulged more when she coughed, yet she had few breathing symptoms. Blood tests showed strong signs of infection.

Ferreira's chest scan showed a consolidated area in the upper left lung with a hollow lesion holding an air-fluid level. The lesion pushed through the gap between the first ribs into the chest wall tissues. Drainage was judged unhelpful because little fluid could be drawn out. Four weeks of intravenous antibiotics brought steady clinical, lab, and scan improvement, and a scan at three months showed both lesions fully gone. The authors flag chest wall swelling as a rare face of lung abscess.
pmc-13525450:
Daniel B. Larach, Miklos D. Kertai, and Stephen Bruehl present a 2026 secondary analysis of opioid misuse-related behavior in the first month after elective surgery. Surgeons and dentists write tens of millions of opioid prescriptions yearly in the United States, and many people with opioid use disorder first encounter these drugs through a medical prescription. Rigorous prospective incidence data, however, were scarce.

Earlier prospective studies gave mixed pictures, one in a trauma cohort using a seventeen-item misuse measure at six months and one in young ambulatory patients using a two-question screen. The authors combined two prospective postoperative cohorts that both used a validated nine-item version of the Current Opioid Misuse Measure, designed for people on long-term opioid therapy. Their analysis focuses on specific aberrant behaviors within the early recovery window.
pmc-13526750:
Alexandra J. Feld and others validate, in a 2026 psychometric study, a quality-of-life questionnaire for hereditary angioedema, a condition of recurrent unpredictable swelling attacks. Proving the seventeen-item instrument measures what it claims was needed before trial results using it can be trusted. Data came from a phase three trial of the drug donidalorsen.

Ninety participants with the condition supplied baseline and week twenty-four data. Factor analysis supported the questionnaire's structure, and reliability was strong for the total score and most domains, with the two-item nutrition domain notably weaker. Scores aligned with disease activity and control measures in expected directions, separated well-controlled from poorly controlled patients, and moved when disease activity changed, except for the fatigue and mood domain. The authors endorse the tool for trial use.
pmc-13526850:
Li and colleagues published a 2026 study on nanoparticles that hitchhike on red blood cells to reach lungs. Getting drugs to lung tissue in useful amounts remains a stubborn problem. Their particles wear a protein-like coat whose building order steers where they land. Certain coat orders make particles cling to red cell skins in the blood.

Riding red cells, the particles piled up in lungs after injection. Up to 37 percent of the dose reached lung tissue that way. Loaded with an antioxidant cargo, they calmed acute lung injury in mice. The coat's amino-acid order, not just its makeup, decided the destination. Sequence tuning may guide carriers to other organs, they suggest. The same trick delivered a working lung treatment in their tests.
pmc-13527250:
Yosuke Suzuki, Akira Iwase, and six co-authors track a growth factor around birth in women with pregnancy diabetes. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, measures FGF21 in blood at three points. Samples come from late pregnancy, near term, and the week after birth. Forty-five women with the condition and thirty controls took part.

Levels of the factor rose across pregnancy in both groups. They stayed high after birth as well. In the diabetes group, the level helped predict insulin resistance after delivery. That outcome matters because it flags later diabetes risk. Stored samples from a single center made the long view possible.
pmc-13527950:
Oisin Stronach and six colleagues analyze health service contacts before methamphetamine-related deaths in two Australian states, using linked ambulance, emergency, and hospital records from 2008 to 2021. The study covers 2,075 deaths in New South Wales and 2,045 in Victoria.

More than ninety percent of those who died had used an acute service at some point beforehand, most often an emergency department. Two-thirds had contact in the final year and one-third in the last thirty days, with visit rates climbing steeply as death approached. Only about one in twelve had no recorded contact at all. The authors argue emergency departments are a key place to connect people who use methamphetamine with ongoing care.
pmc-13528050:
Gumbi and a large South African team ask whether the immune chemistry of the cervix and vagina mirrors what a clinician sees through a colposcope. The work has stakes for HIV prevention, since genital inflammation raises infection risk. Colposcopy is scarce in low-resource settings, so biomarkers that flag cervical changes could matter. Their 2026 study examined 203 adolescent girls and adult women from two provinces, photographing the cervix and measuring a panel of signalling proteins in cervicovaginal fluid, alongside tests for common infections.

Three quarters of participants had at least one visible finding, such as cervical ectopy, discharge, injury, or white patches, underlining how common these changes are. Particular cytokine patterns accompanied particular findings, but the associations differed between the two study sites, which keeps the authors cautious. They stress the design is cross-sectional and hypothesis-generating: a snapshot cannot prove the chemistry causes the appearance or predicts disease.
pmc-13528150:
Zidan Li, Ibrahim Al'Abri, and Nathan Crook report a hitch in phage-based directed evolution in a 2026 study. Their goal was tougher E. coli that shrug off acid. A phage system mutated three stress-control genes at once inside cells. Rounds of growth at low pH picked the winners. Early rounds found two helpful changes in one gene. The lag before growth shrank under acid.

Progress then stalled after the third round. A cheater took over: the plasmid had deleted the cargo genes entirely. Losing the genes beat mutating them, since the added copies dragged fitness down. The empty form could gain no more improvements. Gene readouts showed the early mutations worked much like deletion. The authors warn that evolution systems must guard their cargo. A substrate that costs fitness invites this dead end.
pmc-13529650:
Shiwei Jing and Jianjun Li design an image encryption scheme that hides a secret picture inside an innocent one in a 2026 paper. The hidden result still looks meaningful, unlike noise-like ciphers. A chaotic map supplies the random streams. First the secret image is squeezed by a stairwise method that uses color channel overlap. Bits are then shuffled into a noise-like form.

That form is tucked into a cover photo with a low-bit embedding trick. Extra steps reshape value spreads to keep the cover looking clean. Tests showed faithful decryption and strong security marks. Rebuilt secret images kept high quality. The authors say the joint use of space and color redundancy is the key gain. Their code is public for checking. The scheme targets safe sharing of color images.
pmc-13529750:
Jingwen Liu and three colleagues simulate how rock caves in above deep mines in a 2026 study. Caving mines let ore roofs collapse in a controlled way for cheap extraction. Guessing the collapse shape in three dimensions is hard. Their method treats tension-driven breaking of weakened rock as the trigger. A computer then removes failed blocks step by step.

The model matched classic arch theory for test spans. It was then run on a real orebody at the Anhui Taiping Mine. The cave grew upward in stages, forming an arch-shaped profile. Tests showed the rock's friction angle mattered most. It set cave height and volume by governing sliding and stress flow. The authors pitch the tool for risk review and backfill planning. It runs fast enough for design choices, they say.
pmc-13530250:
Yian Yang and colleagues uncover in 2026 a control chain that keeps the gut mucus shield intact and slows colorectal cancer when restored. The mucin MUC2 needs proper sugar coating to form a protective gel, and that coating fails as cancer advances. A sugar-adding enzyme emerged as the key guardian of that coating.

A gene switch controlled by a known drug target drives both the enzyme and MUC2 itself. The diabetes drug rosiglitazone switched that chain back on in experiments, restoring mucus strength and barrier function. The findings open a fresh treatment angle centered on mucus repair.
pmc-13531350:
Dixon-Ibarra and six co-authors studied functional limits among United States adults with intellectual disability who take part in Special Olympics. They used a short standard question set that covers seeing, hearing, walking, memory, self-care, and communication. The aim was to learn what support these athletes need.

Five hundred twenty-five athletes answered an online survey in twenty twenty-two. Under a strict definition, about twenty-four percent reported a functional limit. Under a broad definition, over eighty-two percent did. Rates exceeded general population figures in all six areas, most sharply for self-care and communication. Answers also differed when a helper replied instead of the athlete. The authors say the findings can guide programs and disability tracking.
pmc-13531750:
Qin Dai and co-authors map in 2026 how feeling alienated from parents interacts with depression symptoms in Chinese teenagers over time. Surveys one year apart covered 1,503 adolescents, with network methods tracing which symptoms drive which others. Loss of pleasure, called anhedonia, drew special attention.

Anhedonia sat at the center of the depression network and formed the main bridge to parental alienation. Each side predicted the other a year later, with depression pushing alienation harder than the reverse. Distance from mothers predicted later symptoms more strongly than distance from fathers. Low self-esteem acted as the main spark, suggesting family and school targets.
pmc-13531850:
Lídia Bezerra Barbosa leads a 2026 study of diet and metabolic syndrome among quilombola women in Alagoas, Brazil. These Afro-Brazilian communities carry high chronic disease loads. A total of 895 women aged 19 to 59 gave diet recalls and health measurements, with syndrome judged by international criteria.

Nearly half met the syndrome definition. Seven eating patterns emerged from the data, and none tied directly to the full syndrome. Specific links appeared instead: one pattern tied to lower blood fat problems, another to lower blood sugar and better cholesterol, while two patterns tied to larger waistlines. Component-level care is the lesson.
pmc-13531950:
Anthony Smith and co-authors survey in 2026 the state of professional sexology training across sub-Saharan Africa. A global survey drew 28 responses from 11 countries, half from South Africa alone, plus seven interviews with clinicians and educators. Training today leans on HIV and reproductive topics while neglecting dysfunction and diversity in sexual health.

Respondents described scattered content across medical fields, no shared curriculum, weak official status, and few advanced routes. Stigma, political and religious pressures, scarce money, and unclear ownership block reform. Cross-border teamwork, standard curricula, and trained faculty form the proposed way forward.
pmc-13534450:

pmc-13536650:

pmc-13536750:

pmc-13536850:

pmc-13540050:

pmc-13540450:

pmc-13540850:

pmc-13540950:

pmc-13542150:

pmc-13542250:

pmc-13542450:

pmc-13543350:

pmc-13543450:

pmc-13543550:

pmc-13546050:

pmc-13546550:

pmc-13547350:

pmc-13548650:

pmc-13550450:

pmc-13551050:

pmc-13551750:

pmc-13551850:

pmc-13551950:

pmc-13554050:

pmc-13554250:

pmc-13554350:

pmc-13554450:

pmc-13556150:

pmc-13560150:

pmc-13560250:

pmc-13560550:

pmc-13562050:

pmc-13562350:

pmc-13562450:

pmc-13562650:

pmc-13563650:

pmc-13563850:

pmc-13563950:

pmc-13564050:

pmc-13566850:

Patient samples from healthy controls, non-eosinophilic disease, and eosinophilic disease were compared for the enzyme's level and location.

ALOX15 ran high in the eosinophilic tissue, and sat inside the M2 macrophages. In lab-grown M2 cells, switching the cells on raised ALOX15 and fat oxidation. Baicalein pushed both back down and cut the release of several immune signals. A known ALOX15 blocker was used to check the target. In mice, a papain-driven model of the disease was treated with baicalein, and nose tissue, IgE, and immune cell entry were scored.
pmc-13567550:
Filiz Akin leads a large team on silage maize under drip irrigation. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with water and nitrogen levels. Poor nitrogen timing can raise nitrate leaching and harm.

A two year field test set three water regimes. Four nitrogen rates ran from zero to a high level. Plots used a split design with three repeats each season. Water totals varied widely across regimes and years. One low nitrogen plus deficit water combo led yield. Green forage, water productivity, and returns were all tracked. Such mixes guide farm input choices.
pmc-13570150:
Tahereh Setayesh comments, in a 2026 article, on new real-world evidence for hydroxyurea in hemoglobin SC disease, the second most common form of sickle cell disease, long labeled milder and often undertreated. The underlying Quebec study followed 110 adults for safety and 75 for effectiveness, comparing crisis rates before and after starting the drug.

Painful crisis events fell by more than half, side effects were mostly mild, and no dangerous blood-thickening complications appeared. Barriers around adherence and prescription renewal still limited routine care. Setayesh urges clinicians to move from hesitation toward evidence-guided use, since the supposedly mild disease still causes serious harm.
pmc-13570550:
Haozhu Liu and co-authors grade, in a 2026 umbrella review, claims linking gum disease to chronic diseases such as cancer and heart disease. Thirty-eight earlier meta-analyses covering fifty-eight links across nine disease groups were rechecked for quality, consistency, and bias with standard credibility tools.

Most links reached statistical significance, yet few stayed convincing once prediction ranges and between-study variation were considered. Only four links reached the highly suggestive tier, covering a stomach bacterium infection and three cancer groupings, and none rested on a top-quality meta-analysis. Readers get a sobering scale for claims that gum disease causes widespread illness.
pmc-13570850:
Melanie A. Amrein and colleagues test, in a 2026 Swiss claims study, whether long-term antidepressant use in adults aged sixty-five and older relates to later dementia, a question earlier evidence left unsettled. More than nineteen thousand people who used antidepressants for over two years were matched with similar non-users in records from 2013 to 2023, with a separate look at older tricyclic drugs.
