pmc-13571050:
Bradley Ong and colleagues measured how product milestones moved public curiosity about migraine therapies that block CGRP, a pain-related peptide. These drugs transformed migraine care, but whether trial news, approvals, launches, or advertising actually drove awareness was unclear. Their infodemiology study tracked monthly Google Trends data from January 2017 to July 2025 for seven therapies in the United States, with a secondary look at one drug across five European countries.

Commercial launches produced immediate search jumps for erenumab and galcanezumab, while several other drugs gained steadily after launch; media exposure also spiked searches. Regulatory approvals and trial publications, by contrast, did not reliably move the needle. The authors conclude that launches and media, more than science or regulation alone, shape when patients start looking for a new migraine therapy.
pmc-13571350:
Meyer and co-authors reported a 2026 case report of topsy-turvy heart, an extremely rare congenital defect where the heart is rotated on its long axis. The ventricles stack vertically instead of side by side, and the airways and neck vessels stretch abnormally. The condition was diagnosed before birth in this newborn.

Fetal ultrasound of the heart combined with fetal cardiac MRI mapped the anatomy and an associated aortopulmonary window, a hole between the great arteries. Meyer notes the imaging also raised strong suspicion of airway abnormalities before delivery. Immediately after birth the newborn developed severe breathing failure needing mechanical ventilation in intensive care. Imaging confirmed severe bronchomalacia, soft collapsing airways, plus lung tissue disease alongside the heart defect. Given the combined findings, the expert team judged the prognosis dismal and recommended redirecting care.
pmc-13571450:
Samantha F. Kennedy leads a 2026 design paper for the DiAL Health pilot trial, which compares five eating strategies over twenty-four weeks in healthy adults aged twenty-five to forty-nine. Two arms restrict calories by a quarter, and two limit eating to an eight-hour daily window. One control arm keeps a usual diet. Each active approach comes in traditional and app-supported adaptive versions.

Adaptive arms use mobile tools that react to each person's progress with timely feedback and support. Outcomes focus on markers of biological aging and health span, plus whether such programs are practical at all. The pilot exists to size up a larger, longer trial of how eating patterns might slow aging.
pmc-13572350:
Rui Chen and colleagues test, in a 2026 prospective cohort study, a simpler way to recheck armpit lymph nodes after drug treatment in breast cancer that had already spread to those nodes. Before treatment, the most suspicious node was injected with a carbon dye under ultrasound guidance; after treatment, surgeons removed only the stained nodes and then cleared the rest for verification.

All 159 patients had their marked nodes found at surgery. About forty-one percent had no cancer left in the armpit, and the method missed residual disease in about five percent of cases, inside the accepted safety limit in every subgroup. The dye technique is cheap and straightforward, offering hospitals an alternative to sentinel node procedures after chemotherapy.
pmc-13572550:
Chang June Lee and Jung Keun Lee released a dataset that bridges lab-grade and wearable movement measurement. Optical motion capture and instrumented treadmills are accurate but confined to laboratories, while wearable sensors work anywhere yet need validation against those gold standards. Their 2026 dataset synchronises four systems, optical capture, inertial capture, an instrumented treadmill, and pressure-sensing insoles, on the same movements.

Twelve healthy young adults performed postures, treadmill walking and running at varied speeds and inclines, squats, weight shifts, and jumps. Raw signals and model-derived biomechanics are included together. The authors present the resource for validating wearables, training machine-learning models, and studying gait and movement beyond simple level walking.
pmc-13573450:
Bettina Toth, with 11 colleagues, ran a 2026 study of immune cells in the mouse ovary. Most of the ovary's egg supply is lost before puberty, and eggs need shelter from immune attack to survive. The team mapped which immune cells live in the ovary and how that mix compares with true immune organs.

Natural killer cells led at 24 percent, with T cells at 21 and macrophages at 17. The spleen and lymph nodes, by contrast, were packed with B and T cells. The ovary's guard thus leans on innate cells, the fast first line. The authors link that lean mix to the egg-protecting role of the organ.
pmc-13573850:
Prapanca Nugraha, Kiki Lukman, and eight co-authors test two tumor traits as guides to chemo response in bowel cancer. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, runs at a hospital in West Java, Indonesia. One trait is microsatellite instability, a DNA repair flaw. The other is the count of killer T cells inside the tumor.

Forty-one patients who got chemo before surgery enter the study. A gene test reads the instability trait, and tissue staining counts the T cells. Response is judged by standard tumor size rules. Only a small share of tumors showed the instability trait. The team asks whether either trait foretells who shrinks on chemo.
pmc-13574650:
Weiyue Zhang, Yifan Zhou, Wei Ma, and Huimin Jiang trace how a gene switch drives breast cancer stem cells. Their study from twenty twenty-six focuses on triple-negative breast cancer. The switch protein ZEB1 is known to support stubborn cancer stem cells. How it controls helpful signals for those cells was less clear.

Drugs that loosen those marks raised IL-6 output further. Extra IL-6 then strengthened stem-like behaviour in cancer cells. Cutting IL-6 weakened those traits, confirming the chain the authors propose.
pmc-13574850:
Five researchers led by Wallace Tavares da Silva compared how two dark-coated farm animals handle heat on Tenerife in the Canary Islands. They studied thirty goats of a local breed and twenty-three sheep of another, kept in like conditions. Body temperature, breathing rate, and coat traits such as thickness and hair length were measured.

Sheep ran hotter and breathed far faster than goats, though both stayed within the normal range. Goats wore thicker, longer coats with wider hairs. Hair length alone split the two groups almost fully in a sorting test. The authors read the goats as better fitted to the island heat, a clue for breed care under warming climates.
pmc-13575150:
Luying Zhang and five colleagues search for gene markers of nasopharyngeal carcinoma, a cancer of the upper throat common in southern China and Southeast Asia, in a 2026 study. Early symptoms are vague, so many cases are found late. The team mined five public datasets with four machine learning methods.

Two genes, BLK and OSBPL10, came through every screen. Both were turned down in tumour tissue, a pattern confirmed in a separate dataset and by staining of tissue samples. Tests of diagnostic accuracy looked strong for the pair. Low levels of each gene also tracked with worse patient outcomes. The genes tie to B-cell signalling and fat metabolism, and to immune cell presence in tumours. The authors call for checks in new patient groups.
pmc-13575250:
Alessandro Mancari and Maria Concetta Morrone test whether timing felt through movement carries over to timing heard through sound, in a 2026 study. Adapting to a set duration normally makes later durations seem repelled away from it. Most work shows this aftereffect stays inside one sense.

Volunteers judged the length of sounds after either listening to repeated sounds or producing timed movements. That sound routine produced the expected aftereffect on later judgements. The movement routine produced none. The pair take this as a sign that the motor system and the hearing system keep separate clocks. Their result adds to the case that the senses time events apart, rather than through one shared timer.
pmc-13575750:
Ting Zhang, Hong Lei, and Chunmei Zhang published a 2026 review of protein arginine methyltransferases, a family of enzymes that attach a chemical mark to proteins. The review asks what that mark does in disease of the heart and blood vessels. The mark is placed on arginine, one of the building blocks of proteins. It controls how genes are read, how code is spliced, and how cells signal.

When these enzymes go off balance, disease can take root. Atherosclerosis, with stiff and fat-lined vessels, is one result. High blood pressure, heart failure, and heart attacks are others. Drugs blocking selected members eased heart enlargement, scarring, and low-blood-flow injury in laboratory models. The authors present them as a rich set of drug targets.
pmc-13576250:
Özkan Kocamış and Hacı Sütiçen examine the cornea's inner cell layer in people with vitiligo in a 2026 eye study. Vitiligo destroys pigment cells in the skin, and pigment cells also sit inside the eye, raising the question of hidden eye effects. Fifty patients and fifty matched healthy controls had full eye exams plus a microscope count of those cells. Cell density, shape regularity, and size variation all matched between groups, as did other eye measures. One surprise emerged: patients with vitiligo around the eyes showed higher cell density than patients without that pattern, with no sign of weaker reserve. The authors judge the layer preserved and call for long-term imaging studies.
pmc-13577250:

A finer targeted method sharpened one map further, pinpointing key binding residues. Diverse antibody and antigen pairs were handled by the same pipeline. Drug developers get a faster route to interface maps without waiting for full experimental structures.
pmc-13579450:
Yizhi Ge and others looked at tiny materials that protect against radiation harm in 2026. Radiotherapy shrinks tumours but hurts healthy tissue. Damage around the tumour is often severe. Classic protective drugs have real drawbacks. Harm and poor supply limit them. Nanotechnology offers a new design path.

Protective ways are explained in detail. New designs are surveyed across studies. Real uses are also covered here. Tiny carriers can target tissues better. They can also lower drug harm. The review aims to inspire new methods. Working nano-therapies are the end goal. Radiation disease care could improve a lot.
pmc-13579950:
ByoungJun Jeon stress tests whether AI explanations for skin allergy predictions rest on real chemistry, in a 2026 study. A graph neural network learned from 436 molecules with animal test labels, then seven explanation tools highlighted which atoms each blamed. Fifty known reactive center patterns, the spots where allergy chemistry starts, served as the truth key for scoring those highlights.

A cruel control ran alongside: the same network retrained on shuffled labels, which should know no chemistry at all. Score gaps between the real and sham models crossed zero for every explanation tool. Much of the seeming insight was habit of the tools, not learned chemistry. One narrow chemistry class hinted at a real signal, but on roughly two molecules, so the author files it as a hunch to retest.
pmc-13581150:
Gerald Weiher and colleagues built a framework describing what therapists need to know and do when therapy mixes in-person sessions with digital tools. Blended care can add video calls, apps, or virtual reality at different stages of treatment, yet terms and expectations have been inconsistent. Writing in twenty twenty-six, the team searched earlier competence models, drafted a version, and refined it with experienced blended care therapists in a workshop. The team then folded in findings from a systematic review of prior studies.

The final framework sorts competence into eight domains. They cover setting up the work, adapting communication and methods, holding the therapeutic relationship, self-care, data security and ethics, technology itself, scientific knowledge, and cultural diversity. Knowledge, skills, and attitudes are treated separately within each domain. The authors offer the framework for training programs and for later testing in practice.
pmc-13582250:
Ramón Garrido-González and colleagues test a mix of clinic and home rehab for patients with heart pumps, in a study from twenty twenty-six. These pumps keep weak hearts going long term. Patients still often stay frail and short of breath. Fifteen patients joined the twelve-week program across centers.

Thirteen finished the program. Peak oxygen use rose a bit but not by a proven margin. Walking distance in six minutes rose clearly and by a useful amount. Quality of life scores were also tracked. Safety and ease of running the program were judged apart. Checks at six months explored whether gains held. The authors call the hybrid model workable and safe. It may widen rehab access for pump patients.
pmc-13584250:
Xian Zhang, Yan Li, Qiang Li, and Quan Zhou study stroke after major surgery in a Korean hospital dataset reported in 2026. A brain infarct, where a blocked vessel kills brain tissue, is a rare but grave outcome after chest or belly surgery. The team checked records for more than 15,000 patients who had major thoracic or abdominopelvic operations and looked for who suffered such a stroke.

Strokes were confirmed in 277 patients, a rate under two in a hundred. Older age and high blood pressure carried the strongest links, joined by an irregular heartbeat, kidney disease, and artery disease in the limbs. Blood tests for inflammation looked higher in stroke patients at first glance, yet lost their link once other factors were counted. Stroke patients also died in hospital far more often.
pmc-13584450:
Hao-qi Wu and colleagues compare drug-free ways to fight oral frailty in older adults in this 2026 review. Oral frailty means a weakening mouth: a softer bite, a weaker tongue, and less saliva, all of which can drag down eating and health. Twenty-six studies fit, and 18 held enough data to pool across methods such as tongue exercises, chewing training, and online health programs. The online programs, which pair remote guidance with mouth exercises and teaching, lifted tongue strength and saliva flow the most. Chewing exercise gave the biggest gain in bite force. The authors add a caution: most trials were small and short, so the rankings rest on shaky ground.
pmc-13585250:
Zhangzhang Qi and nine colleagues link body inflammation to brain wiring changes in people with mild, early depression, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. This in-between state often comes before full depression, so early signs matter. The team studied 126 people with the mild state and 104 healthy peers. They took brain scans, mood surveys, and blood levels of four swelling signals.

The mild group showed stronger links in three circuits of the cingulate cortex, a hub for emotion. Three swelling signals ran higher in their blood. Certain circuit strengths tracked mood and rumination scores. One swelling signal joined with a circuit to track anxiety. The work hints that calming inflammation may help stop full depression.
pmc-13585550:
Durak and seven co-authors break down stubborn water pollutants with light and tiny metal bits in this twenty twenty-six study. The pollutants are long-lived chemicals that shun most clean-up routes and build up in water. Light on the metal bits can spark strong bursts that help split their tough bonds.

Inside, bits of two rare metals on a sand-like base split two named pollutants in room-warm water under mild light. Tests tracked the split step by step and found freed parts near the full count hoped for. No pool of short, burnt waste goods built up in the runs. The team ties the split to free sparks and gas made right at the metal face.
pmc-13587050:
Lanning Xie and eight colleagues published this 2026 letter on food restriction in Chinese children with atopic dermatitis, an itchy skin disease affecting up to a fifth of children. Avoiding a proven allergen can help, but families often cut foods on suspicion alone. The team ran a cross-sectional study at a Shandong dermatology hospital from July 2024 to July 2025. About a quarter of the children (24.92 percent) were on restricted diets, while 30.20 percent tested positive for food sensitisation. The two barely matched: 46.36 percent of restrictions had no test evidence behind them. The most avoided foods, shrimp, fish and crab, reflect stimulating-food beliefs, whereas the commonest sensitisations were egg, milk and wheat. pmc-13587250:
Fatemeh Abdollahi and co-authors study heat-shock genes in the Sunn pest in 2026, an insect that harms wheat crops. Heat-shock proteins help cells cope with stress, and their genes switch on and off across the year. The pest sleeps through part of the year in sheltered spots.

The team read the pest's gene data and picked out parts of three heat-shock genes. They then measured how active each gene was in groups caught across seasons, for both sexes. One gene ran higher in summer-caught pests. The other two showed patterns that mixed season with sex. The authors warn that place and body state also shifted between groups, so the patterns are clues, not proof of a season effect.
pmc-13587350:
Btisème Bendjebour led a team reviewing how living surfaces inspire engineered ones in a 2026 paper. Surfaces in nature handle talking between cells, exchange of materials, defense, and movement. Light-based and chemical signaling on surfaces have guided better sensors, filters, and drug delivery. Camouflage and germ-fighting structures suggest protective designs. pmc-13587650:

The authors present the method as a tight, radical-based entry to group-bearing five-rings for natural-product builds.
pmc-13589650:
Adjaratou Wakha Aidara and two colleagues survey scuba divers in Dakar, Senegal, about tooth trouble caused by pressure change. Fifteen percent reported dental barotrauma and about thirteen percent pressure-related dental pain; together, more than one diver in five had met at least one. Despite the toll, only half had told their dentist about their diving, and fewer than one in five had been given diving-specific dental advice. The authors label the self-reported findings a starting hypothesis.
pmc-13589950:
Wenqi Song and four colleagues present, in 2026, a new lens for an old craft: the processing of traditional Chinese medicines. On their account, active parts and helper stuff in a herb self assemble into soft clusters during processing. Those clusters steer which parts change, which survive, and how the body takes them up. The authors liken a cluster to a template with memory. They suggest the idea could guide smart drug carriers and materials that adapt.
pmc-13590050:

One unusual cluster sat in the rear uvea at the later stage and switched on a distinct gene set. Staining confirmed those cells in fetal tissue. pmc-13590650:

Number and quality measures support uses in ecology, water, climate, farming, woods, and Earth-system science. They also aim to foster data-driven choices at multiple scales.
pmc-13591650:
Lee and colleagues engineer in 2026 an ultrathin stretchable membrane for lung models that breathe, borrowing the physics of soap films. Real alveolar tissue flexes outward with every breath, and lab models need membranes thin enough to flex yet tough enough to survive millions of cycles.

By blending acrylamide into gelatin methacryloyl and tuning the liquid's viscosity and surface tension, the team formed freestanding films. It also changed inflammatory and antiviral responses when influenza A infected the model.
pmc-13593550:
Fady Khoury and colleagues describe a 54-year-old man with repeated fainting whose heart tracing showed only the milder, non-diagnostic form of the Brugada pattern. Daily cannabis use mattered here, because cannabis can block sodium channels and help expose the condition, especially during a fever. The man declined a defibrillator after shared decision making, so the team used an implanted heart monitor instead, combined with strict avoidance of triggers such as fever, alcohol, and cannabis. Screening his close relatives was also arranged, following guideline advice for families facing this inherited risk.
pmc-13593650:
Jada Saunders and co-authors compared robotic and laparoscopic keyhole surgery for acid reflux and hiatus hernia inside one British hospital unit that treats benign upper digestive conditions. pmc-13593850:
Khaled Shaeel Althabaiti, Monica Hunsberger, Sayem Ahmed, and Jahangir Khan break down income inequality in outpatient care use in Saudi Arabia. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. A standard index measured how use tilts by income rank. The team then split the inequality into shares owed to health need and to factors beyond need, such as coverage type. The split tells reformers which part of the gap policy could fairly close.
pmc-13597250:
Yingjie Wang and a team of co-authors report late repeat treatment of a pancreatic tumor that could not be cut out. Their case report, from twenty twenty-six, deals with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. This cancer has a grim outlook, most of all once it spreads. The patient was a sixty-two year old man with blocked bile flow. A team read judged the tumor past surgery, since it wrapped a key vein joint.

He had an electric pulse ablation plus a bile bypass in early twenty twenty-one, then drug care in sequence. Liver spread came ten months on and was treated in place. Proof on late repeat pulse care is thin. Readers learn how one team stretched control of a harsh cancer over years.
pmc-13600950:
Emma Larsson and colleagues lay out the protocol for a Swedish trial of doing less in intensive care. The authors expect the design to show whether trimming routine tests is safe.
pmc-13601550:
Lisowski and colleagues present a 2026 system called STORMS, a robot that automates sampling of solid chemicals at milligram scale. The approach could clear a quiet but real bottleneck in high-throughput chemistry and materials testing.
pmc-13601750:
Sulaiman and six co-authors identify factors tied to ninety-day function after surgery for hypertensive brain bleeding, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Prognosis after such bleeding is well studied generally, but surgical cohorts are less clear. The team uses a Qatar stroke registry from twenty thirteen to twenty twenty-four. Ordinal modeling respects the ranked disability scale as primary analysis. Ninety-five patients have outcome scores, and eighty-seven have complete model data. pmc-13603750:

They suggest campus programs work on activity and emotional states together, since improving either may lift the other.
pmc-13607750:

pmc-13611450:
Xubo Zhao and four co-authors make ultra high expansion nano cell foams from a blend of two bio based plastics with a chain extender, using pressurized carbon dioxide.
