A multi role epoxy extender reacts with end groups of both plastics during mixing, which forms a bridge copolymer on the spot. Melt stretch, surface fit, and gas uptake all improve. The team varies the second plastic share and foam heat, then reads crystal acts, flow traits, cell shape, and crush strength of the foams.
pmc-13611550:
Ren-Chieh Wu and Kuang-Ting Yeh reviewed in 2026 how the Eastern Russell's viper destroys kidneys, and how much of the story is actually proven. Kidney injury is a severe complication of this snake's bite, but much published evidence mixes this species with its close relative or comes from laboratory work. The authors searched PubMed and OpenAlex and sorted species-confirmed human evidence apart from experiments.

They organized the review around four questions, covering human renal evidence, the venom pathways involved, antivenom timing, and long-term kidney risk. Referral hospital cohorts show real burdens of kidney failure and dialysis, but inconsistent methods prevent a pooled rate. Lab studies point to interacting pathways: clotting chaos, vessel damage, blood pressure collapse, pigments, inflammation, and direct kidney toxicity. Separating solid ground from plausible story is the review's main service to clinicians.
pmc-13611850:
Andrey Bogoyavlenskiy and colleagues report a 2026 study of roseofungin, an antibiotic made by a soil microbe, tested against influenza A. Flu drugs face growing resistance, so new options matter. The team checked the compound in lab dishes, in eggs, and in early animal tests, with computer models on the side.

Roseofungin slowed several flu strains, including one that resists a common flu drug. It worked at low doses and seemed to act early, stopping the virus from latching onto cells. It also directly cut the amount of live virus. Safety tests in mice showed low harm at the doses tried. Computer models suggested the compound grips key flu proteins firmly. The authors present roseofungin as a promising lead, while noting that far more testing lies ahead before any human use.
pmc-13613350:
Alexandra Sjöholm and colleagues report a 2026 trial comparing two light treatments for actinic keratoses, rough sun-damaged patches on the skin that can turn into cancer. The standard treatment, photodynamic therapy with red light, works well but hurts. A newer version uses simulated daylight, which most likely hurts less, yet its strength had not been well tested. Adults with matching patches on both sides of a body area joined the trial.

One half of each treated area got the standard red light treatment and the other half got the simulated daylight version, in a single session with the same light-activated cream. Pain was scored from 0 to 10, and patients stated which side they preferred. At three months the team checked how well each half had healed, testing whether the gentler light gives up any real benefit.
pmc-13613850:
Quddus and colleagues published a 2026 field study on nano-boron spray for cauliflower crops. Boron feeds cauliflower growth, but soil doses wash away or miss roots. Tiny nano-boron particles slip into leaves more readily than standard forms. The team sprayed four doses plus a standard boron spray on field plots.

A mid dose, 200 parts per million, gave the best harvest overall. Its curd yield beat the unsprayed control by about 70 percent. It also beat the standard boron spray by about 23 percent. Curds grew firmer, richer in vitamin C, and heavier at that dose. Profits peaked there too, with the best cost-to-gain ratio recorded. The dose also used boron most efficiently of all treatments tested.
pmc-13616350:
Xueli Mei and colleagues make pyruvic acid, a small molecule with roles from food chemistry to drug making, through a two-step cascade that brews its own hydrogen peroxide on site. Peroxide is a clean oxidiser, but shipping and storing it is wasteful and risky. Their method generates peroxide electrically from oxygen and spends it at once to convert hydroxy acids into pyruvate. The hard part is balancing peroxide output, activation, and clean conversion in one pot.

A family of cerium oxide catalysts spiked with different metals was tested, and the nickel version won, producing pyruvate at 19.9 millimoles per gram per hour with 55.3 percent of the electric charge doing useful work. Studies of the surface showed the metal tuning oxygen vacancies, which set how tightly a key intermediate sticks. Greener routes to staple chemicals can start with such coupled designs.
pmc-13618850:
Hua Wu and four colleagues lay out a case for diagnosing melioidosis faster by targeting the weaponry its bacterium, Burkholderia pseudomallei, actually switches on inside the body. Culture misses many cases and takes days, while PCR needs equipment endemic regions often lack, so deaths stay high. Most biomarkers ignore the fact that virulence factors are switched on during active infection, the authors argue, which makes those very factors the smartest diagnostic targets.

Their flagship example is Hcp1, a secretion system component, converted through their pipeline into a point-of-care strip test. Its sensitivity ran near eighty-eight percent and specificity reached one hundred percent in prospective validation in endemic settings. Other upregulated factors wait in line behind it. The authors propose integrating multi-omics data with explainable machine learning to pick factor combinations for multiplex tests. They offer the framework as a template for other intracellular pathogens.
pmc-13618950:
Zhi-Peng Lin and three colleagues introduce a way to judge when a sequence of moving closed sets settles in a metric space. Standard convergence theories fix the test regions in advance, which can hide where a sequence stabilizes. Their construction reverses the order: they measure the worst mismatch between far-out members of the sequence. The sets where that mismatch shrinks to zero form a stabilization family generated by the sequence itself.

They prove this family behaves like a bornology, the mathematical structure used for local convergence, whenever it covers the whole space. Under neighborhood stabilization plus a compactness guard against escape, a sequence must vanish from a region eventually or converge there to a nonempty local closed limit. Compatible local limits then assemble into a global cluster set. Counterexamples show the notion differs from Hausdorff and distance-function convergence, and compactness cannot be dropped.
pmc-13619050:
Marisha Shetty and seven colleagues compare sleep's fine structure in children referred for excessive daytime sleepiness, in a 2026 study of whether spindles help tell diagnoses apart. Spindles are brief bursts of brain activity during sleep whose density, duration, and strength can be measured at scalp sites. The sample covered twenty-eight children with narcolepsy, eleven with idiopathic hypersomnolence, and twenty-six who felt sleepy despite a non-diagnostic nap test, each against matched controls, ages six to nineteen.

Children with narcolepsy showed longer spindle durations at central and frontal sites than their controls and the subjectively sleepy group. Spindle intensity ran higher in the narcolepsy and subjectively sleepy groups than in controls, and in those groups spindles built toward the night's end rather than its start. No spindle measure tracked parents' reports of sleepiness. The authors suggest the signatures may help distinguish narcolepsy from look-alike complaints in children.
pmc-13619250:
Abrar I Alsaadi led a large team on a 2026 study of NAD+, a coenzyme cells need for energy, repair, and stress responses, during gut inflammation. The group used a mouse model of colitis, multi-omics tools, and isotope-labeled building blocks given by vein. Their aim was to map how NAD+ production shifts across body tissues and the gut lumen when inflammation strikes.

Diseased mice leaned harder on a recycling route, called the salvage pathway, to make up for weaker fresh production from the amino acid tryptophan. Gut microbes raised their own fresh NAD+ production at the same time. The authors read that pairing as a cooperative response, with host and microbes adjusting in opposite directions to keep NAD+ levels steady. The picture may help explain how metabolism goes wrong in inflammatory bowel disease.
pmc-13620850:
Fatemeh Shayesteh and four colleagues tested two probiotic bacteria as treatments for ulcerative colitis in rats, aiming at veterinary use. Bowel inflammation troubles pets and livestock as well as people, and standard drugs often fail or carry side effects. Forty male rats were split into five groups: healthy, untreated colitis, colitis treated with the standard drug mesalazine, and colitis treated with one of two probiotics, Bacillus coagulans or Lactobacillus acidophilus.

The chemical used to trigger colitis raised inflammatory signals and scarred the colon lining. Both probiotics pulled those signals down, calmed the inflammasome, the cell machinery that amplifies inflammation, and restored colon shape. Their protection matched the standard drug's effects in this model. The authors suggest either bacterium could serve as an add-on therapy for animals, with possible lessons for human care.
pmc-13621350:
Nilofar Nilofar and ten colleagues profiled two little-studied plants for chemistry and health-related activity in the lab. Extracts of Saponaria pumila and Suaeda confusa were made with three solvents, and a high-end mass spectrometry method named their compounds. Standard assays then measured antioxidant strength, enzyme blocking, and microbe killing, with computer docking adding targets the wet work cannot see.

The methanol extract of the first plant carried the richest load of phenolics and flavonoids, plant chemicals tied to antioxidant power, and it led most radical-scavenging tests. Water extracts from each plant led on blocking enzymes linked to memory loss and skin darkening, while the second plant's methanol extract topped that pair overall. Microbe tests showed the strongest effects against a foodborne bacterium and a lung fungus, while one hardy hospital bacterium resisted. The authors pitch both plants as raw material for functional products, pending deeper study.
pmc-13621950:
Yi-Yang Zhao and colleagues test whether eating foods rich in curcumin, the yellow compound in turmeric, links to lower oral cancer risk. Because few foods were tracked for curcumin content, the team used oranges and carrots as stand-ins. Their data come from a national United States health and nutrition survey carried out in 2003 and 2004.

The analysis covered 2,762 people and compared the oral cancer group with everyone else. People with cancer more often reported never eating the tracked foods, and they faced more social and economic disadvantage. As reported eating of oranges and carrots rose, the share of cancer cases fell in a steady trend. Eating both foods often went with the lowest risk in the combined analysis. The authors built a prediction model that sorted the two groups well, while noting that survey links like these cannot prove that a food prevents cancer.
pmc-13622750:
Advanced Science issued a correction for a 2026 article by M Eason and co-authors on blocking a growth signal in breast cancer. After publication, the authors found copy-and-paste mistakes in the raw data files behind three figures. The notice sets out each error and states that the corrected files have been posted for readers.

For one figure, values for a key protein were duplicated into another protein's rows, and for two others, measurement rows were repeated from the rows above. The graphs were rebuilt from the fixed data and shown beside the originals. Some significance results shifted slightly, with one link growing stronger, while the main outcomes and the article's conclusions stayed unchanged. One duplicated set had never entered the published graphs, because the plotting step used a random selection that skipped those points. The notice lets readers verify exactly what changed.
pmc-13623450:
Chutima Churee, Piya Hanvoravongchai, and Thanapoom Rattananupong published a 2026 nationwide study of access to ultraviolet phototherapy for psoriasis in Thailand. Light treatment is a cheap, guideline-backed option for moderate-to-severe psoriasis, yet nobody had mapped who receives it under the country's universal coverage system. Data covered the whole of 2023.

Insurance records identified 49,219 patients with psoriasis, of whom 16,188 had moderate-to-severe disease judged by their treatments. Only a small fraction of that group, about three in a hundred, received phototherapy. Use clustered in richer provinces, and a formal inequality measure confirmed the tilt toward the better-off. Age, psoriasis type, insurance scheme, region, provincial income, and the local supply of skin doctors and light devices each shaped access. The authors argue that spreading staff and devices more evenly would do more for fairness than coverage rules alone.
pmc-13624950:
Lal, Pathi, and Nanda review removing fibroids during caesarean birth in twenty twenty-six. Fibroids are common in pregnancy, but cutting them out at delivery is controversial. Surgeons fear heavy bleeding from the pregnant uterus. The team reviewed twenty-five such cases at a Bihar tertiary centre over two years.

Patients averaged twenty-nine years old and delivered near term. Fibroids ranged from four to sixteen centimetres. Operations averaged about sixty-eight minutes, with modest blood loss on average. Seven women needed a blood transfusion. Nearly all mothers and babies did well, with three babies needing intensive care. The authors conclude the combined operation is feasible in expert hands. Careful case selection avoids a second surgery later.
pmc-13625350:
Arto Gråstén and three colleagues, publishing in 2026, measure grip strength and movement in young Emirati women at college. Heat, custom, and family expectations can all hold back exercise in this group, and strength data were scarce. The team tested 291 students aged eighteen to twenty-six with a grip meter and motion sensors. Self-reported activity scores came again eight weeks later. The models adjusted for wear time, muscle mass, and hand size.

About four in five students fell short of activity guidelines, and their grip strength sat near the bottom tenth of world values for their age. More sitting time linked weakly to weaker grip, while light everyday movement linked weakly to stronger grip, and harder exercise showed no clear link. Cutting sitting time may matter as much as formal workouts.
pmc-13625650:
Tomoko Hata, Tomoya Ohyama, Jenny Veitch, and Daisuke Takagi survey children's park freedom in Japan in a 2026 paper. Independent mobility means parents let children travel and play unsupervised, and it supports body and mind health. Thousands of mothers reported on their primary school child. Among park visitors, about half the children could go to parks alone, return alone, or play there alone.

Girls were less likely than boys to be allowed the trip home alone. For every freedom type, mothers who trusted the child's self-protection, or trusted local residents to step in, granted it more often. Nearby watchful adults seemed to substitute for child readiness.
pmc-13626250:
Hansol Kang and colleagues estimate how common inflammatory bowel disease is in each American state. The country lacks a single registry for Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. So the team reused a pooled set of insurance claims analyses. Those had put national prevalence at 721 per hundred thousand people, about 2.39 million Americans. They then reweighted those figures by each state's racial mix, since prevalence differs sharply by ancestry.

Earlier pooled work found disease most common in the Northeast and least in the West, and most common among White Americans. State-level numbers matter because clinics, budgets, and screening drives are planned state by state. The estimates also set up fairer comparisons for studies of why place and background shape this chronic gut disease.
pmc-13627450:
Giuseppe Pezzotti and co-authors read the light fingerprints of coronavirus RNA to tell its variants apart without sequencing. They collected Raman spectra, the scatter patterns molecules throw off under laser light. The strands came from twenty SARS-CoV-2 strains. The set ran from the first Japanese isolate through the Greek-letter variants to a dozen Omicron subvariants. All shared the backbone and base signals of similar RNA, yet fine features shifted with each strain's folded structure.

Ordinary statistics could barely separate the strains. Recast as barcodes, though, the spectra distinguished every strain, and several signals swelled in step with hairpin content and stem length in the folded RNA. A barcode library tied to molecular shape, the authors argue, could flag emerging variants fast, a step toward what they call the Raman genome.
pmc-13628550:
Shivam Tikoo and two colleagues report a selenium-based linker for attaching cargo to synthetic oligonucleotides, the short DNA-like strands used as gene-silencing drugs. In their 2026 method, the linker is added at the strand's end during standard solid-phase synthesis, carrying a protected selenium handle.

Once the strand is released from its support, two strands join quantitatively into a diselenide-linked dimer, confirmed by gel, chromatography, and mass measurements. A mild reducing agent then splits the pair back into reactive single strands, which grab onto target molecules to form the final conjugates. The team shows several different attachments succeeding, arguing the platform is flexible enough for broad use in chemical biology.
pmc-13631350:
Junchen Zhou and eight colleagues chart how the brain's white matter joins its functional networks. White matter was long treated as mere cabling between grey matter zones. Their study appeared in 2026. The blood-oxygen signals used in brain imaging were thought to live in grey matter. Sensitive scanning now detects them in white matter too.

Building a joint grey-white connectome from ultra-high-field scans, the team found clear patterns. White matter coupling follows the same sensory-to-abstract ladder as grey matter. It also aligns with neurotransmitter receptor spread. Different white matter networks paired with distinct mental domains. Single differences tracked test performance. The joint map flagged brain disorders more sharply than grey matter alone. Findings repeated in a second scanner cohort.
pmc-13632250:
Maartje Witsen and colleagues mapped the proteins that colorectal cancer cells release into their surroundings. Tumors use these secreted factors to shape nearby tissue and dodge immune attack. Telling cancer-made factors apart from those of healthy tissue has been hard. The team grew organoids, small lab versions of tumors and healthy colon, from patients. They used a click chemistry trick to tag only the proteins each organoid released.

Cancer organoids showed a clearly rewired release pattern compared with healthy ones. Tumors also split into distinct secretory groups matching their two known genetic subtypes. Hunting for factors tied to tumors that keep immune cells out, the team singled out a protein called NOTUM. Tumors releasing more NOTUM held fewer infiltrating T cells across four separate datasets. The method gives researchers a scalable way to connect secreted factors with tumor behavior.
pmc-13634250:
Julia Brechbühl and four colleagues tested a stepping program that mixes movement and thinking tasks for hospital patients with traumatic brain injury. Brain injury survivors often walk poorly, and thinking problems make falls more likely. Training both at once, called dual-task training, has helped in later recovery stages. Their program, StepIt, delivers short individual sessions of about fifteen minutes during the acute hospital stay.

Recruitment, adherence, and compliance rates all came out strong, and no training-related harm occurred. Two weak points stood out: very few admitted patients qualified for the study, and more than four in ten dropped out along the way. Four of six preset feasibility goals were met. The authors judge the program workable in acute hospital care, with design changes needed before a larger trial. They propose testing it next in rehabilitation settings, both inpatient and outpatient.
pmc-13636450:
Lauren Head Zauche and five colleagues published this 2026 report from the United States COVID-19 vaccine pregnancy registry. The registry followed people vaccinated during pregnancy from late 2020 into mid 2021. Phone interviews gathered infant outcomes from birth to three months, with a smaller group followed to fifteen months. The team tracked birth weight, growth size, deaths, and ten prespecified conditions ranging from heart problems to seizures and stroke.

Nearly twenty thousand infants had three-month data. Only a small fraction had any of the ten watched conditions. Rates of low birth weight, small size for age, death, and each listed condition sat within or below the ranges seen before the pandemic. The authors present the registry as reassurance that vaccination in pregnancy showed no excess of these infant outcomes. Their design cannot prove safety for rarer events, yet the scale and the comparison frame make the report a reference point.
pmc-13638050:
Katrine E Dailey and ten colleagues investigate why almost no flu antibody manages to neutralize both influenza A and influenza B. The stem of the virus's surface protein barely changes, making it the prime target for a universal vaccine strategy. One famous antibody, CR9114, crosses the A-B divide alone. The team ran four deep mutational scans, testing thousands of variants of the antibody's ancestor and its mature form against three viral targets.

The trade-offs were stark. Many changes that kept or even improved binding to one influenza A subtype damaged binding to the other subtype or to influenza B. Mutations also interacted with each other pervasively, so gains could not simply be stacked. Together these constraints explain the scarcity of cross-reactive stem antibodies on mechanistic grounds. Vaccine designers chasing breadth, the authors argue, must engineer around epistasis rather than optimize one target at a time.
pmc-13639550:
Hoang Le Huy Nguyen and Tuan Cong Trinh published this 2026 prospective cohort study on frailty and repeated hospitalisation in older Vietnamese adults with chronic heart failure. Frailty is known to predict death in this group, but its link to recurrent admissions, and its worth next to the heart pumping measure, ejection fraction, were unclear in Asian patients. The team followed 150 outpatients aged 60 or over for twelve months.

Fifty-four participants, 36.0 percent of the group, met the frailty cut-off on the Clinical Frailty Scale, and over half were hospitalised at least once. Frail patients had a 73 percent higher rate of recurrent hospitalisation after adjusting for age and sex (hazard ratio 1.73). Prediction accuracy was modest for every model, and frailty performed about as well as ejection fraction; combining them helped only slightly. The authors suggest a frailty check at baseline to flag high-risk patients.
pmc-13642250:
Hantang Huang and six colleagues present a 2026 genome assembly for the fig cultivar Green Peel. Fig is among the earliest domesticated fruit crops, yet high-quality genome references for breeding and evolution studies have been scarce.

Built from long nanopore reads, chromosome-contact data, and short-read polishing, the assembly spans about 307 million bases across thirteen pseudo-chromosomes. Annotation predicted 27,036 protein-coding genes with near-complete coverage of conserved gene sets. Comparison with a climbing fig relative mapped family expansions and wide structural differences. The authors offer the resource for trait mapping, genome-guided breeding, and a future fig pan-genome.
pmc-13642950:
Paulina Czajka-Francuz and twenty-four colleagues present a 2026 analysis of cancer drug trials in the United Kingdom over twenty-five years, with an eye on the 2026 reboot of trial regulation. The review uses the global trial registry to compare the UK with the European Union, the United States, and China.

British trial numbers grew until 2017, then fell with Brexit and the pandemic before partly recovering. China grew fastest, especially in early-phase trials, while population-adjusted intensity declined in the EU and USA. The authors say strong British infrastructure plus the new rules could restore competitiveness, if global rivalry allows.
pmc-13645550:
Abdifatah Ahmed Osman and Hamze G Dahir write a perspective piece on health care seeking in Somaliland, where people often move among healers, drug sellers, clinics, and hospitals during one illness. The pair build their argument from published studies and policy papers. They name the core problem as poorly linked steps between these sources of care. Each extra step can add time, cost, and risk before proper treatment begins.

The authors propose a framework that sorts delay patterns for city, rural, and herding communities, and they present the patterns as ideas to test, not proven facts. Their plan calls for safer pharmacy rules, referral ties with trusted local healers, and mobile services for herding groups. They also want transport and payment links tied to referrals. The piece speaks to wider goals of fair, universal health coverage.
pmc-13646750:
Raafat Mady and six colleagues ask whether a sentinel lymph node biopsy can safely be skipped in older women with the most favorable breast cancers, using records from one British breast unit. Guidelines already question the routine biopsy for women over seventy with hormone-sensitive, early tumors. The team cross-checked hospital coding against pathology records for patients biopsied between January 2015 and December 2020. Ages were verified independently rather than assumed.

In the primary group of thirty-nine women with grade 1, small, hormone-positive tumors, the biopsy found spread in just three patients. Positivity rose in grade 2 disease and sat between the two in grade 3, a pattern read with care given the small numbers. All primary-group patients were followed at least five years. The authors argue the low yield supports selective omission of the biopsy in this narrow subgroup, sparing older women an operation that rarely changes their care.
pmc-13649450:
Ronglang Wu and four colleagues pooled studies on a kidney illness in children that follows a strep infection. The illness can raise blood pressure, swell the body, and in rare cases shut down the kidneys. They searched six sources for studies that reported signs and severe outcomes in young patients.

Eighteen studies with 2,191 children were included, most from hospitals. High blood pressure was the most common sign, seen in about two-thirds of children. Visible blood in urine showed in near half, and sharp kidney injury in about two in five. Severe problems struck about one in eight, and a small share needed dialysis-type care. Rates swung widely between studies, a caveat the authors note.
pmc-13649550:
Arwa Alruwaili led a 2026 study of how body composition and resting metabolic rate relate to two sides of appetite in adults. Fat-free mass, fat mass, and resting metabolic rate are thought to drive food intake, yet their roles in hunger hormones, cravings, food reward, and taste remain murky. The team measured 130 adults averaging twenty-five, tracking metabolic rate by indirect calorimetry, body composition by air-displacement plethysmography, and intake in a lab.

Metabolic rate, not fat-free or fat mass, tracked with energy intake, more strongly in younger, more active, leaner participants and in smokers. Fat-free mass linked to post-meal peptide YY, hunger, craving control, and smell sensitivity, while fat mass showed a contrasting pattern across fasting and post-meal hormones and taste sensitivity. No consistent links emerged for food reward. Metabolic rate drives how much is eaten, while body compartments tune appetite signals in different directions.
pmc-13649750:
Youqi Li and eight colleagues tested a paired drug plan for a kidney filter disease that had resisted past care. The plan joins an antibody drug that drains B cells with low-dose steroids. Their group held 36 adults with the stubborn form of the disease, all new to the antibody drug.

At one year, about three in four patients with outcome data had reached full or partial remission. At two years, rates ran higher still among those who stayed in the study, though a worst-case count that treats all dropouts as failures reads far lower. Harm events struck about a third of patients, and a small share had severe infections. No cancers or deaths were seen. The authors say the open design bars firm claims.
pmc-13650350:
Pirawan Wangupadcha and four colleagues, publishing in 2026, trace nearly two decades of workplace injury and disease across Thailand using workers' compensation records. The nationwide study covers 2007 to 2024, a period when the registered workforce grew while factories, construction, and services changed quickly.

More than two million injury cases were recorded. Overall injury rates fell steeply, and severe injury rates fell as well, yet fatal injury rates dropped less steadily, ending the period at roughly half their starting level per head of workforce. Muscle and joint disorders stayed the most common work-related disease. Looking closely at 2024, deaths clustered among workers aged 55 and over, at construction sites, in vehicle-related events, and in smaller workplaces. The authors conclude that prevention has worked broadly but must now target the settings where fatal harm persists.
pmc-13650450:
Alexander Muacevic and seven colleagues report a 28-year-old woman with acute leukemia whose scans seemed to show fresh internal bleeding but actually showed a harmless contrast quirk. Contrast dye from repeated scans can leave the body through the liver and gut when the kidneys falter, and the leftover dye looks bright on computed tomography, exactly like blood.

Her course included drug-induced pancreas inflammation and heavy bleeding behind the abdomen, treated by blocking a stomach artery with coils after scans suggested active bleeding. A later scan showed bright material in the gallbladder and bowel, raising fears of new bleeding. Comparing the plain images taken before fresh dye was given showed the bright material was already there and unchanged, proving it was excreted dye rather than hemorrhage. The authors warn teams to recognize this pattern before ordering needless vessel procedures or surgery.
pmc-13650750:
Mingyue Ren and five colleagues review how fat-derived hormones may drive obesity-related asthma, a stubborn form of the disease with poor control, frequent attacks, and weak response to standard steroids. Body weight pressing on the chest explains some symptoms, so the authors focus on a hormonal axis: too much leptin and too little adiponectin, two signals secreted by fat tissue.

Evidence from population studies, animals, and airway cells links this imbalance to three connected harms. Immune activation deepens, partly through a fired-up inflammatory complex in macrophages. Airway twitchiness rises through inflammatory, neural, and muscle pathways. Remodeling follows, as repair fails, smooth muscle multiplies, fat around the airways talks directly to them, and scar-like matrix accumulates. Their model moves from systemic hormone signals early to local fat-airway chatter later, ending in fixed structural change, and they propose the hormones as sorting markers for tailored treatment trials.
pmc-13652550:
Zeineb Alaoui Kadiri and nine colleagues study how often heart and metabolic conditions appear alongside knee osteoarthritis, and what that overlap means for care. The joint disease is a leading cause of pain and disability, and conditions such as high blood pressure, abnormal blood fats, and diabetes travel with it often. The team examined consecutive patients with X-ray-confirmed knee osteoarthritis at a rheumatology clinic and recorded their cardiovascular profile, pain, and function.

Coexisting conditions shape treatment directly, because the anti-inflammatory drugs commonly used for joint pain can strain the heart and kidneys. By measuring how burden, pain, and daily function change when cardiovascular disease is present, the study gives clinicians a clearer basis for choosing safer pain relief. It also argues for treating the knee and the heart as one problem rather than two separate charts.
pmc-13654150:
Lin Chen, Dan Liu, Ying-Kun Guo, and Xing-Yuan Zhang describe a rare heart defect found in a baby before birth. In the defect, veins from the lungs drain to the wrong place. This mixed form is uncommon and often blocks blood flow. Blockage forces urgent surgery after birth and worsens the outlook.

The mother was a thirty-six-year-old woman scanned partway through pregnancy. Standard ultrasound can miss the fine layout of these veins. The team used advanced moving 3D ultrasound to map the vessels in detail. They found a single shared vein trunk with flow leaving in two directions, a pattern not reported before. The report also sets out quality checks for the scan method. Careful maps like this help surgeons plan the repair.
pmc-13664850:
Giuseppe Perri and colleagues tested sourdough bacteria against grain toxins in 2026. Toxins from Fusarium fungi contaminate many cereal foods. Clean-label ways to cut them remain limited. Lactic acid bacteria had shown promise in lab tests. Real dough evidence was scarce. The team screened nineteen sourdough strains in wholegrain wheat dough. Their target was a toxin called deoxynivalenol. Three strong strains then faced a wider toxin panel. That panel included changed toxin forms and newer toxins.

After two days of fermentation, toxin levels fell by about half. The main toxin dropped below the European safety limit. All three chosen strains performed much alike. Tests with heat-killed cells cut toxins less well. That gap pointed to cell walls soaking up toxins. Live cell activity may add an effect. The authors caution that lower readings do not prove detoxifying. Still, fermentation looks like a practical defense for wheat foods.
pmc-13668950:
Parcha and Bittner review RNA-based drugs that lower lipoprotein(a), a blood fat tied to heart disease. High levels are set by genes, affect about a fifth of people worldwide, and raise risk of artery disease and aortic valve narrowing. Lifestyle change and current drugs barely move this level.

The review covers the biology that makes lipoprotein(a) a drug target. It then weighs antisense drugs and small interfering RNAs, which block the protein's production in the liver. Newer platforms are also surveyed. The authors judge how far each approach cuts levels and what proof is still needed.
pmc-13679550:
Abisha Marshal Williams leads a team that reviews green nanoparticles in farming. Their review from twenty twenty-six deals with precision crop care. Lasting farm output needs more yield with less harm to nature.

Particles made from plants, microbes, and waste are covered. Uses span nutrient delivery, crop guard, and stress care. Sensors and smart delivery are part of the scope as well. Gains vary with size, dose, crop, and soil type. Risks like plant harm and build up are weighed too. Waste based particles offer a circular path.  Long term effects on ecosystems are covered too.
pmc-2008650:
Kerr, Wyllie, and Currie propose the term apoptosis for a controlled way cells delete themselves. Writing in 1972, they describe a process that had been little recognised before. It appears to balance cell division, keeping animal cell populations in check from the opposite side.

The authors outline the distinct shape changes of dying cells under this programme. Unlike messy death from injury, apoptosis looks active and built into the tissue's own control system. Naming and defining it opened a huge field: faulty cell deletion is now tied to cancer, immune disease, and the shaping of growing bodies.
pmc-3198950:
O'Boyle, Banck, James, and co-authors present Open Babel, an open chemical toolbox for converting molecular structures between formats. Computational modelling constantly hits the problem that chemical data live in many incompatible file types. Standard formats exist, such as Chemical Markup Language, and common ones like SMILES arose by use.

Even so, researchers still need reliable translation between the many formats in daily use. Open Babel supplies that interconversion as free, open software. It quietly underpins cheminformatics work worldwide, letting models, drawings, and databases finally speak to one another.  Drug designers rely on such conversions when merging data from many suppliers.
pmc-3506950:
Morgan, Tickle, Sokol, and co-authors analyse how gut microbes go wrong in Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, and during treatment. Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis arise from changes in intestinal microbes together with the immune system. The precise failures of microbial workings in the gut during these diseases were unclear.

Their analysis compares gut communities and their chemical activity in patients and controls. Naming which microbial jobs are lost or overdone suggests new treatment angles, from diet to live microbe therapies. The work shaped how bowel disease is viewed as a system disorder.
pmc-3810850:
Zhang, Kapli, Pavlidis, and co-authors present a general method for delimiting species from sequence data, with applications to placing species on family trees. Sequence-based delimitation is central to DNA-based taxonomy, to surveys of microbial communities, and to metabarcoding studies. Existing approaches rely either on simple similarity thresholds or on complex, compute-heavy evolutionary models.

Their method seeks a middle path that is both principled and practical. Deciding where one species ends and another begins affects conservation lists, ecological counts, and identification of specimens from environmental DNA.  DNA barcoding of insects and fungi drove much of the demand behind it.
pmc-4287950:
Anders, Pyl, and Huber presented HTSeq in 2014, a Python framework for high-throughput sequencing data. Many tools exist for standard steps in this kind of analysis. Once a project departs from standard workflows, though, researchers must write custom scripts of their own.

HTSeq makes that custom work faster and safer. It provides building blocks for reading, counting, and sorting sequencing data in Python. A common task is counting how many reads fall on each gene. With a solid library for the basics, labs can focus their code on the new question they are asking instead of file handling.
pmc-4687950:
Whiting, Savović, Higgins, and their colleagues developed ROBIS, reported in 2016, to judge bias in systematic reviews. Many tools assessed bias in primary studies, but reviews themselves can also be biased. ROBIS was built to fill that gap for reviewers of reviews.

The team used a four-stage process: set the scope, review the evidence, meet in person, and refine the tool by piloting. ROBIS checks how a review searched, selected, and combined studies, and whether its conclusions follow. Umbrella reviews and guidelines rely on underlying reviews being sound. A tested tool for spotting weak reviews protects the decisions built on them.
pmc-5520850:
Yang, Fan, Mao, and their team found in 2017 that circular RNAs can be turned into proteins on a wide scale. Back-splicing of gene messages creates large numbers of circular RNAs in human cells. What most of these circles do in the cell was still largely unclear.

The team reports that a chemical mark on RNA, the most common such mark, drives the making of proteins from these circles. That was a surprise, since circles lack the start cap that straight messages use to begin protein making. Proteins from circles would add a hidden layer of gene products. The find widened the known roles of circular RNAs in the cell.
pmc-6146950:
James Dahlhamer, Jacqueline Lucas, Carla Zelaya, and colleagues reported United States pain figures for 2016 in this 2018 report. Chronic pain shapes work, mood, and health care use across the country. Knowing how common it is guides policy and funding.

Using a national health survey, the authors estimate that about one in five adults had chronic pain. A smaller share had high-impact pain that often limits life or work. Rates were higher in women, older adults, and rural areas. These baseline numbers are still quoted when pain policy and opioid policy are debated.
pmc-8431850:
David Stirling and co-authors described CellProfiler 4 in 2021, the newest version of a free program that measures features in microscope images. Images hold far more information than the eye can tally, and modern microscopy produces datasets far too large for manual scoring. Automated, objective measurement has become essential for image based biology.

The update focuses on speed, utility, and ease of use, letting researchers process big image sets faster and with less friction. The authors explain what changed under the hood and in the interface. CellProfiler is a workhorse in drug screening and cell biology, so improvements here quietly raise the throughput of many laboratories.
pmc-9438950:
Giulio Formenti and colleagues built Gfastats in 2022, a tool that sums up genome assemblies and helps researchers work with them. Labs now produce new reference genomes at great speed. Each one needs a clear report card: how long it is, how many pieces it comes in, and how far it can be trusted. New data types and new methods keep changing what that report card must show.

Gfastats builds its reports from assembly graphs, the maps that assembly software draws as it works. It can also convert files between formats and let users trim or join pieces of a genome build. Teams check these numbers at each step to judge when a genome is done, so a fast, sound tool sits inside many projects.
pmc-9825450:
Typhaine Paysan-Lafosse, Matty Blum, and co-authors reported in 2023 the recent developments in InterPro, a database that classifies proteins into families. InterPro also marks the domains and conserved sites that reveal what a protein does. This report covers version ninety of the resource and the services associated with it.

The authors describe new member databases and data added, improvements to the website, and growth in the classifications offered. InterPro merges many specialist collections into one search, so a single query checks a protein against all of them. Keeping such an integration current is constant work, and these periodic reports let users see what changed beneath a tool many treat as fixed.
reichenbach-researches-magnetism-1850:
Karl von Reichenbach announces a new force in his Physico-Physiological Researches, in William Gregory's 1850 English version. Sensitive persons, he reports, see flames and glows around magnets and crystals. He names the unseen energy the odic force and builds a vast system of trials to prove its presence in nature.

Earnest and elaborate, the work sought new forces with a chemist's care. Reichenbach had real fame as the finder of creosote and paraffin. Critics could not repeat his sensitives' visions under strict test conditions. The book remains the pivotal work of fringe science in its century, a serious mind's bold reach beyond the known map of nature.
sendivogius-new-light-of-alchymie-1650:
Michael Sendivogius was a Polish adept at the courts of emperors whose Novum Lumen Chymicum taught a generation of chymists. This 1650 English translation, A New Light of Alchymie, carried his treatise to Boyle and Newton. Both men studied Sendivogius with close attention.

He teaches that a hidden food of life, drawn from the air and the sun's rays, feeds metals growing in the earth. The philosophers' stone, in his account, concentrates that food until base metals ripen into gold. His clear, confident system made him the most readable of the great alchemical teachers. His name for that hidden food, the seed of nature, passed into wide use.
smith-dictionary-greek-roman-biography-m:
Volume Two of Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology appeared in 1850, continuing the alphabet of ancient lives. William Smith's team of scholars worked from the Greek and Latin authors directly. The aim was a complete record of the classical world in persons.

Each article weighs the ancient evidence, cites its sources, and untangles fact from myth. Long lives like those of the Caesars sit beside brief notices of minor poets and kings. The volume holds hundreds of engraved coins and portraits as well. Together with its mates, it formed the standard English guide to classical biography.
sydenham-works-vol2-1850:
Thomas Sydenham built his fame on careful notes taken at the sickbed in seventeenth-century London. R. G. Latham translated his Latin writings for the Sydenham Society. This second volume of the English Works followed the first in 1850 and completes the set.

Here Sydenham treats smallpox, gout, and several other common diseases of his day. He explains the cooling treatment he used for smallpox and describes his own painful attacks of gout. Throughout, he trusts what repeated observation shows over what old books claim. The volume rounds out the record of his clinical method, and it shows why later doctors admired his honest, practical style.
tennyson-in-memoriam-1850:
Alfred Tennyson's closest friend, Arthur Hallam, died suddenly at twenty-two in 1833. Tennyson grieved for seventeen years, writing short lyrics whenever sorrow or hope moved him. He published the gathered sequence, 131 lyrics with prologue and epilogue, as In Memoriam in 1850, without his name at first.

The poems swing between despair and a hard-won trust that love survives death. Tennyson wrestles with new geology and evolution, which seemed to make nature careless of human life. Ring out, wild bells and other sections became famous Victorian touchstones. Queen Victoria kept the book beside her Bible after her husband died. It remains the century's deepest meditation on faith and doubt.
the-divine-pymander-in-xvii-books-hermet: The Divine Pymander in XVII Books, 1650. The Hermetic classic. This book preserves that work. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-:
Vol. 1, No. 50 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is dated October 21, 1897. The paper is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Its lead item names the new Prime Minister of Spain: Senor Sagasta. A report went round that General Weyler had sent in his resignation from Cuba. It was also rumored that Sagasta meant to remove him. Weyler does not intend to leave if he can help it.

Before the old ministry fell, Weyler hurried off a long report. He claimed that Western Cuba was pacified. He claimed that trains ran regularly and the telegraph worked. He claimed the troops were in excellent health, though their pay was six months in arrears. Every one of these statements, the paper says, is declared false by those who know the real state of affairs. Soldiers parade the streets crying, Long live Weyler!
the-iliad-pg6150:
Homer's Iliad appears here in English blank verse rendered by Edward, Earl of Derby, a version with an unusual birth. In the spring of 1862, at the request of personal friends, Derby printed a small volume of translations for private circulation only, and it included the first book of the Iliad. Competent judges praised his attempt to infuse an almost literal version with the spirit and simplicity of the original, and their encouragement persuaded him to continue.

The work filled the intervals of more urgent business, meaning a statesman's career, and gave him a steady pleasure that only grew with time. All twenty-four books are listed in the contents. Readers get a Victorian prime minister's Homer: stately blank verse meant to stay close to the Greek line by line, produced as a private pleasure that outgrew its private printing.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
The Mirror's number for Saturday, June 20, 1829, No. 376, remembers Exeter 'Change in the Strand. Who has not heard of it, the article asks: menagerie and merchandise, wild beasts and cutlery, kangaroos and fleecy hosiery, elephants and minikin pins. The building began as Burleigh's magnificent house, where Elizabeth visited her treasurer. Its lower floors became a little nation of shopkeepers, among them Mr. Clarke the cutler, who amassed a princely fortune.

Improvement has now condemned the whole building, and the menagerie removes to the King's Mews at Charing Cross. Mr. Cross's occupation is gone, the article laments in Othello's phrase. Early numbers of the Mirror itself appeared two doors east of the wonder-house. Readers are offered a graphic sketch as preservation, the magazine archiving its own childhood treat: the long bill from the yeoman at the door and the pocket knife from the counters below.

For Saturday, May 7, 1831, the Mirror's No. 488 illustrates St. George's Chapel at Windsor, following an explanation in No. 486. The chapel stands in the castle's lower ward, dividing the court into two parts. Dean and canons' houses line its north side, while the Poor Knights of Windsor live on the south and west. The engraving shows the south front seen through Henry VIII's Gateway.

The entrance was formed by command of George IV, and his remains passed through it, as he had wished before death. The chapel is praised in the purest style of pointed architecture. Edward III founded it in 1377 for the Order of the Garter's honour. Edward IV and Henry VII improved the design, with Sir Reginald Bray helping complete the roof under Henry VII. Its stone vaulting is reckoned excellent workmanship. Readers enter the Garter's chapel by a dead king's chosen door.

Volume 19, No. 540, dated March 31, 1832, walks Bankside, the southern bank of the Thames in London. Engravings show Bankside in 1648, the bull and bear-baiting theatres, and the Rose and Globe playhouses together. Few districts, the writers say, hold more interest for lovers of old drama and old sports.

In 1648 much of the bank was still open crown land. The Globe Theatre and the Bear Garden stood there among places of public show. The Pike Gardens kept fresh-water fish, said to be for the royal table, under an officer titled the king's purveyor of pike. Nearby rose the palace of the bishops of Winchester, built around 1107, and the palace of the bishops of Rochester.
the-pacing-of-the-sentinel-or-the-soul-o: Only the Google Books scanning preamble is present here, followed by the first letters of a title page that breaks off. The preamble explains that the book was scanned from a library copy whose copyright had expired, and it sets out terms for using the file. No author, chapter, or passage of the book itself can be read in what is present. The volume's own pages therefore cannot be described from this opening; only the scanner's wrapper appears.
the-reformed-librarie-keeper-1650: John Dury's tract of 1650 is reprinted by the Augustan Reprint Society in 1983 through the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library at Los Angeles, with an introduction by Richard H. Popkin and Thomas F. Wright. Here only the reprint series pages and editorial board lists are present, so Dury's argument about librarians itself does not appear.
the-vanity-of-human-wishes-1749-and-two-: Samuel Johnson's Vanity of Human Wishes of 1749 is reprinted here with two Rambler papers from 1750 by the Augustan Reprint Society. Bertrand H. Bronson supplied the introduction. The volume is publication number 22, issued at Los Angeles in 1950 by the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library. Only the series title pages and editorial board lists are present in this record, so Johnson's poem and essays do not appear. Long lists name general, assistant, and advisory editors from universities across America and London, including Cleanth Brooks and Arthur Friedman.
three-voyages-for-the-discovery-of-a-nor: Volume two of Sir W. E. Parry's Northwest Passage narrative appeared at New York with Harper and Brothers in 1844. The sibling record in this slice holds volume one and its publishers' advertisement instead. This volume continues the second voyage in its contents. Chapter ten headings describe leaving Winter Island, meeting Inuit travellers, and facing ice and tides. The Barrow River, the Fury and Hecla Strait, Igloolik, and a sledge journey all appear. Only contents pages are present here, so Parry's narrative itself is not shown.
tob-0150:
Aleister Crowley summed up his system in Magick in Theory and Practice, the best-known manual of ceremonial magic of the twentieth century. His definition is famous: magick is the science and art of causing change to occur in conformity with will. The book lays out both his theory and his rites.

Yoga, ritual tools, invocations, and the holy books of Thelema all find their place in the scheme. Crowley writes as teacher, showman, and scold by turns. The work remains under copyright, and no public-domain text is distributed with this entry. Its record here marks the place the book holds in occult history.
tob-10450:
Jakob Boehme, a German shoemaker who became one of the most original religious thinkers of his century, staged Dialogues on the Supersensual Life as conversations between a master and a disciple. The subject is the life beyond the senses. Boehme wrote in dense, image-rich language drawn from craft, nature, and Scripture.

Master and disciple discuss how the soul falls, how it is reborn, and what heaven and hell truly are. Boehme treats both as states within the soul as much as places after death. Readers willing to move slowly get a strange, vivid system that influenced later German philosophy and Protestant mysticism alike.
tob-13150:
F. Max Muller, the German-born Oxford scholar who edited the Rig Veda, surveyed Hindu thought in Six Systems of Indian Philosophy. Muller did more than any other Victorian to bring Indian texts to English readers. The book gathers his long study into one course.

The six systems, or darshanas, are Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa, and Vedanta. Muller explains each one's view of the soul, the world, and release, and shows how they argue with each other. His survey gave the English-speaking world its first ordered map of Indian philosophy and still serves as a clear, if dated, first guide.
tob-13450:
Swami Paramananda, an Indian teacher who carried Vedanta to America, translated the principal Upanishads into clear English. The Upanishads are dialogues and teachings from ancient India, placed at the end of the Vedas. Teachers and students sit in forests and ask what the Self truly is.

Their answer is bold: Brahman, the ground of all things, and Atman, the self within, are one. Famous lines like thou art that sum up the claim. The talks use stories, riddles, and bold images to lead hearers past fear and death. Paramananda's plain style keeps the focus on those central claims.
tob-4050:
Volume three of Wordsworth's Poetical Works collects poems of his middle years, including the lyric England knows best, I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud. The daffodils poem, composed after a walk with his sister Dorothy, turns a remembered field of flowers into a theory of memory itself: nature stored, then repaid with interest in solitude.

Sonnets, memorial verses, and meditations on time surround the famous lyric. The Lake District's poet is at his most musical here, chiming public sonnets about liberty with private recollection. For readers working through the eight volumes, the third shows Romanticism's everyday sublime at working strength, neither manifesto nor epic, but lived attention.
tob-4150:
Nicholson's Mathnawi continues in volume two, covering the middle books of Rumi's vast Persian poem. The reed flute's cry still frames the teaching: the soul, cut from its source, longs to return. Tale follows tale, of lovers parted and seekers tested, each glossed by Nicholson's commentary.

Fools, kings, saints, and talking animals all carry lessons about pride, love, and the polishing of the heart. Nicholson spent his later life on this translation, and its authority rests on that labor. Verified from the 1919 edition record, volume two deepens the poem's argument: behind every story stands the one Beloved.
tob-9350:
Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish thinker of the first century, expounded the commandments of Moses in On Special Laws. His project joins Athens to Jerusalem: the Torah's rules, read with Greek philosophy, yield lessons in virtue that any rational reader can honor. Allegory is his master key.

Festivals, sacrifices, and laws of purity become teachings about the soul's health and the city's order. Philo writes for Jews tempted by Greek thought and Greeks curious about Moses alike. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. His bridge between the two worlds carried traffic for a thousand years, into church and synagogue alike.
turgenev-diary-superfluous-man-garnett-1:
The Diary of a Superfluous Man, written by Ivan Turgenev in 1850, is Englished here in Constance Garnett's translation of 1899. A dying young landowner named Tchulkaturin keeps a journal in his last weeks. He looks back on a life in which he always arrived one step too late.

His one love was taken by a livelier rival, and even his duel ended in farce. Turgenev gave Russian writing a lasting type in this hero: clever, feeling, and unable to act. Other stories in the volume extend the study of missed chances. The superfluous man haunted Russian novels for the rest of the century. Garnett's version kept the tale in English classrooms for decades.
un-ga-res-a-69-50:
Glowing goods in the wrong hands are the fear behind Resolution A/69/50, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. Radioactive goods serve health, farms, and power plants across the world. Yet the text voices deep worry at the risk that terror groups may gain, move, or use such goods in a device that spreads radiation and fear.

Stray and smuggled atomic goods, loose from all state checks, add to the threat. Such a device, if used, would harm health and foul the land. World pacts built to bar and crush that risk are recalled with weight. States are urged to keep radioactive stock under firm guard, in store and on the road.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly resolution 69/50 (2014) aims to keep radioactive sources out of terrorists' hands. The Assembly calls on member states to keep terrorists from getting or using radioactive materials. It calls on them to join the International Convention for the Suppression of Acts of Nuclear Terrorism. It calls on them to strengthen steps to track, secure, and guard radioactive sources. It backs the International Atomic Energy Agency's Code of Conduct on the Safety and Security of Radioactive Sources. It backs its Incident and Trafficking Database, and efforts to recover stray 'orphan' sources.
un-sc-res-1350: An official UN record text, Resolution 1350 is catalogued in this library with a 2001 date. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-1450:
Kenya came under formal Council review in Resolution 1450, adopted on 13 December 2002 by fourteen votes to one. On 28 November a bomb had wrecked the Paradise Hotel at Kikambala near Mombasa. The same day, missiles had nearly hit an Israeli airliner leaving Mombasa. Al-Qaida claimed both attacks.

The Council condemns the hotel bombing and the missile attempt in the strongest terms. It sends deep sympathy to Kenya, to Israel, and to the victims' families. All states are urged to help find and bring to justice those who planned and paid for the attacks. The text restates the Council's resolve to fight every form of terror.
un-sc-res-1550:
Six more months for the Golan Heights observer force came in June 2004. The force, called UNDOF, watches the cease-fire line between Israel and Syria. A report from the Secretary-General on the force was before the Council that month. The file's header date sits a day before the report it cites, so the month is the safe dating. Resolution 1550 was adopted unanimously in June 2004.

The Council called on the parties to carry out Resolution 338 of 1973 at once. That text demanded a cease-fire and peace talks after the October war. UNDOF's mandate was renewed for six months, until 31 December 2004. At the end of that period, the Secretary-General had to report on developments. His report also had to cover the measures taken to put Resolution 338 into effect. The renewal followed the standard pattern for this long-running mission.
un-sc-res-1650: Adopted in 2006, Resolution 1650 is part of the Security Council's formal record, kept here through a Wikisource transcription. Every resolution is a small treaty among fifteen delegations about what the UN will say and do. This entry holds one such agreement entire, in the order and wording the members finally settled on.
un-sc-res-1750:
UNMIL was extended with a drawdown plan attached on 30 March 2007. The Secretary-General's report of 15 March lay before the Council. Liberia's government was improving governance, fighting corruption, and regaining control over the country's natural wealth. Fighters had largely been reintegrated, though jobs for them were scarce. UNMIL worked closely with the United Nations force in Côte d'Ivoire on border security.

The Council extended UNMIL's mandate until 30 September 2007. It restated its intention to let the Secretary-General shift troops between UNMIL and the Côte d'Ivoire mission as needed. He was asked to present a detailed drawdown plan for UNMIL, with benchmarks for handing security to Liberian hands. The government was called to press its reforms in close coordination with the mission. The Council noted the Special Court for Sierra Leone's aim to finish its work in good time.
un-sc-res-1850:
At the end of 2008, Resolution 1850 declared the Council's support for the Israeli-Palestinian peace talks restarted at Annapolis. It was a rare Middle East text that the United States helped draft and all members backed. The members called the negotiations irreversible.

Inside, the text backs the two-state goal, praises both sides' commitments, and urges donors to fund the Palestinian Authority. It also calls on regional states to support the process and cut ties with violence. Adopted days before the Gaza war began, it preserves the last shared statement of a peace effort about to collapse.
un-sc-res-1950:
Resolution 1950, adopted on 23 November 2010, took up Piracy off Somalia. Pirate attacks had spread deep into the western Indian Ocean. Ransom payments kept climbing, and captured suspects were often freed for lack of courts. Somalia's government had asked for the naval powers to be renewed.

The Council renews those powers for twelve more months. States working with Somalia's government may enter its waters and use all necessary means against pirates. Warships, aircraft, and seizures of pirate gear all stay allowed. Kenya and the Seychelles win praise for trying suspects in their courts. The text presses all states to make piracy a crime and to share proof for trials.
un-sc-res-250: Preserved as Resolution 250, this Security Council text carries a 1968 date in the catalog record. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-350:
A new United Nations force for the Golan Heights was created by the Security Council on 31 May 1974. Israel and Syria had just signed an Agreement on Disengagement, worked out under resolution 338 (1973). The Secretary-General had reported on how a force should be set up, with annexes on its terms. The Council welcomed the disengagement agreement as a step in applying the 1973 cease-fire call.

The Council set up the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force at once, under its own authority. It asked the Secretary-General to take the needed steps in line with his report. The force was established for an initial six months, open to renewal by later resolution. The Secretary-General had to keep the Council fully informed of developments. The observer force took its place between the two armies on the Golan, where renewals every six months became a fixture of the region for decades.
un-sc-res-450: Security Council Resolution 450 survives in the official record, and the catalog dates it to 1979. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-50:
Fighting in Palestine after Israel's founding brought a truce call in May 1948. On 29 May 1948 the Security Council ordered a halt to all armed force for four weeks. The call went to every government and authority involved. It was made without judging the rival claims of Arabs and Jews. The aim was simply to stop the shooting.

During the truce, no side could bring fighting men into the region. The ban covered Palestine and seven nearby states, from Egypt to Yemen. Men of military age who did arrive could not be trained or mobilized. Arms imports and exports were also frozen. United Nations mediators used the pause to press for a settlement.
un-sc-res-650:
Nicaragua's contra fighters were set to lay down their arms in 1990. The Central America observer group needed a bigger mandate to help. On 27 March 1990 the Security Council approved the Secretary-General's report on the region. It authorized, on a standby basis, an enlarged role for ONUCA. Armed personnel would be added to its strength. The group could then take part in the voluntary demobilization of the resistance.

The Secretary-General had to keep the Council fully informed. The Central American presidents' own peace agreements drove the process. The Council praised their efforts and urged all parties to honor their pledges. The step turned a small observer team into an armed demobilization mission.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Short-term judges for the Yugoslavia war crimes tribunal are the business of this text, passed on 27 April 2001. These posts, called ad litem judges, let the tribunal run more trials at once without adding permanent seats. The Council had created the system the year before, as the tribunal's workload kept growing.

The text forwards to the General Assembly the nominations the Secretary-General had received, as the tribunal's Statute requires. The list runs to dozens of lawyers and judges named by countries on every continent. From it, the Assembly would elect a pool of ad litem judges, and tribunal panels could then draw on that pool case by case.

A suicide bomber struck a beach hotel near Mombasa, Kenya, on 28 November 2002. The Paradise Hotel was popular with Israeli tourists. The same day, attackers fired missiles at an Israeli airliner leaving Mombasa. They missed. Al-Qaida claimed both attacks in December. Resolution 1450 followed on 13 December 2002, with only Syria voting no.

The Council condemned the bombing in the strongest terms. It offered sympathy to Kenya, Israel, and the victims' families. All states were urged to hunt down those who planned and funded the attacks. That duty flowed from Resolution 1373, the post-September 11 counterterrorism law. Members pledged stronger resolve against terrorism everywhere.

Côte d'Ivoire's path to a UN seat ran through this line of 1960. On 23 August, the Council adopted Resolution 150 without dissent. The Republic of Ivory Coast had claimed freedom from France weeks before, on 7 August. It was one voice in the great chorus of the Year of Africa.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Ivory Coast. The Assembly acted the next month. Seventeen African states joined the UN in 1960 alone. Ivory Coast stood in that cohort. Their arrival changed the world body's balance for good. A new bloc of votes now shaped its debates.

The Golan Heights watch gained six more months in the summer of 2004. On 20 June, the Council adopted Resolution 1550 without dissent. It had read the Secretary-General's fresh report on the observer force. That force, UNDOF, guards the truce line between Israel and Syria. The line dates from the end of the 1973 war.

The text calls on the parties to carry out Resolution 338 at once. That 1973 order links a ceasefire to peace talks. The mandate then runs to 31 December 2004. A closing report from the Secretary-General is due at the end. This text is one link in an unbroken chain of renewals.

Burundi's transition had just ended in success when its United Nations operation, ONUB, was extended on 21 December 2005, until 1 July 2006. Authority had passed peacefully to an elected government and institutions. Burundians are congratulated on that outcome, and the regional initiative, the African Union, and ONUB are thanked for their parts in it.

The mission stays in place to support the new authorities while many challenges remain. Temporary redeployments between ONUB and the Congo mission are authorized, under set conditions, so the two operations can back each other up. The government is urged to complete its disarmament and security reform programme, and donors are called on to keep funding Burundi's development and recovery.

Resolution 1750, passed on 30 March 2007, keeps the UN force in Liberia for six more months. A UN report that March won warm words, as did Liberia's strides at home. The state had curbed graft and won back grip on its mines and woods. Donors, West African states, and the African bloc won thanks for their aid. The force, UNMIL, drew praise too. It worked hand in hand with the UN team in the next-door state on border safety.

The new term ran to September 2007. Sound gains in bringing ex-fighters back to civil life were noted. Yet their fate in the end hung on real jobs in shops, farms, and trades. The growth of the police and the new army also drew the Council's eye.

Support is declared on 16 December 2008 for the Israeli-Palestinian negotiations launched at Annapolis. The November 2007 Annapolis Conference had restarted talks aimed at a two-state settlement under the Road Map. The Quartet's November 2008 statement backed the process, and the Council now added its own weight.

The Annapolis negotiations are declared irreversible, and both parties are called on to meet their Road Map duties, including freezing settlement activity and fighting terrorism. All states and world bodies are called on to support the talks and the Palestinian Authority's institution building. Stronger diplomacy toward a comprehensive Middle East peace is urged, including on the Syrian and Lebanese tracks, and a possible meeting in Moscow in 2009 is welcomed.

Somali piracy authorizations are renewed for another year in Resolution 1950, adopted on 23 November 2010. Pirate range and capacity were growing into the western Indian Ocean. Ransoms and weak embargo enforcement were fuelling the trade. Captured pirates were often released for lack of courts able to prosecute them. The Transitional Federal Government consented and asked for renewal.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews for twelve months the authorizations in Resolutions 1846 (2008) and 1851 (2008). They let states and organizations cooperating with the Transitional Federal Government enter Somali waters, seize pirate boats, and fight piracy and armed robbery at sea. It commends the EU's Operation Atalanta, NATO operations, and Combined Task Force 151. It praises Kenya and Seychelles for prosecuting suspects and stresses the authorizations apply only to Somalia and create no customary international law. Member states are called on to criminalize piracy and cooperate on prosecution.

North Korea's weapons programs stand behind Resolution 2050, adopted on 12 June 2012. Earlier resolutions had punished the country for nuclear and missile work and had created a Panel of Experts to watch over the sanctions. The panel's interim and final reports were now before the Council. Members again called the spread of nuclear, chemical, and biological weapons a threat to peace.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the panel's mandate until 12 July 2013. It sets deadlines for a midterm report and a final report with findings and advice, and asks for a work plan within thirty days of the panel's new appointment. The panel serves the sanctions committee, which is urged to discuss the panel's work with it on a regular basis.

Israel planned to hold a military parade in Jerusalem on 2 May 1968, and the Council moved to stop it. Resolution 250 was adopted unanimously on 27 April 1968, after the Council heard statements from Jordan and Israel. The Council judged that the parade would raise tensions in the area. It would also harm the chances of a peaceful settlement. The short text calls on Israel to refrain from holding the parade. The Secretary-General was asked to report on how the resolution was carried out.

Resolution 350, adopted on 31 May 1974 by thirteen votes to none, creates the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force. Israel and Syria had just signed an agreement pulling their forces apart on the Golan Heights, following up the ceasefire that ended the October 1973 war. The Secretary-General's report, with annexes setting out the force's design, reached the Council the same week.

The Council welcomed the disengagement agreement and set up the observer force under its own authority at once. The Secretary-General was told to take the necessary steps, following his report. The force was created for an initial six months, renewable by later resolutions. Nearly five decades of renewals followed, making this founding text unusually consequential for its length.

Southern Lebanon stayed violent in 1979, and the United Nations force there could not deploy in full. Obstacles blocked UNIFIL's work in the south. Violence against Lebanon had displaced civilians, including Palestinians. Resolution 450, adopted on 24 June 1979, renews the force.

The Council strongly deplored the violence and the loss of innocent life. Israel was called on to stop its acts against Lebanon's unity and territory at once. Its incursions were named, and so was its support for armed groups inside Lebanon. UNIFIL's work was praised, and the force's goals were restated. Its mandate was renewed for six months, until 19 December 1979. The old armistice machinery between Israel and Lebanon was to be revived as well.

The first truce order for Palestine came two weeks into the first Arab-Israeli war. On 29 May 1948, the Council adopted Resolution 50. Israel had declared itself a state days before. Neighboring Arab states had invaded at once. The Council said it sought a halt to the fighting. Neither side's rights, claims, or stance would be judged by the pause.

All governments must order a stop to armed acts for four weeks. No fighting men may enter the region in that span. War goods may not flow in or out either. Jerusalem's Holy Places must be kept safe, with access for worship kept open. The UN Mediator and the Truce Commission will watch the truce. Army observers will back them, and weekly reports are due.

Nicaragua's Contra war was dying in the spring of 1990. A new elected leader was set to take power. The Contra camps had to empty by pact. Resolution 650 passed with no dissent on 27 March 1990. It backed the chief's report of 15 March. The UN team in the area was small and bare of arms.

That changed, on one condition. The team could grow and take on armed staff. Its new job was to help Contra men lay down their guns by free choice. This was a first for UN peace work in the region. Demobilization by consent, not force, was the theme. The chief had to keep the Council fully briefed. Within weeks, the Contras stood down, and the team watched it happen.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s500-150:
Section 500.150 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations deals with access to programs in buildings that are in place. It sits in Part 500, on the bar on bias based on handicap in programs of the National Commission for Employment Policy. The agency must run each program so that the program, seen as a whole, can be reached and used by handicapped persons with ease. That is the core rule set out in the text.

The rule has clear bounds. It does not force the agency to make each of its buildings in place fit for such use. In the case of programs for the care of old sites, it does not force a step that would mar the key old marks of a site. The text goes on to a third bound, cut off in the part shown here.
van-helmont-ternary-of-paradoxes-1650:
Jan Baptista van Helmont argued three strange claims in A Ternary of Paradoxes, Englished by Walter Charleton in 1650. The Flemish doctor and chemist challenged the medicine of his day on wound cures, on wine, and on man's likeness to God. Charleton's version became the key English text of Helmont's new way of healing by chemistry.

The magnetic cure of wounds claims that sympathy can heal at a distance, without touch. The piece on tartar explains the stony crust in wine casks and, by likeness, the stones that form in the body. Readers of the age found here a bold new medical scheme, strange and fertile, that helped turn medicine toward tests and trials.
wordsworth-prelude-1850:
William Wordsworth worked on The Prelude for fifty years and never published it himself. He called it the poem on the growth of his own mind and read it aloud to Coleridge. After his death in 1850, his family published it in fourteen books, and it proved to be his life work.

The poem follows Wordsworth from childhood in the Lake District through Cambridge, London, and revolutionary France. He recalls stolen boats, skating at dusk, and the terror and joy nature taught him. Disillusion with the French Revolution forces him to rebuild his faith in the mind itself. The Prelude is the great autobiographical poem in English, and Romanticism's central document.
zoist-vol-08-1850:
Volume eight of The Zoist covers March 1850 to January 1851. Eight years in, Elliotson's journal remains mesmerism's English headquarters in print. Cases of trance, with and without surgery, lead the contents. Cerebral physiology, the study of brain and mind together, keeps its column.

Somnambulist reports grow stranger as spiritualism dawns next door in America. The journal watches the new rappings with a mesmerist's claim to the ground. Its thirteen volumes, ending in 1856, hold the movement's full primary record. Volume eight marks the run's later middle. The fight with the medical press cools into habit. The archive's weight keeps growing.
